"Whilest we were in hand with these foure parts of the Institutes, we often having occasion to go into the city, and from thence into the country, did in some sort envy the state of the honest plowman, and other mechanics; for the one when he was at his work would merrily sing, and the plowman whistle some selfpleasing tune, and yet their work both proceeded and succeeded: but he that takes upon him to write, doth captivate all the faculties and powers both of his minde and body, and must be only intentive to that which he collecteth, without any expression of joy or cheerfulness, whilest he in at his work."

INTESTATE ACT COMPLETE TEXT OF ACT AN ACT 

Relating to the descent of the real and personal estates of persons dying intestate and the procedure in reference thereto. 

The General Asembly of the Commonwealth of Penn sylvania hereby enacts as follows: 

Section 1. Intestate Descent.-The real and personal estate of a decedent, whether male or female, subject to payment of debts and charges, and not disposed of by will or otherwise, shall descend as hereinafter provided. 

Section 2. Share of Surviving Spouse. The surviving spouse shall be entitled to the following share or shares: (1) More Than One Child. One-third if the decedent is survived by more than one child, or by one or more children and the issue of a deceased child or children, or by the issue of more than one deceased child; or (2) One Child. One-half if the decedent is survived by one child only, or by no child, but by the issue of one deceased child; or (3) No Issue. The first ten thousand dollars in value and one-half of the balance of the estate, if the decedent is survived by no issue; or 

(4) No Issue or Other Designated Person. All of the estate if the decedent is survived by no issue, parent, brother, sister, child of a brother or sister, grandparent, uncle or aunt.

Section 3. Shares of Others Than Surviving Spouse. 

The share of the estate, if any, to which the surviving spouse is not entitled, and the entire estate if there is no surviving spouse, shall descend in the following order: (1) Issue. To the issue of the decedent.

INTESTATE ACT 

(2) Parents. If no issue survives the decedent, then to the parents or parent of the decedent. (3) Brothers, Sisters, or Their Issue. If no parent survives the decedent, then to the issue of each of the decedent's parents. (4) Grandparents. If no issue of either of the decedent's parents but at least one grandparent survives the decedent, then half to the paternal grandparents or grandparent, or if both are dead, to the children of each of them and the children of the deceased children of each of them, and half to the maternal grandparents or grandparent, or if both are dead to the children of each of them and the children of the deceased children of each of them. If both of the paternal grandparents or both of the maternal grandparents are dead leaving no child or grandchild to survive the decedent, the half which would have passed to them or to their children and grandchildren shall be added to the half passing to the grandparents or grandparent on the other side. (5) Uncles, Aunts and Their Children. If no grandparent survives the decedent, then to the uncles and aunts and the children of deceased uncles and aunts of the decedent. (6) Commonwealth. In default of all persons hereinbefore described, then to the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania.

Section 4. Rules of Descent.- (1) Taking in Different Degrees. The shares descending under this act to the issue of the decedent, to the issue of his parents or grandparents or to his uncles or aunts or to their children, shall descend to them as follows: The part of the estate descending to any such persons shall be divided into as many equal shares as there shall be persons in the nearest degree of consanguinity to the decedent living and taking shares therein and persons in that degree who

INTESTATE ACT 

have died before the decedent and have left issue to survive him who take shares therein. One equal share shall descend to each such living person in the nearest degree and one equal share shall descend by representation to the issue of each such deceased person, except that no issue of a child of an uncle or aunt of the decedent shall be entitled to any share of the estate. 

(2) Whole and Half Blood. Persons taking under this act shall take without distinction between those of the whole and those of the half blood. (3) After-Born Persons; Time of Determining Relationships. Persons begotten before the decedent's death. but born thereafter, shall take as if they had been born in his lifetime. (4) Source of Ownership. Real estate shall descend under this act without regard to the ancestor or other relation from whom it has come. (5) Quantity of Estate. Any person taking real or personal estate under this act shall take such interest as the decedent had therein. 1 (6) Tenancy in Estate. When real or personal estate or shares therein shall descend to two or more persons, they shall take it as tenants in common, except that if it shall descend to a husband and wife they shall take it as tenants by the entireties. (7) Alienage. Real and personal estate shall descend without regard to whether the decedent or any person otherwise entitled to take under this act is or has been an alien. 

(8) Person Related to Decedent Through Two Lines. 

A person related to the decedent through two lines of relationship shall take one share only which shall be the larger share. 

Section 5. Spouse's Rights.- 

(a) Widow. The shares of the estate to which the widow is entitled shall be in lieu and full satisfaction of her dower at common law, so far as relates to real estate of

INTESTATE ACT 

www. which the husband dies seised; and her share in real estate aliened by the husband in his lifetime, without her joining in the conveyance, shall be the same as her share in real estate of which the husband dies *seised. The widow shall receive the same share in a future estate owned by the husband as in an estate of which he dies seised, although the particular estate shall not terminate before the death of the husband. (b) Surviving Husband. The shares of the estate to which the surviving husband is entitled shall be in lieu and full satisfaction of his curtesy at common law. The surviving husband shall receive the same share in a future estate owned by the wife as in an estate of which she dies seised, although the particular estate shall not terminate before the death of the wife. 

Section 6. Forfeiture.- 

(a) Husband's Share. A husband who, for one year or upward previous to the death of his wife, shall have wilfully neglected or refused to provide for her, or who for that period or upwards shall have wilfully and maliciously deserted her, shall have no title or interest under this act in her real or her personal estate. (b) Wife's Share. A wife who, for one year or upwards previous to the death of her husband, shall have wilfully and maliciously deserted him, shall have no title or interest under this act in his real or personal estate. (c) Slayer's Share. Any person who participates either as a principal or as an accessory before the fact in the wilful and unlawful killing of any person shall not in any way acquire property or receive any benefits as the result of such killing, but such property or benefits shall be distributed as provided by law. (d) Surviving Spouse as Witness. The surviving husband or wife shall be a competent witness as to all matters pertinent to the issue of forfeiture under this section. *"seized," in original.

INTESTATE ACT Section 7. Illegitimates.- 

(a) Child of Mother. For purposes of descent by, from and through an illegitimate, he shall be considered the child of his mother but not of his father. (b) Marriage of Parents. When the parents of a person born illegitimate shall have married each other, he shall be legitimated for purposes of descent by, from and through him as if he had been born during the wedlock of his parents.

Section 8. Adopted Person. For purposes of descent by, from and through an adopted person he shall be considered the issue of his adopting parent or parents and not the issue of his natural parents: Provided, That if a natural parent shall have married the adopting parent, the adopted person for purposes of descent by, from and through him shall also be considered the issue of such natural parent.

Section 9. Advancements.- 

(a) In General. If any person, other than the surviving spouse taking real or personal estate from the decedent, shall have received any estate by settlement or advancement of the decedent, in either real or personal estate, the value of such settlement or advancement shall be charged against the share of the person who shall have received it, so that the total share received by him, including the value of such settlement or advancement, shall not exceed the share received by each of the other persons who take equally from the decedent. 

(b) Valuation. The settlement or advancement shall be considered as of its value when the advancee came into enjoyment of it or at the death of the decedent, whichever occurred first. 

Section 10. Spouse's Allowance; Procedure.- (a) Right of Selection. Subject to the rights of creditors and to existing liens, the surviving spouse, or his successor in interest, shall have the right to claim all or part

INTESTATE ACT 

of his ten thousand dollar allowance out of real estate of the decedent. (b) From Real Estate. If the allowance is to be set apart in whole or in part out of real estate, the appraisement of the real estate shall be made by two appraisers who shall be appointed by the orphans' court. The orphans' court of the county where letters testamentary or of administration have been granted, or should no letters have been granted then of the county within which was the family or principal residence of the decedent, shall have jurisdiction concerning the allowance, whether the real estate is situate in that county or in any other county of the Commonwealth. If the decedent was a non-resident of the Commonwealth then the appraisers shall be appointed by the orphans' court of any county wherein any real estate of the decedent shall lie, and that court shall thereupon have jurisdiction concerning the allowance with respect to all of the real estate of the decedent within the Commonwealth. When real estate is located outside of the county of original jurisdiction, the orphans' court of the county of original jurisdiction may, in its discretion, direct that an application for the appointment of appraisers shall be made to the orphans' court of the county in which the real estate is located to fix the value of such real estate. The appraisers so appointed shall fix the value of the real estate as of the date the claim is presented in court and shall receive such compensation as shall be allowed by the court appointing them. Exceptions to appraisements wherever made shall be filed with the court of original jurisdiction which may in its discretion refer the exceptions to the orphans' court of the county in which the real estate is located. Upon compliance with such requirements of notice as the court shall prescribe, the court of original jurisdiction may confirm such appraisement and set apart such real estate to the surviving spouse. (c) Real Estate Valued at More Than the Amount

Claimed. Whenever the real estate of the decedent cannot be divided so as to set apart the amount claimed in value without prejudice to or spoiling the whole or any parcel of it, and the appraisers shall value such real estate or parcel thereof at any sum exceeding the amount claimed,

INTESTATE ACT 

it shall be lawful for the orphans' court of original jurisdiction to confirm the appraisement, and to set apart such real estate or parcel thereof for the use of the surviving spouse: Conditioned, however, That the surviving spouse shall pay the amount of the valuation in excess of the amount claimed without interest within six months from the date of confirmation of the appraisement. If the surviving spouse shall refuse to take the real estate or parcel thereof at the appraisement, or shall fail to make payment as provided above, the court, on application of any person interested, shall direct the executor or administrator, or a trustee appointed by the court, to sell the same, and the procedure in such case shall be the same as is provided by law in cases of sales of real estate for the payment of debts of a decedent. (d) Payment of Surplus. The real estate, if taken by the surviving spouse, shall vest in him, upon his paying the surplus above so much of the allowance as shall be claimed out of the real estate, to the parties entitled thereto, or to the personal representatives of the decedent as the court in its discretion shall direct. If the real estate is sold so much of the allowance as shall be claimed out of it shall be paid out of the purchase money to the surviving spouse, and the balance after payment of costs shall be distributed to the parties entitled thereto, or to the personal representatives of the decedent as the court in its discretion shall direct. (e) Income. When the spouse's allowance does not exhaust the entire real and personal estate the income therefrom shall be equitably prorated between the surviving spouse and the others taking the estate. (f) Recording and Registering Decrees. A certified copy of every decree confirming an appraisement of real estate, and setting it apart to the surviving spouse, shall be recorded in the deed book in the office of the recorder of deeds of each county where the real estate shall lie, shall be indexed by the recorder in the grantor's index under the name of the decedent, and in the grantee's index under the name of the surviving spouse, and shall be registered in the survey bureau or with the proper authorities empowered to

INTESTATE ACT 

keep a register of real estate in the county: Provided, That no decree conditioned upon payment of any surplus by the surviving spouse shall be recorded or registered unless there is offered for recording concurrently therewith written evidence of the payment of such surplus. (g) Other Remedies. The surviving spouse may also collect the allowance out of real and personal estate, together with income thereon, in the manner provided by law for the collection of legacies. (h) Costs and Expenses. All costs, appraisers' fees, and expenses of recording and registering incurred in claiming the allowance shall be part of the general administration expenses of the estate. 

Section 11. Procedure to Establish Title to Real Es tate When Spouse Claims Entire Estate.-The surviving spouse or his successors in interest claiming the entire estate under this act may, after the expiration of one year from the death of the decedent, present a petition to establish title to real estate in the orphans' court of the county where letters testamentary or of administration have been granted, or should no letters have been granted then of the county within which was the family or principal residence of the decedent, setting forth that the decedent died leaving no known heirs, other than the surviving spouse, entitled to take under the provisions of this act and seised of real estate which by virtue of this act has vested in the surviving spouse. If the decedent was a non-resident of the 

Commonwealth, the petition may be presented in the orphans' court of any county wherein any real estate of the decedent shall lie and such court shall thereupon have jurisdiction of proceedings under this section with respect to all of the real estate of the decedent within the Commonwealth. 

The court, being satisfied concerning the facts set forth in the petition, aided if necessary by the report of a master, may enter its decree nisi adjudging that the title to such real estate is in the surviving spouse or his successor in interest. Notice of the decree nisi shall be published for such length of time and in such manner as the court shall direct. If within six months from the last publication of 10

INTESTATE ACT 

such notice exceptions shall be filed with the court alleging the existence of other heirs entitled to interests in the real estate, the court after hearing thereon and upon evidence satisfactory to it, aided if necessary by the report of a master, shall vacate the decree nisi, or confirm it absolutely. 

If no exceptions are filed, the decree shall be confirmed absolutely. A certified copy of the decree shall be recorded in the deed book in the office of the recorder of deeds of each county where real estate of the decedent shall lie shall be indexed by the recorder in the grantor's index under the name of the decedent and in the grantee's index under the name of the surviving spouse, and shall be registered in the survey bureau or with the proper authorities empowered to keep a register of real estate in the county. 

Section 12. Property Distributable to the Common wealth.-All of the real and personal estate of the decedent, to which the Commonwealth shall be entitled under this act, shall be sold by the executor or administrator after notice to the Attorney General. The proceeds of sale shall be accounted for by the executor or administrator to the court having jurisdiction of the estate and the net amount remaining for distribution shall be paid by him. through the Department of Revenue into the State Treasury as in the case of unclaimed funds in the hands of fiduciaries. Sales of real estate under this section shall be made in the manner and form prescribed for sales of real estate by the act approved the seventh day of June, one thousand nine hundred seventeen (Pamphlet Laws 388), known as the Revised Price Act, as now or hereafter amended or recodified.

Section 13. Limitations of Claims.- 

(a) Shares Not Claimed Within Seven Years. Any person entitled under this act to a share of the estate of the decedent must make legal claim to his share of the personal estate within seven years of the death of the decedent or be debarred from claiming such share thereof as shall have been distributed pursuant to adjudication or decree: Provided, That if any such person shall be a minor 11

INTESTATE ACT 

at the death of the decedent, the seven year period shall commence to run upon his attaining majority. (b) Pleading Limitation. The bar of this section may be pleaded by any person interested in the estate including the Commonwealth, but it may not be pleaded by a personal representative of the decedent to enable him to retain any part of the decedent's estate to which he is not legally entitled.

Section 14. Personal Estate of Non-Resident.-Noth ing contained in this act with respect to a distribution of personal estate shall extend to the estate of a decedent whose domicile at his death is out of the Commonwealth. 

Section 15. Short Title.-This act shall be known and may be cited as the "Intestate Act of 1947."

Section 16. Repealer.-This act is intended as an entire and complete system regulating the descent of the real and personal estates of persons dying wholly or partially intestate on or after the first day of January, one thousand nine hundred forty-eight. The following acts and parts of acts and all amendments of each are hereby repealed as respectively indicated, but so far only as relates to the real and personal estates of persons dying intestate on or after the first day of January, one thousand nine hundred fortyeight: (1) The act approved the twenty-third day of February, one thousand seven hundred ninety-one (three Smith's Laws four), entitled "A supplement to the act, entitled 'An act to declare and regulate escheats,' '"' in so far as it relates to inheritance. (2) The act approved the seventh day of June, one thousand nine hundred seventeen (Pamphlet Laws 429), entitled "An act relating to the descent and distribution of the real and personal property of persons dying intestate; and to provide for the recording and registering of the decrees of the orphans' court in connection therewith, and the fees therefor," absolutely. |- 12

INTESTATE ACT 

(3) The act approved the twenty-fourth day of April, one thousand nine hundred thirty-one (Pamphlet Laws 46), entitled "An act making the surviving spouse competent to testify in all cases where the right of such spouse to share in a deceased spouse's estate is disputed because of alleged desertion or non-support of the decedent, whether decedent died testate or intestate," in so far as it relates to inheritance. (4) All other acts and parts of acts inconsistent herewith are hereby repealed. 

Section 17. Effective Date.-This act shall take effect on the first day of January, one thousand nine hundred forty-eight, and shall apply to the real and personal estates of all persons dying on or after that day. The existing laws shall remain in full force and effect for the real and personal estates of all persons dying before that day. 

APPROVED-The 24th day of April, A. D. 1947.

Amending Act of 1955-6, P.L. 1037

AN ACT 

Amending the act of April twenty-four, one thousand nine hundred forty-seven (Pamphlet Laws 80), entitled "An act relating to the descent of the real and personal estates of persons dying intestate and the procedure in reference thereto," and repealing parts thereof, limiting right of a spouse on partial intestacy and in selection of allowance, and revising procedure for setting aside spouse's allowance, establishing title to real estate when spouse claims entire estate, and distribution to the Commonwealth as statutory heir.

13

INTESTATE ACT Section 1. Section two, act of April twenty-four, one thousand nine hundred forty-seven (Pamphlet Laws 80), known as the "Intestate Act of 1947" is amended to read: 

Section 2. Share of Surviving Spouse. The surviving spouse shall be entitled to the following share or shares: (1) More Than One Child. One-third if the decedent is survived by more than one child, or by one or more children and the issue of a deceased child or children, or by the issue of more than one deceased child; or (2) One Child. One-half if the decedent is survived by one child only, or by no child, but by the issue of one deceased child; or (3) No Issue. The first ten thousand dollars in value and one-half of the balance of the estate, if the decedent is survived by no issue. In case of partial intestacy, any amount received by the surviving spouse under the will shall satisfy pro tanto the ten thousand dollar allowance; or 

(4) No Issue or Other Designated Person. All of the estate if the decedent is survived by no issue, parent, brother, sister, child of a brother or sister, grandparent, uncle or aunt.

Section 2. Sections ten, eleven and twelve of the act are repealed.

Section 3. The act is amended by adding, after section nine, three new sections to read:

Section 10. Spouse's Allowance Procedure.—The ten thousand dollar allowance shall be set aside and awarded in distribution to the surviving spouse, or his successor in interest, in the same manner as other distributive shares of the estate are awarded, without any right in the surviving spouse to choose particular real or personal property in satisfaction thereof. Nothing herein shall be construed as limiting the right of the surviving spouse and other dis- 14

INTESTATE ACT 

tributees to demand that property, not theretofore sold, be distributed in kind to them.

Section 11. Procedure to Establish Title to Real Prop erty When Spouse Claims Entire Estate.-A surviving spouse entitled, under the provisions of this act, to the entire estate of the decedent shall have it awarded to him in the same manner as a lesser share of the estate would be so awarded.

Section 12. Property Distributable to the Common wealth.-When the estate is distributable to the Commonwealth, as statutory heir under the provisions of this act, it shall be reduced to cash in all cases by the personal representative, and awarded by the court in distribution to the Commonwealth, and paid by the personal representative through the Department of Revenue into the State Treasury.

Section 4. This amending act shall take effect April one, one thousand nine hundred fifty-six, and shall apply to the real and personal estates of all persons dying on or after that day. The provisions of sections ten, eleven and twelve of the "Intestate Act of 1947" repealed hereby shall remain in effect as to the estates of persons dying on or after January one, one thousand nine hundred forty-eight, and prior to April one, one thousand nine hundred fifty-six.

APPROVED-The 10th day of February, A.D. 1956.

known as the "Intestate Act of 1947" is amended by adding, after clause (1), a new clause to read: 

Section 4. Rules of Descent.- (1.1) Taking in Same Degree.

When persons entitled to take under this act other than as a surviving spouse are all in the same degree of consanguinity to the decedent, they shall take in equal shares.

INTESTATE ACT Amending Act of 1963, P. L. 280 AN ACT 

Amending the act of April 24, 1947 (P. L. 80), entitled "An act relating to the descent of the real and personal estates of persons dying intestate and the procedure in reference thereto," prescribing the spouse's rights in the decedent's estate as to real estate conveyed by decedent wife in her lifetime without his joinder. 

Section 1. Section 5, act of April 24, 1947 (P. L. 80), known as the "Intestate Act of 1947," is amended to read:

Section 5. Spouse's Rights.- 

(a) Widow. The shares of the estate to which the widow is entitled shall be in lieu and full satisfaction of her dower at common law, so far as relates to real estate of which the husband dies seised; and her share in real estate aliened by the husband in his lifetime, without her joining in the conveyance, shall be the same as her share in real estate of which the husband died seised. The widow shall receive the same share in a future estate owned by the husband as in an estate of which he dies seised, although the particular estate shall not terminate before the death of the husband. (b) Surviving Husband. The shares of the estate to which the surviving husband is entitled shall be in lieu and full satisfaction of his curtesy at common law so far as relates to real estate of which the wife dies seised, and his share in real estate aliened by the wife in her lifetime without his joining in the conveyance shall be the same as his share in real estate of which the wife dies seised. The surviving husband shall receive the same share in a future estate owned by the wife as in an estate of which she dies seised, although the particular estate shall not terminate before the death of the wife.

Section 2. This amending act shall take effect immediately, and shall apply to the real and personal estates of PRI 18

WILLIAM W. SCRANTON Amending Act No. 474 of 1965 AN ACT 

Amending the act of April 24, 1947 (P. L. 80), entitled "An act relating to the descent of the real and personal estates of persons dying intestate and the procedure in reference thereto," changing provisions relating to grandchildren of deceased uncles and aunts of the decedent.

Section 1. Clause (5) of section 3 and clause (1) of section 4, act of April 24, 1947 (P. L. 80), known as the "Intestate Act of 1947” amended December 10, 1959 (P. L. 

1747), are amended to read:

The 1917 introductory clause was copied from section 1 of the Act of April 8, 1833, P. L. 315.

Section 1 conforms with the prior language except where clarity dictates otherwise. The words "subject to payment" are substituted for "remaining after payment" to eliminate any implication that only title to the net balance passes. It is the whole title which passes "subject to payment of debts and charges." The words "just" and "legal" have been omitted as tending to possible restriction of the "debts and charges." "and not disposed of by will or otherwise" has been substituted for "which shall not have been sold, or disposed of by will, or otherwise limited by marriage settlement," because of the possibility that reference to property "sold" and "marriage settlement" might indicate that other inter vivos dispositions, such as inter vivos trusts, were excluded. "Shall descend" instead of "shall be divided and enjoyed" is used because it denotes the transfer of ownership.

¶ 1. General-Persons to Whom Act Applies 

This introductory section differs only slightly from the language used since the act of 1833, P. L. 315. The scope of the act is here defined-necessarily in broad and general terms. The act applies to the "real and personal estate" of any "decedent" which is "not disposed of by will or otherwise."

In section 16 (repealer) it is reiterated that this act "is intended as an entire and complete system regulating the descent of the real and personal estates of persons 52

¶ 2a §

INTESTATE ACT 

Are there any dying wholly or partially intestate express or implied limitations to this general language? 

In Keen's Estate, 297 Pa. 22 (1929), the appellant attempted to have the court impose an implied limitation on the word "decedent" in the act of 1917-arguing that the disposition of a lunatic's estate was governed rather by the Statute De Prerogativa Regis, 17 Edw. II, c. IX (1324), the most recent legislation expressly referring to the estates of insane persons. Of course the contention was rejected and the Intestate Act construed to mean what it said. The case is valuable merely as an illustration that there is no implied limitation on the meaning of the word "decedent” in this section. The act applies to all decedents—“whether male or female," minor or of age, competent or incompetent. The only limitation on the scope of the act in this respect is the express exception with regard to non-resident decedents in section 14. 

12. Property to Which Act Applies 

Jurisdictional limitations and accepted principles of conflict of laws also qualify the words "real and personal estate." These likewise are discussed under section 14. 

The following comments are confined to whether there are any particular types of estates which survive the decedent but do not pass under this act in cases of intestacy. 

a. Title Held by Decedent as Fiduciary 

One type of interest which is not subject to the act is a legal title held by the decedent in a fiduciary capacity. 

On the death of a trustee, his title might pass to a surviving co-trustee or to a successor named in the instrument. If a sole trustee dies intestate and the trust instrument is silent as to the successor, the legal title passes by intestacy, but not under the act. It is said to pass to his administrator in the case of personalty or to his heir at common law in the case of land.² This is perhaps the one situation where the common law of descent is still in effect 

1. Olney Bank and Trust Co. Case, 116 Pa. Super. 438 (1935). 

2. Jenks v. Backhouse, 1 Binney 91 (1803); cf. Carlisle's Appeal, 9 Watts 331 (1840). 53

§

INTESTATE ACT 

¶2b www in Pennsylvania.³ It is of slight importance, however. The trustee's title passes to his administrator or common law heir, but the power to act as trustee terminates at the decedent's death. Hence, the trust cannot be administered until a new trustee is appointed, and in the usual case it is a matter of no consequence where the bare legal title to the trust property rests in the meantime. 

b. Beneficial Interests in General 

It is clear therefore that the act is concerned only with property owned beneficially. So qualified, the words "real and personal estate," as interpreted by the courts, are sufficiently broad to cover any legal or equitable interest which decedent owned and which does not expire at his death.5 

There is no authority in our cases for giving the word "estate" in this section a narrow or technical meaning. 

Plainly the word is used in its broadest possible meaning and includes any sort of interest which does not expire at decedent's death-regardless of whether or not the interest would have been termed an "estate" by the common law theorists.Ⓡ

Naturally the interest in the heirs in such a case remains contingent and might turn out to be valueless if the life tenant should die leaving issue, but this uncertainty in no way affects the interest's inheritability.

This rather obvious qualification of the rule is often inaccurately stated when it is said that remainders to unascertained persons cannot pass by intestacy or devise.15 It is a rare case indeed where a person might be ascertained as a remainderman after his death, because survivorship is almost always a condition. Indeed, as in the case of contingent interests discussed above, most questions that seem to involve the scope of the act are really questions of whether there is anything left under general property law to which the act could apply. It is sometimes said, for example, that an estate for the life of the owner will not pass by succession; what is really meant is that the interest ceases at the death of the life tenant. The same can be said of the interests of joint tenants with right of survivorship or of tenants by the entireties; by settled principles of property law the whole interest passes automatically to the surviving tenant so that there is nothing left in the estate of the tenant who first died. (See discussion below under ¶ 4f of joint bank accounts in this connection.) 

Many questions as to whether a decedent's interest in property survives his death involve the construction of the will or deed of another.18 Did decedent's death disqualify him as a remainderman of a trust in another estate? Did decedent's interest in the income of a trust expire at his death? Other questions will concern the law of contracts. 

It is unusual but possible, for example, for a contract to be so personal that rights under it will cease with the death of the obligee.19 Other rights and interests might also be so personal that they expire at the owner's death-such as an unclaimed widow's exemption or unasserted right to take against the will of another.20 On the other hand, some interests which seem quite precarious clearly survive the owner's death and can pass by intestacy-such as the unripened interest of an adverse possessor who has occupied for less than the required period.21

a. Partial Intestacy 

It is clear from the wording of the present section and from section 16 that the act applies to property undisposed of in cases of partial intestacy in the same manner as it applies to all of decedent's property in cases of total intestacy. Note, however, that an unintentional failure to dispose of the entire estate might be governed by sections 14 (9) and (10) of the Wills Act so that no intestacy occurs. 

See the discussion of "Undisposed of Gifts" under those sections (15).

The doctrine of advancements (Section 9, infra) does not apply to testamentary gifts. Thus, if T's heirs are 

A and B and by will he leaves half of his estate to A, dying intestate as to the other half, A's share in the part of the estate passing by intestacy is not in any way affected by the fact that he has also received a gift under the will. 

A gets three-quarters and B one-quarter. As more fully explained below (under b and c), even an express provision in the incomplete will that A shall receive no more than the testamentary gift is ineffective to avoid this result-unless the gift is conditional upon A's renouncing his share in the rest of the estate. 

Where the spouse is the beneficiary under the incomplete will in such a case, he will sometimes take the entire estate due to the fact that in the absence of issue he will be entitled to the first $10,000 of the undisposed of property. 

As the court emphasized in Schillo's Estate, 64 Pa. Super. 

85, 89 (1916), he is in no sense taking against the will in this situation. Hence, he takes both his legacy and his full intestate share. The effect of this rule is often quite startling when a testator fails to make a valid disposition of a remainder after a life estate. Cases dealing with the disposition of the reversion in such a situation are discussed below (6) in connection with the general question of "When Heirs Are Determined." 60

13b 

INTESTATE ACT 

cos b. Negative Disinheritance 

In Rorer's Will, 7 Phila. 524 (1870), a duly executed writing stating "I do not wish any of my brothers to have any of my estate," was held not to be a will, so that the decedent died intestate and her brothers took their intestate shares. This is apparently in accord with the general common law rule to the effect that negative words are insufficient to disinherit an heir, where the property is not affirmatively disposed of to someone else. The question frequently arises in cases of partial intestacy. Thus, in 

Gorgas's Estate, 166 Pa. 269 (1895), an undisposed of portion of the estate passed to a niece under the intestate law, although she had been expressly disinherited in the will. 

And in Hitchcok v. Hitchcock, 35 Pa. 393 (1860), the testator bequeathed to a granddaughter "only" $2,000 because "she is the only child of my deceased son, and as such inherits all his estate, while my other grandchildren, who may be left orphans, may not be so well off.' The testator later died intestate as to a large part of his property and it was held that the grandchild took her full intestate share of the undisposed of property. To the same effect, see Gibbons' Estate, 317 Pa. 465, 468 (1935); 

Verner's Estate, 358 Pa. 280, 286 (1948). 

It will be noted that the doctrine of the above cases never applies where there is an affirmative disposition of the estate. If, for example, the decedent in Rorer's Estate had included a provision giving his estate to those entitled under the intestate laws, the express exclusion of the brothers from this class would have been effective to disinherit them. See, for example, McGovran's Estate, 190

Pa. 375 (1899). In effect, the doctrine is merely that the law will not imply a gift to other heirs from a provision disinheriting some of them.

The rule that a positive disposition of property must be made in order to disinherit an heir has apparently been consistently followed in Pennsylvania, except in Kissinger's Estate, 292 Pa. 336 (1928), which suggests a possible exception to the doctrine. There, the decedent had executed a paper directing that $7,500 should be "deducted from the share of" his son X and given to Y, a stranger to his 61

$

INTESTATE ACT 

¶ 3c blood. There was no positive disposition of his estate other than the gift to Y. The decedent was survived by a spouse and several children including X. If the rule against negative disinheritance were applied strictly, it would seem that Y should receive a legacy of $7,500 and that the balance of the estate should pass under the intestate laws to the spouse and children, including X. In other words, the gift of $7,500 to Y is clearly effective, but the direction that X's intestate share should be reduced by $7,500 would seem ineffective under the rule against negative disinheritance, so that the amount should be deducted from the whole estate. The actual holding in the case is probably consistent with this view, as the appeal was from a decree of distribution which merely awarded the $7,500 to Y and apparently made no award of the rest of the estate.24 Both the Orphans' Court and Supreme Court, however, were clearly of the opinion that the $7,500 must be deducted from X's intestate share. The Supreme Court opinion states that "in effect [the decedent] said all my estate is to be distributed under the intestate laws except $7,500 of my son's share thereof and that shall go elsewhere." But the point is that the decedent did not expressly make any affirmative gift of the balance of his estate, and any theory that the decedent makes an implied gift to the other heirs in such cases would apply in any case of negative disinheritance.

It is doubtful that Kissinger's Estate will have any serious effect on the rule against negative disinheritance which seems firmly entrenched in our decisions.25 On the other hand, it is conceivable that the decision will be used as an opening wedge to remove this ancient and not too logical doctrine from our law.

Ordinarily the heir-legatee will not be put to such an election. It has already been seen that where the will is silent on the subject, the heir may take both the gift in the will and the intestate share of undisposed-of property. And, because of the rule against negative disinheritance, the same result will follow even where the testator has expressed an intention that the beneficiary should receive no more of the estate than the amount mentioned in the will. 

But while the decedent may not exclude the heir from undisposed-of property, it is perfectly possible for a testator to make the gift in the will contingent upon the legatee's renouncing any right he might have by reason of partial intestacy. If this intent is adequately expressed, the heirlegatee will then be forced to choose between the share of undisposed-of property and the testamentary gift. Thus, in Jackson's Appeal, 126 Pa. 105 (1889), the decedent left a will giving one-third of his estate to his wife "in lieu of her dower if she shall so elect," but died intestate as to the other two-thirds. It was held that the widow could have taken either the testamentary gift or her intestate share, but she was not permitted to take both. 

On the other hand, it must clearly appear that the testator intended the heir to be put to this election, so that the decision will vary with the wording of the will and the circumstances in the particular case. In Forrestal's Estate, 10 D. & C. 152 (O. C. Phila. 1928), for example, the court refused to follow Jackson's Appeal in a case where the gift to the wife was in lieu of any interest she might have in the estate, but where the testator thereafter attempted 26. The distinction in most cases is unimportant, since the result is the same whichever theory is adopted. 

Where inherited property is more of a burden than a benefit, however, the question sometimes arises. See Edwin Home v. Shattuck, 64 Pa. Super. 239, 242 (1916); Provident Trust Co. v. Gitlin, 52 Montg. 302 (1936); Page, Wills

¶ 3d to dispose of all the rest of his estate by his will. The intestacy arose due to a void gift to charity rather than to deliberate design as in Jackson's Appeal. The court therefore interpreted the will to mean that the testamentary gift was conditional upon her not taking against the will and not upon her renouncing the share arising from an intestacy which the testator did not foresee. d. Renunciation of Gift in Will

Wholly different problems arise where a person renounces not the intestate share but the gift in the will. 

Presumably a refused legacy will fall into the residue or to other residuary legatees under section 14 (9 and 10) of the Wills Act. But if the refused legacy is the sole residuary gift, it will pass by intestacy to those entitled under the act, perhaps including the refusing legatee himself. It is difficult to see how this result can be avoided even where the legatee-heir renounces in order to avoid a condition in the will. In Atkinson, Wills (1937), p. 727, however, there is the following statement which is unsupported by citations and which may be taken for what it is worth: "It would seem that if the person rejecting a residuary devise or legacy is also the heir, his renunciation should prevent him from taking any portion so becoming intestate property; otherwise the beneficiary might avoid the effect. of a testamentary condition in defiance of the testator's intention." 

e. Spouse's Share-Cross-Reference 

A surviving spouse can elect to assert certain rights in property which ordinarily would pass under decedent's will, but when a spouse takes against the will he claims under section 8 of the Wills Act and not under the Intestate Act. Cases of this sort must be distinguished from cases of actual intestacy.

... Otherwise"

a. Disposition by Other Statutes 

It will first be noted that under the revised language of this section, its literal meaning no longer conflicts with other statutes dealing with the disposition of a decedent's property when an attempted testamentary or inter vivos gift fails. The provisions for lapsed and void gifts in causes (8) to (10) of section 14 of the Wills Act might be regarded as rules for construing the will, although in a sense they provide a statutory disposition of the gift that failed. The provisions for cy pres in section 10 of the 

Estates Act will likewise take precedence over the Intestate Act where a gift to charity fails for any of the reasons there set forth.

Particular attention is directed to sections 5 and 8 of the Estates Act. Under these new provisions a void perpetuity will never revert to the estate of the grantor or testator and an invalid accumulation will revert to the settlor's estate only when distribution to the statutory beneficiaries is impossible. 

b. Gifts Inter Vivos-Personalty 

Persons so often make incomplete gifts of personalty with some naive idea of avoiding taxes at their deaths, and disappointed relatives of a decedent so often claim by way of inter vivos gift, that the law of gifts has become closely connected with the law of decedents' estates. Hundreds of pages have been written on the subject,27 but the bare outlines of the problem can be briefly described. Broadly speaking, there must be a manifestation of an intent to make a present gift 28 plus some objective act which will satisfy the requirement of delivery.

c. Gifts Inter Vivos-Real Estate 

Similar rules apply to gifts of real estate. The subject is discussed in Allshouse's Estate, 304 Pa. 481, 488 (1931). An "unmistakable" intent to part with title and vest it in the donee is necessary, and since manual delivery of the land is impossible, an unconditional delivery of a deed (to the donee or in escrow) is required. What constitutes a sufficient "deed” in cases where no formal instrument is drawn up is not entirely clear from the decisions. Note that neither a seal (act of 1925, P. L. 404, 21 P. S. § 10), nor an acknowledgement (Maguire v. Preferred Realty, 257 Pa. 48, 51 (1917)), nor technical words of conveyance (act of 1909, P. L. 91, 21 P. S. § 1 et seq.; 

Auman v. Auman, 21 Pa. 343, 347 (1853)) are necessary, but of course the Statute of Frauds must be complied with. 

Possible exceptions to the above requirements are cases involving a parol gift followed by the donee's taking possession and making improvements (see cases cited in the Allshouse case) and cases involving dedication to a public use (Commonwealth v. First National Bank, 46 D. & C. 

619 (C. P. Montour, 1943)).

That gifts causa mortis are recognized in Pennsylvania is clear from Elliott's Estate, 312 Pa. 493 (1933), and the authorities there discussed. It is thus possible for a person in contemplation of imminent death to make a conditional gift of a chattel to another which will take effect only if the donor does in fact die soon thereafter. e. Gifts of Future Interests-Trusts 

It is possible for a person to limit his interest in property to a life estate and make a present gift of the remainder arising on his death. Such transfers are generally subject to death taxes, but so far as general property law is concerned the present passage of title to the future interest will be recognized so that the donee's rights will be superior to the rights of the donor's heirs. For this result to follow, however, it is essential that an interest vests in the donee at the time of the gift, even though its enjoyment is postponed. If this element is lacking, the attempted gift will be regarded as merely an attempt to make a testamentary transfer so that its validity will depend on conformity with the Wills Act. Since the gift comes into enjoyment only on the donor's death in either case, it can readily be seen why the line of distinction between an effective present gift of a future interest and an attempt to make a future gift is often such a fine one. 38 The neatest way to make a present gift of a future interest is by means of an inter vivos trust. If this device is used, the settlor may retain not only a life interest, but also the power to revoke 88 or to consume principle,39 and at least some power over the management of the trust assets.40 Indeed, the settlor may declare himself to be the trustee, in which event the requirement of delivery is dispensed with. See Glosser's Trust, 355 Pa. 210, 214-15 (1946). However, all such transactions will be examined closely and the attempted gift is sometimes found to be incomplete. Thus, where a third party is trustee, there is always the possibility that the court will find that the alleged settlor lacked the necessary intent to make a present

However, the delivery to the escrow is irrevocable so that the gift is regarded as complete.

The fact that joint bank accounts are recognized at all as accomplishing completed gifts is perhaps more surprising than the limitations stated in rules (2) and (3). 

In the ordinary joint tenancy, neither owner may dispose of the property without the other's joinder, but in the case of bank accounts where either party has the right to withdraw, the donor can at any time during his lifetime withdraw the entire balance. It might appear, therefore, that these cases represent an exception to the general policy of the law (as opposed to equity) against revocable gifts. 

The theoretical answer is that although the donor can withdraw the fund so far as the bank is concerned, the interest of the donee remains in the cash withdrawn, which cannot properly be used for the donor's sole benefit. Hence, there is no revocation by reason of the withdrawal. See Berhalter v. Berhalter, 315 Pa. 225 (1934).

Wholly different problems are raised when a savings account is opened in the name of donor as "trustee" for donee. If in such a case the donor with the intent to make a gift delivers the pass book to the donee, the transaction is viewed as an ordinary case of a present irrevocable gift. 

See McGary's Estate, 355 Pa. 232 (1946), (discussed in the 

December, 1946, issue of the Fiduciary Review), dealing with the inheritance taxation aspects of such transactions.

Cases dealing with such deposits are in a class by themselves, and it is generally recognized that they cannot be explained in terms of traditional concepts. From the citations of the Restatement and Scott, it also seems probable that the doctrine is limited to savings accounts and would not apply to an ordinary drawing account. In proper cases, however, a tentative trust will be recognized, so that the fund will not be considered as part of the depositor's estate, even though he retains complete and exclusive dominion over it until his death. Thus, the tentative trust constitutes a definite exception to the principles of law relating to inter vivos transfers. 

The law relating to certain types of life insurance policies might also be regarded as an exception to the ordinary rule that the law does not permit revocable gifts, although the exception is so well recognized that it is seldom considered as such. Where a policy is payable to a named beneficiary, it is unquestionable that the proceeds form no part of the insured's estate, even though the insured retained complete power over the policy until the moment of his death.52 Here the law is even more liberal than in the case of ordinary bank deposits. As has been seen, a deposit (other than a tentative trust) which the owner alone controls during his lifetime but which is designated as the property of another on the owner's death is regarded as testamentary (rule 3 supra in the discussion of Onofrey v. 15. Meaning of the Word "Descend"

Under the opening words of the old acts, the real and personal estate was said to be "divided and enjoyed" as provided. Under the present act, the estate "descends" as provided. Neither phraseology is technically precise or orthodox in describing the manner in which an intestate's property passes to those entitled, but the change is without significance. The difficulty arises from the fact that traditional terminology was originally used in connection with a dual system of intestate succession which was long ago discarded, although there is no widely accepted language which is more appropriate in modern law. 

Traditionally, real estate "descended" to common law heirs (it could never lineally ascend), and personalty was "distributed" to the next of kin. The trouble first began with the act of 1833, P. L. 315, which provided in section 7 that in default of named relatives, both the real and personal estate of the intestate should "descend to and be distributed among the next of kin of such intestate." It was argued, logically enough, in McDowell v. Addams, 45 

Pa. 430, 434 (1863), that the estate could not "descend" to a grandmother under that section, even though she might be the nearest kin. The court, however, very prop- 75

§

INTESTATE ACT 

「5 erly pointed out that the words "descend," "be distributed," "go," "pass," and "be enjoyed" were used more or less indiscriminately in our statutes and refused to ascribe a technical meaning to the word "descend." The same can be said of the present section. It simply means that the estate passes to those entitled, and no particular significance should be attached to the use of the admittedly anachronistic language.

If the concept of property "descending" to a grandparent can be mastered, little additional difficulty should be encountered in understanding how the term can be used in connection with personal property. It is true, under the present law of decedents' estates, that if a distributee obtains legal title to any particular item of an intestate's personalty, it will be through an agreement or a special decree of court and not by operation of law. The legal title to personal property (or at least powers usually associated with legal title) passes to the administrator who is ordinarily supposed to liquidate it,54 pay debts and charges, and distribute what is left among those entitled, although the modern tendency is to discard the distinction between real and personal property in this respect.55 All that, however, concerns the law of administration which has been divorced from the law of intestacy since 1833.56 The substantive provisions of the intestate act are concerned only with the beneficial interest in the net estate. The Commissioners who drafted the act of 1833, P. They therefore very sensibly transferred these procedural provisions to their act relating to executors and administrators. For better or for worse, certain procedural provisions applicable only in special cases (such as provisions for setting aside real estate for the spouse, escheat, etc.) have since crept back into the intestate act, but the substantive provisions have generally remained unadulterated by provisions relating to the law of administration. 76

It is clear, therefore, that the departure from the language of prior acts in this section and in section 4 (6), infra, cannot be interpreted as having any esoteric effect on the law of administration, which is governed by other statutes and is entirely foreign to the subject matter of these provisions. 

16. When Heirs Are Determined a. In General

Persons entitled to take under the intestate act are determined at the moment of death. The only exception to this rule in Pennsylvania is in the case of a person conceived before the decedent's death but born thereafter; such cases are governed by section 4 (3) of this act. In all other cases, the persons described in the act who are living at the time of death will take both real and personal property to the exclusion of those who predeceased the decedent and those who are begotten after his death. Thus, although the distribution of personalty might be delayed, "the rights of distributees of the personal property of an intestate vest immediately upon his death" and not at the time of distribution.58 The fact that the administrator holds legal title during administration is of no consequence; as already explained, it is the beneficial title which "descends" under the act and this passes immediately. It is true that when the persons entitled are husband and wife (as in the case of a decedent's parents) the interest of one will, upon his death before distribution, shift to the other (see infra under section 4 (6)), but this is because they take by the entireties and does not present any real exception to the rule.

¶ 6b involving estates which come into enjoyment long after that time. It often seems useless to trace the interest in the property through one or more intervening estates, and it must be admitted that the old common law of descent was often more practical than the modern law in this respect. 

The effect of the common law requirement of seisin was that future interests often passed to the heirs of the person last in actual possession as determined at the time the interest came into enjoyment.59 It is clear from our cases, however, that this doctrine of seisin has never been recognized in this state, so that those entitled to future as well as present interests which the intestate owned will be determined immediately.

Often the interest will pass through the estate of the intestate back to a person who had a life interest in the same property. Thus, on the death of the beneficiary under an insurance policy, the unpaid installments certain might revert to the estate of the insured and pass by intestacy to the estate of the named beneficiary.⁰ The question frequently arises in cases of partial intestacy where a remainder after a life estate given by will fails for one reason or another and becomes a reversion vesting immediately in those persons entitled under the intestate law at the testator's death. As explained above (3a) the legatee-heir can take both the gift in the will and the full intestate share. 

A typical case is McFarland's Estate, 155 Pa. Super. 466 (1944). There testator left his estate to his daughter for life, remainder to her issue. The daughter survived, enjoyed her life estate, and died without issue. There was no alternative gift of the remainder, so an intestacy resulted and it was held that the entire principal must be distributed to the executor of the daughter since she was the original decedent's sole heir at the time of his death. 

The court pointed out that "the fact that the life tenant is

Freeman's Estate, 227 Pa. 154 (1910), is a similar case where the testator simply left his estate to his wife for life and made no disposition of the remainder at all, so that his wife's estate became entitled to her intestate share of the reversion as well. The results of the doctrine are often quite harsh in such a case because the lion's share of the property will probably pass through the spouse's estate to her family rather than to the original decedent's collaterals. 

As already explained, the spouse in this situation is not taking against the will, so that her share will include the $10,000 allowance. McGough's Estate, 42 D. & C. 435 (O. C.

Montg., 1941) is an interesting holding on this point. Testator gave the residue of his estate to his wife but provided that if she remarried, two-thirds of the estate should be forfeited and go to "my brother and sisters living.'

Upon the widow's remarriage, the court held that the twothirds was indeed forfeited, but since testator's brother and sisters had all died in the meantime, there was an intestacy as to the gift over, so that the wife could take in fee her one-half of the forfeited share plus her $5,000 allowance under the old act. 

Not only are the heirs determined as of the date of decedent's death, but they are determined under the law as it then existed. For this reason it takes a long time for intestate laws to become obsolete. In Oram's Estate, 21 

Wash. 59, decided in 1941, for example, it was necessary to trace the blood of the first purchaser under the act of 1833 in order to determine who was entitled to the reversion following a life estate.

§ 2. SHARE OF SURVIVING SPOUSE. 

The surviving spouse shall be entitled to the following share or shares: (1) More Than One Child.

One-third if the decedent is survived by more than one child, or by one or more children and the issue of a deceased child or children, or by the issue of more than one deceased child; or (2) One Child.

One-half if the decedent is survived by one child only, or by no child, but by the issue of one deceased child; or 

(3) No Issue. 

The first ten thousand dollars in value and one-half of the balance of the estate, if the decedent is survived by no issue; or

COMMISSIONERS' COMMENTS (4) No Issue or Other Designated Persons. 

All of the estate if the decedent is survived by no issue, parent, brother, sister, child of a brother or sister, grandparent, uncle or aunt. 

Section 2 supplants sections 1, 2, and 17 of the 1917 act.

It is believed that the share of the spouse is set forth clearly, briefly and logically, progressing from a share of one-third in clause (1) to the entire estate in clause (4). 

The present arrangement has the added virtue of setting forth in one place the share of the surviving spouse. The principal changes are: 

1. The $5,000 allowance is increased to $10,000 because of the greatly decreased value of money. 

2. The surviving spouse is given the entire estate in the absence of near relatives. This seems more equitable and reduces administration difficulties by avoiding the necessity of searching for remote relatives, and in many cases giving each of them only a small interest. 

3. The proviso in section 2(a) of the 1917 act to the effect that the allowance does not apply upon an election to take against the will has been omitted because it is not properly in this act. Langerwisch's Est., 267 Pa. 319 (1920), raised the question of the validity of the proviso. While it 101

4. The procedural provisions applicable to the $10,000 allowance and to the spouse's claim of the entire estate have been placed separately in sections 10 and 11 to avoid confusion in defining the extent of the shares received by each beneficiary. [clause (1)]

Old Law 

Section 1. The real and personal estate of a decedent, whether male or female, remaining after payment of all just debts and legal charges, which shall not have been sold, or disposed of by will, or otherwise limited by marriage settlement, shall be divided and enjoyed as follows; namely,— (a) Where such intestate shall leave a spouse surviving and one child only, or shall leave a spouse surviving and no children, but shall leave descendants of one deceased child, the spouse shall be entitled to one-half part of the real and personal estate. (b) Where such intestate shall leave a spouse surviving and more than one child, or one child and the descendants of a deceased child or children, or the descendants of more than one deceased child, the surviving spouse shall be entitled to one-third part of the real and personal estate. 

Section 2. (a) Where such intestate shall leave a spouse surviving and other kindred, but no issue, the surviving spouse shall be entitled to the real or personal estate, or both, to the aggregate value of five thousand dollars, in addition, in the case of a widow, to the widow's exemption as allowed by law; and, if such estate shall exceed in value the sum of five thousand dollars, the surviving spouse shall be entitled to the sum of five thousand dollars absolutely, to be chosen by him or her from real or personal estate, or both, and in addition thereto shall be entitled to one-half part of the remaining real and personal estate: Provided, That the provisions of this clause as to said five thousand dollars in value shall apply only to cases of actual intestacy of husband or wife, entire or partial, and not to cases where the surviving spouse shall elect to take against the will of the deceased spouse. 

There are two important changes:

Section 17. (a) In default of known heirs or kindred, competent as aforesaid, the real estate of such intestate shall be vested in the surviving spouse of such intestate, if any, and the surviving spouse shall be entitled to the whole of the personal estate. 

Intestate Act of 1917, P. L. 429, as amended 1917, P. L. 755. 

(1) The allowance of the surviving spouse in cases where there is no surviving issue is now $10,000 (rather than $5,000). (2) The surviving spouse now takes the whole estate where the decedent is survived by no issue, parent, grandparent or collateral relative as close as an uncle (rather than in default of known heirs). 

The other changes from the wording of the old act are stylistic only and will have no effect on prior law. The entire procedure for setting aside the allowance being dropped to section 10 of the present act. Discussion

¶ 6. Share Taken by Spouse-Whole Estate. 

11. History-Spouse as an Heir

At common law, a husband was entitled to all his wife's personalty upon marriage (2 Blackstone's Commentaries 433) so that no provision for him was necessary in the English Statute of Distribution of 1670. In Pennsylvania, a widower was first mentioned in the act of 1797, 3 Sm. L. 296, which provided in section 5 that the husband of an intestate was entitled to "the whole personal estate." This was continued by section 1 of the act of 1833, P. L. 315 and remained law until 1917, when the widower's share in personalty was reduced to the same share allotted to a widow. 

The widow of an intestate has always taken a share of personal property in the same manner as the intestate's blood relatives. Under the English Statute of Distribution of 1670 this share was one-third of the personalty if there were issue surviving, or one-half if no issue survived. This scheme was adopted by the Pennsylvania act of 1684 (172nd law) and continued through the act of 1833, P. L. 315. The first departure from this rule came with the act of 1909, P. L. 87, which introduced the allowance in addition to the half when there was no issue. The only other significant change was introduced by section 1 (a) of the act of 1917, providing that the spouse is entitled to a half, instead of a 104

2 

INTESTATE ACT 

$cos third, when only one child or the issue of only one child survives.

As to real estate, the common law did not regard the spouse as an heir. The husband took his curtesy and the wife her dower, but the law of descent had nothing to do with the interests of the surviving spouse. The history of the disappearance of common law curtesy and dower is traced briefly in the discussion of section 5 (a) and (b) of the present act. As there explained, the share given the spouse by the present section is the modern substitute for curtesy and dower in property owned by an intestate at his death. It continues the scheme finally adopted in 1917 of increasing the share from a life interest to a fee in the allotted portion of the estate and of making the surviving spouse of either sex an "heir" to both real and personal property, the share of either spouse in both kinds of property now being analogous to the widow's share in personalty under the original Statute of Distribution. The statutory share in both kinds of property now "descends" to the spouse in the same manner as property descends to other persons entitled to share in the estate. (6 

As stated in Barnard's Estate, 351 Pa. 313, 315 (1945), as respects personal property the surviving spouse was always regarded as an 'heir' . . By the Intestate Act of 1917 . a surviving spouse takes an estate of inheritance in both real and personal property. Consequently, a surviving spouse is a statutory heir of the estate of the other." See also Verner's Estate, 358 Pa. 280, 288 (1948). 

2. Special Rules Applicable to Spouse Cross References 

Although the spouse now takes as an "heir" to both real and personal property and the older distinctions have for the most part been abolished, certain special rules still govern the rights of the surviving spouse because of the size and nature of the share and the unique husband-wife relationship. Thus, a special procedure for setting aside the $10,000 allowance in proper cases is set forth in section 10 of the present act. A spouse is also subject to special rules of forfeiture in section 6; the discussion of that section includes not only forfeiture for misconduct but also 105

INTESTATE ACT 

¶ 3a various other possible grounds for barring the spouse from his ordinary intestate share, such as inter vivos agreements. On the other hand, the spouse is in a position superior to other heirs in that he or she can attack certain inter vivos transfers under section 5 of this act and under section 11 of the Estates Act; hence the spouse may sometimes share in property not available to blood relatives of the decedent. Finally, the spouse is permitted to take against the will of the decedent as provided by section 8 of the Wills Act, but this field of the law is quite divorced from the law of intestacy, and the share taken by the electing spouse is now set forth in the Wills Act without reference to the present section. 

¶ 3. Proof of Relationship a. Marriage 

A person claiming under this section must of course. have been legally married to the decedent. A comprehensive treatment of the various questions that arise concerning the validity of domestic and foreign marriages will be found in the excellent work of Abraham and Maurice Freedman, Marriage and Divorce in Pennsylvania (1939), in the Pennsylvania annotations to sections 121, et seq., of the Restatement of Conflicts, and in the chapter on "Marriage" in Hunter's Orphans' Court Commonplace Book (1939). In cases involving common law marriage, reference should also be made to Buradus v. General Cement Co., 159 Pa. Super. 

501 (1946), where the validity of common law marriages without a license is reaffirmed although the dislike of the court for the anachronistic doctrine is apparent, and to Horton's Estate, 357 Pa. 30 (1947), where the rules of proof are discussed. 

b. Divorce 

Where an absolute divorce has been obtained, the parties are no longer married, and it is clear that all rights of succession cease. For questions relating to the validity of foreign divorces and the possibility of attacking such decrees collaterally, the following cases should be exam- 106

¶ 3c 

INTESTATE ACT 

82 ined: Williams v. North Carolina, 317 U. S. 287 (1942), explained in 325 U. S. 226 (1945); Commonwealth v. Esenwein, 325 U. S. 279 (1945), affirming 348 Pa. 455 (1944); and Sherrer v. Sherrer, 92 L. Ed. 1055 (1948). The net result of this flurry of decisions seems to be that foreign decrees of divorce may still be denied full faith and credit on the ground that the moving party failed to establish a bona fide domicile in the state where the divorce was obtained-but only if the divorce defendant did not enter a personal appearance in the foreign proceeding.¹ 

To be distinguished from an absolute divorce is a decree of separation or "divorce a mensa et thoro" which does not affect the marriage status and will not of itself affect intestate succession by either spouse. There might be ground for forfeiture in such cases, however, under section 6 (a) and (b) of this act. 2 c. Estoppel

A person might have been the legal spouse of the decedent at the time of death but be estopped from asserting his status as such. In Richardson's Estate, 132 Pa. 292 (1890), the alleged widow would not be heard to question a divorce which the decedent obtained where she had not only raised no objection to it for many years during decedent's life but had actually remarried on the strength of it. And in Romanski's Estate, 354 Pa. 261 (1946), Pennsylvania joined the majority in holding that an invalid foreign divorce may not be attacked by the person who obtained it. 

Both these cases are in accord with the Restatement of Conflicts § 112, which was cited in the Romanski case. Other cases where estoppel might arise can be imagined. Where the survivor is guilty of collusion he might be barred even though he was not the libellant-especially if collusion is the alleged ground for the invalidity. But where there is

Like any other heir, a person claiming to be decedent's spouse has the primary burden of proving the relationship. 

Once a prima facie case of marriage has been made (as by the introduction of a marriage certificate), the burden shifts to the other heirs to introduce evidence of the alleged marriage's invalidity. This they might do by showing a prior marriage, whereupon the position of the parties is reversed and the claimant must show that the first marriage had been dissolved before the second marriage took place. Helpful cases are Thomas v. Thomas, 124 Pa. 646 (1889), Madison v. 

Lewis, 151 Pa. Super. 138 (1943), and Hudek v. United

Engineering Co., 152 Pa. Super. 493 (1943). It will be noted that the various presumptions that arise in these cases are quite different from those where the legitimacy of a child is in question, as in the cases discussed under section 7 (¶1). 

When a claim is made on behalf of a deceased spouse of the decedent, the problems relating to proof of survivorship are the same as in the case of claims on behalf of any other heir. See the discussion of "Proof of Kinship' under section 3 (¶ 10). 

¶ 4. Share Taken by Spouse-Issue 

The size of the share taken by the spouse will depend primarily on whether there are also issue of the decedent surviving. Clearly step-children of the decedent are not his issue. On the other hand, it would seem equally clear that an illegitimate should be considered the child of his mother but not his father and an adopted person the child of the adopting parent but not his natural parent within the meaning of this section. Sections 7 and 8 provide for these results "for purposes of descent by, from and through" the illegitimate or adopted person. The spouse's allowance of a definite sum in addition to the fractional share where there is no issue first made its appearance in the intestate laws in the act of 1909, P. Later, because of the wording of the act of 1855, P. b. Changes in Present Act 

The present act raises the amount of the allowance to $10,000. The language of the old section is also considerably revised but with little substantial effect on prior law. 

The phrase inserted for the sake of emphasis in the original amendment of 1909 stating that the allowance is "in addition to" the widow's exemption under the Fiduciaries Act is omitted as unnecessary. (See below- 5c.) And the necessity for separate provisions for estates under and over the amount of the allowance is eliminated by the simple expedient of providing that the spouse gets the "first" $10,000 in value.

Also omitted at this point in the act is the phrase in section 2 (a) of the old act to the effect that the value of the allowance may be "chosen" by the surviving spouse "from the real or personal estate or both." One reason for this omission is that the right of selecting personal property has been eliminated as an illogical exception to the theoretical duty of the personal representative to liquidate personalty and the ordinary rules relating to the distribution of an estate. There is still the right to select the allowance out of real estate, but the entire procedure relating to such selection is now set forth separately in section 10. 

Finally, the proviso in the old act stating that the allowance is limited to cases of actual intestacy is omitted as unnecessary in view of the revised language of the provision in the present Wills Act relating to a spouse's election to take against the will. Section 8 (b) of that act now spells out in detail the share which an electing spouse may take against the will of a decedent instead of referring to the Intestate Act. In effect the law under the 1917 act remains substantially the same, because the share described in section 8 (b) of the Wills Act is similar to the intestate share without the $10,000 allowance. 110

1.5c 

INTESTATE ACT 

cos c. Theory of Allowance The theory of the allowance continues unchanged. 

Some confusion in this regard arose from the wording of the original amendment of 1909 and the misunderstanding continued to crop up under the act of 1917. The omission of any language in the present section relating to the choosing of the property to be set apart for the allowance should make it even clearer that the allowance is an intestate share which vests at death. It can, of course, be given or contracted away like any other inheritance, but it is in no sense a personal right contingent upon affirmative action being taken to assert it. In this the allowance differs radically from the widow's exemption under the Fiduciaries Act. This distinction was early recognized in Buckland's 

Estate, 239 Pa. 608 (1913), holding that the right to the allowance survives the death of a spouse who failed to claim it during his lifetime,10 and has been emphasized by the courts ever since. In the words of the court in Hast's 

Estate, 51 D. & C. 314, 317 (O. C. Fulton, 1944), “ it has been consistently held that the $500 exemption allowed to widows is a personal privilege and benefit which, if she does not claim it, she never has. But the $5,000 allowance is a vested interest at the death of her husband, and this she cannot be deprived of except by her own act." It was there held that in an estate of less than $5,000, the lien of the surviving spouse's creditors attached to all the decedent's real estate at the moment of death regardless of inaction on the part of the surviving spouse. Another important distinction between the spouse's allowance and the widow's exemption is that the allowance is "subject to debts and charges" like any other intestate share. This was made clear in Gilbert's Estate, 227 Pa. 

648, 652 (1910) shortly after the provision first made its appearance in the Intestate Act. When the allowance is
