It was held by Judge Gest in Paul's Estate, 26 Dist. 

1011 (O. C. Phila., 1917), that the allowance may be claimed from Pennsylvania real estate by the spouse of a nonresident decedent. The provision might work somewhat illogically in this situation, particularly if the surviving spouse is entitled to another allowance at the decedent's domicile, and still other allowances in other states where the decedent owned real estate, but it is difficult to see how the conclusion could be avoided. Not only is Paul's Estate in accord with general principles of conflict of laws, but since 1931, the act has contained special provisions (now in section 10 (b)) governing procedure for claiming the allowance in cases of non-resident decedents. It would seem, therefore, that the "first $10,000 in value" under clause (3) of the present section means the first $10,000 of property which passes under this act, even though the spouse might be entitled to other property elsewhere. e. Partial Intestacy, Gifts to "Heirs," Etc.-Cross

References As pointed out in the discussion of section 1 (¶ 3a and ¶ 6) the full intestate share, including the allowance in proper cases, may be claimed by the spouse in cases of partial intestacy. Here again, the spouse is entitled to the first $10,000 of property passing under this act, even though he might also receive other property under the incomplete will. The allowance may also be claimed where a spouse, married after the making of the will, takes an intestate share pursuant to section 7 (3) of the Wills Act.. On the other hand, where there is a gift in the will or deed of another to the "heirs," or "next of kin," etc. of the decedent, the allowance cannot ordinarily be claimed under the present statutes: see section 14 (4) of the Wills Act and section 14 (1) of the Estates Act. And, as already pointed out, there is no provision for an allowance when the spouse takes against the will under section 8 of the 

Wills Act.

¶ § 2 

INTESTATE ACT ¶ 6. Share Taken by Spouse-Whole Estate 

Another change from prior law favorable to the surviving spouse is brought about by clause (4) of this section. Under the act of 1917 and prior acts, the spouse took the entire estate only "in default of known heirs or kindred." Since there were no limits on the remoteness of persons who might become entitled under the act of 1917, this meant that the spouse might have to share the estate with distant relatives. If she took the entire estate under the old law, it was only because of the absence of known relatives-i. e., only if there was a failure of proof." The present act makes two distinct changes in this regard. 

First, the class of possible heirs is limited by section 3, discussed infra. Secondly, the wife is given the whole estate as an intestate share under section 2 (4) "if the decedent is survived by no issue, parent, brother, sister, child of a brother or sister, grandparent, uncle or aunt.”

It is important to note that this class of relatives described in section 2 (4) is somewhat narrower than the class of possible heirs under section 3. On chart III (infra § 3-¶ 2), the limits within which there must be a surviving relative to reduce the share of the spouse are indicated by the broken line, while the limits of those who can inherit generally is indicated by the heavy unbroken line. Suppose, for example, that decedent is survived by a spouse and a first cousin, as illustrated in chart I. A first cousin is not mentioned in section 2 (4), so that the spouse will take the whole estate. If, on the other hand, there had been no surviving spouse, the cousin would have taken the estate under section 3 (5).

However, a person not mentioned in section 2 (4) might in certain circumstances take a share even where a spouse survives. Such a case is illustrated by chart II. Here, the same family is represented as in chart I, but one of the decedent's uncles has survived. As a result, the spouse will not take the entire estate under 2 (4); instead he will take merely his $10,000 allowance plus one-half of the balance, and the rest of the estate is shared under section 3

INTESTATE ACT § 3 §3. SHARES OF OTHERS THAN SURVIVING SPOUSE 

The share of the estate, if any, to which the surviving spouse is not entitled, and the entire estate if there is no surviving spouse, shall descend in the following order: 

(1) Issue. 

To the issue of the decedent. (2) Parents.

If no issue survives the decedent, then to the parents or parent of the decedent. (3) Brothers, Sisters, or Their Issue. 

If no parent survives the decedent, then to the issue of each of the decedent's parents. (4) Grandparents.

If no issue of either of the decedent's parents but at least one grandparent survives the decedent, then half to the paternal grandparents or grandparent, or if both are dead, to the children of each of them and the children of the deceased children of each of them, and half to the maternal grandparents or grandparent, or if both are dead, to the children of each of them and the children of the deceased children of each of them. If both of the paternal grandparents or both of the maternal grandparents are dead leaving no child or grandchild to survive the decedent, the half which would have passed to them or to their children and grandchildren shall be added to the half passing to the grandparents or grandparent on the other side. (5) Uncles, Aunts and Their Children. 

If no grandparent survives the decedent, then to the uncles and aunts and the children of deceased uncles and aunts of the decedent. (6) Commonwealth.

In default of all persons hereinbefore described, then to the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania.

COMMISSIONERS' COMMENTS- [General] 

Section 3 is designed to take the place of sections, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, and 19 of the act of 1917. 151

INTESTATE ACT 

[clause (1)] The manner in which persons taking in unequal degrees shall share in the estate is covered by section 4(1). [clause (2)] This takes the place of section 8 of the 1917 act which reads:

[see below] Parents will receive their shares as tenants by the entireties under section 4(6). [clause (3)] This takes the place of section 9 of the 1917 act. Issue of deceased brothers and sisters are recognized without limitation. Thus, great grandnephews share in the estate prior to grandparents. This will seldom be applied. [clause (4)] This takes the place of sections 10 and 12 of the 1917 act. 

Section 10 has been criticized by the Supreme Court in Miles's Est., 272 Pa. 329 (1922), as "vague and indefinite; it fails either to say or suggest what possible groups of the persons indicated are to inherit, how these groups are to be ascertained, and whether those composing them take, as individuals, per stirpes or per capita." Section 12 of the 1917 act attempted to answer these questions but it does not cover all situations. 

Grandparents receive their shares in pairs, maternal and paternal, with limited right of representation where both grandparents on one side are deceased and a grandparent on the other side survives. [clause (5)] This replaces sections 10 and 11 of the 1917 act.

[clause (6)] The rights of the Commonwealth as a participant in an intestate estate are accelerated at the expense of persons more remotely related than first cousins, but not prior to indefinite issue of deceased brothers and sisters. A decedent who does not provide by his will for relations more remote than first cousins cannot be supposed to have much concern for them, and it is desired to avoid tedious and expensive searches for distant relations not expressly favored by the testator. "in default of all persons hereinbefore described" is suggested by the beginning of sections 10 and 24 of the 1917 act. 

Section 24 of the 1917 act as amended sets forth procedural matters with respect to estates escheatable to the Commonwealth. 

These procedural matters are now in section 12.

Section 7. The real and personal estate of such intestate not hereinbefore given to the surviving spouse, if any there be, shall descend to and be distributed among his or here issue according to the following rules and order of succession; namely,- 152

(a) If such intestate shall leave children, but no other descendant, being the issue of a deceased child, the estate shall descend to and be distributed among such children. (b) If such intestate shall leave grandchildren, but no child or other descendant, being the issue of a deceased grandchild, the estate shall descend to and be distributed among such grandchildren. (c) If such intestate shall leave descendants in other degrees of consanguinity, however remote from him, and all in the same degree of consanguinity to him, the estate shall descend to and be distributed among such descendants. 

Section 8. In default of issue, as aforesaid, the real and personal estate of such intestate not hereinbefore given to the surviving spouse, if any there be, shall go to and be vested in the father and mother of such intestate; or, if either the father or mother be dead at the time of the death of the intestate, the parent surviving shall take such real and personal estate. Section 9. In default of issue, father and mother, the real and personal estate of such intestate not hereinbefore given to the surviving spouse, if any there be, shall descend to and be distributed among the collateral heirs and kindred of such intestate, without distinction between those of the whole and those of the half-blood, according to the following rules and order of succession; namely,- (a) If such intestate shall leave brothers and sisters, or either, and no nephew or niece, or child of a deceased nephew or niece being the issue of a deceased brother or sister, the real and personal estate shall descend to and be distributed among such brothers and sisters. (b) If such intestate shall leave neither brother nor sister, and no child of any deceased nephew or niece being the issue of a deceased brother or sister, but nephews or nieces being the children of such deceased brother or sister, the real and personal estate shall descend to and be distributed among such nephews and nieces. (c) If such intestate shall leave neither brother nor sister, nor any nephew or niece being the child of such deceased brother or sister, but children of deceased nephews or nieces, the real and personal estate shall descend to and be distributed among such children of deceased nephews or nieces. Section 10. In default of all persons hereinbefore described, the real and personal estate of the intestate shall descend to and be distributed among the grandparents or descendants of deceased grandparents of such intestate, and, in default thereof, to and among the next of kin to such intestate. 

Section 11. The grandchildren of brothers and sisters and the children of uncles and aunts shall be entitled to take, by representation, the shares of real and personal estate which their parents would have taken if living; but, except as hereinafter provided, there shall be no representation admitted among collaterals after the grandchildren of brothers and sisters and the children of uncles and aunts.

Section 12. If the next of kin of an intestate, entitled to take under the provisions of this act, shall be one or more than one grandparent of such intestate, and there shall be living, at the time of the decease of such intestate, children or other descendants of any deceased grandparent, then the children or other descendants of any such deceased grandparent shall represent the grandparent so deceased, and shall take the share of real or personal estate to which such deceased grandparent would be entitled if living.

The issue of any such deceased grandparent shall take according to the following rules of succession; namely,— (a) If there be only children of such deceased grandparent, the share of such deceased grandparent shall descend to and be distributed among such children. (b) If there be grandchildren of such deceased grandparent, and no other descendants being children of a deceased grandchild, and no child, the share of such deceased grandparent shall descend to and be distributed among such grandchildren. (c) If there be descendants of such deceased grandparent in any other degree, however remote from him, and all in the same degree of consanguinity to 153

§INTESTATE ACT 

him, the share of such deceased grandparent shall descend to and be distributed among such descendants.

Section 24. In default of all such known heirs or kindred or surviving spouse, competent to take as aforesaid, the real and personal estate of such intestate, remaining after the payment of all just debts and legal charges, shall be sold by the executor or administrator of the estate, and the net proceeds of such sale shall be, by him, paid into the State Treasury for the use of the Commonwealth. Intestate Act of 1917, P. L. 429, amended as to Section 24 by Act of 1923, P. L. 70.

The important change is that the class of possible heirs is now limited, and the Commonwealth will now take in preference to the following: (a) ancestors more remote than grandparents (e. g., great grandparent, etc., excluded), (b) issue of ancestors more remote than grandparents (e. g., great uncles, second cousins, etc., excluded), and (c) grandparents' issue more remote than first cousins (e. g., first cousins once removed and other issue of first cousins excluded). However, issue of the decedent and issue of his brothers and sisters still take indefinitely. 

A less significant change is that where there are persons of unequal degrees entitled to take, the limits on representation among issue of brothers and sisters (contained in section 11 of the old act) have now been eliminated. 

Another minor change is that in the rare case where the estate goes to three surviving grandparents the sharing will now be half to the grandparent on one side of the family and half to the two on the other side instead of onethird to each.

[ 1. History 

As with the provision for the spouse, the history of our intestate law with respect to blood relatives has been one of breaking away from the old common law canons for the descent of real estate and providing for inheritance of both real and personal property in accordance with a scheme inspired by the English system for personal property as found in the Statute of Distribution of 1670. As listed by the 1917 Commission, early Pennsylvania statutes dealing with the subject are the act of 1683 (110th Law), act of 1684 (172nd Law), act of 1693, act of 1705, 3 Sm. L. 

156 n., act of 1764, 3 Sm. L. 159 n., act of 1794, 3 Sm. L. 143, and act of 1797, 3 Sm. L. 296. These were all superseded by the act of 1833, P. L. 315.

By 1833 there was no trace of the law of primogeniture, and other canons of descent had been considerably modified, although complete conformity between the rules governing real and personal property had not been attempted. 

Section 2 of the Act of 1833 provided for descent and distribution to issue in much the same manner as the present act. Sections 3 and 5, governing the interests of parents in the absence of issue, represented a compromise between the old and the new theories. The father (or mother if the father was dead) took the personalty absolutely, and the common law canon against the ascent (as opposed to descent) of real estate was modified to the extent of giving the parent a life interest in the real estate in the absence of issue, or an absolute interest therein in the absence of issue or brothers and sisters and their issue. Brothers and sisters and their issue were treated in section 4 of the act of 1833 in much the same manner as they are now, except for the limits on representation in section 8 of that act (see infra ¶ 5b). In default of issue, parents, or parents' issue, the estate both real and personal went to the "next 1 155

§

INTESTATE ACT 

12 of kin" under the provision of section 7. This general reference to next of kin incorporated by implication as to both types of property the rules applied to personalty under the English Statute of Distribution and the earlier principles followed by the ecclesiastical courts (McDowell v. Addams, 45 Pa. 430, 433 (1863)). Relatively minor changes were made by the acts of 1855, P. L. 368 (limits on representation-see infra ¶ 5b), 1885, P. L. 251 (per capita sharing-see § 4 (1) ¶ 2 fn 3) and 1887, P. L. 261 (grandparents-see infra ¶ 7) but the act of 1833 remained the basic law until 1917. Cutting across the various provisions of the act of 1833 were the left-overs of the common law canons relative to half blood and blood of the first purchaser. The history of the final disappearance of these canons is treated under sections 4 (2) and 4 (4) infra. 

By the act of 1917, the last vestiges of the old distinction between real and personal property and between male and female heirs and next of kin were wholly abolished and the general scheme of the present act was established. 

The changes in the present act are in the nature of clarifications and relatively unimportant modifications of the 1917 plan. 

¶ 2. Scope of This Section 

This section deals with the estate, if any, "to which the surviving spouse is not entitled"-whatever that turns out to be after section 2 is applied. It undertakes to answer only two questions: (1) What persons can inherit this part of the estate? and (2) What is the order of priority among such persons? Unlike the corresponding provisions in the act of 1917, the present section does not deal with the proportions taken by each person when more than one person becomes entitled to the estate not passing to the spouse. 

The one exception is in the provision for grandparents, where the estate is split into paternal and maternal halves. 

Aside from this, the size of the share taken by each of several persons entitled to take under any particular clause of this section will be governed primarily by section 4 (1) unless they are husband and wife (as in the case of parents or grandparents) in which event section 4 (6) provides for taking by entireties. 156

Chart III presents the scheme of the present section for the benefit of those who like charts. For readers who do not like charts, little can be added by way of explanation to the wording of the act itself. The following discussion of the history and effect of the various provisions might be helpful, however, if doubts arise as to whether the act means what it says. ¶ 3. Limitations on Who Can Be an Heir

Prior to the present act there was no limit on the remoteness of a relative who could become entitled to the decedent's property by intestate succession, so long as he was the nearest relative surviving. In the absence of persons specifically named in the act of 1917, the estate went to the "next of kin" under section 10. This referred back to the civil law of distribution so that no matter how remote the claimant was, he could take the estate provided there were no closer relatives and provided of course he could prove his relationship.² 1 This was radically changed by the present act which makes no mention of general "heirs" or "next-of-kin" but provides that the estate passes to the Commonwealth in the absence of relatives specifically described. Hence, the lines of possible heirs are chopped off at two places, as indicated by the heavy unbroken line on Chart III. There

However, no ancestor more remote than a grandparent is mentioned, and issue of any ancestor more remote than a grandparent are likewise omitted, so that great grandparents, great uncles, second cousins and the like will no longer inherit in any circumstances. It will also be noted that clauses (4) and (5) provide for "children" and 'grandchildren" of grandparents, and for "children" of uncles and aunts, but the use of any such general term as "issue" is studiously avoided in these clauses; as a result, descendants of grandparents are cut off after first cousins, and cousins once or twice removed will never take or share the estate of an intestate. 

¶ 4. Commonwealth as Heir

Since there was no limitation in the old law on the remoteness of blood relatives who could inherit, and since a decedent always has some blood relatives, the Commonwealth could never be theoretically entitled to the estate in its own right prior to the present act. It took under section 24 of the act of 1917 only in default of "known” heirs. In other words, the Commonwealth took not as an heir but only if those with a prior claim to the estate could not be found. In the present act, the Commonwealth is named in the present section as the distributee which takes the estate in the absence of a relative as close as a first cousin. Thus, it would seem that the Commonwealth now takes in the manner of an heir rather than by escheat or quasi-escheat. Note, however, that a special procedure is still provided in section 12 of this act for the administration of decedent's property when it goes to the Commonwealth under clause (6) of section 3. 

[5. Priority Among Persons Described in Different Clauses a. General

The order of preference among those taking the estate not going to the spouse follows closely the scheme of the act of 1917 which had completely revised the act of 1833, 159

§

INTESTATE ACT 

¶ 5b P. L. 315, in this respect. The only change of this type made by the present act from the act of 1917 is a very minor one with respect to remote issue of brothers and sisters, discussed below. Otherwise, the order of priority within the restricted class of possible heirs remains the same. 

The language has been considerably simplified, however, and the new provision should be easier to follow than the cumbersome wording of the old act. It is clear from the opening words of the present provision that the persons described in each clause are preferred over persons described in subsequent clauses. Hence, in any particular estate, all surviving persons mentioned in the first clause which describes a surviving relative will take to the exclusion of all others.

On Chart III (supra ¶ 2) the primary order of priority provided for in § 3 is indicated by the numbers assigned to each relative. It will be noted that only three priority numbers are given on the chart although there are five classes of takers aside from the Commonwealth described in the act. This is because the priority as between clauses (2) and (3) and between clauses (4) and (5) are implicit in the general rule that descendants will not share with their living ancestor. Hence, parents, brothers and sisters, and their issue are all included in priority "2" on the chart and grandparents and their issue are all included in priority "3." The secondary priorities as between ancestor and descendant in the same line are indicated by the letters “A,” “B,” “C," etc., as this seems part of a more general problem discussed below (6) under the heading "Priorities Among Persons Described in Same Clause." b. Remote Issue of Deceased Brothers and Sisters-Representation

Under the wording of clause (3) of the present section, all issue of deceased brothers and sisters are preferred to grandparents, uncles, aunts, and cousins. In other words, such issue, no matter how remote, will now stand in the shoes of their deceased ancestor and enjoy the preference a brother or sister would have enjoyed if living. This constitutes a slight change from the prior law under which 1 160

¶ 5b cos 

INTESTATE ACT 

83 such preference was limited to children and grandchildren of brothers and sisters. Thus, a great grandnephew whose ancestors of the decedent's blood are deceased will take before a first cousin under the present act although he would not have been so preferred under the old act.³ 

This change will be of little importance to the practitioner since it will be a relatively rare case where the decedent is survived by a great grandnephew or great grandniece whose ancestors of decedent's blood have all died. 

It will be of interest to the legal historian, however, as the latest chapter in the history of the doctrine of representation in this state. Wars for the Crown of England have been fought over the acceptance or rejection of this principle, and the doctrine has had a checkered career under various statutes in Pennsylvania since 1705.

It must be remembered that we are dealing here with the doctrine of representation as a rule of preference. We are not concerned here with the limits on the class of possible heirs; thus, under the present act, a grandchild of a deceased uncle can never share in the estate, even if he is the closest surviving relative, so that there is no question of whether he can represent the deceased uncle in determining a preference. On the other hand, we are likewise not dealing with the portion of the estate which the representative takes; this is governed by section 4 (1), where "taking by representation" is used in the sense of taking a stirpal share. The problem here is preliminary to that question; it is whether or not a person of more remote degree of consanguinity (e. g., great grandnephew) can share with or exclude a person of nearer degree (e. g., first cousin) because the former represents and enjoys the preference of a deceased ancestor.5

Unlimited representation among issue of the decedent has always been permitted, but except for an interval between 1795 and 1833, representation among collaterals has been restricted, to a greater or lesser extent, until the present act. Section 8 of the Act of 1833, P. L. 315, provided that there should be "no representation admitted amongst collaterals after brothers' and sisters' children." This was liberalized by section 2 of the act of 1855, P. L. 368, to permit representation by grandchildren of brothers and.sisters and children of uncles and aunts. This scheme was incorporated into the act of 1917 which in section 11 provided that there should "be no representation admitted among collaterals after the grandchildren of brothers and sisters and the children of uncles and aunts." The provisions did not mean that more remote collaterals could never be heirs under those acts, but simply that they had no preference as representatives of their ancestors. Under the present act, remote representation of deceased uncles and aunts is no longer a problem, because, as we have seen, all descendants after children of uncles and aunts are excluded entirely from the class of possible heirs. The former limitation on representation of brothers and sisters, however, has now been eliminated. 

¶ 6. Priorities Among Persons Described in the Same Clause 

Subject to the rule that a descendent will never share with his living ancestor of decedent's blood, there is no priority among persons of different degrees described in any one clause of section 3, and the estate will pass to all of them-though possibly in unequal shares under section 4 (1). 

6. Among issue of grandparents, this limitation on representation in § 11 of the act of 1917 did not apply to cases under § 12 of that act where grandparents on one side survived. There was no very satisfactory reason for this distinction.

84(1) 2 fn 3) and act of 1887, P. L. 261 (infra, this section ¶7) concern aspects of representation other than that considered here. 162

The first part of this rule-that a living ancestor will always exclude his own issue—is axiomatic to the law of descent, and is also clear from the wording of the act. The only places where the question could arise is under clauses (1) and (3) where descendants take without limitation.

For example, it might be asked whether the child of decedent's living child can share under clause (1). The answer is plainly no, because of the meaning of the word "issue" (as defined in Mayhew's Estate, 307 Pa. 84 (1932)) and because of section 4 (1) of the act which is concerned primarily with the method of sharing, but which incidentally amplifies the meaning of section 3 in this respect. 

The second part of the rule—that all persons mentioned in any one clause share the estate-arises primarily from the absence of any provision in the present act to the contrary, although section 4 (1) is also helpful on this point. 

This is merely another aspect of the doctrine of representation already discussed. Thus, contrary to the prior law, not only will a great grandnephew take in preference to a cousin, as pointed out above, but he can also share with a surviving brother, nephew or grandnephew of the decedent so long as none of those persons is the great grandnephew's own ancestor."

The priority of the first surviving generation of a class of heirs entitled to take is therefore of a qualified nature. 

A member of the oldest generation will exclude his own descendants but will not exclude descendants of his brothers and sisters. On Chart III (supra ¶ 2) this type of qualified priority is represented by the letters "A," "B," "C," etc., in order to distinguish it from the absolute priority between different lines of relatives indicated by the numbers "1," "2," and "3." ¶ 7. Grandparents

Clause (4) of the present section should clarify the law relating to the share to be taken by grandparents. Prior 

7. For examples of contrary holdings under the old law, see Kingston's Est., 28 W. N. C. 284 (O. C. Phila. 1891); and Ebling's Est., 8 D. & C. 319 (O. C.

to 1887, the intestate law made no specific reference to grandparents who took if at all under the general provision for "next-of-kin." As a result it was held in McDowell v. 

Addams, 45 Pa. 430 (1863), that a single surviving grandparent took the whole estate to the exclusion of descendants of deceased grandparents on the other side of the family. 

And in Fister's Estate, 2 Woodward 323 (0. C. Berks, 1871), it was held that three surviving grandparents each took a third of the estate. McDowell v. Addams was corrected by the act of 1887, P. L. 261, which provided that issue of a deceased grandparent could represent the ancestor in cases where at least one grandparent was living. 

The substance of the act of 1887 was incorporated into the act of 1917 as section 12, and in effect remains law today under clause (4) of the present section (except as limited by the fact that descendants of first cousins can no longer share).

Until the present act was passed, however, the law remained ambiguous, and among other things the situation in Fister's Estate was not specifically covered. This remaining uncertainty is eliminated by the present section. It now seems clear that if the decedent is survived by one paternal grandparent and two maternal grandparents, the former will take a half and the other half will pass to the maternal grandparents (who will take by the entireties under section 4 (6)). 

18. Relatives by Affinity

It is perhaps unnecessary to emphasize that relatives by affinity cannot share under this subsection. In common parlance the wife of one's uncle is sometimes referred to as an "aunt," but it is generally realized that this is not accurate; she is no more an aunt than one's sister-in-law is a sister. It has been law since time immemorial that except for the decedent's spouse and except as specially provided by the statute in the case of an adopted child (see section 8. Section 10 of the act of 1917 mentioned "grandparents" but did not indicate how they should share. See Conger, Problems of Inheritance by and through Grandparents, 104 Phila. 8), no person can become entitled by intestate succession other than those of decedent's blood." There is nothing in the present section which affects this rule. ¶ 9. Forfeiture Unworthy Heirs

The only ground for forfeiture by persons other than the surviving spouse under the present act is "unlawful killing” of the decedent under section 6 (c). Hence, other types of misconduct on the part of the decedent's blood or adopted relatives will have no effect on the law of inheritance. "It is the act of the law which casts the descent of estates, and that is not regulated or controlled by the acts, the follies, the frauds, or the crimes of any individual per- ,, 10 sons. 

10. Proof of Kinship

Proof of kinship will be somewhat simpler than in the past in view of the new limitations on the class of possible heirs, although problems of this sort will no doubt continue to arise, particularly where it becomes necessary to trace the descent of a vested future interest through the estates of persons long since deceased. The burden of course is on the claimant. Recent cases dealing with the subject are 

Link's Estate (No. 1), 319 Pa. 513 (1935), and District of Columbia's Appeal (Fink's Estate), 343 Pa. 65 (1941). 

Other cases will be found in Hunter's Orphans' Court Commonplace Book (1939), under the heading "Kinship" and in Vale's Digest under section 71 (4) et seq. of "Descent and Distribution." Proof of legitimacy raises special problems which are discussed under section 7. Attention is also called to the seven years' limitation in section 13, although as there pointed out that section will seldom become operative.

P. S. § 630 et seq. should be consulted.

The failure of a claimant to carry the burden of proving kinship and survivorship will ordinarily inure to the benefit of the other parties in interest. In the case of a missing relative, however, the failure of the absentee to appear and carry his burden will be of little significance unless he has had actual notice of his possible interest. The administrator has a duty to locate and notify the parties and cannot rely on the advertising of his letters for this purpose. If (as in Campbell v. Reed, 24 Pa. 498 (1855), or 

McFarlin's Estate, 267 Pa. 510 (1920)) he distributes voluntarily, he runs the risk of surcharge. Heirs are treated more kindly than creditors in this regard. Likewise, if distribution by decree is sought, the court will be hesitant to award the fund to those apparently entitled when there is reason to suspect the existence of a missing heir. The tendency will be rather to suspend distribution until the facts can be developed. See, for example, Feodor's Estate, 53 D. & C. 95 (O. C. Phila., 1945), and the alternative procedures suggested in Fiduciary Review, Nov., 1945, p. 4.

§4. RULES OF DESCENT 

(1) Taking in Different Degrees. 

The shares descending under this act to the issue of the decedent, to the issue of his parents or grandparents or to his uncles or aunts or to their children, shall descend to them as follows: The part of the estate descending to any such persons shall be divided into as many equal shares as there shall be persons in the nearest degree of consanguinity to the decedent living and taking shares therein and persons in that degree who have died before the decedent and have left issue to survive him who takes shares therein. One equal share shall descend to each such living person in the nearest degree and one equal share shall descend by representation to the issue of each such deceased person, except that no issue of a child of an uncle or aunt of the decedent shall be entitled to any share of the estate. 

COMMISSIONERS' COMMENT- 

The plan of combining the rules of descent in a separate section is new. The 1917 act includes rules of descent in separate sections and in some instances as parts of other sections. Section 4 now presents these rules in a convenient form. [clause (1)] This appears as the first rule of descent to eliminate any question concerning the manner in which the shares shall be divided. The 1917 act refers to "representation" and to rules of representation in numerous places, including 7 (d) 3 (descendants of intestate), 9(d) (descendants of brothers and sisters), 11 (general rule of limitation of representation), 12(d) (issue of grandparents) and 19 (persons in the same degree of consanguinity). Much of the cumbersome language of the places referred to is now avoided by the provisions of section 3 together with this clause (1) of section 4. 

Definition of the words "by representation" is not needed because they are a term of art well known to lawyers and about which there can be no dispute except as to the top level at which the stirpital distribution starts. See 2 Blackstone 217. The definition given here covers that question.

¶ 2. General Rule and History 

The present act continues the basic rule of the prior law that those of the nearest degree of consanguinity to the decedent among the survivors share equally or per capita, while those in more remote degrees share per stirpes as representatives of their deceased ancestor in the same degree as the nearest survivor. 

In this, Pennsylvania departs from the common law of succession to real estate and adopts for all purposes the scheme used for sharing among collateral under the original English Statute of Distribution. The idea is apparently of continental origin 2 and can be rationalized on the ground that the average person is inclined to think of his grandchildren, for example, in terms of family units only as long as at least one of his children survives; after the last child dies, the father is supposedly more inclined to regard his grandchildren as a single class so that he would want them to share his estate equally. The rule is cumbersome to apply and often brings about results offensive to the logical mind. It seems odd, for example, that. the shares of grandchildren and great grandchildren should vary so much between the cases illustrated in Charts IV and V when the only difference is that the first child of decedent predeceased the intestate in the first case and survived in the second. The results seem even more arbitrary when the rule is applied to collaterals, as illustrated in Charts VI and VII (infra ¶4). Be that as it may, this system of distribution is of ancient origin and has been used as to both real and personal property in Pennsylvania at least since 1833.

13. Sharing Among Descendants 

The simplest application of this rule is among decedent's issue. Chart IV illustrates a hypothetical case where decedent is survived by three grandchildren and three great grandchildren. Since no child survived, the three grandchildren take per capita and each takes a fifth even though one grandchild was the child of one of decedent's children and the other two grandchildren were children of another of decedent's children. Each great grandchild, on the other hand, takes his stirpal share of the onefifth which would have gone to his deceased parent. Two things should be emphasized concerning the shares taken by great grandchildren in this case. First, it will be noted that they do not share per capita, although they are all three of the same degree, because they are not of the nearest degree among the survivors. This result is clearer from the wording of the present section than it was under prior law. Section 19 of the act of 1917 which was based on section 14 of the act of 1833 would, if read literally, seem to provide for per capita sharing by all those of like degree, but this has apparently never been the law. Even under the act of 1833, the rule was stated in Clement's Estate, 160 Pa. 391, 398 (1894) as follows:

When there are descendants in different degrees, those in the class nearest to the intestate take (per capita) in their own right and the remoter ones take by representation from deceased members of the same class as the nearest survivors." In that case the distribution was similar to that indicated by Chart IV: four surviving grandchildren took per capita (1/11 each) and thirteen great grandchildren took by representation the shares which would have gone to seven deceased grandchildren. 66 The second point to notice about the shares taken by great grandchildren in Chart IV is that they share by representation of the deceased grandchildren (since grandchildren were the nearest survivors) and not by representation of deceased children (since no child survived). This result is also clear from the wording of 4 (1) and from Clement's Estate. Hence, it is not exact to say that the more remote degrees share per stirpes from the decedent. 207

§(1) 

INTESTATE ACT 

14 More precisely speaking, each member of the more remote degree takes a stirpal share of what would have been taken by his deceased ancestor of the same degree as the nearest survivor.

Chart IV should be compared with Chart V in this respect. In the latter case, a child survived so that the sharing was per stirpes all the way through. In that case, therefore, two of the three great grandchildren took 1/18 (or 2 of 1/3 of 1/3) and the third great grandchild took 1/3 as the sole representative of his line. In Chart IV, on the other hand, the stirpal sharing begins with grandchildren so that the shares of the great grandchildren do not reflect the different sizes of the children's families but only the different sizes of the grandchildren's families. The shares, therefore, are 1/10, 1/10, and 1/5 respectively. ¶ 4. Sharing Among Collaterals-In General 

Subject to the qualification discussed under the next heading (where sharing between grandparents and collaterals is discussed) it seems clear under both the earlier cases and the wording of the present section that the rule of sharing operates in the same manner among collaterals as it does among the decedent's lineal descendants. Hence, if a brother or sister survives, the sharing is stirpal from the parent throughout. If no brothers or sisters survive, nephews and nieces will take per capita and grandnephews and grandnieces by representation of deceased nephews and nieces. And so on down the line-the nearest survivors always sharing equally and the more remote ones taking by representation.

The same rule applies among issue of grandparents, although here we are concerned only with uncles, aunts and first cousins, since all more remote descendants of grandparents are excluded from the class of possible heirs by section 3. The simplest case is Brooke's Estate, 84 Pa. 

Super. 415 (1925), where the only child of a deceased aunt had to share per capita with six children of a deceased

Does this mean that the maternal cousins must take per stirpes as in the case where the paternal uncle survived (Chart VII)? The answer would seem to be No. Section 

4 (1) is not concerned with who is in the nearest degree of all decedent's relatives; rather it prescribes per capita sharing among those of the nearest degree within the class to which the section applies. Where the paternal grandparent survives, therefore, the estate not going to the spouse is split into halves, and the half passing to the issue of the maternal grandparent is considered as a separate unit under section 4 (1). Hence, the cousins, being in the nearest degree within this separate unit, take per capita." 

This result would seem to follow from a careful reading of section 4 (1). The opening words of the section enumerate the classes to which the section applies. One of these classes is the "issue of . . . grandparents." The section then continues: "The part of the estate descending to any such person [i. e., the issue of grandparents] shall be divided into as many equal shares as there shall be persons in the nearest degree of consanguinity to the decedent living and taking shares therein [i. e., taking shares in the part of the estate descending to the issue of grandparents]." The key word is "therein" which refers back to "the part of the estate descending to any such persons," while "such persons" refers back to "issue of grandparents" since that is the only class of persons mentioned in the opening words to which the section could apply in this case. It follows, therefore, that the maternal cousins in Chart VIII are the persons in the nearest degree within the meaning of section 4 (1), and that they therefore take per capita shares in the half passing down the 7. Recapitulation Considered together, the results indicated by Charts VI, VII, and VIII seem quite arbitrary. 17. Meaning of "Degree of Consanguinity"

The civil law and the common law differed in the manner in which degrees of consanguinity were calculated among collaterals. The civil law followed the logical scheme of counting upward to the common ancestor and downward to the relative, counting a degree for each person both ascending and descending. This method is represented by the Roman numerals on Chart IX, and would seem to be in harmony with the average person's concept of the distance between relatives. Under the so-called "common law" method, lineal degrees were counted in the same way, but collateral degrees were computed in an entirely different manner. As described by Blackstone," "we begin at the common ancestor, and reckon downwards: and in whatsoever degree the two persons, or the most remote of them, is distant from the common ancestor, that is the degree in which they are related to each other." This method is represented by the Arabic numbers on Chart IX. 

It will be noticed that under this system, an uncle and a cousin of the decedent are both of the second degree. One of the curious things about the common law system is that it was only used in connection with the descent of real 

8. See Bouvier's Law Dictionary, "Consanguinity." 

9. Commentaries, vol. 2, p. 206. 215

(1) 

INTESTATE ACT 

17 

estate, and in that field of the law (as Blackstone himself points out 10) it made no difference whether the common or civil law method were used, because of the unqualified acceptance of the doctrine of representation in the law of descent. It is even doubtful that the "common law' method is appropriately named, because the English ecclasiastical law (which has been described as "part of the general law of England-and of the common law" ¹¹) adopted the so-called civil law method in computing degrees for the administration of a decedent's personal property even before the Statute of Distribution.12 In other words, in the only cases where it made any difference, the nonstatutory law of England counted degrees according to the so-called civil law method. 

It will be seen immediately that in referring to "degree of consanguinity" in section 4 (1) the Legislature could not possibly have been referring to what is called the "common law" method of computing degrees. In the first place, such a construction would lead to confusion in applying the section to a case involving sharing among uncles and first cousins, a result the Legislature could scarcely have intended. In the second place, for the reasons stated above, it is probably inaccurate to call this method the "common law" method even with respect to the law of descent, and it certainly was never the law with respect to the distribution of personalty. Thirdly, the civil law method was always used in determining remote heirs under the prior acts in this state.13 True, the prior acts referred to "next of kin" which clearly indicated that the civil law of kinship was intended, but the fact remains that the Pennsylvania authorities without exception have computed degrees according to the civil law system. 

Any ambiguity of the term "degree of consanguinity," therefore, is more apparent than real. It seems beyond question that such degrees are to be calculated by the logical and widely understood method of the civil law, as indicated by the Roman numerals on Chart IX.

Discussion The general rule is that persons entitled under the intestate act are determined at the moment of decedent's death; this has already been discussed in connection with section 1, under ¶ 6—"When Heirs Are Determined." The present section sets forth the one exception to that rule. 

This provision has been in our intestate law at least since 1794 and the wording has been substantially the same since 1833. It is based on the ancient civil law which was followed in England with respect to personal property, and is analogous to the similar rule in the law of wills.¹

Old Law

Discussion This subsection is a paraphrase of section 13 of the Act of 1917 which eliminated from our law the rule relating to the blood of the first purchaser in the descent of real estate. Blackstone succinctly explains the common law in this respect in his fifth canon of descent as follows: "

On failure of lineal descendants, or issue, of the person last seised, the inheritance shall descend to his collateral relations being of the blood of the first purchaser. . . . Thus if Geoffrey Stiles purchases land, and it descends to John Stiles, his son, and John dies seised thereof, without issue; whoever succeeds to this inheritance must be of the blood of Geoffrey, the first purchaser of this family."1 "'1 It would 

1. 2 Commentaries 220. 

351

§(4) 

INTESTATE ACT 

follow, therefore, that all of John's maternal collateralssuch as his maternal uncles, aunts, and cousins—would be excluded. It will likewise be noted that if John has a half brother who is not the son of John's father, the half brother would also be excluded under this canon-even in the absence of canon six, discussed above under section 4 (2). 

The common law rule was followed in Pennsylvania and was incorporated into our statutory law by section 9 of the act of 1833, P. L. 315, so that it was necessary to trace the blood of the first purchaser with respect to the descent of land in this state until 1917 when the rule was abolished. 

Indeed, the act of 1833 not only adopted the common law rule but extended it in an important aspect. By the common law, as Blackstone emphasized, "the first purchaser, perquisitor, is he who first acquired the estate to his family, whether same was transferred to him by sale or by gift, or by any other method, except only that of descent."2 

Thus, if John Stiles, in Blackstone's example, had been devised the land by his father, John himself would be the first purchaser and all his collaterals would inherit at common law. The drafters of the 1833 act apparently regarded this distinction as illogical and provided that "no person who is not of the blood of the ancestors or other relations from whom any real estate descended, or by whom it was given or devised to the intestate, shall in any cases before mentioned, take any estate of inheritance therein The extent to which this statute modified the common law rule is illustrated by Reed v. Geddes, 287 Pa. 274 (1926), where it became necessary to apply the act of 1833 to an intestacy which had occurred in 1915. In that case the father deeded real estate to his wife without consideration; the wife died and the property passed by descent to the daughter; then the daughter died intestate survived by both paternal and maternal relatives, and it was necessary to determine whether her mother or her father was the "first purchaser." The court held that the deed to the wife did not break the line and that the father must be regarded as the first purchaser within the statutory rule. 99

(5) Quantity of Estate. 

Any person taking real or personal estate under this act shall take such interest as the decedent had therein. 

COMMISSIONERS' COMMENT This replaces section 18 of the 1917 

act, which reads: [see below] 

Old Law

Section 18. The real estate of such intestate shall be vested in the person or persons entitled thereto, under the provisions of this act, for such estate as the intestate had therein, and such person or persons shall be entitled to the personal estate absolutely. 

Intestate Act of 1917, P. L. 429.

There is no change from the act of 1917.

Discussion This unnecessary provision first made its appearance in the act of 1917. There is possibly a psychological if not a logical explanation for its existence. Prior to 1917 the only mention of the quantity of estates passing by intestacy was in the sections relating to the share of a surviving spouse, where there was some necessity to make a distinction. Under section 1 of the act of 1833, for example, the widow took a share of the real estate "for the term of her life" and a share of the personal estate "absolutely." In 1917 the share of the surviving spouse in a portion of the real estate was increased from a life estate to an absolute interest. The 

1917 Commission probably considered simply substituting the word "absolutely" for "for the term of her life" in the sections relating to the spouse's share, but then began worrying about whether this would be adequate. Would the implication arise that persons other than the spouse took something less than an absolute estate? Was "absolutely" the proper word anyway, if the decedent himself owned 401

(5) 

INTESTATE ACT 

only an estate pur auter vie or an estate subject to divestment? As a solution to these imaginary difficulties, all mention of the quantity of estate taken by the spouse or anyone else was omitted except in section 18, quoted above, which was to be a general provision covering all cases. 

Curiously enough, the 1917 Commission seems to have overlooked the possibility of a limited estate in personal property which might survive a decedent's death, but this oversight is corrected in the present act. 

The law would undoubtedly be exactly the same if this provision had been omitted in its entirety. As presently drafted, however, it is harmless surplusage and might be useful to emphasize the fact that the surviving spouse is not limited to a life interest in her share of the real estate. 402 [The next page is 451]

Discussion ¶ 1. Real Estate

The important part of section 19 of the act of 1917 has already been referred to in connection with section 4 (1) of the present act. Here we are concerned with the last few words of section 19 which provided that several heirs took real estate as tenants in common. For the most part 451

§(6) INTESTATE ACT 

T1 the courts have paid but little attention to this general provision which has been in the act since 1833.¹ Ordinarily, several persons sharing real estate would take as tenants in common anyway.2 Where the persons entitled are husband and wife, however, the provision in the earlier intestate acts about sharing as tenants in common was quite inappropriate, and it seems to have been the rule that parents or grandparents who were married to each other took the decedent's real estate as tenants by entireties in spite of this provision in the old acts. The present section is an improvement over the earleir statutes in that it expressly provides for this result. Even though the parents' or married grandparents' share is not the whole estate, they should nevertheless take their share by the entireties. Suppose, for example, that the owner of real estate dies intestate survived by one paternal grandparent and two maternal grandparents. It is clear from section 3 of the present act, that the paternal grandparent will take half and the maternal grandparents the other half (see § 3, ¶7). By the terms of the present section it is likewise clear that the maternal grandparents will take their undivided half as tenants by the entireties. 

There would seem to be no objection in general law to holding a fractional interest by the entireties in this manner.

12. Personal Estate

Prior to the present act there was no statutory provision concerning the tenancy of several persons entitled to the personal estate. In interpreting the present .provision on this subject it is important to bear in mind what was emphasized concerning the meaning of the word "descend" under § 1, ¶ 5. As there explained, the substantive provisions of the Intestate Act are concerned only with the beneficial interest passing to those entitled and have nothing to do with the law of administration which governs the location of the bare legal title before distribution. The present section, therefore, should have no effect on the current concept that legal title to or the right to control and sell personalty passes to the administrator. The personal "estate" referred to in this clause is the beneficial interest in the net estate, which vests immediately at the decedent's death.5

It is here provided that when the sharing of personal property is between others than husband and wife, those entitled take as tenants in common. Insofar as this has any meaning at all, it is merely a restatement of the well settled rule that the interest of each person will survive his death before distribution. At distribution, there will ordinarily be an automatic "partition" of any tenancy in common which might have existed before then. 

Where the personal estate is shared by parents or by grandparents who are husband and wife, it was settled by the old cases that they took as tenants by entireties, and this rule is continued by the express provision in the present section. One important result of this rule is that if an estate passes to parents, for example, and the father dies before distribution, the entire interest will vest in the mother by right of survivorship and it would be improper

INTESTATE ACT ¶ 1. Descent of Land by and From an Alien 

At common law, an alien could not take real estate by descent. There were also qualifications in the common law on the power of an alien to take real estate by purchase (including devise), but here the prohibition was not absolute. The alien would take a title which would be good during his lifetime against all the world except the state. The state could, however, by proper proceedings appropriate the property, and on the death of the alien intestate the purchased land passed to the state automatically.¹ Whether the alien could make a voluntary transfer of the purchased property inter vivos or by devise, and whether (assuming he could) the title of the transferee was defeasible by action of the state, was not entirely clear.2 

The prohibition against an alien's inheriting land was early removed by the act of 1791, which was the only statute governing descent until the present act. The same act also permitted him to take by devise. Since he could have taken a defeasible title by devise in the absence of statute it is fair to assume that the Legislature by the act of 1791 intended that the title so taken would be indefeasible during the alien's lifetime and inheritable at his death. As to lands acquired by purchase other than devise, the common law was modified by various acts (only some of which have been repealed) giving an alien the right to "purchase" and to "hold" real property subject to various qualifications. The most recent enactment is the act of 1861, P. L. 

274, 68 P. S. § 32, which provides simply that an alien "may purchase and hold real estate in this state not exceeding in quantity five thousand acres, nor in net annual income twenty thousand dollars." Again it may be assumed that the title so acquired is indefeasible and inheritable. 1. For the common law generally as to descent of land to and from an alien, see 3 C. J. S. 546 et seq.; Atkinson, Wills (1937) §§ 15 and 32. See also Reese v. Waters, 4 W. & S. 145 (1842) (overruled by Cooke v. Doron, 215 Pa. 393 (1906), infra note 5), and the Rubeck and Bradley cases considered infra in the text. 

2. See 3 C. J. S. 582 and 586; In re Palmer Co., 183 Fed. 902 (M. D. Pa. 

1911) (indicating that the transferee takes a defeasible estate only). 

3. 68 P. S. § 25 et seq. The earlier acts are reviewed in Rubeck v. Gardner, 7 Watts 455, 456 (1838). 502

¶ 

INTESTATE ACT § 4 (7) 

The net result of the acts of 1791 and 1861 would seem to be that so long as the alien held in the aggregate less land than the generous maximum set forth in the act of 1861, he could be treated as a citizen so far as descent of real property to or from him is concerned; he could inherit indefeasible title from his ancestor and his heirs could inherit freely from him. See, for example, Bradley v. Comber, 19 Dist. 130 (C. P. Sullivan, 1908). If, on the other hand, the limitations of the act of 1861 were exceeded by either the ancestor or the heir, the law was by no means clear. 

In Rubeck v. Gardner, 7 Watts 455 (1838), an alien who had acquired land by deed, without conforming to the statute governing purchases then in effect, was held to own a defeasible title which would pass automatically to the Commonwealth on his death intestate; he had no title which could descend to anyone so that the act of 1791 was irrelevant. This case was properly distinguished in the 

Bradley case, but has never been overruled or even questioned. It was also uncertain how the act of 1861 would operate if the heir's limit was exceeded as a result of the inheritance.

Both the certainties and the uncertainties that existed under the act of 1791 will probably continue under the present section. The power of an alien to inherit an indefeasible title from a citizen (or from another alien who has clear title) should remain unchanged so long as the heir's limit under the act of 1861 is not exceeded. The omission of the provision that the alien inherits "in as full and ample manner as the citizens of this state may do," etc., should be no ground for arguing that the alien heir will take a defeasible estate only; the Legislature could scarcely have intended to take a step backward from what has been the law since 1791. On the other hand, it is doubtful whether the new reference to the alienage of the decedent in the present act will have any affect on the Rubeck decision if the limit of 5,000 acres or $20,000 income is exceeded. If the alien ancestor had an indefeasible title, there was nothing in the law to prevent such title passing to his heirs at his death even before the present act (as shown by the Bradley case); but where the decedent's title 503

§ (7) 

INTESTATE ACT 

12 is defective due to his having purchased more than the maximum allowed by the act of 1861 (which remains law), it can still be argued that there is nothing left to descend on his death intestate under the reasoning of the Rubeck case. The extent to which the Rubeck case would be followed today is an open question. Likewise open are innumerable questions which might arise if the limitations of the act of 1861 are exceeded in situations not covered by our cases. In view of the liberal limits allowed by that act, however, it is doubtful that such questions will arise often, if at all. In the great majority of cases, the alien can be treated as a citizen, because so long as the alien's holdings are within the statutory limits, there will be no obstacle to land descending from or to him. ¶ 2. Dower and Curtesy

It has been said that a surviving spouse in Pennsylvania takes the statutory equivalent to dower and curtesy by descent. Hence there would seem to be no additional problem with respect to an alien widow's share of lands conveyed by the deceased husband during his life without her consent under section 5 (a) of the present act.5 ¶ 3. (a) Widow.

¶ 1. General-Cross References 

This subsection continues one aspect of the makeshift arrangement in our law for the protection of the spouse. 

The distinctions drawn by the early common law between real estate and personalty and between the property rights of men and women have never been revised by any single comprehensive statute governing the respective rights of husband and wife in each other's property. Instead, outmoded rules have been corrected piecemeal, so that the subject is now covered by various sections in at least four principal statutes, to say nothing of other legislation affecting the subject incidentally.¹

The rights of the husband and wife in each other's personal estate are now governed primarily by section 2 of the present act (intestate share), section 8 of the Wills Act (taking against the will), section 11 of the Estates Act (share in property transferred inter vivos reserving power of appointment), and the act of 1945, P. L. 625, 48 P. S. § 31 (married women's power over her property). 

1. Consider, for example, the $500 widow's exemption under § 12 of the 

Fiduciaries Act of 1917, P. L. 447, 20 P. S. 471, although that provision is more in the nature of a debtor's exemption and has a different genesis from ordinary statutes regulating marital property rights. 602

¶ 2a 

INTESTATE ACT  

As to real estate, the situation is even more complicated. At common law all interests of the wife in her husband's land were embraced in the single concept of dower.2 

Dower was a life interest commencing at the husband's death in one-third of real estate of which he was seised at any time during coverture. Until the husband died it was a mere expectant interest but if the wife survived, she could claim her dower against (1) land which the husband devised to another by will, (2) land as to which the husband died intestate, and (3) land aliened by the husband during coverture without his wife's joinder. These three aspects of common law dower are now replaced by: (1) the statutory right to take against the husband's will, (2) the intestate share given the spouse by section 2 of this act, and (3) the interest given by the present subsection in land which the husband conveyed without joinder during his lifetime. The widow's power to take against the will is discussed under section 8 of the Wills Act. The present discussion will be confined to the modification of the other two aspects of dower. 

2. Land as to Which Husband Died Intestate a. General

The share given by section 2 of this act is the present substitute for dower in land owned by an intestate at his death. As to such land dower is abolished absolutely by the present subsection. The provision that the widow's share under the act "shall be in full satisfaction of her dower at common law" has been in the intestate law since 1794.3 As to real estate passing by intestacy, the provision is easily understood and has given but little trouble throughout the years. In effect the widow is now an heir to such real estate and descent to her is no longer governed by peculiar rules-except those required by the nature of the relationship and the size of her intestate share (such as provisions relating to forfeiture and the method of setting aside the $10,000 allowance). Thus, there is no question 

2. For references to general works on common law dower, see infra, note 10. 

3. Act of 1794, 3 Smith L. 143, § 13; Act of 1833, P. L. 315, § 15. 

4. See general discussion § 2 (¶1) supra. 603

2b 

INTESTATE ACT 

that she takes "subject to debts and charges," as provided in section 1, and hence has no interest in land sold for the payment of decedent's debts. In this and other respects, her interest is treated in the same manner as the interest of any other heir.Ⓡ 

b. Requirement of Seisin-Future Interests 

As noted in the discussion of section 1 (¶¶ 2c and 6b) of this act, there is no trace of the ancient doctrine of seisin in the law of descent in Pennsylvania, and the language of that section negatives any suggestion that it still exists as a condition to inheritance in this state. With dower eliminated and the widow in effect made an heir as to an intestate's real estate, it would seem to follow that she would be no more bound than any other heir by the requirement that the decedent be seised of the property owned at death. 

There was, it is true, an independent requirement of seisin in the law of dower, but since dower is abolished as to real property forming a part of the decedent's estate, this would seem irrelevant. For these reasons, it would seem that the last sentence of the present subsection is surplusage with regard to property forming part of the estate. 

¶ 3. Land Aliened Inter Vivos Without Wife's Joinder a. History

The statutory modification of dower in lands conveyed by the husband during coverture without his wife's joinder was new in 1917 and presents problems more difficult of solution. It was early held that the intestate acts of 1794 and 1833 abolished common law dower only with respect to lands which the husband owned at his death, and the surviving widow was permitted to assert her common law dower in real estate conveyed by the husband during his lifetime. Prior to 1917, therefore, the widow on the death of her husband was entitled to (1) her statutory intestate 

5. See Hay v. Meyers, 114 Pa. Super. 269, 273 (1934); but the land might be made subject to the widow's rights by the decree ordering the sale-see Ohio- 

Pa. Bank v. Blough, 119 Pa. Super. 34, 40 (1935). Note that even common law dower was subject to rights of creditors in Pennsylvania-see infra at note 11. 

6. See generally the discussion under § 1 of partial intestacy, negative disinheritance, gifts conditional upon renunciation, etc.

In section 3 of the intestate act of 1917, the provision concerning dower was expanded. The words "so far as relates to lands of which the husband died seised" were added to the sentence abolishing dower, in order to reinforce the conclusion already reached by the courts, and a new provision was inserted stating that the widow's "share in lands aliened by the husband in his lifetime without her joining in the conveyance shall be the same as her share in lands of which the husband died seised." In other words, the share of the widow in aliened lands was enlarged from a life estate in a third to a fractional share in the fee to correspond with the share she received in lands which the decedent owned at his death. This major change in the law was soon tested and it was held that the new provision did not apply to conveyances completed before the act became effective, regardless of when decedent died, but that it did apply to all conveyances after the effective date of the act, even though the marriage took place before that time." 

Section 3 of the act of 1917 is re-enacted with unimportant stylistic changes by the present section. The law therefore will remain the same as to all conveyances by a husband without his wife's joinder since December 31, 1917.

There are, however, many questions in this field of the law which remain unanswered. 

b. General Rule of Construction 

The application of this provision concerning aliened land is not as easy as it looks. As to real estate owned by the intestate at his death, the widow since 1794 has simply taken her share in the same manner as any other heir, and the old rules of dower can for the most part be forgotten. 

8. Merrick v. DuPont, 285 Pa. 368 (1926).

Hence, by enlarging the widow's share in such lands, nothing is 'simplified but new problems are created. 

The basic rule for construing the present provision is set forth in Bridgeford v. Groh (second appeal), 306 Pa. 

566, 575 (1932). In considering the effect of the new provision in the act of 1917, the court there applied the principle that "a statute should be so interpreted that it will accord, as nearly as may be, with the theretofore existing course of the common law," and said that the provision concerning aliened land "gives no evidence of any legislative intent to change the common law further than in the quantum of the interest given to the widow."

d. Open Questions (When and by Whom Dower May Be 

Claimed; Mining Property)

In many cases it will be difficult to predict to what extent the old authorities will be followed. Thus, prior to 

1917 it was apparently law that the widow could claim her common law dower in lands conveyed inter vivos without her joinder regardless of whether the husband died testate or intestate, and regardless of whether the widow elected to take under or against his will. The hardest case is where the husband dies testate and the widow elects to take under his will. In such a case she is not permitted to claim a share of real estate devised by the will to others.25 But if she is permitted to take both her gift under the will and also an intestate share in real estate conveyed inter vivos, her rights against the transferee (who might be an innocent purchaser for value) are greater than her rights against devisees. Nevertheless, it was held in Borland v. 

Nichols, 12 Pa. 38 (1849), that the widow could take both a devise under the will and her dower in land conveyed without her joinder. Presumably, that case is still law, although an argument to the contrary might be developed from the provision in the present section that the widow's share is the same "as her share in real estate of which the husband died seised." In other words, the fiction that the husband died seised of the aliened property might be used as a basis for arguing that the widow is put to an election and cannot take both under the will and against the conveyance.

Another moot question is whether the heirs or devisees of a widow who failed to claim her statutory dower during her lifetime can assert her rights in aliened real estate after her death. This question could not have arisen be- 

24. Clark v. Clark, 6 W. & S. 85, 87-8 (1843); Rudolph's Est., 128 Pa.

By way of analogy, it will be noted that the substitute for dower in devised property established by section 8 of the Wills Act is a personal right to take against the will and this cannot be exercised after the widow's death.26 On the other hand the substitute for dower in lands owned by a decedent at his death and not disposed of by will is an estate which vests immediately in the widow and survives her death regardless of whether she takes any affirmative action to claim it.27 The wording of the present section would seem to favor the latter analogy. The earlier cases held, however, that common law dower remained a mere expectancy even after the husband's death until proceedings were instituted and the dower set apart or “assigned" to the widow.28 This concept might be the basis for deciding that the widow's interest in aliened land under the present statute will not pass to her heirs or devisees if she dies before claiming it.

Other cases can be imagined where the increase of the widow's share from a life estate to a fee might render obsolete decisions dealing with common law dower. One example would be the case of mining property conveyed by the husband without the wife's joinder. Prior to 1917, this presented a problem of waste. If the mines were opened during the husband's lifetime, the widow's life interests in a third would include a third of the proceeds; if the mines were unopened, however, she could not open them.29 These cases will be of little help under the present law as the widow will take her fractional interest in the fee regardless of whether the mines were opened or not. The old cases will probably be followed, however, in denying to the widow any interest in proceeds of mines before the "assignment" of the dower is completed.30

INTESTATE ACT e. Property Subject to Dower 

At common law, inchoate dower attached only to real estate of which the husband was seised during coverture. 

It will first be noted that the present section is in accord with the common law in limiting the rights of the widow to real property. Hence the old cases determining what is real and what is personal property for purposes of dower will continue to be valuable.31 It also seems clear that the widow will have rights under this section only as to land owned by the husband during marriage. The wording of the present section is not as accurate as it might be on this point, but the inter vivos alienation must be "by the husband" as such-that is, during coverture. Transfers before marriage are sometimes attacked on the ground of fraud, but this raises a somewhat different problem discussed below (¶ 3k).

The principal question is what has become of the common law requirement of seisin.32 The main effect of this requirement under the law prior to 1917 was to exclude the widow from a dower interest in a future interest which did not come into enjoyment before the husband's death. 

As pointed out below (¶ 3h-"Future Interests") this result of the doctrine of seisin has been changed by the express provision of the last sentence of the present section. 

But there is no authority indicating to what extent, if any, the 1917 provision has affected the requirement of seisin in present interests owned by the husband during coverture. 

This question is made doubly difficult by the fact that the exact meaning of seisin in this regard was by no means clear at common law. On the one hand, it has been said that "the doctrine of seisin is little known here .; and with us seisin is, for many substantial purposes, the beneficial interest and right of ownership." (Reed v. Morri- 31. See Kelley v. Mahan, 2 Yeates 515 (1799) (equitable title arising from possession and improvements); Shoemaker v. Walker, 2 S. & R. 554 (1816) (trust estate); Shupe v. Rainey, 255 Pa. 432, 438 (1917) (partnership property --but note that the land in that case was originally owned by the husband individually); see, generally, Tiffany, Real Property (3d ed. 1939) § 492 et seq. 

Note that the question as to whether the interest was real or personal property often overlaps the question of whether the husband had the necessary seisin see infra in the text at notes 33 and 34. 

32. Compare discussion of seisin in the law of descent under § 1 ( 2c) of this act. 611

INTESTATE ACT 

¶ 3e son, 12 S. & R. 18, 21 (1824)). Consistent with this view are the decisions indicating that dower attached to an equitable interest in real estate held in trust, although technical seisin is in the trustee.33 On the other hand, there are decisions indicating that dower does not attach to the equitable interest of a vendee under a contract of sale (at least before the purchase money is paid) because the husband is not seised.34 Conversely, however, where the husband is the legal owner at the time of the marriage, but the land is subject to an antenuptial contract of sale or option agreement, the wife is also excluded. See Detwiler v. 

Capone, 357 Pa. 495 (1947). If a complete survey were made of the Pennsylvania cases on this topic, the conclusion would probably be reached that even before 1917 there was little left of the technical requirement of seisin (except with regard to future interests), and that dower would attach to any present interest in real estate, legal or equitable, which the husband actually owned beneficially during coverture, although the fictions of equity would not be strained to bring about unrealistic results where the husband's interest was unsubstantial. Assuming that this was the effect of the older cases, there is nothing in the provision of the 1917 or the present act to change this sensible, if somewhat indefinite, rule.

It will be noted, however, that the length of time title is held by the husband before conveying it continues to be irrelevant. Thus in Bridgeford v. Groh (second appeal), 306 Pa. 566 (1932), the widow was permitted to claim her statutory dower even though the husband had held title "only for an instant" before conveying to another. Judge (now Justice) Stern in the court below (13 D. & C. 704, 706) illustrated the point "by a quaint case in Wales, where a father and a son were hanged simultaneously, but the son was supposed to have survived the father by appearing to struggle longer, and, accordingly, it was held that he thereby became seised of an estate in fee by survivorship, in consequence of which seisin his widow obtained a verdict for her dower."
