f. Size of the Widow's Share—the $10,000 Allowance 

The share of the widow in real estate aliened without her consent is said to be the same as in land "of which the decedent died seised." In other words, it will be the full intestate share as provided by section 2. Where there are issue, this share will be either one-third 35 or onehalf 36 under section 2 (1) or 2 (2), and where there are no close relatives other than the spouse, it would seem clear that the spouse can claim the whole property from the transferee under section 2 (4). There is but little logic in making the rights of the transferee depend on whether decedent is survived by close relatives other than the spouse, but this result seems unavoidable as the present section is worded.

A real difficulty is presented, however, by the provision for the $10,000 allowance in clause (3) of section 2. No case since 1917 has been found where this problem was presented to the court. In the analogous situation where the spouse takes against the will, no allowance is now provided by section 8 of the Wills Act, but as explained under that section (and under § 2, ¶ 5a, of the present act), prior to 1917 the electing spouse could take the allowance. The problem with respect to land conveyed inter vivos under the present section, however, is a little different. Suppose the husband dies testate survived by no issue and leaves the bulk of his estate to his widow. Can she claim one-half plus $10,000 from real estate conveyed by him during his lifetime without her joinder, as well as the gifts under the will? 37 Or if he dies intestate, will the widow be permitted under section 10 of this act to take her entire allowance from the land which he conveyed without her joinder?

g. Conflict With Section 11 of Estates Act 

The present section might conflict with the Estates Act in cases where the husband has conveyed without his wife's joinder a life estate in his real estate reserving to himself a power to appoint the remainder. Section 11 of the Estates 

Act provides that the surviving spouse in such cases may treat "as testamentary" the transfer of any estate not vested in enjoyment before the husband's death; in other words she may elect to take against an inter vivos transfer of this nature in the same manner as she is permitted to take against the decedent's will under section 8 of the Wills Act. As already pointed out, however, the share of the spouse taking against the will is considerably smaller in many cases than her full intestate share allowed by the present section in land conveyed without joinder. Suppose, for example, A, during coverture, conveys Blackacre in trust to pay the income to his sister B for life with remainder to such person as he might by will appoint. 

Later A dies, survived by both his sister B and his wife X. 

By his will appoints the remainder in Blackacre to his nephew C, and leaves most of the rest of his property to his wife X. If X claims her statutory dower under the present section, she can probably take her full intestate share

Plainly it would be to her advantage to elect the former alternative and claim under the present section, and this would seem to be her proper remedy. The transferee of Blackacre and the other heirs at law might argue that section 11 of the Estates Act supersedes the present section in this situation, but it is doubtful that the drafters of that act intended to interfere with the law under the present section of the Intestate Act. 

h. Future Interests 

Not to be confused with the case just discussed where the husband owned Blackacre in fee and conveyed to others future estates in it, is the case where the husband never owned Blackacre outright but has been given a future interest in the property by the will or deed of another and dies before his estate comes into enjoyment. This case is governed by the last sentence of the present section which is a revision of a similar provision first added in 1917. 

This provision was inserted to change the common law relating to dower in property which was not seised by the husband during his lifetime. In the words of Simes, "At common law seisin was a pre-requisite for dower and curtesy. Therefore, if a future interest in land followed a freehold possessory estate, there could be neither dower nor curtesy, for the possessory owner was seised and not the owner of the future interest." 40 As to future interests owned by the decedent at his death, the last sentence of the present subsection is probably surplusage, since common law dower in such property is abolished by the previous sentence, and the widow in her capacity of heir would take a share in the future estate anyway. 41 As to future

i. Liability of Husband's Estate on Warranty in Deed 

Where the husband has given a general warranty deed to the purchaser the widow will do well to consider whether a recovery of her statutory dower in the land conveyed will be profitable to herself and her family. It has long been the law that the transferee may not set-off or counterclaim for breach of the husband's warranty in the widow's action of dower.43 However, it would seem that the husband's estate would be liable in a separate suit by the purchaser for whatever damage the breach of warranty caused. This will make little difference to the widow if the estate is insolvent or of less value than her share in the deeded land, but other cases can be imagined where the ultimate effect of claiming dower in aliened lands will be robbing the left hand to pay the right. j. Hence, her misconduct at the time of death and not at the time of the conveyance will be controlling.44 k. Transfers in Fraud of Dower (Antenuptial and Postnuptial)

We have seen above (1) that dower attaches only to land owned by the husband during the marriage, and (2) that in Pennsylvania the wife's interest is subordinate to the husband's creditor. It follows that a husband's conveyance before marriage or his mortgage after marriage is prima facie effective to transfer or encumber the whole title without the wife's joinder. In certain circumstances, however, equity will step in to protect the wife from the normal legal consequences of such transactions. 

Antenuptial conveyances have often been used by prospective husbands for the purpose of barring dower. 

Formerly a secret conveyance on the eve of marriage was "presumed" to be fraudulent and equity would permit the wife to assert her dower interest therein to the same extent as she could have if the husband had conveyed during coverture. These early cases were overruled, however, in 

Kirk v. Kirk, 340 Pa. 203 (1940), where the court laid down the following rule: "Either spouse may challenge, as fraudulent, a conveyance of real estate or a gift of personal property made during a treaty of marriage, but mere proof of the conveyance or gift, without the knowledge of the other party, does not constitute a prima facie case of fraudulent transfer. In addition, it is necessary for the party alleging it to prove the fraud, or 'actual fraud,' to use an expression common in the decisions. Mere conjecture or suspicion does not take the place of evidence." Thus, while the wife is not precluded from attacking such conveyances and claiming her statutory dower in the property after the husband's death, the rule of presumed fraud is

13k discarded and she must prove something more than the secret conveyance. Exactly what the widow must prove to show actual fraud in an antenuptial conveyance remains an open question, but apparently the conveyance must be secret, without consideration, not in satisfaction of any moral obligation, and "with the intention of depriving her of rights which, expressly or by implication, he induced her to believe she would receive by marrying him.'' 45

The common law relating to antenuptial conveyances will be affected by section 11 of the Estates Act wherever the husband retains a power of appointment or revocation. In that limited class of cases, it would seem that the widow will be relieved of the burden of proving actual fraud. See discussion of that section on this point. 

After the marriage, the husband can no longer bar dower by a conveyance, but the device of creating liens against the property has been used in attempts to accomplish the same result. If the husband gives a mortgage or confesses a judgment in a bona fide loan transaction, it cannot be questioned by the non-joining wife, but if he does so voluntarily for the sole purpose of barring his wife from a share in the property after his death, equity will view the transaction as the sham that it is. A clear case of this sort was presented in Cancilla v. Bondy, 353 Pa. 249 (1945). 

There the husband without receiving consideration gave to his grandson bonds and mortgages payable at his death and bearing interest only after that time. One of the mortgages even provided that if the mortgagor conveyed the property the bond and mortgage would become "absolutely void." The court had little trouble in finding that the transaction was ineffective to bar the wife's dower even as to a subsequent purchaser of the mortgage, although the wife lost her opportunity to attack its validity by her failure to raise a defense at the foreclosure proceedings after her 45. 340 Pa. at 208. McHale, 354 Pa. 177 (1946), where a man's antenuptial conveyance to himself and others as joint tenants with rights of survivorship was upheld; there the conveyance was supported by consideration. For an analysis of the Kirk decision and the earlier cases see Bregy and Wilkinson, "Antenuptial Transfers as Frauds on Marital Rights in Pennsylvania," 90 U. of Pa.

The court stated the rule as follows (at 252): " a wife has an inchoate interest in her husband's real property; therefore, while he may mortgage such property if the transaction is bona fide and for a consideration, he cannot deprive his wife of her dower rights, without her consent, by creating a voluntary mortgage or judgment, since the giving of such a mortgage or judgment would be equivalent to a pro tanto conveyance of the real estate in fraud of her dower rights." How much more must be proved by the wife than the mere fact of a voluntary creation of a lien against the property is not entirely clear from the cases, but it would seem that the burden here is somewhat lighter than in the case of an antenuptial conveyance.

The Cancilla opinion will also be of value in determining the rights of bona fide purchasers in cases of fraudulent transfers 46 and in determining when and how such transactions should be attacked by the injured wife.47

11. Background

The amendment of 1963 brings about such a basic change in the law respecting inter vivos conveyances by a married woman that the original discussion of this section of the act of 1947 will be almost entirely obsolete with respect to land conveyed inter vivos by married women who die on or after July 25, 1963. The original text has therefore been relegated to the "Repealed Sections" portion of this volume.

The history of curtesy in Pennsylvania is set forth in the original text and is traced in more detail in Commissioners of Rouse Estate v. Poor District, 169 Pa. 116 (1895), and Scaife v. McKee, 298 Pa. 33 (1929). Useful commentaries on the general law of a husband's marital estates, published since the original text was prepared, are Haskins, American Law of Property (1952) § 5.50 et seq., and Powell, 

Real Property (1950) ¶ 214 et seq.

For present purposes, it is sufficient to recall that sections 3 and 4 of the Intestate Act of 1917, P. L. 429, made two basic changes in the Pennsylvania law of marital rights in real estate: (a) It confirmed the earlier abolition of dower as to all property owned by a husband at his death (the wife's interests in such property being adequately protected by her intestate share and her right to take against the will) but retained dower in modified form as to property conveyed by the husband during his life without his wife's joinder. (b) Curtesy, on the other hand, was abolished altogether, because it was felt that, as to property owned at the wife's death, the husband's interest was protected by his intestate share and right to take against her will and, as to her inter vivos conveyances, his interest was protected by her absolute disability to convey her property without her husband's joinder under the Married Women's 

Property Act of 1893, P. L. 344. 

652

INTESTATE ACT 

 These two sections of the 1917 act were re-enacted as sections 5(a) and 5(b) of the Intestate Act of 1947. From 

1917 until recently, therefore, the wife was protected from her husband's inter vivos conveyances through her statutory dower interest in the land, while the husband had no interest in his wife's land and was protected from her inter vivos conveyances only by her inability to convey any title. 

So matters stood until several heavy-handed amendments to the Married Women's Property Act, beginning with the act of 1945 and culminating with the act of 1957. 

These amendments were drafted by persons with inadequate knowledge of the curious history of marital rights in Pennsylvania and the confusion they caused was almost unbelievable. The act of 1945, P. L. 625 (which provided that a married woman could convey real estate without joinder but could not make a deed) is discussed under ¶ 3b of unamended § 5(b) under "Repealed Sections". The act was again amended by the acts of 1947, P. L. 60 and P. L. 352, but without curing the ambiguity. Nevertheless, it was held in Bosses v. Mahlasky, 365 Pa. 184, 186 (1950), that the provisions in these amendments were ineffective to give a married woman the power to pass title without her husband's joinder. The act of 1951, P. L. 1416, further amended the act to confirm this result and returned matters to the status quo so far as the wife's conveyances were concerned. (The earlier amendments had also given a wife the power to mortgage to the same extent as a husband and this was preserved by the 1951 act. However, since a husband can mortgage free of his wife's dower in Pennsylvania, that portion of the amendment did not raise any problems.) 

Then came the act of 1957, P. L. 969, 48 P. S. § 32.1, when the confusion was revived and compounded by the insertion of a provision that a married woman can convey her real estate "... in the same manner and to the same extent as a married man." No one knew what this meant. 

As noted in the August 1957 issue of the Fiduciary Review, the act pointedly avoided giving married women the same right to convey as "an unmarried person" (the language which was used with respect to contracts in the Married -653

(b) 12 

INTESTATE ACT 

Women's Property Act of 1893), so it seems unlikely that the legislature intended to give married women the unfettered right to convey free of any interest in the husband. 

It is reasonably obvious that the drafters had some vague idea of equalizing the sexes but failed to realize that curtesy had been abolished. The effect of the 1957 act was considered in Campbell v. Shick, 35 D. & C. 2d 772, 14 Fid.

Rep. 304 and 15 Fid. Rep. 185 (C. P. Lyc. 1965) which held that the act had resurrected curtesy in the form of an intestate share in the conveyed land, but whether this would be followed in other counties remained uncertain. 

Faced with this situation, the Advisory Committee on Decedents Estates recommended to the Joint State Government Commission that dower be abolished altogether by the deletion of that part of section 5 (a) of the Intestate Act which saved dower as to lands conveyed inter vivos without joinder. If this had been done, the act of 1957 would have become intelligible and the requirement of joinder in conveyances by married persons would have been completely eliminated. The proposal was introduced as H. B. 977 of 

1961 and again as H. B. 75 of 1963, but both bills failed to pass. As an alternative, therefore, the Advisory Committee recommended that section 5 (b) be amended to conform to section 5 (a)-thus giving husbands an interest in their wives' real estate comparable to the dower interest preserved for wives. This recommendation was accepted and became the act of 1963, P. L. 280. Thus, coherence is provided for the act of 1957 by another route, but at best the 1963 amendment is a solution born of desperation. Logical symmetry is attained at the expense of turning back one hand of the clock so that it will match the other one which is a couple of centuries behind the times. 

¶ 2. Effect of the 1963 Amendment 

The wording of section 5 (b) as amended now corresponds exactly to the wording governing the wife's rights in section 5 (a) which in turn is identical to section 3 of the Intestate Act of 1917. The problem of construing new section 5 (b), however, will be somewhat different from the problem of construing section 3 of the 1917 act. In Bridge- 654

ford v. Groh (2d Appeal), 306 Pa. 566 (1932), the court was faced with a situation where common law dower, an existing estate, was modified and continued as to lands conveyed inter vivos. Hence, the court followed the principle that "... a statute should be so interpreted that it will accord as nearly as may be, with the theretofore existing course of the common law." (306 Pa. at 575) It will be seen immediately that this approach is impossible with respect to the 1963 insertion of similar language to govern a husband's rights-bearing in mind that curtesy had been absolutely abolished in 1917 and, even before, had little significance, so far as a wife's inter vivos conveyances were concerned, because of her inability to pass any title. The provision of the 1963 act comes, not as a continuation of something old, but as the initiation of something new and unique.

It would be a mistake, therefore, to try to interpret the 1963 amendment as in any sense an attempt to revive curtesy. Curtesy initiate at common law was entirely different from inchoate dower. Any attempt to pick up the pieces of curtesy (either in its original form or as modified by 

Pennsylvania statutes for many years before 1917) would only lead to confusion and could bring about a situation where the rights and remedies of the two spouses would once more be entirely different.

Furthermore, there would be no justification for such an approach in the language of the amendment. The word "curtesy" is not used in the provisions concerning the husband's interest in land conveyed without joinder. The amendment simply copies the provision which has governed the wife's rights since 1917. Thus, the amendment shows on its face a legislative intention to conform the rights of the husband to the rights of the wife and this is confirmed by the Commissioners' comment. It is to be hoped, therefore, that the courts will forget all about curtesy and construe the new amendment in the light of the authorities governing a widow's statutory dower in aliened lands under the 1917 and 1947 acts. 

Take, for example, the question of "assignment. 

There was no such thing as assignment of common law cur- 

6.55

§(b) 12 

INTESTATE ACT 

tesy; upon the wife's death, the husband's life estate in the entire property simply continued. The husband's new interest under amended section 5 (b), however, is now an intestate share-a fee interest in a half or third in most cases. Thus, the surviving husband is faced with the same problem of defining his interest in lands conveyed without joinder as the surviving wife. In Balkiewicz v. Asenavage, 406 Pa. 501 (1962), the court reaffirmed that something equivalent to an "assignment" of dower is necessary under section 5 (a) and held that a partition proceeding would have to be instituted before the wife could bring ejectment against the grantees. The same rule should apply to the identical interest a surviving husband would have in such a case under section 5 (b).

The same would hold true as to the various other rules governing a widow's interest in aliened lands-principles which were inherited from the law of dower and in many instances were foreign to the law of curtesy but which, it seems plain, the legislature intended to incorporate into section 5 (b) by copying the provision of section 5 (a). 

Thus, the authorities holding that the rights of a husband's mortgagee are not subject to dower and cases concerning other creditors' liens, condemnation, valuation, effect of election against the will, forfeiture under section 6, and other matters discussed in connection with statutory dower under section 5 (a) should be the controlling authorities in construing the husband's interests under section 5 (b). One open question is what effect the 1963 amendment will have on the Feme Sole Trader Acts of 1855, P. L. 430, and 1915, P. L. 639, as amended, 48 P. S. §§ 42-44, and the act of 1927, P. In Moninger v. Ritner, 104 Pa. 298 (1883), and in Scaife v. McKee, 298 Pa. 33 (1929), it was held that these acts not only removed the wife's disability but also permitted her to convey free of the husband's common law curtesy. 13. Effective Date and Constitutionality 

Section 2 of the 1963 amendment provides that "This amending act shall take effect immediately [July 25, 1963] and shall apply to the real and personal estates of all persons dying on or after that day. The existing law shall remain in force and effect for the real and personal estates of all persons dying before that day." This was based on a similar provision in the act of 1917 but it will be seen that somewhat different problems of constitutionality are raised by the act of 1963 which creates a new estate in a surviving husband where none existed before. 

In Scaife v. McKee, 298 Pa. 33 (1929) the validity of the 1917 abolition of curtesy was raised indirectly. The primary question was whether the act of 1927, P. L. 181, under which a married woman who had obtained a divorce a mensa et thoro was given the right to convey her real estate "... in all respects as if she were a feme sole. . .", constitutionally deprived the husband of his alleged curtesy in her land. The court found no constitutional objection to the suspension of curtesy in this situation and, as an alternative ground for the decision, said that the husband's 657

§(b). 

INTESTATE ACT 

13 argument was unsound anyway because he ". never had any curtesy in the properties the subject of this controversy." (298 Pa. at 40) The relevant dates were as follows: The parties were married in 1896. The title to the real estate in question was taken by the wife on December 

25, 1917. A few months before, on June 7, 1917, the Intestate Act abolishing curtesy became law but it contained a provision that it was to take effect on December 31, 1917, and "... shall apply to the estates, real and personal, of all persons dying intestate on and after said day." By a curious but plausible interpretation of that provision, the court held that curtesy was abolished as of June 7th with respect to real estate of married women dying on or after December 31. Hence, since the wife was still alive and must necessarily die after 1917, the husband had no curtesy in the land in question which had been purchased between those two dates. Language earlier in the opinion, however, might be relied on for the proposition that the act would have been constitutional even if title had been taken by the wife before June 7, 1917, and this proposition would find some support in statements in earlier cases (such as Moninger v. Ritner, 104 Pa. 298, 302 (1883)) to the effect that marital rights are not constitutionally protected while both spouses are living. 

A distinction must be drawn, however, between statutes which cut down marital rights and statutes, such as the 1963 amendment, which enlarge them as to property conveyed inter vivos. In the latter case, the rights affected are not the marital rights of the spouse but those of the spouse's grantee, who in many cases will be an innocent purchaser for value. Hence, cases dealing with whether dower and curtesy were constitutionally protected are of little value. 

A closer analogy is presented by cases dealing with the extent to which the provisions of section 3 of the Intestate Act of 1917, enlarging the wife's dower interest in land conveyed inter vivos, could be validly applied to interests of her husband's grantee. Unfortunately, the cases on this question are inconclusive. 

In Merrick v. DuPont, 285 Pa. 368 (1926) land was conveyed without joinder in 1902 by a husband who died in 658

INTESTATE ACT 

1924. It was held that the wife could claim only common law dower, unaffected by the 1917 act. The decision was based, however, on a forced construction of certain wording in section 1 of the 1917 act which is omitted in section 1 of the present act. Hence, the holding is of little value, although it is apparent from the opinion that in construing the act not to apply to past conveyances the court was influenced by the constitutional doubts a contrary construction would raise. 

In Bridgeford v. Groh (1st appeal), 305 Pa. 554 (1932) the dower section of the 1917 act was attacked on the grounds of insufficient title and two subjects. No objection based on vested rights was raised-apparently because the conveyance by the husband took place after 1917 and, since it is recited that he held title "only for an instant" (13 D. & 

C. at 706) it is clear that the conveyance to the husband was also after 1917. No case has been found testing section 

3 of the 1917 act where title was acquired by the husband before the act and conveyed without joinder after the act. 

Against this background, consider the following factual situations with respect to the amendment of 1963, in all cases assuming the wife dies after July 25, 1963: (a) Property both acquired and conveyed after July 25, 1963. Here, there would seem to be no question of constitutionality, even though the parties were married before 1963. (b) Property acquired and conveyance attempted by an unemancipated wife without joinder before 1957. This will present no problem because before 1957 a married woman had no capacity to pass any title to her grantee without her husband's joinder. Hence, her deed was absolutely void and the question of the husband's interest would never arise. (c) Property acquired and conveyed by the wife before 1957 but conveyed after she had been emancipated from her disability by a divorce a mensa et thoro or a feme sole trader decree. This is similar to Merrick v. DuPont, supra, and presents the strongest case for unconstitutionality. It would indeed be shocking if the legislature could 659

§(b) 

INTESTATE ACT 

13 in 1963 take away a portion of the clear title obtained by a purchaser for value before 1957. (d) Conveyance by the wife between 1957 and 1963, regardless of when acquired. The answer here depends on the interpretation to be given to the act of 1957, P. L. 969, 48 P. S. § 32.1, discussed above. If that act is construed to have given the wife an unfettered right to convey full title, then the act of 1963 would be just as objectionable constitutionally as in the case of a conveyance by a feme sole trader. 

If, on the other hand, Campbell v. Shick, 14 Fid. Rep. 304 (C. P. Lyc. 1964) is correct, then the act of 1963 would seem to be valid as merely confirming what was already implicit in the 1957 act. (e) Parties married and property acquired before 1957; conveyance by wife without joinder in 1964. This, perhaps, is the most difficult case. On the one hand, it is hard to see how the legislature can create interests in the husband with respect to land in which he had no such interest before the 1963 amendment. On the other hand, when the wife acquired the property it was in a sense already indirectly encumbered by her disability to convey title without joinder; and, what is more important, the party contesting the constitutionality of the 1963 amendment will normally be, not the wife, but her grantee who had no interest in the property until 1964. 660 [The next page is 701]

INTESTATE ACT 

§ 6. FORFEITURE 

(a) Husband's Share.

A husband who, for one year or upwards previous to the death of his wife, shall have wilfully neglected or refused to provide for her, or who for that period or upwards shall have wilfully and maliciously deserted her, shall have no title or interest under this act in her real or personal estate. 

(b) Wife's Share. 

A wife who, for one year or upwards previous to the death of her husband, shall have wilfully and maliciously deserted him, shall have no title or interest under this act in his real or personal estate.

1. History and Scope. 

At common law, neither spouse was barred by his misconduct from asserting his rights in the real or personal estate of the decedent.¹ It follows that forfeiture for misconduct will arise from statute or not at all. The Statute of Westminster II, 13 Edw. I, c. 34, provided that a voluntary leaving by the wife, followed by her adultery, would bar dower. This statute was held to be in effect in Pennsylvania in Reel v. Elder, 62 Pa. 308 (1869), a case involving a common law action for dower in aliened lands.² 

By section 5 of the act of 1855, P. L. 430, a husband who had deserted or failed to support his wife for one year prior to death was barred from intestate succession. 

This provision was amended in 1915, P. L. 234, by adding a corresponding provision barring a deserting wife. In 1917 section 5 of the act of 1855 as amended was repealed and substantially identical language inserted in the Intestate Act in the sections quoted above. The present section repeats the 1917 provision almost verbatim. 

These subsections state the law of forfeiture for marital misconduct in all four situations where marital property

These provisions (together with subsection (c) concerning the Slayer Act discussed separately infra) are, moreover, the exclusive provisions for forfeiture in our law of marital property interests. As above noted there is no common law or forfeiture, and the Statute of Westminster is clearly superseded by the act of 1855 as re-enacted here. 

The possibility that the unrepealed sections of the femme sole trader statutes might present alternative grounds for forfeiture is discussed below (6), but for most practical purposes those acts can be ignored insofar as they overlap this section. The femme sole trader acts and the act relating to divorces a mensa et thoro do provide for a wife's emancipation from her inability to convey inter vivos without her husband's joinder. As explained in connection with section 5 (b) (¶ 3f), however, those acts raise a question distinct from forfeiture in this respect. 

Also to be distinguished from forfeiture of marital property rights is forfeiture of the $500 widow's exemption under the Fiduciaries Act. As pointed out in Mehaffey's Estate, 102 Pa. Super. 228, 231 (1931), the requirements for foreiture of the exemption are different from the requirements for general forfeiture under the Intestate Act. 

12. Desertion-Problems Covered by Divorce Law 

The words "wilfully and maliciously deserted” in both these subsections are plainly taken from the divorce law which since 1815 has listed "wilful and malicious desertion" 4. See summary of the various statutory provisions governing marital property rights under § 5(a) (1) of the present act. 703

¶ 3a as one of the grounds for divorce a v. m. As might be supposed, the cases under the two laws for the most part have followed the same general principles. The careful analysis in Chapter 20 of Freedman's Marriage and Divorce in Penn sylvania (1939) covers the subject in divorce law, and the corresponding cases in decedents' estates law are collected in Hunter's Orphans' Court Commonplace Book (1939), “Intestate Act" § 4. The discussion here will be confined to matters where the law or forfeiture for desertion is or might be different from the law of divorce. 

13. Desertion-Problems Distinct from Divorce Law a. The One Year Period. 

One obvious departure from the divorce law is the shorter period prescribed by the present section, which states that the desertion must be "for one year or upwards previous to the death" of the decedent. It is plain from common sense, as well as such cases as there are, that the one year period must immediately precede the death; otherwise, the words "previous to death" would be meaningless surplusage. The easiest case is where there has been a reconciliation after the period of misconduct. There the spouse will not be barred for two reasons: (1) the period of desertion did not immediately precede the death, and (2) the offense was condoned by the innocent party. If the second of these two reasons is eliminated, however, the case becomes more difficult. Suppose, for example, a man deserts his wife for more than one year, but then several years before her death makes a bona fide offer to return which the wife refuses. In the law of divorce, an offer to return within the two year period breaks the desertion," but an offer after the two year period has run is ineffective

b. Other Misconduct Affecting Issue of Desertion 

An important difference between the law of divorce and the law of forfeiture so far as desertion is concerned arises from the fact that there are many grounds for divorce but only desertion, non-support or unlawful killing will cause forfeiture in the law of decedents' estates. This distinction comes into play in situations where other misconduct, serious enough to constitute an independent ground for divorce, becomes relevant in determining whether there has been a desertion. If adultery is used as a typical example of such other misconduct, its effect on the issue of desertion in divorce law may be summarized as follows: (1) Where the libellant committed adultery before respondent left, the leaving is justified and respondent is not a deserter. (2) Where libellant commits adultery after respondent leaves (even within the two-year period) an illogical line of cases holds that this is irrelevant to the issue of desertion; for some reason the courts do not regard this as reasonable grounds for respondent's continuance of the desertion.10 (3) Adultery by respondent is sometimes raised in cases of alleged constructive desertion-where the libel- is insufficient.

Note that anything short of reasonable ground for divorce 10. Id. at § 250. Note, however, that the effect of the rule is diminished by the cases holding that the libellant's continued adultery is admissible to negative the bona fides of his willingness to take the deserting spouse back. 705

¶ 3b lant is the leaving party but alleges that he has been "turned out of doors." Here, the divorce law will not regard adultery by the respondent followed by the libellant's leaving as constructive desertion on the part of respondent. In the words of Freedman, "desertion is not made out where the conduct of respondent amounts to ground for divorce and causes libellant to withdraw, but there is wanting a turning out of doors, actual or constructive. The remedy of the injured party in such a case is to assign the cause for divorce which compelled the departure." 11 The italics are supplied in order to emphasize one reason for this rule in divorce law. 

Turning now to the law of forfeiture for desertion under the present section, there would seem to be no reason to depart from the first two rules stated above-concerning the effect of adultery (or other misconduct amounting to an independent ground for divorce) by the deserted party, here the decedent. Thus, there are cases in decedents' estates law which follow the divorce cases in holding (1) that adultery by the decedent before the surviving spouse's departure will constitute justification for the alleged desertion,12 but (2) adultery by the decedent after the surviving spouse's departure will not excuse the desertion.13

There is reason to believe, however, that the third rule of divorce law stated above has no proper application in the law of forfeiture under the present section. Where, for example, a husband leaves his wife because of her adultery and then sues her for divorce on the ground that she constructively deserted him, the courts quite reasonably ask, "Why didn't you sue on the ground of adultery?"

This question cannot be asked where forfeiture of the intestate share is claimed, however, because adultery is not a ground for forfeiture. An important case indicating that a different rule applies in decedents' estates is Lodge's Estate, 287 Pa. 184 (1926). It was there held that adultery by the surviving spouse during a period of separation

They worked together for the same family for a while and then "failing to obtain another suitable place together decided to take separate places." They worked in different cities most of the time and saw little of each other, although relations between them apparently continued amicable until she died. On its facts, Kvist's Estate seems to stand for the proposition that even though the wife voluntarily supports herself and never asks for help, the husband is barred from an interest in her estate. However, conclusions cannot be drawn too hastily in this field of the law. As every lawyer familiar with marital cases knows, Kvist's Estate might be distinguished in any case where the husband sends his wife Christmas cards. The doctrine that the failure of a selfsupporting wife to ask for financial help does not excuse the husband has been subsequently followed, but usually the husband in such a case is guilty of some other blameworthy conduct.24 In no case examined has the doctrine been applied where the parties lived together and each earned his own living.25 Logically, since desertion is not

In short, it is doubtful that Kvist's Estate and cases following it eliminate the possibility of an implied release by the wife of the husband's duty to support her. True, the court will not assume that the woman did not want support merely because she failed to ask for it. But if it appears from the circumstances that the wife was content to support herself and it is reasonably clear that she would have refused an offer of support, an express release would probably not be required. Where the parties live separately and the wife has to work for a living, however, it will be difficult to show that she would not have appreciated a weekly check. 

5. Proof, Collateral Decrees, Etc.

Freedman's analysis of the various rules concerning burden of proof, presumptions and evidence in suits for divorce on the ground of desertion is equally valuable in cases involving the issue of forefeiture on this ground.27 

The heirs at law or beneficiaries under the will are in the position of libellants and have the primary burden of proof, although the burden of going forward with the evidence might shift to the spouse if an unexplained absence is proved.28

Where non-support is the issue, the same pattern is followed. The heirs show the fact that the husband did not provide for the decedent and the burden shifts to him to 26. The indications are rather that the husband would not be barred. "If any exception exists to the penalty which is affixed to the neglect of a husband to provide for his wife, it can be in those cases only where the wife has a competence in her own right, and not in any event where she is driven to labor by actual necessity." Hilker's Est., 22 W. N. C. 148 (O. C. Phila. 1888). 

27. Marriage and Divorce in Pennsylvania (1939) §§ 249, 253 et seq. 

28. See, generally, Buckley's Est., 348 Pa. 311 (1944); Heath's Est., 156 

Pa. Super. 597 (1944); Hunter, O. C. Book, "Intestate Act" § 4(e). 711

¶ show that his failure was justifiable. An interesting and somewhat puzzling case on this point is Buckley's Estate, 348 Pa. 311 (1944). There the surviving husband was a professional criminal and seems to have spent most of his married life in jail. In February of 1940 he was sentenced to 22 to 5 years for burglary and was serving this term when his wife died in 1941. No other facts are given in the Supreme Court opinion. Apparently there were "intervening periods of freedom" between his various jail terms, but it is not indicated whether there was any evidence that he supported his wife during those times or not. His claim to share in her estate was resisted on the ground of desertion, non-support, or both. The opinion on appeal is very short. After some general remarks and useful citations concerning the burden of proof in cases of forfeiture the court said (at 312): "While the incarceration of the husband for a year and upwards might not of itself establish either wilful desertion or non-support, yet in the facts of this case the persistent course of criminal conduct and the various imprisonments since 1926, in this and another state, raise a presumption that during such period, and particularly since 1940, the husband failed to support his wife. The burden was therefore placed upon the husband to establish that during the intervening periods of freedom from imprisonment the husband did in fact support his wife, and that his failure to support his wife for a year or upwards previous to her death was not wilful neglect or refusal to provide for the wife, but was due solely to his incarceration. This the husband wholly failed to do." The exact basis for the decision is difficult to determine. It might be argued, for example, that the court's interest in whether the husband supported decedent during the intervening periods of freedom shows that the one year period of non-support need not be immediately preceding the death, since he had been in jail for more than that time before the wife died.20 Yet the court specifically mentioned the non-support "since 1940" and he was sentenced in February of that year. A more reasonable explanation of the decision is that the husband's inability to support his wife 

29. See discussion of "The One Year Period" (¶ 3a) supra in the text. 712

INTESTATE ACT 

was presumably due to his own fault-that being an habitual (and unsuccessful) criminal is the same as being an habitual drunkard.30 On the whole, however, it would be risky to rely on this case as authority beyond its peculiar facts. It is valuable mainly as an illustration of how proof of the fact of non-support shifts the burden of justification to the surviving spouse. 

When a burden of proof is met to the satisfaction of the hearing judge, his finding is apparently binding on appeal if based on adequate and competent evidence. However, the force of this rule has been considerably lessened in forfeiture cases by recent decisions emphasizing the qualification that inferences or conclusions drawn by the hearing judge do not bind the reviewing court. Jac's Estate, 355 Pa. 137 (1946), illustrates the extent to which the appellate court can go in ignoring findings which it views as mere inferences. And Nixon's Estate, 104 Pa. 

Super. 506 (1931) (which the Supreme Court cited with approval), contains a discussion of the effect of findings by an auditor appointed by the court and some remarks on the puzzling problem of whether such findings attain added dignity by being approved by the lower court.

An interesting question of res adjudicata in forfeiture cases, which has no analogy in divorce proceedings, arises from the concurrent jurisdiction of the orphans' court and common pleas in matters concerning the decedent's real estate. If the surviving spouse is held to have forfeited his interest in decedent's land in an ejectment proceeding in the common pleas, can he thereafter claim against personalty in the orphans' court? Although some doubt existed on this question in the past, it now seems settled that a decree in either court based on a finding of fact will be res judicata in the other court so that factual issues will not be re-litigated, assuming of course that the first court had jurisdiction.39 It will be noted that this is one aspect of the far broader problem of res judicata and jurisdiction in decedents' estates. 

The dead man rule used to play a large part in forfeiture cases, but this has been changed by statute. See subsection (d) of this section, infra. 

16. Substantive Effects of Divorce a Mensa et Thoro and 

Femme Sole Trader Decree

Although, as explained above, separation and femme sole trader decrees might have certain probative value in proving forfeiture under the present section, it seems fairly clear that neither decree in itself has any substantive effect on the right of a spouse to inherit. This can be said without qualification in the case of a divorce a mensa et thoro. 

Such a decree does not affect the marriage status,40 and the act of 1927, P. L. 181, 48 P. S. § 117a, says nothing about forfeiture of inheritance rights. Thus, after a divorce a mensa et thoro has been granted, a married woman may 38. Query whether service by publication would have been sufficient in

The present substantive effect of the femme sole trader acts on inheritance rights is not so plain. There can be no question that the unrepealed sections of the act of 1855, P. L. 430, 48 P. S. § 42, and the act of 1915, P. L. 639, 48 

P. S. § 44, although they are concerned primarily with inter vivos transfers, both expressly provide for forfeiture of inheritance rights. The misconduct mentioned in these femme sole trader acts-desertion or non-support-is substantially the same as that described in the present section of the Intestate Act, so that no serious conflict can arise.42 

The act of 1915 presents no conflict at all because that act has a one-year requirement similar to the Intestate Act.43 

Section 2 of the act of 1855, however, declares a forfeiture of inheritance rights for desertion or non-support with no mention of the period during which such misconduct must continue. It has been held that this act is still law and is superseded neither by the femme sole trader act of 1915 ** nor by the Intestate Act.45 Does this mean that a husband will be barred from his wife's estate under the act of 1855 if he has failed to support her for only a few months prior to her death? Apparently not, in view of the decision in 

Walsh's Appeal, 330 Pa. 502 (1938), which seems to read into the act of 1855 a one-year requirement. That case did not involve inheritance rights, but it did involve a petition for a femme sole trader certificate where the non-support had continued for only five months. The court quoted both the act of 1855 and the act of 1915, and concluded that the certificate must be denied, because (inter alia) the misconduct had lasted for less than one year.

¶ 7. Other Situations Where Spouse May Be Barred—Inter Vivos Agreements 

Although desertion, non-support, and unlawful killing are the sole grounds for forfeiture for misconduct, a person claiming marital rights might be barred from sharing under the Intestate Act, or taking against the will or inter vivos conveyances for other independent reasons. Thus, it is clear that the marriage status must exist at the time of death. If the marriage was invalid from the beginning or has been terminated by a valid divorce a v. m., no marital rights can be claimed. Or a spouse might in certain circumstances be estopped to assert his status as such. 

These matters are discussed under section 2 (¶3) of the present act.

Another situation where the spouse will be barred is where he renounces his rights by accepting a testamentary gift. This will clearly bar him from taking against the will" and might also bar him from an intestate share in undisposed of property if (but only if) the testamentary gift is expressly made conditional upon renunciation.48 

The most important type of case where the spouse is barred in the absence of misconduct is where marital rights are released by inter vivos agreement. There is a useful summary of the law on this subject in the January 1947

It is now well settled that contracts between husband and wife concerning their respective interests in each other's property are valid and enforceable, whether they are made before 49 or after marriage,50 and regardless of whether they are part of a separation agreement.51 Although antenuptial and postnuptial agreements are usually treated separately, there is no clear indication that different rules apply in modern law.52 There is also no reason to believe that the applicable rules of law depend on whether the husband or the wife is the complaining party.53 The tacit assumption of the old common law that a woman had no mind of her own has for the most part disappeared, although as a matter of proof a surviving wife will usually have a better chance of showing fraud, overreaching or coercion than will a surviving husband. 

In a general way, it may be said that agreements between husband and wife are governed by ordinary principles of contract law-as affected by the peculiar relationship of the contracting parties. Thus such agreements are strictly construed and will not alter marital rights unless they so provide, expressly or by "necessary implication.'' 54 

Rescission, on the other hand, is more readily found. A subsequent reconciliation, for example, will ordinarily operate as an implied rescission of a separation agreement.55

INTESTATE ACT § 6 (c) § 6. FORFEITURE (Continued) 

(c) Slayer's Share.

Any person who participates either as a principal or as an accessory before the fact in the wilful and unlawful killing of any person shall not in any way acquire property or receive any benefits as the result of such killing, but such property or benefits shall be distributed as provided by law.

COMMISSIONERS' COMMENT This subsection overlaps some of the provisions of the "Slayer" Act of 1941, P. L. 816. It is not intended to supplant the provisions of the Slayer Act, but is included here for completeness and to avoid any suggestion of partial repeal of the Slayer Act. 

Old Law

Between 1941 and the enactment of the present act there was no provision in the Intestate Act concerning unlawful killing of the decedent. However, the subject was covered by the Slayer Act of 1941, P. L. 816, 20 P. S. § 3441 (quoted in part infra), which remains law and to which the present section refers. 

The Slayer Act of 1941 continues in effect and the law since that act was passed remains unchanged. The act of 

1941, however, made important changes from the act of 1917.

Discussion As pointed out under section 3 (19) and under subsections (a) and (b) (¶ 1) of the present section, our cases have never recognized any common law doctrine of forfeiture for misconduct. Thus, it was held in Carpenter's 

Estate, 170 Pa. 203 (1895), that even though the heir murdered the decedent, his right to inherit was unaffected. This was changed by section 23 of the Intestate Act of 1917, P. L. 

429, which barred from inheritance anyone who was "finally adjudged" guilty of murder of the decedent in the first or second degree. In Tarlo's Estate, 315 Pa. 321 (1934), this act was construed to require a conviction in a criminal court before the murderer would be barred; hence the estate of a murderer who had committed suicide was permitted to share in the estate of the victim. 751

§(c) 

INTESTATE ACT 

Section 23 of the act of 1917 was repealed with the enactment of the Slayer Act of 1941, P. L. 816, 20 P. S. § 3441-a comprehensive statute carefully drafted in order to prohibit the slayer from reaping the harvest of his crime in a number of situations, including intestacy. The present provision in the Intestate Act is new, but it in no way disturbs the Slayer Act. The purpose was rather to avoid an implied repealer of the Slayer Act, in view of the language of section 16 of the present act stating that "this act is intended as an entire and complete system regulating" descent. 

The first part of the present provision is taken almost verbatim from the definition of a "slayer" in section 1 of the act of 1941 which reads as follows: 

"The term slayer shall mean any person who participates, either as a principal or as an accessory before the fact, in the wilful and unlawful killing of any other person."

The balance of the present section is based on section 2 of the Slayer Act which reads as follows: 

"No slayer shall in any way acquire any property or receive any benefit as the result of the death of the decedent but such property shall pass as provided in the sections following.

For the words, "in the sections following," the present provision has substituted "by law," thus clearly incorporating by reference the subsequent provisions of the Slayer Act or any future amendments or revisions thereof. 

In cases of intestacy the relevant provision of the 

Slayer Act is section 3, which reads as follows: 

"The slayer shall be deemed to have predeceased the decedent as to property which would have passed from the decedent or his estate to the slayer under the statutes of descent and distribution or have been acquired by dower, by courtesy or by statutory right as surviving spouse."

It will be seen that any problem that might arise under the present subsection of the Intestate Act is really a 752

INTESTATE ACT 

§ 6 (c) problem under the Slayer Act which is partly copied and partly incorporated by reference. The Slayer Act has at the time of writing not yet been judicially construed in a case involving intestate rights.¹ However, the model upon which the Pennsylvania Slayer Act is based is analyzed in detail by its drafter, John W. Wade, in 49 Harv. L. Rev. 

715 (1936), and the Pennsylvania act is discussed by Harold 

S. Irwin, in 46 Dickinson L. Rev. 99 (1942), and by the editors of the Fiduciary Review in the October, 1941, issue (see also June, 1947, issue referring to the present section of the Intestate Act). Only the effect of the act on intestate succession will be discussed here. 

It will first be observed that a criminal conviction of the slayer is no longer necessary, so that Tarlo's Estate, 315 

Pa. 321 (1934), supra, and Hoffman's Estate, 39 D. & C. 

208 (O. C. Armstrong 1940) (where the slayer became insane) are no longer law. Conversely, however, a conviction is no longer conclusive on the issue of forfeiture as it was under the act of 1917. Under section 14 of the Act of 1941, the conviction is merely admissible evidence when rights under the Intestate Act are being determined. (See 

Pinder's Estate, 61 D. & C. 193 (O. C. Del. 1947).) Note, however, there is no provision making a record of acquittal admissible, although that is equally incompetent at common law. This omission cannot be presumed to have been unintentional, because there is a theoretical argument that since the burden of proof is heavier in a criminal proceeding, an acquittal is of less probative value than a conviction when used in a civil suit. Furthermore, the other heirs would not have had the opportunity to cross-examine the witnesses of the defendant in the criminal suit, so that an acquittal based on such testimony would come within the policy of the hearsay rule.

It will also be noted that the definition of "slayer" is different from the corresponding provision of the act of 1917, which applied only where there had been first or second degree murder. It is clear, for example, that the act

337, 341 (1930), where a surviving spouse's claim was resisted by those taking under the will on the ground of desertion. This was changed by the act of 1931, quoted above, which is re-enacted in simplified form by the present provision.

1. Proof of Illegitimacy-Presumptions 

This section will be applicable wherever it can be shown that a child is in fact illegitimate, but this will not always be easy. It will first be noted that any child born while his parents are married is in fact legitimate-regardless of when he was conceived. Furthermore, when a child is born during the marriage of his mother, there is a strong presumption that he is the child of his mother's husband and this can be rebutted only by proof of non-access or impotency, to which neither husband nor wife is competent to testify. All these points are illustrated by Dennison v. 

Page, 29 Pa. 420 (1857).¹ In that case the plaintiff's right to inherit depended on whether she was the legitimate daughter of the decedent. It appeared that she was born to the wife of decedent three months after the marriage. 

The defendant attempted to prove illegitimacy in various ways, including the testimony of the mother as to the nonaccess of her husband during the period of conception. Objections to all this testimony were sustained and a verdict was directed for plaintiff. On appeal the decision was affirmed. The court ruled: (1) "A child born in wedlock, 1. Quoted and followed as late as Com. v. DiMatteo, 124 Pa. Super. 277 (1936) (criminal case). For other cases, see Fiduciary Review, April, 1946, p. 

2; Hunter, O. C. Book (1939) "Legitimacy" §1(a); and cases infra notes 2 and 3. 852

¶ 7 

INTESTATE ACT 

cos though born within a month or a day after marriage, is legitimate by presumption of law" and the presumption is not "weakened" by a showing of antenuptial conception. (2) "This presumption can only be rebutted by clearly proving that no sexual intercourse occurred between the two at any time when the child could have been begotten. 

Nothing short of this will bastardize one born in wedlock. "2 Hence all the testimony of the family scene following the birth, the tears of the husband, and the reputation of illegitimacy was properly excluded. (3) Finally, the testimony of the mother as to non-access was inadmissible because "non-access cannot be proved by either the husband or the wife, whether the action be civil or criminal, or whether the proceeding is one of settlement or bastardy, or to recover property claimed as heir at law.” 3 The rules set forth in Dennison v. Page are applicable when the child was admittedly born while his mother was married, and the question is whether the husband was the father. If, on the other hand, the child is able to prove who his father is, but the question is rather whether his father was married to his mother, different presumptions apply. 

This situation is governed by the rules and cases reviewed in Mays' Estate, 141 Pa. Super. 479 (1940). There the child was able to prove that the decedent was his father, but there was no convincing proof that his mother ever married the decedent. The child was nevertheless found to be legitimate under the following rules as to burden of proof: (1) The child "had the burden of proof of his relationship to the decedent, that is, the decedent's paternity, apart, primarily, from any question of his own legitimacy," but (2) the child's "kinship to decedent having been thus shown, it was not incumbent upon him to go further to prove his legitimacy; it was for the appellants to disprove it, and that by proof that was clear, direct, satisfactory, and irrefragable." proof of a negative is not an easy thing. The cases cited in Mays' Estate also make it clear that the same rules apply where the validity rather than the fact of a purported marriage is attacked; actually the problem is the same because an invalid marriage is no marriage at all. Thus where the purported marriage of the parents is attacked on the ground of bigamy, the "burden of showing the first marriage not dissolved was on the" other heirs." 

To summarize the effect of Dennison v. Page and Mays' 

Estate, a child can either (1) prove that his mother was married when he was born, in which event the mother's husband is presumed to be his father, or (2) prove who his father is, in which event it is presumed that the father was married to the mother. Both presumptions are rebuttable, but only by evidence which will not be available in many cases. ¶ 2. Inheritance With Respect to Mother and Her Family 

Assuming the illegitimacy is shown-either by proof of birth out of wedlock or by proof of non-access or impotency of the mother's husband-and assuming that the child was not subsequently legitimated or adopted, the present provision will govern questions of inheritance by, from and through the illegitimate. 

At common law an illegitimate was the child of no one. 

Since 1855, however, the class of cases where the relationship between an illegitimate and his mother is recognized has been progressively enlarged. The present provision simplifies the language of the act of 1917 and should remove any doubt that might have existed. The illegitimate is the child of his mother for all purposes of inheritance. Not only can the illegitimate and his mother inherit from each other, but the barriers to inheritance are also removed between the illegitimate's issue and his maternal collaterals. 13. Inheritance With Respect to Father and His Family 

Although an illegitimate can be considered the legitimate child of his mother for all purposes of inheritance, he still remains a child without a father in the eyes of the law. 

Unless the child is legitimated by a subsequent marriage, or unless the father adopts him, there would seem to be no exception to this rule in the law of succession. Even an acknowledgment of parenthood by the father is insufficient in Pennsylvania, because of the common law doctrine and the express provision of the present section. The possibility of the illegitimate's claiming as a creditor against the estate of his father, however, should be investigated in such a case. ¶ 4. Subsequent Marriage of Parents-Legitimation 

Legitimation by special act of assembly was popular before it became impossible due to article 3, section 7, of the Constitution of 1874. Today, the father might adopt his illegitimate child but the only method of legitimation available is the subsequent marriage of the parents. The act of 1857, P. L. 507, 48 P. S. § 167 (requiring marriage and "cohabitation") governs this subject generally, and the present section (requiring merely a subsequent marriage of the parents) is based on section 15 of the act of 1917 which superseded the general act of 1857 for purposes of intestate succession."

The present provision no longer requires "lawful wedlock" as did the act of 1917, but the change is without significance. Even under the old act a voidable marriage (as in Thorn's Estate, 353 Pa. 603 (1946)) fulfilled the requirement. Conversely, a purported marriage which has no legal effect is no marriage at all even under the present act. 

As already noted, however, the courts are reluctant to declare a marriage invalid where the legitimacy of a child is in question. There is no reason to believe that a questionable marriage will be more vulnerable in a case of alleged legitimation than in the case of a child born during the marriage, discussed above (¶ 1).10

On the other hand, a child relying on legitimation by subsequent marriage will not have the advantage of the presumption, available to a child born in wedlock, that his mother's husband is his father. It is his "parents" who must be married, and "there is no presumption that the man who marries the mother of a bastard child is the father 9. 5. Conflict of Laws 

Assuming, as we must, that we are dealing with inheritance of Pennsylvania land, or personalty of a Pennsylvania decedent (see section 14, infra), it would seem plain that whether the child is legitimate might depend on foreign law, but the effect of illegitimacy on inheritance will be governed by this section. Thus, if the marriage is invalid in the state where it took place (even though it might have been valid here), the law of that place will fix the status of the child born there as illegitimate.¹¹ Inheritance from or through the father in this state will therefore be impossible, but if the mother dies owning Pennsylvania real estate the child will inherit his statutory share pursuant to this provision of our Intestate Act, regardless of what the law is in the state of domicile. 

In cases involving legitimation, these principles give the child a double chance of success; he can argue that he was legitimated under the law of his foreign domicil and hence must inherit as a legitimate here, or that he may inherit under subsection (b) of this section if his parents subsequently married, even though this would not have resulted in legitimation by the law of his domicil.12 Thus, in Moretti's Estate, 16 D. & C. 715 (O. C. Phila. 1932) (approved in Thorn's Estate, 353 Pa. 603 (1946) 13), the estate of a decedent (who the court was willing to assume died domiciled in Pennsylvania) was awarded to his natural 11. See also authorities on conflicts discussed under $8 (5) relating to adoption. Strictly speaking, the law of the state of marriage will determine the validity of the marriage; the law of the state where the child was born will determine its legitimacy (conceivably a child born of unmarried but cohabitating parents might be legitimate in a foreign state); and the law of the domicil of decedent or the situs of his land will determine inheritance rights. ¶ 6. Controlling Date 

Since the present provision makes little if any change in the law since 1901, a determination of which statute is applicable will not be important in many cases. However, it will be noted that it is the date of decedent's death which is controlling and not the date when the illegitimate was born or when the subsequent marriage (in cases of legitimation) takes place. As said in Taylor's Estate, 57 D. & C. 

311, 312 (O. C. Phila. 1946) (aff'd, 357 Pa. 120 (1947)), "If the statute does no more than to put the child among the next of kin of the mother for purposes of inheritance from or through her, the applicable statute would be that which was in effect at the time of her death."

§ 8. ADOPTED PERSONS 

For purposes of descent by, from and through an adopted person he shall be considered the issue of his adopting parent or parents and not the issue of his natural parents: Provided, That if a natural parent shall have married the adopting parent, the adopted person for purposes of descent by, from and through him shall also be considered the issue of such natural parent. 

COMMISSIONERS' COMMENT This section is intended to retain the rule of Cave's Est., 326 Pa. 358, and Reamer's Est., 331 Pa.

(a) Any minor or adult person adopted according to law, and the adopting parent or parents shall, respectively, inherit and take, by devolution from and through each other, personal estate as next of kin, and real estate as heirs, under the provisions of this act, as fully as if the person adopted had been born a lawful child of the adopting parent or parents. (b) The person adopted shall, for all purposes of inheritance and taking by devolution, be a member of the family of the adopting parent or parents. 1. Who is an "Adopted Person" a. General 

As the Supreme Court said in Fisher v. Robison, 329 

Pa. 305, 308 (1938), "Adoption was not a common law act; it depends altogether on the statute, and in this state may be defined as taking the child of another in the manner provided by, and with the consequences specified in, the statute." Formerly, adoption could be accomplished by deed under the act of 1872, P. L. 31, or by petition and decree of court under the act of 1855, P. L. 430, as variously amended and supplemented,' but the earlier statutes were repealed and superseded by the act of 1925, P. L. 127, as amended, 1 P. S. § 1, which eliminates adoption by deed and provides only for adoption by court proceeding. 

It follows that unless adoption has taken place under the law of another state (see below ¶5), the present section will apply only where the child has been adopted pursuant to the applicable Pennsylvania statute and retains such status at the decedent's death. The proper procedure for adoption under the 1925 and prior acts, and whether a defective or improper proceeding is nevertheless effective to preclude collateral attack cannot be discussed here. Suffice it to note that under our law, neither an intention to adopt, the treatment of the child as if adopted, an adoption by the other spouse, nor a promise to adopt 41; Lein-

b. Contract to Treat as Heir Distinguished 

Although a person not legally adopted cannot claim under the present section, he might have certain rights as a third party beneficiary under a contract by the foster parents to treat the child as their own. Proof of such contracts is often attempted without success, but in Mc- 

Daniel's Estate, 305 Pa. 17 (1931), a contract between the decedent and a children's home, providing that an unadopted child should have a natural child's interest in the promisor's estate, was held binding and enforceable against the estate of the promisor who died intestate. It seems important to distinguish such cases from cases where a legal adoption has taken place. The child's share is the same, but the fact that he claims as creditor under the contract, rather than under the present section of the Intestate Act, might make a difference in the disposition of the balance of the estate when the decedent is also survived by a spouse. 

Suppose, for example, the intestate is survived by a spouse but no natural children. The spouse and a legally adopted child would share the estate equally (see § 2 ¶ 4 of this act). 

On the other hand if there is merely a contract and no adoption, the foster child would receive the same share, but it would seem that the spouse would be entitled only to the allowance plus one-half of what remained. The creditor would be paid and the net estate distributed to those entitled. Although strict logic would seem to make this result inevitable, such cases as there are leave the question in doubt. 12. Inheritance By, From and Through Adopted Person a. Adoptive Parents, Ascendants and Collaterals 

The history of the statutes and cases on inheritance with respect to adopted children is summarized in Cave's 

Estate, 326 Pa. 358 (1937), Long, "Adoption as Affecting 

Inheritance in Pennsylvania," 39 Dick L. Rev. 179 (1935), and Hutton, "Concerning Adoption and Adopted Persons as Heirs in Pennsylvania," 42 Dick. L. Rev. 12 (1937).

Generally speaking, the law since 1855 has progressed by degrees toward making the adopted person the child of the adopting parent for all purposes of intestate succession. In Cave's Estate, the Supreme Court was finally convinced that the Act of 1917 was sufficient to enable the child to inherit from collateral relatives of the adopting parent. Since the failure to provide for this result was the principal inadequacy of the pre-1917 statutes, it is safe to assume that since 1917 it has been law that an adopted person can be treated under the Intestate Act in the same manner as a natural child of his adopting parent. 

As the court said (326 Pa. at 366) the act "severs the child from his natural family tree and engrafts him upon that of his new parentage 'for all purposes of inheritance.' '' 

The simplified language of the present provision should make this even clearer by the elimination of any specific reference to the persons from whom the adopted child inherits or the persons who are inheriting from or through him. He is "the issue of his adopting parent or parents" regardless of who is inheriting from whom. It follows necessarily that he is also the grandchild of the adopting parent's parent, the nephew of the adopting parent's brother, the cousin of the adopting parent's nephew, and so forth. 

7. Reamer's Est., 315 Pa. 148 (1934), where the court adopted a different view, was distinguished in Cave's Estate, but later was overruled in Reamer's 

Est., 331 Pa. 117 (1938). See also Finegan's Est., 30 Erie 292 (O. C. 1947). 904

cos b. Natural Parents, Ascendants and Collaterals 

Prior to 1917, the statutes were not clear as to inheritance rights between an adopted child and his natural ascendants and collaterals in all situations. The act of 

1887, P. L. 53, provided that the natural parents could not inherit from the adopted child, and in Morgan v. Reel, 213 

Pa. 81, 89 (1905), the court held the converse to be truefinding a general intent by the Legislature that inheritance by the child from both lines should not be permitted. This was made clear in the act of 1917, and the same rule is continued by the present section. It is also clear that since the connection with the natural parents is severed, all relationships traced through the natural parents are likewise lost. Fisher v. Robison, 329 Pa. 305 (1938) (natural parent); Crossley's Estate, 135 Pa. Super. 524 (1939) (natural grandparent); and Zoell's Estate, 345 Pa. 413 (1942) (natural uncle), are the more recent authorities on the general subject, if authority is needed. It will be noted that when there is only one adopting parent, the child is forced to exchange two parents for one, but this is what the statute provides. The only exception under present law is where the natural and adopting parents marry each other a situation discussed below (4). 

c. Spouse and Issue of Adopted Person 

Although a child's parents, ascendants and collaterals are changed by the adoption, there is nothing in the present law or any prior statute which affects the adopted person's relationship to his own spouse and issue. Thus, there can be no question that the adoption is irrelevant with regard to inheritance of the adopted child, his spouse and descendants among themselves. It further follows, however, that these descendants are transferred along with the adopted person to the family tree of the adopting parent. In the words of the present provision, the descendants inherit "through" the adopted person who is treated as the child of the adopting parent. In Webb's Estate, 250 Pa. 179 (1915) (deciding that the child of an adopted child inherits from the adopting parent), this was held to be the law even under the act of 1889, P. L. 168, which was much less 905

§

INTESTATE ACT 

cos ¶ 3 clear on this point than either the 1917 act or the present section. See also the well-phrased analysis of the question under the 1917 act in Thomas's Estate, 2 D. & C. 89 (0. C. Wash. 1922), which was quoted with approval in 

Fisher v. Robison, 329 Pa. 305, 310 (1938). Conversely, as that opinion points out, the child of an adopted person cannot inherit from his natural grandfather, as the relationship between the adopted person and his natural parent is severed for all purposes of inheritance. 

13. Controlling Date 

It is plain that the child's status at the time of decedent's death will be controlling. This has been clearer since the adoption statutes were segregated from the provisions for intestate succession with relation to adopted children. There can now be no question that (1) whether the child is effectively adopted will depend on the law in force when the attempted adoption takes place, but (2) the handling of problems of intestacy, once the child's status has been determined, will be governed by the law in effect at decedent's death. The distinction between the two questions is more dramatically demonstrated in cases of foreign adoption discussed below (5) under "Conflict of Laws.'

The one possible qualification to the rules stated above is in connection with cases where the natural and adopting parent marry each other-see the last paragraph of the discussion under the next heading. 

¶ 4. Marriage of Natural and Adopting Parent 

It has already been pointed out (1) that for inheritance purposes the relationship between the child and the natural parent is lost by the adoption, and (2) that the mere fact that one spouse adopts the child does not mean that the other spouse becomes an adoptive parent unless he too joins in the petition. Combining these two rules under the 1917 act, the court in Fisher v. Robison, 329 Pa. 305 (1938), held that where a husband adopted his stepchild the child lost his right to inherit from his mother. In that case, the parties were divorced prior to the mother's death, 8. See cases supra note 4. 233 194445 906

¶ 8 

INTESTATE ACT 

cas but in view of earlier decisions, it is fairly certain that the decision would have been the same even in the absence of the subsequent divorce. 

Where only one of two married people adopts a child, the failure of the other to join in the petition is sometimes intentional or the result of carelessness. Where the other spouse is the natural parent, however, there is some doubt as to whether it is legally possible for a parent to adopt his own legitimate child and in any event it is not a thing that a parent ordinarily thinks of doing. The rule of 

Fisher v. Robison was therefore changed by the act of 

1941, P. L. 424, which is paraphrased as the proviso in the present section. The provision will apply whether the marriage takes place before or after the adoption. It would likewise seem to make no difference whether or not the parties remained married until the decedent's death. Thus, if the proviso is construed literally, the Fisher case is no longer law even on its facts, and improbable cases of divorce and remarriage can be imagined where the adopted child will end up by having three or more parents. 

15. Conflict of Laws 

Most questions of conflicts arising where a child is adopted in a foreign jurisdiction and the decedent dies domiciled in Pennsylvania should be answered by the decision in Zoell's Estate, 345 Pa. 413 (1942), cert. denied 

318 U. S. 778, following Crossley's Estate, 135 Pa. Super. 

524 (1939). It is plain from these cases that (1) a foreign decree of adoption by a court having the necessary jurisdiction is entitled to recognition in this state so far as the child's status is concerned, but (2) our own intestate law governs the question of inheritance by, from and through adopted children with respect to personalty of a Pennsylvania decedent or Pennsylvania real estate (see section 14).

Thus, even though the foreign decree or law attempts to limit or preserve inheritance rights, it will be ignored, insofar as it is inconsistent with our law of inheritance.

89. ADVANCEMENTS 

(a) In General.

If any person, other than the surviving spouse, taking real or personal estate from the decedent, shall have received any estate by settlement or advancement of the decedent, in either real or personal estate, the value of such settlement or advancement shall be charged against the share of the person who shall have received it, so that the total share received by him, including the value of such settlement or advancement, shall not exceed the share received by each of the other persons who take equally from the decedent. (b) Valuation.

The settlement or advancement shall be considered as of its value when the advancee came into enjoyment of it or at the death of the decedent, whichever occurred first.
