¶ 1. General "An advancement as defined by this Court is a pure and irrevocable gift, by a parent in his lifetime, to his child, on account of such child's share of the estate, after the parent's decease . 

Smith's Estate, 350 Pa. 418, 419 (1944). The definition is not too precise,¹ but it has become something of a classic and is useful as setting forth the general outlines of the concept. 

The rule that inter vivos gifts must be taken into account in attempting to make equal distribution among an intestate's children dates back to the original Statute of Distribution in England and survives today as a relic of an age when wills were the exception rather than the rule. 

For better or for worse, provisions for equalizing advance- 1. The reference to irrevocability is somewhat puzzling. A gift not in trust is by definition irrevocable and there seems to be no reason why a gift in a revocable trust should not be an advancement if it were so intended and remained unrevoked at the donor's death. It is believed that the words "pure and irrevocable" are used rather to emphasize the difference between an advancement and a loan. It will also be noted that the doctrine of advancements is not limited to gifts to children, although that is the typical case. 952

INTESTATE ACT 

89 ments have appeared in our intestate acts since 1705.2 Section 16 of the act of 1833 P. L. 315, literally applied only to gifts to "children" but it was judicially construed to include gifts to other descendants as well.³ In 1917, the language was revised (according to the Commission) "to include all persons entitled under the act (other than the spouse) and to simplify the language." Subsection (a) of the present act was intended to be merely a stylistic revision of the 1917 provision.

Apart from its great antiquity, there is little to be said in favor of the doctrine of advancements. It represents an anachronistic concern for carrying out the supposed intent of an intestate, at the expense of admitting all sorts of oral evidence and speculating on what the decedent would have wanted. Fortunately for the speedy administration of decedents' estates, the provision seems to be falling into disuse. References to the rule in wills cases (12 below) are fairly numerous, but reported decisions actually applying this section of the Intestate Act have been relatively rare in the last fifty years-perhaps because on the modern scene persons who can afford to make substantial inter vivos gifts generally take the trouble to make a will. 

12. Wills Cases Distinguished 

Precisely speaking, the doctrine of advancements applies only in cases of intestacy. There is no objection to using the term in a broader sense to cover closely analogous principles in the law of wills, but it is important to remember that no statutory provision is being applied in such cases, and that anything said by the court is dictum insofar as the interpretation of the Intestate Act is concerned. The law of "advancements" enters into the law of wills in two principal classes of cases. The first is where a testator makes a gift to one of his children and later

However, the rules relating to ademption by satisfaction are wholly a matter of case law; there is nothing in the Wills Act corresponding to the present provision of the Intestate Act. Hence, cases involving wills can never be quite controlling for the proper interpretation of the present section-persuasive as they might sometimes be. 

3. Partial Intestacy-Gifts by Will Not Advancements 

There are dicta in O'Connor v. Flick, 271 Pa. 249, 253 (1921), and in the Superior Court opinion in Laughlin's

There may be Pennsylvania cases so holding, although a superficial search has disclosed none. In Atkinson on Wills (1937) § 239, p. 679, it is said that "in most jurisdictions the doctrine of advancements does not apply to cases of partial intestacy, as the testator is conclusively presumed to have considered prior and future advancements in his calculations of bequests." This seems by far the more sensible solution. Certainly, if the doctrine of

¶5. Parties to Transaction and in Favor of Whom Doctrine 

Applies a. General

For a problem of advancements to arise, there must have been an inter vivos gift by the intestate to or for the benefit of an heir other than the spouse, and the decedent must also be survived by other heirs entitled to equalization. That the decedent must have been the donor of the gift is plain from the wording of the provision. Thus, a gift by the mother will not be equalized in the distribution of the father's estate; the presumption in favor of equality is not carried this far. Surprisingly enough, this point is sometimes litigated (as in Christy's Appeal, 1 Grant 369 (1856)), but the question in such cases is largely one of the proper interpretation of the facts in complicated family transactions.

The other two requirements—that the gift must be to or for the benefit of an heir other than the decedent's spouse, and that persons entitled to equalization must also survive can best be considered together in connection with various types of relationships. b. Spouse

As expressly set forth in the statute, the doctrine of advancements applies only to gifts to heirs "other than the surviving spouse," so that gifts to the spouse need never be equalized.12 She is entitled to both the gift and her intestate share unless she has released the latter by contract.13 

12. Even in cases involving the satisfaction of a legacy inter vivos, it is said that "the doctrine of advancements does not apply as between husband and wife." 

Loesch's Est., 322 Pa. 105, 109 (1936), but there the question seems rather one of intent. See Alexander's Est., 83 Pa. Super. 210 (1924), supra (2) in the text and compare Dermond's Estate, infra note 15. 

13. See discussion of such contracts under §6 (7) of this act and discussion of voluntary release of intestate share under 4, supra, and under § 1 (f3c) of this act. 957

INTESTATE ACT 

Conversely, the spouse may not benefit from the equalization of an advancement to another party. This is clear from settled principles elsewhere 14 and from the wording in the statute to the effect that the equalization is for the benefit of "other persons who take equally from the decedent." Similar wording in the 1917 act was discussed in 

Whyte's Estate, 13 D. & C. 380, 381 (O. C. Phila. 1930), expressly ruling that the share of the widow could not be enlarged because of an alleged advancement to a child. 

After quoting from the old act the provision for equalization among "other persons who are equally entitled," the auditing judge said: "The share of the widow is not always equal to an heir's share. Among the heirs, however, the shares are equal, except where some take by representation, and in the latter case, the aggregate of their shares is equal to the share of one who takes in his own right. The 

Auditing Judge, therefore, rules that the trust fund does not constitute an advancement as respects the widow." 15 

Thus, if an advancement to a child is brought into hotchpot at all, it will be only for the benefit of other descendants; the widow will take only her share of the estate before the amount of advancement is added. Note that this is one situation where an advancement differs materially from a debt-see ¶ 6b below. c. Other Heirs in General

An inter vivos gift to any heir other than the spouse might be shown to be an advancement. In discussing general questions of advancements, it is common to speak in terms of gifts to children. Even under the act of 1833, however, the doctrine was applied to other descendants 16 and since 1917 the statute has expressly provided for equalization of gifts to any person entitled under the act other than the spouse. A literal reading of the 1917 and the present provision might lead to the belief that while a gift to any heir other than the spouse might be an advancement, the gift will be equalized only in favor of persons of the same degree of consanguinity who share the estate per capita with the donee. It is certain, however, that the Legislature did not intend so to restrict the doctrine. Advancement provisions in intestate statutes have always referred to equality in one way or another, but the proper construction of such language is indicated by the quotation supra from Whyte's 

Estate, 13 D. & C. 380, 381 (O. C. Phila. 1930). Where persons of unequal degrees share the estate, the equality referred to is among the shares of those of the nearest degree and the aggregate share of any group taking by representation.17 d. Children and Grandchildren 

The opinions in Eshleman's Appeal, 74 Pa. 42 (1873), Person's Appeal, 74 Pa. 121 (1873) and Storey's Appeal, 83 Pa. 89, 96-7 (1876) provide by way of decision and dicta a complete set of rules governing advancements with respect to grandchildren. They may be summarized as follows: (1) Where grandchildren take by representation of their deceased parent (in estates where other children of the decedent survive) an advancement to the deceased child will be charged against the grandchildren claiming through him. (2) Where, on the other hand, the decedent is survived by none of his children, so that the grandchildren take

(3) Where the advancement is made directly to the grandchild, however, this will be charged against the donee regardless of whether he takes by representation or in his own right. It is only necessary to add that in the third case the gift to the grandchild will ordinarily be regarded as an advancement only if made after the death of the grandchild's parent; otherwise the circumstances would rebut the intent necessary for an advancement.18 In other words, a gift to a grandchild while his parent is still living could not be deemed to be in contemplation of eventual equalization, for the decedent could scarcely have contemplated that the grandchild's parent would not survive. e. Collaterals 

No case has been found where the doctrine of advancements was applied where the estate went to collaterals, although since 1917 the statute has been expressly applicable with respect to any heir other than the spouse. In cases involving collaterals the showing of the necessary intent will be difficult and the presumption applicable to gifts to children might not arise-see discussion of intent, ¶ 6 below.

Most of the problems that might arise in such cases can be answered on the analogy of the cases dealing with grandchildren; the heir will be chargeable with any advancement made to him personally, but will be charged with advancements made to his parent or ancestor only when he takes by representation. The question of when a collateral takes by representation and when he takes in his own right is discussed under section 4 (1) (¶¶ 4 & 5). ¶ 6. Intent a. Advancement Distinguished from Preferential Gift 

Whether or not a gift is an advancement is said to depend on the donor's intent at the time of the transac-

Patterson's Appeal, 128 Pa. 269, 281 (1889). The nature of the required intent cannot be understood apart from this presumption, and it is probably more helpful if the rule is put in the negative: An advancement is distinguished from a preferential gift by the absence of an intent by the donor to prefer one child over another with reference to his entire wealth. He is presumed to have intended eventual equality among his heirs, and the burden of showing the contrary is on the donee. 

It would seem that the presumption is less realistic today than it might have been in the past when wills were not so popular. In literate communities, it might be more sensible to reverse the old presumption and assume that when a person of wealth makes an inter vivos gift without providing for equalization by will, he intends to favor the donee in the absence of proof to the contrary. This would seem especially advisable in the case of a gift to a collateral; the presumption in favor of equality would seem to have no proper application in such a case, and since there is no controlling authority on the subject, a court should find a preferential gift in the absence of evidence of actual intent. Where the gift is to a lineal descendant of the donor, however, the old presumption that an advancement was intended is apparently still in force, although a modern court would probably be more ready to find that it had been rebutted. In Grissinger's Estate, 104 

Pa. Super. 184 (1931) the presumption was not even mentioned.

Sometimes the presumption is rebutted (or in a sense does not arise) because of the nature of the gift itself, even in the absence of extrinsic evidence of intent. The subject is treated by Justice Sharswood in Weaver's Appeal, 63 Pa. 309 (1869). Advancement Distinguished from Loan

In some cases it makes little difference whether an advancement or a loan was intended because both must in a sense be repaid to the estate. However, the distinction becomes important in the following respects: (1) Disability, alterations, the statute of limitations, etc. are defenses to a debt but will not prevent equalization of an advancement; 30 (2) The debtor must repay the debt regardless of its amount, but there is no obligation on the part of the donee to bring into hotchpot an advancement in excess of his share of the estate; 31 (3) Interest usually runs against a debt from the time it was incurred, but interest does not run against an advancement until the time for distributing the decedent's estate; (4) The spouse or any party in interest can benefit by the repayment of a loan, but (as already pointed out) only those "who take equally from the decedent" can benefit from the bringing in of an advancement.33 32 The rules of presumption are about the same as in the case where the dispute is whether the transfer is an advancement or a preferential gift. ¶ 7. How Advancement is Equalized a. Hotchpot

The method of equalizing an advancement is succinctly described in Smith's Estate, 350 Pa. 418, 420 (1944): “It is to be treated as if repayment had been made to the estate, the total divided among the heirs, and the advancement deducted from the share of the one advanced. The whole is placed in hotchpot, the advancement added and the total divided " Thus, if a net estate of $12,000. goes to three children, but one child has received an advancement of $3,000., the advancement is theoretically added and the total of $15,000. divided by three. The advanced child takes $5,000. less his advancement-or $2,000.-and the other two children take $5,000. each.87

The contribution of the value of the advancement is of course purely theoretical. It need not be actually paid to

In adjusting advancements under our statute, there is no distinction between real and personal property. Not only can the subject matter of an advancement be either real or personal property, but its value can be charged against the advancee's share in either the real or personal property of the decedent. Hence, if the personal estate is insufficient to equalize the shares, the advancee's fractional interest in decedent's real estate will be reduced. The procedure in such cases is under the Partition Act, and the jurisdiction of the Orphans' Court is said to be exclusive.40 b. Interest

An advancement does not bear interest in the sense that a debt bears interest. It is said, however, that an advancement does bear interest "after the legal period for the settlement of the estate . . . or from the time when the other heirs received the balance due." 41 Exactly how this is worked out is not entirely clear from the cases. 

The one thing that is absolutely clear is that the donee is not chargeable with interest prior to the donor's death. It also seems to be established that between the date of death and the time when distribution is or should be made,*2 no interest is charged against the advancement, and income actually earned by the estate is divided equally among the 38. Thus, the amount theoretically added is in no sense a part of the estate.

Plainly, this method brings about equality only in the rare case where the estate actually earns income at the legal rate, or in the equally improbable case where the donee is able to earn 6% on the advancement. Moreover, the cases in support of this view concern the construction of wills and might be distinguishable on that basis. 1 A much fairer method is to determine the respective shares in the net estate as of the time for distribution, and divide the income accruing thereafter in the proportion so ascertained—thus, in effect, charging the advancee interest only at the rate actually earned by the estate. It is believed that this method is more in accord with the general purpose of bringing about equality and is not precluded by any controlling authority.

D. & C. 380 (1930), the court neatly dodged the question by holding that the donor could not have intended the gift to be an advancement in the circumstances. It is difficult to imagine what else the court could have done, and it is certainly reasonable to assume that no person in his right mind would intend a contingent gift to be an advancement. 

46. See the English case involving an annuity, cited in Gore's Estate; but cf. Wagner's Appeal, 38 Pa. 122 (1861), where the remainder was to the issue of the advancee and the principal amount was charged--this seems equitable but difficult to justify logically. 967 [The next page is 1001]

Discussion ¶ 1. Real Estate

As pointed out under § 2, ¶ 5c, and in the discussions of §-10 (h) of the 1947 Act under "Repealed Sec tions," when the spouse's allowance was first introduced by the Act of 1899, real estate was not subject to administration, so that it was necessary to insert procedural provisions to define the spouse's rights in real estate in such cases. Otherwise, it would have been impossible to determine what portion of the estate represented "the first $5,000" (now $10,000). These procedural provisions, with some modifications, were continued in the Acts of 1917 and 1947. 

By the Fiduciaries' Act of 1949, P.L. 512, 20 P. S. § 320.1 et seq., real estate was brought into administration in estates of decedents dying on or after January 1, 1950.

Provisions were made for inclusion of real estate in the inventory and account and its distribution pursuant to an award by the court in the same manner as personal property. The pertinent provision with respect to distribution in that act reads as follows:

SECTION 734. Distribution in Kind.-The court, for cause shown, may order the estate to be distributed in kind to the parties in interest, including fiduciaries. 

In such case, when there are two or more distributees, distribution may be made of undivided interests in real or personal estate, or the personal representative or a distributee may request the court to divide, partition and allot the property, or to direct the sale of the property. If such a request is made, the court, after such notice as it shall direct, shall fairly divide, partition and allot the property among the distributees in proportion to their respective interests, or the court may direct the personal representative to sell at a sale confined to the distributees, or at a private or public sale not so confined, any property which cannot be so divided, partitioned or allotted. 1002

INTESTATE ACT 

§ 10 See also 736 providing for the recording of the award of the decedent's real estate.

With real estate thus made subject to administration and award, § 10 of the Intestate Act of 1947 became superfluous. It was not repealed at that time, however, so that in estates of decedents dying between January 1, 1950, and

April 1, 1956, the two Acts contained overlapping provisions with respect to the distribution of real estate in cases involving the $10,000 spouse's allowance. This naturally resulted in some confusion. In Golden Estate, 78 

D. & C. 599, 1 Fid. Rep. 498 (O.C. Allegh. 1951) the court was asked to award real estate to a surviving husband as part of his $10,000 allowance at the audit of the administrator's account under § 734 of the Fiduciaries' Act of 1949. 

The court refused to do so, stating that § 10 of the Intestate Act of 1947 set forth the exclusive procedure for setting aside the allowance; distribution was suspended and the spouse was ordered to proceed with appraisals under that Act.1

The apparent conflict between the two sections was also noted in Tumolo Estate, 3 Fid. Rep. 57 (0.C. Phila. 1952) where the spouse had proceeded under old $10 of the Intestate Act and secured a decree setting aside real estate for the allowance. The question then arose as to whether a further decree of distribution should be entered under 734 of the Fiduciaries' Act, and the court held that it should. See also Polanco Estate No. 1, 2 Fid. Rep. 124 (O.C. Del. 1952), annotated in Fiduciary Review, March 

1952, where the spouse's right to select real estate in satisfaction of the allowance under old § 10 of the Intestate Act was mentioned as a reason for restraining the administrator from selling the property the spouse intended to select. 

Effective July 5, 1954, the Supreme Court in § 12, R. 2 of its Orphans' Court Rules, supplemented the procedure for setting aside the allowance under old $ 10 of the In- 

1. This holding is inconsistent with Roberts v. Ulsh, 67 D. & C. 297 (C.P. Cumb. 1949), annotated in Fiduciary Review, Sept. 1949, where it was held that the comparable procedure set forth in the Intestate Act of 1917 was not exclusive as a procedure for fixing the spouse's rights to the allowance so that the matter could be raised and decided in an action to quiet title. 1003

¶ 1 testate Act and then provided in R. 2 (c) that "The court may, at the request of the surviving spouse, award in distribution, specific real estate included in the account in satisfaction of, or on account of, the spouse's allowance of $10,000 without the necessity of compliance with the procedure outlined in subparagraphs (a) and (b) of this rule, provided, however, that all parties in interest agree in writing to the valuation at which the real estate is to be awarded." This partially modified the rule of Golden 

Estate but it will be noted that the consent of all parties had to be obtained if the procedure described by old § 10 of the Intestate Act was to be avoided.

The confusion has now been eliminated by rejecting § 10 of the Intestate Act of 1947 and replacing it with the present section which simply states that the allowance will be awarded and distributed in the same manner as any other distributive shares.

The only substantive change in the law is the elimination of the power in the spouse to choose particular real estate in satisfaction of the allowance. Under the old law, this right of choice was a by-product of the necessity for setting up machinery to fix relative rights in real estate. 

Under the present law the spouse will no longer have the absolute right to select particular real estate, but, as the second sentence of the new section states, the spouse or any other heir can still request the allocation of any real or personal property to his or her distributive share and the court in its discretion has the power under § 734 of the Fiduciaries Act to honor such a request if it is considered reasonable. In the absence of agreement by all parties, the court will probably require some sort of reappraisal of the property in question at the time of distribution, but so far as the statutory law is concerned there are no special requirements.

It is interesting to note that with the exception of this section and §§ 11 and 12 infra (which for all practical purposes merely restate what the law would have been if these sections were entirely eliminated) the Intestate Act is once more free of procedural provisions, as it was from 1833 to 

1909. See § 1, 15, Footnote 56.

The right of the spouse to choose specific items of personal property in satisfaction of the allowance was eliminated by § 10 of the Intestate Act of 1947 which simply omitted any provision for such selection. This change in the law was recognized by the court in Polanco Estate (No. 2), 80 D. & C. 457, 2 Fid. Rep. 129 (O.C. Del. 1952), annotated in Fiduciary Review, March 1952. The present amendment confirms this decision by expressly eliminating any right of selection in either real or personal property and providing for distribution in the same manner as other distributive shares. Hence a spouse or any other heir can always ask for a distribution of specific property at the audit under § 734 of the Fiduciaries' Act, but since 1947 there has been no absolute right to such selection in the case of a spouse claiming the allowance and no special provision for its award. 1005 [The next page is 1401]

Discussion The history of this provision in the Intestate Law is set forth in the discussion of old § 11 (see "Repealed Sections"). There was never any need for such a provision with respect to personal property and this was eliminated by Act of 1947. However, that act continued a special procedure for fixing title to real estate in cases where the spouse took the entire estate, although the need for such a provision probably vanished with the change in the substantive provision in § 2 of the same act which gives the wife the entire estate when the decedent is not survived by certain designated relatives (rather than in the absence of “known heirs" as in the Intestate Act of 1917).

With the passage of the Fiduciaries Act of 1949, P.L. 

512, P.S. § 320.1 et seq., effective January 1, 1950, real estate was brought into administration and a procedure established for its award in kind under $ 734 of that act. Hence 1401

11 of the Intestate Act of 1947 became worse than superfluous in that it seemed to provide an alternative procedure for fixing title to real estate in this particular type of case. 

By the amendment of 1955-56 the Legislature has now removed this conflict by in effect repealing § 11. The present provision which takes its place merely confirms what would have been law anyway in the absence of any provision on the subject. The spouse who takes the entire estate will now have both real and personal estate awarded at the audit pursuant to the Fiduciaries Act, just as the estate is awarded in any other type of case. 1402 [The next page is 1451]

INTESTATE ACT 

§ 12 

§ 12. PROPERTY DISTRIBUTABLE TO THE COMMONWEALTH 

When the estate is distributable to the Commonwealth, as statutory heir under the provisions of this act, it shall be reduced to cash in all cases by the personal representative, and awarded by the court in distribution to the Commonwealth, and paid by the personal representative through the Department of Revenue into the State Treasury. -As amended 1955-6, P.L. 1037 applicable to estates of decedents dying on or after April 1, 1956.

COMMISSIONERS' COMMENT This replaces the more cumbersome lan guage of Section 12 of the 1947 act, which was required until real property was included in the administration of the decedent's estate.

Old Law See § 12 the Act of 1947 under tab entitled "Repealed Sections."  

(1) The requirement of special notice to the Attorney General before the estate is reduced to cash is eliminated; (2) the special provision for sale of real estate as provided by the Price Act is eliminated so that such sales will now be made pursuant to the power of the administrator as set forth in the Fiduciaries Act; (3) also eliminated is the provision that distribution to the Commonwealth is to be made "as in the case of unclaimed funds in the hands of fiduciaries," thus eliminating the suggestion that the award is in the nature of an escheat rather than an award to the 

Commonwealth as an heir.

Discussion As set forth in the discussion of old $ 12 (see "Repealed Sections"), prior to 1947 the Commonwealth took only in the absence of "known heirs," and there was no limitation on the remoteness of blood relatives who could inherit. A pre-1948 decedent necessarily had heirs with a superior right to the Commonwealth's, even if his ancestry 1451

§ INTESTATE ACT 

had to be traced back to Adam. The Commonwealth took only when these heirs were not known, so that the Commonwealth necessarily claimed by escheat or analogy thereto, and not as an heir. This concept of the Commonwealth's rights in an intestate's estate was radically changed by the Act of 1947.

As set forth in the discussion of § 3 (4), the Commonwealth is now an heir and takes as such when there is no relative as close as a first cousin. Hence there is really no need to provide any special procedure in this type of case. For better or for worse, however, such a special provision was continued in § 12 of the Act of 1947. Included in this section, as originally worded, was a puzzling provision that the estate be distributed to the Commonwealth "as in the case of unclaimed funds in the hands of fiduciaries." The reference was presumably to § 1314 of the Fiscal Code of 1929, P.L. 343, 72 P.S. § 1314, which provides generally for payment to the Commonwealth of unclaimed fiduciary funds, subject to the rights of the owner to recover them when and if he appears. This caused confusion. On the one hand § 3 (6) clearly made the Commonwealth an heir, while old § 12 seemed to imply that the Commonwealth took merely because the real owner could not be found. 

In Davis Estate, 365 Pa. 605, 608 (1950), annotated in

Fiduciary Review, December 1950, this inconsistency between the two sections came to light. In that case, one claiming to be a half brother of the intestate failed to prove his relationship and no other relatives were known. The 

Orphans' Court held that the evidence submitted was insufficient and, without expressly dismissing the claim, awarded the fund to the Commonwealth "under the provision of § 12 of the Intestate Act of 1947, P.L. 80." The 

Supreme Court, while affirming the decision on the merits, held that the form of the decree was wrong, saying ". § 12 is merely a procedural section and cannot be the basis for an award. It is § 3 (6) of that Act which provides that the Commonwealth shall take as an heir where there are no first cousins or other closer relatives." (365 Pa. at 

608.) The Supreme Court went on to say that if the court 1452

INTESTATE ACT 

§ 12 did not wish to dismiss the claim of the half brother finally, it could have made the award under § 1314 of the Fiscal Code, 72 P.S. § 1314,—presumably with the thought that the fund thereupon would remain subject to claims for refund by this or other alleged heirs under § 504 of the Code, as amended, 72 P.S. § 504, or the Act of 1937, P.L. 2063, as amended, 27 P.S. § 443. The record was therefore remanded for the Orphans' Court to choose between an award under § 3 (6) of the Intestate Act and an award under 

§ 1314 of the Fiscal Code.¹ 

As already noted, however, old § 12 of the Intestate Act, which provided the procedure for awards under § 3 (6), by implication seemed to incorporate the procedure of § 1314 of the Fiscal Code. Hence, it is hard to avoid the conclusion that under § 12 as originally worded all roads led back to the Fiscal Code and the fund would have remained subject to refund to later-appearing heirs, regardless of which alternative form of award was selected.2 

The amendment of 1956 should eliminate the source of the confusion by taking out the illogical reference to "unclaimed funds in the hands of fiduciaries" in § 12. The result reached by the Supreme Court in Davis Estate, 365 Pa. 605, 608 (1950) is now confirmed and it should now be clear that when there is no relative as close as a first cousin, the Commonwealth takes in the same manner as any other heir.

Still to be distinguished is the case where a close relative is known or suspected to exist but cannot be found. 

In such a case the Commonwealth would have no claim as heir, but an award to the Commonwealth as custodian for unclaimed funds under the Fiscal Code might be appropriate, as the Supreme Court in Davis Estate suggested.

The provision that the limitation applies only to property distributed pursuant to court decree is new, but the old provision was so little used that the change will be of little consequence.

Discussion This is section 21 of the act of 1917, restricted so as to prohibit claims only when there has been distribution pursuant to decree of court. As presently worded, the provision might be startling to the casual reader until it is realized that the converse does not necessarily follow. This section, barring claims seven years after decedent's death, does not mean that a claim within the seven years will necessarily be successful. As a matter of fact, claims to property which has been distributed pursuant to decree are subject to numerous other possible defenses so that the present provision will be controlling only in the relatively rare case.

Curiously enough, this provision limiting claims to intestate's estates can trace its ancestry back further than most statutes now on our books. In the words of the court in Vogest's Estate, 31 D. & C. 169, 171 (O. C. Phila. 1937), "The first appearance of a limitation of this nature in our statutes is found in the 110th law passed in 1683, just two years after Charles II granted Pennsylvania to William

Penn. This act imposed a limitation of three years. This same limitation is found in the Act of 1684 (172d law) and the Act of 1693, 3 Sm. L. 154. The Act of 1700, 3 Sm. L. 

155, increased the limitation to seven years. Almost the identical language used in the section under discussion [section 21 of the Act of 1917] is found successively in section 5 of the Act of 1705, 3 Sm. L. 157, section 18 of the Act of 

April 19, 1794, 3 Sm. L. 143, and section 19 of the Act of 

April 8, 1833, P. L. 315." 1502

INTESTATE ACT § 13 

In spite of its great antiquity, however, the provision has been little used. A review of the few reported cases under the prior acts will be found in the February, 1947, issue of the Fiduciary Review. As there pointed out, there are only two lower court cases on the books where the limitation was controlling and they were probably incorrectly decided in the light of subsequent decisions. 

One reason for the lack of popularity of this provision is that the courts had restricted its application even when the language was much broader than it is now. The present provision expressly incorporates the restrictions earlier imposed by the courts and also adds some new ones. Thus, like the old act, it does not apply to real estate¹ or to creditors' claims (because it bars only persons "entitled under this act"). §14 

§14. PERSONAL ESTATE OF NON-RESIDENT 

Nothing contained in this act with respect to a distribution of personal estate shall extend to the estate of a decedent whose domicile at his death is out of the Commonwealth.

COMMISSIONERS' COMMENT-This is based on section 25 of the 1917 

act, which in turn was section 20 of the Act of 1833. 

Old Law

Section 25. Nothing in this act contained relative to a distribution of personal estate among kindred shall be construed to extend to the personal estate of an intestate, whose domicile at the time of his death was out of this Commonwealth. 

Intestate Act of 1917, P. L. 429.

There is no change.

Discussion This provision, which has been in the Intestate Act since 1833, merely restates one aspect of settled rules of conflict of laws concerning descent and distribution. See 

Barton's Trust, 348 Pa. 279, 284 (1944). These rules, which are definitely established in this state and elsewhere, are: (1) The descent of real estate is governed by the law of the state where the land is situated, regardless of where the decedent lived.¹ (2) The inheritance of personal property is governed by the law of decedent's domicile, regardless of where the property is situated.² 

The law of conflicts with regard to succession to personalty is simpler than in other fields of the law, because here there is no distinction made between tangibles and intangibles or between property having a situs and property which follows the owner. Thus, even if the personalty is a tangible situated in another state, or an intangible which has a "business situs" in another state, the law of decedent's domicile still controls the inheritance rights therein. Possibly the only exceptions to this rule are where the state of the property's situs has changed the common 

1. See Wolfe v. Lewisburg Trust Co., 305 Pa. 583, 589 (1931). See also discussion of "foreign decedents" under §2 (15d) (spouse's allowance). 

2. Welles's Est., 161 Pa. 218 (1894); Ehrhart's Est., 31 Pa. Super. 120 (1906); Crossley's Est., 135 Pa. Super. 524, 527 (1939); Restatement, Conflicts (1934) § 303. 1551

INTESTATE ACT 

law rule by statute, or where the decedent is survived by no relatives and the property escheats. In the latter case the indications are that the state where the property is located will appropriate it rather than turn it over to the state of decedent's domicile.¹

The general principles of conflicts with regard to succession are too well settled to be questioned, although difficulties sometimes arise in applying them. It is particularly important to distinguish between questions of succession and collateral questions which might affect inheritance indirectly. Thus, it might be uncertain whether a specific item of property is real or personal within the meaning of the above rules. This preliminary question should be determined according to the law of the state where the property is situated.5 A reference to the general property law of a foreign state might also be necessary in order to determine what property the Pennsylvania resident owned when he died, even though the Pennsylvania law will determine the inheritance of rights in personalty thus established. The legal status of the person claiming to be an heir under our law likewise might depend on the law of another state. The most obvious case of this sort is where it is necessary to determine the validity of a foreign marriage or divorce. Similar questions arise in determining whether a child was legally adopted or whether an illegitimate child was subsequently legitimated. Such questions are all preliminary to the question of inheritance which arises only after the nature and ownership of the property has been determined and the status of the parties fixed.

4. Restatement, Conflicts (1934) §§ 309 and 310; Goodrich, Conflict of 

Laws (1938) p. 435. 

5. Restatement, Conflicts (1934) § 208; cf. Welles's Est., 161 Pa. 218, 223 (1894). 

6. Cf. Mallory's Est., 300 Pa. 217 (1930). 

7. See authorities referred to in discussion of § 2 (¶3). Such a reference to foreign law in Pennsylvania estates might become necessary wherever our law refers to a legal status rather than factual situations. Thus, if our law says a "spouse" may inherit, the question of whether the claimant is the spouse is a mixed question of fact and law, and the law of the state where the alleged marriage took place might enter the picture. On the other hand, if our law states that a spouse may not inherit if he has deserted the decedent, only our law need be looked to on the question of desertion (as in Mallory's Est., 300 Pa. 

217 (1930)) because there is no reference to a legal status, but merely a wrongful act. 

8. See discussion of "Conflict of Laws" under §§ 7 (¶5) and 8 (¶5). 1552 [The next page is 1601]

§ 17 

§17. EFFECTIVE DATE 

This act shall take effect on the first day of January, one thousand nine hundred forty-eight, and shall apply to the real and personal estates of all persons dying on or after that day. The existing laws shall remain in full force and effect for the real and personal estates of all persons dying before that day.

COMMISSIONERS' COMMENT 

This is almost identical with the language of section 27 of the 1917 act. See also section 16 hereof which preserves existing legislation until January 1, 1948. 

Old Law

Section 27. This act shall take effect on the thirty-first day of December, nineteen hundred and seventeen, and shall apply to the estates, real and personal, of all persons dying intestate on or after said day. As to the estates, real and personal, of all persons dying before that day, the existing laws shall remain in full force and effect. 

Intestate Act of 1917, P. L. 429.

Discussion As to property owned by the decedent at his death this provision, which is almost identical with that in the 1917 act, is clear and precise. It is often important to bear this section in mind in cases where it becomes necessary to trace the ownership of reversions and other future interests through the estates of decedents who died prior to 1948as where there is an intestacy of the estate remaining after a life estate (see discussion of "When Heirs Are Determined" under section 1 (6)) or where the owner of a vested remainder dies before the estate comes into enjoyment. The old acts will continue to be effective in such cases for some years to come.

As to living persons to whose estates the present act will apply if they die intestate, it is important to remember the new limitations in section 3 of this act on the class of relatives who may inherit and the corresponding new preference given to the Commonwealth. Persons who have no close relatives but who were satisfied to let their estates descend to remote kindred under the act of 1917 will do well to make a will if they wish to prefer a second cousin to the Commonwealth. The same can be said of living per- 1701

§ INTESTATE ACT 

sons who have executed wills in the past, bequeathing alternative remainders to persons entitled under the intestate laws (see Wills Act $14 (4)). Unless such wills are changed, the estate might go to the Commonwealth and this might be contrary to the testator's intention. 

Sometimes it will not be possible for a person to make or change a will to avoid the effect of the present act. In 

Keen's Estate, 297 Pa. 22 (1929), the decedent had been insane and hence had no choice but to die intestate. It was held, nevertheless, that the act of 1917 applied and it is difficult to see how the court could have decided otherwise. 

The one qualification to the broad language of this effective date provision is that section 5 (a), which governs dower in real estate conveyed inter vivos without the wife's joinder, cannot affect the rights of the husband's grantee under a prior conveyance. See Merrick v. Dupont, 285 Pa. 

368 (1926), and discussion under section 5 (a) (3a). Since the present act merely re-enacts the 1917 provision concerning dower, however, this limitation on the effect of section 5 (a) will be important only in cases where the conveyance was made before 1917. 1702 [The next page is 1951]

WILLS ACT COMPLETE TEXT OF ACT AN ACT 

Relating to the form, execution, revocation, operation, and interpretatation of wills; to nuncupative wills; to the appointment of testamentary guardians; to elections to take under or against wills and the procedure in reference thereto. 

Section 1. Who May Make a Will. 

(a) Persons Twenty-one or Older. Any person of sound mind twenty-one years of age or older may by will dispose of all his real and personal estate subject to payment of debts and charges. 

(b) Persons in Military Service and Mariners. Dur ing any war in which the United States is engaged, a person of sound mind eighteen years of age or older and being in the Armed Forces of the United States in active service at home or abroad, or being a mariner on land or at sea, may by will dispose of all his real and personal estate subject to payment of debts and charges, and may thereafter revoke such will whether or not the United States is engaged in war and whether or not he is still in such service or is a mariner. 

Section 2. Form and Execution of a Will.-Every will, except nuncupative wills but including wills of mariners and persons in the Armed Forces of the United States, shall be in writing and shall be signed by the testator at the end thereof, subject to the following rules and exceptions: 

(1) Words Following Signature. The presence of any writing after the signature to a will, whether written before or after its execution, shall not invalidate that which precedes the signature. (2) Signature by Mark. If the testator is unable to sign his name for any reason, a will to which he makes 1953

WILLS ACT 

his mark and to which his name is subscribed in his presence before or after he makes his mark, shall be as valid as though he had signed his name thereto : Provided, He makes his mark in the presence of two witnesses who sign their names to the will in his presence. (3) Signature by Another. If the testator is unable to sign his name or to make his mark for any reason, a will to which his name is subscribed in his presence and by his express direction shall be as valid as though he had signed his name thereto : Provided, He declares the instrument to be his will in the presence of two witnesses who sign their names to it in his presence. 

Section 3. Nuncupative Wills. 

(a) When Permissible. A nuncupative will may be made only by a person in imminent peril of death, whether from illness or otherwise, shall be valid only if the testator died as a result of the peril, and must be declared to be his will by the testator before two disinterested witnesses, reduced to writing by or under the direction of both of the witnesses within ten days after such declaration, and submitted for probate within three months of the death of the testator. (b) Property Disposable. A nuncupative will attempting to dispose of personal property of an aggregate value in excess of five hundred dollars, or of real estate in any amount, shall be wholly void. (c) Effect on Prior Will. A nuncupative will shall neither revoke nor change an existing written will. 

Section 4. Witnesses.-No will shall be valid unless proved by the oaths or affirmations of two competent witnesses.

Section 5. Revocation of a Will.-No will or codicil in writing, or any part thereof, can be revoked or altered otherwise than: (1) Will or Codicil. By some other will or codicil in writing, 1954

WILLS ACT (2) Other Writing. By some other writing declaring the same, executed and proved in the manner required of wills, or (3) Act to the Document. By being burnt, torn, canceled, obliterated, or destroyed, with the intent and for the purpose of revocation, by the testator himself or by another person in his presence and by his express direction. If such act is done by any person other than the testator, the direction of the testator must be proved by the oaths or affirmations of two competent witnesses. 

Section 6. Revival of Revoked or Invalid Will.—If, after the making of any will, the testator shall execute a later will which expressly or by necessary implication revokes the earlier will, the revocation of the later will shall not revive the earlier will, unless the revocation is in writing and declares the intention of the testator to revive the earlier will, or unless, after such revocation, the earlier will shall be re-executed. Oral republication of itself shall be ineffective to revive a will. 

Section 7. Modification by Circumstances.-Wills shall be modified upon the occurrence of any of the following circumstances, among others: 

(1) Death Within Thirty Days; Religious and Chari table Gifts. Any bequest or devise for religious or charitable purposes included in a will or codicil executed within thirty days of the death of the testator shall be invalid unless all who would benefit by its invalidity agree that it shall be valid. The thirty-day period shall be so computed as to include the day on which the will or codicil is written and to exclude the day of death. Unless the testator directs otherwise, if such a will or codicil shall revoke or supersede a prior will or codicil executed at least thirty days before the testator's death, and not theretofore revoked or superseded and the original of which can be produced in legibile condition, and if each instrument shall contain an identical gift for substantially the same religious or charitable purpose, the gift in the later will or codicil shall be valid; or if each instrument shall give for sub- 1955

WILLS ACT 

stantially the same religious or charitable purpose a cash legacy or a share of the residuary estate or a share of the same asset, payable immediately or subject to identical prior estates and conditions, the later gift shall be valid to the extent to which it shall not exceed the prior gift. (2) Divorce. If the testator is divorced from the bonds of matrimony after making a will, all provisions in the will in favor of his spouse so divorced shall be thereby revoked. (3) Marriage. If the testator marries after making a will, the surviving spouse shall receive the share of the estate to which he would have been entitled had the testator died intestate, unless the will shall give him a greater share. (4) Birth or Adoption. If the testator fails to provide in his will for his child born or adopted after making his will unless it appears from the will that the failure was intentional, such child shall receive out of the testator's property not passing to a surviving spouse, such share as he would have received if the testator had died unmarried and intestate owning only that portion of his estate not passing to a surviving spouse. (5) Slaying. Any person who participates either as a principal or as an accessory before the fact in the wilful and unlawful killing of any person shall not in any way acquire property or receive any benefits as the result of the wilful and unlawful killing but such property or benefits shall be distributed as provided by law. 

Section 8. Change by Election of Surviving Spouse. 

(a) Right of Election. When a married person dies testate as to any part of his estate, the surviving spouse while living shall have a right of election under the limitations and conditions hereinafter stated. (b) Share of Estate. The surviving spouse, upon an election to take against the will, shall be entitled to onethird of the real and personal estate of the testator if the testator is survived by more than one child or by one or more children and the issue of a deceased child or children 1956

WILLS ACT 

or by the issue of more than one deceased child, and in all other circumstances the surviving spouse shall be entitled to one-half of the real and personal estate of the testator. (c) Powers of Appointment. The surviving spouse, upon an election to take against the will, shall not be entitled to any share in property passing under a power of appointment given by someone other than the testator and exercised by the will of the testator whether or not such power has been exercised in favor of the surviving spouse and whether or not the appointed and the individual estates have been blended.

Section 9. Forfeiture of Right of Election. 

(a) By Husband. A husband, who for one year or upwards previous to the death of his wife, shall have wilfully neglected or refused to provide for her, or who for that period or upwards shall have wilfully and maliciously deserted her, shall have no right of election. (b) By Wife. A wife, who for one year or upwards previous to the death of her husband shall have wilfully and maliciously deserted him, shall have no right of election. (c) Slayer. Any surviving spouse who participates either as a principal or as an accessory before the fact in the wilful and unlawful killing of the testator shall have no right of election. 

(d) Surviving Spouse as Witness. The surviving hus band or wife shall be a competent witness as to all matters pertinent to the issue of forfeiture under this section. 

Section 10. How Election Made.-The surviving spouse electing to take under or against the will shall manifest the election in writing signed by him and acknowledged before an officer authorized by law to take acknowledgments of deeds. The election or a copy thereof shall be mailed or delivered to the personal representative of the testator or his attorney. The election shall be filed in the office of the clerk of the orphans' court of the county where the will was probated, and a record shall be made of such filing by the clerk. When the estate includes real estate 1957

WILLS ACT 

the election or a duplicate original or a certified copy thereof shall be recorded in the office of the recorder of deeds of each county in which any of the real estate of the testator lies, and shall be indexed by the recorder in the grantors' index under the name of the testator, and in the grantees' index under the name of the surviving spouse. 

The costs of filing and recording the election shall be paid out of the estate as a part of the administration expenses. 

Section 11. Time for Making Election.-As between the surviving spouse and other legatees and devisees, the spouse's election shall be in time if within one year after the probate of the will the surviving spouse shall (1) mail or deliver the election or a copy thereof to the personal representative of the testator or his attorney or (2) file it in the office of the clerk of the orphans' court and mail or deliver a copy to the personal representative or his attorney or (3) record such election or a duplicate original or certified copy thereof in the office of the recorder of deeds of any county in which real estate of the testator lies and mail or deliver a copy to the personal representative or his attorney. The orphans' court, on application of the surviving spouse made within one year after the probate of the will, may extend the time for making the election for such period and upon such terms and conditions as the court shall deem proper under the circumstances. A certified copy of the decree of the court extending the time for making the election may be recorded and indexed in the office of the recorder of deeds in any county in which any of the real estate of the testator lies in the manner provided in section 10 hereof. 

Section 12. Failure to Make an Election. 

(a) Effect. Except as provided in section 7 (3) hereof, failure to make an election in the manner and within the time limits set forth in section 11 hereof shall be deemed an election to take under the will or an acquiescence in the provisions thereof. No payment or distribution from the estate, except the exemption allowed by law to the widow, shall be required to be made to the surviving spouse 1958

WILLS ACT 

within one year after the probate of the will unless his election to take under or acquiesce in the will shall have been made and filed as provided in section 10 hereof. (b) Personal Right. The right of election shall be personal to the surviving spouse and shall not be exercised after his death.

Section 13. Grantee or Lienholder.-An election shall be void as against a bona fide grantee of or holder of a lien on real estate in any county unless (1) the election or a duplicate original or certified copy thereof is recorded in such county within one year after the probate of the will or if thereafter then before the recording or entering of the instrument or lien under which such grantee or lienholder claims, or (2) a certified copy of the decree of the court extending the time for making the election has been recorded in such county within one year after the probate of the will or if thereafter then before the recording or entering of such instrument or lien and the election or a duplicate original or certified copy thereof has been recorded in such county within the time set by the court or if thereafter then before the recording or entering of such. instrument or lien.

Section 14. Rules of Interpretation.- (1) Wills Construed as if Executed Immediately Before Death. Every will shall be construed, with reference to the testator's real and personal estate, to speak and take effect as if it had been executed immediately before the death of the testator. (2) After-Acquired Property. The real and personal estate acquired by a testator after making his will shall pass by a general devise or bequest. 

(3) Devises of Real Estate. All devises of real estate shall pass the whole estate of the testator in the premises devised, although there be no words of inheritance or of perpetuity. 1959

WILLS ACT 

(4) Meaning of "Heirs" and "Next of Kin" etc. 

Time of Ascertaining Class. A devise or bequest of real or personal estate, whether directly or in trust, to the testor's or another designated person's "heirs" or "next of kin" or "relatives" or "family" or to "the persons thereunto entitled under the intestate laws" or to persons described by words of similar import, shall mean those persons, including the spouse, who would take under the intestate laws if the testator or other designated person were to die intestate at the time when such class is to be ascertained, a resident of the Commonwealth, and owning the estate so devised or bequeathed: Provided, however, That the share of a spouse, other than the spouse of the testator, shall not include the ten thousand dollar allowance under the intestate laws. The time when such class is to be ascertained shall be the time when the devise or bequest is to take effect in enjoyment. (5) Meaning of "Die Without Issue" and Similar Phrases. In any devise or bequest of real or personal estate, the words "die without issue" "die without leaving issue" "have no issue" or other words importing either a want or failure of issue of any person in his lifetime or at the time of his death, or an indefinite failure of his issue, shall be construed to mean a want or failure of issue in his lifetime or at his death, and not an indefinite failure of his issue. (6) Adopted Children. In construing a will making a devise or bequest to a person or persons described by relationship to the testator or to another, any person adopted before the death of the testator shall be considered the child of his adopting parent or parents and not the child of his natural parents: Provided, That if a natural parent shall have married the adopting parent before the testator's death, the adopted person shall also be considered the child of such natural parent. (7) Illegitimates. In construing a will making a devise or bequest to a person or persons described by relationship to the testator or to another, an illegitimate per- *"or," omitted in original. 1960

WILLS ACT 

son shall be considered the child of his mother and not of his father; Provided, That when the parents of a person born illegitimate shall have married each other, he shall thereafter be considered legitimate. 

(8) Lapsed and Void Devises and Legacies. Substi tution of Issue. A devise or bequest to a child or other issue of the testator or to his brother or sister or to a child of his brother or sister whether designated by name or as one of a class shall not lapse if the beneficiary shall fail to survive the testator and shall leave issue surviving the testator but shall pass to such surviving issue who shall take per stirpes the share which their deceased ancestor would have taken had he survived the testator; Provided, That such a devise or bequest to a brother or sister or to the child of a brother or sister shall lapse to the extent to which it will pass to the testator's spouse or issue as a part of the residuary estate or under the intestate laws. 

(9) Lapsed and Void Devises and Legacies. Shares not in Residue. A devise or bequest not being part of the residuary estate which shall fail or be void because the beneficiary fails to survive the testator or because it is contrary to law or otherwise incapable of taking effect or which has been revoked by the testator or is undisposed of or is released or disclaimed by the beneficiary, if it shall not pass to the issue of the beneficiary under the provisions of clause (8) hereof, and if the disposition thereof shall not be otherwise expressly provided for by law, shall be included in the residuary devise or bequest, if any, contained in the will. 

(10) Lapsed and Void Devises and Legacies. Shares in Residue. When a devise or bequest as described in clause (9) hereof shall be included in a residuary clause of the will and shall not be available to the issue of the devisee or legatee under the provisions of clause (8) hereof, and if the disposition shall not be otherwise expressly provided for by law, it shall pass to the other residuary devisees or legatees, if any there be, in proportion to their respective shares or interests in the residue. 1961

WILLS ACT (11) Lapsed and Void Devises and Legacies. Adopted 

Persons and Illegitimates. For the purposes of the foregoing clauses of this section, the words "child" or "issue" shall include persons claiming by or through adoption and an illegitimate person shall be considered the child of his mother and not of his father; Provided, That when the parents of a person born illegitimate shall have married each other, he shall thereafter be considered legitimate. (12) Real Estate Subject to a Mortgage. The devisee of real estate which is subject to a mortgage shall take subject thereto, and shall not be entitled to exoneration out of the other estate of the testator, real or personal; and this whether the mortgage was created by the testator or by a previous owner or owners, and notwithstanding any general direction by the testator that his debts be paid. (13) Lien of Pecuniary Legacies. Pecuniary legacies of one hundred dollars or less shall not be a charge on any of the testator's real estate. All pecuniary legacies in excess of the principal sum of one hundred dollars shall be charged upon, and payable out of, any real estate not specifically devised, where the personal estate is or becomes insufficient for their payment. (14) Power of Appointment. A general devise of the real estate of the testator, or of the real estate of the testator in any place, or in the occupation of any person mentioned in his will, or otherwise described in a general manner, shall be construed to include any real estate, or any real estate to which such description shall extend, as the case may be, which he shall have power to appoint in any manner he shall think proper, and shall operate as an execution of such power. In like manner, a bequest of the personal estate of the testator, or any bequest of personal property described in a general manner, shall be construed to include any personal estate, or any personal estate to which such description shall extend, as the case may be, which he shall have power to appoint in any manner he shall think proper, and shall operate as an execution of such power. 

In like manner, a general pecuniary legacy, when the assets. 1962

WILLS ACT 

of the individual estate of the testator are not sufficient for its payment, shall, to the extent necessary to make possible the payment of the legacy, be construed to include any estate which the testator shall have power to appoint in any manner he shall think proper, and shall to such extent operate as an execution of such power. 

Section 15. Devise in Fee Tail Abolished.-Whenever by any devise an estate in fee tail would be created according to the common law of the Commonwealth, it shall pass an estate in fee simple, and as such shall be inheritable and freely alienable.

Section 16. Rule in Shelley's Case.-The rules* in 

Shelley's Case and its corollaries shall not be applied, and a devise or bequest directly or in trust which shall express an intent to create an estate for life with remainder to the life tenant's heirs or the heirs of his body or his issue or his next of kin or persons described by words of similar import, shall not operate to give such life tenant an estate in fee in real estate or an absolute estate in personalty. 

Section 17. Alienage.-Real and personal estate shall pass without regard to whether the testator or any devisee or legatee is or has been an alien. 

Section 18. Testamentary Guardian. 

(a) Guardian of the Person. A person competent to make a will, being the sole surviving parent or adopting parent of any unmarried minor child, may appoint a testamentary guardian of the person of such child during his minority, or for any shorter period: Provided, That no father who, for one year or upwards previous to his death, shall have wilfully neglected or refused to provide for his child, and no mother who for a like period, shall have deserted her child or wilfully failed to perform her parental duties, shall have the right to appoint a testamentary guardian of the person of such child. (b) Guardian of the Estate. Any person may by will appoint a testamentary guardian of the real or personal * [Should be "rule"-Ed.] 1963

WILLS ACT 

estate which he shall devise, bequeath, or appoint to a minor.

Section 19. Personal Estate of Non-Resident.-Noth ing contained in this act shall be construed to apply to the disposition of personal estate by a testator whose domicile at the time of his death is out of the Commonwealth. 

Section 20. Short Title. This act shall be known and may be cited as the Wills Act of 1947.

Section 21. Repealer.-The following acts and parts of acts of assembly and all amendments of each are hereby repealed as respectively indicated, but so far only as relates to the estates, real and personal, of any person or persons dying on or after the first day of January, one thousand nine hundred forty-eight: (1) The act, approved the twenty-third day of February, one thousand seven hundred ninety-one (three Smith's Laws, four), entitled "A supplement to the Act, entitled 'An act to declare and regulate escheats,' '"' in so far as it relates to dispositions of real or personal estate by wills. (2) The act, approved the seventh day of June, one thousand nine hundred seventeen (Pamphlet Laws 403), entitled "An act relating to the form, execution, revocation, and interpretation of wills; to nuncupative wills; to the appointment of testamentary guardians; to spendthrift trusts; to forfeiture of devise or legacy in case of murder of testator; to elections to take under or against wills, and to the recording and registering of such elections and of decrees relative thereto, and to the fees therefor," absolutely. (3) The act, approved the twenty-fourth day of April, one thousand nine hundred thirty-one (Pamphlet Laws 46), entitled "An act making the surviving spouse competent to testify in all cases where the right of such spouse to share in a deceased spouse's estate is disputed because of alleged desertion or nonsupport of the decedent, whether decedent died testate or intestate," in so far as it relates to dispositions of real or personal estate by wills. 1964

WILLS ACT 

(4) All other acts and parts of acts inconsistent herewith are hereby repealed. 

Section 22. Effective Date.-This act shall take effect on the first day of January, one thousand nine hundred forty-eight, and shall apply only to the wills of all persons dying on or after that day. As to the wills of persons dying before that day, the existing law shall remain in full force and effect.

AN ACT 

To amend section 1 of the act, approved the twenty-fourth day of April, one thousand nine hundred forty-seven (Pamphlet Laws 89), entitled "An act relating to the form, execution, revocation, operation, and interpretation of wills; to nuncupative wills; to the appointment of testamentary guardians; to elections to take under or against wills and the procedure in reference thereto," by changing the provisions which permit minors in military service and mariners to dispose of their property by will. 

Section 1. Section 1 of the act, approved the twenty fourth day of April, one thousand nine hundred forty-seven (Pamphlet Laws 89), entitled "An act relating to the form, execution, revocation, operation, and interpretation of wills; to nuncupative wills; to the appointment of testamentary guardians; to elections to take under or against wills and the procedure in reference thereto," is hereby amended to read as follows: 

1965

WILLS ACT Section 1. Who May Make a Will.— 

(a) Persons Twenty-one or Older. Any person of sound mind twenty-one years of age or older may by will dispose of all his real and personal estate subject to payment of debts and charges. 

(b) Persons in Military Service and Mariners. 1. Persons Who May Make Wills 

Insofar as this provision describes the type of person who is competent to make a will (other than soldiers and mariners provided for in section 1 (b)), the only change from the prior act is the elimination of the redundant phrase "whether married or single." Since wills of married women are no longer a novelty, it was considered unnecessary to continue the specific reference to married status even for the sake of emphasis.¹ Plainly a married woman is a "person."

The requirements of age and mental capacity have remained the same since 1833 when the Legislature rejected the Commissioners' recommendation that the age be reduced to eighteen. That these requirements refer to the date of the will's execution rather than the date of decedent's death is clear from common sense, and from the cases on mental capacity (discussed below). The act of 

1833 was a little more explicit on this point, but the present act follows the act of 1917 which caused no confusion. 

As to the age requirement, it might be mentioned in passing that there is authority in other jurisdictions to the effect that a person becomes of age the day before his twenty-first birthday.2 This seems to be the reductio ad 

1. The act of 1833, P. L. 249, specifically excepted married women in section 1 but make special provision for exercising powers and disposing of personalty. Later, the married women's property act of 1848, P. L. 536, permitted devises by a will witnessed by the husband. The act of 1893, P. L. 344, gave married women broad powers to "dispose of" their property and in section 5 gave them specific power to dispose of their property by will. Section 5 of the act of 1893 was repealed by the Wills Act of 1917 which, in section 1, eliminated the exception relating to married women in the act of 1833, and in order to avoid any doubt on the subject, provided that any person "whether married or single" could make a will. The present act eliminates these words as unnecessary. Aside from the fact that the word "person" is broad enough to include married women, it will be noted that section 1 of the act of 1893, as amended in 1945, P. L. 625, 48 P. S. § 31, still remains on the books giving married women broad powers to "dispose of" property. As to the requirement that the testator be "of sound mind," there is a good résumé of the distinctions drawn in the numberless cases on the subject in Hutton's Wills in Pennsylvania (1933) p. 18 et seq., and more recently in 

Sturgeon's Will, 357 Pa. 75, 81 (1947). The decisions are often of little value beyond the facts of the particular case, but the broad principles which the courts are supposed to apply can be summarized briefly. It is said that the testator must have "a full and intelligent knowledge of the act he is engaged in, a full knowledge of the property he possesses, an intelligent perception and understanding of the disposition he desires to make of it and of the persons and objects he desires shall be the recipients of his bounty." As every lawyer knows, however, none of these requirements is very strict. The testator's knowledge of his property can be pretty vague, and the mere fact that he disinherited natural objects of his bounty does not prove that he lacked a clear idea of whom he intended to favor.5 

Even an adjudicated lunatic may make a will in a lucid interval, and any number of infirmities, including incapacity to transact ordinary business does not preclude capacity to make a will. Finally, and perhaps most important, it is well settled that there is a presumption of sanity, so that the contestants always have the burden of proof or at least the burden of going forward with the evidence—even where there are no subscribing witnesses.8 

The one qualification of this rule is that an adjudication of general incompetency will shift to the proponents the burden of showing that the will was made during a lucid interval."

2. Property Which May Pass by Will-In General 

With regard to property which may pass by will, the present act eliminates all the references in the old statute to special types of property and provides simply that the testator may dispose of "all his real and personal estate subject to payment of debts and charges." It is clear, however, that the omitted provisions were unnecessary in the act of 1917 and that the law will remain unchanged. 

In general, it may be said that in this state a person may devise or bequeath any interest which he owns and which survives his death-or, in other words, any interest which would have passed by intestacy in the absence of a will. Thus, the discussion under section 1 of the Intestate 

Act of what interests the decedent owns at his death and which of those interests survive him is equally relevant here.

Possible exceptions to the rule that a person may devise or bequeath any estate of inheritance are discussed below in connection with the non-beneficial title which the decedent held as a fiduciary and interests which are subject to a valid restraint on testamentary alienation. In all other cases the question turns out to be simply one of whether the particular interest in fact survived the decedent's death. As the subsequent discussion will show, the Pennsylvania courts have been unusually free from the inhibitions of the old common law with respect to testamentary power over certain types of property. Of course, it is assumed that the will is broad enough to cover the property and that obligations to spouse and creditor are satisfied. If this is so, then under our cases the phrase "real and personal estate" is broad enough to cover anything of value which remains as an asset of the decedent's estate. 2004

WILLS ACT 

§1 (a) • • 

3. Interests Specifically Mentioned in Old Act 

The provisions in the old act relating to estates pur auter vie, joint tenancies, emblements and accrued rents were inherited from the act of 1833. Whatever reasons might have existed for making specific references to these types of property in 1833 no longer exist today. 

> 10 Thus, the Commission of 1917 followed the act of 1833 and specifically mentioned in section 1 an "estate . . . held for the life or lives of any other person or persons. 

There was some reason for this, because the estate pur auter vie at common law was not an estate of inheritance. 

When the tenant died before the cestui que vie, the interest in the property during the remainder of the term passed to whoever happened to take possession.11 Statutory correction of this legal curiosity is therefore necessary, but the Wills Act is scarcely the place for it, in that a similar problem arises in case of intestacy and the problem is essentially one of property law. The estate pur auter vie must be converted into an estate of inheritance which will survive the death of the owner. For these reasons, the reference to estates pur auter vie was omitted in this act and a provision relating to them inserted as section 15 of the Estates Act of 1947.12 By the terms of that provision, estates for the life of another are made into estates of inheritance, so that they will necessarily be included as property of the decedent which he can dispose of by will under the general language of the present section of the Wills Act.

The present section likewise omits the specific reference to joint tenancies found in section 1 of both the act of 1917 and the act of 1833. The Commission of 1833 explained that it "followed the Act of Assembly of 31 March, 1812, [P. L. 259, 20 P. S. § 121] in providing that the interest of a joint tenant shall pass by devise." That act, which is still in effect, eliminates the right of survivorship as a 10. The provision was based on a similar provision in the English Statute of Frauds, 27 Chas. II, c. 3, § 12. 

11. A different result followed where the estate was limited to the tenant "and his heirs." See fuller discussion and authorities cited under $15 of the 

Estates Act. 

12. The subject is also dealt with in § 11 (g) of the Fiduciaries Act of 1917, P. L. 447, 20 P. S. § 448. 2005

§(a) 

WILLS ACT 

¶ 3 normal incident to joint ownership, and expressly provides that the interest of the deceased tenant shall "descend or pass by devise The drafters of the 1947 act properly felt that the act of 1812 was now old enough to stand on its own feet. It must be borne in mind, however, that the act of 1812 merely provides a rule of construction to be used when the intent of the conveyor is not clear 13 and that the act has no application to a conveyance to husband and wife.¹4 Hence, it is still possible that the interest of a joint owner will pass automatically to the surviving tenant and that there will be nothing to pass under the decedent's will.1 15 99 The origin of the curious reference to emblements and accrued rents of a deceased life tenant in the act of 1833 and section 7 of the act of 1917 is more obscure. The part about "emblements or growing crops on lands held by a widow in dower" was inspired by a similar provision in the Statute of Merton.18 Whatever may have been the reason for such legislation in thirteenth century England, there is certainly no need for it in Pennsylvania todayif only for the reason that common law dower has long been abolished and the statutory share of a widow is no longer limited to a life interest. The 1833 commission went further than the Statute of Merton, however, and included emblements, rents, and "other periodic payments accruing to any tenant for life." The propriety of this extension was "conceived to be apparent," 17 and no further explanation was given. Granted that there are difficulties in enforcing the rights of a deceased life tenant against his lessee arising from the law of landlord and tenant,18 no

The elimination of these provisions will therefore have no effect on prior law. 

4. Future Interests-Vested, Contingent, and Expectant

It would seem elementary that the mere fact that an interest does not take effect in enjoyment until after the owner's death in no way interferes with his power to dispose of it by will. Thus, no one has ever questioned that a reversion or a vested remainder may be bequeathed or devised, and this is so regardless of whether the interest is subject to divestment or is vested in a member of a class subject to open.20 Where the future interest is not vested in the decedent, the law elsewhere is not so clear, but the Pennsylvania courts have on the whole taken a very liberal attitude in such cases. Thus, it seems well established under our decisions that an executory or contingent interest in an ascertained person can pass under his will.21 

As pointed out in the discussion of contingent interests under section 1 of the Intestate Act, it is sometimes said that remainders to unascertained persons cannot pass by will or descent upon the death of the presumptive remainderman before the class is ascertained.22 What is really meant is that the decedent's death would probably disqualify him as a possible remainderman in ninety-nine of such cases out of a hundred.
