§1 (a) It appears, therefore, that a Pennsylvania testator has full power to dispose by will of future interests which are not certain to take effect. Of course, the beneficiary takes only what the testator had, so that the gift may turn out to be worthless. Until this is determined, however, the testator has an interest of speculative value which will survive his death. There is some reason to draw a distinction between property and a mere "expectancy” in the law of attachment, because if the future enjoyment of the interest is too uncertain, the amount bid at the sheriff's sale will be quite arbitrary.29 In the law of wills, however, there is no necessity to draw such a distinction or to declare an enforced intestacy, no matter how uncertain it is that the interest will eventually take effect in enjoyment. 

Insofar as they have passed on the subject, the Pennsylvania decisions are in accord with this principle. 

¶ 5. Property Adversely Held 

There is an almost forgotten doctrine in the old common law that a person could not alienate that which was adversely held by another. A real action might survive the owner's death, but a voluntary transfer of it, even by will, was thought to be champertous. Here again, however, the inhibitions of the common law have given little trouble to the Pennsylvania courts which rejected the doctrine long ago. The cases and relevant statutes on the subject are reviewed in English's article on the Uniform 

Property Act, 46 Dick. L. Rev. at 149 (1942). 

¶ 6. Title Held by Testator as Fiduciary 

When a trustee dies, the title to the trust property might pass to a co-trustee or to a successor named in the instrument. Where there is no co-trustee or successor named, the Restatement of Trusts (1935) § 105 provides as follows: "Upon the death of a sole trustee who has devised or bequeathed the trust property, the title to the trust property passes subject to the trust to the devisee or legatee, unless it is otherwise provided by the terms of 

29. See Pennsylvania Company v. Youngman, 314 Pa. 277, 282 (1934); for general discussion of voluntary and involuntary inter vivos alienation of contingent interests see English, "Uniform Property Act in Pennsylvania," 46 

Dick. L. Rev. 37, 144 (1942). 2009

§(a) WILLS ACT 

17 the trust or by statute." In Dunlap v. Dunlap, 92 Pa. 

Super. 602 (1927), the legal title to personalty of a sole trustee was said to pass to his executor, but no Pennsylvania case has been found passing on whether trust property may be devised and bequeathed. Ordinarily the question is of no practical importance because it is clear that neither executor, legatee nor devisee would have the power to administer the trust.30 Such power is suspended until a substituted trustee is duly appointed, so that whoever theoretically succeeds to the property at the moment of the trustee's death is a mere depository of the legal title in the meantime. 

¶7. Interests Subject to a Valid Restraint on Alienation 

It is possible that the terms of the conveyance to the decedent might validly prohibit the alienation by will of an interest which decedent owned and which survived him. 

Such a case, however, would be unusual. Most disabling or forfeiture restraints on the alienation of a legal interest are void. But even assuming a valid restraint on inter vivos transfers by the owner, it is doubtful whether the restraint would be construed as prohibiting testamentary disposition.32 Thus, a spendthrift provision applicable to an equitable estate of inheritance might be valid, but should not be construed to restrict the power of the owner to dispose of the interest by will. The purpose of such a provision is usually to protect the beneficiary during his lifetime and not to force an intestacy at his death.34 At

8. Unowned Property Subject to Testamentary Power a. General

A type of problem which does not arise in cases of intestacy is presented in cases where the decedent by will purports to exercise a power over property which he does not own.

The simplest case is where the decedent has reserved or has been given a general power to appoint the principal of a trust by will. Under section 14 (14) of the present act, even a general devise or bequest not specifically referring to the power is ordinarily sufficient to exercise a power of this sort. In other cases, the terms of the instrument creating or reserving the power do not make it clear whether it may be exercised by will. It then becomes necessary to construe the particular instrument in order to determine what was intended. It has been held, for example, that a power to consume must be exercised during the donee's lifetime or not at all. A general power to "dispose" of property, however, is said to be broad enough to permit disposal by will.37 36 An interesting line of cases dealing with this general subject are those in which the decedent has transferred to others certain interests in property but has reserved a power to destroy such interests and regain complete title to the property up until the moment of his death-as in cases of revocable trusts, life insurance policies, and the like. Certain transactions of this type have been discussed in connection with section 1 (4) of the Intestate Act. 

There, the question was whether the attempted inter vivos transfer was effective to begin with. Plainly, if no inter vivos transfer was effectively completed, the decedent still

Revocable Trusts

In the case of a revocable inter vivos trust, the terms of the reserved power apparently must be strictly complied with. Where the instrument stated that the trust could be revoked by a signed writing, it was held to be revocable by will.39 But where the trust provided that it could be revoked by "written notice" to the trustee, one lower court held that a will attempting to exercise the power did not fulfill the requirement.40 The latter decision is strongly supported by Shapley's Trust, 353 Pa. 499 (1946), where the inter vivos trust reserved the power to revoke it by an "instrument in writing executed by me and lodged with the Trustee." The trust was not revoked during the settlor's lifetime but the will was delivered to the trustee by the executor after the settlor's death. c. Life Insurance 

A similar problem is presented where a person has purchased life insurance reserving the power to change the named beneficiary.. It has been noted under section 1 (¶ 4f) of the Intestate Act that insurance policies constitute an historical exception to the ordinary rules of law relating to inter vivos transactions having a testamentary character. 

Assuming, therefore, that the proceeds of a policy with a named beneficiary will not ordinarily form a part of the insured's estate, can the insured change the beneficiary by will? The question under various types of policies is dis cussed in Couch on Insurance (1929) §§ 318 and 319. Or dinarily, policies provide for certain formalities for changing the beneficiary, such as endorsement on the face of the policy, but there is general authority to the effect that such provisions are merely for the protection of the company and are irrelevant in disputes between rival claimants.1 This has led at least one lower court to hold that the beneficiary of such a policy can be changed by an express provision in a will.42 d. Tentative Trusts

As noted under section 1 (¶ 4f) of the Intestate Act, there is a split of authority as to whether the registration of undelivered bonds in these forms is sufficient to pass any title at all. A recent adjudication in the Philadelphia Orphans' Court adopted an intermediate position on the question. The will made a specific bequest to A of all bonds in the testator's safe deposit box. Some bonds were found in the box registered in the name of decedent and payable on death to B. Other bonds were found outside the box payable on death to C. It was held (1) that the naming of the alternative beneficiary was sufficient to pass title to the named person in the absence of a will specifically revoking the gift so that C took his bonds, but (2) that the will effectively revoked the gift to B as to the bonds in the safe deposit box, so that these were made part of the estate and passed to A under the will. In other words, the bonds were treated in the same manner as a tentative trust-effective to pass title but revocable by will. The decision seems questionable in view of the Treasury regulations prohibiting the transfer of such bonds. It would appear that these regulations are closely connected with the Government's program for inflation control and that the prohibition against transfers is something more than a mere facility of payment clause for the convenience of the Government. The court considered this aspect of the case, however, and decided that in the absence of an act of Congress, the state law was not superseded.

WILLS ACT 

§ 1 (b) (b) Persons in Military Service and Mariners.

During any war in which the United States is engaged, a person of sound mind, eighteen years of age or older and being in the Armed Forces of the United States in active service at home or abroad, or being a mariner on land or at sea, may by will dispose of all his real and personal estate subject to payment of debts and charges and may thereafter revoke such will whether or not the United States is engaged in war and whether or not he is still in such service or is a mariner.

COMMISSIONERS' COMMENT Subsection (b) takes the place of sec tion 5 of the 1917 act which reads: [see below] 

Subsection (b) changes the law in the following respects: 

1. It permits a person in the armed forces of the United 

States or a mariner, in time of war, to dispose of real as well as personal estate if he is eighteen years of age or older. 

2. It invalidates wills made by all persons who have not attained eighteen years of age. 

3. It makes all persons comply with the safeguards of the 

Wills Act. 

4. It recognizes expressly the right to revoke such a will before attaining the age of 21, whether or not the status giving the privilege has been retained. 

5. It permits mariners and soldiers between eighteen and twenty-one years of age to have their wills written at home without requiring them to be in "actual military service" or "at 

sea. 

The term "active service" as distinguished from "reserve" service has a recognized meaning. It is not the equivalent of the words "actual military service" included in section 5 of the 

1917 act. 

Old Law

Section 5. Notwithstanding this act, any mariner being at sea, or any soldier being in actual military service, may dispose of his movables, wages, and personal estate as he might have done before the making of this act. 

Wills Act of 1917, P. L. 403. 

The principal change is that wills of soldiers and mariners are now subject to the formal requirements of the Wills Act, the only special dispensation now being the 2051

WILLS ACT 

T1 lower age requirement. The situations to which the new provision applies are also considerably changed. It applies only during a war (even as to mariners); it applies to persons in the Armed Forces in active service (instead of "actual military service"); it applies to mariners at sea or on land; and it applies to wills of both real and personal property.

Discussion ¶ 1. General. 

2. Cases Where Lower Age Requirement Applies. 

13. Revocation. ¶ 1. General

This section for the first time since Julius Caesar subjects the wills of soldiers and mariners to the formal requirements for ordinary wills. The quaint history of legislation, or rather the absence of legislation, dealing with such wills was traced by Judge Gest in Henninger's Estate, 30 Dist. 413 (O. C. Phila. 1921). As there pointed out, every Wills Act in Pennsylvania since 1705 had followed the Roman and English tradition of exempting from its provisions wills of personalty by soldiers and mariners. 

As a result, such wills were governed by the principles applied by the ecclesiastical courts in England prior to the 

Statute of Frauds. If the required testamentary intent could be shown, the will could be oral and the testator could be as young as fourteen. For the old exemption to apply, however, the soldier had to be "in actual military service" and the mariner had to be "at sea" when the will was made-requirements which caused many questions under the old law.2 

1. In Pennsylvania, at least, the requirement of testamentary intent seems to have been the factor on which most of the cases turned. Smith's Est., 308 Pa. 

265 (1932) (where the question did not actually arise) seemed to indicate a very liberal interpretation of this requirement, but Buehrer's Will, 349 Pa. 353 (1944), represents a very strict holding on the issue of intent and removed all doubt that the intent requirements were just as stringent in this type of case as in cases of ordinary wills. Other interesting cases on this point are Satar's

1935). See general discussion of testamentary intent infra under section 2 (2a).

WILLS ACT 

§1 (b) The present act retains only a vestige of the ancient exemption. A soldier's or mariner's will is now subjected to the provisions of the Wills Act and for nearly all purposes is treated as any other will. Thus, it must be in writing and executed as provided in section 2 (which now expressly applies to all wills "including wills of mariners and persons in the Armed Forces'), except in the rare case where the strict conditions for nuncupative wills are complied with under section 3. The only remaining special exemption is that during a war the age requirement is lowered to eighteen for testators who are in the military service or who are mariners. 

[[2. Cases Where Lower Age Requirement Applies 

Several changes will be noticed in the class to which the remaining dispensation under the new provision applies: (1) The lower age requirement is effective only when the will is executed "during any war in which the United States is engaged." That the necessity for a state of war refers to the time the will is executed and not to the date of death is plain for the same reasons already mentioned in connection with the requirements of mental capacity and age under section 1 (a) (¶1). (Note also the language in the present subsection relating to revocation in this respect.) Whether the courts will adopt a technical or a realistic construction of the word "war" is impossible to predict. Probably less trouble will be encountered in the long run if the popular meaning of the word is adopted and the fact of war determined in each case independently of what Congress or the President has declared to be the theoretical condition. As can be seen from a moment's reflection, the appearance of certainty presented by a technical construction is deceiving. A full scale war might never be declared, and on the other hand we might be theoretically at war with a nation years after the last gun has been fired. 

3. Query whether a state of war was necessary for the soldier's exemption under the old act to apply. The indications are that war was implied in the requirements of actual military service. See authorities supra note 2 and infra note 4. 2053

13 (2) The new provision applies to persons "in the Armed Forces of the United States in active service at home or abroad" rather than to "soldiers in actual military service" as under the old act. It will first be observed that the test is no longer whether the testator is a "soldier" but whether he is in any branch of our "Armed Forces." 

The significance of the change from "actual military service" to "active service at home or abroad" is not immediately apparent but is explained by the notes of the Commissioners. The intention was to distinguish between the reserve and "active" service in the military sense, and to eliminate the fine spun distinctions concerning the meaning of "actual" military service, under the old act. Thus, it would appear from the additional words "at home or abroad" that a soldier on furlough is in "active service" within the intended meaning of this clause. (3) Consistent with the broadening of the class of soldeirs covered by the section is the broadening of the class of mariners to include mariners on land as well as on sea.5 

Notice, however, that the requirement that the will be made during a war applies to mariners as well as persons in the armed forces. §1 (b) charged soldier who is still under age may revoke his prior will but cannot make a new one until he reaches twenty-one. 

No mention is made in this section of partial revocation, and the omission is pointed in view of the express reference to partial revocation in section 5. Since any revocation of a part only of a will ordinarily enlarges the residuary gift indirectly, it probably should not be permitted in the absence of specific statutory authorization, although it is difficult to predict how the courts will treat this question. See, generally, 62 A. L. R. 1367, 1376 and compare Lightner's

The mechanics of revocation under this provision are, of course, governed by section 5, where the permissible methods of revocation are enumerated. It will be seen that the first method of revoking a will mentioned in that section is "by some other will or codicil." Suppose a discharged soldier, while still a minor, purports to make a will which is inconsistent with a will made when he was in the service. Would this be effective as a revocation, although ineffective as a will? Probably not, because the new writing would not be a "will" within the meaning of clause (1) of section 5. However, if the new writing expressly revoked the former will, it should qualify as a revocation by "other writing" under clause (2). Note that dependent relative revocation might be argued in such a case; see discussion of this doctrine under section 5 (¶ 8). 2055 [The next page is 2101]

§2. FORM AND EXECUTION OF A WILL 

Every will, except nuncupative wills but including wills of mariners and persons in the Armed Forces of the United States, shall be in writing and shall be signed by the testator at the end thereof, subject to the following rules and exceptions:

COMMISSIONERS' COMMENT "Every will *** shall be in writing and shall be signed by the testator at the end thereof" has been taken from section 2 of the 1917 act. The words "including wills of mariners and persons in the Armed Forces of the United States" are intended to take the place of section 5 of the 1917 act and change the policy of the law in respect to such wills. With the liberal provisions concerning the form and execution of written and oral wills contained in this act, with the liberal provisions for surviving spouses contained in the Interstate Act of 1947, and with facilities for those in military service to write wills, it is inadvisable to permit a distinction for those in military service and mariners beyond the provisions of section 1(b) of this act.

¶ 1. General-Cross References 

This general provision governing ordinary wills (as opposed to the subsequent provisions governing special cases) contains the law as it has existed for over a century.¹ So far as the general requirement of a signature by testator at the end of the will is concerned, the only change made by the present act is that this provision is now completely separated from the miscellaneous provisions governing special cases. In the 1917 act, section 2 included (a) the general provision for signature at the end of the will, (b) an exception to the requirement of any signature in case of extremity, (c) a provision for signature by another, (d) the two-witness requirement, and (e) the proviso relating to writing following the signature. It will be seen that the present provision includes only the general requirement of signature at the end. All the other matters treated in old section 2 are now dropped to other clauses in this section and to section 4 governing witnesses, with the exception of the provision for unsigned written wills which is eliminated entirely. These special provisions are of course discussed under the relevant clauses and sections infra. As to wills of soldiers and mariners, see discussion of section 1 (b), supra. The present discussion will be confined to the general requirements of due execution in the ordinary case.

12. Requirements of General Law Apart from Statute a. Testamentary Intent in General 

It is obvious that any dispositive writing signed at the end is not necessarily a will. Nowhere in the act is there a complete definition of the term will. The present provision merely adds formal requirements to the common law. 

As a practical matter, however, the common law definition of a will is so broad that the only nonstatutory requirement is that of testamentary intent. This general nonstatutory requirement will be discussed briefly because questions concerning testamentary intent frequently overlap questions of due execution under the statute. Kent's definition of a will as "a disposition of real and personal property to take effect after the death of the testator" is probably as useful as any other.2 Note that it is the “disposition" which takes effect after death and not merely the enjoyment by the beneficiary. In this, a will differs from a present inter vivos gift of a future interest. 

The questions of property law that arise in this connection (when a deed of trust is considered testamentary, etc.) are discussed under section 1 (¶ 4e) of the Intestate Act. 

Often the question is less one of property concepts than of arriving at the most reasonable construction of an informal declaration by a person who himself had no very definite idea of what he meant. A typical case is McCune's 

Estate, 265 Pa. 523 (1920), where a paper signed by the decedent read "I want you, E. A. Kerr, to look after my property and if I don't sell it, I will sign it over to you. 

Received from E. A. Kerr $140 in cash and tax recits. $32.15." The court held that no testamentary intent appeared. There was nothing in the paper "from which any inference could be derived that it was intended as a posthumous destination of the property Every expression and every intendment to be derived contemplates

Page, Wills, (3d ed. 1941) §§ 5 and 6. Note that there must be an affirmative "disposition"; negative words are not enough-see discussion of "Negative Disinheritance" under section 1 (3b) of the Intestate Act. The exception is where testator merely appoints executors without disposing of anything; this is nevertheless a will: Douglas's Est., 303 Pa. 227, 232 (1931). Compare the muchadmired Blackstone definition (quoted in McCune's Est., 265 Pa. 523, 526 (1920)), which seems less exact than Kent's. 2103

In Hengen's Estate, 337 Pa. 547 (1940), on the other hand, the intent to make a posthumous gift was inferred from an informal writing in the present tense. Plainly this is a field of law where general rules are not of much help. (As to the necessity for and admissibility of extrinsic evidence of testamentary intent in cases of this sort, see § 4 ¶ 2a fn. 5.) 

Another type of case is where the intention of the decedent was unquestionably focused on what should happen after his death but it is doubtful whether he intended the particular writing to be the operative disposition in view of his expressed intention to execute another more formal instrument in the future. In such cases the decision will depend on whether the informal document was a mere declaration of what the writer intended to do and didn't, or was intended to be effective until the more formal writing was executed. The line of distinction runs somewhere between Tyson's Estate, 336 Pa. 497 (1939), denying probate of a letter reading "I am making out my will leaving securities to you," and Wenz's Estate, 345 Pa. 393 (1943), permitting probate of a letter beginning "In case of my death without having made a will.. 

A third type of case is the conditional will, where testator provides that the writing should be his will only in the event of a named contingency. See, for example, Trevaskis' Estate, 345 Pa. 525 (1942), where testator declared a writing to be his will only if an earlier writing, believed lost in the Pittsburgh flood, could not be found.

The earlier writing was in fact found and the court gave effect to the condition by denying probate of the later instrument. Sometimes, however, the courts hold that the testator did not really mean what he said in such cases.

Capacity, Influence, Fraud, and Mistake

Also related to the common law requirement of testamentary intent are the cases dealing with such matters as mental capacity, undue influence, fraud and mistake. 

The requirement of mental capacity has already been discussed briefly in connection with section 1 (a) (¶1). The many cases on undue influence deal mostly with questions of fact. The law on the subject is simply that the influence must be such as "to prejudice the mind of the testator, to destroy his free agency and to operate as a present restraint upon him in the making of the will." Ash's Will, 351 Pa. 317, 322 (1945). The all-important rules of burden of proof in applying this general test to the facts of a particular case are also reviewed in the same case. The contestant must show both confidential relationship and a weakened intellect in order to shift the burden of going forward with the evidence to the proponent. For a collec-

The clearest case of fraud and mistake negativing the necessary intent to make a will is where the testator has signed the wrong paper. See Alter's Appeal, 67 Pa. 341 (1871); Bryen's Estate, 328 Pa. 122, 128 (1937); cf. 

Thomas's Will, 349 Pa. 212, 216 (1944). There is simply no will in such a situation and the case is really no different from where the signature is forged or where pages are fraudulently inserted by another after execution; see 

Kane's Estate, 312 Pa. 531 (1933).

Similarly, a will is invalid if it can be shown that the alleged testator did not know its contents; see, for example, Blume v. Hartman, 115 Pa. 32 (1886). There is a heavy burden on contestants in such cases, however, which is seldom successfully carried. There is a presumption that testator knew the contents of the instrument, and proof that the will was read to him is not necessary. See Wetzel v. Edwards, 340 Pa. 121, 127 (1940) and other cases under § 4 (¶ 2a fn. 8). One more step removed is where the testator read the will but it is claimed that he did not understand the legal import of the words used. In such a case evidence of the mistake is absolutely inadmissible; see 

Penrose's Estate, 317 Pa. 444, 448 (1935). Different rules would no doubt apply, however, in the case of fraud on the part of the scrivener. 

Another type of case is where the fraud or mistake relates not to the fact of execution or the nature of the contents but to a collateral matter constituting testator's motive for making the will. Pennsylvania authorities in this type of situation seem to be rare and a superficial search has disclosed none directly in point. There are fairly clear indications, however, that a mistake of fact of this nature negatives the required intent only when the mistaken reason is stated by testator in the will (Gifford v. Dyer, 2 R. I. 99 (1852)), and even then only when the mistake related to a fact "not in the personal knowledge of the testator." See 

Mendinhall's Estate, 124 Pa. 387, 397 (1889) dealing with a similar problem in the case of revocation (§ 5, ¶ 8d), and the cases discussed in Shelly's Estate, 154 Pa. Super. 433 2106

2 cas (1943) dealing with directions to deduct debts and advancements from legacies. Thus it would seem that if testator recited in his will that because his son was dead he left everything to his daughter, the will might be ineffective if the son was in fact alive. But if the testator said that he left his entire estate to his daughter because he had already given his son an inter vivos gift, the fact that he had not actually made any such gift to his son would seem to be irrelevant. 

However, if fraud can be shown on the part of the party benefiting by the will, the same restrictions should not apply, even though the fraud related only to the inducement and not to the execution. See Carson's Estate, 184 

Cal. 437, 194 P. 5 (1920) for a rather extreme case where a will was refused probate because of fraud in the inducement. Note that this sort of fraud is really a form of undue influence, so that the Pennsylvania cases on influence generally should control.

4. Signature by the Testator 

Whether a will is signed by the testator is often a question of pure fact. The rules relating to burden of proof, presumptions and when an issue will be awarded in cases where forgery is alleged can be found in Young's 

Estate, 347 Pa. 457 (1943) and Lare's Will, 352 Pa. 323 (1945) (see Hutton's comments in 50 Dick. L. Rev. 104 

More interesting are the cases where the facts are admitted or have been proved in such a way that the findings are binding on appeal. Thus, it has been questioned whether a testator who has received assistance in writing his name can be said to have signed his will. The general answer to this question was early given in Cozzens' Will, 61 Pa. 196, 201 (1869) where the court expressly declared that in such a case the act of signing was testator's own "with the assistance of another, and not the act of another under authority from him." Hence such a signature is sufficient under this general provision and it is not necessary to show that the special requirements of clause (3), infra, have been complied with. However, exactly how much the testator must contribute to the joint effort is not entirely clear, and proof of execution by those familiar with the decedent's handwriting of course becomes impossible wherever substantial assistance has been given." 

Many questions of law relating to the requirement of a signature concern abbreviated or informal executions. 

There is a careful analysis of the cases of this sort in

From these cases the Superior Court in Wilson's Estate reasoned that a mark could qualify as a signature under the general requirements of section 2 of the Act of 1917, although the special requirements for wills executed by mark in section 3 of that act had not been complied with. 

This seems wrong. The reasoning is sound so far as it goes. If something other than the name can be a signature within the meaning of the general requirement, why not a mark? The opinion failed to take into account, however, the collateral effect of the special statutory provision for wills executed by mark. The Legislature in 1917 did not simply provide that a mark was a signature (as might have been the effect of the act of 1848) but enacted a special provision for wills of this sort, thus unmistakably indicating an intent that all wills executed by mark should comply with the special provision. The same can be said of the present act. Reading the present general provision by itself, it would be possible to conclude that a mark could be a signature. However, if the section is read as a whole, it becomes clear that if the will is signed by a mark, it must comply with the special provision of clause (2), just as a will signed by another is now governed exclusively by clause (3). It would seem, therefore, that the present general provision calls for something more than a mere mark, and this conclusion is supported by Hunter's Estate, 328 Pa. 484, 490-491 (1938) where Wilson's Estate was explained away as a case dealing with a testator in extremis so that no execution at all was required under the 1917 act (see § 2 (2) and (3) ¶ 1 fn. 4).

15. "At the End Thereof"

The history and purpose of the requirement that the signature be at the end of the will are reviewed in Knox's 

Estate, 131 Pa. 220, 228 (1889). The provision was new in 1833 and was inserted in order to make certain that the 99 The testator had "completed his testamentary purpose. requirement played a more important part in the law of wills prior to 1917 than it does today. In that year, the proviso was added concerning writing below the signature -now in clause (1) of this section, discussed separately infra. Even as qualified by clause (1), however, the general requirement that the signature be at the end continues to be important in many cases, because (as pointed out in the discussion of that clause) only that part of a writing which precedes the signature can be regarded as the will in any event, and even that portion cannot be probated when it represents a mere fragment. 

Before questions relating to the location of the signature are reached, it must first appear that the name sub-

This more basic requirement has already been discussed, and the distinction between the question of whether there is any signature at all and whether the signature is at the end of the writing will again be emphasized in the discussion of clause (1). But assuming that the testator wrote his name intending it as an execution of the writing, the statutory requirement that the signature must appear at the end of what is probated must be satisfied. 

Passing for the moment wills written on several detached sheets (discussed separately below-6) and cases where other writing follows the signature (discussed under clause (1)), the following rules may be laid down concerning the general requirement that the will be signed "at the end thereof": (a) When the signature appears at a place which would normally be understood as the end of a paper, the statute is satisfied even though the signature is physically closer to the beginning than other parts of the writing, and even though there is no internal or literary connection between the text and the signature. Thus, in 

Morrow's Estate (No. 1), 204 Pa. 479 (1903), the probate was upheld where the dispositive provisions appeared on one side of a single sheet and the signature at the top of the reverse side. "Who that writes or reads a letter does not involuntarily turn over leaf after leaf seeking the continuation until he comes to the signature? . . . After all, it is the common understanding and practice which must determine questions of this kind." (b) Where, however, widely accepted rules of sequence are not followed, it must appear that the signature is at the literary end of the instrument by the internal connection between the various parts thereof. 10 It is this second type of case that most frequently causes disputes. Suppose, for example, a single-sheet is signed in the margin. There is no widely accepted custom of proceeding from the bottom of a page to the margin

In such a case, it is said that the will is signed at its "literary" or "logical" end. An example of this is Swire's Estate, 225 Pa. 188 (1909), where marginal writing connected by paragraph numbering with the rest of the instrument was admitted to probate. 

One step removed from marginal writing is Coyne's 

Will, 349 Pa. 331 (1944),12 where the writing was signed at the top of a single sheet. Here the physical arrangement used by the alleged testator was in direct conflict with accepted usage. Hence the requirement of a literary connection was more strict. The normal reader would have read the writing in the following order: "Signed Francis Coyne

My last will and testomony is left to Eva and Genevieve Coyne." The lower court had decided that the word "signed" established a literary connection between the dispositive provisions and the signature, but the Supreme Court reversed, finding insufficient internal connection. 

Another type of case is where the decedent has written on the various sides of a folded sheet of paper, thus making a folio of four pages. Here there are no widely accepted rules relating to which page follows which, as anyone who receives letters could testify. However, the courts seem to favor reading such papers in the same order as pages in a bound book. Hence, if the book sequence is departed from, at least some internal or literary connection between the various sheets seems to be necessary. In both 

Stinson's Estate, 228 Pa. 475 (1910), and Bogart's Estate, 96 Pa. Super. 26 (1929), the alleged wills proceeded from book page 1 to book page 3 to book page 2. In Stinson's 

Estate, there was clear literary connection between the pages and the probate was upheld. In Bogart's Estate, the

On the one hand, the statutory requirement must be complied with regardless of whether there is any real probability of fraud. Hence (as in

WILLS ACT ¶ 6. Wills on Separate Sheets 

The three opinions filed by Justices Maxey, Stern and 

Drew in Covington's Estate, 348 Pa. 1 (1943), 92 U. of Pa.

L. Rev. 217, contain most of what is known concerning the 

Pennsylvania law of wills written on separate sheets. The authorities are exhaustively reviewed and the different points of view presented by the divided court constitute an unusually complete picture of the state of the law today on this difficult subject. According to Justice Stern, the rule governing this type of case "stems entirely from decisional law" (348 Pa. at 18) rather than anything in the statute.

It is immediately apparent, however, that the cases are closely related to the requirement that the will be signed at the end. Indeed the reasoning used is almost identical. 

The dogma is that the separate pages must be either physically attached to one another or show some sort of internal or literary connection. The cases will not be understood, however, if this rule is interpreted too literally. 

By stating the requirements in the alternative-either physical or internal connection-the courts give a misleading impression of what they actually require. The fact seems to be that the two requirements are related to each other, so that the degree of necessary internal connection varies according to the degree of physical detachment. 

Thus, as in the cases discussed under the previous heading, no absolute standard of internal connection can be stated, even in general language. 

The holding of Covington's Estate is a good example of this. The will, which the majority permitted to be probated, was written on three unattached sheets. There was no paragraph or page numbering and no sentence running from one page to another. In fact, the only literary connection at all seemed to be a negative one-the absence of any inconsistency in style or incoherence in meaning when the pages were read together. If this factor alone controlled, it would be easy to see why the dissenting justices regarded the decision as a radical departure from the earlier decisions. Justice Stern in his concurring opinion, however, emphasized two additional factors which without doubt 2114

¶ 

WILLS ACT 

§ 2 played a large part in the decision of the majority: "The first is that the pages of this will were enclosed in a sealed envelope; this served as effectually to unite the separate pages as a clip or other metal fastener would have done. 

The second vital circumstance in this case is that all the sheets were admittedly in the handwriting of the testators. The possibility, therefore, that there was a fraudulent insertion of a page, as there might have been in the case of a typewritten document, is practically negligible." (348 Pa. at 19-20.) In other words, because of these two factors a lesser degree of internal connection was required. 

Had the pages been found scattered in various parts of the room, the decision might well have been different. Also note that the three sheets were "identical in form and apparently taken from [the same] pad " (348 Pa. at 2.)

This also undoubtedly entered into the decision. Thus, the standard of internal connection will vary with the facts of the particular case and proponents in future cases will be disappointed if Covington's Estate is regarded as relaxing the requirement generally. Indeed, the limitations of Covington's Estate were demonstrated four years later in Baldwin's Will, 357 Pa. 432 (1947). There three sheets were found rolled in a rubber band, but they were not in decedent's handwriting and were not identical in form. The court distinguished Covington's Estate and denied probate. Conversely, it would seem that the mere fact of physical attachment will not alone suffice in all cases, as a too literal reading of the rule might indicate. Certainly physical attachment of one page to another is important, and the amount of necessary internal connection might diminish to the vanishing point as the firmness of the physical connection increases. But the decisions show that an insecure physical attachment is not enough where the papers do not present the appearance of having been written at one time.14 

It would seem, therefore, that in the average multi-page will prepared by attorneys, the paragraph and page numbering together with literary coherence between the various pages is fully as important as the staples at the top. 

14. See Baker's Est., 331 Pa. 33 (1938); Davis's Est., 344 Pa. 520 (1942); cf. Rosenthal's Est., 339 Pa. 488 (1940). 2115

The danger of such fraud is frequently mentioned in the Covington type of case, but even if there is sufficient connection between the sheets to make out a case for probate in the absence of evidence, it can always be shown affirmatively that a sheet was in fact inserted later. ¶ 7. Qualifications to Requirements of Writing and Execution-Incorporation by Reference, Etc. 

Apart from the limited type of nuncupative will permitted by section 3, there are strictly speaking no exceptions to the formal requirements of a writing and due execution as set forth in this section. There are, however, what might be called qualifications to the rule that every will must be in writing and signed by the testator at the end thereof. 

a. Incorporation by Reference 

One such qualification arises from the doctrine of incorporation by reference. As stated in Clark v. Dennison, 283 Pa. 285, 289 (1925), "The general rule, followed in . Pennsylvania, is that reference in a will to an extrinsic document or writing incorporates the latter as part of the will itself, provided it is clearly identified and in existence at the time the will was written." The Clark case and the cases there cited and discussed adequately illustrate how the incorporated document need not itself be signed by testator. See also Hogue's Estate, 135 Pa. Super. 

543 (1939). The theory is that the extrinsic writing becomes a part of the will so that in effect both papers are executed when testator signs the will. As to the probate of the extrinsic document, see Galli's Estate, 250 Pa. 120 (1915), indicating that such document, if properly incorporated, should be probated with the will. 

b. Oral Trusts 

It is said that oral statements may not be incorporated into a will 15 so that the doctrine of incorporation by refer- 

15. Page, Wills (3d ed. 1941), § 267. 

2116

¶7c 

WILLS ACT 

2 cos ence presents no qualification to the requirement of a writing as it does to the requirement of due execution. However, a similar result is sometimes reached through trust concepts where a will makes a gift to a person who orally agrees to dispose of it to others. Thus, in Hartman's Estate (No. 2), 320 Pa. 331 (1936), cash and personal effects were directed by the will to be distributed "according to directions privately given to my hereinafter named executor" and the court approved distribution according to the oral instructions.18 

c. Reference to Future Acts 

Another type of case which might be regarded as a qualification of the requirement of a writing is illustrated by Reinheimer's Estate, 265 Pa. 185 (1919), where the court upheld a gift of the residue in a duly executed will to the "party or parties who may be farming my farm and taking care of me at the time of my death." The interesting aspect of the case is that the designation of the beneficiary depended on a subsequent act by the testator himself. 

The extent to which this sort of thing will be permitted is discussed in the dissenting opinion in Atwood v. Rhode 

Island Hospital Trust Co., 275 Fed. 513, (C. C. A. 1st 1921). 

Citing Reinheimer's Estate, the dissenting judge pointed out that the subsequent acts of testator which designated the beneficiaries "were not regarded as testamentary for they related directly to making provision for working his farm and caring for him at the time of his death, though incidentally they made it certain who was intended by the language of his will to take the residue of his estate." It would seem from these cases that the subsequent act must have an independent significance making its testamentary aspect incidental. Note, however, that gifts of the contents of a certain box and the like are often upheld (see Gaff v. 

Cornwallis, 219 Mass. 226, 106 N. E. 860 (1914)), although the testator can put things in the box or take them out after the will is executed. In some situations, such acts have little or no significance apart from the testamentary

[Every will... shall be in writing and shall be signed by the testator at the end thereof, subject to the following rules and exceptions:] (1) Words Following Signature. 

The presence of any writing after the signature to a will, whether written before or after its execution, shall not invalidate that which precedes the signature.

COMMISSIONERS' COMMENT This is similar to the proviso in section 2 of the 1917 act. Between the Act of 1833, P. L. 249, which first required that wills be signed "at the end thereof" and the effective date of the Wills Act of 1917, any writing of a testamentary nature following the signature invalidated the whole will: Wineland's Ap., 118 Pa. 37. This proved to be too harsh and hence the proviso in section 2 of the 1917 act which is hereby preserved. What is considered to precede or follow a signature will of necessity be a matter for judicial determination in each case, but the numerous decisions and articles on the subject will be helpful: See Covington Est., 348 Pa. 1, 92 Pa. 

L. Rev., 217; Coyne Will, 349 Pa. 331, 93 Pa. L. Rev., 110.

Old Law Section 2. [Every will shall be in writing, etc.] 

Provided, That the presence of dispositive or testamentary words or directions, or the appointment of an executor, or the like, after the signature to a will, whether written before or after the execution thereof, shall not invalidate that which precedes the signature.

Wills Act of 1917, P. L. 403. 

There is no change from the proviso in the 1917 act insofar as it has been judicially construed. Discussion This is the first qualification to the general requirement, discussed above, that a will be signed at the end thereof. The provision was new in 1917 and the present clause is merely a stylistic improvement of the older language.

The provision should not be given more effect than what was intended or what it literally provides if carefully read. There must be a validly executed testamentary 2151

§(1) 

WILLS ACT 

writing before the clause has any application. The writing below the "signature to a will" does not invalidate the whole document, but there must be a will, properly signed, when the additional writing is ignored. This depends on whether the writing above the signature is complete and coherent as a will if considered by itself, and whether it appears from the face of the writing that when testator wrote his name he intended it as an execution of the document. 

Consider, for example, Churchill's Estate, 260 Pa. 94 (1918), where the testator died before the proviso of 1917 became effective. There the decedent had written his name in the testimonium of a holographic document but not in the place for the signature, so that the last paragraph (all in decedent's handwriting) read: "In witness whereof, I, P. Churchill, the Testator above named, have hereunto subscribed my name and affixed my seal. . . . . (SEAL)" 

The real difficulty with the proponents' case was that there was no signature at all. If the incompetent oral testimony were ignored, it appeared that although testator wrote his name he did not intend it to be an execution of the paper. 

The case was really no different from Stinson's Estate, (No. 2), 232 Pa. 230 (1911), considered in the discussion of the opening sentence of section 2 (4). Instead of denying probate on the ground that the paper was simply unsigned, however, the Supreme Court in Churchill's Estate rather ambiguously stated that the paper was not signed "at the end thereof." This language led the proponent in Bridge's Estate, 139 Pa. Super. 606 (1940) into a trap. 

The facts of the later case were about identical, but the proponent reasoned that the rule of Churchill's Estate had been changed by the proviso to section 2 of the act of 1917. The Superior Court rejected the contention, however, and held that proper execution was still lacking in spite of the new provision. The proper rationale of both cases seems to be that the papers were not signed at allat the end or at any other place. 2152

WILLS ACT 

§2 (1) Bridge's Estate is important as demonstrating the limited effect of the present provision. Prior to 1917 there were two types of cases where writing appeared under the testator's name and probate was denied: (1) where because of the additional writing it was clear that the name could not be considered as a signature to what preceded it (as in Churchill's Estate, supra); and (2) where the additional writing was plainly an afterthought in no way affecting the completeness of the preceding writing, as in Wineland's Appeal, 118 Pa. 37 (1888), where decedent had merely appointed his executor under the signature and the court held that the whole writing was thereby invalidated.¹ It was only the latter type of case which the Commissioners of 1917 wished to change and the courts have realized this in the subsequent decisions. 

In the above distinction lies the answer to whether the part above the signature can be probated in cases where the whole writing cannot be because the will is not signed at the end, or because it is on detached sheets showing no internal connection. Plainly the court will not order probate of the part above the signature, or the signed sheet, when it is evident that this part of the writing represents a mere fragment. If, on the other hand, it appears that the writing preceding the signature was regarded as a complete will and signed as such by the testator, only the additional writing will be ignored and the signed portions can be probated.2

COMMISSIONERS' COMMENTS— 

[clause (2)] This is taken in part from section 3 of the Wills Act of 1917. The requirement that two witnesses sign the will in the presence of the testator is new. It is believed that no mark should be recognized unless there are subscribing witnesses. 

This clause is intended to eliminate arbitrary requirements without removing any of the essential safeguards. The testator's name may be subscribed "before or after he makes his mark" but it must still be subscribed in his presence. If it is subscribed out of his presence, the execution will be faulty: cf. 

Orlady's Est., 336 Pa. 369. The mark must be made in the presence of the witnesses. A later acknowledgment to one or to both of them will not suffice. [clause (3)] This also is taken in part from section 3 of the Wills Act of 1917. Reasons for the precautions are slightly greater in this case than where execution is by mark. The requirements in addition to those where execution is by mark are: (1) Testator's name must be subscribed at his "express direction," and (2) Testator must declare the instrument to be his will in the presence of the witnesses. As a practical matter this clause seldom will be employed. Whether testator is able to sign his 2201

No special provision was made for the extremity of the decedent's last illness as is contained in sections 2 and 3 of the 1917 act. If a testator is so ill that he can neither make his mark nor direct another to sign for him, he cannot be supposed to have testamentary capacity. 

Old Law 

Section 2. Every will shall be in writing, and, unless the person making the same shall be prevented by the extremity of his last sickness, shall be signed by him at the end thereof, or by some person in his presence and by his express direction.

Section 3. These clauses completely revise the provisions for disabled testators in the act of 1917. The reason for the disability (extremity or other reason) is now irrelevant and the same provisions apply to both types of cases. If the testator is able to make his mark, he must do so, and his name must be subscribed in his presence, although authorization for the subscription is no longer necessary in such a case. If the testator is unable to make his mark, his name must be subscribed in his presence and by his express direction and he must declare the writing to be his will. 

The provision for wills with neither mark nor name has been eliminated. As before, all the necessary facts must be proved by two witnesses (see section 4) and in addition there is a new requirement for subscribing witnesses in cases governed by these clauses. Discussion

1. History 

These two clauses will be considered together because they represent an attempt to untangle the various provisions for disabled testators in sections 2 and 3 of the act of 1917.

Ironically, those very sections in the act of 1917 themselves represented a singularly unsuccessful attempt to bring order out of chaos dating back to the acts of 1833, P. L. 249, and 1848, P. L. 16. The history of the provisions for incapacitated testators is traced in detail in Chapter VI of Hutton's Wills in Pennsylvania (1933). Apparently the confusion started with the poorly drafted provision of section 6 of the act of 1833, which was almost identical with section 2 of the act of 1917, quoted above. This section was construed, rightly or wrongly, to mean that signature by name and by the testator personally was necessary in all cases except where the testator was prevented from doing so by the extremity of his last illness, in which event signature by another or no signature at all would suffice. 

This was altered somewhat by the act of 1848 which permitted signature by mark in general terms, and so the law remained until 1917. In that year the Commissioners rather woodenly copied the ambiguous language of section 6 of the act of 1833 and made it section 2 of the act of 1917, but the act of 1848 was revised. It was required that testator's name be subscribed "in his presence" to wills signed by mark and such execution was limited to cases where the testator was prevented from signing his name personally for a reason other than his last illness. 

The net effect of the 1917 revision was that new difficulties were added without solving the old ones. There 2203

§(2) & (3) 

WILLS ACT 

¶ 1 are several good analyses of these sections of the act of 1917 in the law reviews,¹ and the courts have from time to time made brave efforts to rationalize the conflicting and overlapping requirements as construed and misconstrued by the earlier cases.

Very briefly and dogmatically, the law relating to disabled testators under the act of 1917 seems to have been applied according to the following rules: (1) When testator was disabled by the extremity of his last sickness,2 he could either (a) have his name subscribed in his presence by his "express" direction,³ or (b) simply approve a will with no signature at all, if he was too ill even to give an express direction. (2) When testator was disabled for reasons other than the extremity of his last illness ("whether from lack of education or from physical weakness" in the words of the Commission of 1917) he could do either of the following, depending on the extent of his disability: (a) make his mark and have his name subscribed in his presence "by his direction and authority" (note that "express" direction was not necessary in this case); or (b) simply have his name subscribed in his presence and by his direc-

¶2. New Provisions in General 

The new act eliminates most of the illogical distinctions and arbitrary provisions of the act of 1917, but tightens up the remaining requirements in several respects. 

As presently arranged, this section makes clear what was implicit in the old act that wills of incapacitated testators under clauses (2) and (3) are also subject to the more general requirements in the opening provision of the section that wills must be in writing and signed in one way or another at the end thereof. Special requirements are added when testator signs with his mark or has someone else sign for him, but what has been said in the discussion of the opening provision of this section concerning the requirements that the will be in writing and that the signature appear at the end applies equally to wills under clauses (2) and (3).

Before discussing the details of these clauses, it will be noted that there is no longer a provision for execution in the absence of either a mark or an expressly authorized signature by another. The little used parenthetical provision of doubtful meaning which seemed to provide for this in section 2 of the act of 1917 has been completely eliminated. Thus, unless the decedent is at least able to comply with either clause (2) or clause (3) he cannot make a will. 

3. Extent of Incapacity 

To qualify under clause (2) it is necessary to show that decedent was unable to sign his name, and to qualify under clause (3) it must be shown that he was unable to sign his name or make a mark. It is no longer relevant whether the disability arises from the extremity of testator's last illness or from some other cause, such as 6. This was to cover the case of "a man who has lost both arms or is paralyzed" according to the Commission of 1917. A cursory examination has disclosed no actual cases of this sort, in the absence of extremity, but the language of the old act seems plain. 

7. See supra note 4. 2205

illiteracy or physical handicap. Only the fact of disability is now important; it may be "for any reason." 

The showing of such disability should not be too difficult in most cases. Under the analogous provisions of section 3 of the act of 1917, the courts were not strict in determining whether the necessary incapacity appeared.s 

As pointed out in the Commissioners' Comments, Rosato's 

Estate, 322 Pa. 229 (1936), represents a liberal decision in this respect. There, the court went so far as to say that a testator, who is able to write his name, may nevertheless sign by mark "if he chooses to do so." In that case, however, the decedent who "chose" to sign by mark was suffering from a nervous disorder which made his hand shake, so that the holding falls somewhat short of the dictum.

In the same volume of the state reports is Kline's Estate, 322 Pa. 374 (1936), where an issue was directed on the question of forgery partly on the ground that a literate and healthy decedent's signature by mark remained unexplained. Of course, Kline's Estate is not direct authority on the question, but it suggests that at least some excuse must be furnished for the informal execution. Rosato's 

Estate demonstrates that incapacity is a relative rather than an absolute concept, but it would seem that as a bare minimum it must be proved that the testator chose the easier method of execution because of some sort of disability. As to proof of such fact by two witnesses, see discussion under section 4 (3). 

4. Signature by Mark

If, then, it can be shown that a testator was unable (or relatively unable) to sign his name for any reason, a signature by mark is permissible, but the requirements of clause (2) must be strictly complied with. Several changes from the old act will be noted. The requirements now are: (1) testator must make his mark in the presence of two witnesses; (2) his name must be subscribed to the will in his presence; and (3) the witnesses must subscribe their names to the will in the presence of the testator.

a. The Mark 

In Kelly's Estate, 306 Pa. 551 (1932), the court quoted with approval Blackstone's definition of a mark as "a cross made in a little space left between the Christian name and the surname" with the word "his" above the mark and "mark" below it. This is useful as a description of the orthodox method of signing by mark, but it is evident that much less than this is required. Obviously the "his mark" is unnecessary, and as explained below under ¶ 4c, the name need not be subscribed before the mark is made. A cross is the traditional form of a mark, but no doubt any figure intended to be an execution of the document will suffice. The subject is well considered in Plate's 

Estate, 148 Pa. 55 (1892), where the court indicated that no particular form of a mark is required, but that it must appear that the figure was made "with the intent to execute the will thereby." Hence an incomplete name was held not to be a mark in that case, because there was nothing which testator intended to be a complete signature. That a testator may be assisted in making his mark seems to follow from the cases dealing with assistance in making a signature by name discussed under the opening provision of this section 2 (¶4). So long as it can be shown that the testator made a voluntary contribution to the joint effort of making the mark it would seem that the stricter requirements of clause (3) need not be complied with. Authority for this proposition will be found in Vandruff v. 

Rinehart, 29 Pa. 232 (1857), and Morris's Will, 349 Pa. 387, 389-390 (1944); see also Novicki v. O'Mara, 280 Pa. 411, 416-17 (1924).

The principal change in the provisions of clause (2) is the elimination of any requirement that the testator authorize the subscription of his name. Under section 2 of the old act the testator had to direct expressly that his name be subscribed, 10 and even under the more liberal provisions of section 3, it was necessary that the testator both be present and at least impliedly authorize the subscription of his name." Under clause (2) of the new act, however, it is only necessary that the name be subscribed in testator's presence. Thus, a subscription of the name while testator is in a coma would apparently comply with the new provision-although it is conceivable that the court would hold that the testator was mentally absent in such a case so that the subscription was not in his presence.

In the average case, the elimination of the requirement of authorization in clause (2) will be of little significance. By definition, the testator in such a case has made or will make his mark to the instrument, so that he presumably knows what is going on. The distinction between a subscription in testator's presence with his implied authority is not likely to be much different from a subscription in testator's presence with no authority at all.

Hence, the cases construing clause (2) will probably follow the general pattern of the cases under section 3 of the old act.

The requirement that the name be subscribed in the testator's presence remains the same and will probably continue to present a major difficulty in complying with the statute. Hunter's Estate, 328 Pa. 484 (1938), James's

c. Order of Events 

It was pointed out by Judge Gest in Picconi's Estate, 4 D. & C. 245, 247 (O. C. Phila. 1924), that it was immaterial under the act of 1917 whether the mark or the subscription was made first. Later there was some doubt thrown on the subject by some general language in Kelly's

15. Signature by Another Without Mark 

With respect to wills signed by another without the testator's mark, clause (3) combines the requirements of sections 2 and 3 of the act of 1917 and adds a new requirement for oral publication in the presence of subscribing witnesses. The first requirement is proof of the testator's inability either to sign his name or to make a mark. This was derived from section 3 of the old act, but the inability can now be for any reason, rather than for a reason other than last illness. The showing of such inability should be subject to the same rules as in cases governed by clause (2) discussed above.13 In addition, it must appear that the subscription of testator's name was made in his presence and "by his express direction." This latter requirement is peculiar to clause (3). 

Since the language with respect to the express direction is identical with section 2 of the act of 1917 (which in turn was copied from the act of 1833), the cases dealing with testators in extremis under those acts should govern 12. This addition to the clause was made after the draft of the new act was first circulated among the members of the bar.

¶ 6 the construction of the present act in this respect. It is important not to confuse these cases with those construing the different language of section 3 of the act of 1917. As already pointed out, implied authority was sufficient under old section 3, but the phrase "express direction" in section 2 of the old act was always construed to mean exactly what it said. As Chief Justice Gibson said in Greenough v. 

Greenough, 11 Pa. 489, 496 (1849), in construing the same phrase in the act of 1833, "Why use emphatic words, if there was no design to distinguish between an express and an implied direction?" Thus, the direction may not be inferred from the circumstances or from testator's silence,¹4 and a subsequent ratification or acknowledgment (even if express) is insufficient.15 Patti's Estate, 133 Pa. Super. 81 (1938), probably represents the minimum requirement in this respect. There, the testator answered "Yes" when asked if his will should be subscribed by another, and this was held to be sufficient as an express direction. 

Finally, the testator who cannot make his mark must declare the writing to be his will in the presence of two witnesses. The requirement of a declaration is new to 

Pennsylvania law, but it is not an uncommon requirement in other jurisdictions, so that authorities will not be wholly lacking.16

§3. NUNCUPATIVE WILLS. 

(a) When Permissible.

A nuncupative will may be made only by a person in imminent peril of death, whether from illness or otherwise, shall be valid only if the testator died as a result of the peril, and must be declared to be his will by the testator before two disinterested witnesses, reduced to writing by or under the direction of both of the witnesses within ten days after such declaration, and submitted for probate within three months of the death of the testator. 

(b) Property Disposable. 

A nuncupative will attempting to dispose of personal property of an aggregate value in excess of five hundred dollars, or of real estate in any amount, shall be wholly void. 

(c) Effect on Prior Will. 

A nuncupative will shall neither revoke nor change an existing written will.

In putting a limit on the amount which can be disposed of, it is believed that section 3 will serve a useful purpose. See

Old Law.

Section 4. Personal estate may be bequeathed by a nuncupative will, under the following restrictions:- (a) Such will shall in all cases be made during the last sickness of the testator, and in the house of his habitation or dwelling, or where he has resided for the space of ten days or more next before the making of such will, except where such person shall be surprised by sickness, being from his own house. (b) Where the sum or value bequeathed shall exceed one hundred dollars, it shall be proved that the testator, at the time of pronouncing the bequest, did bid the persons present, or some of them, to bear witness that such was his will, or to that effect; and, in all cases, the foregoing requisites shall be proved by two or more witnesses who were present at the making of such will. (c) No testimony shall be received to prove any nuncupative will after six months elapsed from the speaking of the alleged testamentary words, unless the said testimony, or the substance thereof, were committed to writing within six days after the making of said will. 2251

WILLS ACT 

Section 20 (b) No will in writing, concerning any personal estate, shall be revoked, nor shall any bequest or direction therein be altered, otherwise than as hereinbefore provided in the case of real estate [section 20 (a) quoted under section 5 of the present act], except by a nuncupative will made under the circumstances set forth in section four of this act, and also committed to writing in the lifetime of the testator, and, after the writing thereof, read to or by him and allowed by him, and proved to be so done by two or more witnesses. 

Wills Act of 1917, P. L. 403. 

The old act is changed in a number of important respects. The place where the will is made is now irrelevant and the requirement that testator "bid the persons present . . to bear witness" has been eliminated. On the other hand, new restrictions have been added such as the $500 limitation. Other less important changes will also be noted, such as the requirement that testator declare the words to be his will in the presence of witnesses, and the stricter requirements for reduction to writing and prompt probate. 

The provision of subsection (c) is likewise new although based on section 20 (b) of the old act. Discussion In the English statute of Frauds and in all Pennsylvania wills acts since the original act of 1705, 1 Sm. L. 33, there has been a carefully limited exception with regard to nuncupative wills of personality. Clauses (a) and (b) of section 4 of the act of 1917 were taken almost verbatim from section 7 of the act of 1833, P. L. 249, while section 4 (c) and section 20 (b) of the 1917 act were based on section 11 of the act of 1832, P. L. 137.¹ As pointed out in the Commissioner's Comments, the present section was inspired by section 6 of the Model Execution of Wills Act and makes several changes from the prior law. A number of the more arbitrary requirements of the old act have been eliminated, but other restrictions have been added which, together with the new limitation confining the section to personal estate of less than $500, will tend to make successful proof of a 1. In view of this new limitation, cases dealing with nuncupative wills will no doubt tend to disappear from the appellate court reports. (2) Intent. The attempted disposition must be a will, so that the ordinary requirements of testamentary intent must be fulfilled under this section just as in any other type of will. In addition, it must be shown that the testator intended to make an oral disposition of his property. (3) Peril of Death. "Imminent peril of death" is substituted in the new act for "last sickness" under the act of 1917. In a sense this is a relaxation of the requirement, in that the testator expecting to die need not be sick. However, the new language gives greater emphasis to the necessity for the imminence of death—a requirement already read into the old act by judicial construction. As the court said in McClellan's Estate, 325 Pa. 257, 262-3 (1937), the cases "have uniformly construed this provision to require that the nuncupation take place in such extremity of the testator's last sickness as to preclude the making of a written will." As the decision in that case and the authorities cited show, the rule had been extremely strict in this respect, and it will certainly not be any less strict under the revised language. In other words, "imminent peril of death" means so imminent that the making of a written will is impossible. It will also be noted that the alleged testator

¶ 1. General.

This section continues what has been the law as to proof of ordinary wills since the act of 1705, 1 Sm. L. 33.

It takes the place of identical provisions in sections 2 and 3 of the act of 1917, which in turn were copied from sec- 2301

¶ 2a сор 

WILLS ACT 

tion 6 of the act of 1833, P. L. 249.¹ As in the past, all that is required is that the will be "proved" by two witnesses at probate. Nothing in this section requires subscribing witnesses or witnesses who were present at execution. 

The provision now appears as a separate section instead of being repeated in the various sections governing execution of different types of wills. It applies to all wills-those signed in the ordinary manner, those signed by mark or by another, and nuncupative wills. In cases of disabled testators and nuncupation, it seems plain that the requirement of this section is in addition to and independent of the special provisions for subscribing witnesses in clauses (2) and (3) of section 2 and in section 3. The way this section operates with respect to the three types of wills will be discussed in turn. 

2. Ordinary Wills

With respect to ordinary wills governed by the opening provision of section 2, this section embodies the only witness requirement. Together, the two sections make the proof of such wills much easier in Pennsylvania than in most other states. 

a. Substance of Proof 

Part of the liberality of Pennsylvania law in this respect arises from the simplicity of the part of section 2 governing the ordinary will signed with testator's name. 

There is no requirement that the testator declare the writing to be his will or that he sign it in the presence of witnesses. As pointed out in the discussion of the opening words of section 2, the only statutory requirement is that there be a writing signed by the testator at the end thereof to which might be added the requirement of testa1. Formerly there were special requirements for wills of married women, gifts to charity, etc., but except for the provisions for disabled testators (§2 (2) & (3)), these have all been discarded. For a general discussion of the witness requirement and the many cases on the subject, see Hutton, Wills in Pennsylvania (1933) p. 120 et seq. and Hunter, O. C. Book, (1939) "Execution of

Almost all these elements, however, are ordinarily selfevident as a matter of law upon the production of the writing, or are governed by presumptions in favor of the proponents until rebutted by evidence to the contrary. Thus, whether the document offered is a writing within the meaning of the statute, and whether the signature appears at "the end thereof" present questions of law for the court.* 

The same is true for the most part as to testamentary intent; except in the most extraordinary cases, the paper will indicate on its face whether a posthumous disposition of property was intended. The other necessary elements raise questions of fact, but in the absence of evidence to the contrary it is presumed that testator had mental capacity," that the writing preceding his signature was there when he signed it (at least in the absence of interlineations not in testator's handwriting),' that he knew its contents, and that he affixed his signature with the intent to execute.⁹ As a result, except in extraordinary situations the only fact which the witnesses must prove to make out a prima facie case for an ordinary signed will is that the purported signature is that of the testator.10

WILLS ACT b. Method of Proof (Best Evidence) 

Turning now to section 4, the only requirement is that the will must be proved by the "oaths or affirmations of two competent witnesses." The courts have held that the witnesses required by this section do not have to be disinterested 11 and do not have to subscribe their names to the will.12 Thus, the signature of the testator-which, as pointed out above, is ordinarily the one fact necessary for proof of a signed will-can be established by the oaths or affirmations of any two witnesses so long as they are "competent" in the sense that they have knowledge of the facts they declare.13 As in all types of cases covered by this section, every necessary fact must be proved by each of two witnesses, so that if the testimony of one were stricken from the record, the necessary proof by one witness would still remain.14 In view of the simplicity of proving wills executed by signature, however, this rule is of more importance in connection with wills executed by mark, etc. (infra) than it is here.15

As to the permissible methods of proving the testator's signature by each of the two witnesses, our courts have sanctioned the following: (1) the direct testimony of a person (regardless of whether or not such person subscribes his name to the will) who was present when testator signed the will 16 or when testator acknowledged a signature to be his own,¹7 (2) proof of the signature of a subscribing wit- 17

That case involved an execution by mark, but it is plain that the same reasoning would apply to the proof of any sort of will under the identical statutory provision.

It would seem clear, therefore, that the mere fact that the subscribing witnesses are present does not make inadmissible other evidence of execution. 13. Wills by Incapacitated Testators 

There is nothing in the present section limiting its application to wills signed by the testator with his name. 

Thus, although there are special provisions in clauses (2) and (3) of section 2 calling for subscribing witnesses to be present when certain acts are done, it would seem clear that the broader requirements of this section 4 must also be complied with.

So applied, the present section continues the witness requirements which have governed cases of incapacitated testators in the past. These requirements under the present section will be discussed generally before discussing the relation of this section to the provisos of clauses (2) and (3).

WILLS ACT a. Substance of Proof 

The requirements of section 2 for execution by mark or by another must be examined carefully. As in the case of a will signed by testator with his name, testamentary capacity will be presumed and the paper will ordinarily speak for itself on questions of whether there was testamentary intent and whether the writing was signed at the end.31 All the other requirements for a will signed by mark or by another, however, raise simple questions of fact to which no presumption applies. The applicable clause must be read carefully, therefore, and each requirement proved by two witnesses.

Special attention is directed to the first requirement in each clause that testator be unable to sign his name or unable either to sign his name or make his mark, as the case may be. As pointed out in the discussion of those provisions (¶ 3 under § 2 (2) & (3)), the courts do not require proof that it was absolutely impossible for testator to sign in the ordinary manner. It would seem that some incapacity must be shown, however, and under the terms of the present section it must be proved by two witnesses. In recent decisions there is little mention of the witness requirement in this respect, but Cavett's Appeal, 8 W. & S. 21, 26 (1844), is a clear holding that two witnesses are necessary to prove incapacity,32 and there is no definite indication in the later cases that this is not still the law.33 This aspect of the proof should be the least of proponent's worries, but care should be taken at the hearing to make an adequate record on the fact of disability in order to avoid embarrassment later. 

b. Method of Proof
