Note, however, that the same two witnesses do not necessarily have to testify to all the facts. Suppose A testifies to facts 1, 2, and 3; B testifies to facts 1 and 2; and C testifies to fact 3. Such proof would be sufficient-see for example Cohen's Will, 356 Pa. 161, 165 (1947), discussed under the next subheading. 

Proof by two witnesses is difficult in these cases not only because of the number of facts that must be proved, but also because the available methods of presenting the evidence of due execution are necessarily limited. Proof of testator's handwriting is of course impossible, so that the only remaining methods are (a) proof by the direct testimony of persons who were present, or (b) proof of the handwriting of unavailable or forgetful subscribing witnesses. 

If proof of the latter type is relied upon, however, it would appear from recent decisions that the subscribing witness must have signed an attestation clause setting forth all the necessary facts. Where testator has personally signed his name to a will in the ordinary manner, it has been noted that no special attestation clause is required so long as it appears that the subscribers signed as witnesses.34 

This is because the entire substance of the proof in such a case is that the testator signed his name. It would appear from earlier cases-such as Barker v. McFerran, 26 Pa. 211 (1856) and Vernon v. Kirk, 30 Pa. 218 (1858)—that this was formerly the law even as to wills of incapacitated testators; the subscription by a forgetful witness was apparently sufficient to constitute prima facie proof of all facts necessary to a proper execution. In recent casessuch as Kelly's Estate, 306 Pa. 551 (1932)-however, the court seems to regard the loss of memory by one of the two

witnesses to such a will as fatal even where the witness had subscribed his name to the will unless there is an adequate attestation clause. The point was squarely raised in 

Drew's Estate, 32 D. & C. 297 (O. C. Phila. 1938). There was an attestation clause signed by two witnesses, but the clause was incomplete, and the witnesses could not remember facts sufficient to prove that the name of testator was subscribed in his presence and by his authority pursuant to section 3 of the act of 1917. The court ruled that the presumption of regularity could not be relied upon in a case of this sort and probate was refused. 

If, however, the forgetful or unavailable witnesses have signed a carefully drawn attestation clause reciting all the facts necessary to due execution under clauses (2) or (3), it would seem clear that proof of the witnesses' signatures would suffice. See, for example, Lawrence's Estate, 286 Pa. 58, 63 (1926), where in another connection the court said that a signed attestation clause may be used not only to refresh an available witness's recollection but "also may be used as substantive proof to establish validity." 35

True, the two provisions will overlap in many cases, 36

Suppose, for example, the scrivener can testify that he subscribed testator's name to the document in testator's presence and the subscribing witnesses can testify that they saw testator make his mark in their presence and that they subscribed their own names in his presence. The proviso in clause (2) of section 2 would be satisfied in such a case, but proof under the general provisions of section 4 would be defective, because only one witness (the scrivener) testified that the testator's name was subscribed in the testator's presence.

It is important, therefore, that both provisions be kept in mind when the execution of a will by mark is being arranged or when proof in a contested case is being prepared. 

Ordinarily, of course, the subscribing witnesses should be present when all the acts necessary to a proper execution under this clause are being performed, and an attestation clause should be carefully prepared so that all the necessary facts will appear over the signatures of the two wit- 87 nesses. 

Where this is not done, proof of execution will be more difficult but not necessarily impossible. There is nothing in the act which requires that the subscribing witnesses be the ones who satisfy the requirements of section 4, and the cases under the old act are persuasive to the effect that other witnesses can supply any deficiency in the subscribing witnesses' testimony. In Morris's Will, 349 Pa. 387 (1944), for example, probate was allowed, even though the subscribing witnesses contradicted themselves, because other witnesses testified as to all the necessary facts. Another example is Cohen's Will, 356 Pa. 165 (1947), where A (a subscribing witness) testified to all the relevant facts, the testimony of B (the other subscribing witness) established the proper affixation of the mark, and the testimony of C (a non-subscribing witness) established the proper subscription of testator's name; since the joint story of B and C corroborated the story of A, the proof was held sufficient.38

In the same way, it would seem that non-subscribing witnesses could supply any deficiency of proof under clause (2) of section 2 so long as (a) the testimony of at least two witnesses established each necessary fact, and (b) the testator made his mark in the presence of the subscribing witnesses who in turn signed their names to the will in his presence.

Thus, even if there was no attestation clause and the subscribing witnesses were dead, it would seem that other persons who were present could supply the necessary proof, if all the necessary facts could be established by two witnesses-including the facts that the deceased subscribing witnesses and the testator were in each other's presence when testator made his mark and the deceased witnesses signed their names.39 

14. Nuncupative Wills 

The operation of section 4 with respect to nuncupative wills governed by section 3 is much the same as in cases of wills signed by mark or by another. The substance of the proof will of course be different, but for the reasons already discussed it would seem that the special provision for disinterested witnesses to nuncupative wills in section 3 is in addition to the general requirement of this section 4 that all facts necessary for a proper execution must be proved by two witnesses.

In all except the most unusual case, the witnesses before whom testator declared his oral will and who reduced it to writing will be the ones who will prove it under this section. Conceivably, however, these witnesses will be unable to testify as to all the necessary facts--they might even be unavailable. In such a case it would seem that other witnesses who were present could testify as to the necessary facts, including the fact that the unavailable disinterested witnesses reduced the will to writing within ten days.

¶ 5. Lost Wills 

The rule relating to proof of lost wills is set forth in 

Hodgson's Estate, 270 Pa. 210, 213 (1921), as follows: "Proof of a lost will is made out only by proof of execution and of contents, by two witnesses, each of whom must separately depose to all the facts necessary to complete the chain of evidence. "' 40 In that case the scrivener produced a copy of the alleged will and his testimony was sufficient for proof by one of the two witnesses. The attesting witnesses, however, did not know the contents of the will so that their testimony was insufficient "without aid borrowed from" the scrivener in order to establish the connection between the will which was executed and the copy produced. Probate was therefore denied. 

In addition to proof of execution and contents, it is also essential for the proponents to overcome the presumption that a will which cannot be found was revoked by the decedent. This presumption can be rebutted by showing that someone else destroyed it, that decedent did not have access to it, or that decedent made statements up until the time of his death indicating that his will was still in existence. Such evidence, however, must be "positive, clear, and satisfactory.' See Dalbey's Estate, 326 Pa. 285 (1937), and 

O'Neill's Estate, 58 D. & C. 351 (O. C. Bucks 1946), for a complete discussion of the Pennsylvania authorities governing this presumption. 

Finally, an additional barrier to proving lost wills arises from Koehler's Estate, 316 Pa. 321 (1934), holding that revocation of an earlier will cannot be shown by oral testimony of a lost will in any circumstances. Thus if an earlier will is produced, proof of a later lost will is absolutely impossible.

§ 5. REVOCATION OF A WILL. 

No will or codicil in writing, or any part thereof, can be revoked or altered otherwise than:

Two changes are made. No distinction is made between wills of realty and wills of personalty. Thus a written will of personalty cannot be revoked by a nuncupative will. ¶ 1. History 

The present provision enumerates substantially the same modes of revocation that have been in our statutes since the act of 1833, P. L. 249. The only change is that it is no longer possible to revoke a written will by a nuncupa- 2352

¶2a 

WILLS ACT § 5 

tive will (see section 3, supra). As the notes of the Commissioners point out, the word "torn" has been added, but this method has always been recognized as a method of "destroying" a will under the acts of 1833 and 1917 (see infra ¶6). The provision requiring proof by two witnesses of a direction to another to destroy a will is new, but that also is probably declaratory of existing law (see infra ¶ 7). 

Other rules of presumption and proof and the law relating to intent, being based entirely on the cases, will of course continue the same. Hence, except where a nuncupative will is involved, the law of revocation (as opposed to the kindred subjects distinguished under the next heading) remains unchanged. 

¶ 2. Distinctions a. "Revocation" by Inter Vivos Conveyance

The term "revocation" has been used rather loosely in describing a number of transactions relating to wills. 

If a will purports to leave to X a particular watch which testator owned when he made his will but sold later, the case is one of ademption. There is simply no watch upon which the will can operate. Even the old common law theorists did not call this a revocation. If the testator did the same thing with real estate, however, a subsequent sale of the land inter vivos used to be called a revocation of the devise. There was some sense to this distinction because at common law a will of land was something like a revocable deed. If the testator in the case suggested reacquired title to his watch it would pass under the will, but if he reacquired title to the aliened land it would not. Even a general devise would not pass after-acquired land for this reason.

This rule of law relating to devises was changed by section 10 of the act of 1833, P. L. 249, and the act of 1879, P. L. 88, which now are sections 14 (1) and (2) of the present act. By reason of these statutory provisions, afteracquired land passes under a general devise and the will speaks as of the date of death with respect to both real and personal estate. Hence, it is now absurd to call an inter 2353

§ 

WILLS ACT 

2b vivos conveyance of land a "revocation" of a devise in an earlier executed will. In all cases the question is simply whether the testator owned the property when he died.

Occasionally, however, echoes of the old law continue to be heard with resulting confusion. In Gensimore's 

Estate, 246 Pa. 216 (1914), the court seemed to hold that an attempted, though unsuccessful, inter vivos conveyance of land revoked a prior will. No reference was made to the 

Wills Act and the decision seems plainly wrong. The actual holding may be explained away,' but it is doubtful if it will ever be followed as authority for the general proposition that a will can be revoked by an inter vivos conveyance. b. "Revocation" by Change of Circumstances

Another field of the law where the term "revocation" is loosely applied is covered by section 7 of the present act dealing with modification of a will by circumstancessuch as a later marriage, etc. This is sometimes called "revocation by operation of law," but of course the problems in such cases are quite different from those arising under the present section. c. Contracts Not to Revoke

Finally, it is sometimes said that the ability of a testator to revoke a will is qualified in cases where he is bound by contract not to revoke it. It seems, however, that this statement is incorrect. There would seem to be no obstacle to the actual revocation in such a case. The new will might violate the contract, but it is nevertheless a valid will and can be probated-see Norris's Estate, 329 Pa. 483 (1938). The promisee should claim as a creditor rather than as a beneficiary under a will which no longer exists. 

Even if the obligee takes land by specific performance, it -see

¶3. General Principles 

To revoke a will or codicil, in whole or in part, it is necessary to do certain acts with a certain intent. The statute prescribes the available methods so far as the objective act is concerned. Unless one of these methods is used, no revocation is accomplished, regardless of how clear the intention to revoke may be. Thus in Williams' 

Estate, 336 Pa. 235 (1939), the testator wrote "this will to be destroyed" at the top of one of the pages of his will, but probate was nevertheless ordered because none of the methods enumerated in the statute for revoking a will had been followed. The notation was unsigned so that it did not qualify as a revocation by another writing; and since the provisions of the will remained untouched by the added words they did not constitute a cancellation, obliteration or destruction.3

The intent necessary to revoke a will is wholly a matter of case law but is of equal importance. In doing the statutory act, there must be an intention to accomplish a present revocation, as opposed to the mere contemplation of a future change. See generally Evans's Appeal, 58 Pa. 238, 248 (1868). Tearing, for example, has always been recognized as a method of destroying even under the old act which did not mention "tearing" specifically. However, as the court pointed out in Ford's Estate, 301 Pa. 

183, 198 (1930), "it is not the tearing up of a will that works its revocation, it must be torn up animo revocandi. 

Hence, if a testator tears his will inadvertently (as in Cook's Estate, 5 Clark 1 (C. P. Phila. 

1850)) it is clear that no revocation takes place.*

Since mental state is important, it follows that for revocation to be effective, testator must have mental ca- 99

Burns, 4 S. & R. 295 (1818), decided before the act of 1833.

The law relating to intent to revoke is closely parallel to the law relating to testamentary intent in all the above respects. The cases discussed in connection with section 

2 (¶ 2a and ¶ 2c) of this act should therefore be persuasive in cases concerning intent to revoke. 

Act and intent, then, are the two elements necessary for a valid revocation. The subject is further complicated, however, by the fact that partial revocation has always been permitted under our statute. The statute itself recognizes that a will may be revoked "in whole or in part," but no distinction is made between the methods prescribed for a partial and a total revocation. Hence, how much of a will is revoked is simply a question of what testator intended in the circumstances. See generally Sheaffer's Estate, 240 Pa. 83 (1913), discussed more fully below under ¶ 6b. 

Thus, the principal questions in all cases of revocation are: (1) Did the decedent perform one of the acts enumerated in the statute? (2) If so, was the act performed with the intention to revoke? (3) If so, how much of the will did the decedent intend to revoke? How these questions will be answered in a particular case will depend to a large extent on various rules of presumptions and proof that have been developed by the courts. For example, the necessary intent will sometimes appear from the mere doing of the act, so that no independent proof of intent is necessary. On the other hand, the act might conform to the statute but be ambiguous so that the intent must be proved by testimony. These and other rules of presumptions and proof (such as those relating to whether the testator or someone else defaced a document) form an intricate pattern of rules and exceptions which as a practical matter are fully as important as the rules of substantive law in this field. The first method of revocation mentioned in the statute is by later will or codicil. Whether the act prescribed by the statute has been performed in this type of case is simply a question of whether the later writing is in fact a properly executed will under the requirements discussed under sections 1 and 2. Note, however, that the "will” within the meaning of this section is not necessarily testator's last will. Logically, this might be a contradiction. 

How can a document be a will but not be entitled to probate as a dispositive writing? So reasoned Justice Patterson in his dissenting opinion in Burtt's Will, 353 Pa. 

217, 235 (1946). This dissent, however, merely serves to point up the decision of the majority that the second of two wills (which contained no revocation clause but was wholly inconsistent with the earlier will) was effective to revoke the first will although the second will itself was later revoked by cancellation of the signature. Burtt's Will is further discussed under section 6. Suffice it to note here that a later "will" within the meaning of this section 5 is a writing which would qualify as a will if testator had died immediately after its execution. Unlike a will, a revocation is not ambulatory in Pennsylvania, even when it is accomplished by a later will. The first will is revoked at the instant the second inconsistent will is executed, and this 2357

4b 

WILLS ACT 

revocation remains effective regardless of the subsequent fate of the revoking document. It is possible to revive a revoked will by a writing under section 6, but, aside from that, it is impossible to revoke a revocation. 

The one qualification to this principle is the curious doctrine of Koehler's Estate, 316 Pa. 321 (1934), holding that evidence of a lost will cannot be introduced to revoke or modify an earlier available will. As already noted under section 4 (15) there is nothing in the statutory language to justify this rule, but it may be regarded as a sort of judge-made statute of frauds. Thus, logically or illogically, the revoking will must be produced in some form or other. It may be cancelled, torn, or otherwise mutilated, but it cannot be lost.

Subject to this qualification any writing which exhibits testamentary intent and is executed according to the statute may revoke a prior will at the instant of execution. 

Whether and to what extent it does so in a particular case is solely a matter of what testator intended. Did he intend to revoke the prior will at all, and, if so, how much of it? b. Intent 

The general rules for construing intent in cases of revocation by later will were set forth in Price v. Maxwell, 28 Pa. 23, 38 (1857): (1) Where there is an express clause of revocation in the later will, the earlier will is revoked thereby, even though the two wills are not inconsistent. 

See also Teacle's Estate, 153 Pa. 219 (1893); Hartman's 

Estate (No. 1) 320 Pa. 321, 326 (1936). (2) Where there is no express clause of revocation, the second will of course supersedes the earlier one so far as it is inconsistent and hence revokes the earlier will to that extent, but in the absence of inconsistency both wills are permitted to stand.

A testator might bequeath his personal property by one will and his real estate by another. Where the two wills overlap partially, more difficult problems arise. Suppose the first will leaves 

Blackacre in fee to A and the second will (containing no revocation clause) leaves a life estate in Blackacre to B without disposing of the remainder. Or suppose the case is taken a step further, and the second will leaves a life estate in Blackacre to B with remainder to his issue, but with no gift over in default of issue. In the absence of an express clause of revocation, can the first will stand to pass to A any interest not covered by the second will? 

Perhaps. But Hoffner's Estate and Hartman's Estate indicate that something less than total inconsistency between the two wills is sufficient for an implied total revocation of the first one. Hence, in the second hypothetical case suggested, the court might well hold that the later will in favor of B and his issue revoked the will in favor of A, and that there was an intestacy when B died without issue.12

c. Revocation by Codicil

Where the alleged revocation is by a paper labelled a codicil (or where it is necessarily a codicil, although labelled a will, in that it expressly saves gifts in the prior instrument—as in Bingaman's Estate, 281 Pa. 497 (1924)), roughly the same rules apply, but there is a considerably stronger presumption against revocation. Thus, even an express clause of revocation will sometimes be disregarded in extraordinary cases if it appears that testator's real intent was to modify a gift rather than to revoke it. See 

Sloan's Appeal, 168 Pa. 422 (1895), followed in Morrow's 

Estate (No. 2), 204 Pa. 484 (1903).13

Where there is no express revocation, the courts are loath to find an implied one. Of course, the provisions of the codicil must prevail (Elkins' Estate, 339 Pa. 193 (1940)), but the will should not be disturbed any more. than absolutely necessary. See Chauncey's Estate, 335 Pa. 

73 (1939).

Suppose the will leaves $500 to X, and a codicil provides that X shall have $600. It may well be in such a case that testator intended merely to increase X's gift from five to six hundred dollars, but the presumption against revocation results in X's getting $1100, unless the codicil expressly revoked the $500 gift or expressly stated that the $600 gift was in lieu thereof. Sigel's Estate (No. 1), 213 Pa. 14 (1905), is a strong case to this effect. There the residue in the will was given to heirs and the codicil made a pecuniary bequest to X of a certain amount "and no more." It was held that X, who was an heir, took both the pecuniary gift under the codicil and the share of the residue under the will.

The presumption against revocation by codicil might also prevent the whole estate's passing under a "codicil" which literally disposes of all testator's property. See, for example, Mifflin's Estate, 49 Pa. Super. 605 (1912). There covered enumerated items which at the time of execution comprised the entire estate, although there was other property at testator's death. Held: Second will revoked first will completely so that there was intestacy as to the rest of the property.

The word "estate" was construed to mean "residuary estate" so that while X's gift was necessarily revoked, the specific and pecuniary gifts to A and B were allowed to stand.14 

15. Revocation by "Other Writing"

Revocation by "some other writing declaring the same, executed and proved in the manner required of wills" is governed by principles similar to those governing revocation by later will. A provision substantially the same as the present one has been in our Wills Act since 1833.15 It was considered in Rudy v. Ulrich, 69 Pa. 177, 182 (1871), where its purpose is discussed. Ford's Estate, 301 Pa. 183 (1930), is the leading case although its importance is now somewhat diminished by reason of the broader decision in 

Burtt's Will, 353 Pa. 217 (1946), discussed above (¶ 4a).

In Ford's Estate, a later will expressly revoking an earlier will was held effective as a revocation by "other writing" even though the second instrument was itself cancelled so that it could not be probated as a will. As already noted, Burtt's Will later extended this same reasoning to revocation by later will containing provisions wholly inconsistent with the first will but no express clause of revocation. 

Hence, the fine distinctions drawn by the court in Ford's Estate are no longer significant, but the decision itself is confirmed. Contrary to the argument of the dissenting justices, the statutory requirement that the other writing must be "proved in the manner required of wills" merely means that the signature must be proved by two witnesses; it does not mean that the writing must be capable of probate.

On the other hand, the limitations of Koehler's Estate, 316 Pa. 321 (1934), clearly apply so that the later writing must be produced to be effective. The "other writing" can

With regard to revocation by act to the instrument the new statute again simply repeats what has been Pennsylvania law at least since 1833. The only innovation in the language is the addition of the word "torn," but as pointed out in the Commissioners' Comments, this has always been recognized as a method of destroying a will. 

There are many cases in the books explaining what acts are sufficient under this provision. On the whole the statutory requirements have not been over-strictly applied. 

A destruction need not be a complete destruction and a "cancellation or obliteration does not mean an effacing so that the letters or words cannot be read." Heller's Estate, 158 Pa. Super. 194, 196 (1945). In that case the names of the beneficiaries were crossed out in lead pencil in such an indefinite way that the court below thought the marks were mere "smudges." Nevertheless the Superior Court held that the marks were sufficient under the statute. 

On the other hand, there must be some act to the instrument, however slight, which will fall within one of the descriptions in the statute. Williams's Estate, 336 Pa. 235 (1939), where the marginal notation "This will to be destroyed" was held insufficient, has already been discussed above under ¶ 3. A similar holding is Lewis v. Lewis, 2 W. & S. 455 (1841), where the word "obsolete" in the margin was insufficient as cancellation because the word did not cover to any provision in the will.16 Other examples of acts done to the instrument which the court held insufficient under the statute are Curry's Estate, 317 Pa. 565 (1935), where testator struck out the names of the subscribing witnesses, and Wetzel v. Edwards, 340 Pa. 121 (1940), where the will was merely crumpled.

E. 748 (1934), Evans's Appeal can be said to stand for the following, assuming in all cases that the requisite intent appears: (1) Even a partial tearing, if it extends into the actual writing, is sufficient for revocation by destruction. (2) The striking out of the testator's signature is sufficient to cancel the whole will. (3) Marginal notations such as "cancelled" are ineffective in themselves to accomplish a revocation when they do not run across the writing, but they may be considered in determining the intent if other acts of destruction or mutilation have been performed.

Of course, the acts to the instrument must be performed by the testator (or by his direction-see ¶ 7 below) to be effective. Parole evidence is naturally admissible to establish or rebut this fact, but ordinarily evidence is unavailable so that the case turns on the applicable presumptions. These are reviewed in Heller's Estate, 158 Pa. 

Super. 194 (1945), discussed above, and in O'Neil's Estate, 58 D. & C. 351 (O. C. Bucks 1946). Where the will is found in testator's possession, the presumption is that he did the cancelling or destroying. O'Neil's Estate illustrates how this principle might be applied even though others also had access to the document. It was there held that in the absence of evidence the presumption against fraud is sufficiently strong to establish that testator did the acts even though the will was not in his exclusive possession. But in 

Wenrich's Will, 43 Schuyl. L. Rec. 77 (1947), the court refused to apply the presumption where both the testator and others had access to the will. 

A similar problem arises when a will cannot be found. "The rule is that where testator retains custody of his will and following his death the paper cannot be found, the presumption in the absence of proof to the contrary, is that he intentionally destroyed the instrument." Bates's Estate, 286 Pa. 583, 585 (1926). In that case an executed carbon 2363

con 

WILLS ACT 

5 ¶ 6b was offered for probate, but there was evidence that testator had followed the deplorable practice of signing his will in duplicate; hence in the absence of explanation of what had become of the original, the executed carbon was denied probate. b. Intent

The second element necessary for revocation by act to the instrument is the intent to revoke. As already pointed out (¶ 3), a tearing by mistake is no revocation. And even if it appears that the act of cancellation or destruction was done animo revocandi, it becomes necessary to decide how much of the will testator intended to revoke. This being a pure question of fact, the rules of presumption and proof become all important. 

It would seem that in all cases parole evidence is admissible to show what testator actually intended where the alleged revocation is by an act to the instrument. "It is always competent to show in cases of this character, the actual intention, and that the intention implied by the physical acts did not in fact exist." Sheaffer's Estate, 240 Pa. 83, 85 (1913).¹ 17 In the absence of evidence, it would appear that certain acts of destruction and obliteration are sufficient in themselves to make out a prima facie case of intention. 

A close case is Heller's Estate, 158 Pa. Super. 194 (1945), ¶ 6a above. There the lines drawn through the names of the beneficiaries (which were so indistinct that the lower court had regarded them as mere smudges) were considered definite enough by the Superior Court to raise a presumption of intent to revoke even in the absence of supporting evidence. On the other hand, certain acts of mutilation might be so ambiguous that supplemental proof would be required. For example, a partial tearing (as in Evans's 

Appeal, 58 Pa. 238 (1868), discussed above-¶| 6a) might indicate either an intentional revocation or an accidental mutilation. Hence, it would seem that something more than the mere fact of the tear must be shown before the necessary intent would be established.

c. Will Modified by Cancellation 

The questionable policy of allowing partial revocation by acts of destruction and cancellation can raise some interesting problems. Suppose a simple case where testator writes a will leaving a pecuniary legacy of $10,000 to A and the residue to B. Later, testator draws a line through 

A's legacy, intending to revoke it. This would plainly constitute a sufficient partial revocation of the will, and B as residuary legatee would get the whole estate. The implications of such a decision generally pass unnoticed in this simple type of case.19 Yet it cannot be doubted that without conforming with any of the requirements of execution testator by drawing lines through the provision for A has in effect made an affirmative testamentary disposition of $10,000 to B.

Speculation as to how far this sort of thing can be carried can be intriguing. In Guth's Estate, 19 Lehigh 351 (O. C. 1941), the testatrix marked up her will after its execution and did not re-execute it. At her death, part of her will read as follows: "I give and bequeath to Mrs. Edward

[7. Directions to Another to Destroy or Cancel 

The last sentence of clause (3) (providing that when the act to the instrument is done by another, the direction of testator must be proved by two witnesses) is said in the Commissioners' Comments to be declaratory of prior case law, a reference being made to Simrell's Estate, 154 Pa. 604 (1893). That is a curious case, the facts of which presented a problem similar to the cases discussed under the subheading immediately above. Erasures had been made in the will which would have had the effect of changing the entire scheme of distribution rather than merely enlarging the residue. Thus, even if testatrix herself had made the erasures, the case would have presented an interesting problem. However, an additional complication arose due to uncontradicted testimony that the erasures were made not by testatrix but by another at her direction. Possibly because the erasures, if recognized, would indirectly make a new and different disposition of the estate, the court treated the case as one of alteration by interlineation rather than simple cancellation. Hence, it was reasoned that proof by two witnesses was necessary, and since the "proof of the will in its altered state depends on the testimony of one witness" probate of the paper as originally written was ordered. The reasoning is not too clear. If the case were one of alteration rather than simple cancellation, it is difficult to see how the testimony of an additional witness would rectify matters, because proof of re-execution would seem to be necessary. Thus, there is some reason for regarding the decision as standing for the rule that even where simple cancellations or a total destruction is performed by another at testator's direction, the direction must be proved by two witnesses. In any event, that is the rule now written into the statute, so that two witnesses will now be required, not only in unusual cases like Simrell's Estate, but in all cases of partial or total revocation by 2367

Dependent Relative Revocation a. General

The perplexing subject of dependent relative revocation was recently treated in Braun's Estate, 358 Pa. 271 (1948), affirming 59 D. & C. 563 (O. C. Phila. 1947). Testator in his will provided for his wife, his sons and certain charities and gave $50,000 to trustees to pay the income to his adopted daughter until she reached the age of 35 and then to pay her the principal. Some years later the testator executed a codicil, which made certain changes in the provisions for the wife, sons, and charities and contained the following provision in one of the clauses: "I hereby revoke the Trust Fund in favor of my daughter Mildred, and substitute a lump sum of dollars in cash." Due to the testator's failure to insert an amount, there was of course no effective gift to the daughter in the codicil. The argument concerned whether the express clause of revocation in the duly executed codicil should nevertheless be effective so that the daughter would take nothing. Both the Orphans' Court and Supreme Court agreed that there was no effective revocation of the gift in the will, so that the daughter (who was over 35 when the testator died) took $50,000 under the will. In reaching this result the Supreme Court used the doctrine of dependent relative revocation and made it clear that in spite of some disparaging remarks in earlier cases Pennsylvania has in no sense rejected this doctrine. 

Judge Hunter (59 D. & C. at 564) quotes the following definition of the doctrine from an old English case. spite of the cumbersome language, the definition is prob- In 2368

¶ 8a 

WILLS ACT 

5 cos ably as good as any other and far more precise than some: "Where a disposition is made, so as to have legal effect, and afterwards another, by which the former would be revoked, but the other substituted, and it is evident that the testator, though using the means of revocation, could not intend it for any other purpose than to give effect to another disposition, though, if it had been a mere revocation, it would have had effect, yet, the object being only to make way for another disposition, if the instrument cannot have that effect, it shall not be a revocation."

It can now be said that this doctrine in some form or other is part of the law of Pennsylvania. The difficulty lies in its application. As pointed out in Warren's article on the subject in 33 Harv. L. Rev. 337, 338 (1920) (quoted in Stevenson's Estate, 48 D. & C. 140, 143 (O. C. 

Phila. 1943)), "dependent relative revocation" is a confusing term applied loosely to a number of situations. 

It will first be noted that the question arises only where there has been an act and intent sufficient to constitute a revocation under general law. If, for example, a second will is denied probate on the ground of mental incapacity, the prior will stands, not because of the doctrine of dependent relative revocation, but because there was simply no intent to revoke under the general requirement. The very incapacity which destroyed the necessary intent to make the new will also destroyed the intent to revoke the old one. See Kapp's Estate, 317 Pa. 253 (1935). This seems elemental, but it is important to keep the distinction in mind in considering cases discussed below where the absence of intent is not so obvious. It is only when the testator has the intention to revoke and performs one of the acts enumerated in the statute that the problem of dependent relative revocation arises.21 

The heart of the problem is how far the courts will go in relieving the testator from the consequences of his own. intentional and otherwise effective act. The precise limits to the doctrine of dependent relative revocation are difficult to define. In the Supreme Court opinion in Braun's 

21. Thus, if the second document is not executed, there is clearly neither a new will nor a revocation of the old one. See Melville's Est., 245 Pa. 318, 324-5 (1914). 2369

Estate, there is language indicating that the doctrine is limited to cases where "the dispositive part of the revoking instrument fails because of a defect intrinsic to the instrument." It is doubtful, however, that this or any other artificial limitation is workable, and it does not seem to fit in with prior decisions.22 After all, the reason for the failure of the substituted gift seems quite irrelevant in determining whether the old gift should be saved. 

A more practical limit to the doctrine of dependent relative revocation is that stated by the English court in the definition quoted above: It must appear that "the testator, though using the means of revocation, could not intend it for any other purpose than to give effect to another disposition." This test, in spite of its necessary vagueness, seems the only reliable one in that it describes how the court will probably think in such cases regardless of what the dogma might be.23 The court will not indulge in conjecture but will be more likely to grant relief where it is a moral certainty that testator's only purpose for the revocation was the making of the ineffective second gift. Hence, important factors are the extent of the attempted change and whether a change of beneficiaries is involved. An attempt (as in Braun's Estate) to substitute an outright gift for a gift payable at age 35 in favor of the same beneficiary is a more appropriate occasion to apply the doctrine than an attempted substitution of a gift to B for a gift to A. In the latter case the attempted change might have been motivated by a dislike for A as much as an affection for B.24

b. Ineffective Gift in Second Will or Codicil 

Under ¶ 4b above, it was pointed out that a will revokes a prior will either if it contains an express clause of revocation or if it is inconsistent with the prior will. Under 14c it was pointed out that neither of these results follows necessarily if the second paper is labelled a codicil. 

The cases dealing with later wills represent a rather strict view against the doctrine of dependent relative revocation and, before Braun's Estate was decided, there was serious doubt as to whether the doctrine was acceptable at all in Pennsylvania. Where the beneficiary was changed by the new will, as in McClure's Estate, 309 Pa. 370 (1933), it was not surprising that the first will was regarded as revoked in spite of the invalidity of the substituted charitable gift. As pointed out above, the doctrine of dependent relative revocation should not be applied where a complete change of beneficiaries is attempted. The cases dealing with invalid gifts in later wills go considerably further than this, however, and refuse to consider the revocation conditional even when the beneficiary of each gift is the same. Thus, in both Price v. Maxwell, 28 Pa. 23 (1857), and Hartman's Estate (No. 1), 320 Pa. 321 (1936), there were gifts to the same charity in both the earlier will and the later will. Yet, the invalidity of the second gift (due to the death of the testator within thirty days) resulted in intestacy, because the court refused to apply the doctrine of dependent relative revocation.

The cases on revocation by codicil are as liberal as the cases on revocation by will are strict. Where the beneficiary is the same in both instruments, the court will even 25. The doctrine was mentioned in Rudy v. Ulrich, 69 Pa. 177 (1871) infra in the text under ¶8c, but seemed unnecessary to the decision. 2371

§ 

WILLS ACT 

¶ 8b ignore an express clause of revocation in a codicil—as in 

Sloan's Appeal, 168 Pa. 422 (1895), and Morrow's Estate (No. 2), 204 Pa. 484 (1903). These decisions were based on the proposition that testator did not mean what he said when he "revoked" the earlier gift, because he actually intended only to modify it. The similarity of this reasoning to that of dependent relative revocation is apparent and the decisions can be regarded as applications of the doctrine. It will be noted that Braun's Estate is an example of this sort of case and the court used both types of reasoning in finding that the gift in the will had not been revoked. 

Thus, whatever the theoretical basis for such decisions might be, it seems to be settled that an invalid gift to the same beneficiary in a codicil, with or without an express revocation clause, will not ordinarily revoke the gift in the will which it was supposed to replace. Lutz's Estate, 27 

W. N. C. 403 (0. C. Phila. 1890, Penrose, J.); Rice's Estate, 16 D. & C. 123, 127 (O. C. Montg. 1930), and Stevenson's Estate, 48 D. & C. 140 (O. C. Phila. 1943), are examples of lower court decisions reaching the same conclusion in cases dealing with non-charitable gifts. In the first case, testator by codicil provided for an unlawful accumulation out of income given to his wife by the will. In the latter two cases, the codicil purported to extend for another generation a trust created in the will in a way which violated the rule against perpetuities. In all three cases the gift in the will was allowed to stand when the changes in the codicil were stricken down. 

Again, however, it is clear that the earlier gift cannot be saved-even in cases of revocation by codicil—if the testator has attempted to change the beneficiary from one person to another. Melville's Estate, 245 Pa. 318 (1914), is a clear decision to this effect. A possible qualification to this principle is presented by the perpetuity cases mentioned in the preceding paragraph. The gift to the parent in each case was attempted to be cut down to a life estate and a new gift of remainder given to the original beneficiary's issue. Strictly speaking this would have resulted in a partial change of beneficiaries. However, both gifts were in favor of the same family and it was clear that 2372

¶ 8c 

WILLS ACT 

§ 5 the attempted change could not have been motivated by a lack of affection for the beneficiary in the will. The court noted this in Stevenson's Estate and indicated that its decision might have been different if the invalid gift in the codicil had been in favor of an entirely different family. 

Another possible qualification to the general rule is illustrated by McDermott's Estate, 1 D. & C. 789 (O. C. Phila. 

1922), where testator had expressly stated in the codicil that the only reason for revoking the earlier gift was to make possible the substituted gift to another beneficiary, who then predeceased testator.

To recapitulate, our courts have refused to apply the doctrine of dependent relative revocation where the revoking document containing an invalid gift was a new will. 

Where the paper was a codicil, however, the gift in the will has been saved except where a complete change of beneficiaries was attempted. Whether there is sense in drawing such a sharp distinction between wills and codicils in this regard is questionable. However, it seems to be the law of our cases at least for the present. Bingaman's 

Estate, 281 Pa. 497 (1924), presented a slight relaxation of the rule where what was labelled a "will" but expressly saved certain gifts in an earlier will was held to be in effect a codicil. In Hartman Estate (No. 1), 320 Pa. 321 (1936), however, the court refused to extend the rule of Bingaman's Estate beyond its facts and held that a paper labelled a will must be considered as such even though it repeats certain provisions of an earlier will. 

As already pointed out, the cases dealing with invalid gifts in later wills and codicils will be less important in the future than they have in the past. Cases dealing with charitable gifts will be subject to the special provision in section 7 (1) of this act while the disposition of invalid accumulations and perpetuities will be governed by sections 5 and 8 respectively of the Estates Act. The old cases should continue to be valuable, however, as the leading general authorities on dependent relative revocation. c. Undue Influence

Suppose the second of two wills is the result of undue influence. Ordinarily the same influence which induces the 2373

§ 

WILLS ACT 

¶8c new will induces the revocation of the old one. Hence, as in the case of mental incapacity discussed above under subheading a, there is no effective revocation of the older instrument which remains as the testator's only valid will. 

Rudy v. Ulrich, 69 Pa. 177 (1871), and Ash's Will, 351 Pa. 

317 (1945), are cases of this sort. In each case the revocation of the earlier will (at least insofar as it was altered by the later will) was necessary to accomplish the purpose of the person influencing testator to make the second will. 

Therefore, the earlier will was reinstated when the influenced will was declared invalid.

A more difficult case is presented if the second will is entirely different from the first, but only part of the new instrument was the result of undue influence. It has been held that only the particular gift induced by undue influence is ineffective and the rest of the will must be allowed to stand: see Widdowson's Estate, 189 Pa. 338 (1889). It would seem to follow that the revocation of the old will is also effective except as to that part of the revocation which was necessary to make room for the unduly influenced gift in the second will. Suppose, for example, the first will gave $1,000 to A and the residue to B, while the second will, which was unduly influenced by Y, gave $1,000 to X and the residue to Y. It would seem that the estate should be distributed $1,000 to X and the residue to B, for the revocation of only the residuary gift was brought about by the undue influence. No Pennsylvania authority has been found to this effect, however, and it remains uncertain how the courts would handle a case of this sort. 

The important thing to note is that dependent relative revocation is not involved in either type of case, although the court in Rudy v. Ulrich mentioned the doctrine. 

The problem is rather the more basic one of how much, if any, of the revocation was induced by the undue influence-thus destroying the necessary intent. 

A somewhat unusual case of undue influence where the question of dependent relative revocation was reached is McCalla's Estate, 33 D. & C. 643 (O. C. Phila. 1938). In that case testatrix was influenced by X to set up an inter vivos trust in his favor. At the same time testatrix exe- 2374

¶ 8d 

WILLS ACT § 5 

cuted a codicil saying that by reason of having created a trust for X she revoked a smaller legacy to him in her will. 

After testatrix's death, the inter vivos trust was set aside on the ground of undue influence, and X argued that if this were the case, the revocation of his legacy should also be declared of no effect. The court, however, held the revocation effective. It will be seen that this case differed from the ordinary case of undue influence because the revocation of the legacy was collateral to the setting up of the trust. X's influence made testatrix set up the trust, but it scarcely could be said that X influenced testatrix to revoke the testamentary gift in his favor. Hence X's only chance of success was in the doctrine of dependent relative revocation, but the court refused to apply the doctrine for reasons explained under the next sub-heading. d. Mistake

A third type of problem involving principles similar to dependent relative revocation is presented by the cases dealing with mistake as to a collateral fact. Where a mistake goes to the very act of revocation (as where a testator tears a will inadvertently-see 13 above) it will negative the necessary intent. Suppose, however, that a testator intentionally revokes a gift but for a mistaken reason. The facts of McCalla's Estate, 33 D. & C. 643, supra, also raised a question of this sort, once it became clear that the undue influence did not go directly to the revocation. The testatrix in that case had revoked the testamentary gift to X intentionally and of her own free will, but as a result of the mistaken belief that she had made a valid gift to X inter vivos. The court followed Mendinhall's Appeal, 124 Pa. 387 (1889), in holding that a mistake of this sort, which is said to concern a matter "in the personal knowledge of the testator," is insufficient to avoid the revocation. See also Cummins's Estate, 37 Pa. Super. 580 (1908). 

By way of dictum in all three of the above cases, the courts recognized that if it appears on the face of a written revocation that it was made because of a mistake as to a 2375

$

WILLS ACT 

¶ 8e collateral fact "not in the personal knowledge of the testator but assumed upon information derived from others" the revocation will not stand. In the English case cited for this proposition, a codicil purporting to revoke a gift to grandchildren for the stated reason that they were dead was held to be ineffective when it appeared that they were in fact alive. It would seem that even in such a case, it must appear on the face of the revoking instrument that the supposed fact was the only reason for the purported revocation. Apparently, a mistaken motive (at least in the absence of fraud) cannot be shown by parole evidence. 

See Gifford v. Dyer, 2 R. I. 99 (1852).20 26 e. Cancellations and Interlineations

The effect of cancellations plus interlineations presents a field for speculation in Pennsylvania. If a testator draws a line through the provision for a legacy, it has been seen that this is sufficient under our statute for a partial revocation. On the other hand, if without in any way obliterating the writing a testator writes in the margin words indicating a change of mind-such as "Increase this $500 legacy to $1000"-the marginal note is of no effect unless it is executed in the manner required for wills. 

Suppose, now, testator instead of merely making a marginal note, crosses out the figure "$500" and above it writes the figure "$1000" intending to double a legacy to X in the will but without re-executing the document. Or, suppose he writes in "$250" intending to reduce it. It seems plain that the interlineation cannot be admitted as part of the will, but there remains the question of what, if anything, X takes.

Apparently, our cases have skirted but never decided this question. The indications are, however, that the cancellation, as well as the interlineation, will be disregarded in this type of case. Dixon's Appeal, 55 Pa. 424 (1867), raised the problem on its facts, but the point was not

Where a testator attempts to decrease the amount of the gift by crossing out the "$500" and inserting "$250" the case is not so easy. Here some sort of animus revocandi coincides with the act of cancellation. It could be argued that the gift in the reduced amount should be awarded by admitting the interlineation, not as part of the will, but as extrinsic evidence of how much of a partial revocation the testator intended to accomplish by his act to the instrument. § 6 WILLS ACT 86. REVIVAL OF REVOKED OR INVALID WILL 

If, after the making of any will, the testator shall execute a later will which expressly or by necessary implication revokes the earlier will, the revocation of the later will shall not revive the earlier will, unless the revocation is in writing and declares the intention of the testator to revive the earlier will, or unless, after such revocation, the earlier will shall be re-executed. Oral republication of itself shall be ineffective to revive a will. 

COMMISSIONERS' COMMENT This section was suggested by the problem of Burtt Will, 353 Pa. 217, and Ford's Est., 301 Pa. 

183. Under the decisions there has been a chance, depending on oral evidence, that a will which has been "revoked" and forgotten may be given new life by the revocation of a later will. 

The language used was suggested by the wording of Nevada and New York statutes referred to at pages 239 and 240 of Burtt Will. However, the last sentence does not appear in either of these statutes. It was added to eliminate any doubt on the open question of oral republication. Cf. Baum's Est., 269 Pa. 

63; Holmes Est., 240 Pa. 537; Broe v. Boyle, 108 Pa. 76; 

Shaeffer's Est., 240 Pa. 83; 8 Temple L. Q. 80. 

Old Law

There was no earlier statute. Under our cases the earlier will was revived if the testator so intended and there was a rebuttable presumption that he did so intend.

The case law is changed and a writing or re-execution is now necessary for revival in all cases. Discussion ¶ 1. General.

a. Revocation by Lost Will. 

b. First Will Revoked by Other Writing.

¶ 1. General 

In Burtt's Will, 353 Pa. 217 (1945), testator executed a will in 1906 and a wholly inconsistent will in 1939. Later he cancelled the signature of the 1939 will, thus revoking it. 2401

§ WILLS ACT 

T1 The question was whether the 1906 will could be probated. 

The court denied probate and declared an intestacy. The facts presented two distinct questions which it is important not to confuse: (1) Was the 1939 paper (which admittedly had been revoked and could not be probated) a later "will" within the meaning of the section of the Wills Act dealing with revocation, so that although ineffective as a testamentary disposition it was nevertheless effective to revoke the 1906 will? (2) Assuming that the 1906 will was revoked by the 1939 will, does the revocation of the 1939 will revive the 1906 will?

The first question was considered in the discussion of section 5 (4a). As there explained, the majority decided in Burtt's Will that the first will was effectively revoked when the second inconsistent will was executed, even though the second instrument was itself revoked at a later time. 

Only after that question was passed did the question of revival arise. Assuming the first will was revoked, was it revived by the revocation of the second will? 

On this question the majority in Burtt's Will ruled as follows: "The remaining question is whether the finding of the hearing judge 'that testator had no intention, at the cancellation of the will of 1939, to revive the will of 1906, but on the contrary the cancellation was made with the intention of making a new will,' is supported by the evidence. 

It was overwhelmingly established that testator did not intend to revive the 1906 will. [When a later will is revoked] the earlier will is presumptively revived. 

However, in this case, such presumption has been rebutted by evidence which overwhelmingly establishes testator's intention not to revive the prior will." (353 Pa. at 232.) The unsatisfactory part of this holding was not the result but the reason given. The question of revival in such a case was made to depend on oral evidence, in spite of the general policy against oral republication of wills enunciated in a different connection in Baum's Estate, 269 Pa. 

63 (1920).¹

The present section changes this part of the rule of Burtt's Will and makes oral republication or revival of the 1. Discussed in connection with §7 (2), (3) & (4) (¶6) of this act. 2402

¶ 2a $

WILLS ACT 

earlier will impossible. As explained in the Commissioners' Comments, the wording is based on similar statutes in other states referred to in Burtt's Will, 353 Pa. at 239-40.

Suppose, then, a testator makes a will leaving his estate to A, then makes a later will leaving his estate to B, and still later cancels the second will, making an express oral declaration of his intent to revive the first will. Under the present act there will be an intestacy because: (1) the second will revoked the first (see § 5, 14a) and (2) the revocation of the second will, even accompanied by an oral declaration of testator's intention, is insufficient under this section to give life to the first will. On the other hand if the testator revokes the second will by a duly executed writing (under section 5 (2)) and in that writing expressly declares his intention to revive the first will, or if the first will is reexecuted, the case will fall within the exception stated in the statute and the revival will be effective. 

2. Particular Types of Cases 

So much for the cases where the result under section 6 is clear. In other types of cases some difficulty might be encountered. a. Revocation by Lost Will 

Suppose, in the example above, testator burned the second will (instead of canceling it) so that it could not be produced to show that it revoked the first will, although witnesses are available to prove the second will's contents. 

Here, the contestants would be faced with the doctrine of Koehler's Estate, 316 Pa. 321 (1934), discussed in connection with section 4 (¶ 5) and section 5 ( 4a). That case decided that a revocation of a prior will by a later will cannot be shown by oral evidence alone. Hence, if the later paper cannot be produced at least in some condition, the first will stands. There would seem to be nothing in the present section to change this judge-made rule. Under 

Kohler's Estate no revocation of the earlier will can be shown so that the question of revival is never reached. 

b. First Will Revoked by Other Writing 

The first sentence of section 6 would not cover the following facts: Testator makes a will and later executes a 2403

$

WILLS ACT 

¶ 2c writing other than a will expressly revoking the will pursuant to section 5 (2). Still later testator cancels the second writing intending to revive the original will. Under 

Ford's Estate, 301 Pa. 183 (1930) (as buttressed by Burtt's

Will, 353 Pa. 217 (1945)), the will was revoked when the second writing was executed. Was it later revived when the revoking instrument was cancelled? Or can oral evidence of intent to revive be admitted? 

The first sentence of section 6 would not be applicable since by its terms it is limited to cases where the first will is revoked by a later "will." The second sentence of the section, however, states generally that "oral republication of itself shall be ineffective to revive a will." This broader provision should be sufficient to cover the case suggested so that under the statute no revival could be shown. 

c. Second Will Cancelled and Written Revival 

Under the statute, revival of the first will is impossible "unless the revocation [of the second will] is in writing and declares the intention of the testator to revive the earlier will, or unless, after such revocation, the earlier will shall be re-executed." Suppose testator writes inconsistent wills in 1906 and 1939, then cancels the second will by crossing out his signature, and then in 1940 duly executes a writing reading, "I hereby revive my will of 1906." Could it be argued that the statute was not complied with because the revocation of the second will was not in writing and the first will itself was not re-executed? Such an argument could be easily answered by use of the doctrine of incorporation by reference.2 The 1940 paper incorporated the 

1906 writing. Hence the 1906 will was re-executed pursuant to the statute, and even apart from the statute the writing of 1940, incorporating the 1906 writing, would be testator's last will.

§7. MODIFICATION BY CIRCUMSTANCES 

Wills shall be modified upon the occurrence of any of the following circumstances, among others: 

(1) Death Within Thirty Days-Religious and Charitable Gifts. 

Any bequest or devise for religious or charitable purposes included in a will or codicil executed within thirty days of the death of the testator shall be invalid unless all who would benefit by its invalidity agree that it shall be valid. The thirty-day period shall be so computed as to include the day on which the will or codicil is written and to exclude the day of death. Unless the testator directs otherwise, if such a will or codicil shall revoke or supersede a prior will or codicil executed at least thirty days before the testator's death, and not theretofore revoked or superseded and the original of which can be produced in legible condition, and if each instrument shall contain an✓ identical gift for substantially the same religious or charitable purpose, the gift in the later will or codicil shall be valid; or if each instrument shall give for substantially the same religious or charitable purpose a cash legacy or a share of the residuary estate or a share of the same asset, payable immediately or subject to identical prior estates and conditions, the later gift shall be valid to the extent to which it shall not exceed the prior gift. 

COMMISSIONERS' COMMENTS— 

[General] The grouping of what were several separate sections of the 1917 act in one section is believed to be logical and convenient. 

A will may be affected vitally by the happening of any one of the circumstances listed in the clauses. In addition it may be changed by the election of the surviving spouse. All of the circumstances mentioned in this section must occur at or before testator's death. The importance of the surviving spouse's election warrants separate consideration, and therefore was excluded from this section. 

While marriage of the parents of children born illegitimate and death of legatees or devisees are changes in circumstances, they also concern rules of construction and are included thereunder in section 14 so that they can appear with other rules with which they are closely associated and which are properly included in that section alone. 2451

§(1) 

WILLS ACT 

[clause (1)] The first two sentences take the place of the 1917 act, section 6, as amended, which reads: [see below] "and go to the residuary legatee or devisee, heirs or next of kin according to law" in the 1917 act has been omitted as unnecessary, especially since this act expressly provides the manner in which void devises and legacies shall be distributed. "for religious or charitable purposes" has been substituted for "to any body politic, or to any person in trust for religious or charitable uses" for simplicity. "The thirty-day period shall be so computed as to include the day on which the will or codicil is written and to exclude the day of death" is necessary because under the Statutory Construction Act "Whenever the last day of any such period shall fall on Sunday, or on any day made a legal holiday by the laws of this Commonwealth or of the United States, such day shall be omitted from the computation." In some instances the Statutory Construction Act allows thirty-one days. 

The addition of the words "unless all who would benefit by its invalidity agree that it shall be valid" will preserve the testator's wish with the least mechanical difficulties where all parties are agreed.

The last sentence of the new clause covers the case in which a testator has been charitably inclined and then changes his will in some respect within thirty days of death. Cf. Hartman's 

Est., 320 Pa. 321.

Of course, a testator may still provide expressly in his new will that it shall not revoke charitable gifts in his former will if he dies within thirty days.

1. History-Questionable Policy of the Statute 

The genesis of this sort of legislation is the English Mortmain Statutes dating from the thirteenth century. 

Originally such statutes had a very practical purpose. 

Conveyances to the Church defeated the privileges of the feudal lords and it was plainly to the advantage of the nobility to restrict them. In later years the emphasis shifted. The concentration of wealth in the Church became less of a threat to the secular society but there remained the spectre of the bedside priest inducing the dying man to buy his way into heaven at the expense of his family. 

Thus, the act of 9 Geo II c. 36 (1736) prohibited gifts for charitable purposes only if the instrument was executed. within a year of death or was not properly attested. 

Pennsylvania apparently got along without such legislation until the act of 1855, P. L. 328, which in section 11 prohibited conveyances for charitable purposes "except the same be done by deed or will attested by two credible, and at the time, disinterested witnesses, at least one calendar month before the decease of the testator or alienor."

In the light of subsequent experience it might be questioned whether this legislation has not caused more trouble than it is worth. Frequent amendments have been required in order to avoid unnecessary litigation and obviously unjust results.

By the amendment of 1911, P. L. 702, the wording was changed to provide that the attesting witnesses need not 2453

§(1) 

WILLS ACT 

11 be disinterested generally, in the sense of taking nothing under the will or deed, if they were not interested in the particular charity. The provision as to wills in the act of 1855 was superseded by section 6 of the Wills Act of 1917, P. L. 403, which changed the period from one month to 30 days in the interest of uniformity throughout the year. By the act of 1935, P. L. 573, the requirement of disinterested witnesses, which had caused so much litigation,2 was dropped entirely so far as wills were concerned. 

By the act of 1939, P. L. 141 No. 71, the Wills Act was again amended to make it clear that the 30 day period was to be "so computed as to exclude the first and include the last day thereof," and at the same session the act of 1855 as amended was superseded by a new act (1939, P. L. 141 

No. 70) relating to inter vivos transfers and conforming with the changed provision in the Wills Act. 

The present section of the Wills Act re-enacts the old legislation with a new provision to eliminate injustice in a special type of case and with other minor changes discussed below. The act of 1939, P. L. 141 No. 70, 10 P. S. § 17, remains in effect so far as inter vivos transfers are concerned.

Remick and Hutton, in 51 Dickinson Law Review 201 

(1947), question the policy of the legislation as it now stands. They point out that the provision can be easily evaded by making an outright gift to a bishop or other person who the testator can feel sure will use it for the purpose in question. As to other cases, the authors of the article. believe that "a negligible few of the gifts for such purposes can be imputed to overweening influence on a mind clouded by approaching death and bent on a belated ransom. Where such is the purpose that impelled the gift and such the condition of the testator, our law has adequate

In spite of the above considerations, neither the 1917 nor 1947 Commission felt at liberty to change the policy of the law with respect to charitable gifts. Thus, the 30 day requirement remains on the books. Except for two matters discussed under separate headings below, the law will remain as it has been since the requirement of attesting witnesses was eliminated in 1939. 14. Gifts in Performance of Promise or Trust

If the testator holds title to property in trust for himself for life with remainder on his death to a charity, the property passes to the charity under the trust rather than under the will so that this section of the statute obviously has no application. Sometimes, however, the trustee affirms an existing oral trust in his will executed within 30 days of his death and makes it appear that he is making a charitable devise or bequest. This might raise a difficult problem of proof, but the way is always open to show the pre-existing oral trust by testimony and thus save the gift from the statute. See McAuley's Estate, 184 Pa. 124 (1898).

Similarly, if the testator is obligated to leave property to charity under an enforceable promise made to another, the performance of this duty by a will executed within 30 days of death is not condemned by the statute. See 

Gredler's Estate, 361 Pa. 384 (1949); Heim's Estate, 50 

D. & C. 239 (0. C. Lack. 1944). ¶ 5. Powers of Appointment

If A by will executed within 30 days of death makes a gift to charities to be selected by his executor B, the gift to the charities is made by A rather than by B and the gift is void. See Linde's Estate, 58 Montg. 214 (O. C. 1942).

The same is equally, if less obviously, true if A provides for a life estate to B with remainder to such charities as B might appoint by his will, but with no gift over in default of appointment. The power is imperative (i. e., if 

B fails to select the charity, the court will do it for him—see discussion under Estates Act § 3-1 4) so that the property is unconditionally destined for charity under A's will.

By the same token it would seem plain that if A's will were made more than 30 days before his death, the gift is valid and it would make no difference how soon B died after making his will selecting the charities. On the other hand, if A gives a life estate to B and a general power to appoint the remainder by will, the realities of the situation demand that the will of B be considered the operative one. Hence it makes no difference when 

A dies, but if B appoints to charity by a will executed within 30 days of his death the gift is void. See Graff's

Estate, 16 Dist. 518 (O. C. Phila. 1907). The theory that the donor of a power is the one who makes the appointed gift must be discarded for the purpose of applying the statute if unrealistic results are to be avoided. 

The exercise of the power rather than the giving of it should also be determinative where the power is to appoint among a limited class, including charities, such as a power to appoint to issue or charities. The test should be whether the power is imperative, not whether it is special. Suppose 

A gives to B a power of appointment which is limited to charities, but there is a gift over to an individual in default of appointment. The gift in default of appointment prevents the power from being imperative and distinguishes the case from Fowler's Estate, supra. Hence it is 

B's will which actually commits the property to the charitable purpose, and it is believed that the appointment should be void only if B dies within 30 days of exercising it. No decisions have been found on this point, however. 

16. Meaning of "Religious or Charitable Purpose"-Gifts on Secret Trusts

A question that frequently arises in applying this section is whether the attempted gift is "for religious or charitable purposes." Cases on what is a charitable gift are reviewed in connection with section 1 (1) of the Estates Act where the term is defined. That definition will not apply to the Wills Act, but the provision was based on sec- 2457

§(1) 

WILLS ACT 

¶ 6 tion 368 of the Restatement of Trusts which is in accord with our cases.

A special aspect of the question of what is a charitable gift is presented by such cases as Schultz's Appeal, 80 Pa. 

396 (1876), Flood v. Ryan, 220 Pa. 450 (1908), and Bickley's Estate, 270 Pa. 101 (1921), which permit the subterfuge of making an outright gift to the bishop in order to evade the prohibition of the statute. These cases have been criticized but it is difficult to see how the court could have decided otherwise. In none of the cases did the devisee or legatee even know of the will until after the testator's death and by its terms each gift was outright. Hence it would have been difficult to impress a trust on the assets merely because the beneficiary indicated that he would voluntarily carry out testator's wishes. If the court had decided that any gift to a cleric was to be considered charitable unless it affirmatively appeared in the will that the testator had the legatee's personal comfort in mind, the next case would have involved a gift to a person who happened to be president of a charitable association, or to a rich cousin with charitable inclinations. In short, while the objections to these decisions are full of superficially convincing talk about "fraud on the law," the absence of any legal duty on the beneficiary to apply the property to the charitable use cannot be escaped. 

On the other hand, it is important to note the limitations on the rule of these cases. Any language in the will suggesting a legal obligation on the named beneficiary to carry out the purpose would undoubtedly be seized upon as a ground for distinction. Likewise, if a secret trust can be shown to be "assented to by the devisee either expressly or impliedly, by knowledge and silence before the death of the testator, a court of equity will fasten a trust on him on the ground of fraud, and consequently the Statute of Mortmain will avoid the devise if the trust is in favor of a charity." 10
