[7. Similar Gifts in Earlier Will a. Prior Case Law 

Many of the cases discussed in connection with section 5 of this act (¶s 4 and 8b) involved gifts to charity in wills or codicils executed within 30 days of death. In each case the testator's charitable inclinations appeared in an earlier will and the question was whether the earlier gift was revoked by the second instrument which could not be effective. 

Where the second writing was a will, the courts took a rather strict view. The cases can be summarized as follows: (1) Where the first will was expressly revoked by the second, the revocation was complete regardless of similarity between the two instruments. (Price v. Maxwell, 28 Pa. 23, 38 (1857); Hartman's Est. (No. 1), 320 Pa. 321 (1936)); (2) Where the second will disposed of the entire estate in a different manner from the first will, the first will was revoked even in the absence of an express revocation (McClure's Estate, 309 Pa. 370 (1933)). This latter principle was applied in Hoffner's Estate, 161 Pa. 331 (1894), where there was something less than total inconsistency between the two wills and indeed the charitable gifts were identical in both papers. See also Hartman's 

Estate (No. 1), 320 Pa. 321, 324-6 (1936).

On the other hand, if the instrument executed within 30 days was a codicil, the following more liberal rules applied: (1) A formal republication of the will by the codicil did not for this purpose have the effect of making the 2459

§(1) 

WILLS ACT 

¶ 7b date of the codicil the date of the will; hence, if the charitable gift in the will was unaffected by the codicil, it was valid (Darlington's Estate, 289 Pa. 297, 306 (1927)). (2)

An express revocation plus total inconsistency (as a change from Charity A to Charity B) resulted in revocation of the will regardless of the invalidity of the gift in the codicil (Melville's Estate, 245 Pa. 318 (1914)). (3) Where the two gifts were not totally inconsistent (as where there was merely a modification of a gift to Charity A), there was no revocation of the gift in the will where the gift in the codicil was invalid, even where the codicil contained an express clause of revocation (Sloan's Appeal, 168 Pa. 422 (1895); 

Morrow's Estate (No. 2), 204 Pa. 484 (1905)). This principle was applied in Bingaman's Estate, 281 Pa. 497 (1924), where the second paper was labelled a will although it was really a codicil in that it expressly saved certain gifts in the earlier paper, but the principle was not extended beyond this. A second instrument disposing of the entire estate without reference to the earlier paper is necessarily a will and was subject to the rules stated in the preceding paragraph.

Thus, where the second paper was a codicil there was a good chance of saving the earlier gift even before the present statute. Of course the codicil itself was invalid to the extent that it increased the benefit to the charity. 

Lightner's Appeal, 57 Pa. Super. 469 (1914), is a rather extreme example of this. The will left the residue after certain pecuniary legacies to a charity. A codicil executed within 30 days of death did not mention the gift to charity but reduced the pecuniary legacies by $700. It was held that the charity could take only the residue minus $700 because its gift was indirectly increased by that amount by the codicil.11 

b. Continued Importance of Prior Cases 

The present clause of the statute will relax the prior case law as to revocation by later will. As to revocation by codicil, it is questionable whether the statute has not 11. What was done with the $700 does not appear from the report. Presumably it would go to the heirs at law unless the doctrine of dependent relative revocation could be argued by the pecuniary legatees whose gifts were reduced. 2460

¶ 7b 

WILLS ACT 

§7 (1) provided a stricter rule than has hitherto been applied. In 

Morrow's Estate (No. 2), 204 Pa. 484 (1903), the codicil executed within 30 days of death purported to revoke a gift to a charity of one-sixth of the residue and substitute a gift to the same charity of one-seventh of the residue. Here the statute would have had the same effect as the case law -the gift is good as to the one-seventh. In Sloan's Appeal, 168 Pa. 422 (1895), on the other hand, testator by will left an outright sum to a charity and then by codicil executed within 30 days of death purported to revoke the gift and make a gift of the same amount in trust to A for life with remainder to the same charity. The court held that the charity could take the remainder on the ground that the gift in the will was not really revoked but only postponed. This case would not fall within the exception of new statute, because the gift in the second instrument was not "subject to identical prior estates." 

The failure to provide for such cases as Sloan's Appeal in the statute was due largely to the difficulty of drafting a provision which could be easily understood and which would work fairly in all cases. The facts in Sloan's 

Appeal presented a relatively easy case, but suppose the codicil, instead of adding a life estate, had eliminated one. 

Could the charitable gift be accelerated or should there be sequestration during the life of the excluded life tenant? 

Or suppose the life tenant had been changed from A to B. 

Or suppose a contingency which was attached to the prior gift to the charity had been eliminated. On the whole, it was thought wiser to cut the Gordian knot and require "identical" prior estates or conditions in both papers rather than attempt an elaborate provision to bring about perfect justice in all cases. 

It is suggested in spite of what has been said, however, that the statute does not change the rule in Sloan's Appeal or in any way require a stricter rule as to revocation by codicil than our case law provides. By its terms the new statutory provision applies only when the second will or codicil "shall revoke or supersede 12 a prior will 12. The words "or supersede" were added in a late draft of the act in order to cover implied revocation by an inconsistent gift. They do not have any esoteric significance. 2461

§(1) 

WILLS ACT 

¶ 7c or codicil." In other words, the statute has no application unless under general principles of our law the earlier gift has in fact been revoked or superseded. The holding in 

Sloan's Appeal was that the gift in the will had not been revoked by the codicil. Hence, if the same case were to arise today, there should be no occasion to apply this section of the Wills Act. Thus, in all cases it is important to determine preliminarily whether there has been a revocation under general principles discussed under section 5. 

If there has not been, no problem under this section arises.13 

c. The Present Statute 

Assuming, then, that under general principles of case law there has been a revocation of the earlier gift and the substituted charitable gift is in a will or codicil executed within 30 days of death, the last sentence of the present section must be read with care to determine if the gift can nevertheless be saved. The simplest type of case is where there are identical gifts for the same charitable purpose in both instruments. Here the gift will plainly be saved even though the second paper, which was executed within the 30 days, was a will and expressly revoked the former will. The difficulty arises when the two gifts are not identical. The statute recognizes three possible types of dif ferences: 

(1) The object of the gift might be changed. In this respect the statute will operate to save the gift only if the gift in each instrument is "for substantially the same religious or charitable purpose." This intentionally general standard should leave considerable leeway to the court in applying the statute. It is correspondingly difficult to predict exactly how much leeway will be permitted. A gift to X hospital for its general endowment would undoubtedly be "substantially the same" as a gift to the X hospital for a memorial bed. A gift to the X Committee for 

13. Sometimes the testator takes the precaution of making the revocation See by the later instrument conditioned upon his surviving for 30 days. 

Bradish v. McClellan, 100 Pa. 607 (1882). If that is done and death occurs within 30 days, there is of course no revocation and no occasion to apply the statute. 2462

¶ 

WILLS ACT §7 (1) 

Emancipation of the Working Man on the other hand could scarcely be termed substantially the same as a gift to the Y Art Museum. Somewhere between these cases, the line must be drawn. (2) The two gifts might differ in value. Where both gifts are outright pecuniary legacies, the statutory solution is simple and logical. The lower of the two amounts is the measure of the effective gift. Thus, the will executed within 30 days of death can reduce the charitable gift but cannot increase it. In either case, the second gift is effective but only "to the extent to which it shall not exceed the prior gift." Thus if the prior gift is $10,000 and the substituted gift is $20,000, or if the first gift is $20,000 and the second gift is $10,000, the charity will get $10,000 in either case. If the two gifts, instead of being pecuniary legacies, are framed in terms of fractional shares "of the residuary estate" or "of the same asset," again the lower of the two fractions constitutes the measure of the effective gift. Note, however, that one standard of measure may not be substituted for another. If the revoked gift is a pecuniary legacy of $10,000 and the substituted gift within 30 days of death is one-third of the residue, the statute, construed literally, would not apply. (3) The difference between the two gifts might be in terms of conditions or preceding life estates. Here the statute is unbending. For reasons explained above, the slightest change is fatal to the operation of the saving clause. To take an extreme case, suppose the first will gave the X hospital the remainder of the residue after A's life estate and the second will (expressly revoking the first) gave X hospital the residue outright. In such a case the 

X hospital would get no help from the statute. 

18. Agreement to Let Charity Take 

The words "unless all who would benefit by its invalidity agree that it shall be valid" were added as a qualification to the general rule of the section for the purpose of preserving the benefit of the deduction allowed for charitable gifts under the Federal estate tax law when the parties in interest decide to let the charity have the gift. 2463

(1) 

WILLS ACT 

¶ 8 The Federal cases had drawn a distinction between states where a gift to charity is voidable and where it is void. Generally speaking, in those states (such as New 

York) where the benefit of the statutory prohibition can only be asserted by a certain class of relatives, the statute has been construed as making the gift voidable rather than void by the state courts. It has therefore been held by the Federal courts that if the parties waive their rights to attack the gift the charitable deduction is allowed. See 

Humphrey v. Millard, 79 F. 2d 107 (C. C. A. 2nd 1935);

Commissioner v. First National Bank of Atlanta, 102 F. 

2d 129 (C. C. A. 5th 1939). In determining the effect of the Pennsylvania act in cases of this sort the Federal courts have indicated that our act of 1917 made the gift to charity within 30 days of death absolutely void so that the reasoning of the Humphrey case did not apply. See Marine National Bank (Carey's Estate) v. Commissioner, 9. T. C. 1047 (1947), aff'd 168 F. 2d 400 (C. C. A. 3d 1948).14

The wording of the present section would seem sufficient to change the above rule and to bring Pennsylvania within the rule applied in New York. Under the revised wording the gift is void only if the parties do not agree to let the charity take. If the parties do so agree, therefore, the charity takes under the will rather than from the beneficiaries.15

87. MODIFICATION OF CIRCUMSTANCES (Continued) 

Wills shall be modified upon the occurrence of any of the following circumstances, among others: 

(2) Divorce. 

If the testator is divorced from the bonds of matrimony after making a will, all provisions in the will in favor of his spouse so divorced shall be thereby revoked. 

(3) Marriage. 

If the testator marries after making a will, the surviving spouse shall receive the share of the estate to which he would have been entitled had the testator died intestate, unless the will shall give him a greater share. (4) Birth or Adoption.

If the testator fails to provide in his will for his child born or adopted after making his will, unless it appears from the will that the failure was intentional, such child shall receive out of the testator's property not passing to a surviving spouse, such share as he would have received if the testator had died unmarried and intestate owning only that portion of his estate not passing to a surviving spouse. 

COMMISSIONERS' COMMENTS— 

[clause (2)] This is taken from section 53 of the Model Probate Code. 

There is no similar provision in the 1917 act. A will in favor of a named spouse remained good in Pennsylvania without regard to a subsequent divorce: Jones's Est., 211 Pa. 364. It is not a complete answer to say that the will can be changed or revoked. The testator may delay the change too long or may forget to make it or may be incompetent to make it. The real question is whether most persons so circumstanced (as in the case of later marriage or birth) would wish their wills changed or would wish them to remain the same, and there is no doubt that most would wish them changed. [clause (3)] Clauses (3) and (4) as proposed take the place of section 21 of the 1917 act, as amended, which reads: [see below] 

The division of the substance of the 1917 act, section 21, into two clauses is a step toward clarity. This is especially necessary with the substantive changes made. 

The Model Probate Code makes no provision for the aftermarried spouse because it is considered that his right to take 2501

§(2)-(4) 

WILLS ACT 

against the will is a full protection. Pennsylvania places the after-married spouse in the more gracious position of receiving a full intestate share, including the spouse's allowance (Shestack's Est., 267 Pa. 115), without requiring that there be an election to take against the will. "unless the will shall give him a greater share" is declaratory of existing law. See Lintner's Est., 297 Pa. 428 where a will written prior to marriage gave the surviving spouse the entire estate which he was permitted to retain. In most instances it will be obvious which is the greater share, and such a share of personal property will be awarded in the adjudication or in the decree of distribution. 

This clause is believed to be a distinct improvement over section 21 of the 1917 act. It avoids the necessity for nominal gifts to after-born or after-adopted children or the re-execution of a will after the birth of a child. The revised form gives ample protection to the child and will avoid frequent occasions for the disruption of well laid plans. 

Old Law 

Section 21. When any person, male or female, shall make a last will and testament, and afterwards shall marry, or shall have a child or children, either by birth or by adoption, not provided for in such will, and shall die leaving a surviving spouse and such child or children, or either a surviving spouse or such child or children, although such child or children be born after the death of their father, every such person, so far as shall regard the surviving spouse or child or children born or adopted after the making of the will, shall be deemed and construed to die intestate; and such surviving spouse, child or children shall be entitled to such purparts, shares, and dividends of the estate, real and personal, of the deceased, as if such person had actually died without any will. 

Wills Act of 1917, P. L. 403, as amended 1921, P. L. 937. 

Clause (2) providing for divorce is entirely new and will change the prior case law.

Clause (3) relating to marriage substantially restates the prior law. The qualification that the spouse takes under the statute only when the will does not give him a larger share represents a theoretical change from prior case law under which the spouse had the choice of taking under the will or under the statute. 

Clause (4) relating to after-born children, contains two new limitations on the child's right to take under the statute. The child does not take if it appears from the will that the failure to provide was intentional, and in any 2502

WILLS ACT 

§7 (2)-(4) event the child does not share in property passing to a surviving spouse.

The revised language of clauses (3) and (4) might exclude the spouse and child from property which testator appointed under a power of appointment in all cases. Under prior case law the spouse or child could ignore the will and become entitled to any gift made to him in default of appointment under the will of the donor of the power. Discussion

17. How Share is Measured-Effect of Will-Abatement, Etc. 1. History 

At common law "the will of a feme sole was revoked by her marriage, whilst marriage and the birth of a child conjointly revoked the will of a man, whether of real or personal estate; marriage and the birth of issue did not procure revocation, where there was a provision made for the wife and children by the will itself, or perhaps by settlement executed previously to the will." Walker v. 

Hall, 34 Pa. 483, 484 (1859).¹ Following this statement of the common law rule there is a review of the early legislation on the subject in Pennsylvania culminating with sections 15 and 16 of the Wills Act of 1833, P. L. 250. 

Section 16 of the act of 1833 followed the common law doctrine and provided that a woman's will was revoked

¶ 1 absolutely by her subsequent marriage. This theory of absolute revocation had the following results prior to 1917: (1) Even if the after-married husband predeceased the testatrix, the will nevertheless remained a nullity.2 (2) 

Even if the testatrix left her entire estate to her intended husband, the marriage nevertheless revoked it and the husband could not elect to take under it.³ (3) The question under that act was clearly one of probate rather than distribution; hence if such a will were probated and the time for appeal elapsed, the effect of the subsequent marriage could no longer be raised.*

The corresponding provisions for the after-married wife in section 15 of the act of 1833 were based on an entirely different theory. The word "revoked" was not even mentioned. The section merely provided that the after-married wife, if she survived the testator, was entitled to her full intestate share, but it was clear that the will remained effective with respect to other property.5 

Hence, the results under this section were just the reverse of those mentioned in the case of the woman who married after making her will: (1) The after-married wife would share only if she survived the testator. (2) If the widow was given a larger share by the will she could waive her rights under the statute and elect to take under the will.' (3) The question was one of distribution rather than probate, so that the decree of the register was irrelevant in determining the widow's right to share. The act of 1917, P. L. 403, abolished the old distinction between wills of men and women with regard to the effect of a later marriage. The language of section 15 of the act of 1833 was adopted and made applicable to the will of "any person, male or female" with respect to both aftermarried spouses and after-born children. It would seem that the other results reached under section 15 of the act of 1833 would also have followed in all cases.

The first and most important change made by the present act is accomplished by clause (2) which is entirely new. 

Under the older acts, divorce had no effect on the will and the divorced spouse took any gift in the previously written will which the testator failed to revoke. This was established by Jones's Estate, 211 Pa. 364 (1905), where testator made a will making a gift to his "wife Mary." Later 

Mary secured a divorce a v. m. The court held (1) that

Hence the gift to Mary remained effective in spite of the divorce. The same result was reached in Darrow's Estate, 164 Pa. It was held that the woman who was testator's wife at the time the will was written was intended, and she took the estate in spite of their subsequent divorce.

The new provision will change the result in this type of case.

It is phrased in simple and direct terms and should cause little trouble. A few points should be noted: (a) The provision is confined to divorces a v. m. Separations, divorces a mensa et thoro, or acts of misconduct on the part of the spouse named in the will are still not grounds for implied revocation.12 To this extent the general principle of Jones's Estate and Darrow's Estate-that there is no implied revocation except as set forth in the statute-remains law. (b) There is no provision for a contrary intent appearing in the will. Thus, the act will probably be held to cause a revocation even in a case where the will indicates on its face that the testator contemplated the divorce but wanted to make the gift anyway. In this respect the provision is similar to section 16 of the act of 1833, discussed above, which, prior to 1917, governed wills of an unmarried woman and provided that such a will was revoked by subsequent marriage regardless of intent.13 (c) The new provision is also similar to section 16 of the act of 1833 in that it provides for a revocation. It differs in that it does not provide for total revocation but 12. It is important to bear in mind that we are dealing here with the power of the misbehaving spouse to take under the will-not his powers to take against a will or under the intestate law which are governed by $9 of this act and §6 of the Intestate Act.

§7 (2)-(4) only a revocation of the provisions for the divorced spouse. 

Nevertheless, it seems clear that this clause (as opposed to clauses (3) and (4)) raises a question of probate rather than distribution.14 Thus, the other legatees and heirs must be alert to attack the will in this sort of case by objecting to the probate of the provisions in question rather than waiting for the audit when the time for appeal might have elapsed. (d) The revocation is of "all provisions in the will in favor of his spouse so divorced." This might require judicial interpretation before its meaning becomes entirely settled. It would seem reasonably clear, however, that this wording would cover not only gifts to the divorced spouse but also provisions appointing him executor and the like. (Contrast the cases dealing with a spouse taking against the will under section 8 (4) in this respect.) (e) The provision only applies where the testator himself is divorced after making his will. If testator provides for a legacy to his son's wife, who is divorced between the date of the will and the date of testator's death, the statute will clearly have no application and presumably the divorced spouse will take the gift. For an interesting case of this sort see Teesdale v. McClintock, [1925] Ch. 

287. There, a gift was made to "A's wife," and A obtained a divorce and remarried between the date of the will and the date of testator's death. Fortunately there was an intervening republication by codicil which the court grasped upon to avoid awarding the gift to A's former wife. (Cf. § 14 (1) & (2) (15) of the present act.)

14. Birth of Children a. General

The new provision for after-born children contains a number of interesting features and has already been the subject of a note in 10 U. of Pitts. L. Rev. 219 (1948). It will first be observed that, as in the case of a subsequent marriage, the birth of children after the making of the will does not revoke the will, although in certain circumstances the child might be entitled to an intestate share of the estate. 

Hence the birth of a child after the date of the will presents no obstacle to probate.21

As heretofore, it is the birth (or adoption-see ¶ 4d below) of a child which brings the statute into operation. 

The fact that the child was conceived before the will was written is of no consequence if he was in fact born thereafter. This was early held in M'Knight v. Read, 1 Wh. 

213 (1836).22 The provision will also continue to apply to posthumous children. These were specifically mentioned in the old act,23 but under the revised language of the present clause the specific reference is no longer necessary; certainly such a child is born after the making of the will. 

And, as heretofore, the clause is confined to children. The birth of a grandchild after the making of a will, even if the child's parent predeceases the testator, has no effect in itself. Where both child and grandchild are born after the will, however, a special problem is raised which is discussed under the next subheading. 24 b. Representation of After-born Predeceased Child 

Suppose T (at a time when he is childless) makes his will leaving his entire estate to his friend X; then T's child 

A is born who has issue of his own; then A dies; then T

24. Alburger's Est. (No. 1), 274 Pa. 10 (1922). 2509

¶ 4c dies, a widower, but survived by his friend X and his grandchildren. Plainly, if A had survived T, he would have taken under this section of the statute. If, as in the case suggested, A predeceases T, can A's issue represent him for this purpose? Matter of Horst, 264 N. Y. 236, 190 

N. E. 475 (1934), holds that A's issue take under such facts, but it is doubtful if the Pennsylvania court would follow this decision. The wording of the acts of 1833 and 1917 would seem to have precluded such a result under the old law. The new statute is a little less definite on this point, but it still seems that the benefit of the statute runs only in favor of the "child" and not of his representatives. Section 14 (8) of the Wills Act (saving lapsed gifts for issue) is confined to cases where a "devise or bequest" is made to the child and would seem to have no application in this situation. Hence, it is difficult to see how our courts could follow the Horst decision merely because (in the words of the New York court) "the principle of representation is ancient." However, the result reached in the Horst case is morally appealing and the possibility of Pennsylvania's following it cannot be dismissed in the absence of controlling authority in this state. 

c. When Child Exluded 

Since the earliest statute, the after-born child could not share under the statute if he was "provided for" in the will. Many cases that arose under this limitation merely raised questions of construing the will. Did a gift to "children" in the will include after-born children so that the child would share under the will rather than under the statute? 25

In another type of case, the question was whether a gift to the after-born child was sufficient to satisfy the statute. In this regard, it was held in Newlin's 

Estate, 209 Pa. 456 (1904), that the size of the gift was irrelevant because there was no requirement that the provision be adequate. Following this case, a gift to surviving children conditional upon the spouse not surviving was 25. Generally, a class gift to "children" includes after-born children, so that the statute has no application in such cases: see Schaper v. Pittsburgh Coal 

Co., 266 Pa. 154 (1920), and infra, § 14 (8) of the Wills Act, fn. 13. 2510

¶ 4c 

WILLS ACT 

§7 (2)-(4) held to be a sufficient provision in Randall v. Dunlap, 218 

Pa. 210 (1907), even though the primary legatee survived so that the children in fact took nothing. However, the provision had to appear in the will itself. In Patterson's 

Estate, 282 Pa. 396 (1925), the legatee alleged that he had entered into a parole trust with testator under which he agreed to distribute a part of the estate to the after-born child, but the court held that this sort of "provision" did not fall within the meaning of the statute. Where, however, the extrinsic trust was in writing and subject to incorporation by reference, it was quite properly held that the provision for the child became part of the will itself, so that the statute did not apply. See Glatfelter's Estate, 60 York 77 (O. C. 1946), discussed in Fiduciary Review,

Oct. 1946, p. 2. 

The limitation that the child must be unprovided-for in the will remains in the statute, so that the above authorities will remain law so far as they go. The new act, however, adds two new limitations on the child's right to share: (1) the statute does not apply if it appears from the will that the failure to provide for the child was intentional; and (2) in any event the after-born child does not share in property passing to the surviving spouse. 

There were no such limitations in the prior acts, and as a result the testator's plans were frequently upset for no good reason. Children in existence could be disinherited at will, but the unborn child had to be "provided for” if the effect of the old act were to be avoided. There was some language in Newlin's Estate, 209 Pa. 456 (1904), indicating that even under the act of 1833 the child was "provided for" if it appeared that the testator had the child in mind when he wrote the will. Judge Gest in McIllvain's 

Estate, 2 D. & C. 501 (O. C. Phila. 1922), however, concluded after a careful review of the cases that a "provision" under the act of 1917 must be some sort of gift, large or small; 26 hence a clause in the will expressly disinheriting after-born children was held to be ineffective to avoid the effect of the act of 1917. 

26. For decisions in other states and varying statutory provisions, see 

Matthews, "Pretermitted Heirs," 29 Col. L. Rev. 748 (1929), and infra, note 27. 2511

§(2)-(4) 

WILLS ACT 

¶ 4c The rule of McIllvain's Estate will be changed by the present statute. Anything in the will indicating that the testator had the possibility of after-born children in mind and intentionally disinherited them will suffice to take the case out of the statute. The clearest case would be a clause in the will expressly disinheriting such children. It is uncertain how much less than this will be considered sufficient.27 Would the mere fact that testator disinherited children who were living at the date of the will be enough to indicate an intentional disinheritance of after-born children appearing "from the will?'' 28

In many cases the question of whether intentional disinheritance appears will be avoided because of the second qualification added by the new statute: the after-born child shares only in property not passing to the surviving spouse. 

This provision will eliminate entirely from the operation of the statute the common case where the testator disinherits his children by leaving his entire estate to his wife. 

In cases where the spouse survives but is not given the entire estate in the will, the wording of clause (4) describing the size of the after-born child's share should be read with care. Suppose, for example, the will purports to give three-quarters of the estate to the wife and the remaining quarter to child A who was living when the will was made. 

Child B is later born and testator is survived by his wife and children A and B. The widow gets the three-quarters, unaffected by the statute. Child B, under this clause, will get an intestate share of the remaining quarter of the estate-assuming (for the purpose of determining B's share) that the wife had predeceased and the estate had 27. The case sugested in the text is a little different in that it could be argued that the intent to disinherit the after-born children appeared in the will as interpreted in the light of the circumstances. See 10 U. of Pitts. L. Rev. at 220. But see Frank's Est., infra 29, holding that the fact that the child was born within two months of the will is insufficient to rebut the rule of the statute because the intent to exclude the child "appears from collateral circumstances rather than from the will itself," cf. supra, ¶ 4a at note 22. 2512

¶ 4c 

WILLS ACT 

§7 (2)-(4) consisted of only the quarter which the widow did not take. 

Hence, B would take one-eighth, and A would take the remaining eighth. Plainly this is a fairer result than if B took a full intestate share of the whole estate. Of course the provision will not work this easily in all cases. Suppose, for example, the will gives $1,000 to child A and the residue to the spouse. What does after-born child B get, and where does it come from? Probably an exception should be made to the ordinary rules of abatement in such a case, and A and B should each be awarded $500.29 

By way of summary, the after-born child will be excluded (1) where there is a provision for him in the will which would satisfy the requirements of the old act, (2) where an intentional disinheritance of after-born children appears in the will, and (3) when the entire estate is given by the will to the surviving spouse. For examples: 

1. T makes a will leaving his entire estate to his brother X, if X survives, but if X does not survive, to T's surviving children. After making this will, T has a child. If X survives T, he will take to the exclusion of the after-born child, because even under the old act a conditional gift to "children" has been held to be a sufficient "provision" for the after-born child. Randall v. Dunlap, 218 Pa. 210 (1907). 

2. T leaves his entire estate to his sister "knowing that she will take care of any children I might have." 

Under the present act, the sister will take the entire estate to the exclusion of the after-born child because "it appears from the will that the failure [to provide for the child] was intentional." This would be so under the present act even though the sister had no legal obligation to provide for the children. Contrast 

Walker v. Hall, 34 Pa. 483 (1859), reaching a contrary conclusion under the old act. 

3. T makes a will leaving his entire estate to his wife X if she survives him, or if she does not survive him to charity Y. The after-born child will be excluded

As explained above under ¶ 1, the provision for children adopted after the making of the will was inserted by the amendment of 1921. This changed the rule of Boyd's 

Estate, 270 Pa. 504 (1921). The present act continues to apply to children adopted after the will. See generally 

Russell's Estate, 284 Pa. 164, 168-9 (1925). e. Illegitimates

There is no express provision in the Wills Act governing the rights of illegitimate children in this type of case. The situation is covered, however, by the general act of 1901, P. L. 639, 11 P. S. § 1 abolishing the doctrine of nullius filius "as between the mother and her illegitimate child." In Patterson's Estate, 282 Pa. 396 (1925), it was held that the act of 1901 was applicable to this kind of case so that an after-born illegitimate child was permitted to share in the estate of its mother. Section 7 of the Intestate Act would also aid the child in such a case because of the reference in this clause of the Wills Act to the hypothetical intestacy of the testator.

As to the father, the common law doctrine of nullius filius still applies, so that the child will be excluded unless it is adopted or legitimated. In case of legitimation by the subsequent marriage of the parents, the requirement that the child must be born after the will still applies. Thus, if the illegitimate child is born, the will written, and the child legitimated, in that order, the statute does not apply: 

McCulloch's Appeal, 113 Pa. 247 (1886). 

15. Powers of Appointment 

In Shoch's Estate (No. 1), 271 Pa. 158 (1921), A gave a part of his estate to his son T for life with remainder to T's appointees under a general testamentary power of appointment, or in default of appointment to T's children. 2514

གླ 

WILLS ACT 

§7 (2)-(4) T made a will appointing outright to his wife, but after the date of T's will, T's child X was born. Admittedly X took an intestate share in T's individual estate, but X's guardian also claimed the appointed property under the gift in default of appointment--and, surprisingly enough, he succeeded. The court reasoned (a) that as to the afterborn child, T died intestate; and (b) that therefore there was no appointment so far as the child was concerned; and (c) that therefore X took, not merely one-half under the intestate laws, but the whole appointive estate under the provision in the grandfather's will in default of appointment. There was some basis for this decision in the wording of the old act. Section 21 of the act of 1917 stated that as to the after-born child the testator "shall be deemed and construed to die intestate 

This wording was apparently thought to be sufficient by the court in Shoch's Estate to allow the child to take against the appointment where he would have taken in default of appointment if testator had in fact died intestate. The subsequent sentence in the act of 1917 stating that the child should share in the "estate. of the deceased" apparently did not limit the preceding provision. 

It will be seen that there is no general statement in the statute as now worded to the effect that the testator shall be deemed to have died intestate. In fact, the share of the child under clause (4) is expressly limited to the "testator's property." The language of clause (3) (relating to the after-married spouse) is less definite in this respect but even under that clause the spouse is limited to a share in "the estate" which must mean the estate of the testator. 

It is likely, therefore, that Shoch's Estate is no longer law, although an argument to the contrary might be made on the ground that there is no express exclusion of appointed property in this section as there is in section 8 (c) infra dealing with a spouse's right to take against the will.30 

30. The strongest case for the spouse would be where T is given a general power of appointment with a gift to T's heirs in default of appointment. These were the facts in Young's Appeal, 39 Pa. 115 (1861). In such a case, the spouse can argue that T in effect has a fee, even though the power is given by someone other than T himself. In cases where the testator himself reserves the power, see § 11 of the Estates Act concerning the right of the surviving spouse. 2515

In any event, the doctrine of Shoch's Estate, even if accepted, will have no application (1) where the after-born child would not share under the gift in default of appointment (because such child takes, if at all, under the will of the donor of the power and not under the intestate law), or (2) where the appointment is in favor of testator's spouse, as in fact occurred in Shoch's Estate (because of the express exclusion of property passing to the spouse in the new act). 

6. Republication

Although there was some uncertainty expressed in the early cases on the subject, it was definitely laid down in 

Baum's Estate, 269 Pa. 63 (1920), that an attempted oral republication after the birth or marriage is insufficient to take the case out of the statute. A duly executed written republication, on the other hand, would seem clearly sufficient to bar the spouse or child who was married or born between the date of the will and the date of the republication. In Revercomb's Estate, 315 Pa. 424 (1934), testator made his will, then married his second wife, then executed what was construed to be a codicil expressly stating that he did not want to give anything to his second wife. It was held that this was a sufficient republication so that the second wife could not claim a full intestate share under this provision of the act (although she could of course take against the will under what is now section 8). The same result should follow regardless of whether the spouse (or child) is expressly referred to and regardless of whether the codicil contains an express clause of republication. If the testator makes any sort of a codicil to his will after a change in family circumstances, this at least shows that he was thinking of his will at that time, and the fiction of dating a will as of the date of the codicil seems realistic in this type of case.

Wills shall be modified upon the occurrence of any of the following circumstances, among others: (5) Slaying.

Any person who participates either as a principal or as an accessory before the fact in the wilful and unlawful killing of any person shall not in any way acquire property or receive any benefits as the result of the wilful and unlawful killing but such property or benefits shall be distributed as provided by law.

COMMISSIONERS' COMMENT— 

This clause overlaps some of the provisions of the Slayer

It is not in tended to supplant the provisions of the Slayer Act, but is included here for completeness and to avoid any suggestion of partial repeal of the Slayer Act of 1941. A similar provision is included in section 6 (c) of the Intestate Act of 1947. 

Old Law 

Between 1941 and the enactment of the present act there was no provision in the Wills Act concerning unlawful killing of the decedent. However, the subject was covered by the Slayer Act of 1941, P. L. 816, 20 P. S. § 3441, which remains law and to which the present section refers. Prior to 1941, the subject was covered by section 22 of the Wills Act of 1917, P. L. 403. 

The Slayer Act of 1941 continues in effect and the law since that act was passed remains unchanged. The act of 1941 made important changes from the act of 1917, however.

Discussion This section which confirms and incorporates by reference the Slayer Act of 1941, P. L. 816, as amended, 20 PS § 3441, is comparable to section 6 (c) of the Intestate Act which contains a similar provision barring the slayer from intestate succession. 18. Conflict of Laws. 

1. History 

These provisions substantially re-enact the law as it has existed since 1917. Prior to that time there had been a confusing series of statutes by which the Legislature in a haphazard sort of way had attempted to whittle down the common law distinctions between real and personal property, and between the rights of husband and wife. 

As to real estate, a married woman at common law had her dower and that was all. As explained under section 5 (a) of the Intestate Act, common law dower embraced what in modern law has been replaced by (1) the widow's intestate share under section 2 of the Intestate Act, (2) her statutory dower under section 5 (a) of the Intestate Act in lands conveyed inter vivos by her husband without her joinder and (3) her right to take against her husband's will under this section of the Wills Act. Dower in the case of intestacy was replaced by a statutory provision as early as 1794. In the case of land conveyed inter vivos it was replaced by statutory dower in 1917. The substitution of the statutory right of election for dower in devised land came more gradually. 

Dower at common law, being an estate in the wife, could not be divested by a husband's devise of the land. 

When a widow asserted her right to the estate, she was not making an election in the modern sense, since she could also take what was given to her by the will unless she was forced to elect by the will itself. The early history of election is traced in Cunningham's Estate, 137 Pa. 621, 628 (1890): "The common law rule was that a devise or bequest to a wife was not in satisfaction or lieu of dower unless so expressed in the will: Co. Litt. 36 b. The courts of equity relaxed this rule by holding that where the provisions of 2603

cas 

WILLS ACT 

¶1 

LIRI 

ba 

LIL! !! !!* the will would otherwise be materially deranged, an intention to make the devise in lieu of dower would be implied. 

This gave rise to frequent litigation as to the inconsistency of dower with the provisions of wills, (see Webb v. Evans, 1 Binn. 565) and the Act of 1833 (P. L. 249) § 11 was meant to diminish this by establishing a fixed general rule." 

The section of the act of 1833 referred to stated that any devise or bequest to a widow "shall be deemed and taken to be in lieu and bar of her dower-provided, that nothing herein contained shall deprive the widow of her choice either of dower or of the estates or property so devised or bequeathed." This was construed to mean that if the widow elected to take her dower, she took her common law dower in the decedent's land (a life estate in a third) rather than the statutory substitute which she was entitled to in case of actual intestacy. This was corrected by the act of 1869, P. L. 77, which provided that the widow taking against the will should take her intestate share of real estate rather than common law dower. 

In the meantime the widow was given a right to take her intestate share of personal property against her husband's will by section 11 of the act of 1848, P. L. 536. This was an entirely novel idea. At common law a woman had no interest in her husband's personalty and her intestate share therein could be defeated by a transfer either inter vivos or by will. The act of 1848 took away this power of the husband with respect to testamentary disposition. (As to inter vivos transfers of personalty by the husband, see discussion of section 11 of the Estates Act.) 

Thus by 1869 the modern pattern of a widow's right of election had been established. She could take either her intestate share of real or personal property owned by the decedent at his death, or what was given to her by the will. An additional complication arose with the act of 

1909, P. L. 87, which increased the widow's intestate share by the $5,000 allowance in the absence of issue. This was held in Guenthoer's Estate, 235 Pa. 67 (1912), to apply also to the share taken by the widow who took against the will. 

The 1917 Commission, however, decided that the allowance 

1. Hinnershits v. Bernhard, 13 Pa. 518 (1850). 2604

[

WILLS ACT § 8 

should apply only in cases of actual intestacy and inserted the proviso in section 2 (a) of the Intestate Act of 1917, P. L. 429, 755, to that effect.

The rights of the husband in his wife's property at common law consisted primarily of his estate of curtesy in her real estate and his absolute interest in her personalty. As explained under section 5 (b) of the Intestate 

Act, curtesy, like dower, had a three-fold aspect which has been replaced (1) as to intestate real estate by the husband's share under section 2 of the Intestate Act, (2) as to inter vivos conveyances by the wife's absolute incapacity to convey land without his joinder, and (3) as to devises in the wife's will, by this section of the Wills Act. Even at early law, the estate of curtesy was not important with respect to inter vivos conveyances by the wife because of her inability to convey without his joinder. It was also of no significance with respect to devises until married women were given the power to devise their lands by the act of 1848, P. L. 536. That act contained a proviso in section 10 that the new provision should not "deprive the husband of his right as tenant by curtesy." With regard to personalty, on the other hand, the husband had no protection against testamentary disposition by the wife under the power to bequeath personal property which was given to married women at least as early as the act of 1833, P. L. 249.

So the law stood until the act of 1855, P. L. 430, which provided that the husband might, "against [the wife's] will, elect to take such share and interest in her real and personal estate as she can, when surviving, elect to take against his will in his estate, or otherwise to take only her real estate as tenant by curtesy." (See the general discussion of this and prior acts relating to curtesy in Clarke's 

Appeal, 79 Pa. 376 (1875).) In other words, the husband had three choices: (1) to take under the wife's will, (2) to take the share in real and personal estate which she could have taken against his will, or (3) to take his common law curtesy.

Note that the husband's share under the second of his three choices was not his intestate share in the deceased wife's real and personal etate, but what she would have 2605

WILLS ACT 

¶ 2 *** WIL LI! 1 LIBU? ??** been entitled to if he had died intestate before her. Hence when the widow was given the extra $5,000 allowance in cases where there were no issue by the Act of 1909, P. L. 87, the electing husband's share was indirectly increased by that amount, although he had no right to the allowance if the wife died intestate.³

These inconsistencies were eliminated in 1917 when the rights of the surviving husband and surviving wife in both real and personal property were made identical. Curtesy was eliminated, and in cases of actual intestacy the surviving husband took a share in the real and personal estate identical with that of the surviving wife-including the allowance if there were no issue. The rights of either spouse to take against the other's will were also kept identical, but the right to the allowance was eliminated as to both husband and wife in this type of case. 

12. Present Statute in General

The present act continues the scheme of the Act of 1917 with some changes in the general arrangement. The substantive rule is now set forth in this section 8 where the size of the share is spelled out in detail rather than by reference to the Intestate Act. The formalities which must be followed in making the election and the time limit within which the election must be made are now governed by sections 10, 11 and 12 of this act. Under those sections will be discussed not only procedural matters but also such general questions of whether an election once made can be changed (section 10-¶9) and whether it can be made after the death of the spouse or by a guardian for an incompetent spouse (section 12 (b)). Also treated in a separate section is the subject of forfeiture; in view of the omission of any reference to the Intestate Act, it was necessary to repeat the provisions for forfeiture in the Wills Act, and this is done in section 9. 

¶ 3. Share of Electing Spouse 

Under the present act, as under the act of 1917, the electing spouse takes a smaller share in certain situations 

2. Moore's Est., 50 Pa. Super. 76 (1912); Buckland's Est., 239 Pa. 608 (1913). 

3. Ellermeyer's Est., 255 Pa. 610 (1917). 2606

cos than in cases of actual intestacy. The $10,000 allowance, which an intestate's spouse takes in the absence of issue, is eliminated just as the $5,000 allowance was denied to the electing spouse by the Intestate Act of 1917. Similarly the electing spouse can never take the whole estate. This result is also the same as that reached under the act of 1917, although the reasoning will be a little different. Under prior law the spouse of the intestate was never theoretically entitled to the whole estate as an intestate share; it was awarded to the spouse only when there were no "known heirs." Hence, it was decided in Petterson's Estate, 195 

Pa. 78 (1900), that the electing spouse was not entitled to this special right which accrued to the intestate's spouse only when the true heirs were unknown. Under the present 

Intestate Act, on the other hand, it is clear that in situations covered by section 2 (4) the intestate's spouse takes the entire estate as an inheritance and not merely because those with a prior right cannot be found. Hence the reasoning of Petterson's Estate would no longer apply, but the present section of the Wills Act preserves the same result by omitting any right of the electing spouse to take the whole estate. 

4. How Share is Measured-Effect of Will 

Since 1917, when the share of the electing spouse was clarified, there have been few if any questions raised concerning what fraction of the estate can be claimed. The way the share is calculated in detail, however, remains a matter of case law.

Thus, it has been held that the right of the spouse relates back to the date of decedent's death, both as to principal and income. The personal representative should therefore beware of distributing income until the election is made unless enough is withheld to make necessary adjustments.

With few qualifications the share is calculated as if the will did not exist, both as to testamentary provisions which might work to the spouse's advantage and as to pro- 4. Fitzgibbon's Est., 276 Pa. 105 (1923). It is assumed, of course, that the election is made in time-see § 11. 2607

§ WILLS ACT 

14 visions which might reduce the share. This principle had important effects where testator had exercised a power of appointment. Such cases are now covered by subsection (c), considered separately below (15). The principle was also applied, however, in a variety of other cases dealing with the effect of the will on what the spouse could take.5 

Thus, an electing spouse must renounce not only the devises and bequests but also the benefit of other provisions in the will which have the effect of increasing the size of the estate. It has been held, for example, that an electing widow cannot take advantage of a provision in the will requiring a child to bring into hotchpot an advancement or an uncollectable debt: Dermond's Estate, 55 Pa. Super. 

453 (1913). Likewise, an electing widower cannot take advantage of a testamentary provision relieving him of his obligation to pay for his wife's funeral: Mitchell's Estate, 79 Pa. Super. 208, 210-211 (1922). The qualification to this principle is that the electing spouse can take advantage of provisions in the will which are not dispository and do not affect the property taken. 

Thus, it has been held that the electing spouse is not required to renounce an appointment as executor, trustee," or guardian of a minor's estate. There is even a curious dictum in Lonergan's Estate, 303 Pa. 142, 149 (1931), suggesting that the electing spouse might not be required to renounce a power of appointment given her in the will-a suggestion which probably should not be taken too seriously. On the other hand, the spouse's interest in the estate cannot be adversely affected by provisions in the will. Although the size of the share might be different than in cases of actual intestacy, the fiction of intestacy is preserved in determining how the share is measured. Thus, a

cos provision in the will providing for an executor's commission in excess of what would be allowed by law, or admitting a "debt" which does not exist, can be ignored in determining the value of the net estate in which the spouse shares: Chamberlain's Estate, 54 Pa. Super. 434 (1913).

As to real estate, the spouse is entitled to an undivided fractional interest in each parcel owned by decedent at his death, including land specifically devised: Heineman's Appeal, 92 Pa. 95 (1879). And this interest cannot be affected by the exercise of a power of sale given to the executor in the will or by a direction to sell resulting in an equitable conversion as to the other parties in interest: 

Petterson's Estate, 195 Pa. 78, 79 (1900) (but see cases on estoppel considered under § 10, 17). To what extent these principles will be changed if administration of real estate is provided for in the new Fiduciaries Act remains to be seen. 10

As to the personal estate, the spouse's share is a fractional interest in the abstract value rather than an interest in any specific item. This interest will ordinarily be awarded in cash after liquidation (in the absence of an agreement or special order for distribution in kind) and the spouse cannot claim an interest in any particular item of personalty-especially when it has been specifically bequeathed. Gallagher's Estate, 76 Pa. 296 (1874). See also 

Williams's Estate, 45 D. & C. 207 (O. C. Phila. 1942) discussing the same problem with respect to the rights of a spouse married after the date of the will under what is now section 7 (3) of this act. 

5. Powers of Appointment 

Subsection (c) is new and will hereafter govern cases where the decedent has exercised a power of appointment by will. As stated in the Commissioners' comments, the 11 10. If the law (as opposed to the will) were to give the personal representative power to sell real estate, it would seem that the spouse's right would be subject to this power and the spouse's interest would be transferred to the proceeds. 

11. We are dealing here with cases where the decedent owned the power. 

Contrast the case mentioned by way of dictum in Lonergan's Est., 303 Pa. 142, 149 (1931) considered under 4 supra, where the decedent gives his spouse a power in the will. 2609

¶ 5 cos 

WILLS ACT 

Milta tft iz xti fizi new provision reaffirms Kates's Estate, 282 Pa. 417 (1925), and changes the rule of Huddy's Estate, 236 Pa. 276 (1912).

The cases where a decedent had a power of appointment given to him by another can be divided into four categories: (1) The appointment might not be exercised, in which event the gift in default of appointment in the instrument creating the power takes effect and the existence of the power is irrelevant in distributing the estate of the donee of the power. The present provision does not cover this case, but the result seems plain. In no sense was the appointive fund part of the donee's estate in which the electing spouse can claim the share given by the statute. By the same token, if the gift in default were to the donee's spouse there is nothing in this section or in the cases to prevent such spouse from receiving it under the donor's will even though he takes against the donee's will. 99 12 (2) The donee of the power might appoint it to one other than his spouse. Here again, it was plain under the cases that the donee's electing spouse could not share in the appointive fund. The general theory of appointments is that the donee of the power is merely "employed to manage the conduit pipe of another's munificence . and, in the absence of blending, the appointive fund cannot be considered any part of the donee's estate in which the electing spouse takes his share. The reasoning of the court in Huddy's Estate, 236 Pa. 276 (1912), (as opposed to the actual decision) makes this clear, and the present statute confirms this result. (3) The donee's will might appoint the property to his spouse who thereupon claims what is appointed in the exercise of the appointment and also the statutory share in the donee's individual estate against the donee's will. This was Huddy's Estate, 236 Pa. 276 (1912), where the court sustained the spouse and permitted him to take both under the appointment and against the will. Subsection (c) of the present section changes this rule and forces the electing spouse to forego the benefit of the appointment and take only his statutory share in the individual estate. 

12. Com. v. Duffield, 12 Pa. 277, 280 (1849). 2610

¶ 6a 

WILLS ACT §8 

(4) Finally, the donee of the general power might in effect appoint to his own estate by "blending" the appointive property with his own. In such cases the general theory is that the appointive property becomes part of the donee's estate so that, for example, it is available to his creditor. In Kates's Estate, 282 Pa. 417 (1925), however, the court refused to follow this general theory in determining the rights of the electing spouse, and it was held that the electing widow could not take advantage of the blending and claim her statutory share in the appointive fund, even though it had been awarded to the executors of the donee as part of the donee's estate. The present act confirms this decision. In fact it probably goes further. 

Suppose the donee blends the appointive estate with his own and then gives his wife one quarter of the combined funds. The widow elects against the will and takes one half of the individual estate. Under Kates's Estate she could not claim one half of the appointive fund, but prior to the present act could she have claimed one quarter thereof under the theory of Huddy's Estate? Kates's Estate does not make this clear, but the present section would require a negative answer, since the electing spouse is barred entirely from any property passing under the power.

Note that subsection (c) is confined to cases where the power is given to the decedent by another. Where the decedent himself has reserved a power over property which he formerly owned, the case will be governed by section 

11 of the Estates Act. 

16. Effect of Election on Remaining Estate a. General

Except for the two types of cases discussed below, the estate not taken by the electing spouse is divided among the other devisees and legatees as if the spouse had predeceased the testator and the testator's estate had consistd of only that portion of his property not taken under the election. If there is not enough to go around, ordinary rules of abatement are followed and the problem is no different than it would be if testator had simply overesti- 2611

¶ 6b cos 

WILLS ACT 

:: 22 au 

MY ??? · mated the value of his estate by the amount the electing spouse took out of it. Subject to an intent appearing in the will to give a special preference to a particular beneficiary, specific gifts will first be satisfied, then pecuniary legacies, and finally the residuary gifts if there is anything left,13

Suppose a testator, with an estate of $30,000 consisting entirely of personalty, left his watch to A, $10,000 to B, $10,000 to his wife, and the residue to C. If there was no issue and the wife took against the will, the result would be no different than if the wife had predeceased testator and he had left an estate of $15,000 rather than $30,000. 

A would get the watch, B would get $10,000, and C would get what remained. If the estate were less, C might be out entirely and B's pecuniary gift might be reduced, but A would still get the watch. Such cases present problems no different from any other case of abatement. 

Where real estate is involved, again no special problem arises unless there is a specific devise. Pecuniary legacies are a charge against residuary real estate under section 14 (13) of this act. This principle is applied in the ordinary way in cases of election, the only difference being that the electing spouse's share in such land cannot be so charged. Hence the legacy will be charged only on the onehalf or two-thirds interest in the land which passes to the residuary devisees or heirs. See Beck v. Beiter, 146 Pa. 

Super. 114, 119 (1941). b. Specific Devises

A problem peculiar to election arises where testator has made a specific devise of real estate to one other than his spouse. A testator gives his watch to A, Blackacre to 

B and the residue to C. His spouse, X, takes against the will. As explained above (14), X (assuming there is no issue) is entitled to one-half of the general value of the personalty and an undivided one-half interest in each parcel of real estate. Hence A gets his watch, but only onehalf interest in Blackacre remains for B. In order to make

If Blackacre is worth $20,000, B will get a one-half interest therein plus $10,000 from the personal estate. Gallagher's Appeal, 87 Pa. 200 (1878), is a case of this sort. There, the electing widow was bought off in order to free the real estate for the specific devisee. See also Edelman's Estate, 336 Pa. 4, 6-7, 8-9 (1939), where the principle is recognized. 

c. Income Estate Given to Spouse-Sequestration 

The other type of case in which election by a spouse raises peculiar problems is where the will has given the spouse an interest in income which is necessarily renounced due to the election. In this type of case the "ordinary rule" is that the renunciation of the life estate is equivalent to the prior death of the life tenant so that the remainder, vested or contingent, is accelerated to the testator's death. Disston's Estate, 257 Pa. 537 (1917), is an example of the application of the rule of acceleration, even though the remainder was contingent. Somewhat simplified, the facts were that a portion of the residuary estate was left to the wife for life with a direction to distribute the principal on the wife's death to the son if living or otherwise to his issue. The wife took against the will and necessarily renounced her life estate. The son was living at testator's death and the question was whether the gift over to him on the wife's death should be accelerated to testator's death following the fiction that the election by the spouse was equivalent to her death. It was held that the postponement of the son's estate was only for the purpose of allowing the wife to enjoy her life estate so that the general rule of acceleration was followed and the son took the principal at testator's death even though it was uncertain whether he would actually outlive his mother. 

Exceptions to the rule are made in two general types of cases. In the first place, acceleration will not be de- 2613

cas ¶ 6c 

WILLS ACT 

Mill! 2 1 * ** : 10 101 Hi!!

LIUMI 

creed if it is found that testator had some purpose in postponing the remainders independent of making room for the spouse's rejected income estate. A gift in remainder, for example, might be postponed until the beneficiary reached the age of 21, the income to be paid to testator's spouse in the meantime. In such a case acceleration would seem quite inappropriate. France's Estate, 352 

Pa. 522 (1945), may be cited as an instance of this sort of case, although the will was peculiar and the decision was far more complex than in the case suggested. Actually the remainder in France's Estate was partly accelerated and partly postponed in a manner which is scarcely worth explaining since a case similar on its facts is not likely to arise again.

The second and far more common exception to the rule of acceleration is typified by Lonergan's Estate, 303 Pa. 

142 (1931). The distinguishing feature of that case was that the income estate given to the wife was carved out of a pecuniary legacy, rather than the residuary estate. In effect the testator left $50,000 to his wife for life with remainder to X.14 The residue of the estate was left to 

Y. The estate, even as reduced by the election, amounted to over $500,000.15 If the rule of acceleration had been followed, Y would have borne the full burden of the election and X would have received more than he would have received in the absence of election, because he would have received his $50,000 at testator's death instead of later when the wife died. The court decreed that the $50,000 fund should be sequestered and the income paid to Y during the life of the electing spouse, the principal to be distributed to X when the wife actually died. Thus X got all he was ever intended to receive and the burden of the election which necessarily fell on Y was somewhat reduced.

It is important not to confuse the rights of the spouse who takes against the will under this section with the rights under section 7 (3) of the spouse who is married after the execution of the will. The after-married spouse takes a full intestate share and is not required to file any sort of election. The electing spouse, on the other hand, takes under section 8 a share which might be somewhat smaller in certain cases and the formalities prescribed in sections 11, 12 and 13 must be complied with to protect his rights. 

18. Conflict of Laws 

As in other branches of decedents' estates law, the law of decedent's domicile governs rights in personalty while rights in real estate are governed by the law of the state where the land is situated. Thus, in Eckels' Estate, 16. Annotated in Fiduciary Review, Nov. 1941. 2615

§WILLS ACT 

18 

THE 2 2 38 :: 

37 D. & C. 383 (O. C. Montg. 1940), it was held that the foreign law governs the right of the spouse in proceeds of real estate situated in another state. And in Paul's Estate, 26 

Dist. 1011 (0. C. Phila. 1917), it was held that our law governs the right of a spouse to take against a devise of Pennsylvania land regardless of where the decedent lived.¹7 

That the domicile of the surviving spouse is irrelevant was decided in Mallory's Estate, 300 Pa. 217 (1930), holding that our law governs the spouse's rights in personalty of a Pennsylvania decedent even though the widow (for justifiable cause or by mutual consent) lived elsewhere. The heirs in that case argued that this result was unfair since the law of the spouse's residence was less favorable to election and the decedent would not have had similar rights if the survivor had died first. The court decided, however, that this could make no difference. 

Note that in cases involving real estate, the result of the above rule might be that the spouse takes under the will in one jurisdiction and against the will in another. 

Thus in Eckels' Estate, 37 D. & C. 383 (O. C. Montg. 1940), the spouse of the Pennsylvania decedent took against the will here but took the life estate given to her by the will in the proceeds of foreign real estate. If that decision is right, this is one situation where the spouse can take both under and against the will.

§ 9. FORFEITURE OF RIGHT OF ELECTION. 

(a) By Husband. 

A husband, who for one year or upwards previous to the death of his wife, shall have wilfully neglected or refused to provide for her, or who for that period or upwards shall have wilfully and maliciously deserted her, shall have no right of election. 

(b) By Wife. 

A wife, who for one year or upwards previous to the death of her husband shall have wilfully and maliciously deserted him, shall have no right of election. (c) Slayer. 

Any surviving spouse who participates either as a principal or as an accessory before the fact in the wilful and unlawful killing of the testator shall have no right of election. 

(d) Surviving Spouse as Witness. 

The surviving husband or wife shall be a competent witness as to all matters pertinent to the issue of forfeiture under this section.

12. Agreements. 

1. General-Cross Reference 

This section is copied almost verbatim from section 6 of the Intestate Act. It was necessary to insert it here because the present act no longer refers to the Intestate Act in setting forth the spouse's right to elect. The law remains unchanged, however, and as in the past the same conduct which would bar a spouse from taking by intestacy bars the spouse from taking against the will. The cases on the subject are discussed under section 6 of the Intestate Act. Actually, most of the cases there discussed are election cases. ¶ 2. Agreements

Agreements under which the spouse has relinquished the right to share in the estate are also considered under section 6 of the Intestate Act. It is clear from the cases there considered that the right of election can be waived by agreement between, the husband and wife during their lives. Of special significance in election cases are the authorities considering agreements noted on the will itself. 

In both Kreiser's Appeal, 69 Pa. 194 (1871), and Mc- 

Bride's Estate, 81 Pa. 303 (1876), there were signed statements by the spouse appended to the will renouncing the 2652

WILLS ACT § 9 

right to take against it. In McBride's Estate, the survivor was the husband and he was held to his bargain. In 

Kreiser's Appeal, the surviving wife was permitted to avoid the effect of her waiver on the ground that a married woman had no power to make such a contract because "she is presumed to be under [the husband's] control and coercion." It is very doubtful that Kreiser's Appeal would be decided the same way today.' It is true that agreements between spouses are closely examined for fraud and overreaching. The sex of the promisor is no doubt still a factor in this examination, but a much less important one than it was in the last century. The modern rule seems to be that either a fair provision or full disclosure of the value of the estate is sufficient to uphold the agreement, even when the survivor is the wife.2 

As to agreements made after the decedent's death between the surviving spouse and the beneficiaries under the will, see discussion under section 10 (¶7) of the present act.

§ 10. How ELECTION MADE 

The surviving spouse electing to take under or against the will shall manifest the election in writing signed by him and acknowledged before an officer authorized by law to take acknowledgments of deeds. The election or a copy thereof shall be mailed or delivered to the personal representative of the testator or his attorney. The election shall be filed in the office of the clerk of the orphans' court of the county where the will was probated, and a record shall be made of such filing by the clerk. When the estate includes real estate the election or a duplicate original or a certified copy thereof shall be recorded in the office of the recorder of deeds of each county in which any of the real estate of the testator lies, and shall be indexed by the recorder in the grantors' index under the name of the testator, and in the grantees' index under the name of the surviving spouse. 

The costs of filing and recording the election shall be paid out of the estate as a part of the administration expenses. 

COMMISSIONERS' COMMENT-Section 10 should be compared with the first sentences of section 23 (b) and section 23 (e) of the 1917 act. Section 10 provides simply and clearly what shall be done to perfect the election. Later sections define the time limits and the effect of failure to comply with the procedure herein directed.

19. Change of Election. 

¶ 1. General

Prior to 1911 there were no special formalities prescribed for the spouse's election to take under or against the will. As a result there were frequent disputes over whether the surviving spouse had committed himself one way or the other by his conduct following the decedent's death (see § 11, ¶ 1, fn. 2). With the act of 1911, P. L. 79, it was provided that the election must be by a writing properly acknowledged and delivered to the personal representative, and formalities for filing the election were prescribed. These provisions were incorporated into section. 

23 of the Wills Act of 1917, and a time limit of two years. was set, later reduced to one year in 1925 (see discussion of § 11, 1). The present act continues these requirements with some modifications.

The procedure to be followed is now set forth separately in this section 10, while the time limit, the effect of failure to elect, and a new provision to protect bona fide purchasers of real estate are set forth in sections 11, 12 and 13, infra. Generally speaking, section 10 is the guide for the careful practitioner and describes what is supposed to be done in all cases. Section 11 and the subsequent sections will become important only when the procedure in section 10 has not been followed in all details. 

Omitted entirely from the new act is the procedure formerly in section 23 (d) of the act of 1917 for citing the spouse to elect after six months from the decedent's death. 

A failure to elect within a year of probate still has the effect of forcing the spouse to take under the will (section 12 (a)) but it is no longer possible to compel the spouse 2703

§ 

WILLS ACT 

12 FANHUji i Asi! 10 -041 ∙ARS to act before the year expires.¹ This omission makes unnecessary any reference in the present section to filing or recording the decree obtained in such a proceeding. Note also that the present section omits the exception in the old act which provided that an election was not required when the spouse was given the entire estate by the will. 

Since the worst that can happen to a dilatory spouse is to be forced to take under the will (section 12 (a)), the exception was thought to be unnecessary. 

There are four things to be done according to section 

10: (1) execution and acknowledgment of the writing, (2) delivery to the personal representative, (3) filing with the Orphans' Court, and (4) (if there is real estate) recording with the Recorder of Deeds. 

12. Execution of the Election 

2 The requirements for the form and execution of the election remain the same. There must be a writing signed and acknowledged. In this respect the language is identical with the act of 1917, so that the effect of the earlier cases on the subject will remain unchanged. No special words are necessary, but there must be a definite and unqualified election. Thus, a paper which purported to make a qualified election-conditional upon the children receiving a certain share was held to be no election in Powell's Estate, 225 Pa. 518 (1909). Likewise an ambiguous statement that the spouse has a claim against the estate is insufficient: Minnich's Estate, 288 Pa. 354 (1927).

The requirement of the spouse's signature was considered in Celenza's Estate, 308 Pa. 186 (1932), where it was held that the spouse may act through an agent in making the election, so that an election signed by her duly authorized attorney-in-fact complied with the statute. The same reasoning would apply in cases of election by the guardian of an incompetent spouse. The subject of election by agents, guardians, etc., is considered further under section 12 (b) infra.

WILLS ACT 13. Delivery to Personal Representative 

4 The delivery of the election to the executor or administrator c. t. a. remains a prime requisite of an effective election. The statute now specifically authorizes (1) a delivery of either the original or a copy, (2) either manual delivery or mailing and (3) delivery to either the personal representative or his attorney. These optional methods would probably have sufficed under the old act, but they are now expressly authorized by the statute. 

14. Filing with Orphans' Court

As in the old act, it is required that the election "shall be filed with the clerk of the Orphans' Court of the County where the will was probated." Presumably the court will refuse to order distribution unless this requirement is complied with or unless more than a year elapsed from probate and it is set forth in the statement of proposed distribution that no election was made (see section 12 (a)). It would seem to be the primary duty of the personal representative to attend to this filing, but if he fails to do so the electing spouse should see that it is done or take the risk of an erroneous decree of distribution. ¶ 5. Recording

The requirements for recording in cases where the estate includes real property are substantially changed. 

The election ("or a duplicate original or certified copy") must now be filed in the Recorder's office of each county where the real estate lies, rather than in the county where the will was probated. A failure in this respect might defeat the spouse's rights with respect to bona fide purchasers, as set forth in section 13, infra."
