Under the present act, Hunter concludes that the recording "may and should be done by the spouse to protect his rights, especially against grantee or lienholder." 8 Also omitted is the provision in the old act for registering the election with the survey bureau. 

6. Election by Conduct Impossible 

Since 1911, when formalities for making the election were first established, it would seem that election by conduct without complying with the statutory formalities has been impossible. In Beck's Estate, 265 Pa. 51 (1919), the widow had signed a written election to take under the will and had filed it with the Register of Wills but had not delivered it to the personal representative as required by the act of 1911, P. L. 79. She also accepted income payments under a trust created by the will. Later she changed her mind and decided to take against the will. The court said that the purpose of the act "was to promote certainty in the settlement of estates" and held that the widow's prior conduct did not amount to an election because the act had not been strictly complied with. Hence she was permitted to elect against the will by a writing properly delivered to the executor.9 

17. Estoppel and Agreements 

Although election by conduct other than that prescribed by the statute is impossible for reasons explained above, it would still seem possible for a spouse to be estopped from asserting all or part of the statutory right. 

Thus, in Cunningham's Estate, 137 Pa. 621 (1890), it was decided that if an electing widow acquiesces in a sale made by the executor under a power in the will, she is estopped from pursuing her interest in the land itself and must look to the proceeds for her statutory share. By the same reasoning, it would seem that if a spouse induces the executor 

7. See Cramm's Est., 127 Pa. Super. 446 (1937), aff'd. 329 Pa. 528 (1938). 

8. O. C. Book (1939) "Election by Spouse" §5 (d). If the personal rep resentative took care of recording and filing of the election he was not estopped from questioning it under the old act: Mahoney's Est., 56 D. & C. 286 (O. C. 

Allegh. 1945); this should remain the law in spite of the change in the act. 

9. See also McCutcheon's Est., 283 Pa. 157, 161 (1925); cf. Hoehl's Est., 321 Pa. 66 (1936), and cases under § 8, 14, fns. 7-9. 2706

to make a distribution which turns out to be erroneous in view of a later election and cannot be adjusted, the spouse should not be permitted to complain.10 This is not election by conduct but merely the application of general principles of estoppel.

Note that such a case is not likely to arise because after a year from probate the spouse who has yet not taken formal action will be compelled to take under the will (section 12 (a)) and the executor will be on his guard before that time. Also note that the principle of estoppel would have no application where the acts induced by the vacillating spouse cause no real hardship. Ordinarily, for example, a premature partial distribution can be adjusted in the light of a later election from funds remaining in the executor's hands.11

Principles of estoppel might also become relevant in considering conduct by the spouse before the decedent's death-as where the spouse has impliedly or expressly agreed with the decedent not to elect against the will. This type of case is treated under section 9 (¶ 2) of this act where the discussion of the general subject under section 6 of the 

Intestate Act is referred to. 

Another type of case where the spouse's conduct affects the statutory right is where the spouse and the beneficiaries under the will agree among themselves after the decedent's death as to the distribution of the estate. Assuming such an agreement is entered into with full knowledge of the facts, it will be favored by the law and will supersede the statutory procedure. See generally McCutcheon's Estate, 283 Pa. 157 (1925). 

8. When Election Becomes Final 

Aside from cases of estoppel or cases where the rights of the parties are governed by agreement, it has been seen that within the year no election can be made without complying with the statutory formalities. Suppose a spouse complies with some of the formalities of section 10 but not all of them. At what point is the election complete? 

10. See McCutcheon's Est., 283 Pa. 157, 161 (1925). 

11. As in Beck's Est., 265 Pa. 51, 55 (1919). 2707

§ 

WILLS ACT 

¶ 8 

The question might arise in three types of cases: (1) 

The question might be whether the spouse has acted in time. (2) The question might be whether the spouse, who himself has died shortly after the decedent, has sufficiently complied with the act to make the election effective. (Under section 12 (b), the personal representative of a deceased spouse cannot act for the spouse in making the election, but it is not clear whether all the formalities prescribed by section 10 must be completed before the spouse's death.) (3) The question might be whether the spouse has gone far enough in complying with the formalities of section 10 to preclude him from changing his mind within the year. (As explained under the next heading, a final election cannot be changed even within the year in the absence of fraud or mistake. Here we are assuming that no fraud or mistake can be shown.)

The statute provides the answer to only the first of these three types of problems. Section 11, infra, says that the election is in time as between the spouse and other beneficiaries under the will if a duly executed writing is delivered to the personal representative within a year of probate, regardless of when the filing and recording are done. Section 13, infra, has comparable provisions to cover. disputes between the spouse and the bona fide purchaser when the recording requirements have not been complied with. In the other two types of cases (i. e. where the spouse dies or changes his mind within the year before all the formalities are complied with) the statute is not clear as to when the election is complete. 

Under the 1917 act, delivery of a properly executed writing to the personal representative was essential (Beck's Estate, 265 Pa. 51 (1919)), but more than this was not required (Cramm's Estate, 127 Pa. Super. 446 (1937), aff'd. 329 Pa. 528 (1938)).12 In the act of 1917, however, the requirements of execution and delivery were set forth in 23 (b) as primary requirements, while the provisions for filing and recording were in subsequent subsections and were viewed as merely setting forth what the personal representative was supposed to do after the election had been 

12. But see McCurdy's Est., 50 D. & C. 403 (O. C. Montg. 1944). 2708

¶

WILLS ACT 

§ 10 made. In the present act, the provisions for filing and recording (not necessarily by the personal representative) are now in section 10 along with the provisions for execution and delivery. 

It could conceivably be argued, therefore, that all the requirements of section 10 must now be complied with before the spouse is precluded from changing his mind. Such a construction, however, would cause uncertainty and confusion in the settlement of estates. A more reasonable construction is that an election is binding on the spouse and on his estate when a proper writing is delivered to the executor. Such a rule would be in harmony with section 

11 and the cases under the old act. The converse of this proposition that until delivery is made there is no election (as held in Beck's Estate 265 Pa. 51 (1919) supra)would also seem to follow, although this might lead to difficulties under section 13 where the problem will again be discussed at ¶ 3. 

¶9. Change of Election 

Let it now be assumed that section 10 has been sufficiently complied with to make the election effective. Can the spouse thereafter withdraw or change the election? 

The general answer is that an election once made is binding, and the spouse cannot change it even though the time limit has not expired. See Baily's Estate, 285 Pa. 

408 (1926). The exceptions are as follows: (1) Within a year from probate, a spouse may withdraw and change an election if it was made "in ignorance of the value of the estate, or of the rights which would accrue under the provisions of the will as compared with the interests given by" the statute: McCutcheon's Estate, 283 Pa. 157, 162 (1925). (2) After the year, an election can be changed only upon a showing of actual fraud: Daub's Estate, 305

§ 11 

§ 11. TIME FOR MAKING ELECTION 

As between the surviving spouse and other legatees and devisees, the spouse's election shall be in time if within one year after the probate of the will the surviving spouse shall (1) mail or deliver the election or a copy thereof to the personal representative of the testator or his attorney or (2) file it in the office of the clerk of the orphans' court and mail or deliver a copy to the personal representative or his attorney or (3) record such election or a duplicate original or certified copy thereof in the office of the recorder of deeds of any county in which real estate of the testator lies and mail or deliver a copy to the personal representative or his attorney. The orphans' court, on application of the surviving spouse made within one year after the probate of the will, may extend the time for making the election for such period and upon such terms and conditions as the court shall deem proper under the circumstances. A certified copy of the decree of the court extending the time for making the election may be recorded and indexed in the office of the recorder of deeds in any county in which any of the real estate of the testator lies in the manner provided in section 10 hereof. 

COMMISSIONERS' COMMENT-The proviso of section 23 (b) of the 

1917 act has not been preserved. It is considered unnecessary because of the privilege of applying to the court for extension of time to file the election. This avoids the uncertainties of when there is a "final adjudication of the contest." 

The provisions of section 23 (f) of the 1917 act, added by amendment of 1939, P. L. 705, have been preserved, but the time of making application to the court has been extended from seven months to one year from the date of probate. This gives the surviving spouse a better opportunity to know what his share will be and whether there will be a will contest. Compelling action to be taken with one year is not considered unduly harsh. If a will contest is initiated within the year, application may be made to extend the time. If the contest is initiated after the year, the surviving spouse will have his share under the election if the will is sustained. If the will is not sustained, he will have an additional period of one year from the probate of a former will or, in case of intestacy, will have an intestate share which may be more than the share which would be acquired by an adverse election.

The provisions of section 23 (d) of the 1917 act for enforcing an earlier election after six months have been omitted in 2751

If these simple requirements have been met, the spouse is protected against legatees and devisees. His rights against third persons are covered in the following sections.

Discussion ¶1. History. 

12. Changes in Present Act. 

13. When Limitation is Tolled-Fraud. 

¶ 1. History 

Prior to 1917 the spouse could be cited to make an election after a year,¹ but in the absence of such a proceeding there was no time limit for making the election and sometimes the question of what the spouse had elected was litigated years after the probate of the will.2 In the act of 

1917, a two-year limitation was inserted on pain of being compelled to take under the will and this was reduced to one year by the amendment of 1925. In 1935 a proviso was added to section 23 (b) extending the time to 30 days. after the "final adjudication" of a will contest, and in 1939 the spouse was given the additional right in section 23 (f) to petition the court for an extension. The provision for citing the spouse to elect was retained in section 23 (d) of the act of 1917, the time after which this could be done being reduced to six months from decedent's death. 

12. Changes in Present Act 

The present section (together with section 12 (a) infra) continues the general scheme of the old act with the following changes: 

1. The section applies only "as between the surviving spouse and other legatees and devisees." The rights of third parties are treated separately in section 13. 

2. The one year runs from the probate of the will rather than the grant of letters. 

3. It is now definitely stated which of the formalities prescribed by section 10 must be completed within the year. 

1. Section 35 of the Act of 1832, P. L. 190. 

2. E. g. Boileau's Est., 201 Pa. 493 (1902), where the question was raised

MAU LA DOWN 

If a properly executed election is delivered to the personal representative within the year, the election is in time and the other formalities can be completed later. This restates the result reached under the old act in Cramm's Estate, 127 Pa. Super. 446 (1937), aff'd. 329 Pa. 528 (1938).³ The new provision reads as if the spouse had a choice of three possible procedures listed as (1), (2) and (3) for making the election in time. A careful reading of this part of the section, however, will reveal that "(2)" and "(3)" are superfluous. In effect the new provision states that the election is in time if within the year there is (1) delivery alone or (2) delivery and filing, or (3) delivery and recording. This curious duplication was the result of an oversight and should cause no concern; "(2)" and "(3)” can simply be ignored. 

4. The proviso of old section 23 (b) automatically extending the time in case of a will contest has been omitted for the reasons set forth in the Commissioner's comments. 

Remember that the year now runs from probate. If the contested will has been refused probate, no problem arises. 

If the will is admitted and the probate appealed, the spouse should make up his mind whether he likes the probated will and act accordingly, regardless of what he thinks of other papers which might be offered if the order of probate is reversed. Then if the contested will is sustained the spouse will have made his election with respect to it. If the order of probate is reversed the election with respect to it will be a nullity, and if a different will is thereupon probated the spouse will have an additional year to make up his mind. Of course if things get too complicated the spouse can always petition for extension, but a will contest in itself should not make extension necessary. 

5. The spouse may still apply to the court for an extension of the time limit which will be granted in proper cases. Such an application may now be made at any time within the year from probate (rather than within seven months). A provision for recording the decree extending the time has also been added in view of the new protection

3. When Limitation is Tolled-Fraud 

It is clear from Freer's Estate, 353 Pa. 351 (1946), that nothing short of "active fraud" will toll the limitation of this section. In that case letters had been advertised in the county where they were granted but the executors made no further attempt to inform the surviving husband of his wife's death. The husband (who seems to have been something less than attentive, although he was absolved from the charge of desertion) learned of the death 21 months later and filed an election to take against the will about two and a half years after the grant of letters. 

The court decided that the attempted election was ineffective because it had not been filed within the year. It was said that the executors had no duty to give the husband special notice of the probate and their failure to do so was no fraud.*

Discussion The law remains substantially the same but for some reason the ability of the spouse to force distribution before the year is now limited to where the election is to take under the will.

This subsection continues the provisions contained in section 23 (b) and 23 (c) of the old act. Such changes as there are will not materially affect prior practice. 

Thus, the words, "except as provided in section 7 (3) hereof," were to distinguish the case of the spouse married after the execution of the will. As explained under section 

8 (17) ("After-Married Spouse Distinguished") the two types of cases are entirely distinct. The after-married spouse is in no sense put to an election; he simply "receives" a full intestate share unless the will gives him. 2801

§ (a) WILLS ACT 

CI Mo 

MDIVI? 

more. The express exception of such cases from the operation of section 12 (a) merely confirms what is implicit in the statute.

The conclusive presumption that the spouse who has not acted in time has elected to take under the will remains the same, except as it is indirectly affected by the changes made in section 11 with reference to what the time limit is and how it can be extended. 

The second sentence of this section 12 (a) substantially re-enacts the old law in prohibiting an award to the spouse until the election is made. The prohibition now is expressly limited to awards within the year, because after the year the spouse who has not elected must take under the will. An unimportant change is made by the addition of the words "and filed." The old act merely required execution and delivery. The change is theoretical, however, because the provision only operates when the court is being asked to make an award so that the spouse would ordinarily see that the election was filed as a matter of course. (Note that there is no requirement in this section or sections 10 and 11 that the filing must be done within the year.) 

A more important change is made by the language of the second sentence relating to the election. Under the old act the spouse could demand accounting and distribution after the delivery of his "election"-whether it was under or against the will. Under the present act it would seem that the court is not permitted to order any distribution to the spouse within the year unless the spouse has elected to take under the will. Apparently the spouse who early elects to take against the will must nevertheless wait out the year before citing the personal representative to account and distribute. The change was probably unintentional.

Note that the prohibition only applies to enforced distribution-i. e., by decree of court after a proper accounting. Nothing in this section or elsewhere interferes with the power of the personal representative to make partial distribution at his own risk prior to accounting-as he will ordinarily be willing to do in cases where the spouse gets something regardless of which way the election is made. 2802 [The next page is 2851]

Discussion ¶ 1. General.

¶ 1. General 

This new provision was intended to be declaratory of prior case law. That no change was intended is clear from the Commissioners' comments and from the fact that the language is derived from the Supreme Court decisions. on the subject. The latter part of the subsection covers the particular case where the surviving spouse dies without having made an election. The first part of the sentence, referring generally to the personal nature of the right, might arise in a variety of situations. 

2. Death of Spouse 

It has long been the law under our cases, even though the statute formerly had no provision governing the case, that an election to take against the will cannot be made on behalf of the spouse's estate after the latter's death.¹ The 

1. See cases collected in Harris's Est., 351 Pa. 368, 379, fn. 10 (1945), and

Hunter, O. C. Book (1939) “Election by Spouse" §7 (c). 

2851

§ (b) 

WILLS ACT

theoretical basis for these decisions was that until the right was exercised it was not property which could pass as part of the deceased spouse's estate. The policy behind the rule was that the right was intended for the benefit of the spouse and not of the spouse's heirs or beneficiaries under the spouse's will.

Neither the present statutory provision nor the earlier cases, however, prevent the representative of the spouse from enforcing an election which the spouse made before his death even though the spouse died before actual distribution. This seems unavoidable and it was so held in 

Buckland's Estate, 239 Pa. 608, 613 (1913), and Mallon's 

Estate, 253 Pa. 29, 32 (1916). The present statutory provision merely states that the right shall not be "exercised" after the spouse's death. Hence the law remains that the benefit of an election made prior to death will inure to the spouse's estate.

As a result of this distinction it might become important to determine whether a spouse went far enough in following the procedure set forth in section 10 prior to his death. In Roberts's Estate, 82 Pa. Super. 251 (1923), it was held under the act of 1917 that the mere execution of the election (without delivery, filing or recording) was insufficient to constitute an election so that the procedure could not be completed by the widow's executor after her death. 

The general question of when an election becomes final arises in a number of situations and is discussed under section 10 (8) where other types of cases are considered and differences between the present act and the act of 1917 are noted. For reasons there explained, it is believed that the election should become final when a properly executed writing is delivered to the personal representative. Hence, if the spouse dies after delivery but before filing or recording, the representative of the deceased spouse should be permitted to complete the formalities. ¶ 3. Insolvent Spouse

Consistent with the theory that the right of election is not present property but is merely a personal right for the benefit of the spouse himself, it was held in Fleming's 2852

¶ 

WILLS ACT 

Estate, 217 Pa. 610 (1907), that creditors of a spouse who was given a spendthrift interest in income by the will could not compel him to exercise his right to take against the will. The wording of the present provision should confirm this result. 

14. Incompetent Spouse

A reading of this subsection by one unfamiliar with the earlier case law might lead to the erroneous impression that the spouse must act personally and hence that it would be impossible for a mentally incompetent spouse to elect. Such was not the intent of the drafters, as the Commissioners' comments indicate.

The earlier cases had, like the present statute, laid down the rule that the right of election was a "personal right.' 

By this was meant that the right, prior to its exercise, was not inheritable or transferable property and that it was intended for the spouse's personal benefit. That the right is a "personal" one, however, does not mean that it must in all cases be exercised by the spouse in person. "It is a personal right as distinguished from a property right, not necessarily a right to be exercised only by direct personal action." Celenza's Estate, 308 Pa. 186, 192 (1932). Thus, it has long been law that the guardian of an incompetent spouse may exercise this personal right on behalf of the incompetent, subject to the court's supervision. Since the language of the act is based on the language of the prior cases there is no reason to suppose that the act changes this rule in any way. 

A recent and leading case on the subject is Harris's 

Estate, 351 Pa. 368, 382 (1945). The Pennsylvania authorities on the power of the guardian or committee of a mentally incompetent spouse to make the election and the supervisory power of the court ("which is the real guardian of the incompetent") are there reviewed. Because it is the court which must make the ultimate decision, a petition by the guardian for instruction would seem necessary in all cases. Harris's Estate demonstrates how the court's decision will by no means be based on simple mathematics. "It is common knowledge that not every widow 2853

§ (b) WILLS ACT 

14 

BODYPAL THEY 

MAR disregards her husband's last wishes for the disposition of his property merely because she would obtain a greater quantum of his estate by so doing; sentiment enters into such situations quite as much as considerations of material advantage, and, if she is reasonably provided for in her husband's will or her wants are otherwise adequately supplied, it does not follow, just because such provision may not be as much as she might elect, that she would file an election to take against his will. Therefore, when the court acts on behalf of a mentally defective widow it should not be controlled by mere mathematical calculations of the financial results that would accrue to her one way or the other." (351 Pa. at 383) It was decided that even though the spouse in Harris's Estate was excluded entirely from the will, the guardian should not take against it. The decision was based on a number of considerations including the fact that the spouse would be adequately provided for from income of the decedent's grandfather's trust and that a large portion of the decedent's estate consisted of a vested interest in the principal of that trust which the spouse would probably not live long enough to enjoy.

The proper court to make the decision in this type of case is the court of common pleas which appointed the guardian (not the orphans' court administering the estate). 

This raises problems in cases of foreign decedents. Mac- 

Gregor's Estate, 40 D. & C. 519 (C. P. Warren 1940), followed to its logical extreme the theory that the right of election is not property in a case of this sort. The decedent was a non-resident but owned Pennsylvania real estate, so that the right of the spouse therein was governed by Pennsylvania law. The surviving spouse, who also resided in the foreign state, was incompetent, and a petition was filed by the domiciliary guardian for the appointment of a committee here to elect against the will. The court decided that it was without authority to do so because the statute authorizing such appointments was limited to cases where the incompetent had "real or personal estate" in

Pa. 368, 372, fn. 3 (1945).

SAT MAR 3`Agataka 

2854

Pennsylvania, and the personal right of election was neither. It is difficult to answer this logic, but the decision seems unduly theoretical. That the right of a non-resident spouse should depend on the accident of whether he has an interest in Pennsylvania property other than his unripened interest in the decedent's estate is scarcely just, and it is doubtful that the appellate courts would adopt such a technical construction of the statute providing for guardians.3 

¶ 5. Other Situations Where Right Is Exercised by Another 

The pattern set by the cases dealing with deceased, insolvent, and mentally incompetent spouses gives a fair indication of the rule to be applied in analogous situations. 

The right is not to be exercised for the benefit of others, but if the spouse will personally benefit, an election by another on his behalf is permissible.

Thus, the cases dealing with mentally incompetent spouses would undoubtedly be followed in the case of a minor spouse. The guardian would be permitted to execute the election subject to the approval of the court which appointed him. The Supreme Court said as much by way of dictum in Celenza's Estate, 308 Pa. 186, 192 (1932).

The actual holding of Celenza's Estate was that the election could be signed by the spouse's authorized attorney in fact. Not only is the signature of the agent a compliance with the formal requirements of what is now section 10 of the act, but it would seem from the facts and the court's reasoning that even the discretion of whether to elect or not can be delegated by the spouse to another. In that case the widow who was illiterate and resided in Italy executed a power of attorney authorizing her agent "to act in her behalf in matters pertaining to her husband's estate." Plainly such an agent was acting as something more than a rubber stamp, but his election on behalf of the widow was upheld.

§ 13. GRANTEE OR LIENHOLDER 

An election shall be void as against a bona fide grantee of or holder of a lien on real estate in any county unless (1) the election or a duplicate original or certified copy thereof is recorded in such county within one year after the probate of the will or if thereafter then before the recording or entering of the instrument or lien under which such grantee or lienholder claims, or (2) a certified copy of the decree of the court extending the time for making the election has been recorded in such county within one year after the probate of the will or if thereafter then before the recording or entering of such instrument or lien and the election or a duplicate original or certified copy thereof has been recorded in such county within the time set by the court or if thereafter then before the recording or entering of such instrument or lien.

COMMISSIONERS' COMMENT The purpose of this new section is to protect bona fide grantees, mortgagees, and judgment creditors when the election is recorded in the county where the real estate is located after the one year period has expired. The spouse who has failed to record his election is allowed to take ahead of devisees, if he has complied with the minimum requirements of section 10, but must perfect the election in each county where real estate lies if he wishes to be protected against bona fide grantees, mortgagees or judgment creditors of the devisee. 

Old Law

Prior to the present act there was no specific provision dealing with the rights of a bona fide grantee or lienholder except the general requirement of recording (now in section 10). There was dictum in the cases, however, to the effect that an innocent third party would be protected where the election was not recorded.

Discussion 

This section probably restates the results that would have been reached under the old law. Note, however, that under section 10 the election must now be recorded in the county where the real estate is situated, regardless of the county of probate.

¶ 1. General 

This is a new provision intended to simplify title searches by setting forth in detail the effect of failing to record the election pursuant to section 10. Perhaps the effect of this section was implicit in the requirement of recording in the acts of 1911, P. L. 79, and 1917, P. L. 403, but the law on the subject was not clear. No case has been found since 1911 where the rights of bona fide purchasers were directly involved. In Dalsen's Estate, 310 Pa. 190, 194, 195-6 (1933), the court considered the question incidentally. The dispute was between legatees and spouse in that case, so that what was said on the subject must be considered dictum so far as the rights of third parties are concerned. It seems clear from the opinion, however, that the court would have given protection to a third party who had acted in ignorance of an unrecorded election even in the absence of a specific provision to this effect in the old act.

The present section spells out the exact effect of failure to record and should provide comfort to the searcher in tracing titles through devises by persons dying on or after January 1, 1948. As already noted under section 10, the recording is now done in the county where the land is situated rather than where the will was probated. 

There is no time limit on when the recording may be done, but if the election is recorded after a year from probate the intervening rights of third parties are superior. If a bona fide purchaser buys the land from the devisee and records his deed after ten months and the spouse records an election the eleventh month, the spouse's rights are superior. After the year has run, the spouse may still prevail if the election is recorded before the deed of the bona fide purchaser. The net effect is that the title searcher may rely on the record after a year from probate. 

Although this section does not say so in so many words, the "election" referred to must mean an election against the will. In other words, if nothing appears of record after the year, the third party (in the absence of actual knowledge to the contrary) may assume that no election was made and hence that the spouse has acquiesced 2902

WILLS ACT § 13 

in the will under section 12 (a). Otherwise section 13 would be meaningless.

Protection is given to a "bona fide grantee of or holder of a lien on" real estate. A bona fide purchaser has been held to mean one who has taken without notice of the title infirmity and has given value. See Cancilla v. Bondy, 353 

Pa. 249, 253 (1945). Absence of notice is plainly implicit in the words "bona fide". "Grantee", however, seems broader than "purchaser". Literally, it would seem that the giving of value is unnecessary for protection under this section of the Wills Act, although this would be a rather marked departure from analogous rules applied under recording acts generally. Furthermore "grantee" would not include a devisee and it would seem illogical to give protection to a volunteer who takes by inter vivos. gift when no such protection is given to one who takes by will. For these reasons the words "for value" might be read into the statute.

In the case of a lienholder, it may be questioned whether reliance on the apparent ownership of the devisee must be shown. A mortgagee of the devisee will necessarily rely on appearances, but a judgment creditor might not even know of the debtor's colorable title until after the lien is acquired. Unless reliance is implicit in the concept of bona fides, however, it would seem that such a judgment creditor would nevertheless be protected. 

¶ 2. Indexing 

Section 10 describes how the election should be indexed by the recorder of deeds. The present section says nothing about indexing but it would seem from general principles that the spouse must see that the proper indexing is done if he wishes to take advantage of the protection section 13 purports to give. 

The dictum in Dalsen's Estate, 310 Pa. 190, 195-6 (1933), is also helpful on this point. "The act provides the election shall be indexed in a certain way, but improper indexing does not condemn an election. Indexing is an act of a county officer; if not proper, courts will compel proper indexing. It may be that intervening rights of 2903

Añāž BORAN

OV third parties could not be prejudiced without notice through failure to properly index an election, and that responsibility for such failure might fall on the officer. 

The validity of the election as such would not be affected by these acts. In the present case the grantor's index was in order, and such indexing gave notice of the spouse's interest to all persons dealing with decedent's property. 

Title could not be safely taken without an examination of an election so indexed. This conclusion is not in opposition to anything we have said in Prouty v. Marshall, 225 

Pa. 570. We distinguish the facts in that case from the present case: Crippen v. Bergold, 258 Pa. 469. It would be better, however, to have the grantee's index corrected. We conclude, therefore, that the court in banc did not err in sustaining the election."

The holding of Dalsen's Estate was merely that improper indexing does not invalidate the election as between the spouse and legatee. The significance of this decision was later overshadowed by Cramm's Estate, 127 Pa. Super. 

446 (1937), aff'd. 329 Pa. 528 (1938), deciding that no recording at all was necessary for an effective election as between the spouse and those claiming under the will. 

The quoted language in Dalsen's Estate indicates, however, that improper indexing of an election will have the same effect as improper indexing of deeds and mortgages generally. Briefly, the rule applied in the cases cited in the above quotation is that the third party will be protected if a reasonable search of the index fails to disclose the recorded instrument. A mere technical error in indexing (as the omission of a middle initial in the Crippen case) will not excuse the careless title searcher, but the third party's title will be superior if a prior instrument is indexed in a manner which the court considers misleading to a reasonably diligent searcher (as the indexing under the wrong initial in the Prouty case). The person recording in instrument "cannot hide behind the mistake of the recorder," in a dispute with a bona fide purchaser. He must "look at the record and see that the instrument has been properly entered." If he fails to do so he might lose his title to an innocent purchaser, although he may 2904

WILLS ACT 

§ 13 have an action for damages against the recorder. See 

Prouty v. Marshall, 225 Pa. 570, 577 (1909). 

13. Recording Without Delivery

Suppose a duly executed election against the will is recorded but never delivered to the personal representative pursuant to sections 10 and 11 or delivered after the time limit has expired. In Wilson's Estate, 297 Pa. 348 (1929), it was held that such an election was a nullity and it is reasonable to suppose that the same result would follow under the present act. The devisee's title would be superior to the spouse's under section 11, and there is nothing in the act requiring the devisee to see that the records are not falsified (consciously or unconsciously) by the spouse.

Thus, a record showing an election might not give a true picture of the title. This should not be of any real concern to the title searcher, however. If nothing appears of record after a year from probate, the innocent third party can rely on the apparent title of the devisee. If an election against the will appears of record it might not be valid, but in such a case the third party will need the joinder of the devisee in any event since even if the election is valid the spouse will only own a fractional interest. 

Many such title problems will disappear if administration of real estate is provided by the new Fiduciaries Act—at least in cases which are fully administered so that the title to the decedent's land will be fixed by the decree of distribution. 2905 [The next page is 2951]

§14. RULES OF INTERPRETATION 

 (1) Wills Construed as if Executed Immediately Before Death.

Every will shall be construed, with reference to the testator's real and personal estate, to speak and take effect as if it had been executed immediately before the death of the testator. (2) After-Acquired Property. 

The real and personal estate acquired by a testator after making his will shall pass by a general devise or bequest.

COMMISSIONERS' COMMENTS- 

[General] This section includes rules for the interpretation of wills, some of which are new and some of which are separate sections of the 1917 act. [clause (1)] 

Clause (1) is identical with section 9 of the 1917 act. [clause (2)] Clause (2) is similar to section 10 of the 1917 act, but has been made applicable to personal estate as well as to real estate. 

Old Law

Section 9. Every will shall be construed, with reference to the real and personal estate comprised in it, to speak and take effect as if it had been executed immediately before the death of the testator, unless a contrary intention shall appear by the will.

Section 10. The real estate acquired by a testator after making his will shall pass by a general devise, unless a contrary intention be manifest on the face of the will.

¶5. Designation of Beneficiaries Not Included. 

1. History 

There is a good history and analysis of these statutory provisions in Fidelity Company's Appeal, 108 Pa. 492, 499 (1885). "The general rule of the common law was, that a will of realty was construed to speak from its date; real estate which the testator did not have at the time of making of his will, but which he subsequently acquired, would not pass under it, however express, comprehensive and general the words of the will, or however manifest the intention of the testator. A will of personalty, however, was not referable to the state of the property at the time of the making of the will, but was construed to take effect from the date of the testator's death, unless there were expressions in the will showing it was intended to describe the property with reference to the former and not the later date. By Sec. 10 of our act of April 10th, 1833 [P. L. 249] 

it was provided 'that the real estate acquired by a testator, after making his will, shall pass by a general devise, unless a contrary intention be manifest on the face of the will.' It will be seen that this section placed wills of realty and personalty on the same footing in part only, and the first section of the act of 4th June, 1879 [P. L. 88 providing that wills should be contrued to speak and take effect as if executed immediately before the testator's death as to both real and personal estate] was enacted to complete what had only been partially effected by the act of 1833.' 

The act of 1879 is now section 14 (1) of the present act, while section 10 of the act of 1833 has become section 14 (2). Clause (1) would seem broad enough to make clause (2) unnecessary. The Commission of 1917 recognized this in its comment. However, it was thought advisable to include both provisions in the act of 1917 to avoid any implication that a change was being made, and the drafters of the 1947 act followed the same policy. 

The language of the older acts has been followed closely. The only change is to make clause (2) apply to 2952

WILLS ACT 

 personal as well as real estate. This has no significance because a general bequest always passed after-acquired personalty even at common law, and as already noted, clause (2) is probably unnecessary anyway. Clause (1) on the other hand has always expressly applied to both types of property since its original enactment in 1879. 

These provisions were no doubt inserted in our statutory law simply for the purpose of making the common law rule as to personalty apply to real estate as well. The court in Fidelity Company's Appeal, 108 Pa. at 500, pointed out, however, that the effect of what is now section 14 (1) has been somewhat more than this. The common law presumption as to personal property has been fortified and the courts now require "a clearer proof and the use of more decided terms in the will, to establish a contrary intention."

A simple example of the operation of clause (2) of the present section is where a will makes a gift of "the residue of my estate, real and personal." At common law this would pass any personal property owned at death regardless of when acquired but it would pass only such real estate as testator owned when he wrote the will. Under what is now clause (2) any real and personal estate owned at death passes under a testamentary provision of this sort. See Hackett v. Commonwealth, 102 Pa. 505, 514 

A case where the broader provision of clause (1) would have to be relied upon is the following: Testator writes a will giving to X "all my personal effects and all my Pennsylvania coal lands." When testator dies some years later it appears that the personal effects and Pennsylvania coal lands he owned at his death are not the same as those he owned when he wrote the will. At common law, X would get the personal effects but not the after-acquired coal lands. Clause (2) of the present section would not change this result because the devise was not general.¹ Clause (1) 

1. Compare discussion of section 14 (13) infra for meaning of "general devise." Thus, if a specific gift was made of "Blackacre", a conveyance after the will revoked the devise at common law and Blackacre would not pass even if testator subsequently reacquired title to the same land before his death. These clauses come into play in a variety of situations. Only a few of the innumerable cases on the subject can be treated. 

12. General, Specific or Demonstrative Gifts

The first question that is likely to arise is whether the testamentary gift in question is general or specific. If it is general, the beneficiary can rely on clause (2) without going into the more complex questions covered by clause (1). Sometimes the solution to this problem involves construing a home-made will to determine whether a word or phrase literally having a restricted meaning was intended to be all inclusive. For example, a testator makes a gift of his "money." In Jacobs's Estate, 140 Pa. 268 (1891), the court decided that testator referred to all his property, including real estate, when he used the word "money." 

See also Bricker's Estate, 335 Pa. 300, 303 (1939). In 

Miller v. Bower, 260 Pa. 349 (1918), on the other hand, the court came to an opposite conclusion when the word was used in a different context. Of course the whole will must be read in such cases and authorities are of little value. 

Sometimes, a testator refers to his "property” and then begins enumerating it. The tendency in such cases seems to be to hold that the enumeration does not restrict the broader phrase preceding it, so that the gift is held to be general-at least where intestacy is thereby avoided. Again, however, the particular wording and surrounding circumstances are important. See Rzedzianowski's Estate, 148 

Pa. Super. 361, 370 (1942), for the relevant authorities.

Another kind of case where it becomes important to determine whether a gift is general or specific is where 2. The court cites three cases for this proposition, two of which seem to hold just the opposite. 

See also Martin's Est., 135 Pa. Super. 136, 146 (1938). For other cases, see 

Fiduciary Review, Nov. 1947. 2954

WILLS ACT 

Sg., Glad wall be 3 property is admittedly described in particular terms and testator owns nothing at his death which fills the description. If the gift is construed as specific, the beneficiary will lose regardless of whether the will is read as of its date or as of the time of death, because the subject matter of the gift no longer exists. In such a case the only argument available to the beneficiary is that although the kind of property was particularly described, testator intended a general legacy of a certain value. A clear case where such an argument would prevail is where a testator who owns no bonds leaves X "$5000 worth of government bonds." The construction is that testator was not referring to bonds he owned or expected to own but that he intended his executor to purchase the bonds and turn them over to X. Sometimes courts will go to great length to avoid disappointing the named beneficiary in cases of this sort. In Snyder's Estate, 217 Pa. 71 (1907), testatrix owned twenty-six shares of bank stock having a par value of $2600. The will gave "to Ina Stuart six hundred dollars of bank stock of the Second National Bank of Mercer..." and to "Peter Myers two thousand dollars of the Bank stock of Bank referred to above." Later testatrix sold her bank stock and died owning none of it. The court held the gift general. "What she intended to give them was a certain amount of bank stock, measured by its par value, and what they are entitled to get from her estate is the market value of the same." (217 Pa. at 77.) Apparently the decision in such cases depends on whether testator uses the possessive pronoun. If he says "my 100 shares of 

X stock" the gift is likely to be found to be specific, but if he simply says "100 shares of X stock" the gift can be construed to be general. 

The so-called "demonstrative legacy" is a general gift of a certain amount payable out of specifically designated property,—a gift of "$500 to A, to be paid from the proceeds of my X stock." Such a gift is treated like a specific gift if the designated property is in existence and there 3. But see infra under "Tracing" (4). It is here assumed that we are dealing with a case where even under the doctrine of tracing the property described cannot be identified. 

4. Note that when the gift is so construed the legatee is given the option of taking cash if he wants to. 2955

WILLS ACT 

12 is a problem of abatement. On the other hand, if the designated property has been sold by testator during his lifetime, the demonstrative legacy is treated as general, so that there is no ademption. Again, courts will stretch the wording of a will to its limit in order to avoid ademption in this type of case. In Shearer's Estate, 346 Pa. 97 (1943), there was a gift to trustees for a son of "my farm and tract of land situated in Conroy Township. "The farm was sold shortly before testator's death. The court admitted that if the will had said no more, the gift would necessarily have been specific and adeemed by the sale. 

After stating the terms of the trust, however, the will went on to say, "The value of said farm and contents I fix at the sum of Six Thousand Dollars ($6000), so that my said son shall receive the use and benefit of the said amount out of my estate." This, together with the fact that the other children were given amounts each of which, together with inter vivos gifts, totalled $6000 convinced the court that testator did not intend a specific gift of the farm, but a general gift of $6000 payable out of the proceeds of the farm. It has been said that "a demonstrative legacy is a mere creation or fiction of law, intended to cover a situation arising from some uncertainty or ambiguity in the language of a will, where the real intent of the testator is not apparent. I venture to say that no attorney, much less a layman, would ever intentionally attempt to create a demonstrative legacy by language so uncertain as to require judicial construction." In re Low's Will, 232 App. 

Div. 414, 421, 250 N. Y. S. 192, 200 (1931). This is no doubt true. The point is, however, that the court must translate testator's muddled thoughts into a precise intent. In all cases of this sort there is a combination of motives: The testator wants to make a gift of a certain value, and he also wants to make a gift of a certain thing. Where the thing has disappeared so that testator's purpose cannot be fulfilled in this regard, it is reasonable to attempt to give effect to the other part of testator's purpose. Suppose the extreme case of a testator who gives his aging dog Rover to his wealthy friend A, for the sole reason that he knows A loves the dog and will take care of it. Certainly, SESTED 2956

WILLS ACT 

 if Rover dies before testator, there is no reason to give A anything. On the other hand, a gift of 100 shares of General Motors stock is not likely to have the same connotations. Hence, if there is something in the will indicating that testator was thinking in terms of monetary rather than sentimental value, the court will try to construe the gift as general or demonstrative.

Mechem would go a step further than the courts in this respect. In "Specific Legacies, Gifts of Unspecific 

Things," 87 U. of Pa. L. Rev. 546 (1939), he suggests that more attention should be paid to the form of the gift. The gift of "my horse Bessie" should not be treated in the same way as "my General Motors stock" regardless of the use of the possessive pronoun and regardless of whether the testator places any monetary value on the property.

He admits, however, that the decisions have not gone this far. For better or for worse, the courts seem to require either the absence of "my" or the ascribing of a monetary valuation before they will find against ademption. 

13. Specific Gifts-Date of Will or Death 

When a gift in the will is clearly specific, then clause (2) has no application, but clause (1) is relevant in determining whether testator referred to a particular item of property owned by him when he wrote his will or to any property of the kind described which he might own at his death. The statute merely provides the presumption; the decision in the particular case depends on what the courts require as an expression of a contrary intention. 

Suppose the gift is of "my piano." As already pointed out, if testator owns no piano at his death, the beneficiary clearly takes nothing regardless of how the will is construed. Suppose, however, that the testator owned a piano when he wrote his will but later sold it and bought another one which he died owning. If the will is read as if it were executed immediately before death, then the beneficiary takes the second piano, but if it is found that testator was referring to the piano owned at the time he wrote the will, then the "contrary intention" will take the case out of the statute and the legacy will fail. 2957

WILLS ACT 

13 There is general authority for making the case turn on whether reference is made to "that which is genericthat which may be increased or diminished" or to "a particular thing such as a ring or a horse." Thus, "my personal effects" or "my annuities" would refer to whatever filled the description at the testator's death. But "my piano" in the case described above was held by an English court (under a statute identical with clause (1) of our statute) to mean the piano owned by testator when he wrote his will, so that the legacy was adeemed by a later sale even though testator died owning another piano. It is doubtful, however, that the decision would have been the same in Pennsylvania, as our courts have given a very strong effect to the presumption of the statute and seem to require something more than a reference to a particularized object as a manifestation of the contrary intent. 

Lusk's Estate, 336 Pa. 465 (1939), is a rather striking decision in this respect. Testator devised to his wife "my house and lot in which I now reside, situate in the Second Ward, City of New Castle, Lawrence County, Pennsylvania." At the time the will was written, testator owned a house in the second ward which he later sold. He then purchased another house where he resided at his death. 

Apparently by pure coincidence, this house also was in the second ward of the city of New Castle. It was held that the second house passed, no intent being found contrary to what is now clause (1) of the present section. The court looked with favor on the wife's argument that testator "presumably knowing the law provided his will would speak as of his death, found it unnecessary, when he substituted one residence for another, to change the phraseology of the devise because the general testamentary description already in the will sufficiently identified the subsequently acquired residence "The case is a strong one; not only was the gift of a particular thing (rather than a class of things) but the phrase "in which I now reside" was used to identify it. Hence, neither of these factors or even a combination of them can be regarded as controlling in Pennsylvania.

An example of a Pennsylvania decision going the other way is Fidelity Company's Appeal, 108 Pa. 492 (1885), already referred to. There, a gift was made of "eightyone shares of the Provident Life and Trust Company of Philadelphia, now standing in my name on the books of said company.'

After the date of the will, the corporation revised its capital structure and issued new shares to replace the old at the ratio of one for two-thus reducing testatrix's nominal holdings to forty and a half shares, although the actual value of her interest remained the same. 

Later, the testatrix purchased additional shares and at the time of her death she again owned exactly eighty-one shares although each share now represented twice the actual value of the ones she owned when she wrote her will. 

The court regarded the use of the word "now" in the description as significant and held that the presumption of the statute had been rebutted. The will was construed to refer to the stock owned at the date of execution, and the legatee took only forty and a half shares of the new stock. (See below 4 under "Tracing.") 

One cannot help wondering if the decision in Fidelity

Company's Appeal would have been the same if the facts had come before the court after Lusk's Estate had been decided. The fact that both decisions remain on the books demonstrates that cases of this sort are always distinguishable. There are so many factors, both articulated and unarticulated, entering into the decision that it is impossible to reduce these cases to a rule of thumb. For example, the difference between the relative value of the property owned at the date of the will and the property owned at death undoubtedly plays a part, although the point is seldom mentioned. In Waldo v. Hayes, 96 App. Div. 454, 89 

N. Y. S. 69 (1904), "my diamond brooch" written at a time when testatrix owned a brooch worth $1500 was held sufficient to pass another brooch worth $2350 owned at the time of death. It may be wondered whether this decision would be controlling on the same court if a brooch worth $500 was owned when the will was written and one worth $10,000 was owned at death. 4. Tracing-Change in Form of Corporate Shares 

Suppose a gift is specific ("my shares in X corporation") and there is nothing which literally fits the description of the subject matter at testator's death. The beneficiary still has a chance if he can show that there is property owned at death "which has been changed in name and form only, but which is substantially the same thing" as property owned by testator when he wrote his will. It would seem, for example, that if testator makes a gift of "my shares in X corporation" and before his death the corporation merely changes its name to the Y corporation the legacy is not adeemed. In this very limited sense, the property can be "traced," but it is doubtful that our courts would go much beyond the case suggested. Certainly, there can be no "tracing" as the word is used in cases dealing with the misappropriation of trust property. 

In Horn's Estate, 317 Pa. 49 (1934), the will made a gift of "my Ohio Fuel Corporation stock." The corporation later consolidated with another corporation to form the Columbia Gas and Electric Corporation and the testator's common shares were exchanged for common and preferred shares in the new company. Subsequently, there was a stock split-up, a stock dividend, and the issuance of voting trust certificates. The named legatee claimed the conglomeration of interests owned at death representing the original Ohio Fuel Corporation stock owned at the date of the will. The court held there had been an ademption, indicating that the consolidation alone was sufficient to accomplish this result. 

Note that the problem of tracing can arise only when it is first conceded that testator was referring to specific 

8. Compare Goode v. Reynolds, 208 Ky. 441, 271 S. W. 600, 63 A. L. R. 

631 (1925) reaching a contrary conclusion on similar facts. As to stock and liquidating dividends after the date of the will, see generally Hicks v. Kerr, 132 

Md. 693, 104 A. 426, 10 A. L. R. 1323 (1918). 2960

WILLS ACT 

 property owned at the date of his will. The problems are distinct. In Fidelity Company's Appeal, discussed under the preceding heading, both problems were really present. 

Testatrix owned stock fitting the description in the will both at the time the will was made and at the time of death, but the shares owned at death were considerably different from those owned at the time of the will because of the intervening change in the capital structure. In effect the court held (1) that the stock held at the date of the will was intended to be the subject matter of the gift, and (2) this could be traced into a one-half interest in the new shares owned at death. In Horn's Estate, on the other hand, the court indicated by way of dictum that if there had been stock owned at death literally fitting the description in the will (e. g. if the name of the corporation had remained unchanged) the legatee would have taken it in spite of the intervening changes. But since this condition. did not exist, the legatee was forced to argue (1) that the will spoke as of its date and (2) that the property could be traced. The legatee probably lost on the first point as much as on the second. The court seemed to construe the will as if it read "whatever shares of Ohio Fuel Corporation stock I own at my death." Since no such stock was owned, the legacy failed. Hence, in a sense, the problem of tracing was never reached. The opinion also indicates, however, that tracing would have been impossible on the facts of that case even if the will had been construed as making a gift of stock owned at the date of the will. 

The rather strict rule against tracing adopted in Horn's Estate does not apply if the gift is of the "proceeds" of property. Here the courts seem to allow unlimited tracing, subject only to difficulties of proof. Thus in

as time passed. What was left of the old rule was finally abolished by section 9 of the act of 1833, P. L. 249, the grandfather of the present clause. In the words of Chief 

Justice Gibson, "The court ought to have done at first, in regard to words of inheritance, what our legislature has done at last, by declaring every devise to be a fee, which is not specially restricted."'4

The effect of this clause of the Wills Act, therefore, is merely to relieve the court of the ordeal of searching for an excuse to avoid what had become an artificial rule of construction. The presumption is changed so that a devise "to A" with nothing more now carries the fee, but only in the absence of a contrary intent appearing in the will. 

In view of what has been said, little would be gained by reviewing the cases which have applied the similar provision in the acts of 1833 and 1917.5 For the most part, the statutory provision has merely. been mentioned preliminarily by way of clearing the decks for consideration of other problems.  (4) Meaning of "Heirs" and "Next of Kin,” etc.—

Time of Ascertaining Class. 

A devise or bequest of real or personal estate, whether directly or in trust, to the testator's or another designated person's "heirs," or "next of kin," or "relatives," or "family" or to "the persons thereunto entitled under the intestate laws, or to persons described by words of similar import, shall mean those persons, including the spouse, who would take under the intestate laws if the testator or other designated person were to die intestate at the time when such class is to be ascertained, a resident of the Commonwealth, and owning the estate so devised or bequeathed:

COMMISSIONERS' COMMENT-This clause is new. It is an extension of the Act of 1923, P. L. 914, 21 PS Section 11, to include gifts in remainder to heirs of a person other than the testator. In all such cases it is desirable to have the class determined as of the time the remainder falls in, unless the testator directs otherwise.

It has also been suggested by the recommendation of the Pennsylvania Bar Association Committee on the Law of Decedents' Estates, submitted in June 1942, which was as follows: "The present law is by no means clear as to what is normally meant by a testator's use of the word 'heirs.'

19. Contrary Intent. ¶ 1. General 

Devises and bequests to "heirs," "next of kin” and the like have raised a variety of questions in the law of wills. For a general treatment of the subject, see Casner, "Construction of Gifts to 'Heirs' and the Like," 53 Harv.

L. Rev. 207 (1939). The first legislation on the subject in 

Pennsylvania was the act of 1923 set forth above. That act applied only when there was a gift to testator's "heirs," etc. following an income estate. The present clause continues that act and expands it so that more cases will be covered and more questions answered. 

2. Cases Where There Is No Class Gift Distinguished 

The statutory provision applies only when there is a gift to a class of persons described in one of the manners enumerated. Hence, it is important to determine preliminarily that a class gift is intended. Not all devises and bequests which mention "heirs," etc. are subject to this clause.

Thus, the word "heirs" and other similar expressions are frequently used as words of limitation to describe the quantum of estate given rather than the class of persons to take. The clearest example is a gift to "A and his heirs." By settled principles such a phrase is merely equivalent to a gift to "A in fee" or to "A absolutely.' 

Hence the present clause of the statute would plainly have no application.

On the other hand, if the gift is to "A or his heirs" there is a substitutionary gift to the heirs, who take as purchasers directly from testator if A predeceases the testator.¹ Hence, this clause of the statute would apply to 

1. See, for example, Clark v. Scott, 67 Pa. 446 (1871). 3054

3a 

WILLS ACT 

814 (4) determine who those heirs are. Often the distinction between words of limitation and words of purchase is not so clear as in the examples given,2 but it must first be determined that the "heirs," etc. take as purchasers before the problems covered by the present clause are reached. The abolition of the Rule in Shelley's case is important in this respect and the discussion of section 16 of the act should be consulted. Other cases dealing with words of limitation and words of purchase are discussed under section 

14 (8) (¶ 4).

Another type of case where the present clause has no application is where the gift to "heirs," etc. never takes effect. This seems obvious but there are cases where it is possible to confuse the question of when heirs should be determined with the question of when to determine whether a substitutionary gift to heirs is operative. Such cases are discussed below under ¶ 7a. 

3. Class Gifts to Which Act Applies 

For this clause to apply there must be a gift to a class (as above noted) and this class must be one of those specifically mentioned or to "persons described by words of similar import." The general idea is that the testator must intend distribution directly to those who would be entitled to inherit from the designated ancestor if such ancestor had died intestate. The act does not apply if testator intended the property to go to the estate of the designated person, or to those entitled under that person's will, or to a class of persons other than those entitled by intestacy.3 a. Heirs

The first type of case specifically mentioned in the statute is the common one of a gift in a will to "heirs." This has always been held to mean those entitled to inherit from the person designated as the ancestor under the applicable 

2. See, for example, Thorne's Est., 344 Pa. 503 (1942). 

3. But see discussion below in the text under ¶ 3f.

343 (1947). 3055

§(4) WILLS ACT 

¶ 3b intestate act, rather than common law heirs or those entitled under the named ancestor's will.5 There was some confusion in the cases construing such gifts in the days when the real estate and the personal property of an intestate went to different persons. Thus, prior to 1917 a spouse was excluded from a devise to heirs, because neither spouse took land by descent from the other. 

The wife had her dower and the husband his curtesy, but the estate taken by a spouse of an intestate at early law was not inherited in the strict sense. Similarly, there was ambiguity prior to 1917 when a testator bequeathed personal property to "heirs," because technically "heirs" meant those entitled to inherit real estate. It would seem that the above problems ceased to exist with the Intestate Act of 1917, which, as the court pointed out in Barnard's 

Estate, 351 Pa. 313, 315 (1945), made each spouse the "statutory heir" of the other and abolished all distinction between those who succeed to the real and the personal property of an intestate. The present clause of the Wills Act, like the act of 1923, in this type of case merely confirms the conclusion implicit in the case law that the term "heirs" means those who would inherit under the intestate law-including the spouse. b. Next of Kin

The term "next of kin" was the artistic way to describe those entitled to an intestate's personal property under the applicable statute of distribution. The courts had difficulty with the term, however, when it was used in a will. Usually the spouse was excluded and sometimes the principle of representation was ignored so that child-

c. Relatives 

Gifts to "relatives" or "relations" under our case law were viewed as referring to intestate succession 10 but prior to this act the term was construed to mean blood relatives so that the spouse was again excluded.11 The act of 1923 did not mention such gifts so probably did not affect the rule of the earlier cases. The present clause specifically covers gifts to "relatives" and will change the law accordingly. The act should also cover gifts to "relations" which is certainly a "word of similar import." 

d. Family 

Some earlier cases also excluded the spouse in gifts to a person's "family," 12 and the act of 1923 did not specifically mention gifts of this sort. The present clause specifically covers such gifts and requires distribution in such a case to all those entitled by the Intestate Act in the absence of a contrary intent. e. Persons Entitled Under the Intestate Laws 

Wills which refer specifically to the intestate law have naturally always been construed to mean what they say.18 

The significance of the statute in such cases, therefore, will be limited to the time for ascertaining the class and the choice of the particular statute to apply (see ¶ 7 and ¶8 below).

¶ 3f f. Words of Similar Import 

The phrase "words of similar import" should cover cases where the words in the will are very similar to those specifically mentioned in the statute (as a gift to "relations" already mentioned) and cases where different words are used but there is a general intent to refer to those who would take by intestacy. In the latter respect the cases prior to the act should be of considerable assistance. 

As already mentioned, the statutory rule should have no application when the gift is to classes which are not the same as those who would take by intestacy. A border-line case in this respect is presented when intestate succession is referred to but the class of heirs is limited. The question then arises whether the present clause has no application at all because there is no gift to the whole class of heirs, or whether the clause is applicable in a limited sense to determine who are entitled within the restricted class. The latter solution was reached in Bonsall's Estate, 288 Pa. 

39 (1927), where there was a remainder to "lineal descendants according to the intestate laws." The court held that the act of 1923 was applicable to require determination of the class at the end of the life estate because the testator had used a phrase "similar" to the phrases mentioned in the statute.

The decision seems sensible, but it is difficult to say how far the reasoning can be carried. Suppose the will had simply said "descendants." The court hinted that even this word alone might have been regarded as "similar" to heirs and even indicated that the words "similar or equivalent phrase" in the act of 1923 might embrace gifts to "issue," "children," or "grandchildren." See 288 Pa. at 42. This suggestion seems untenable as a general proposition. The Legislature could easily have made this provision applicable to all class gifts but chose not to. However, the dictum in Bonsall's Estate, which finds some support in Laughlin's Estate, 336 Pa. 529, 536 (1939), seems to open the door to arguments that the act applies to any gift to a class even remotely resembling the class which would take by intestacy. 3058

¶ §14 (4) 

WILLS ACT 

Another type of case is presented when the question is whether the class intended is those who would take by intestacy or those who would take under the designated person's will. Plainly the act would not apply to a gift of the latter sort. Nor would the statute apply if a legacy to the estate of the named person were intended; in such a case the property would presumably be awarded to the named person's executor or administrator to be administered as part of such person's estate, subject to debts and charges, and ultimately distributable under his will if he left one. A legacy to a person's executor or administrator would probably be so construed 14 and the present statute held inapplicable, unless there was something else in the will to indicate that the heirs or next of kin were intended.15 

A gift to a person's "representatives" presents a close case in this respect. When the subject matter of the gift is real estate, it has been held that the word is equivalent to "heirs," so that this clause of the statute should apply.16 

When the gift is of personal property, it could well be argued that the primary meaning of "representatives" is executors or administrators so that the award should be made to the named person's estate. Even when personal property is involved, however, it is said that the word has the "secondary meaning" of those entitled to inherit, and this meaning seems to have been favored in cases construing legacies of this sort. So construed, the present statutory clause would of course apply. 17

With this exception, the spouse will get the share which he would have received if there had been an actual intestacy-including the whole estate in cases governed by clause (4) of section 2 of the Intestate Act. ¶5. Adopted Persons and Illegitimates

There is a possible conflict between this clause (4) and clauses (6) and (7) of this section of the Wills Act in cases where the rights of adopted persons and illegitimates are involved in testamentary gifts to "heirs," etc. Clause (4) requires reference to the Intestate Act and the beneficiaries are those who would take by intestacy from the designated ancestor if the ancestor had died at the time the gift comes into enjoyment. Thus sections 7 and 8 of the Intestate Act would control where adoption or illegitimacy are involved. Clauses (6) and (7) of section 14 of the Wills Act, on the other hand, set forth somewhat different rules to determine the rights of adoption and illegitimates where there is a gift to "persons described by relationship to the testator or to another."

It is believed that clause (4) should prevail where the gift is to "heirs," etc., and that in this type of case the rights of those claiming by or through adoption or ille-
