gitimacy should be governed by sections 7 and 8 of the Intestate Act rather than clauses (6) and (7) of section 

14 of the Wills Act. Kohler's Estate, 199 Pa. 455 (1901) (adoption), and Seitzinger's Estate, 170 Pa. 500, 528 (1895) (illegitimacy), are persuasive to this view. See also Stevenson's Estate, 47 D. & C. 215, 229 (O. C. Clinton 1943).

The main difference will be where a child is adopted after the testator's death but before the gift to heirs takes effect in enjoyment. Suppose, for example, a legacy is given in trust to A for life with remainder to A's heirs, and A adopts child X after testator's death. If clause (6) of section 14 of the Wills Act were applied, X would be excluded. But it is believed that X should share in the remainder under this clause (4) read in connection with sections 7 and 8 of the Intestate Act. ¶ 6. Commonwealth

In applying this clause of the statute and in drafting wills which will be governed by it, it is well to remember that the Commonwealth under section 3 (6) of the Intestate Act enjoys a new status as one entitled by intestacy in certain cases rather than merely as one entitled to unclaimed property by escheat in the absence of "known" heirs as heretofore. See discussion of "Commonwealth as

Heir" under section 3 (4) of that act. 

Under prior law the Commonwealth could not claim as a beneficiary of a gift to the "heirs" of A. because theoretically there were always individual heirs of any decedent under the Intestate Act of 1917. If such individual heirs were unknown the property reverted back to testator's estate to pass under his residuary clause to his heirs by actual intestacy as of the time of his death. See 

Leopold's Estate, 356 Pa. 543 (1947). It would seem that the result reached in that case will be altered by the present Intestate Act under which the Commonwealth is a party entitled to an intestate's estate as the statutory heir in the absence of relatives as close as a first cousin. 

The effect of the new act in this respect might be avoided by arguing contrary intent or that the Common- 3061

§(4) WILLS ACT 

¶ 7a wealth is not a "person" within the meaning of the present clause of the Wills Act, but it is questionable whether such an argument would succeed. 

¶ 7. Time for Ascertaining Class 

Under the statute, gifts to "heirs,' ""next of kin," etc. mean those who would take the property under the Intestate Act. But even assuming that the proper intestate act to apply is decided upon (see 8 below), the class of persons enumerated therein will change from time to time as the ancestor's relatives die and as new relatives are born. It is therefore important to have a definite rule as to when the class of heirs is ascertained. a. Gifts to Heirs Which Never Become Effective Distinguished Before reaching the question of when the class of "heirs," etc. is to be determined, it is important first to ascertain that there is an operative gift to such heirs. This seems elementary but there is likely to be confusion in cases where the gift to heirs is in the alternative. If the condition precedent to the gift to heirs is never fulfilled, there is nothing upon which the statute can operate. In such cases, therefore, it is necessary first to determine the time for ascertaining whether the condition has been satisfied, and this preliminary question will be governed by ordinary rules of construction rather than by the statute. 

The distinction can be illustrated as follows: 

(1) T leaves property in trust to pay the income to A for life and on A's death to distribute the principal to B if B survives T or otherwise to B's heirs. Plainly, if B survives T he has a vested remainder and the statute will have no application; even if B predeceases A the principal will be awarded to B's estate because the gift to heirs never took effect. On the other hand, if B predeceases T, there is a gift to B's heirs and the statute will apply to determine who those heirs are. (2) T leaves property to A for life with remainder in fee to "B or his heirs." B survives T but predeceases A. 3062

¶ 7b 

WILLS ACT 

This is where the confusion arises because it is necessary first to construe the will by ordinary rules of construction in order to determine whether there is a gift to B's heirs upon which the statute can operate. If the will means that 

B must survive A to take, the alternative gift to B's heirs becomes effective and the statute applies. Actually, however, such a will would probably be construed as in example (1) above so that B would have a vested remainder upon surviving T. Hence, there would be no operative gift to B's heirs and nothing to which the statute could apply.19 b. Common Law Rule

Assuming, then, that we are dealing with a case where there is an operative gift to "heirs" or others who are to be ascertained by reference to the Intestate Act, the problem arises as to when such class is to be ascertained. At common law the general rule was that heirs were determined at the death of the designated ancestor regardless of whether such ancestor was the testator himself or another, and regardless of whether the gift was immediate or postponed.20 This rule worked well enough where the gift came into enjoyment simultaneously with the ancestor's death-as an outright gift to testator's heirs, or a gift by testator to A for life with remainder to A's heirs.21 

The rule worked poorly when the death of the ancestor and the enjoyment of the gift did not coincide-as a gift to A for life with remainder to testator's heirs. In such cases it was often necessary to award the fund in whole or in part to the estate of a deceased heir, a result which the testator could scarcely have contemplated, particularly when one of the heirs so ascertained was the life tenant himself. In recent years the courts have often attempted to avoid such a conclusion by basing a finding of a contrary

The act of 1923, P. L. 914, changed this rule in the common type of case mentioned as an example above-a life estate to A with remainder to testator's heirs. Under that act the testator's heirs were determined as of the life tenant's death. However, the case law rule of determining heirs at the death of the ancestor was also unsatisfactory in more unusual types of cases illustrated below, which were not covered by the act of 1923 because that act was confined to gifts to the heirs of testator following a life estate.28 

d. Present Act-Examples 

The last sentence of the present statutory provision was intended to continue the act of 1923 and supplement it so as to present a comprehensive rule of construction to cover all cases of gifts to heirs and the like in the absence of a contrary intent appearing in the will. The class of heirs is to be ascertained as of the time the gift comes into enjoyment regardless of whose heirs are referred to and regardless of whether the gift is immediate or postponed. 

Examples of its operation as compared with prior law would be the following: (1) Life estate to A, remainder to A's heirs. Heirs will be determined at A's death just as they were at common law.24 (2) Life estate to A, remainder to testator's heirs. 

Heirs will be determined at A's death-contrary to the common law rule,25 but in harmony with the act of 1923. (3) Life estate to A, remainder to heirs of B. Heirs will be ascertained at A's death-contrary to the common

In any devise or bequest of real or personal estate the words "die without issue," "die without leaving issue," "have no issue," or other words importing either a want or failure of issue of any person in his lifetime or at the time of his death, or an indefinite failure of his issue, shall be construed to mean a want or failure of issue in his lifetime or at his death, and not an indefinite failure of his issue.

1. History-Explanation of Common Law Rule 

This, like clause (3) (words of inheritance), merely eliminates an arbitrary rule of construction which was inherited from medieval times and has been obsolete for centuries. At common law, a gift "to A and his heirs or if A dies without issue to B and his heirs" was construed as if it read "to A and the heirs of his body or if at any time neither A nor any of his issue is living then to B and his heirs." In effect the words "if A dies" was translated into "if A's issue should fail at any time in the indefinite future"-hence the phrase "indefinite failure of issue" to refer to the contingency.¹ 

How such an unnatural construction was ever adopted in the first place is difficult for the modern mind to understand. The rule originated prior to the Statute of Uses when executory interests were impossible so that a construction which gave B a remainder after an estate tail was thought to be least objectionable. It is no tribute to the common law that the rule was followed long after the reason for it vanished. The courts of one or two American jurisdictions repudiated the doctrine, but most states, including Pennsylvania, continued the old rule until it was changed by statute.2

Prior to 1897, our courts followed the common law rule with respect to both real and (apparently) personal property. As to real estate A would take a fee tail and B a remainder subject to being barred by A or a subsequent tenant in tail by a conveyance of the fee. After the act of 1855, P. L. 368, which converted fees tail into fees simple (see section 15 of the present act) A took a fee simple, and B took nothing, because his interest was executory and void as a perpetuity. As to personal property there was some doubt as to whether the rule applied at all, but it would seem that it did and that since fees tail in personalty were 1. For a full and clear discussion of the rule see Simes, Future Interests (1936) § 334 et seq. and § 326 et seq. The Pennsylvania cases are collected in 

Hunter, O. C. Book (1939) "Estates" § 12 and "Vested and Contingent" §§ 9 (c) 

and 9 (d). 

2. Simes, Future Interests (1936) § 339. 

3. Eichelberger v. Barnitz, 9 Watts 447 (1840). 

4. Ray v. Alexander, 146 Pa. 242 (1891); see infra, note 11. 3102

WILLS ACT §14 (5) 

impossible, A took an absolute interest.5 These rules were of course subject to a contrary intent appearing in the will or deed and the courts would frequently find such an intent, particularly in the cases of bequests of personal property." The rule was finally changed by the act of 1897, P. L. 

213, which was applicable both to deeds and wills. As to wills, this act was continued by section 14 of the Wills Act of 1917, now superseded by the present clause. As to deeds, the act of 1897 remained in effect until it was superseded by section 14 (2) of the present Estates Act. 

2. Present Act 

The act of 1917 and the present clause follow almost verbatim the act of 1897, the rather awkward language being retained in order to preserve the benefit of prior authorities. This language has been explained as follows: "In Dilworth v. Schuylkill Imp. Land Co., 219 Pa. 527, the constitutionality of the Act of 1897 was sustained; it being there held that the legislature had power to fix the legal meaning of words or phrases for future use, and that, by this statute, the lawmakers evidently intended (p. 529) 'certain words and phrases, in regard to failure of issue, which, standing by themselves,. [had heretofore] imported a fee tail, and thus a fee simple . . ., should thereafter indicate a life estate, unless otherwise indicated in the will. . [and, to this end] [p. 531] that, if words are used which, in themselves [that is to say disregarding all prior judicially determined meanings thereof], leave it doubtful whether the failure of issue intended is definite or indefinite, they [the words in question] shall mean a definite failure of issue, unless something else in the instrument shows that they are not so intended.' By 'something else in the instrument,' is meant something in addition to the words under investigation; that is to say, some context 5. Biddle's Appeal, 69 Pa. 190 (1871). The cases where the rule was not applied to personalty can best be explained on the basis of a contrary intent appearing in the instrument.

In short, the provision "if A dies without issue" now means what it says "if A dies and none of his issue is living at his death." The statutory construction will also be favored even when the will is less explicit as where, after referring to the death of A, the will makes a gift over "in default of issue of A." The failure of issue now refers to a definite time-i. e., the death of A-or a "definite failure of issue" in the words of the cases. 

3. Time for Ascertaining Contingency of Death Distin guished Confusion will be avoided if too much is not expected of this clause of the statute. The statutory provision resolves a judge-made ambiguity by eliminating an unnatural rule of construction; it does not resolve ambiguities inherent in the language of the will. Specifically, the statute states at what time the existence of issue should be determined, but it does not state at what time the primary beneficiary must die for the gift over to take effect." Take the original example of a gift "to A in fee, but if A dies without issue, to B." The statute requires the natural construction of "to A in fee, but if A dies and none of his issue is living at his death, then to B." This eliminates the indefinite failure of issue construction, but an inherent ambiguity still remains: At what time must A die in order that B may take? Does the testator mean "If A dies during my lifetime. "thus merely providing a gift over to prevent a lapse? Or does he mean "If A dies before or after my death. . . "thus subjecting A's fee to a con- •" 8. As in Dilworth v. Schuylkill Land Co., 219 Pa. 527 (1908).

Indeed, the question of when the death of the first taker must occur for the gift over to take effect can arise in all sorts of cases, regardless of whether death without issue is the contingency. ¶ 4. Death of "A" Survived by Issue Who Also Die Before Testator 

Bearing in mind the above distinctions, consider the following case: The will makes an immediate gift to A or if A dies without issue to B. If A survives testator he takes absolutely under the rules already discussed. If he predeceases testator survived by no issue, then the substituted gift to B takes effect. Suppose, however, that A dies before testator survived by a child who also predeceases testator, so that neither A nor any of his issue is living when testator dies. Under the definite failure of issue rule of the statute, A has not died without issue, so that literally the condition precedent to B's gift has not been fulfilled; the gift to B would therefore fail, and there would be a lapse.12 In this case the common law rule would have worked better than the statute. No Pennsylvania case of this sort has been found, although a complete search 11. Other cases will be found in Hunter, O. C. Book, "Vested and Contingent" §9 (c) & (d). There are statements in some of these cases that the rule governing the immediate gift (where the contingency is construed as death during testator's lifetime) is the same under the statute as it was before: see 

Eichenlaub's Est., 307 Pa. 357, 364 (1932), and cases there cited. This is not strictly so, although the difference is largely theoretical in this particular type of case. Before 1897 where there was an immediate gift to A with gift over to 

B if A died without issue and A survived testator he took a fee tail which the act of 1855, P. L. 368 converted into a fee simple making the condition subsequent and gift over to B upon indefinite failure of issue void as a perpetuity: see Crawford v. Withrow, 314 Pa. 497, 501 (1934), and supra note 4. After the statute, A likewise took a fee but for an entirely different reason-i. e., that the contingency of A's death during testator's lifetime simply never took effect. 

The statute makes a real difference in the result only when the death of A is construed to mean death after the testator (during a life tenancy, etc.).

This, like the other clauses of this section, is subject to a different intent appearing in the will. Thus, if it clearly appears that a fee tail was intended with a gift over if the first taker's issue should fail at any time, presumably the will would be so construed and the estate converted by section 15 of this act into a fee simple defeasible. (Note that B's interest will no longer necessarily be bad as a perpetuity under the statutory rule in section 4 of this act, although A's estate will be freed of the condition if it is not divested within the permissible period.) 

Since this clause merely eliminates an arbitrary construction which few testators would have intended, however, and since the fee tail has long ago gone out of fashion, cases of contrary intent are likely to be rare. The Supreme 

Court has said that whenever either an indefinite or a definite failure of issue could have been contemplated by the natural meaning of the language (disregarding the common law rule) the statute applies.13 The one possible exception might be the one suggested under the preceding heading where the rejection of the statute would attain a more just result.

WILLS ACT 

§ 14 (6) 

 (6) Adopted Children.

In construing a will making a devise or bequest to a person or persons described by relationship to the testator or to another, any person adopted before the death of the testator shall be considered the child of his adopting parent or parents and not the child of his natural parents: Provided, That if a natural parent shall have married the adopting parent before the testator's death, the adopted person shall also be considered the child of such natural parent. 

COMMISSIONERS' COMMENT This takes the place of section 16 of the Wills Act of 1917. It makes several important changes: (1) 

It makes no distinction as did the 1917 act between adopted children of the testator, and adopted children of others. (2) 

It permits children of others adopted after the date of the will and before the testator's death to be included. In requiring adoptions to be made before the testator's death, it avoids the possibility of adoptions for the sole purpose of preventing a gift over in default of issue. (3) It prevents adopted children from receiving gifts as natural children, except through a natural parent who is the spouse of an adopting parent. The purpose of the clause is to conform with the theory of adoption as expounded in Cave's Est., 326 Pa. 358, and as embodied in the

Intestate Act of 1947. The child is considered the child of the adopting family and not of the natural parents. 

Old Law

Section 16- (a) Whenever in any will a bequest or devise shall be made to the child or children of the testator, without naming such child or children, such bequest or devise shall be construed to include any adopted child or children of the testator, unless a contrary intention shall appear by the will. (b) Whenever in any will a bequest or devise shall be made to the child or children of any person other than the testator, without naming such child or children, such bequest or devise shall be construed to include any adopted child or children of such other person who were adopted before the date of the will, unless a contrary intention shall appear by the will. 

Wills Act of 1917, P. L. 403. 

The law with respect to gifts to testator's own children remains the same, but as to gifts to children of others, 3151

§ (6) WILLS ACT 

¶ 1 the act now includes persons adopted at any time before testator's death (instead of before the execution of the will as under the act of 1917). The provision that the adopted child loses his status as the child of his natural parent is new in the Wills Act; under the act of 1917 the proper construction of a gift to children of the natural parent was in doubt. The revised language also makes it clear that the provision applies to any gift to persons described in terms of relationship and is not limited to gifts made expressly to "children."

11. Who Is Adopted Person-Conflict of Laws-Cross References 

This and the following clause were designed to make the rules governing the construction of wills conform as nearly as possible with the corresponding sections of the Intestate Act. Problems under the two acts are quite different, but the discussion of "Who is Adopted Person" (11) under section 8 of the Intestate Act is, of course, equally relevant in determining whether the present section has any application. The discussion of "Conflict of 

Laws" (5) under section 8 of the Intestate Act will also 3152

WILLS ACT §14 (6) 

be helpful in construing domestic wills in relation to foreign adoptions. The foreign decree will fix the status of the child, although the construction of the will of a Pennsylvania decedent is ordinarily governed by our law at least as to personalty. See section 19 of this act, infra. 

2. Gifts to Heirs Distinguished

Theoretically, a gift to the heirs of a person might be a gift to persons "described by relationship," but it is clear that neither the present provision nor the corresponding provision in the act of 1917 has any application to wills which refer to intestate succession. The rule of construction governing gifts of this sort is set forth in clause (4) of the present section, and even before the present act, such wills were governed by special rules which sometimes required reference to the intestate law in force when the named ancestor died. Thus, in Kohler's Estate, 199 Pa. 

455 (1901), where the testator gave his son a life estate with remainder to the persons who would take if his son died intestate, the son's adopted daughter took the remainder even though she had been adopted twenty years after the testator's death, because the law in force when the son died provided for inheritance by adopted persons.¹ 

In construing gifts to heirs where the rights of an adopted child are involved, therefore, reference should be made to section 14 (4) of this act and section 8 of the Intestate Act, rather than to the present provision.

5. Present Provision a. Date of Testator's Death Controlling 

The present act again changes the law by making a single provision to cover all cases: any child adopted before testator's death is to be regarded as the child of his adopting parent for purposes of will construction, unless a contrary intent appears in the will. Thus, the rule under the act of 1917 will remain unchanged in construing gifts to testator's own children, but gifts to children of others will now include persons adopted after the will is executed, so long as the adoption takes place before the testator dies. As pointed out in the Commissioners' comments, the controlling date was made the testator's death and not later in order to "avoid the possibility of adoptions for the sole purpose of preventing a gift over in default of issue. 

Thus, an adopted child will still not share in a gift of a future interest when the adoption takes place after the testator's death but before the class is ascertained. 

b. Natural Parents

For the first time, the act now includes a provision governing gifts to the "children," etc. of the natural parents. The adoption before testator's death not only

1 makes the child a part of the family of the adopting parents but also eliminates him from his natural family, in a manner analogous to the similar provision which has been in the Intestate Act since 1917. See further discussion of this point, infra under ¶ 5d. 

c. Description "by Relationship" 

The new provision applies to any description of beneficiaries in terms of relationship (other than gifts to "heirs," etc., as explained above, ¶2). It is uncertain whether the act of 1917 was limited to wills which expressly referred to a "child" or "children." In Coble's 

Estate, 58 D. & C. 632 (O. C. Frank. 1947), it was held that the 1917 act did not apply where the gift was to "issue" which the court thought implied a blood relationship. The present provision will eliminate the question on this point. 

The adopted person will be included not only in a gift to the "children" or "issue" of his adopting parent, but also in gifts to his adoptive grandparent's "grandchildren," his adoptive uncle's "nephews and nieces," and so forth. 

d. Contrary Intent-Extrinsic Evidence 

The rule remains a rule of presumed intent in the absence of a showing that the testator intended otherwise. 

And the contrary intent must appear in the will itself. 

Thus, the strict rule of Yates' Estate, 281 Pa. 178 (1924), holding extrinsic evidence of intent inadmissible, presumably remains law. This should cause little if any hardship in cases where the adopted person is claiming as a child of his adopting parents, because a construction favorable to him is now presumed in all cases where the adoption occurred prior to the testator's death. On the other hand, where an adopted person attempts to share in a gift to his natural parents' children, the rule against extrinsic evidence might operate quite harshly-especially where the testator is the natural parent or where the will of another was executed before the adoption. It is uncertain, however, exactly how the rule operates in this situation. In 3156

¶ 5e 

WILLS ACT 

both Yates' Estate, 281 Pa. 178 (1924), and Corr's Estate, 338 Pa. 337 (1940), the court ruled the evidence inadmissible but then proceeded to consider it anyway. It would seem that proof of such facts as the date of adoption and whether the testator knew of it should be admissible to show the background of the intent expressed in the will, but how much more or less than this can be shown remains uncertain. 

e. Incidental References to "Children," etc.-Powers of 

Appointment, etc.

The present provision, like the act of 1917, applies only to "wills making a devise or bequest" to persons described in terms of relationship. Suppose A gives his daughter B a life estate and a power to appoint the remainder among her "issue." Can B appoint to a child adopted by her before A's death? At first blush, it might seem that the wording of the statute would exclude from the operation of this clause a description of the class within which a donee of a special power can appoint. Corr's Estate, 338 Pa. 337 (1940), however, indicates by way of dictum that the provision would apply to such descriptions so that B could appoint to her adopted daughter in the case suggested. This seems theoretically defensible, since in a sense the donor of the power is the one who makes the gift to the appointees. 

Unfortunately, the same cannot be said of a reference to children or issue in a will where no gift is made to such children or issue even indirectly by way of giving a power to appoint to them. Suppose, for example, a testamentary gift is made to X absolutely, the fund to remain in trust, however, with the further provision that if X dies without issue his estate is to be divested and the gift is to go to Y (cf. Conner's Estate, 346 Pa. 271 (1943)). Often the courts will construe such wills as making an implied gift to the issue of X if X has issue, but let us suppose that no such implied gift is found, so that X simply has a fee subject to divestment if he dies without issue. Is the gift divested if X dies survived only by a child adopted before the testator died? It should not be, but literally the pres- 3157

§ WILLS ACT 

8 14 (6) ¶ 6 ent section would not apply because there is no "devise or bequest to a person described by relationship to the testator or another." For a case midway between the cases suggested in this and the preceding paragraph, see Adamson's Estate, 58 D. & C. 511, 514 (O. C. Phila. 1947). There, testator gave his daughter a general power of appointment conditioned upon her being survived by issue. The daughter was survived by an adopted child only, and it was held that the condition was unfulfilled. Unfortunately the case was not governed by the act of 1917, so that what was said on this point is of little help. 

¶ 6. Marriage of Natural and Adoptive Parents 

The proviso to cover cases where the adopting parent has married the natural parent corresponds to an identical provision in section 8 of the Intestate Act. With the child now definitely cut off from his natural parents in the ordinary case, this special provision is necessary to avoid a decision in the law of wills similar to Fisher v. Robison, 329 Pa. 305 (1938), dealing with intestate succession. See discussion under Intestate Act § 8-1 4.

 (7) Illegitimates.

In construing a will making a devise or bequest to a person or persons described by relationship to the testator or to another, an illegitimate person shall be considered the child of his mother and not of his father; Provided, That when the parents of a person born illegitimate shall have married each other, he shall thereafter be considered legitimate.

COMMISSIONERS' COMMENT This provision is new. It is intended to give the illegitimate (whose parents do not marry each other) full rights as a child of his mother, but not of his father, as in the Intestate Act of 1947, section 7. Heretofore, an illegitimate's status under any general description such as "issue" or "children" has been questionable. Cf. Seitzinger's Est., 170

Pa. 500. The proviso is believed to be declaratory of existing law (cf. Thorn Est., 353 Pa. 603) except that cohabitation is not required. The Act of 1857, P. L. 507, 48 PS 167 which requires cohabitation plus marriage was repealed by the Intestate Act of 1917 only insofar as it relates to inheritance. As heretofore, legitimation of a child by marriage of the parents after the testator's death may alter rights which have not vested. 

Cf. Thorn Estate. 

Old Law

There was no provision in the former Wills Act relating to illegitimates. 

However, the following sections of the acts of 1901 and 1857 (which remain law for general purposes) were considered applicable in the construction of wills: 

Section 1. In any and every case where the father and mother of an illegitimate child or children shall enter into the bonds of lawful wedlock and cohabit, such child or children shall thereby become legitimated, and enjoy all the rights and privileges as if they had been born during the wedlock of their parents.

Act of 1857, P. L. 507, 48 P. S. § 167. 

Section 1. Illegitimate children shall take and be known by the name of their mother, and the common law doctrine of nullius filius shall not apply as between the mother and her illegitimate child or children. But the mother and her heirs, and her illegitimate child and its heirs, shall be mutually liable one to the other, and shall enjoy all the rights and privileges one to the other, in the same manner and to the same extent, as if the said child or children had been born in lawful wedlock.

Act of 1901, P. L. 639, 11 P. S. §1.

The proviso relating to legitimation continues the act of 1857, P. L. 507, 48 P. S. § 167, although the requirement of "cohabitation" by the marrying parents has been eliminated.

1. Proof of Illegitimacy and Conflict of Laws-Cross References 

Like clause (6), above, this provision is based on a similar provision in the Intestate Act.. The construction of wills presents entirely different problems than those arising with regard to inheritance, but the question of whether a child is in fact illegitimate is of course the same under both statutes, and problems in conflicts are also analogous. For discussion of such matters, therefore, see section 7 (1 and ¶ 5) of the Intestate Act. 

12. Gifts to Heirs Distinguished

As pointed out in the discussion of clause (6) (¶2), gifts to persons who would be entitled under the intestate law are governed by clause (4) of the present section. 3202

¶ 3a 

WILLS ACT § 14 (7) 

Under that clause such a will is regarded as incorporating the intestate act in force at the time the class of "heirs" is to be determined. A similar result has been reached even before the statute. Thus, in Seitzinger's Estate, 170 Pa. 

500, 528 (1895), the testator died in 1850, giving a life estate to his daughter and a remainder to those who would take her estate if she had died intestate; the daughter died in 1867, and it was held that the estate passed to her two illegitimate children, who were given the right to inherit from her by the act of 1855. Where the rights of an illegitimate are questioned under a will referring to intestate succession, therefore, the case will be governed by section 14 (4) of the Wills Act and section 7 of the Intestate Act, rather than by the present provision, which applies only to gifts to "children" and the like. 

3. Gifts to "Children," Etc. a. Law Prior to 1901

Since the present provision (which is new to the Wills Act) applies only to wills of testators who die on or after January 1, 1948 (see section 22), the prior law will continue to be important for some years in cases where a remainder after a life estate is given to a class described in terms of relationship.

At common law, illegitimates were the children of no one, so that gifts to "children," "issue," etc. were construed to exclude them.¹ Although the law of intestacy was changed with respect to illegitimates as early as 1855,2 the corresponding rule in the law of wills remained untouched by legislation at least until 1901, and it remained "the well-established rule of law that the word 'children' and like words are to be applied only to the legitimate children unless the illegitimate children are otherwise described so as to leave no doubt that they are to be in-

Section 1 of the act of 1901, P. L. 639, 11 P. S. § 1, quoted above, unlike the previous acts relating to illegitimacy, is not confined to intestate succession but is drawn in general terms. The cases indicate that this act destroyed the doctrine of nullius filius entirely as between. mother and child, and as to the mother legitimated the child born out of wedlock for all purposes.* Taylor's

d. Controlling Date 

From what has been said, it is evident that a case might turn on what law is applicable to the particular facts. Assuming that no subsequent legitimation by marriage has taken place (see below), the date the will was executed, the date of testator's death, the date a future gift vests, or the date of the child's birth might be controlling. A special case is the remainder to the mother's heirs. As pointed out above,5 such a case is governed by another line of statutes, and the "heirs" might be determined according to the intestate law in force at the time of the mother's death, regardless of when the testator died. Where the gift is to a class described as "children, "issue," etc. of the mother, the proper law to apply was not clear prior to the present act. Certainly, the provision in the present act will apply to the will of any testator who dies on or after Januuary 1, 1948, as provided by section 22. As to wills of testators who died prior to 

1948, Taylor's Estate, 357 Pa. 120 (1947), holds that the act of 1901 applies where the child was born, the will drawn, and the testator died between 1901 and 1939. No other authority examined discusses the problem. It would

14. Subsequent Marriage of Parents-Legitimation a. General

Most of what was said in the discussion of legitimation under the Intestate Act, §7 (¶4), is equally applicable here. As there pointed out, the courts will be loath to find that a legitimating marriage is invalid, but on the other hand, the child will have the burden of proving that the man his mother married was in fact his father. 

In the case of wills, it will be noted that this provision is new to the Wills Act. Prior to the present act, the subject was governed by the general act of 1857, P. L. 507, 48 P. b. Controlling Date 

In cases involving legitimation, there can be no question that the date of the subsequent marriage is controlling and will enable the child to share in any testamentary gift to the father's "children," etc. which vests after the legitimation takes place, even though the testator died earlier. 

Thus, in Thorn's Estate, 353 Pa. 603 (1946), the testator died in 1886, leaving a contingent gift of income to the "issue" of deceased life tenants. Children of a son of a deceased life tenant were born illegitimate between 1907 and 1923, but the parents married each other in 1929. It was held that the children thereupon became legitimate and on their father's death shared as "issue" of their grandmother. "While testator, by his bequest to the issue of the nephews and nieces, is presumed to have intended only lawful and not illegitimate issue . . the requirement of legitimacy, as far as the rights of the Bullock children in this controvery are concerned, is met by their having been legitimated before their life estates in the trust became operative." § 14-RULES OF INTERPRETATION (Continued) 

(8) Lapsed and Void Devises and Legacies-Substitution of Issue. 

A devise or bequest to a child or other issue of the testator or to his brother or sister or to a child of his brother or sister whether designated by name or as one of a class shall not lapse if the beneficiary shall fail to survive the testator and shall leave issue surviving the testator but shall pass to such surviving issue who shall take per stirpes the share which their deceased ancestor would have taken had he survived the testator; provided, that such a devise or bequest to a brother or sister or to the child of a brother or sister shall lapse to the extent to which it will pass to the testator's spouse or issue as a part of the residuary estate or under the intestate laws. 

COMMISSIONERS' COMMENT This clause takes the place of sections 

15 (a) and (b) of the 1917 act.

In addition to simplifying the language, clause (8) states expressly that the issue shall receive their shares "per stirpes". 

The proviso, unlike the condition of section 15 (b) of the 1917 act, includes the spouse as well as the issue among those who will defeat the rights of issue of deceased brothers, sisters, nephews or nieces, if they would benefit as residuary beneficiaries or by intestacy, on the lapse of the gift. 

Under 15(b) of the 1917 act the words "shall not leave any lineal descendants who would receive the benefit of any lapsed or void devise or legacy" presented the question of whether the lapsed share would go wholly to the issue of the testator or partially to others sharing in the residue. The new provision is intended to make it clear that the gift to the named collaterals will fail only to the extent that the spouse and issue will benefit by the lapse. For example, $250 of a $500 bequest to a predeceased nephew will be paid to the nephew's issue and $250 to the surviving widow if the residuary estate is given onehalf to the widow and one-half to a charity. 

Gifts to named individuals within the favored group, who were dead when the will was written, subject to the rights of testator's spouse or issue will remain available for their issue (Spencer's Est., 37 Pa. Super. 67), but when the gift is to 3251

§(8)

a class, issue will not take the ancestor's share unless the ancestor was living when the will was written or was born thereafter prior to the testator's death: See Harrison's Est., 202 Pa. 331, 334. Old Law

Section 15- 

(a) No devise or legacy in favor of a child or children, or other lineal descendant or descendants of any testator, whether such children or descendants be designated by name or as a class, shall lapse or become void by reason of the decease of such legatee or devisee in the lifetime of the testator, if such devisee or legatee shall leave issue surviving the testator; but such devise or legacy shall be good and available in favor of such surviving issue, with like effect as if such devisee or legatee had survived the testator, unless the testator shall in the will direct otherwise. (b) Where any testator shall not leave any lineal descendants who would receive the benefit of any lapsed or void devise or legacy, no devise or legacy made in favor of a brother or sister, or of brothers or sisters, of such testator, or in favor of the children of a brother or a sister of such testator, whether such brothers or sisters, or children of brothers or sisters, be designated by name or as a class, shall be deemed or held to lapse or become void by reason of the decease of such devisee or legatee in the lifetime of the testator, if such devisee or legatee shall leave issue surviving the testator; but such devise or legacy shall be good and available in favor of such surviving issue, with like effect as if such devisee or legatee had survived the testator, unless the testator shall in the will direct otherwise.

Wills Act of 1917, P. L. 403. 

The only change is in the proviso of the new section: 

The spouse of testator is added to the persons who will prevent the substitution of a collateral's issue, but the gift to the collateral lapses only to the "extent" that it will benefit testator's spouse or issue.

¶ 13. How Issue Take (Conditions, Advancements, Debts, Etc.) 1. History 2 At common law it "has been repeatedly and uniformly decided, in conformity with a principle of law, which is said to have been borrowed from the civil law, that every legacy implies a condition that the legatee shall survive the testator, and that where the legatee dies in the lifetime of the testator the legacy lapses."1 The same was true of devises. Many of the cases concern the question of whether the will makes a substitutionary gift to the heirs of the beneficiary. Thus, where testator makes a gift to A "and his heirs," the phrase is usually construed merely as words of limitation-the traditional way to describe a fee so that a lapse occurs when A dies before testator.3 On the other hand, if the will makes a gift to A "or his heirs," there is a sufficient substitutionary gift and the heirs take if A dies before testator.4

The common law rule concerning lapse was first modified in Pennsylvania by the act of 1810, P. L. 96, which saved for the issue of the beneficiary legacies or devises

The similar provision for the issue of brothers, sisters, nephews, and nieces first appeared in section 2 of the act of 1844, P. See general discussion of the 1917 provision in the March, 1946, issue of the Fiduciary Review.

The present clause combines subsections (a) and (b) of old section 15 and again changes the provision governing the case where the testator's immediate family competes with issue of a deceased collateral beneficiary. The changes made in this provision in 1917 and the present clause are discussed below under ¶ 12. 

12. Meaning of "Child" and "Issue" says.

The statutory language describing the preferred rela- As tives must be construed to mean precisely what it under section 3 of the Intestate Act, and throughout both statutes, child means child and issue means issue. Thus, the clause will apply when the deceased devisee or legatee is any lineal descendant of testator, no matter how remote, but gifts to collaterals more remote than a nephew or niece will not be covered. On the other hand, so long as the beneficiary named in the will is within the preferred class, any of the beneficiary's issue may be substituted. Thus, a great grandnephew might take a legacy intended for his 3254

14. Contrary Intent

An intention contrary to this clause will frequently be found in well drafted wills. In general, anything in the will which expressly or by necessary implication makes the gift contingent upon survivorship supersedes the provision for issue in this clause. The simplest case is illustrated by 

Kunkel v. Kunkel, 267 Pa. 163 (1920), where the legacy was to testator's brother "if living at the time of my decease" so that the gift was not saved for the benefit of the deceased brother's issue.

Another common case of an intention contrary to the present clause is where an alternative beneficiary is named by the testator in the will, thus necessarily implying a condition of survivorship by the first legatee. As already seen (¶1), a gift to A "and his heirs" is equivalent to A “in fee," so that no substitutionary gift is implied and the present clause applies if A predeceased the testator. On the other hand, a gift to A "or his heirs" implies a substitutionary gift to heirs; hence it did not lapse at common law but passed to A's heirs if A predeceased testator." It seems plain that the statute does not change the result in the latter case if A happens to be testator's child or other close relative mentioned in this clause of the statute. If the child predeceases the testator, the child's heirs (including his surviving spouse 8), will take the gift regardless of whether the child leaves issue. In other words, if 

5. Walton's Est., 2 Montg. 189 (O. C. 1886); Hoover's Est., 9 Dauph. 258 (O. C. 1906). 

6. Harding's Est., 2 D. & C. 298 (O. C. Phila. 1922). 

7. Supra, note 4. 

8. See clause (4) of this section, supra; Stevenson's Est., 47 D. & C. 215 (O. C. Clinton 1943); cf. generally 1, "Spouse as Heir" under § 2 of the Intestate Act. 1 1 3255

the testator himself designates an alternative beneficiary capable of taking, there is no lapse and the statute has no application.

A more difficult case arises where neither the first named nor the alternative beneficiary survives. Such a case is Hammond's Estate, 103 Pa. Super. 503 (1931). The will left $6,000 to testator's brother and then provided that “in the event of his decease, the bequest is to go to his wife, Francis Hammond, absolutely." First the brother died, then the brother's wife died, then testator died, but a child of the brother survived. It was held that the gift lapsed and the brother's child was not substituted because an intention contrary to the statute was found in the will. Some emphasis was placed by the court on the fact that the brother died before the sister-in-law, but it is hard to imagine that a different result would have been reached if the sister-in-law had died first. The best basis for the decision seems to be that, as in Kunkel v. Kunkel, the testator in Hammond's Estate "made the gift to the brother contingent upon his surviving him, because he made a different disposition 'in the event of his death.'"' (103 Pa 

Super. at 506.) 9

Other cases where the will shows an intention that issue should not be substituted are discussed below under ¶ 7 where the application of this clause to class gifts is considered. 

5. Types of Gifts Saved-in General 

In the absence of a contrary intent the statute will continue to govern all legacies and devises-whether specific, general or residuary 10-to any of the relatives specified in the act where the intended beneficiary predeceases the testator leaving surviving issue. Thus, it applies to class gifts, to remainder interests, to contingent gifts, and to gifts made through the exercise of a power of appointment. The

¶ 6. Death Before Will 

"We cannot doubt that the act [of 1844] saves this bequest to the testator's sister from being void, though she was dead when the will was written, having left children that survived the testator. This interpretation of the law is so just, and presents itself so naturally that we need waste no words about it. No amount of verbal criticism can make it clearer, but, as is usual in such cases, would only darken and confuse the thought." Minter's Appeal, 40 Pa. 111, 114 (1861).

The decision was repeated in Spencer's Estate, 37 Pa. 

Super. 67 (1908), where the court placed some emphasis on the fact that the old statute expressly provided that the legacy should neither lapse nor "become void." This was viewed as significant because at common law where the legatee was dead at the time the will was executed the 1 3257

§(8) 17 

WILLS ACT 

It legacy was termed "void" rather than "lapsed." ¹¹ could conceivably be argued that the rule of Minter's Appeal is changed by the omission of the phrase "or become void" after the words "shall not lapse" in the present statute, but such an argument would be unsound for several reasons. That no such change was intended by the drafters is clear from the Commissioners' comments. Apart from this, the omitted language actually contributed nothing toward the question of whether the act applies to this sort of case. If the legatee is dead at the time the will is written, the legacy can scarcely be said to "become" void, since at common law it was void from the beginning. Furthermore, the statute as it now reads is not restricted to gifts which technically speaking would otherwise lapse. It applies whenever the designated "beneficiary shall fail to survive the testator." Hence, the technical meaning of lapse does not enter into the interpretation of the positive provisions of the clause.12 

It would seem reasonably certain, therefore, that the law with respect to beneficiaries dead at the time the will is executed remains unchanged. It should be noted at this point, however, that the rule of Minter's Appeal does not apply to class gifts. Gifts to "children," etc. generally are governed by different rules which are discussed under the next heading. 

17. Class Gifts 

Neither the act of 1833 relating to lineals nor the act of 1844 relating to collaterals expressly referred to class gifts, but, curiously enough, they were construed in exactly opposite ways in this respect. The question first arose under the act of 1844 in Gross's Estate, 10 Pa. 360 (1849), where testator left the residue of his estate to the "children" of his brothers and sisters, and the court held that the act of 1844 was ineffective to save the share of the deceased niece for her issue. In Bradley's Estate, 166 Pa. 

300 (1895), however, the court refused to follow the impli-

cations of Gross's Estate in construing the identical language in the act of 1833, relating to gifts to lineals. It was held that the act of 1833 applied regardless of whether the gift was to a class or to individuals. 

By the act of 1897, P. L. 256, Gross's Estate was corrected and since then the statutory provision for issue of collaterals has expressly applied regardless of whether the beneficiaries are "designated by name or as a class." This wording was retained in section 15 (b) of the act of 1917 and was also inserted in 15 (a) relating to lineals in order to remove any possible doubt. The present clause combining the two sections retains the identical language with respect to class gifts.

It will be seen immediately that when a class gift is involved, the problem is entirely different from the case where the primary beneficiary is individually named or described. If the statute is to have any effect on class gifts, it is necessary not only to provide for the substitution of issue but also to change the ordinary rules of construction with respect to the time for ascertaining the class of primary beneficiaries.

Ordinarily, where there is an outright legacy or devise to a class, its membership is determined at the testator's death.13 Thus, unless this is changed, there could never be a predeceased beneficiary of a class gift. In order to give effect to the statute in such cases, the courts have solved the dilemma by accelerating the time for determining the class of primary beneficiaries. The rule in this regard, as found in Worstall's Estate, 125 Pa. Super. 133, 137 (1937), and cases there cited,¹¹ is that the class of primary beneficiaries for whom issue will be substituted is composed of persons fitting the description in the will at any time between the date of its execution 15 and the date of testator's

Since the application of the act to class gifts involves the additional step of accelerating the determination of the class of primary beneficiaries to some time prior to the testator's death, an intention contrary to the statute is clearly indicated when the will expressly designates the time for determining the membership of the class. It would seem in such a case that the statute should operate to save the predeceased child's share for his issue because he was within the class of primary beneficiaries under the literal terms of the will. WILLS ACT 8. Life Estate and Remainder 

This clause is not restricted to outright gifts and it is reasonably clear that it will apply to other types of gifts where such application is possible and not contrary to the terms of the will. It will be a rare case where the substitution of issue is possible with regard to a gift of income to a person who predeceases the testator, because ordinarily the estate which the will attempts to give is measured by the life of the named donee. Hence, it is not so much a question of lapse as the disappearance of the subject matter of the gift.21 Presumably, however, a gift of income for the life of another, or for a term of years, would be saved for the issue of a lineal or close collateral who predeceases the testator.22 

With regard to remainders, a sharp distinction must be drawn between cases where the named remainderman dies before testator and those where he dies after the testator but during the life tenancy, for only in the former case does the present statutory provision have any application. 

Suppose the will gives a life estate to A with what would be a vested remainder in fee to B. If B dies before testator, there is just as much a lapse as if he had been named as the beneficiary of an outright gift. Hence, if B is not a relative of decedent, neither his estate nor his family takes anything. But if B is a lineal descendant or brother, sister, nephew or niece of decedent, any of his issue who survive testator should take as vested remaindermen under this clause.28 On the other hand, if B survives testator but dies before the life tenant, there is no lapse. Whether B is a relative or a stranger, his estate takes the remainder which had already vested in him. Thus, if B in this case left his entire estate to his wife, she will ultimately take

Suppose now that the remainder given to B is not in the form of a vested estate but is contingent upon his surviving A, the life tenant. In most cases, this will present no problem because B must be alive when the life tenant dies to fulfill the condition in the will. It would seem immaterial whether B died before or after testator if he failed to survive A. In either event, neither B, nor his estate, nor his issue, would have any interest in the remainder.24 

But suppose in such a case that A dies first, then B dies, and then testator dies. If the will were literally construed, it would seem that since B survived A, the condition in the will is satisfied and B would be disqualified only because the gift lapsed due to his death before testator. 10. Powers of Appointment 

Where a power of appointment is exercised in favor of a person who predeceases the donee of the power, the courts have had some trouble with the dogma of general property law that the appointee takes directly from the donor of the power-the donee of the power being a mere "conduit.'' 26 

Suppose A leaves his estate to B for life with remainder to whomever B designates by will. B then appoints to C who predeceases B. If the theory that C takes directly from A in such a case is taken too seriously, some strange results would follow in the law of lapse. No appellate court case has been found dealing with the operation of the lapse statute in this situation, but lower court decisions suggest that the artificial theory of the effect of an appointment will not be applied in this type of case. Such decisions as there are take the realistic view that for this purpose the donee of the power, B, should 

26. See Commonwealth v. Duffield, 12 Pa. 277, 280 (1849), for a rather colorful statement of this dogma in another connection. 3263

§(8) 10 

WILLS ACT 

be regarded as the one who actually makes the gift. The applicable rules in various types of cases, so far as they can be predicted in the absence of appellate authority, can be summarized as follows (in all cases assuming that A gives a power to B who appoints to C): 

1. If C is a stranger and does not survive B, the gift fails, regardless of whether C survived A. And this is so whether the power was general or special. In other words 

B (not A) is viewed as the actual testator in applying the common law rule of lapse in the absence of statute.27 

2. If C is a child or other close relative of A, but not of B, the statute will not save the gift for C's issue. Thus in Rowland's Estate, 17 D. & C. 477 (0. C. Phila. 1932), the husband (A) gave his wife (B) a general power of appointment and she appointed to his nephew (C) who predeceased B, leaving issue. Since C was no blood relative of B, it was held that the statute did not apply and the gift passed in default of appointment. The same result would seem to follow even if the power had been specialsee below under 4. 

3. If the appointee (C) is a close relative of the donee of the power (B), the lapse statute applies to save the gift for C's issue, regardless of C's relationship to A, at least where B's power is general. Thus in Lyndall's Estate, 2 

Dist. 476 (O. C. Phila. 1893), where a general power was exercised, the statute saved for issue of the appointee an appointment to a predeceased brother of the donee of the power.28 

4. Whether the rule of Lyndall's Estate should be followed in the case of a special power is not clear from the general authorities. The Restatement of Property § 350 

treats this case in a caveat and the court in Lyndall's Estate expressly limited its decision to a case where a general power was exercised.29 In Grubb's Estate, 36 D. & C. 

1 (0. C. Phila. 1939), however, the gift was regarded as 

27. Restatement, Property § 349; Page, Wills (3d ed. 1941) § 1416; 75 A.

§14 (8) that of the donee of the power even where a special power was exercised. In that case A gave B a special power to appoint among B's "descendants." B appointed to his daughter C who predeceased B leaving issue, and the court held that the issue of C took under the statute. The question was carefully considered in the opinion and the decision seems sound, even though it is contrary to some English authorities. Note, however, that the court itself limited its decision to a case where the issue of the appointee were within the class of permissible appointees. Thus, C's issue were B's "descendants" just as much as C was. A different result would no doubt have been reached if B's power had been limited to appoint to his "children"; in such a case the gift would probably have passed in default of appointment, although no actual decision on this point has been found.

Thus, in all four cases, the donee of the power, general or special, is regarded as the testator in applying common law and statutory rules of lapse, subject to the qualification that the ultimate takers probably have to be members of the class of permissible appointees. The appellate courts might depart from these rules, but there is no reason to suppose that they will. After all, the statute provides a rule of construction and it is the will of the donee of the power which is being construed. 

11. Relation to Clauses (9) and (10) 

Clause (8) clearly takes precedence over clauses (9) and (10) which deal with the passing of ineffective gifts to residuary devisees and legatees. It is now expressly provided in the latter clauses that they apply only if the ineffective gift "shall not pass to the issue of the beneficiary under the provisions of paragraph (8)." Hence, if testator dies childless leaving his residuary estate equally to his brother and sister, and the brother predeceases testator but is survived by issue, the issue of the brother take his half under clause (8) rather than the sister under clause (10). In this respect, the present act merely states the result reached in Desh's Estate, 321 Pa. 286 (1936), under the act of 1917 which was ambiguous on this point. 3265

§(8) 12 

WILLS ACT 

It is possible, however, for both clause (8) and clause (9) or (10) to operate on the same will. Thus, in Denny's 

Estate, 22 D. & C. 175 (O. C. Phila. 1934), the residue was given to the childless testator's brother and sister, both of whom died before testator. The sister died childless but the brother was survived by issue, and it was held that these issue took the entire residue. The sister's share passed under section 15 (c) of the act of 1917 (clause (10) of the present act) to those who represented the brother under section 15 (b) (clause (8) of the present act). The result seems sound and there is nothing in the present act to change it.

For another type of case where clause (8) and clauses (9) and (10) must be considered together, see the discussion under the next heading. 

1 12. Proviso as to Gifts to Brothers, Etc. Where Testator Leaves Spouse or Issue 

The proviso states that a gift to a deceased brother or sister or child of a brother or sister shall lapse to the extent that the testator's spouse or issue would benefit by such a lapse. Under the acts of 1844 and 1897, gifts to such collaterals lapsed whenever testator was "survived" by issue, but this was clarified by the act of 1917 which made the provision in favor of collateral issue operative only when the "testator shall not leave any lineal descendants who would otherwise receive the benefit of any lapsed or void devises or legacies." In other words, it was realized that the mere survival of testator's issue should not defeat the provision for collaterals if the testator's issue would not take in any event.

The present clause again revises the language and makes the following changes: (1) It adds testator's spouse to the class of survivors who will defeat the provision for collateral issue. (2) It re-emphasizes the correction made in 1917 by making it clear that the lapse is permitted only when the testator's immediate family will actually receive the lapsed gift, "either as part of the residuary estate or under the intestate's laws." (3) It carries this idea a step further by providing that the lapse is permitted only 3266

¶ 

WILLS ACT 

§14 (8) "to the extent" that the testator's spouse or issue would benefit. Thus, as the illustration given in the Commissioners' comments indicates, a gift to a brother might partly lapse for the benefit of testator's widow and partly pass to the legatee's issue.

In all cases where a lapse would clearly cause an intestacy, the proviso is easy to apply, and except for the new provision for testator's widow, the law has remained unchanged since 1844. Thus, if testator is survived by a widow and children but leaves his entire estate to his brother who dies before testator but is survived by issue of his own, the gift to the brother will clearly lapse and the property will pass to the spouse and testator's children under the Intestate Act. See, for example, Barnett's 

Estate, 104 Pa. 342 (1883). Note that the testator's spouse in such a case is not required to take against the will, for an actual intestacy occurs. 

There seems to be little authority, however, governing cases where a lapse would not cause an intestacy but the gift would pass to residuary legatees under clauses (9) and (10), infra. Suppose, for example, that testator is survived by children A and B and by will leaves the residue of his estate half to his brother X and half to child A-excluding B. X predeceases testator survived by child Y. It seems plain that the gift intended for X will lapse because of the present proviso and the entire estate will pass to A as the other residuary beneficiary under clause (10) infra, although no decision has been found covering this set of facts. 

On a slightly different set of facts there are conflicting decisions in the lower courts. Suppose, as above, testator is survived by children A and B but leaves the residue of his estate half to his brother X (who predeceases testator but is survived by child Y) and the other half to charity. 

It seems to the present writer that the residuary estate in this case should be distributed half to Y and half to charity, because if the gift to the brother were allowed to lapse, the whole residue would have gone to the charity, as the other residuary legatee under clause (10). Hence, A and B would not have benefited in any event, and the proviso to clause 3267

§(8) WILLS ACT 

¶ 12 (8) has no application. This was the decision in Mohl's 

Estate, 5 Schuyl. Reg. 180 (0. C. 1938), under the similar provision in the act of 1917.

In Spangler's Estate, 31 Berks 258 (1939), however, the court reached the rather curious conclusion that testator's issue have an interest in this type of case, although they were excluded by the will. The reasoning is not too clear, but apparently the provision in section 15 (b) of the act of 1917 (corresponding to the present proviso) was construed to give testator's issue an interest superior to the other residuary beneficiaries under section 15 (c) (corresponding to present clause (10)) in this situation. That such was not the intent of either the 1917 or the 1947 Commission seems plain from the Commissioner's comments of both years and from the wording of both acts. The difficulty arises from the fact that the case bears a deceiving resemblance to Desh's Estate, 321 Pa. 286 (1936), discussed under the previous heading. There testator died childless and it was held that the issue of his predeceased brother took ahead of the other residuary legatees. Hence, there is apparent logic in the proposition that if a brother's issue comes ahead of residuary legatees (Desh's Estate) and if testator's issue come ahead of a brother's issue (the proviso to clause (8)), testator's issue necessarily come ahead of other residuary legatees in all cases. The fallacy lies in the second assumption. The proviso to clause (8) does not put testator's issue ahead of a brother's issue in all cases, but only when testator's issue would otherwise take the gift if it were allowed to pass under the general law as modified by other sections of the act. In other words, Spangler's Estate would be correct only if clauses (9) and (10) contained provisos similar to the proviso in clause (8), but they do not. 

The revised language in the present proviso might make it clearer in cases where there are other residuary beneficiaries that the issue of testator will defeat the substitution of the brother's issue only where the testator's issue would take the lapsed gift under clauses (9) and (10). 3268

WILLS ACT 

13. How Issue Take (Conditions, Advancements, Debts, Etc.) 

Assuming a case where the statute applies, it is clear that the issue take per stirpes. This was so under the prior act,30 and it is now expressly provided in the present clause that the issue share in this manner. 

It is also clear from the wording of the present act that the issue take as representatives of the deceased parent "the share which their deceased ancestor would have taken had he survived the testator." This language more accurately than the old act describes the results reached in Newbold v. Prichett, 2 Wh. 46 (1836), on the one hand, and Callery's Estate, 333 Pa. 258 (1939), on the other. In the first case it was held that the issue take directly and not through the estate of the predeceased ancestor; hence where testatrix provided for a bequest to her son who died before her but left issue who survived, it was held that the son's executor had no interest in the mother's estate. The court in Callery's Estate, on the other hand, while admitting that the issue took directly, decided that they took as representatives of the deceased legatee and hence took subject to a debt owed by the legatee to testator. 

The general theory of Callery's Estate seems beyond question. The issue take as substitutes and should certainly not take more than their parent would have taken if he had survived. Thus if the gift in the will is conditional or subject to a charge, it is obvious that the issue take it cum onere-as in Blackwell v. Scouten, 199 Pa. 446 (1901), discussed above under ¶9. Likewise, if the named legatee received during the testator's lifetime a payment on account of his legacy-or a so-called "advancement" after the will is executed 31-the amount of the gift passing to the issue should be reduced just as it would have been if the beneficiary had survived.

In applying this general theory so as to deduct from the legacy a debt owed by the named legatee to the testator, however, Callery's Estate goes about as far as it is

The decision seems sound if it is assumed that the estate of the predeceased legatee was insolvent so that the debt could not have been recovered except by setting it off against the legacy passing to the issue. If, on the other hand, the estate of the named legatee is solvent, there would be no good reason to make the legatee's issue pay the legatee's debt. Suppose, for example, A makes a will giving his son B a legacy of $10,000. 

B dies first, owing A $5,000, survived by a child C, and leaving his entire estate to his wife X. B's estate after payment of all other debts is $20,000, but before his estate is settled, A dies. On these facts, it would seem questionable whether the doctrine of Callery's Estate should require the deduction of the $5,000 from the legacy passing to C, thus giving X a windfall of this amount. Ordinarily it would seem fairer to let B's estate pay its own debts wherever it is able to do so. (9) Lapsed and Void Devises and Legacies-Shares 

Not in Residue.

A devise or bequest not being part of the residuary estate which shall fail or be void because the beneficiary fails to survive the testator or because it is contrary to law or otherwise incapable of taking effect or which has been revoked by the testator or is undisposed of or is released or disclaimed by the beneficiary, if it shall not pass to the issue of the beneficiary under the provisions of clause (8) hereof, and if the disposition thereof shall not be otherwise expressly provided for by law, shall be included in the residuary devise or bequest, if any, contained in the will. 

(10) Lapsed and Void Devises and Legacies-Shares in Residue.

When a devise or bequest as described in clause (9) hereof shall be included in a residuary clause of the will and shall not be available to the issue of the devisee or legatee under the provisions of clause (8) hereof, and if the disposition shall not be otherwise expressly provided for by law, it shall pass to the other residuary devisees or legatees, if any there be, in proportion to their respective shares or interests in the residue.

COMMISSIONERS' COMMENTS- 

This takes the place of the first sentence of section 15(c) of the 1917 act. The wording has been changed for clarity, and additions have been made. "or is undisposed of" has been added to avoid the disposition of such shares to the heirs and next of kin and to make them the same as lapsed shares: cf. 

Rickenbach Est., 348 Pa. 121. "or is released or disclaimed by the beneficiary" has been added through an abundance of caution to make it clear that such shares are included. The words "released or disclaimed" rather than "renounced" are used because they are the words employed in section 3 of the Estates Act of 1947. "and if the disposition thereof shall not be other- 3301

¶ 1. History 

At common law, a lapsed devise passed to the heirs at law but a lapsed bequest fell into the residue-except where the bequest was itself part of the residuary clause, in which event it too passed by intestacy. This rule was first changed by the act of 1879, P. L. 88, which saved specific devises for the residuary devisees. Under that act, all non-residuary gifts, whether of real or personal property, fell into the residue, but ineffective gifts of part of the residue itself continued to go to the heirs at law.² 

In 1917 the Legislature restated the rule of the earlier act as to non-residuary gifts and took the additional step of saving lapsed and void residuary bequests and devises for the other residuary beneficiaries "if any there be."

The present clauses continue that rule with certain changes in the class of cases to which the provision is applicable. 

2. Contrary Intent 

Moore's Estate, 101 Pa. Super. 39 (1930), discussed below (5) under "Undisposed of Gifts," was decided on the ground that an intention contrary to the statute appeared in the will, although as pointed out in ¶5 it might have been decided on the ground that there was no residuary gift. Another type of case which might be mentioned under this heading is where the testator has specifically provided for the failure of the gift to the beneficiary first named and has named alternative beneficiaries to take the property. The cases discussed under section 14

On the whole, it is difficult to imagine a case where an attempted gift fails entirely and yet an intention contrary to the present clauses appears in the will containing a residuary clause. At least there are no typical cases which it would be profitable to discuss. Griscom's Estate, 70

¶3. Class Gifts 

In one respect the present clauses are narrower than clause (8) because class gifts are not specifically mentioned. 

Hence, unlike clause (8), clauses (9) and (10) have no application to such gifts. In the discussion of clause (8), it was pointed out that if testator made a bequest to his own "children" without saying more, the result under that 3. Further references to contray intent will be found infra under ¶5 (“Undisposed of" Gift) and ¶9 (Powers of Appointments). 3304

WILLS ACT 

clause was quite different than where the gift was to testator's children "living at my death." In the first case, the issue of a deceased child would share, but not in the second. Under clauses (9) and (10), however, this distinction is unimportant. If testator gives a pecuniary legacy to the "children" of X, a deceased friend of testator, the class will be determined at testator's death so that a child of X who died before testator is simply excluded from the class. There is no lapse or failure of any kind so long as at least one person fulfilling the description is alive to take. Hence, in the absence of a special provision governing class gifts in clauses (9) and (10) they have no application unless no one qualifies and the entire gift fails. By the same token, it becomes important under the present clauses to determine whether a gift to a group of persons is a gift to a class or a series of gifts to several individuals, a question which was unimportant under clause (8). Suppose, for example, testator's deceased friend X had three children (A, B, and C) living when testator wrote his will, and child A died before testator. If the will simply gave $600 to be divided among X's "children," it would be a class gift so that B and C would take $300 each. If, on the other hand, the will gave $600 to be divided among "A, B, and C," naming them, B and C would each take $200, and the remaining $200 would lapse and fall into the residue under clause (9). Of course, there are many border-line cases where testator's intent is not so clear. 

The general rules for determining when there is a true class gift are discussed in Billings's Estate (No. 1), 268 Pa. 67 (1920), and additional cases are collected in Hunter's Or phans' Court Commonplace Book (1939) "Legacies and De vises' § 12 (j).

5. "Undisposed of" Gifts

The new provision is broader than the act of 1917 due to the addition of the words ".. or is undisposed of or is released or disclaimed by the beneficiary That renounced gifts should be subject to the act is logical and this part of the addition is a restatement of what probably would have been held even under the old law. The concept of a "devise or bequest" which remains "undisposed of," however, is something to wrestle with. 

The Commissioners' comments refer to Rickenbach's 

Estate, 348 Pa. 121, 125 (1943). There, a remainder interest in one-half the residuary real estate was construed as being vested in decedent's daughter subject to divestment, and since no divestment occurred the daughter's estate took the gift although she had died during the life tenancy. 

Hence, no problem under section 15 (c) of the old Wills Act arose. By way of dictum, however, the court indicated that section 15 (c) would have had no application even if the daughter's interest had been contingent and had never vested due to the failure of the contingency. 

This construction of the act of 1917 is also supported by Knox's Estate (No. 2), 328 Pa. 188 (1937), where testator apparently forgot to provide for distribution of onefourth of the residuary income between the death of one of his sons and the termination of the trust. The court held that section 15 (c) of the act of 1917 had no application. Admittedly there was no lapsed or void bequest and

What is "Residuary Devise or Bequest"

In determining both whether and how to apply these provisions, it is necessary to decide what, if any, part of the will constitutes the residuary clause. As already pointed out under the preceding heading, if there is no residuary clause there is nothing upon which the statute can operate.18 Likewise, if the ineffective gift comprises the entire residue, there will plainly be no "other" residuary beneficiaries to take the property.14 And even when there is admittedly no intestacy as to the ineffective gift, it is necessary to determine who are the residuary beneficiaries entitled to the property under the statute.
