¶ 6 Act is said to exist "where a testator manifests an intent to dispose of everything not otherwise disposed of by the will . . "It is emphasized that "no technical mode of expression is necessary . . ." In that case it was held. that a clause disposing of testator's entire estate was a residuary clause notwithstanding the absence of prior specific provisions. The authorities on the general question are further discussed in Bricker's Estate, 335 Pa. 300 (1939), where a disposition of the "balance" of the estate in the middle of the will was held to be a residuary clause. 

Haak's Estate, 342 Pa. 93 (1941), is an interesting case on this question, although there were three dissents and it is questionable whether the case was correctly decided. 

Testator directed that the estate not given to his wife should be distributed as he would "enter off and on in a book in this desk . . . to relatives, etc." He then provided "If any remains, [it is] to be divided equally among" X, Y, and Z. The attempt to incorporate the future document was admittedly ineffective and the unsigned memoranda in testator's account book had been denied probate. The only question was whether X, Y and Z or the next of kin should take the property. The majority held for the latter saying the provision for X, Y, and Z was not a residuary clause within the meaning of the Wills Act. The reasoning seems to be that X, Y and Z were not given the rest of the estate but only such property as testator did not mention in his memoranda. Hence, both gifts failed and not only the attempted gift to relatives. The fallacy lies in the fact that the same reasoning would apply to any residuary clause and would make a nullity of the statutory provisions in all cases where a specific or pecuniary gift is ineffective. 

It is doubtful, therefore, that Haak's Estate will be of much use as an authority beyond its peculiar facts, although there are helpful analyses of the earlier cases in both the majority and dissenting opinions. 

It seems clear from the definition of a residuary gift in Armstrong's Estate, 347 Pa. 23, and from the discussion in Bricker's Estate, 335 Pa. 300, that these provisions of the Wills Act refer to the general or ultimate residuary clause and not to gifts of the "residue" of particular property or a specified sum. (This is where Haak's Estate 3310

WILLS ACT 

differs from the cases the court relied upon.) Whether a given provision in a will is a gift of the balance of special property or of the estate generally, however, is often difficult to determine.15 

Sometimes the testator creates another sort of problem by making a complicated disposition of the "residue" of his estate and then disposing of the residue of the residue.16 In other cases, the testator gives a fractional share of his estate to A and the rest to B and it is uncertain whether B alone or A and B are the residuary beneficiaries.17 There are many cases on what constitutes a residuary clause in these and other kinds of wills, collected in Hunter's Commonplace Book under "Legacies" § 19, but only a few of them concern the application of these provisions in the Wills Act. Decisions on questions of abatement and the like are helpful by way of analogy but are not necessarily controlling. Furthermore, as in all cases dealing with interpretation of wills, the decision usually rests on the peculiarities of the will in question.

It will be noted in this regard that under the present cy pres provision in section 10 of the Estates Act the requirement of a "general" charitable purpose has been eliminated so that there will be fewer cases where cy pres is impossible. The only question of this sort under the new cy pres law is whether the purpose named by the testator is in fact a charitable purpose within the broad definition of section 1 (1) of the Estates Act. 

It is also obvious that the gift cannot be subject to cy pres when it fails by reason of decedent's death within thirty days (see section 7 (1) of the Wills Act). Whenever cy pres is possible, however, it is clear that section 10 of the Estates Act takes precedence over the present clauses of the Wills Act. 

Void perpetuities at common law reverted to the estate of the donor, so that section 15 (c) of the act of 1917 presumably would have applied to cases where a specific gift or gift of part of the residue violated the rule.19 This has been radically changed, however, by section 5 of the Estates Act which provides an exclusive statutory method for disposing of void perpetuities in all cases. That act will therefore take precedence over the present clauses as a disposition "otherwise expressly provided for by law." 

The same is true of unlawful accumulations. Under the old law a gift of income subject to an invalid direction to accumulate sometimes reverted to the donor's estate and presumably was subject to section 15 (c) of the old 

Wills Act in proper cases.20 Section 8 of the Estates Act, however, sets forth a comprehensive method for handling the released income in such situations. Residuary legatees are not entirely excluded by the new provision (see Estates Act § 8—¶ 4d), but cases where the present clauses have any application to unlawful accumulations will be rare.

The general rule is that income goes to income and principal to principal, although only a few of the possible situations have been passed upon, and some of those only by lower courts.

The simplest type of case is where the whole residue is left to A for life with a void remainder to X. Since A was given income only, it is said that he cannot share in the void gift of principal as an "other residuary legatee" within the meaning of the statute, so there is an intestacy of the remainder. This was the view expressed by Gest, J. in McNulty's Estate, 29 Dist. 709 (O. C. Phila. 1920)—a decision which is difficult to justify from the literal terms of the statute, but which is probably consistent with what

In Morgan's Estate, 340 Pa. 465 (1941), the will gave a life estate to A with remainder to X and Y in equal shares. Only the gift to X was ineffective. Consistent with 

McNulty's Estate the court held that A could not share in the void gift. However, here there was another residuary gift of the same quality as the ineffective gift, so that the Wills Act was held to vest the entire remainder in Y as "the other residuary legatee" within the meaning of this provision.

So far the law seems clear. Income beneficiaries will not share as other residuary devisees or legatees in an ineffective gift of principal, but other remaindermen do share under this provision of the act. 

Suppose the situation is reversed and the gift of income is ineffective while the gift of principal is validan ineffective gift to A for life with a valid remainder to X.24 As already pointed out (8a), the case suggested presents a problem of acceleration which is preliminary to the problem under the present statutory provision. If the remainder to X is accelerated due to the failure of the life estate to A, no problem under the present clause arises. 

Assuming, however, that the valid succeeding estate is not accelerated for one reason or another, such cases as there are follow the logic implicit in McNulty's Estate and Morgan's Estate and hold that the ineffective gift of income (a) will not pass to the remainderman or even to a succeeding income beneficiary, but (b) will pass to persons currently entitled to other income, or to the next of kin if there is no other income beneficiary named in the will.

9. Powers of Appointment 

Suppose A gives B a power of appointment which B attempts to exercise in favor of C, but the appointment is void or ineffective for one reason or another. Should these provisions of the Wills Act apply to save the appointment for B's residuary beneficiaries, or should the property pass in default of appointment under A's will? Darling v. 

Edson, 4 Pa. Super. 498, 504 (1897), indicates that B's residuary legatees take the property. This is consistent with the cases discussed under 14 (8) (¶ 10) where the donee of the power is regarded as making the devise or bequest in applying that clause. A superficial search has disclosed no other cases on the subject.27

Limitations on the doctrine of Darling v. Edson are self-evident. In the first place, the residuary beneficiaries (or other residuary beneficiaries, if the appointment is in the residuary clause) must of course be within the class of permissible appointees. In the second place, the residuary clause must be sufficient to exercise the power and no intent to the contrary must appear. In the Darling case, there was no express reference to the power but the donee (who had no property of her own) exercised it by her whole will by necessary implication. See section 

14 (14) infra. Suppose, however, B's will in one paragraph expressly exercised the power in favor of C and in a separate paragraph left the residue of his estate to D. In such a case, it would probably be held that if the appointment to C was void the property would pass under A's will in default of appointment, because B had expressed an intent that his residuary clause was to operate only on his individual estate.

Old Law

Section 18. Unless the testator shall otherwise direct by his will, the devisee of real estate which is subject to mortgage shall take subject thereto, and shall not be entitled to exoneration out of the other estate of the testator, real or personal; and this whether the mortgage was created by the testator or by a previous owner or owners, and notwithstanding any general direction by the testator that his debts be paid.

This is an almost verbatim re-enactment of section 18 of the act of 1917, where the provision was new. Under 3401

WILLS ACT 

T2 the case law prior to 1917, a devisee could usually insist that the mortgage be paid out of residuary personalty where the mortgage debt represented the direct obligation of the testator-as where the testator had created the mortgage or had expressly assumed an old one.¹ Even before the statute, however, the devisee took subject to the mortgage in any of the following situations: (1) to the extent that residuary personalty was insufficient after payment of claims, specific legacies and pecuniary legacies,2 (2) where the mortgage did not represent the testator's primary obligation-as where the testator had purchased "under and subject to" a mortgage but had not otherwise assumed the debt (the secondary obligation of the grantee to re-imburse the grantor being insufficient to constitute a debt of the grantee-testator within the meaning of the general rule), or (3) where it affirmatively appeared that the testator intended the devise to be charged with the payment of the mortgage debt.5 The 1917 Commission decided that the above distinctions were "technical" and that "the historical justification of the rule has been long outgrown." It was therefore provided that all devisees take subject to any mortgage on the property-regardless of whether the testator was personally liable as mortgagee and regardless of a general direction in the will to pay debts (see ¶ 3, below). 

The provision was inspired by the English "Locke King 

Acts" of 17 and 18 Vict. c. 113, 30 and 31 Vict. c. 69, and 

40 and 41 Vict. c. 34.

On the other hand, there are plainly limits to what can be called a devise. The present provision, for example, would clearly not apply to a bequest of personal property subject to a chattel mortgage. By analogy to the pre-statutory rule as to mortgages it would seem that if such lien or charge is coupled with a primary personal liability on the part of the testator, the devisee can insist on payment of the debt out of the general estate. Analogies are dangerous, however, in any field of law dealing with a testator's presumed intention. The purpose here is merely to call attention to the limited scope of the present provision. 

3. Contrary Intent

This, like the other clauses of section 14, is subject to a contrary intent appearing in the will, but here it is expressly stated that a mere general direction to pay debts is not sufficient in itself to rebut the rule of the statute.

5. Marshalling, Subrogation, Etc.

Ordinarily the mortgagee will proceed against the property and if there is no deficiency no special problems will arise. If there is a deficiency after foreclosure, the mortgagee must claim against the executor of the testatormortgagor's estate because even if the devisee is liable over to the general estate (see preceding heading) no direct personal action can be brought by the mortgagee against the devisee under principles already referred to." 

Suppose the mortgagee, instead of foreclosing the mortgage, merely claims on the testator's bond against the personal estate at the audit. If the mortgagee is successful in collecting the full mortgage debt in this way, there can be no doubt that the executors would be subrogated and have a claim over against the devisee. Could this circuity of actions be avoided by forcing the mortgagee first to proceed by foreclosure against the land, limiting his claim at the audit to any deficiency so established? PROPOSED COMMISSIONERS' COMMENT TO 1963 REPEALER (not yet adopted by the Commission as this goes to press)-This clause is repealed. It has been an anomaly in our law since the Fiduciaries Act of 1949. It is no longer required for the protection of legatees and creates some confusion in the application of the rules of abatement and in the administration of estatesespecially as to legacies of $100 or less: cf. Morgan Est., 1 

Fiduc. Rep. 91. 

Note to Repealer

The repeal of section 14 (13) of the Wills Act is the result of a belated recognition that the section had become unnecessary and confusing with the passage of the Fiduciaries Act of 1949, P. L. 512, 20 P. S. § 320.101 et seq., providing for the administration of real estate. 

The recognition of the inconsistency came gradually. 

In 1961 it was realized that as originally drafted section 3451

§(13) 

WILLS ACT 

14 (13) was in conflict with section 751 of the Fiduciaries Act dealing with the order of abatement and eliminating the preference formerly given to gifts of real estate over gifts of personalty. Thus, since residuary devises and bequests are now on a par so far as abatement is concerned, it is a matter for the judgment of the personal representative whether to sell residuary real or personal property to pay the pecuniary legacies. The 1961 amendment to section 

14 (13) of the Wills Act, by eliminating the words in inner brackets, removed this particular inconsistency between the two acts.

Two years later, however, it was realized that the entire concept of liens of pecuniary legacies was inconsistent with the system of real estate administration adopted by the Fiduciaries Act of 1949 and that the lien of legacies was not only unnecessary for the protection of the pecuniary legatee but created difficulties for the title searcher and continued to confuse the law of abatement. 

As explained in the original text (see discussion under "Repealed Sections" tab), the statutory lien of pecuniary legacies performed a real function prior to the Fiduciaries Act of 1949. Real estate did not pass through administration; hence, if the personal property in the estate were insufficient, the pecuniary legacy simply would not be paid in the absence of some provision in the statute or an express or implied provision in the will making a legacy a charge on the real estate. With the Fiduciaries Act of 1949, however, all this was changed. Regardless of whether the pecuniary legatee has a lien, he has the same remedies available to him against both real and personal property as any other distributee of an estate. 

Suppose, for example, a will of a post-1949 decedent leaves $1,000 to A and the residue to B. Suppose further that the estate consists of nothing but a piece of real estate worth $5,000. Under the present Fiduciaries Act the legatee can pursue his remedies against the real estate in much the same manner as he could have enforced his rights if the estate had consisted of $5,000 of personal property. Thus, his pecuniary legacy is preferred over the residuary devise under section 751 of the Fiduciaries Act governing the order 3452

WILLS ACT 

§14 (13) of abatement, and under section 541 the personal representative has ample powers to sell residuary real estate to give effect to this preference. If for some reason the personal representative does not sell the real estate, then at the audit of the account the legatee can insist that the court order a sale of the real estate prior to distribution under section 734 or make some other arrangement for its payment. For example, even in the absence of old section 

14 (13) of the Wills Act, the court can nevertheless declare the legacy to be a lien under section 752 of the Fiduciaries Act, if for some reason it is not advisable to force a sale of the real estate. Suppose the personal representative, prior to accounting, had distributed the real estate to the residuary beneficiary under section 732 of the Fiduciaries Act. Here also the beneficiary of the unliened legacy has an adequate remedy. Such a distribution is at the risk of the personal representative; he is relieved of liability to creditors who have not given notice but is not relieved of liability for distributing to the wrong person. Hence, the legatee not only can surcharge the personal representative but presumably can force the return of the land to the estate, because the first $1,000 of its value had been distributed wrongfully.

Before the repeal of section 14 (13) of the Wills Act, the $1,000 pecuniary legatee in the above case, in addition to all other remedies described, would have an automatic lien on the real estate and could proceed with foreclosure under section 801 of the Fiduciaries Act. Why he would want to do this instead of raising the matter in the normal way at the audit of the account of the personal representative is difficult to understand. It may be suggested that proceeding under section 801 would be convenient for the legatee if no letters had been granted and the estate had not been administered. In such a case, however, it would be doubtful that the courts would have enforced the payment of the legacy without being satisfied that debts, funeral expenses, etc., had been paid first: see Vassilakis v. Vassilakis, 371 Pa. 268, 272 (1952). In short, it is difficult to imagine a situation where the additional remedy of a lien would be of any real value to a pecuniary legatee. 3453

§(13) 

WILLS ACT 

The lien of legacy was not only useless to the legatee but was harmful to other parties in interest because it was likely to create a cloud on title. Where real estate was sold by the personal representative there was no problem because the purchaser took free of the liens under section 547 of the Fiduciaries Act. A real problem arose, however, when real estate was distributed in kind and the devisee wanted to sell it before the expiration of the 20-year period after which the lien of legacies lapsed under section 804. 

The title searcher could not rely on the excerpt from the decree of distribution in the Recorder's office of the county where the real estate was situated (§ 736) because he had to search the Orphans' Court record of the county where the decedent died to find out if there were any unsatisfied pecuniary legacies. And even when the legacy had been paid, the title would still be clouded if the executor had failed to file a satisfaction of award. The problem was particularly acute where real estate had been distributed to the devisee voluntarily without an accounting. 

The repeal of section 14 (13) of the Wills Act should eliminate these difficulties.

Finally, the existence of section 14 (13) of the Wills Act tended to create confusion with respect to the law of abatement. Thus, in Morgan Estate, 1 Fid. Rep. 91 (0. C.

Phila. adj. 1950) the court construed the 1947 exemption of legacies of $100 or less from the lien under section 14 (13) in such a way that it was concluded that such legacies could not be paid when the personal estate was insufficient. This would have been correct under pre-1949 practice but it seems wrong under the Fiduciaries Act of 1949 for the reasons set forth above. The case is a good example of the confusion caused by sections of two different acts dealing with almost, but not quite, the same subject matter. It is to be hoped that the repeal of section 14 (13) will also eliminate this area of confusion. 3454 [The next page is 3501]

(14) Power of Appointment. 

A general devise of the real estate of the testator or of the real estate of the testator in any place, or in the occupation of any person mentioned in his will, or otherwise described in a general manner, shall be construed to include any real estate, or any real estate to which such description shall extend, as the case may be, which he shall have power to appoint in any manner he shall think proper, and shall operate as an execution of such power. In like manner, a bequest of the personal estate of the testator, or any bequest of personal property described in a general manner, shall be construed to include any personal estate, or any personal estate to which such description shall extend, as the case may be, which he shall have power to appoint in any manner he shall think proper, and shall operate as an execution of such power. In like manner, a general pecuniary legacy, when the assets of the individual estate of the testator are not sufficient for its payment, shall, to the extent necessary to make possible the payment of the legacy, be construed to include any estate which the testator shall have power to appoint in any manner he shall think proper, and shall to such extent operate as an execution of such power.

1. Rule Prior to Statute 

Prior to 1879 there was no statute on this subject and the rule of the cases was that a power was not exercised unless an intention to do so appeared expressly or by necessary implication in the will of the donee. Three classes of cases where such an intention was found in the absence of statute are mentioned in Bingham's Appeal, 64 

Pa. 345, 349 (1870) ¹: (1) when the donee expressly refers to the power, (2) "when he disposes of the subject of it by such a description as identifies it" (as where the donee makes a specific devise of Blackacre which he does not own but has the power to appoint), or (3) "when the instrument of execution cannot have any operation except on the ground that the donee intended to execute his power; as 

1. See also Penna. Company's Account, 264 Pa. 433, 436 (1919); Hupp v. Union Coal and Coke Co., 284 Pa. 529, 534 (1925); Barton's Trust, 348 Pa. 

279, 282 (1944); Jones v. Mackie, 49 D. & C. 459, 474 et seq. (C. P. Susq. 1943). 3502

where it is a power to dispose of real estate and he has none of his own." To these may be added: (4) where the donee of a special power makes a general devise or bequest to all the members of the restricted class.2 This fourth category represents a recent liberalization of the old rule, although it was developed in cases not governed by the statute so that it must be considered as part of our case law. The subject is further discussed below under ¶ 6. 

2. The Statute in General 

The presumption against the exercise of a power was reversed by section 3 of the act of 1879, P. L. 88, which was based on a provision in the English Wills Act. The act of 1917 reenacted the 1879 provision almost verbatim and the first two sentences of the present clause contain language identical to the prior acts. The third sentence, relating to pecuniary legacies, is new but is in harmony with prior cases interpreting the earlier act-see ¶ 3 below. "The statute proceeds on the assumption . . . that an ordinary man considers property which he may dispose of by will as his own . . . and, shifting the burden of proof theretofore prevailing in such cases, the rule is ordained that he who, in any instance, denies that a general devise [or bequest] executes a general power of appointment, must prove 'by what appears on the face of the will' that it was the testator's 'clearly expressed' intention the devise in question 'should not do so'.. "Thompson v. Wanamaker's Trustee, 268 Pa. 203, 214 (1920).³ 

3. Types of Provisions Which Exercise Power 

The statute has been liberally applied by the courts who welcomed the statutory recognition of the fact that a man ordinarily regards himself as the owner of property which he has the power to appoint to whomever he pleases. 

The instrument offered as exercising the power must, of course, be a will or codicil, but there are few, if any, re- 4

The statute also applies, however, to gifts of shares of the donee's estate. In Blackburne's Estate, 290 Pa. 55 (1927), the donee gave his wife "such share of my estate as she is entitled to under the intestate laws. . 

It was held that the words "my estate," in view of the statute, included appointive property so that the wife's share was measured by the combined funds, in contrast to what she would have taken if there had been actual intestacy. Likewise, even before the addition of the last sentence of the present clause, the statute was held to apply to all general devises and bequests, including pecuniary legacies.5 With the status of pecuniary legacies further clarified by the present clause, it would seem that any type of legacy or devise would be sufficient to exercise a general power under the statutory rule in the absence of a contrary intent. 

The only type of gift not mentioned is the specific legacy or devise, but such provisions take care of themselves because a specific gift of an item of property subject to the power exercises it under the case law prior to the statute. 

As for semi-specific gifts (such as "all my securities" or "all my real estate in Delaware County") where property owned outright and property subject to the power both fit the description, these would seem to be covered by the wording of the statute which is not confined to what are technically general legacies or devises, but to any testamentary gift "described in a general manner." Thus, so far as the will of the donee of the power is concerned, the effect of the statute is limited only by the provision for a contrary intent. And even this is difficult to show in this type of case, as indicated below under ¶ 7.

15. Types of Powers Which Are Exercised 

The present clause, like the acts of 1879 and 1917, applies to powers "to appoint in any manner [the donee of the power] thinks proper." It could conceivably have been argued that the statute applies only to powers which are absolutely unrestricted in the sense that they can be exercised either by will or inter vivos deed. It is too late to raise the point now, however, as the statute has frequently been applied to powers which can be exercised by will only, and this is plainly in conformity with the legislative intent. The fact that the power is restricted to exercise by will, therefore, does not prevent it from being a power in the donee "to appoint in any manner he shall think proper." 8 7.

Special powers, then, continue to be governed by case law. Perhaps under the influence of the statute, however, the courts have tended to liberalize the rules as to what is necessary to exercise a special power of appointment. 

As explained above (¶1) in the discussion of the law applicable to all powers prior to the statute, it was originally necessary for the donee either specifically to refer to the power, or to make a specific gift of the particular items of property subject to the power, or to make a general gift of a certain type of property of which the donee owned none but over which he had the power of appointment. 

In Lafferty's Estate (No. 1), 311 Pa. 455, 464 (1933), however, it was held that a special power was exercised by the residuary clause of the donee's will which fulfilled none of the above requirements but which named all the members of the permitted class.

The decision was based partly on the fact that an effective exercise had been assumed in a prior appeal in the same estate and hence had become the law of the case. 

The point was reaffirmed, however, in Biddle's Estate, 333 Pa. 316, 318 (1939) where a life tenant with a special power to appoint to his issue left the residue of his estate (without mentioning the power) in trust for his children and grandchildren. The court said that in Lafferty's Estate "we did intend the general principle that a limited power of appointment may be exercised without direct reference to the creating power, by a clause which names all the members of the permitted class as beneficiaries." 

Note that the doctrine of Lafferty's Estate and Biddle's Estate would not apply if the donee's residuary beneficiaries include other than those in the permitted class.¹4

17. Contrary Intent

The language of the court in Thompson v. Wanamaker's Trustee, 268 Pa. 203, 214 (1920), to the effect that an intent contrary to the present clause must appear "on the face of the will" and be "clearly expressed" has already been quoted under ¶ 1.15

This strict rule against finding a contrary intent was reaffirmed in Provident Trust Co. v. Scott, 335 Pa. 231 (1939), where testatrix had two general powers of appointment-A and B. The will contained a special exercise of power A (specifically referring to it) and a general residuary clause but made no reference to power B. It was held that power B was nevertheless exercised by the residuary clause because no intention contrary to the statute clearly appeared in the will. "We cannot held that Miss Scott's failure to mention the other power amounts to an 'appearance' in the will of an intention on her part not to exercise that power." 335 Pa. at 235. To the same effect is Barton's

Trust, 348 Pa. 279 (1944), where the donee made a bequest of the residue of her estate "including" property subject to power A and it was held that the provision was sufficient to exercise power B. But see Safe Deposit Company v. Friend, 201 Pa. 429 (1902), where the individual estate and power A were referred to in a codicil explaining the scope of the will and an intent contrary to the statute was found so that power B was not exercised. This decision was limited to its facts in the Scott case (335 Pa. at 

236) and in the lower court opinion in Barton's Trust (49 D. & C. at 278). 

15. The provision upon which the argument for contrary intent which was unsuccessfully advanced in that case is of no general interest. In answer to a secondary argument, however, the court ruled that references in the donee's will to property "of which I may die seized" and of which "I may be possessed at the time of my death" included the property over which he had the power and was insufficient to rebut the construction required by the statute. 3508

WILLS ACT § 14 (14) ¶8. Conflict of Laws 

Suppose a power of appointment is given by the will of a donor who dies domiciled in Pennsylvania and the donee of the power dies domiciled in New Jersey. Does this section of our Wills Act govern the question of whether the donee's residuary clause exercises the power? It would appear that it does, even as to personalty. 

In Bingham's Estate, 64 Pa. 345 (1870), the residuary clause in the will of an English decedent was held not to exercise a general power given by a Pennsylvanian, because our law applied and at that time we had no statute on the subject—although the Locke King acts (upon which our present statute is based) were then in effect in England. The court seemed to recognize that if the question were one of interpretation the English law would have governed (64 Pa. at 351), but for some reason the question was held to be one of validity so that the law of the domicile of the donor of the power governed. 

Since that decision, Pennsylvania has adopted the present statutory provision which clearly is a rule of interpretation to prevail only in the absence of a contrary intent. 

Nevertheless in Barton's Trust, 348 Pa. 279 (1944) (aff'g 

49 D. & C. 273 (O. C. Phila. 1942)), it was held that the present statutory provision governed the will of a New Jersey domiciliary merely because the power was contained in a trust subject to Pennsylvania law. Hence the residuary clause in the New Jersey will executed the power over personalty in the Pennsylvania trust although it was assumed that under New Jersey law the decision would have been otherwise. Presumably, the converse would also hold, so that the provisions of our statute would not govern the will of a Pennsylvania donee if the power was created in the will of a non-resident. 

Barton's Trust is supported by the Restatement of Conflicts (1934) § 288 and apparently by the weight of authority, but in the opinion of some the rule is unsound.10

Note that Barton's Trust is inconsistent in theory with Aubert's Appeal, 109 Pa. 447, 459 (1885), supra note 6; see discussion under § 22 (5) of the present act. 3509

Otherwise, the same words in a residuary clause might mean one thing as to the individual estate and another as to the appointive estate. 11. General

16. Contrary Intent ¶1. General

This addition to the Wills Act and the comparable addition in § 14 (5) of the Estates Act were made in connection with the enactment of almost identical provisions in section 718 of the Inheritance and Estate Tax Act of 1961, P. L. 

373, as amended by Act of 1963, P. L. 325, 72 P. S. § 2485-718.

It was thought advisable to include similar provisions in the Wills and Estates Acts to avoid any objection to the provisions in the Inheritance and Estate Tax Act on the ground that their inclusion violated the constitutional prohibition against an act dealing with more than one subject. 

Such an argument would have had some plausibility in view of the fact that the tax imposed is still in the form of an inheritance tax on each transfer, while the provisions of section 718 shift the burden to the residue or trust principal only in the absence of a contrary intent appearing in the will. Hence, it could have been argued that section 718 is a rule of construction having no place in a taxing statute. It is doubtful that such an argument would have prevailed, but it was thought that the addition of the provisions to the Wills and Estates Acts would do no harm and might avoid litigation.

Be that as it may, most practitioners probably associate this subject with inheritance tax law rather than the 3524

WILLS ACT 

§14 (16) law of wills. A complete discussion of the prior law and the effect of the new provisions will be found in Grossman and Smith, Pennsylvania Inheritance and Estate Tax (1961) 718, beginning at page 404. See also Hunter,

Orphans' Court (2d ed. 1959) Vol. 3, p. 224 et seq., under "Inheritance Tax." 

¶ 2. Limited Scope of Provision 

The new statutory provisions, while representing a radical departure from the old law, are very similar to those frequently found in tax clauses in wills. However, the statutory provisions are quite limited in their scope. They do not, for example, throw on the testamentary estate the burden of inheritance taxes on extra-testamentary property as do many tax clauses in wills. The present section deals solely with property passing by the will; taxes on inter vivos transfers in contemplation of death, joint property, etc., are not covered. Also unlike many tax clauses in wills, the present statutory provision throws on the residue the burden of taxes only on outright pre-residuary gifts. A pecuniary or specific bequest or devise in trust pays its own way, although the tax on the life estate or term of years is charged against the principal rather than the income of pre-residuary as well as residuary trusts. ¶3. Estate Taxes Not Affected 

The various statutory provisions deal only with the Pennsylvania inheritance tax. Estate taxes (federal and state) are not covered by these provisions. They will continue to be governed by the Estate Tax Apportionment Act of 1951, P. L. 1405, as amended, 20 P. S. § 881 et seq. 

From 1961 to 1965, that act still provided for apportionment of estate taxes against specific and pecuniary devises and bequests, contrary to the spirit of the present provisions for inheritance taxes. However, Act No. 484 of 

1965, effective December 22, 1965 corrects this and provides for apportionment of estate taxes in a manner consistent with the inheritance tax amendments of 1961 and 1963. 3525

§(16) 14 

WILLS ACT 

4. Charging Taxes Within Residue (1963 Amendment) 

As originally drafted, the first sentence of this section. of the Wills Act and corresponding section 718 (a) of the Inheritance Tax Act raised a question with respect to the charging of taxes within the residue because the provisions were not confined to pre-residuary gifts. Thus, where the residue was left half to a child and half to a brother it was uncertain whether the tax on both halves was deducted before the residuary shares were determined or whether each residuary beneficiary paid his own tax at the 2% and 15% rate respectively. The latter construction was the more plausible (particularly when these sections were read in connection with 718 (c) of the Inheritance Tax Act) and it was so held in Johnson Estate, 29 D. & C. 2d 495, 13 Fid.

Rep. 34 (O. C. Montg. 1962). However, the answer was far from clear: compare Uber's Estate, 330 Pa. 417 (1938) with Spangenberg Estate, 359 Pa. 353, 356 (1948) and Audenried Estate, 376 Pa. 31 (1954); see also Haehnlen Esstate, 10 Fid. Rep. 567 (O. C. Montg. 1960) and other cases cited in Hunter, Orphan's Court (2d ed. 1959) "Inheritance 

Tax"§ 24 (a) and "Estate Tax" § 13. 

The amendment to this section of the Wills Act and the corresponding amendment to section 718 (a) of the Inheritance Tax Act in the Act of 1963, P. L. 325, confining this provision to pre-residuary gifts, should eliminate this problem and confirm the result reached in Johnson Estate. 

The second sentence of section 14 (16) of the Wills Act and section 718 (b) of the Inheritance Tax Act providing for charging principal with the tax on the life estate of course continue to apply to both pre-residuary and residuary gifts. ¶5. Effective Date

There is an unfortunate discrepancy between the effective date provision of the Inheritance and Estate Tax Act of 1961 (which in section 103 provides that that act applies to estates of decedents "dying on or after" January 1, 1962), section 2 of the 1961 amendment to the Wills Act (which provides simply that the amendment "shall take effect January 1, 1962" with no reference to the date of 3526

T§14 (16) 

WILLS ACT 

the decedent's death), and the 1963 amendment to the Wills Act (which has no effective date provision at all). Presumably an act of this sort can constitutionally be applied to undistributed estates of decedents who died before its enactment in cases where the legislative intent is clear: see 

Jeffery's Estate, 333 Pa. 15, 20 (1939). The naked statement that an act shall "take effect" on a certain day is far from clear in this regard, however, and in view of the correlation between this amendment and the Inheritance and Estate Tax Act, it would seem reasonable to construe it in accordance with the effective date provision of that act.

 (17) Ademption.

A specific devise or bequest shall not be adeemed when the testator or the testator's estate receives an asset in exchange for the subject of the devise or bequest and the act which otherwise would have caused the ademption occurs while the testator is an adjudged incompetent, In such case the devise or bequest shall be deemed to apply to whatever was received in exchange. 

-Added by Act No. 477 of 1965, ef fective December 22, 1965. 

Old Law

There was no prior statutory law on the subject. Case law was contrary to this provision. 

Sales and exchanges during legal incompetency will not cause ademption, at least where the proceeds can be traced. Discussion In the absence of the present statute a sale of a specifically devised or bequeathed property by the guardian of an incompetent necessarily caused an ademption because ademption is not based on intention but arises from the fact that the subject matter of the gift is not in the estate. 

Where the subject matter of the gift changed in form only (as where stock was exchanged pursuant to a merger) somewhat more liberal rules of tracing were applied in a case where the change took place during incompetency than in the ordinary case; see Neal Estate, 32 D. & C. 2d 322, 14 Fid. Rep. 277 (O. C. Warren 1963); cf. discussion under 

Wills Act § 14 (1) and (2) ¶ 4. However, no case has been 3529

§(17) 

WILLS ACT 

found where the subject matter of the gift was sold and the attempted specific gift was applied to the proceeds. 

The present addition to the Wills Act is intended to soften the common law rule in cases of sales or exchanges during legal incompetency. It represents a modification of a suggestion which appeared in the September, 1964 issue of Fiduciary Review.

Note that the amendment operates only when the disposition of the property is made while the testator was "an adjudged" incompetent. The mere fact that it can be proved that he was in fact incompetent at the time of the disposition is not enough. Hence, the present amendment will not affect Smith Estate, 415 Pa. 569 (1964). In that case the testatrix, who had not been adjudged incompetent, sold some stock, which she had specifically bequeathed by her will, at a time when in the opinion of her adviser she lacked the competency to make a substitutionary gift to the legatee in her will, so no codicil was suggested to her. Nevertheless, the court held that the gift was adeemed. The same result would follow under the present amendment in any case where there is no adjudication of incompetency at the time of the sale or exchange. 

In the case of a sale or exchange by a guardian of an adjudged incompetent, it must first be determined that the devise or bequest in question is in fact specific (as opposed to general or demonstrative) and that the subject matter of the gift is not still in existence by the application of rules of tracing applicable in ordinary cases. See the discussion of various problems in this respect under Wills Act § 14 (1) and (2), ¶¶ 2-4. 

Assuming an appropriate case, the new provision will be easy to apply if the money or other property received in exchange for the property specifically devised or bequeathed is still intact and unmingled with other funds at the time of the testator's death. Otherwise, problems will arise. Suppose specifically devised real estate is sold and the proceeds are deposited in a bank account and a few days later the money is invested in bonds which remain intact at the testator's death. It would seem fair to award the bonds to the specific devisee, Note however that this involves 3530

WILLS ACT 

§ 14 (17) applying the statute twice. First, the devise must be "deemed to apply" to the cash deposited in the bankwhich, by the terms of the statute, thereby becomes the subject matter of the specific gift. Then, when the cash is converted into the bonds, the statute can be applied again so that the bonds become the subject matter of the gift. Even assuming that this interpretation of the act is accepted, however, far more difficult problems can be imagined—as where the subject matter of several different specific gifts and property not specifically devised or bequeathed are sold by the guardian, the proceeds all mingled together, some of it reinvested, and some of it used for the incompetent's support during the balance of his life. Such problems will be difficult-but not insoluble, and with a little imagination the courts should be able to bring about results considerably fairer than they were at common law. 3530a [The next page is 3531]

WILLS ACT § 14.1 § 14.1. DEVISE OR BEQUEST TO TRUST 

A devise or bequest in a will may be made to the trustee of a trust (including an unfunded life insurance trust, although the settlor has reserved any or all rights of ownership in the insurance contracts) established, in writing, by the testator or any other person before or concurrently with the execution of such will, or to such a trust to be established, in writing, at a future date; provided, that any such future trust instrument or amendment thereto shall be signed by the settlor. Such devise or bequest shall not be invalid because the trust is amendable or revocable, or both, or because the trust was amended after execution of the will. Unless the will provides otherwise, the property so devised or bequeathed shall not be deemed held under a testamentary trust of the testator but shall become and be a part of the principal of the trust to which it is given to be administered and disposed of in accordance with the provisions of the instrument establishing such trust and any amendment thereof. An entire revocation of the trust prior to the testator's death shall invalidate the devise or bequest unless the will directs otherwise. -Added by Act No. 378 of 1957, effective July 11, 1957.

12. The Statute 

Discussion 

¶ 1. Background 

So-called "pour-over" wills, which add the residue to an inter vivos trust, have been popular in Pennsylvania for many years. A man has a taxable estate consisting of $200,000 of life insurance and an interest in a close corporation worth $200,000. He makes the life insurance payable to a revocable unfunded insurance trust and adds the residue of his estate to this same trust by his will. In this way, (a) the draftsman can work with a single fund in providing for a division of the estate into marital deduction and nonmarital deduction portions, (b) the insurance and testamentary property are administered under a single instrument to provide maximum flexibility for the care of the family, and (c) the insurance proceeds are readily available for the payment of death taxes and other cash demands against the estate. (The same result could have been obtained by making the insurance payable to the estate or trustees under the will but this would have unnecessarily subjected the insurance proceeds to Pennsylvania inheritance tax: Myers's Estate, 309 Pa. 581 (1933).)

Because of the advantages and convenience of pourover wills, they became favorites of the practitioner. The property theorist, however, was likely to take a dim view of this procedure because of the doubtful validity of such wills under the laws of various states. The classic discussion of the problem will be found in the various opinions in Atwood v. Rhode Island Trust Company, 275 Fed. 513 (C.C.A. 1st 1921). Since that time the subject has been a favorite of the law reviews and text writers. See generally 

Lauritzen, "Pour-over Wills" 95 Trusts and Estates 992 3532

WILLS ACT 

§ 14.1 (Nov. 1956) and the various cases, statutes and articles cited therein.

Very generally speaking, pour-over wills can be justified in the absence of special legislation on the subject under one of three theories, none of which is entirely airtight: (1) The trust instrument, if in existence at the time the will was made, can be regarded as incorporated by reference into the will; the difficulty here is that such a theory would not help if the trust were amended after the last publication of the will, and it is possible to argue that an instrument which by its terms can be amended in the future cannot be incorporated by reference, regardless of whether the power to amend is exercised. (2) The doctrine that the meaning and effect of a will can be controlled by a subsequent act of independent significance can be relied upon, at least where the trust instrument controls a substantial amount of extratestimentary property so that it has significance independent of the will which adds to it; it can be argued that a gift to a revocable trust is no worse than a gift of whatever furniture happens to be in a particular house at the time of decedent's death or whatever cash happens to be deposited in a particular bank. Query, however, whether a revocable trust to which a will adds ever has significance independent of the settlor's testamentary plan. (3) A possible third ground for upholding pour-over wills, closely related to the second, is that the inter vivos trust is a sort of legal entity to which a gift may be made by willjust as a legacy may be made to a corporation whose purposes can be changed by the stockholders (perhaps the testator himself) after the execution of the will and without complying with the Wills Act.

Naturally some of these theories for upholding a pourover will were stronger in some jurisdictions than others. 

New York, for example, with its aversion to the doctrine of an incorporation by reference, was less hospitable to such wills than other jurisdictions. Also, the objections to wills adding to trusts varied in seriousness according to type of case involved. For example, in few, if any, jurisdictions could objection be made to a will adding to an irrevocable trust of securities already in existence at the time the will 3533

§14.

WILLS ACT 

¶ 1 was executed. On the other hand, the possible objection was most serious in the case of a testamentary addition to an unfunded revocable insurance trust where the settlor retained ownership of the policies so that there was no corpus, and hence no real trust, until the settlor's death. 

In Pennsylvania there was very little reported authority one way or the other prior to the present amendment. 

The closest thing to approval of pour-over wills is in Wilson Estate, 363 Pa. 546, 549 (1950) where the court had before it a pour-over will adding to an insurance trust and said that the inter vivos trust "became incorporated in the will and formed part of it under the doctrine of 'incorporation by reference' ". However, that statement was in the nature of a passing remark by the court at the beginning of an opinion dealing mainly with other questions. Pourover wills adding to insurance trusts have also appeared in lower court decisions where, in the absence of objection, they were given effect without discussion: Ballantyne Estate, 1 Fid. Rep. 445 (O.C. Montg. Adjud. 1951); Clark Estate, 8 D. & C. 2d 665, 7 Fid. Rep. 73 (O.C. Allegh. 1956). Cf.

Lochrie's Estate, 340 Pa. 145 (1940) (trust of securities). 

The Pennsylvania case law on the subject prior to the present amendment is discussed generally in the March 

1957 issue of the Fiduciary Review. Thus, so far as reported Pennsylvania cases are concerned, there was little useful authority one way or another on the subject of pour-over wills. However, in view of 

Pennsylvania's full acceptance of the doctrine of incorporation by reference, and its apparent approval of the doctrine of acts of independent significance and even gifts to oral trusts (see discussion under § 2¶7 of the Wills Act), Pennsylvanians had much less to worry about than attorneys in other jurisdictions. In actual practice, wills adding to existing trusts were very common and were given effect in the absence of objection in countless uncontested cases. 

Furthermore, in view of the liberal requirements in the Pennsylvania Wills Act for execution of wills, the practitioner could always, as a last resort, have probated the deed of trust or amendment as a will or codicil if it were found to be testamentary-a solution not usually available in other 3534

} 14.1 

WILLS ACT 

jurisdictions requiring subscribing witnesses. Hence, there was no desperate need for statutory reform in Pennsylvania, but the present amendment will certaintly be valuable in clearing the air. Also, in validating pour-over wills with respect to future amendments and future trusts, the way is opened to practices which would never have been attempted in the past. 

2. The Statute 

In enacting a statutory provision providing for the validity of pour-over wills, Pennsylvania followed the lead of Indiana (Ind. Stat. Ann. § 6-601 (1953)), Illinois (Ill. 

Stat. Ann. c. 3, § 194a (Smith-Hurd Supp. 1956)), North

Carolina (N.C. Gen. Stat. § 31-47 (Supp. 1955)), and Wisconsin (Wis. Stat. Ann. § 231.205 (West 1957)). However, the Pennsylvania provision in some respects goes much further than these statutes in other states. The following points will be noted: (1) The Pennsylvania act specifically mentions the testamentary addition to an unfunded revocable life insurance trust where the settlor has retained ownership of the policies. As noted above, this was the case where the objection to pour-over wills was most serious. In the absence of the specific language, it could have been argued that no trust was "established" in such a case because there was no corpus. (2) The trust must be in writing. Query whether this by implication changes the rule of Hartman's Estate No. 2, 320 Pa. 331 (1936) (discussed under Wills Act $2¶7b) where a testamentary gift to what seemed to be an oral trust was upheld. (3) If the trust is in existence prior to the date of the will, the trust does not have to be signed, although if the trust is amended or created after the date of the will it must be signed by the settlor. This language requires close examination. In the ordinary case where the testator adds to his own trust the result is scarcely startling. Existing writings, signed or unsigned, could have been incorporated 3535

§ 14.

WILLS ACT 

12 by reference under our case law, and a trust or amendment signed by the testator after the will would comply with the Pennsylvania requirements for execution of wills so it could probably be probated in any event. The rather startling result of the statute will exist in cases where the trust is created or amended by someone other than the testator. 

Suppose, for example, a wife's will gives the residue of her estate to her husband's revocable insurance trust which at the time is set up in favor of their children. Thereafter the husband, without the knowledge or consent of the wife, amends his trust and changes the beneficiaries to persons unrelated to the wife. Under the wording of the present section the wife's will upon her death would be effective to carry her estate to beneficiaries she may not even know. 

It may be suggested that the wording of the statute in this respect was the result of an oversight, that the requirement that the later amendment or trust must be signed by "the settlor" was intended to require signature by "the testator". However, that was not the case. The matter was fully discussed in the Advisory Committee and a large majority were in favor of the statute in its present form. 

The reasoning was that even under traditionally accepted concepts of the law there could have been no objection to the wife's giving her husband a general power of appointment over her estate, and if he survived her he could have exercised such a power in any way he chose. Hence, there is no policy in the law against allowing her in effect to delegate to him a power to dispose of her property regardless of whether he survives her or not. (4) The third sentence of the section, providing that the property added to the trust by will shall not be considered as held under a testamentary trust of the testator but shall be considered a part of the trust to which the addition is made, is based on a similar provision in the North Carolina statute. The full implications of this provision are not entirely clear to the present writer. One possible result is to eliminate any question as to whether the trust instrument should be probated. (Under prior practice the inter vivos trust was seldom ever probated, although if the theory for upholding it was incorporation by reference 3536.

probate may well have been required under our cases if the question had ever been raised-See Galli's Estate, 250 Pa. 

120 (1915).) Another probable result is that after the fund has been turned over to the trustee by the executor, it will be accounted for under the term and number of the inter vivos trust, the situs of which will govern venue. 3537 [The next page is 3551]

The Statute De Donis Conditionalibus, 13 Ed. I. c. 1 

(1285), was reported by the Commission of Judges of 1808 to be in effect in Pennsylvania as part of our common law.¹ 

Under this statute conveyances to a person "and the heirs of his body" or other similar language created an estate 

1. Report of the Judges, 3 Binn. 593 (1811). See early history of the estate tail under section 4 (a) & (b) of the Estates Act. 3551

§ ¶ 1b 

WILLS ACT 

tail. This meant that the ownership passed automatically from the first taker successively to his lineal descendants forever with a reversion in the grantor if the issue of the, grantee died out. The estate did not descend as part of the first taker's estate but the succeeding interest was determined by reference to the common law of descent. Thus, in the ordinary estate tail, male issue had priority according to age and females took equally in the absence of males. Since the property passed automatically rather than as part of the original grantee's estate, the changes made in the law of descent by the various intestate acts did not affect succession to the estate tail, which continued to be governed by the English common law of descent.² 

b. Methods of Barring the Entail 

It was early held in England that the estate tail could be "docked" or destroyed by common recovery or fine. 

These were collusive actions used by the tenant in tail as a means of indirectly conveying a fee, thus cutting off the interests of his descendants. These methods of "barring the entail" were specifically recognized as legitimate in 

Pennsylvania by our act of 1750, 1 Sm. L. 203, 68 P. S. § 121. The destruction of the estate tail was made easier by the act of 1799, 3 Sm. L. 338, 21 P. S. § 13, which permitted the tenant in tail to bar the entail by simply conveying a fee without the hocus pocus of fines and recoveries. Finally, the act of 1874, P. L. 221, 68 P. S. § 126 permitted the tenant in tail to convert his estate into a fee simple by a sealed and recorded declaration of intention to do so without the necessity of any conveyance at all. 

c. Abolition of New Estates Tail 

While the methods of barring existing entails were thus being progressively liberalized as this type of estate went out of fashion, the Legislature passed the act of 1855, P. L. 368, 68 P. S. § 124, which abolished new estates tail by providing that thereafter any devise or inter vivos

There is a similar provision covering both wills and deeds in section 16 of the Estates Act. 

¶ 2. Old Estates Tail Not Affected 

In spite of the impossibility of new estates tail since 1855 and the ease with which old entails can be barred, it is understood that some estates tail created before 1855 are still in existence in Pennsylvania. If this is so, it will be noted that these estates are not affected by the act of 1855 or the present clause. Any such estate can be converted into a fee by the tenant in tail under the statutes enumerated above, which are still in effect, but if the tenant dies without having barred the entail the estate will presumably pass automatically to the next tenant as determined. by the old canons of descent unaffected by the Intestate Act or the deceased tenant's will. Note in this connection that the acts of 1799 and 1874 do not permit barring the entail by will, while the present section of the Wills Act concerns only the creation of new estates and not the destruction of old ones. 

13. Types of Devises Covered-in General 

The traditional manner of creating an estate tail was by a deed or devise to "A and the heirs of his body." 

Under the statute, such words now create a fee simple. 

In addition, the statute presumably converts into fees post-1855 conveyances purporting to create other forms of the estate tail, such as the estate tail male (which was restricted to male descendants), the estate tail female, and the estate tail special ("to A and the heirs of his body by his wife B").3

The estate tail at common law could also be created by provisions in wills which did not conform to the tradi- 

3. See Tiffany, Real Property (3rd ed. 1939) § 34 et seq. and § 421; Simes,

Such an intent has been found, for example, where the devise was to "A and his descendants" or "A and his issue."' 5 On the other hand, Pennsylvania has rejected the rule of Wild's Case, so that a gift to "A and his children" has been held not to create a fee tail. In each case, however, it is a question of what the particular testator intended. If the reference to issue, etc. is construed as merely describing the estate given to A (words of limitation) the statute converts the attempted estate tail into a fee simple. But if it appears that a direct gift to A's issue was contemplated (words of purchase) there is no attempt to create a fee tail and no occasion for applying the statute. The modern tendency, quite understandably, is away from finding that words are used as words of limitation in cases of this sort, so that occasions for applying the present provision are becoming rare. 

4. Relation to Section 16-Shelley's Case 

The principal class of cases where an estate tail was created by implication at common law was where the Rule in Shelley's Case was applied--as in the case of a devise to A for life, remainder to the heirs of his body. Prior to 

1935, such a devise vested a fee tail in A which was converted into a fee simple by the act of 1855 or section 13 of the Wills Act of 1917. By the act of 1935, P. L. 1013, how ever, the Rule in Shelley's Case was abolished and that statute is continued by section 16 of this act. Hence, such a devise now operates to give only life estate to A with remainder to his issue, and the present section has no application.

¶ 5. Interpretation Based on Intention Not Affected. 

1. Law Prior to Statute 

1 Prior to 1935 the Rule in Shelley's Case ¹ was in force in Pennsylvania and there is a great body of case law dealing with the rule's exact meaning and when it was proper to apply it. Although the rule was abolished by the act of 1935, P. L. 1013, which is continued by the present section of the Wills Act and by section 17 of the Estates Act, the effect of its abolition and the extent, if any, to which its influence will continue to be felt cannot be understood without some familiarity with the rule and the theory behind it. 

a. The Rule Stated 

On its surface the rule is a model of precision and clarity. As stated by Kent, it is: "Where a person takes an estate of freehold, legally or equitably, under a deed, will, or other writing, and in the same instrument there is a limitation by way of remainder, either with or without the interposition of another estate, of any interest of the same legal or equitable quality, to his heirs, or heirs of his body, as a class of persons to take in succession from generation to generation, the limitation to the heirs entitles the ancestor to the whole estate."2 The rule's effect in the simplest type of case is that where a grant or devise of real estate is to "A for life, remainder to his heirs" A takes a fee rather than a life estate.

WILLS ACT b. Background of Medieval Concepts 

Shelley's Case itself was decided in 1581 but the rule there enunciated dates back at least to the fourteenth century and reflected a way of thinking which is becoming obsolete. Some understanding of this way of thinking is essential to an understanding of the rule. The modern mind thinks in terms of individuals. Particularly in 

America, land changes hands frequently, both inter vivos and by will, and rarely stays in one family for long; in many instances it is regarded virtually as an item of commerce. Intestacy is rare among people of wealth. 

Families are dispersed, not only by divorce, but by the children's seeking new occupations as individuals rather than following in their fathers' footsteps. Hence when we speak of "A's property" we think in terms of personal ownership, whether we are speaking of his land, his car, or his toothbrush. We are not likely to speak of A's "heirs" at all, but if we do we are likely to think of his children or a group of individuals whom the law designates as those entitled to A's property if he happens to die intestate. If this mode of thinking had always prevailed, the Rule in Shelley's Case would never have been invented. 

The medieval mind, on the other hand, thought in terms of families-not in the sense of groups of individuals as we think of families today, but in the sense of lines of descent. This was particularly true with respect to the ownership of land. Real property, which was the only important form of wealth, tended to stay in one family from generation to generation. Inter vivos conveyances without the consent of the heir apparent were of doubtful validity in Bracton's time, and devises were impossible until the sixteenth century. Hence, in a very real sense the line of descent was the owner rather than its individual representative at any particular time. This mode of thinking was particularly evident with respect to the fee tail, but even the fee simple was viewed in this light. 

The difference between medieval and modern thinking in this respect is well illustrated by the meaning of the phrase "A and his heirs," which was considered in connection with section 14 (3) of this act. That this was the 3603

§

WILLS ACT 

¶ 10 artistic way to describe a fee was by no means the result of an arbitrary whim. The owner was in fact A and his heirs; A was merely the temporary representative of the line of descent which really owned the land. On the other hand, it is doubtful that the phrase has any natural meaning today outside the legal and conveyancing professions. A is one person, his heirs are a group of other individuals, and it would be difficult to predict what the modern layman would understand by the phrase "A and his heirs." See also the discussion under section 14 (1) of the Estates Act of the common law rule governing gifts to one's own heirs in this connection. 

With respect to many legal problems this difference between medieval and modern thinking is unimportant. A could convey Blackacre to B in the old days just as he can today. That he formerly conveyed as the representative of his line while today he conveys as an individual is frequently, of merely psychological significance. In other situations, however, the changing concepts must be borne in mind in examining doctrines which have been inherited from another age. 

c. Rule of Law or Intention 

The old concept of a fee being held by the grantee or devisee as the representative of a line rather than as an individual is particularly important in considering the nature of the Rule in Shelley's Case. It is frequently said that it was a rule of law and not a rule of construction. 

This is only half true. It was not a rule of construction because it was said to apply even if the grantor or testator expressly stated that it should not. On the other hand, it was not a pure rule of policy (like the rule against perpetuities) because even at early law there was nothing which prohibited the limiting of the first taker's interest to a life estate with remainders to others. 3 This paradox constitutes the central problem of the Rule in Shelley's Case and much has been written in attempts to explain it. As will appear, the question of to 

3. Doebler's Appeal, 64 Pa. 9, 17 (1870). 3604

¶ 1c 

WILLS ACT § 16 

what extent the intention of the testator was relevant is particularly important in determining what is meant by the present statute which says that the rule is abolished. 

There are good discussions of this aspect of the rule in Hileman v. Bouslaugh, 13 Pa. 344 (1850), and Guthrie's 

Appeal, 37 Pa. 9 (1861). As understood by the present writer, the part which the intention of the testator played in the application of the Rule in Shelley's Case can be stated as follows: The intent that the first taker's interest should be limited to the legal incidents of a life estate was ignored if it appeared that the so-called remainder was to descend to the first taker's heirs as the representatives of his line of descent. But if the will showed an intention that the remaindermen were to take as individuals rather than as representatives of the line, the intention was respected and the rule was not applied.* 

Suppose, for example, a will read: "I devise Blackacre to A for life. It is my intention that A shall have no more than a life estate. However, at A's death the property shall descend to A's heirs in the same manner as if A owned a fee." It is plain to see why such a provision was repugnant to medieval concepts. The testator was not thinking of A's heirs as a group of individuals to whom he wished to make a gift. Rather, his mind was focused on 

A and his heirs as a unit. In effect the testator was attempting to give a fee to A's line of descent and then to limit A's power over it and the method by which it would. descend to his heirs by imposing the restrictions of a life tenancy on the estate during A's life. On the other hand, suppose the will read: "To A for life, remainder in fee to his heirs-that is to say, his children X and Y." Here the Rule in Shelley's Case would not have been applied even though X and Y were in fact A's only heirs so that for the purpose of identification the latter part of the phrase was superfluous. Here it was clear that the remaindermen were thought of as individuals rather than as representatives of A's line and, there being no policy against devising property in this manner, this intention was permitted to prevail. 

d. Examples of When Rule Was Applied 

Most cases concerning the Rule in Shelley's Case fall somewhere in between the two hypothetical cases suggested. 

When the remainder was simply to the life tenant's "heirs" or "heirs of his body" with no further intention disclosed, the rule would apply to raise the first taker's estate to a fee simple or fee tail respectively. Something else had to be found in the will to show that the testator was using the word "heirs" in a non-technical sense-as in the sense of "children" in the second illustration given above. The presumption was also in favor of applying the rule where the remainder was to "issue," which was said to have a primary meaning of "heirs of the body," but in such cases the intent that the remaindermen were to take as purchasers was somewhat easier to show." Where the remainder was to "children" the presumption was against applying the rule, as that word was primarily a word of purchase although the intent to use it as a word of limitation could be shown. And so on, through the many phrases

One important limitation on the rule was that it did not apply if the estate of the first taker and that of the remainderman were of different quality-i. e., if one was equitable and the other legal. Thus, according to our cases, the rule would not have applied if Blackacre were devised to X as trustee (with active duties to perform) to pay the net income to A for life with remainder in fee to A's heirs. In such a case, it was said that A's estate was equitable (since X held the legal title during A's life) but the gift to A's heirs was of the legal title after the trust had terminated; or, even if the remainder was considered equitable during the continuance of the trust, it was said to be executed into a legal estate by the Statute of Uses at the first taker's death when the trustee's active duties ceased. Hence, the two estates being of different quality, they could not coalesce, and the Rule in Shelley's Case did not apply.10 On the other hand, if the trust was passive, as where the trustee had no active duties to perform, the whole trust was executed by the Statute of Uses, both estates became legal, and the Rule in Shelley's Case applied.¹ 11

12. Reason for Abolition of the Rule 

The Rule in Shelley's Case has little place in modern law. If the courts had kept in step with the times, the rule would have fallen into disuse, because the concept of real property belonging to a line of descent has become foreign to modern thinking. As previously noted, the popularity of wills and the frequency of inter vivos transfers. has rendered obsolete the concept of a fee as something which passes down a line of heirs. The word "heirs" is more likely to connote a group of individuals, and (except when used as a technical term in conveyancing) it is seldom if ever used as a word of limitation in the medieval sense. In short there is no more reason to apply the Rule in Shelley's Case today when the remainder is to the life tenant's "heirs" than there was to apply it in early times where the remainder was to "children." 

For the most part, however, the courts were blinded by the half truth that the rule was one of law rather than intent, and the rule was continued. As a result the courts felt obliged to ascribe to testators ancient modes of thinking which gave a flavor of unrealism to recent cases dealing with the subject. 

In many states and in England the rule has been abolished or partly abolished by statute.18 Pennsylvania finally followed suit by the act of 1935, P. L. 1013, which is now replaced by this section of the Wills Act and section 17 of the Estates Act.

¶ 3. Explanation of Present Section-Changes from Act of 

1935 The revision of the language of the 1935 law was untaken in the light of the unfortunate experiences in other states where such statutes have been strictly construed. 

The fates of several such statutes are reviewed in Simes, Future Interests (1936), § 136. As there pointed out, Kentucky and Ohio had statutes similar to our act of 1935 and there is authority in both states for the proposition that since remainders to heirs of the body are not mentioned in the statutes, the Rule in Shelley's Case still applies to create a fee tail in such cases. In Vest Virginia a similar statute was held to be ineffective to abolish the Rule in Shelley's Case in cases where there was an intervening estate between the life estate to the ancestor and the remainder to his heirs. 

Perhaps the Pennsylvania courts would have taken a more liberal view of our act of 1935, but it was considered advisable to drive another stake through the heart of the rule to make sure that it was dead. The opening twelve words of the present section should be sufficient in themselves for the purpose. "The Rule in Shelley's Case" is not to be applied. By referring to the rule by name the danger of failing to spell out one of its ramifications is avoided. 

Not only is the rule itself abolished but also "its corollaries." These words were inserted through an abundance of caution because the rule itself, as stated by Coke in the case which bears its name, only mentions remainders to "heirs" and "heirs of the body" although, as noted above under ¶ 1d, the rule has subsequently been applied to remainders to "issue" and even to remainders to "children" in special cases. The abolition of the "corollaries" of the rule should prevent a possible argument that the statute did not affect the latter decisions. No other rule is known which is in effect in Pennsylvania and which could be called a corollary to the Rule in Shelley's Case. The rule in 

Wild's Case ("to A and his children" creates a fee tail in A in certain circumstances) might conceivably be so 3609

WILLS ACT 

termed but that rule has been rejected by the Pennsylvania courts.14 As to whether the analogous rule of intention applicable to personal property could be termed a corollary to the rule, see discussion under the next heading. 

The portion of the section following the first dozen words was added by way of explanation. Even this part of the section is broader than the 1935 provision (in that remainders to heirs of the body, issue, etc. are covered), but it would still have been theoretically possible for our courts to follow the West Virginia construction referred to above, were it not for the opening phrase of the section abolishing the rule in its entirety. 

4. Effect on Prior Rule as to Personalty 

As noted under ¶ 1f, the Rule in Shelley's Case did not govern gifts of personal property, although an "analogous" rule of interpretation was said to be applicable. 

There is some confusion as to the exact nature of this analogous rule. Cases can no doubt be found holding that a legacy to A for life with remainder to his heirs gave A an absolute estate.15 It is possible to explain such cases on the theory that there was a rule of construction requiring such a holding in the absence of an intent to the contrary appearing in the will. Such a rule of construction. would bear some similarity to the Rule in Shelley's Casethe only difference being that in the case of personalty a contrary intent affirmatively appearing in the will would be respected.

The proposition that such a rule of construction is part of our law today can be answered in two ways. In the first place, it is doubtful if such a rule ever existed in Pennsylvania and, if it did, it must be regarded as discarded by recent authorities. Dull's Estate, 217 Pa. 358 (1907), and 

Mitinger's Estate, 132 Pa. Super. 475 (1938), are clear holdings to the effect that a bequest of personalty to A for life, remainder to his heirs, will not be construed to vest an absolute interest in A. Mitinger's Estate is a par-

§ 18. TESTAMENTARY GUARDIAN 

(a) Guardian of the Person.

A person competent to make a will, being the sole surviving parent or adopting parent of any unmarried minor child, may appoint a testamentary guardian of the person of such child during his minority, or for any shorter period: 

Provided, That no father who, for one year or upwards previous to his death, shall have wilfully neglected or refused to provide for his child, and no mother who, for a like period, shall have deserted her child or wilfully failed to perform her parental duties, shall have the right to appoint a testamentary guardian of the person of such child. (b) Guardian of the Estate.

Any person may by will appoint a testamentary guardian of the real or personal estate which he shall devise, bequeath, or appoint to a minor.
