WILLS ACT 1. Limited Scope of Section 

The law relating to guardians for minors is governed primarily by the Fiduciaries Act.¹ That act and the cases construing it governs the appointment of guardians by the court and the powers and duties of both court-appointed and will-appointed guardians of a minor's estate. The powers and duties of guardians of the person are left to case law. Questions of jurisdiction (as between the Orphans' Court and Common Pleas (cf. Dougherty's Adoption, 358 Pa. 620 (1948) and Act No. 197 of 1949) are likewise not treated here. In short, this section of the Wills 

Act deals only with a small corner of the subject of guardians for minors—the right to appoint such guardians by will. 

12. History of Prior Statutes 

There is a good review of the earlier statutes on testamentary guardians in Sheetz's Estate, 6 Dist. 367, 19 

County 583 (0. C. Phila. 1897) and Klein's Estate, 38 D. & C. 632 (0. C. Berks 1940).

The rights of the feudal lord with respect to minors were abolished by the statute of 12 Charles II, ch. 24 (1660), which gave to the father the power by his will to appoint a guardian to take care of both the person and the estate of his children during their minority. The relevant sections of that act were reported in force by the judges of the Supreme Court in 1808.2 The English statute was in part superseded by section 4 of the Wills Act of 1833, P. L. 249, which confirmed the right of the father to appoint a guardian of the person but did not affect section 9 of the English statute setting forth the powers of the testamentary guardian over both the person and the property of the ward. The Act of 1833 was followed by section 6 of the act of 1855, P. L. 430, providing for forfeiture of the father's right to appoint "any" guardian in cases of desertion or non-support, and the acts of 1881, P. L. 96, 1. At the time of writing, the act of 1917, P. L. 447, section 59, as amended, 20 P. S. § 1021 et seq., soon to be replaced by the Fiduciaries Act of 1949. The cases are collected in Hunter, O. C. Book (1939) "Guardian and Ward." 

2. 3 Binn. 595 (1811). 

3. See Sheetz's Est., 19 County at 585, 6 Dist. at 369. The two acts were apparently construed together-see Vanartsdalen v. Vanartsdalen, 14 Pa. 384, 387 (1850). 3703

§ ¶ cop 18 

WILLS ACT 

and 1887, P. L. 264, giving the mother a qualified right to appoint a guardian (presumably of both person and estate) when the father had not done so or had forfeited.* 

Further changes were made by the act of 1915, P. L. 124, which gave co-extensive rights to either father or mother to appoint a guardian of the person with the consent of the survivor, and the act of 1915, P. L. 145, which confined the mother's power to appoint a guardian for the estate of the minor to a power to appoint a guardian for the particular property which she left to the child. 

All the foregoing acts were repealed and replaced by section 8 of the Wills Act of 1917. This gave the father the primary power to appoint a general guardian for the minor's person and estate, although the custody of the person of the minor was subject to the superior right of the mother while she survived. The mother was given a secondary power to appoint a general guardian of estate and person when the father had not acted, and the primary right to appoint a special guardian for any estate which she left to the child. The act of 1917 was in turn amended by the act of 1919, P. L. 443, which clarified the right of the mother when the father had forfeited for misconduct.5 

The rights of father and mother were not made equal until the amendment of 1925, P. L. 689, which (1) gave to the surviving parent the right to appoint guardians for (a) the person or (b) the general estate of his or her minor child, and (2) gave to either parent, regardless of survivorship, the right to appoint a guardian for the estate which he or she left to the child. 

13. Guardians of Person and Estate Distinguished 

As shown by the wording of the present section and the foregoing discussion, two broad types of guardians are recognized the guardian of the person and the guardian of the estate. The sharp distinction between the two was recently emphasized in Daniels v. Metropolitan Life Insur- 4. The right existed only when the mother "shall leave to such child an estate." The holding of Sheetz's Estate, supra in the text, was that this did not confine the guardian so appointed to the property left by the appointing mother. This was changed temporarily by the act of 1915, infra in the text. 

5. A provision which had been added by the 1887 act but which had been omitted in the act of 1917. The provision was again omitted in 1925 and in the present act. 3704

¶ 

WILLS ACT 

§ 18 ance Company, 135 Pa. Super. 450 (1939), where the defendant who had paid insurance proceeds to the guardian of a minor's person had to pay again." 

The distinction dates back to Roman law where the tutor of a minor "had charge of the maintenance and education of the minor," while an entirely different person known as the curator was charged with "the care of [the minor's] fortune."7 In feudal times the distinction was blurred because the feudal lord acted in both capacities. 

The potential confusion of the two functions was continued by the earlier statutes on testamentary guardians which for the most part treated both types of guardians together and seemed based on the assumption that the same guardian would control both the person and the estate of the minor. 

That the two functions were separate, however, was frequently recognized-particularly in cases dealing with the rights of a living parent with respect to a minor child's property. The parent during his lifetime was plainly entitled to the child's custody and services and charged with the care of the child's person. However, "the father, as the natural guardian of the person of his child, during infancy, has, by virtue of such relationship, no authority whatever to exercise any control over the estate of the minor." It is to the rights and duties of the parent that the guardian of the person succeeds. The guardian of the estate, on the other hand, might be appointed before or after the parent's death to look after the minor's property as fiduciary pursuant to the powers and duties set forth in the Fiduciaries Act. 

4. General Guardian of Estate and Guardian for Particular Estate Distinguished The present act, like the prior statute, makes a further distinction within the class of guardians of minors' estates.

However, there was nothing to prevent any person from giving property by will or inter vivos to a trustee to apply it for the minor's benefit. 

In that event the legal title was in the trustee (rather than the minor) so that the authority of the general guardian for the minor's estate would not extend to it. 

The concept of a special guardian, whose authority extended only to property devised or bequeathed by a particular person, arose in cases where a testator who had no power to appoint a general guardian for the minor's estate (for example, the child's grandparent) made a testamentary gift to the minor and then purported to appoint a "guardian" (instead of a "trustee') to manage the property until the beneficiary came of age. Where such a will imposed active duties on the "guardian" it was early held in Vanartsdalen v. Where such a will did not expressly impose active duties on the named "guardian," however, it was held in such cases as Huston's

5. Present Act

Thus, prior to the present act three types of testamentary guardians for minors had been recognized: (1) guardian of the person, (2) general guardian of the estate, and (3) special guardian for the particular estate devised or bequeathed. The present act continues these distinctions and makes the following provisions as to each type of guardian: a. Guardian of Person

The provisions with regard to the appointment of a testamentary guardian for the minor's person remain the same as under the amendment of 1925. The exclusive right is in the surviving parent unless the child is married or the parent has forfeited his right by neglect of parental duties (see 8 below). Note that once again the statute fails to give the non-surviving parent the power where the surviving parent has forfeited. b. General Guardian of the Estate

No provision is made for the appointment by anyone of a testamentary guardian for the minor's general estate. 

Any such guardian can now be appointed only by the court pursuant to the Fiduciaries Act.10 

The elimination of the parents' right in this respect, which had been in our law since Penn's time, was the result of several considerations. In the first place, no logical reason could be advanced why the parent should appoint a guardian to take care of property coming to the minor from other sources. No such right existed prior to the parent's death,¹¹ and it seemed inconsistent to permit the parent to name by will a person to fill an office which the parent had no control over during his lifetime. 

Secondly, the springing up of this right in the parent upon his death was likely to cause practical complications. 

10. Supra note 1. 

11. Supra note 8. 3707

WILLS ACT 

¶ 50 During the parent's life the court had exclusive authority to appoint such a guardian but the right of the parent to appoint such a guardian by will was said to supersede the court's power. Hence a shift in the administration from the court-appointed to the will-appointed guardian would apparently have been required.12

Thirdly, under the old law practical difficulties had been encountered arising from the fact that in some cases there was no way of obtaining a court record of the fact that a guardian named in the will had qualified. If, for example, a testator left his entire estate to his second wife and named X guardian of the estate of his child by a former marriage, there was no way for an insurance company with proceeds payable to such minor to be certain whether the testamentary appointment was valid. The risk was not entirely theoretical, because the validity of such an appointment might depend on a number of intangibles-such as whether the testator had forfeited his right, whether X was a competent person,13 whether a bond should be required, or whether the will was sufficiently clear to the effect that X was appointed guardian of the estate rather than only of the person. 14 Of course, none of the above considerations made the elimination of general testamentary guardians of the estate imperative. On the whole, however, it was thought to be simpler and more logical to discontinue the practice of allowing a parent to designate by will the fiduciary for property coming from another source. 

c. Special Guardian for Property Given to the Minor 

The present act continues to recognize a class of special testamentary guardians whose authority extends only to the property "bequeathed, devised or appointed" by the 12. No actual case of this sort has been found. The cases where the court refused to appoint a guardian after one has been appointed by will, however, indicate that the testamentary guardian would have had the right to take over.

13. See 7 infra in the text. 

14. Under the Fiduciaries Act, § 59 (g), 20 P. S. § 1027, the court had discretion to require a bond of any guardian: see cases in Hunter, O. C. Book, "Guardian and Ward" §3 (b). 3708

particular testator. As already noted (¶4), even in the absence of statute any person had the power to appoint a trustee for property given to a minor and if active duties were imposed such a trustee was permitted to act even though the testator referred to him as a "guardian." 

Where no active duties were spelled out in the will, however, the courts felt compelled to declare the appointment ineffective. The soundness of these latter decisions might well have been questioned (on the ground that active duties are implied by the very use of the word "guardian"), but they seem to have been well supported by lower court authority.

The rule of these cases where no active duties were specifically imposed was changed as to parents as early as 1915. Subsection (b) of the present section now quite logically extends to "any person" the power to appoint a testamentary "guardian" for the particular estate devised, bequeathed or appointed. Since this could have been done by a careful draftsman in the absence of statute, the only effect of this provision is to eliminate the necessity of expressly imposing active duties in such cases. 

Some confusion is likely to continue as the result of the statute's designating such a fiduciary as a "guardian." 

It is believed, however, that in cases where this designation might cause a conflict the special guardian under subsection (b) of this section will be treated as the trustee which he really is. Suppose, for example, the minor already has a general guardian appointed by the orphans' court. Does a guardian subsequently appointed by will have prior claim to the particular property bequeathed? It seems clear that the testamentary "guardian" should prevail, just as he would if the will had designated him trustee and had spelled out active duties identical to those of a true guardian. 

The authority of the special guardian under subsection (b) extends only to the particular estate which the testator "shall devise, bequeath, or appoint." Property given by someone other than the testator would clearly be excluded. 

So would property given by the testator himself in an inter vivos transaction--such as a deed of trust or insurance policy. If an inter vivos instrument or insurance policy names a "guardian," his authority will presumably 3709

§ 

WILLS ACT 

¶ 6 be recognized under general principles already discussed, if active duties are imposed, or under the act of 1945, P. L. 

253, 20 P. S. § 1178 (quoted in the Commissioners' Comments), regardless of active duties, but no guardian appointed by will would be recognized as to extra-testamentary property.

In this connection, it seems clear that the words "which he shall appoint" in subsection (b) of the present section must necessarily refer to appointment by will in the exercise of a power given to the testator by another or reserved by the testator in an inter vivos deed. 

The words were inserted in order to avoid the contention that property appointed by will in the exercise of a power is not devised or bequeathed, since under strict property theory the gift is that of the donor of the power. There was certainly no intention to permit the testator in his will to designate a guardian for property appointed inter vivos. Thus, it could not be plausibly argued that a testamentary guardian could receive insurance proceeds under the present act on the theory that the testator "appointed" such proceeds to a minor by naming him beneficiary in the policy. Such a construction would extend this section of the Wills Act beyond the scope of the act's title, would cause a conflict with the act of 1945, and would be contrary to what was plainly the legislative intent-i..e., to limit the testamentary guardian to property passing, by gift or appointment, under the will itself. Any uncertainty as to this should be removed by the Commissioners' Comments.15 ¶ 6. Adoption and Illegitimacy

¶7. Supervision of Court 

The Fiduciaries Act 18 gives the Orphans' Court the power to remove any guardian "whether testamentary or otherwise" where mismanagement or misconduct is shown. 

It would seem to follow that a testamentary appointment could be disapproved at the beginning if ground for removal exists.19 Indeed, the cases dealing with guardians of the person go further than this and indicate that the testamentary appointment can be disregarded whenever the interests of the minor would be better served by awarding his custody to another. Brown's Estate, 166 Pa. 249 (1895), is an example.

¶9. Interpretation of Provisions Appointing Guardians 

The careful draftsman will follow the statutory language in appointing a "guardian of the person" or a 'guardian of the estate" given to the minor, and will make it clear whether after-born children are to be included. 

Little can be said concerning the interpretation of wills where precise language is not used, as the intent must be derived from the particular will. Even the word "guardian" need not be used, if the normal duties of a guardian are imposed upon the designated person. See Palumbo's 

Estate, 15 Dist. 188 (0. C. Phila. 1906), and cases there cited.

As to after-born children, it is clear from Hollingsworth's Appeal, 51 Pa. 518 (1866) that the appointment can extend to such children, and it would seem from principles applied to class gifts that a reference to "children" generally would include at least all those born before the parent's death.2

If the will of a surviving parent simply appoints a "guardian" for his minor child without specifying whether a guardian of the person or of the estate left to the child is intended, the designated person could probably act in both capacities in the absence of something showing contrary intent. This seems to have been assumed in the old cases (Hollingsworth's Appeal itself is an example), and the more precise distinction between the two offices in the more recent statute would probably not change this construction.

Discussion This, like section 14 of the Intestate Act, dates back to 1833. The Commissioners of that year explained that it "merely confirms the existing doctrines of the law, and has been added for the purpose of preventing any misconstruction of the general expressions used in the preceding sections." The provision was regarded as harmless and was included in the 1917 and the present act in order to avoid any implication that a change was intended. 

The section is seldom cited because in practically all cases it merely states one aspect of accepted principles of conflicts which would be applied anyway. Thus, with regard to personal property, the law of decedent's domicile at his death almost always controls-whether the question is one relating to the formal requirements for execution of the will,¹ the validity of the attempted gift,² or the construction of the language used.³

14 (14) 8, where consideration is given to one of the rare situations where section 19 of the Wills Act is in conflict with the case law. The question was whether the residuary clause in the will of a New Jersey domiciliary exercised a power of appointment given to her in a Pennsylvania trust of personalty. If what is now section 14 (14) of our 

Wills Act applied, the power was exercised. The weight of case law authority favored applying the law governing the instrument creating the power in this type of case.

¶ 6. Case Law Rules Distinguished. 

¶ 1. General

The Wills Act of 1833, P. L. 249, contained (in section 

18) only a general provision that it should "take effect from and after the first day of October next. . ." and it was held that it did not apply to wills executed before its effective date even though the testator died thereafter. 

See Gable's Executors v. Daub, 40 Pa. 217, 223 (1861) where the authorities on the subject are extensively reviewed. On the other hand the act of 1879, P. L. 88 (relating to powers of appointment-now section 14 (14) of the present act) contained an effective date provision which, like the present section, referred specifically to the death of the testator, and in Aubert's Appeal 109 Pa. 447, 459 (1885), it was held that the act applied to a will exe- 3901

§ 

WILLS ACT 

12 cuted in 1876. The similar provision in the act of 1917 came before the court in Spain's Estate, 327 Pa. 226 (1937), where it was held that a charitable gift in a will was valid under the law at testatrix's death, even though the will was imperfectly executed under the law at the time of execution. The opinion was a well considered one in which the earlier authorities were reviewed, and its force is increased by the lone dissent which pointed to the various results which this construction must lead to. 

It would seem to be well settled, therefore, that this provision means exactly what it says and that there is no longer any doubt as to the power of the legislature to make the Wills Act retroactive in this limited sense. The present act applies whenever the testator dies on or after January 1, 1948, whether the question is one of execution, revocation, validity or construction and it makes no difference when the will was executed or other relevant facts occurred.¹ 

2. Execution, Revocation, Etc.

In the field of execution, revocation, validity, and the like the rule of this section might seem startling, since a change in the statute might make effective past acts which were ineffective when performed, or vice versa, but this is the very point which Spain's Estate, 327 Pa. 226 (1937), decides.

Analogous questions could arise under the present act. 

Suppose, for example, a case involving an oral revival of a previously revoked will. The will might have been validly revived in 1947 under the law as it then existed but such revival would nevertheless be ineffective under section 6 of the present act if the testator died in 1948. 

¶ 3. Construction 

Similarly, in the field of construction, Aubert's Appeal, 109 Pa. 447, 459 (1885), is definite authority for the proposition that a will might mean one thing when it was written and something else when testator died. This is 

1. See, generally, Fiduciary Review, Nov. 1947, referring to an annotation in 111 A. L. R. 910. 3902

WILLS ACT § 22 

really not so illogical as it might appear. In most disputed cases the testator does not have a very precise idea of what he means anyway-otherwise he would not be likely to use language which requires reference to the statute for interpretation. If, on the other hand, it is assumed that he knew the law when he wrote his will and consciously relied upon it, it is just as reasonable to assume that he also learned of the change by the new statute and consciously decided against changing the provision by codicil. 

4. Amendments to Statute 

Spain's Estate, 327 Pa. 226 (1937), also covers the question of amendments. The actual decision of that case was that a will executed in 1934 was governed by the amendment of July 2, 1935, when the testator died on July 20, 1935. The amendment of 1935 itself merely stated that it was effective upon enactment, but the more precise provision of section 26 of the 1917 act was read into the amending statute. Note, however, the court did not decide that the 1935 amendment applied to all cases where decedent died after 1917. The decision is merely that the amendment applies whenever the testator died after its effective date (1935). A well drafted amendment to a statute should make all this clear, but where the effectivedate provision is ambiguous, Spain's Estate will control. 

5. Powers of Appointment 

Aubert's Appeal, 109 Pa. 447, 459 (1885), is also valuable in deciding what act to apply in cases dealing with the exercise of a power of appointment where the donor of the power has died before the new act and the donee of the power dies thereafter. Clearly the meaning and effect of the donor's will should be governed by the old act, but questions relating to the will of the donee should be governed by the act in effect when the donee died. This was the decision in Aubert's Appeal, and it seems clearly correct. Barton's Trust, 348 Pa. 279 (1944), dealing with con- 

2. But see § 1 (2) (2a) of the Estates Act suggesting a contrary inter pretation of the effective date provisions of that act which deals with all "conveyances" rather than specifically with wills. 3903

§ cas WILLS ACT 

22 ¶ 6 flict of laws where the donor lives in one jurisdiction and the donee in another, might seem theoretically inconsistent with the above conclusion; but as explained under section 

14 (14) of this act (8), Barton's Trust is probably unsound in principle and should be confined to the particular field of conflicts. 

¶ 6. Case Law Rules Distinguished 

This section of the Wills Act plainly does not affect decisions which turn on case law which changes between the date of the will and the date of death. In the November, 1947 issue of the Fiduciary Review (p. 2) it is said "Rules of interpretation not reduced to statutory form, which are to be applied, are those existing when the will was written, not those under case law existing at the date of death: 

Hood v. Penna. Soc., 221 Pa. 474 (1908); cf. Crozer's Est., 257 Pa. 241 (1917); 129 A. L. R. 859." The cases cited certainly seem to stand for this proposition. The Hood case is a rather extreme holding to this effect-the court presuming that testator when he wrote his will knew the law so well that he said just the opposite of what he meant because he thought the court would give his language an artificial meaning. Apparently, however, it was presumed that he did not keep up with the cases after the will was executed, because the artificial rule he was supposed to have relied upon was discarded by the courts before he died. Whether such subtle reasoning will always be followed is at least questionable. Note that the cases cited were decided before the 1917 act became effective. Today the court might be more inclined to look to the law at the date of death so that the statutory and case law rule will be in harmony. 3904 [The next page is 4951]

ESTATES ACT COMPLETE TEXT OF ACT AN ACT 

Relating to the incidents of legal and equitable interests in real and personal property, including the validity thereof, the powers, rights, and duties of persons with respect thereto, and the disposition of interests which fail, and containing provisions concerning termination of trusts, releases and disclaimers of powers and interests, perpetuities, accumulations, charitable estates, rights of a surviving spouse in property as to which the decedent has retained certain powers, spendthrift trusts, limited estates in property, rules of interpretation, estates pur auter vie, estates in fee tail, and the Rule in Shelley's Case. 

The General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Penn sylvania hereby enacts as follows: 

Section 1. 

Definitions.-The following words and phrases, when used in this act, unless the context clearly indicates otherwise, shall have the meanings ascribed to them in this section: (1) "Charity" or "charitable purposes" includes but is not limited to the relief of poverty, the advancement of education, the advancement of religion, the promotion of health, governmental or municipal purposes, and other purposes the accomplishment of which is beneficial to the community. (2) "Conveyance" means an act by which it is intended to create an interest in real or personal property whether the act is intended to have inter vivos or testamentary operation. (3) "Trust" means any testamentary trust or trust inter vivos. 

Section 2. Termination of Trusts. 

(a) Failure of Original Purpose. The court having jurisdiction of a trust, regardless of any spendthrift or similar provision therein, in its discretion may terminate 4953

ESTATES ACT 

such trust in whole or in part, or make an allowance from principal to a conveyor, his spouse, issue, parents, or any of them, who is an income beneficiary, provided the court after hearing is satisfied that the original purpose of the conveyor cannot be carried out or is impractical of fulfillment and that the termination, partial termination, or allowance more nearly approximates the intention of the conveyor, and notice is given to all parties in interest or to their duly appointed fiduciaries. But, distributions of principal under this section, whether by termination, partial termination, or allowance, shall not exceed an aggregate value of twenty-five thousand dollars from all trusts created by the same conveyor. (b) Distribution of Terminated Trust. Whenever the court shall decree termination or partial termination of a trust under the provisions of this section, it shall thereupon order such distribution of the principal and undistributed income as it deems proper and as nearly as possible in conformity with the conveyor's intention. (c) Other Powers. Nothing in this section shall limit any power of the court to terminate or reform a trust under existing law. 

Section 3. Release or Disclaimer of Powers or In terests. (a) Powers and Interests Releasable. Any power of appointment, or power of consumption, whether general or special, other than a power in trust which is imperative, and any interest in, to, or over real or personal property held or owned outright, or in trust, or in any other manner which is reserved or given to any person by deed, will or otherwise, and irrespective of any limitation of such power or interest by virtue of any restriction in the nature of a so-called spendthrift trust provision, or similar provision, may be released by disclaimed, either with or without consideration, by written instrument signed by the person possessing the power or the interest and delivered as hereinafter provided, but nothing in this section shall authorize an income beneficiary of a spendthrift trust to release or disclaim his right to such income. 4954

ESTATES ACT 

(b) Form of Release or Disclaimer. A power or interest which is releasable or disclaimable may be released or disclaimed either absolutely or conditionally, and may also be released or disclaimed with respect to the whole or any part of the property subject to such power or interest, and may also be released or disclaimed in such manner as to reduce or limit the persons or objects or classes of persons or objects in whose favor such power or interest would otherwise be exercisable. No release or disclaimer of a power or of an interest shall be deemed to make imperative a power or interest which was not imperative prior to such release or disclaimer unless the instrument of release or disclaimer expressly so provides. (c) Delivery of Release or Disclaimer. Such release or disclaimer may be delivered to any one of the following: (1) Any person specified for such purpose in the in-. strument creating the power or interest; (2) Any trustee of the property to which the power or interest relates; (3) The clerk of the court having jurisdiction of the trust for filing in said court; (4) The recorder of deeds for recording in the county in which the person possessing the power or interest resides, or in which the deed, will, or other instrument creating the power or interest is recorded or filed. (d) Grantee or Lienholder. A release or disclaimer shall be void as against a bona fide grantee of or holder of a lien on real estate in any county unless the release or disclaimer or a duplicate original or certified copy thereof is recorded in the county where the real estate lies before the recording or entering of the instrument or lien under which such grantee or lienholder claims. (e) Application of Section. This section shall apply to releases and disclaimers heretofore and hereafter delivered, but shall not invalidate any release or disclaimer delivered pursuant to the law in effect prior to the effective date of this act. 4955

ESTATES ACT Section 4. Rule Against Perpetuities. 

(a) General. No interest shall be void as a perpetuity except as herein provided. (b) Void Interest; Exceptions. Upon the expiration of the period allowed by the common law rule against perpetuities as measured by actual rather than possible events any interest not then vested and any interest in members of a class the membership of which is then subject to increase shall be void. This subsection shall not apply to: 

(1) Interests Exempt at Common Law. Interests which would not have been subject to the common law rule against perpetuities; (2) Cemetery Trusts. Interests which are directed to be used for the maintenance, care, or adornment of any cemetery, churchyard or other place for the burial of the dead, or any portion thereof, or any grave therein or any improvement on or about the same, and which are subject to no condition precedent at the end of the period described in subsection (b); (3) Pension or Profit-Sharing Plans. Interests created by a bona fide trust inter vivos primarily for the benefit of business employees, their families or appointees, under a stock bonus, pension, disability or death benefit, profitsharing or other employee benefit plan; (4) Administrative Powers. Powers which contribute to the effective management of trust assets, including powers to sell, mortgage, or lease trust assets, powers relating to investment of trust assets, powers to determine what is principal and what is income, and powers to name successor trustees; (c) Time for Beginning Period. The period allowed by the common law rule against perpetuities under subsection (b) of this section shall be measured from the expiration of any time during which one person while living has the unrestricted power to transfer to himself the entire legal and beneficial interest in the property. 4956

ESTATES ACT Section 5. Rule Against Perpetuities; Disposition 

When Invalidity Occurs. 

(a) Valid Interests Following Void Interests. A valid interest following a void interest in income shall be accelerated to the termination date of the last preceding valid interest. 

(b) Void Interests on Condition Subsequent or Special 

Limitation. A void interest following a valid interest on condition subsequent or special limitation shall vest in the owner of such valid interest. (c) Other Void Interests. Any other void interest shall vest in the person or persons entitled to the income at the expiration of the period described in Section 4 (b). 

Section 6. Income Accumulations; When Valid.-No direction or authorization to accumulate income shall be valid except: (1) Judicious Management. For the purpose of creating a temporary reserve of a reasonable amount for administration of the trust, or periodic distributions in specified amounts, or the needs of a beneficiary; 

(2) Lifetime of the Settlor. For a period expressly measured by the lifetime of the settlor; (3) Minority. During the minority of any beneficiary who if living at the age of twenty-one will be entitled to such accumulations and earnings thereon or to the entire income from such accumulations and earnings thereon; and a direction or authorization to accumulate income until a person reaches a designated age over twenty-one and thereafter to pay to such person, if living, such accumulations and earnings thereon or the entire income from such accumulations and earnings thereon, shall be valid during minority and shall take effect as though twenty-one had been the designated age; (4) Incompetency. For the exclusive benefit of a person who, in the opinion of the trustee, is incompetent to receive or judiciously use the income; 4957

ESTATES ACT 

(5) Charity. For any charitable purpose or purposes; (6) Pension or Profit-Sharing Plans. In a bona fide trust inter vivos primarily for the benefit of business employes; their families or appointees, under a stock bonus, pension, disability or death benefit, profit-sharing, or other employee benefit plan; (7) Insurance Premiums. In a trust consisting of, or including a policy or policies of insurance, a direction or authorization that the dividends on such policies may be applied in whole or in part for the payment of premiums on such policy or policies; 

(8) Apportionment Between Principal and Income. 

The following directions or authorizations shall be valid: a. To apply to principal in whole or in part extraordinary dividends, regardless of the form in which they are paid, and rights to subscribe to stock; b. To amortize from income premiums paid for investments which are callable or have a fixed maturity; c. To amortize from income the waste represented by the return from a wasting asset or dividends from a wasting asset corporation; d. To pay carrying charges on unproductive or underproductive property from income; e. To apply to principal in whole or in part the proceeds of the conversion of unproductive or under-productive property.

Section 7. Disposition of Valid Income Accumulations. 

(a) During Lifetime of Settlor. Except as may be otherwise directed or authorized in the conveyance, accumulations during a period measured by the lifetime of the settlor shall be added to and form a part of the principal from which they originated. (b) During Minority. Except as may be otherwise directed or authorized in the conveyance, accumulations during the minority of a beneficiary shall be added to any 4958

ESTATES ACT 

principal from which the beneficiary is to receive the income. Notwithstanding any direction or authorization to accumulate income during the minority of a beneficiary, it shall be lawful for the court, where other means for his maintenance and education shall be insufficient, to make an adequate allowance from income for such purpose. (c) During Incompetency. Notwithstanding any direction or authorization to accumulate income for the benefit of an incompetent person, it shall be lawful for the court, where other means for such incompetent's maintenance shall be insufficient, to make an adequate allowance from income for such purpose. 

(d) Upon Competency or Death. Accumulations dur ing the incompetency of a person shall be distributed to him when he shall become competent, or to his personal representative at his death.

Section 8. Disposition of Invalid Income Accumula tions. (a) Unlawful Authorization. Any income authorized but not directed to be accumulated unlawfully shall be distributed as if no such accumulation had been authorized. (b) Unlawful Direction. Any income directed to be accumulated unlawfully shall be distributed in the absence of a valid alternative direction in the following order of preference: (1) To the person or persons, if any, who are entitled to the immediate enjoyment of the income from which such accumulations were directed; (2) To the person or persons, if any, who would be entitled to the accumulations if the time fixed by the conveyance for the payment of the accumulations were accelerated to the time of the accrual of the income; (3) To the person, or proportionately to the persons, any, who, when the income accrues, are entitled to other income from the same trust; if (4) To the person or persons, if any, entitled under the residuary clause of the conveyance; 4959

ESTATES ACT 

(5) To the person or persons entitled to property undisposed of by the conveyance. 

Section 9. Combination of Charitable Trusts.-When ever two or more trusts heretofore have been or hereafter shall be created for substantially the same charitable purposes, and the court having jurisdiction over any such trust, upon the application of any party in interest, shall find that they can be more effectively administered if they are combined, the court in its discretion, after such notice as the court shall direct, may combine them in the manner and to the extent that the court shall approve, but not so as to violate any express provision to the contrary in any conveyance creating any of the trusts so combined. 

Section 10. Administration of Charitable Estates. Ex cept as otherwise provided by the conveyor, if the charitable purpose for which an interest shall be conveyed shall be or become indefinite or impossible or impractical of fulfilment, or if it shall not have been carried out for want of a trustee or because of the failure of a trustee to designate such purpose, the court may, on application of the trustee or of any interested person or of the Attorney General of the Commonwealth, after proof of notice to the Attorney General of the Commonwealth when he is not the petitioner, order an administration or distribution of the estate for a charitable purpose in a manner as nearly as possible to fulfill the intention of the conveyor, whether his charitable intent be general or specific.

Section 11. Powers of Appointment.-Rights of Sur viving Spouse. A conveyance of assets by a person who retains a power of appointment by will, or a power of revocation or consumption over the principal thereof, shall at the election of his surviving spouse, be treated as a testamentary disposition so far as the surviving spouse is concerned to the extent to which the power has been reserved, but the right of the surviving spouse shall be subject to the rights of any income beneficiary whose interest in income becomes vested in enjoyment prior to the death of the conveyor. 4960

ESTATES ACT Section 12. Spendthrift Trusts.-Income of a trust subject to spendthrift or similar provisions shall nevertheless be liable for the support of anyone whom the income beneficiary shall be under a legal duty to support. 

Section 13. Limited Estates in Personalty and in the 

Proceeds of the Conversion of Real Estate.-A person having a present interest in personal property, or in the proceeds of the conversion of real estate, which is not in trust, and which is subject to a future interest, shall be deemed to be a trustee of such property, and not a debtor to the remainderman, with the ordinary powers and duties of a trustee, except that he shall not be required to change the form of the investment to an investment authorized for Pennsylvania fiduciaries, nor shall he be entitled to compensation as trustee. Such person, unless given a power of consumption or excused from entering security by the terms of the conveyance, shall be required to enter such security for the protection of persons entitled to the future interests as the court in its discretion shall direct. If a person having a present interest shall not enter security as directed, the court shall appoint a trustee who shall enter such security as the court shall direct, and who shall exercise all the ordinary powers and duties of a trustee, except that he shall not be required to change the form of the investment to an investment authorized for Pennsylvania fiduciaries.

Section 14. Rules of Interpretation.-In the absence of a contrary intent appearing therein, conveyances shall be construed, as to real and personal estate, in accordance with the following rules. (1) Meaning of "Heirs" and "Next of Kin” etc. 

Time of Ascertaining Class. A conveyance of real or personal property, whether directly or in trust, to the conveyor's or another designated person's "heirs" or "next of kin" or "relatives" or "family" or to "the persons thereunto entitled under the intestate laws" or to persons described by words of similar import, shall mean those persons, including the spouse, who would take under the in- * family, in original. 4961

ESTATES ACT 

testate laws if such conveyor or other designated person were to die intestate at the time when such class is to be ascertained, a resident of the Commonwealth, and owning the property so conveyed: Provided, That the share of a spouse other than the spouse of the conveyor, shall not include the ten thousand dollar allowance under the intestate laws. The time when such class is to be ascertained shall be when the conveyance to the class is to take effect in enjoyment. (2) Meaning of "Die Without Issue" and Similar

Phrases. In any conveyance of real or personal estate, the words "die without issue" "die without leaving issue" "have no issue" or other words importing either a want or failure of issue of any person in his lifetime or at the time of his death, or an indefinite failure of his issue, shall be construed to mean a want or failure of issue in his lifetime or at his death, and not an indefinite failure of his issue. (3) Adopted Children. In construing a conveyance to a person or persons described by relationship to the conveyor or to another, any person adopted before the effective date of the conveyance shall be considered the child of his adopting parent or parents and not the child of his natural parents: Provided, That if a natural parent shall have married the adopting parent before the effective date of the conveyance, the adopted person shall also be considered the child of such natural parent. (4) Illegitimates. In construing a conveyance to a person or persons described by relationship to the conveyor or to another, an illegitimate person shall be considered the child of his mother and not of his father: Provided, That when the parents of a person born illegitimate shall have married each other, he shall thereafter be considered legitimate. 

Section 15. Estates Pur Auter Vie.-An interest con veyed to a person for the life of another, whether or not such conveyance is to him and his heirs, shall, on his death before expiration of the interest, be considered as personal 4962

ESTATES ACT 

property forming a part of his estate and shall be subject to distribution in like manner as a lease for a term of years.

Section 16. Estates in Fee Tail Abolished.-Whenever by any conveyance an estate in fee tail would be created according to the common law of the Commonwealth, it shall pass an estate in fee simple and as such shall be inheritable and freely alienable.

Section 17. Rule in Shelley's Case.-The rule in Shel ley's case and its corollaries shall not be applied, and a conveyance directly or in trust which shall express an intent to create an estate for life with remainder to the life tenant's heirs or the heirs of his body or his issue or his next of kin or persons described by words of similar import, shall not operate to give such life tenant an estate in fee in real estate or an absolute estate in personalty. 

Section 18. Severability.-If any provision of this act, or the application thereof to any person or circumstances, is held invalid, the remainder of this act and the application of such provision to other persons or circumstances shall not be affected thereby, and to this end the provisions of this act are declared to be severable. 

Section 19. Short Title.-This act shall be known and may be cited as the Estates Act of 1947.

Section 20. JAMES H. DUFF 

Amending Act of 1955-6, P.L. 1073

AN ACT 

Amending the act of April twenty-four, one thousand nine hundred forty-seven (Pamphlet Laws 100), entitled "An act relating to the incidents of legal and equitable interests in real and personal property, including the validity thereof, the powers, rights, and duties of persons with respect thereto, and the disposition of 4966

ESTATES ACT 

interests which fail, and containing provisions concerning termination of trusts, releases and disclaimers of powers and interests, perpetuities, accumulations, charitable estates, rights of a surviving spouse in property as to which the decedent has retained certain powers, spendthrift trusts, limited estates in property, rules of interpretation, estates pur auter vie, estates in fee tail, and the Rule in Shelley's Case," revising and changing provisions relating to power of court to terminate trusts heretofore created; release or disclaimer by beneficiary of spendthrift trust; income accumulation; conveyances to defeat marital rights and elections against such conveyances, the conveyor's will and the procedure therefor. 

Section 1. Section two and subsection (a) of section three, act of April twenty-four, one thousand nine hundred forty-seven (Pamphlet Laws 100), known as the "Estates 

Act of 1947," are amended to read:

Section 2. Termination of Trusts.- 

(a) Failure of Original Purpose. The court having jurisdiction of a trust, heretofore or hereafter created, regardless of any spendthrift or similar provision therein, in its discretion may terminate such trust in whole or in part, or make an allowance from principal to a conveyor, his spouse, issue, parents, or any of them, who is an income beneficiary, provided the court after hearing is satisfied that the original purpose of the conveyor cannot be carried out or is impractical of fulfillment and that the termination, partial termination, or allowance more nearly approximates the intention of the conveyor, and notice is given to all parties in interest or to their duly appointed fiduciaries. 

But, distributions of principal under this section, whether by termination, partial termination, or allowance, shall not exceed an aggregate value of twenty-five thousand dollars from all trusts created by the same conveyor. (b) Distribution of Terminated Trust. Whenever the court shall decree termination or partial termination of a 4967

ESTATES ACT 

trust under the provisions of this section, it shall thereupon order such distribution of the principal and undistributed income as it deems proper and as nearly as possible in conformity with the conveyor's intention. (c) Other Powers. Nothing in this section shall limit any power of the court to terminate or reform a trust under existing law.

Section 3. Release or Disclaimer of Powers or 

Interests.- (a) Powers and Interests Releasable. Any power of appointment, or power of consumption, whether general or special, other than a power in trust which is imperative, and any interest in, to, or over real or personal property held or owned outright, or in trust, or in any other manner which is reserved or given to any person by deed, will or otherwise, and irrespective of any limitation of such power or interest by virtue of any restriction in the nature of a socalled spendthrift trust provision, or similar provision, may be released or disclaimed, either with or without consideration, by written instrument signed by the person possessing the power or the interest and delivered as hereinafter provided, but nothing in this section shall authorize an income beneficiary of a spendthrift trust to release or disclaim his right to such income, unless as a result of the release or disclaimer the released or disclaimed income will pass to one or more of the beneficiary's descendants. 

Section 2. Section six, section seven and section eight of the act are repealed.

Section 3. The act is amended by adding, after section five, two new sections to read:

Section 6. Income Accumulations; When Valid.-- 

(a) General. No direction or authorization to accumulate income shall be void, except as herein provided. 4968

ESTATES ACT 

(b) Void Accumulations; Exceptions. Upon the expiration of the period allowed by the common law rule against perpetuities as measured by actual rather than possible events, any direction or authorization to accumulate income shall be void.

This subsection shall not apply to: (1) Directions or authorizations to accumulate income in a trust for any charitable purpose or purposes; (2) Directions or authorizations to accumulate income in a bona fide trust inter vivos primarily for the benefit of business employes, their families or appointees, under a stock bonus pension, disability or death benefit, profitsharing or other employe benefit plan; (c) Time for Beginning Period. The period allowed by the common law rule against perpetuities under subsection (b) of this section shall be measured from the expiration of any time during which one person while living has the unrestricted power to transfer to himself the entire legal and beneficial interest in the property. 

Section 7. Income Accumulations Disposition When 

Invalidity Occurs.—Income subject to a void direction or authorization to accumulate shall be distributed to the person or proportionately to the persons in whom the right to such income has vested by the terms of the instrument or by operation of law.

Section 4. Sections eleven and twenty-one of the act are amended to read:

Section 11. [Powers of Appointment; Rights of Surviving Spouse] Conveyances to Defect Marital Rights.- 

(a) In General. A conveyance of assets by a person who retains a power of appointment by will, or a power of revocation or consumption over the principal thereof, shall at the election of his surviving spouse, be treated as a testamentary disposition so far as the surviving spouse is concerned to the extent to which the power has been re- 4969

ESTATES ACT 

served, but the right of the surviving spouse shall be subject to the rights of any income beneficiary whose interest in income becomes vested in enjoyment prior to the death of the conveyor. The provisions of this subsection shall not apply to any contract of life insurance purchased by a decedent, whether payable in trust or otherwise. 

(b) Determination of Share. The spouse may elect to take against any such conveyance and shall be entitled to one-third thereof if the conveyor is survived by more than one child, or by one or more children and the issue of a deceased child or children, or by the issue of more than one deceased child, and in all other circumstances one-half thereof. 

(c) Election Against Other Conveyances. A spouse electing under this section also must elect to take against the will, if he is a beneficiary thereunder, and against all other conveyances within the scope of subsection (a) of which he is a beneficiary. (d) Procedure. The election to treat a conveyance as testamentary shall be made in the same manner as an election to take against the will. If there is a will, such election shall be made within the same time limitations as an election to take against the will. If there is no will, such election shall be made within one year of the conveyor's death, and the orphans' court, on application of the surviving spouse made within such period, may extend the time for making the election. It can be made only if there has been no forfeiture of the right to make an election. The court having jurisdiction of the deceased conveyor's estate shall determine the rights of the surviving spouse in the property included in the conveyance. 

Section 21. Effective Date.-This act shall take effect on the first day of January, one thousand nine hundred forty-eight, and, except as set forth in [section 3] sections two, three and nine hereof, shall apply only to conveyances effective on or after that day. As to conveyances effective before that day, the existing laws shall remain in full force and effect. 4970

ESTATES ACT 

Section 5. This act shall take effect April one, one thousand nine hundred fifty-six, and, except as set forth in sections two, three and nine of the act amended hereby, shall apply only to conveyances effective on or after that day. As to conveyances effective before that, day, the existing law shall remain in full force and effect. 

APPROVED-The 17th day of February, A.D. 1956. 

GEORGE M. LEADER Amending Act of 1957, P. L. 792 AN ACT 

Amending the act of April 24, 1947 (P. L. 100) entitled "An act relating to the incidents of legal and equitable interests in real and personal property, including the validity thereof, the powers, rights, and duties of persons with respect thereto, and the disposition of interests which fail, and containing provisions concerning termination of trusts, releases and disclaimers of powers and interests, perpetuities, accumulations, charitable estates, rights of a surviving spouse in property as to which the decedent has retained certain powers, spendthrift trusts, limited estates in property, rules of interpretation, estates pur auter vie, estates in fee tail, and the Rule in Shelley's Case," clarifying the status of designations of beneficiaries of life insurance and of funds or other property passing under a will to a trust. 

Section 1. The act of April 24, 1947 (P. L. 100) known as the "Estates Act of 1947" is amended by adding, after section 7, a new section to read: 

Section 8. Designation of Insurance Beneficiaries Not 

Testamentary. The designation of beneficiaries of life insurance shall not be considered testamentary, regardless of whether the insurance contract designates the ultimate beneficiaries or makes the proceeds payable, directly or indirectly, to a trustee of a trust under a will or under a separate trust instrument which designates the ultimate 4971

ESTATES ACT 

beneficiaries, and regardless of whether any such trust is amendable or revocable, or both, or is funded or unfunded, and notwithstanding a reservation to the settlor of all rights of ownership in the insurance contracts. Unless otherwise expressly provided in the conveyance, funds or other property so passing to a trust under a will shall become and be a part of the testamentary trust to be administered and disposed of in accordance with the provisions thereof, without forming any part of the testator's estate for administration by his personal representative.

1. Background and General Effect 

"Charitable purposes" are referred to in sections 6 (5) (accumulations), 9 (combination of charitable trusts) and 10 (cy pres).1 The prior statutes dealing with these

12 subjects used a variety of different phrases to describe the types of gifts which were covered by their provisions. The old accumulations statute, for example, referred to "any literary, scientific, charitable, or religious purpose". The language of the former cy pres statutes varied from a simple reference to "charitable use" to a spelling out of "religious, charitable, literary, educational or scientific use or purpose. The language used made little difference, however, as the courts paid no attention to the wording of the particular statute.2

In the absence of any traditional statutory phraseology, the drafters of the present statute decided to use the single phrase "charitable purpose" throughout the act and to include the present definition in order to eliminate any suggestion that the scope of the prior statutes was being narrowed. The provision was copied from section

Not only are "other purposes beneficial to the community" included, but through an abundance of caution it is stated that the term merely "includes but is not limited to" the kinds of gifts specified. Hence, the limits of the legal concept of charity will continue to be a matter of case law. 99

A statement from Perry on Trusts which has been frequently quoted in our cases reads: "A charitable use, where neither law nor public policy forbids, may be applied to almost anything that tends to promote the well-doing and well-being of social man." 5. Gifts to Individuals and Limited Groups

Even more difficult than defining what gifts are beneficial is distinguishing between those which are beneficial to society generally and those which benefit an individual. 

Theoretically the distinction might be illusory, but it is clear that a gift is not legally charitable if the testator has his attention focused on particular individuals rather than on an abstract purpose. This seems to be the idea behind the requirement that the gift be "for the benefit of an indefinite number of persons." 11 In Philadelphia v. Fox, 64

That the motive of the donor is immaterial in determining whether a gift is charitable is worth noting, if only because Pennsylvania has a rather neat case illustrating the principle. In Fire Insurance Patrol v. Boyd, 120 Pa. 

624 (1888), it appeared that a fire patrol organization was supported by contributions from fire insurance companies whose motives were plainly other than "love of God or neighbor free from the stain or taint of every consideration that is personal, private or selfish." The court held that the organization was nevertheless charitable, pointing out that a requirement of unselfish motives would lead to embarrassment "in this wicked world". (120 Pa. at 643.) 

17. Fees, Tuition, Etc.

Many charitable institutions require the payment of fees or tuition by those who share in their benefits. This, of course, does not prevent the institution from being charitable if "the money derived from such source is insufficient to run [the institution], and the deficit is made up by charitable contributions". Channon's Estate, 266 Pa. 417, 426 (1920). Here again the tax cases are distinguished. The qualification to the effect that the fees must be insufficient to run the institution would probably not be controlling so long as any profit that is made is not devoted to a noncharitable use. See section 376, comment d of the Restatement of Trusts, and Barnes Foundation v. Keely, 314 Pa. 

112, 118-19 (1934). 

8. "Benevolent", "Worthy", Etc. Purposes as Charitable

Sometimes the question is not whether a specific purpose is charitable but whether a gift for purposes defined by the donor in broad terms is confined to charitable objects. A charitable trust cannot fail for indefiniteness. 

Hence, a gift in trust to apply the income perpetually to 5006

ESTATES ACT 

§1 (1) such charitable purposes as the trustee sees fit is clearly valid: Kimberly's Estate (No. 1), 249 Pa. 469 (1915). But if the discretion of the trustee "can by any possibility be exercised outside the limits" of what the law considers charitable such a gift would be invalid.15 Thus, in Wilbur's 

Estate, 334 Pa. 45, 76 et seq. (1939), the trustees were given the power to distribute the property "to such persons, corporations and public charities as they may deem fit” and it was held that the gift was not charitable. 

The courts in other jurisdictions have sometimes adopted a rather technical approach to wills and deeds which do not define in artistic words the purposes to which the gift is to be applied. Thus, the words "benevolent" "worthy" etc. have been said to be more comprehensive than the artistic word "charitable" and gifts for the former purposes have been held void for indefiniteness by some courts.18 In Funk's Estate, 353 Pa. 321 (1946), our court had an opportunity to pass on such a will and, to its credit, a realistic construction was adopted. The gift in a holographic will was "to some worthy cause or institution". 

The court conceded that "such words as 'worthy', 'benevolent', 'useful', 'philanthropic', etc. do not have a technical meaning in the law and therefore, if plainly used in a will to characterize a class of beneficiaries broader than charities," the gift cannot be construed as charitable. What the particular testatrix probably meant, rather than the technical meaning of the words, was used as the criterion, however, and an intent to favor only charities was found in the 

Funk will. 

¶9. Incidental Benefits to Individuals 

In a sense, nearly all charities result in incidental benefit to non-charitable objects if only by way of commissions paid to trustees or salaries to employees. The problem of incidental benefits becomes serious only when gratuitous payments to non-charitable objects are involved. 

As indicated by Wilbur's Estate, 334 Pa. 45, 76 (1939), discussed under the preceding heading, a gift in trust to

There is nothing in Wright's Estate, 284 Pa. 334 (1925), contrary to the above principle. In that case, the direction was to pay the income from a perpetual trust for an admittedly charitable purpose with an additional direction to pay such sums as the trustees might see fit to testator's nephews and nieces. There is mention in the opinion of the rule that a trust is charitable although non-charitable objects receive minor and incidental benefit. It would seem, however, that the principle of incidental benefit was in no way involved. The decision turned rather on the construction of the will to mean nephews and nieces living at testator's death. There the will attempted to give the trustee a power to divert a fixed portion of the income (from an otherwise charitable remainder) to deceased life tenants' needy relatives. Notwithstanding Wright's Estate and Yeager's Estate, therefore, it seems clear that a gift is not charitable if an indeterminate amount of the property might be diverted to non-charitable objects. Such trusts must be construed to be exclusively charitable or not charitable at all, although it does not follow that all non-charitable trusts are necessarily bad, or that an invalid non-charitable gift might not be stricken down without affecting charitable gifts in the same trust.17

¶ 1. General

As the Commissioners' comments indicate this definition was taken from section 1 of the Uniform Property 

Act and section 11 of the Restatement of Property. The word "conveyance" is used in various places throughout the present act for the same reason that it was adopted by the Restatement and the Uniform law: there was need for a term which could be used as to both real and personal property and would include inter vivos transfers as well as devises and bequests. Unfortunately, there is no such generic legal term with a long settled artistic meaning. 5051

§(2) 

ESTATES ACT 

¶ 2a The word "conveyance", which had been arbitrarily selected by the Restatement, was chosen for lack of a better one.

The definitions in both the Restatement and the Uniform Act include the phrase "irrespective of whether the act is effective to create such interests." This phrase is omitted in the present clause, but the idea is nevertheless implicit in the words, "an act by which it is intended to create an interest." This phrase in itself makes it clear that the word conveyance is not limited to effective conveyances. 

[2. Problems in Connection with Effective Date of Act 

The meaning of the word "conveyance" is most likely to be in dispute in connection with section 21 of the act, which states that (with certain exceptions) the act applies only to "conveyances effective on or after" January 1, 1948, and preserves prior law as to "conveyances effective before that day." In many cases it will not be entirely clear when a conveyance as here defined takes place. 

a. Powers of Appointment 

Suppose A dies in 1947 giving a life estate and a testamentary power of appointment to B who dies in 1948. 

B appoints in further trust by his will, which contains provisions which would be valid under the present act but which would violate the prior law as to perpetuities or accumulations. Does the Estates Act apply to the will of 

B? The answer will hinge on whether the appointment in

B's will is a "conveyance" by him at his death under the definition in the present section. Did B "create an interest" by his will or did A create the interest which B appointed?

In the introduction to Chapter 25 of the Restatement of Property (preceding § 318, Volume 3, p. 1811 et seq.) it is said: "A power of appointment was originally conceived to be merely an authority in the donee to do an act for the donor. Thus, where A effectively devised Blackacre to B for life, remainder to such person (or such 5052

¶ 2a 

ESTATES ACT 

§1 (2) children of B) as B should appoint, B's power was considered in substance as an authority to fill in a blank in A's will. When B exercised the power by making an appointment to C, C was considered to receive the property by transfer from A, not from B; and the appointment was said to 'relate back' to the time of creation of the power and to operate as if it had been originally contained in A's will. . . However, the 'relation back' theory has never been consistently followed. . The current American law of powers is the outgrowth of the fundamental acceptance of the 'relation back' doctrine with fairly frequent and important departures in situations where the proprietary aspect of the power is most apparent. . 

The above statement is in accordance with Pennsylvania cases. The "relation back" doctrine is still the rule. 

See, for example, Commonwealth v. Duffield, 12 Pa. 277, 279-80 (1849) where this theory is explained by Gibson in characteristically colorful language. The theory is departed from in a number of cases (see, for example, the discussion of powers under section 14 (8) of the Wills Act), but it can fairly be said that these cases are still regarded as exceptions to the general rule. 

In determining whether the Estates Act is applicable to a particular transaction, it would seem impossible to make the answer depend on what particular section of the act is being applied. All sections are governed by the same effective date provision in section 21 and the same definition of "conveyance". Hence, on strict property principles it would seem that the "general rule" must be followed and that the exercise of a power must relate back to the will or deed creating it. Thus, in the hypothetical case suggested, B's appointment in 1948 would relate back to A's will which took effect in 1947, so that the present act would not apply. This conclusion is fortified by the fact that the term "conveyance" is apparently not used to include appointments in the Restatement of Property and the Uniform Property Act. In the Restatement, "conveyance" is defined in section 11, and "appointment" is defined separately in section 322. The definitions are similar 5053

§(2) 

ESTATES ACT 

¶ 2b but the fact that separate definitions were deemed necessary indicates that an "appointment" was not regarded by the authors of the Restatement as a new "conveyance". Similarly, in the Uniform Property Act "conveyance" and "appointment" are treated separately in sections 4 and 5, dealing with the quantum of interest conveyed or appointed.

On the other hand, it could be argued that the exercise of the power actually creates the interests in the appointees and that it is pure fiction to relate the appointment back to the will or deed creating the power. In favor of this position it could be pointed out that the new Wills Act applies to appointment by will whenever the donee of the power dies after January 1, 1948, regardless of when the power was created (see discussion of Wills Act § 22) and it would be illogical to have one rule apply to the Wills Act and another to the Estates Act. 

An intermediate position would be that the exercise of a general power should be considered a conveyance by the donee of the power, while the exercise of a special power relates back to the conveyance of the donor. It is true that the relation back of an appointment to the will or deed of the donor of the power seems most artificial in cases where the power is so broad as to be tantamount to ownership-a general power to appoint by either will or deed, for example. Conversely, it would seem unnatural not to relate back the exercise of a narrowly restricted power-as a non-exclusive power to appoint among children where all the donee can do is fix the size of the shares. 

A distinction between general and special powers in this respect, however, would be apt to lead to endless confusion. 

For historical and practical reasons, probably the best solution is to adopt the strict property view and relate all appointments back to the instrument creating the power in cases of this sort. Cogent arguments can be advanced, however, for any of the three views. mentioned, and a lot will depend on the equities of the first cases to arise. b. Powers to Revoke or Amend An analogous but somewhat different problem will be presented in cases of revocable trusts created before the 5054

2c §(2) 

ESTATES ACT 

effective date of the act where the settlor dies thereafter. 

If the power to revoke remains unexercised, it seems reasonably clear that the act would not apply. Such trusts are not considered testamentary and a power to revoke, which is not exercised, is said to be a "dead thing." See 

Murphey v. C. I. T. Corp., 347 Pa. 591, 594-5 (1943). On the other hand, the act will obviously apply if the trust is actually revoked and a new trust created after January 

1, 1948. 

Suppose a power to revoke or amend is reserved in a trust created before 1948 and thereafter the settlor, without revoking, amends his deed so radically that there is little or no resemblance between the original trust and the trust as amended. Would such an amendment be a new 'conveyance" and hence subject to the act? The legal title remains in the trustee but certainly new equitable interests are created whenever a new beneficiary is named or a gift to a former beneficiary is enlarged. Hence, an amendment changing the dispositive provisions of the deed would constitute a conveyance at least to the extent of the changes, but an amendment, like an appointment, might relate back to the date of the original deed. 

No authority governing this question has been found. 

Note that cases dealing with wills modified by subsequent codicils present a false analogy because a will remains ambulatory until death while an amendable deed takes effect immediately. It would seem that a power to modify is more analogous to a power of appointment, and that whatever rule is adopted as to appointments should govern amendments to deeds of trust. 

c. Prior Ineffective Transfer 

It is assumed in the above discussion that the original transfer before January 1, 1948, was effective in the first place to divest the donor of ownership. As explained under section 1 (4e) of the Intestate Act, a settlor of an inter vivos trust may, without destroying the effectiveness of the transfer, reserve to himself the income for life, a power to revoke and amend, and power to appoint the principal by will. If he goes further, however, and reserves 5055

§(2) 

ESTATES ACT 

¶ control over administration, the conveyance might be held to be merely colorable, so that any "appointment" the settlor makes by will would operate as a new conveyance of property which he still owned. 

The same can be said of unfunded insurance trusts. 

In such cases the trustee is named beneficiary of the insurance, but the policies themselevs are generally not assigned to the trustee. Hence, there is no trust until the settlor dies because until that time there is no corpus. 

Whether a payment of a premium on an insurance policy is itself a "conveyance" is a separate question discussed below. The only point here is that putting the policies under an unfunded insurance trust should not affect the question one way or another. 

¶3. Other Problems-Insurance, Etc. 

In the foregoing discussion it has been assumed that a conveyance took place at one time or another but the applicability of the act depended on whether it took place before or after January 1, 1948. In other cases all the significant events will take place after the effective date of the act, but the question will be whether there was any "conveyance" at all.

As explained above under ¶ 1, the drafters of the act were thinking primarily of wills, inter vivos deeds of legal estates in real estate and inter vivos trusts, when the word "conveyance" was chosen to include all these transactions. 

It might be asked, however, whether the act as drawn is broad enough to cover other transactions of a contractual or partly contractual nature. Is there a "conveyance" to which this act applies when a joint bank account or a tentative trust is created, when an option is given, or when an insurance policy is purchased or a premium paid thereon? Insurance is likely to give the most trouble in this respect, not only because of the similarity of insurance options to trusts, but because the policies themselves are frequently assigned or made payable to trustees, thus further complicating the problem. 

Under section 4 (b) (1) (18) (dealing with perpetuities) there is discussion of a different but somewhat anal- 5056

ESTATES ACT 

§1 (2) ogous problem. Contractual rights were generally exempt from the common law rule against perpetuities unless (as in cases of options or easements) a contract created interests in particular property. But, while a pure contract was exempt as between the parties, it became subject to the rule if the obligation itself was assigned to a trustee under a deed of trust. Perhaps distinctions similar to those which have been drawn in the law of perpetuities will be developed in determining what transactions constitute "conveyances" subject to the present act. 

Suppose A pays B $100 in cash and B gives his note for $100 in return. A has certainly "conveyed" the $100 in cash to B, but it would strain the meaning of the present definition to say that either A or B has made a conveyance with respect to the note. Actually B, in giving his note, created new property rather than created an interest in property which already existed. 

Is the situation any different in this respect if the note runs in favor of C, a third party beneficiary? Probably not, because C's interest resulted from the very act of creating the property and the present definition seems to be based on the assumption that there is property already in existence in which an interest is created. It will be observed in this respect that the case is quite different from a transfer by A of $100 to B in trust for C; in such case, A gives C an interest in the $100, which is property already in existence. In the third party beneficiary contract case, on the other hand, B obtains an absolute interest in the $100 and that passes out of the picture-C's interest being in the newly created note. 

However, once the note has been executed, it plainly becomes property which can thereafter be conveyed. Thus, going back to the original example of the simple note payable to A, if A assigns this note to C (or to T in trust for C), A has made a conveyance by creating interests in existing property.

Insurance presents additional problems because the popular policy, which builds up a cash surrender value and under which the insured reserves the power to cash it in and to change beneficiaries, is sui generis in the law of 5057

§(2) 

ESTATES ACT 

$3 contracts. The nature of such transactions has been the subject of careful analysis in community property states. 

See Latta and Gemmill, Observations on Community Property, 96 U. of Pa. L. Rev. 188, 208 (1947), and Huie, Community Property Laws as Applied to Life Insurance, 17 

Tex. L. Rev. 121, 18 Tex. L. Rev. 121 (1939-1940). Various theories are possible, but it would seem that if the analogy of the perpetuities cases is followed, such insurance policies must still be regarded in the same light as simple contracts. Hence, there would be no "conveyance"-at least where the policy itself has not been assigned. 

All this, to be sure, is highly theoretical and formalistic. Admittedly, there is little real difference between creating a trust for C of an existing note and making the note payable to C in the first place. Hence, it could plausibly be argued that the act should apply to all such transactions without distinction between contract and property. The disadvantages of such an approach are that it would be likely to carry the scope of the act far beyond what its drafters contemplated and unforeseen difficulties would no doubt arise. It would seem that if the scope of the act is to be kept within reasonable bounds, distinctions such as those suggested, or others equally arbitrary, will be necessary.

The equities of each case will vary and the propriety from a practical viewpoint of extending the act to insurance and other transactions will depend on which section of the act is involved. For example, the temptation might be to apply section 14 (3) of the act in construing an insurance policy in order to favor an adopted child. Unfortunately, however, such a decision would be authority for the proposition that other sections of the act (such as section 11 dealing with the spouse's rights against trusts reserving powers) also apply to insurance in cases where the equities might not be as strong and where applying the act might cause endless difficulties. 5058 [The next page is 5101]
