Discussion Consideration was given to inserting here an elaborate definition of trusts subject to the act so as to exclude resulting trusts, constructive trusts, receiverships, etc. It was decided, however, that the term could not be misunderstood in the context in which it is used in the act. The present truncated definition was retained merely to make it clear that both inter vivos and testamentary instruments were being dealt with. This was thought to be advisable in view of the novelty of the present act which deals with both wills and deeds. 5101 [The next page is 5151]

§ 2. TERMINATION OF TRUSTS 

(a) Failure of Original Purpose.

The court having jurisdiction of a trust, regardless of any spendthrift or similar provision therein, in its discretion may terminate such trust in whole or in part, or make an allowance from principal to a conveyor, his spouse, issue, parents, or any of them, who is an income beneficiary, provided the court after hearing is satisfied that the original purpose of the conveyor cannot be carried out or is impractical of fulfillment and that the termination, partial termination, or allowance more nearly approximates the intention of the conveyor, and notice is given to all parties in interest or to their duly appointed fiduciaries. 

But, distributions of principal under this section, whether by termination, partial termination, or allowance, shall not exceed an aggregate value of twenty-five thousand dollars from all trusts created by the same conveyor. (b) Distribution of Terminated Trust.

Whenever the court shall decree termination or partial termination of a trust under the provisions of this section, it shall thereupon order such distribution of the principal and undistributed income as it deems proper and as nearly as possible in conformity with the conveyor's intention. (c) Other Powers.

Nothing in this section shall limit any power of the court to terminate or reform a trust under existing law. 

COMMISSIONERS' COMMENT- 

[Subsection (a)] Termination of trusts, which have failed in their purpose and which have become oppressive or otherwise undesirable, has been impossible in numerous instances due to inability to secure the consent of persons unborn, unascertained, or not sui juris. The purpose of this section is to give relief in such cases, but only as to trusts created after the effective date of the act. The relief to be given is in the nature of cy pres, thus preventing a complete frustration of the conveyor's intention. 

The only other legislation on the subject of termination is section 4 of the Act of 1855, P. L. 415, 20 PS 2982, and 5151

$ESTATES ACT 

cos the Act of 1931, P. L. 29, 20 PS 3251. Section 4 of the 

Act of 1855, P. L. 415, which was repealed, insofar as it relates to testamentary trusts, by the Fiduciaries Act of 1917 reads: "Whenever, by the agreement of competent parties, the further execution of any trust has become useless, it shall be lawful for such court to decree a reconveyance, as provided by the act to which this is a supplement, in case of a trust executed or expired."

The Act of 1931, P. L. 29, provides for termination of trusts by agreement between charitable remaindermen and owners of prior interests. That act apparently was passed for the sole purpose of making possible the termination of the trust involved in Biddle's Ap., 99 Pa. 525, Derbyshire's Est., 239 Pa. 

389, 16 D. & C. 200, 306 Pa. 278. The 1931 act has no application unless the remainder is vested in a charity: Yeager 

Est., 354 Pa. 463. Provisions for charitable trusts, accumulations, and general rules of law permitting termination of trusts upon consent of all interested parties, avoid the possibility of a problem such as that of Derbyshire's Estate. The 1931 act, being an amendment to section 9 of the Act of 1853, P. L. 503, is repealed in section 20 (1) of this act.

A provision for the termination of trusts without the consent of all parties in interest is inspired by similar legislation in several other states including California, Texas, Oklahoma, North Carolina and New York. The allowance from principal for maintenance of the income beneficiary has its analogy in the allowance from income of a spendthrift trust, as authorized in section 12 of this act. "regardless of any spendthrift or similar provision therein" is included to eliminate any doubt about the effect of such a provision on the right of termination. Cf. Rehr v. Fidelity-Phila. 

Trust Co., 310 Pa. 301; Bowers' Trust Est., 346 Pa. 85; Rehr v. Fidelity-Phila. Trust Co., 37 D. & C. 324. 

This subsection is required to eliminate the possible claim that the trust, upon failure of its original purpose, reverts to the settlor or to the settlor's or testator's estate. While courts apparently have ignored this possibility, it nevertheless exists. See 

Restatement, Trusts, section 411 et seq.; Overbeck v. McHale, 354 Pa. 177; Conrad's Est., 341 Pa. 451. 

This subsection is added in an abundance of caution to make it clear that this section does not purport to be a codification of all circumstances under which a trust can be terminated. 

Old Law 

There was no prior statute of any significance. Certain lower court cases were in accord with this section but there was no appellate authority approving them. 5152

¶ 1. General

There is a carefully annotated article on this section. by Mark E. Lefever in 96 U. of Pa. L. Rev. 305 (1948).

As there explained, this is a new provision in our statutory law intended to broaden the court's authority to "lighten or eliminate the burden of the oppressive trust." The power to do so, however, is carefully qualified and much is left to the court's discretion. Hence, whether the new legislation accomplishes its purpose will depend largely on how much responsibility the courts are willing to assume under it.

On the whole, the main effect of this section will probably be to give statutory sanction to what several lower courts have been doing in the absence of statute. A leading example is Auchu's Estate, 38 D. & C. 33 (O. C. Cameron 

1. 96 U. of Pa. L. Rev. at 323. 5153

$cos 

ESTATES ACT 

12 1939), in which the court terminated a small trust without the consent of unascertained remaindermen where it was manifest that because of unforeseen circumstances neither the testator nor anybody else would have wanted it continued. Auchu's Estate and other lower court cases to the same effect are discussed further below ( 3c). This sort of thing had never been approved by the Supreme Court, however, and the usual distribution of the released fund to the life tenant (rather than back to the settlor or to the testator's estate) was difficult to justify in theory. As to trusts created on or after January 1, 1948, the present section will remove the serious doubts concerning the court's authority in such cases. The court must still be moved by the equities of the case to exercise its discretion, however, so that the importance of the statute might vary from county to county. A judge who looks with disfavor upon judicial paternalism will be less likely to act than one who chafes under the dictatorial authority of the dead hand. 

2. Prior Statutes 

As indicated by the Commissioners' comments, prior legislation on termination of trusts was of no significance. 

The act of 1855, P. L. 415, 20 P. S. § 2982, was construed as merely restating common law principles regarding termination by consent of all beneficiaries. It was repealed as to testamentary trusts by the Fiduciaries Act of 1917, P. L. 

447, without appreciable effect on the law. The proviso added in 1931 (P. L. 29) to the accumulations statute of 

1853, P. L. 503, was passed to cover the particular case noted in the Commissioner's comments. Apart from that case, no one was quite sure what it meant. As explained under section 6 (2) of the present act, this proviso was omitted from the new accumulations law, and it is unlikely that it will be missed. 

3. Termination Under Case Law a. Invalid Transfers

Fraud, undue influence, mental or legal incapacity or mistake of fact, destroy the necessary intent and make an alleged trust ineffective ab initio, so that no problem of 5154

¶3b 

ESTATES ACT 

82 3 termination arises.2 The same result follows if the object of the trust is illegal or impossible. Likewise, there is no trust to begin with if the alleged settlor has retained so much interest in the property and power over its administration that the instrument is testamentary in character and superseded by a later will.¹ 

b. Termination by Agreement 

Assuming a trust has been validly created, it may of course be terminated or revoked if the power to do so has been expressly given or reserved, although if the instrument is silent on the subject, no such power is implied.5 

In the absence of such a power, our appellate courts have permitted termination of trusts only where all possible parties in interest, vested and contingent, have agreed. 

And even then, termination is refused if the trust has an unaccomplished special purpose (such as a support trust, or one with a spendthrift provision) unless the settlor is living and joins in the agreement to terminate. The law on the subject of termination by agreement was recently clarified by Bowers' Trust Estate, 346 Pa. 85 (1943), where the relevant sections of the Restatement of Trusts are cited and adopted, and prior inconsistent cases dealing with the special purpose doctrine are disapproved. 

Termination under case law is expressly saved by subsection (c) of the present section. Since termination by agreement must be allowed as a matter of right, the present section should not be employed if it is possible to secure (1) the consent of all possible parties in interest, 2. 4. The Present Statute 

An examination of the present section will show that its minimum effect will be to clarify the court's authority to terminate trusts created on or after January 1, 1948, on grounds similar to those used in the cases just discussed. a. Consent Unnecessary

On the enabling side, it will be noted that the consent of all beneficiaries is not necessary. Notice must be sent to them or "to their duly appointed fiduciaries”—i. e., to any already-appointed guardian or committee for minors or incompetents, and to a guardian or trustee ad litem for minor, incompetent, or unascertained interests not already represented. Such parties will of course have the opportunity to oppose the petition, but there is no requirement for their consents, and theoretically the court could grant the petition over their protests. It is also expressly stated that a spendthrift "or similar" restriction (which would include a separate use clause) will not be a barrier to termination or an allowance from principal even though the creator of the trust is dead and cannot release it. b. Discretion of Court 

On the other hand, the statute merely confers a discretionary power in the court, so that the petitioner has no absolute right to relief. A showing of abuse of discretion might be theoretically possible but it is hard to imagine a case where an appeal by an unsuccessful petitioner would be anything but a waste of money. 5159

$

ESTATES ACT 

¶ 4c c. Grounds for Relief 

The grounds for relief stated in subsection (a) are necessarily vague, and little can be gained by dissecting the language used. The emphasis is on some change of circumstances or the discovery of some previously unknown fact between the drawing of the instrument and the time of the petition, so that the original "intention" of the settlor or testator can be better carried out by permitting the termination or allowance than by a strict compliance with the terms of the instrument. The word "intention" is not too precise in this connection; repetition of the word "purpose" or perhaps "primary purposes" would have been better. But the meaning is clear enough. Plainly it is this general intention or purpose at the time the instrument was drawn that must control. A mere change of heart on the part of the conveyor is obviously not enough. As in the cases discussed above there must be a showing that had the settlor or testator foreseen the way things would work out, he would not have drawn the trust as he did. 

Thus, the statute should at least cover the situations where relief has been granted in the past. As shown above (1 3c), these cases are of two general types--the starving life tenant type (such as the Rehr case) and the nuisance trust type (such as Anchu's Estate). 

With the authority to alter trusts now definitely established, it is also possible that the courts will go further than they have in the past and not insist on such strong equities in all cases. There is no requirement, for example, that the life tenant be unable to live on the income. This would be the requirement if the "intention" or purpose were to support the income beneficiary, but other types of cases can be imagined. A testator might direct that income from a trust be used to send his son through college. If tuition fees rise and income dwindles, an allowance from principal might well be appropriate under this section. On the whole, it is impossible to predict how liberally a particular court will interpret its powers under this section. Most courts will probably proceed cautiously for fear of encouraging a flood of petitions. 5160

4d $

ESTATES ACT 

cas d. Nature of Relief 

Assuming a proper case for relief, the court's powers to deal with the particular problem are broad. Termination, partial or total, is permitted, and under subsection (b) distribution can be made to such persons and in such manner as the court thinks proper to carry out what the conveyor originally had in mind. The provision for permitting an allowance from principal is illogically limited to cases where the income beneficiary is a spouse, descendant or parent of the settlor or testator. Since the same result can be obtained for persons not in this favored class by a series of partial terminations, the reason for this distinction is not clear. A decree operating in the future to permit a periodic allowance is permitted only when the beneficiary is of the favored class. Apparently, others must get relief in a lump sum and come back for more when it is needed. e. $25,000 Limit

The last sentence of subsection (a) puts an overall limit of $25,000 upon all trusts created by the same conveyor.¹7 

This limitation is impliedly criticized by Lefever,18 and it might constitute an unfortunate limitation in an extraordinary case, although in the average case it will do no great harm. One effect will be to impel the court to be conservative in acting under this section for fear more principal will be required later. Another effect will be to discourage petitions in large trusts. Wealthy life tenants will not receive much relief even though the income which was supposed to support them in the manner they were accustomed to falls short of fulfilling the purpose. It will be noted, however, that the limitation is on the distribution of principal and not on the size of the trust. Theoretically, up to $25,000 could be taken from a million dollar trust if a proper case were shown. 

The limitation was inserted primarily for federal tax purposes. The supposed danger in this respect was not so much that because of the statute a reversionary interest 17. 15 or control over principal might be held to remain in the settlor of an otherwise irrevocable trust; it is doubtful that even a tax agent would so argue.19 The fear was rather that an unlimited power in the court to invade principal might have destroyed the deduction for a charitable remainder under such cases as Merchants National Bank of 

Boston v. Commissioner, 320 U. S. 256 (1943). Whether this danger was real or imaginary, it was felt that the primary usefulness of this section would be in small trusts anyway, and that it was better to avoid even a remote danger of an unfavorable tax effect on large trusts where the statute would probably never be used. ¶ 5. Effective Date

This section is prospective only, and under section 21 will apply only to conveyances made on or after January 1, 1948. As to whether the exercise of a general power of appointment or a radical amendment to a revocable trust is a "conveyance", see discussion under section 1 (2) of this act.

Although the new provision has no application to old trusts it might have the psychological effect of adding weight to cases discussed above under ¶ 3c, where similar results were reached in the absence of statute. See

§3. RELEASE OR DISCLAIMER OF POWERS OR INTERESTS. 

(a) Powers and Interests Releasable.

Any power of appointment, or power of consumption, whether general or special, other than a power in trust which is imperative, and any interest in, to, or over real or personal property held or owned outright, or in trust, or in any other manner which is reserved or given to any person by deed, will or otherwise, and irrespective of any limitation of such power or interest by virtue of any restriction in the nature of a so-called spendthrift trust provision, or similar provision, may be released or disclaimed, either with or without consideration, by written instrument signed by the person possessing the power or the interest and delivered as hereinafter provided, but nothing in this section shall authorize an income beneficiary of a spendthrift trust to release or disclaim his right to such income. 

(b) Form of Release or Disclaimer. 

A power or interest which is releasable or disclaimable may be released or disclaimed either absolutely or conditionally, and may also be released or disclaimed with respect to the whole or any part of the property subject to such power or interest, and may also be released or disclaimed in such manner as to reduce or limit the persons or objects or classes of persons or objects in whose favor such power or interest would otherwise be exercisable. No release or disclaimer of a power or of an interest shall be deemed to make imperative a power or interest which was not imperative prior to such release or disclaimer unless the instrument of release or disclaimer expressly so provides. 

(c) Delivery of Release or Disclaimer. 

Such release or disclaimer may be delivered to any one of the following: (1) Any person specified for such purpose in the instrument creating the power or interest; (2) Any trustee of the property to which the power or interest relates; (3) The clerk of the court having jurisdiction of the trust for filing in said court; 5201

§ESTATES ACT 

(4) The recorder of deeds for recording in the county in which the person possessing the power or interest resides, or in which the deed, will, or other instrument creating the power or interest is recorded or filed. (d) Grantee or Lienholder. 

A release or disclaimer shall be void as against a bona fide grantee of or holder of a lien on real estate in any county unless the release or disclaimer or a duplicate original or certified copy thereof is recorded in the county where the real estate lies before the recording or entering of the instrument or lien under which such grantee or lienholder claims. 

(e) Application of Section. 

This section shall apply to releases and disclaimers heretofore and hereafter delivered, but shall not invalidate any release or disclaimer delivered pursuant to the law in effect prior to the effective date of this act. 

COMMISSIONERS' COMMENTS- 

Subsections (a), (b), and (c) are similar to sections 1, 2, and 3 of the Act of 1943, P. L. 797, as amended by the Act of 

1945, P. L. 1337, 68 PS 581, et seq.

An effort has been made to preserve the tax advantages which led to the amendments of 1945 and at the same time to eliminate certain collateral questions which have been raised by those amendments.

The Act of 1943 was prompted by a change in the Federal tax laws by the Revenue Act of 1942. A complete or partial release or disclaimer of a power of appointment or other property right is now often desirable. The purpose of the Act of 

1943 was to establish an orderly method by which the releases, partial releases and disclaimers could be evidenced. 

The 1945 amendment went much further than the original act. The amendments were intended to make it possible for life beneficiaries to disclaim interests in favor of charitable remaindermen before the due date for filing the Federal estate tax return, and in this manner secure full deductions for the charitable gifts in such tax returns. See section 812(d) of the 

Internal Revenue Code as amended by the Revenue Act of 1942. 

As now amended it is possible for the life beneficiary to relinquish his right to consume principal or to receive principal in the discretion of the trustee, and thus secure deduction for the charitable gift. See Schoonmaker Est., 6 T. C. 404. 5202

ESTATES ACT 

cos 83 

[Subsection (a)] 

The subsection preserves the right to relinquish rights in principal which otherwise might make the principal taxable or prevent the deduction of a gift to a charitable remainderman. 

It does not continue the right to release or disclaim the income of a spendthrift trust. In thus avoiding the possibility of defeating the conveyor's plans, it also avoids difficult questions concerning acceleration of remainders: Cf. Disston's Est., 257 Pa. 

537; Gunning's Est., 234 Pa. 144. 

[Subsection (b)] 

The words "except that no power or interest, subject to a spendthrift trust provision or similar provision may be released or disclaimed except in favor of a remainderman" which are in the 1943 and 1945 Acts, are here omitted as unnecessary. A release or disclaimer as distinguished from an assignment can only benefit remaindermen or persons taking in default of appointment. The omitted words raise difficult questions if there is no remainderman and the conveyor or his estate has a reversion. The reference to "imperative" powers in the last sentence is necessary because if the donee of a general power releases his power to appoint to anyone except members of a special class, it might be argued that an interest vests in the members of such class who will take even in default of appointment. See 

Jones v. Mackie, 49 D. & C. 459, 488. 

[Subsection (c)] 

Clauses (1) and (2) are in accordance with the 1943 and 1945 acts. Clause (3) is considered a proper addition as the most natural place where the release or disclaimer should be filed. 

There has been omitted as inadvisable and unnecessary the following clause appearing in the 1943 and 1945 acts: "(c) Any person other than the person possessing the power or interest who could be adversely affected by an exercise of the power or interest."

Clause (4) takes the place of clause (d) in the 1943 and 

1945 acts. 

[Subsection (d)] 

Some protection should be given to persons who give value for an interest in the estate and have taken a reasonable precaution before such value is given. The style of the subsection is based on the language of section 13 of the Wills Act of 1947. 

[Subsection (e)] 

The first part of this subsection is identical with section 4 of the 1943 act. The addition makes it clear that the changes made in subsection (c) will not invalidate what was previously effective.

11. Background

This is a continuation and modification of the act of 1943 as amended in 1945. The background of these statutes is well known. By the Federal Revenue Act of 1942,¹ property subject to a power of appointment was made taxable

In order to avoid the harsh results of the Revenue Act's retroactive application, Congress provided that the owners of taxable powers under old instruments could release or partially release such power if this was done before a certain date. This deadline has been extended from time to time. As the Commissioners' comments indicate, there are also other tax advantages to disclaiming powers and interests as where such disclaimers make definite or increase the value of a deductible gift to charity.* As most people apparently would rather avoid taxation than own a power, there was a general rush to release. powers after the Revenue Act of 1942 became law. To the dismay of attorney and client, however, it was found that considerable doubt existed as to the validity of such releases under state property law in certain situations. Along with other states, therefore, the Pennsylvania Legislature obligingly passed the 1943 act to clarify the subject. In 

1945 the act was amended primarily to provide for the disclaimer of interests and powers of consumption. The present section revises the mechanics of release in certain respects and eliminates the power to release or disclaim spendthrift interests in income.

2. Release of Powers at Common Law a. Validity

There is considerable material by property theorists on release of powers at common law. A partial list is: 

Gray, "Release and Discharge of Powers", 24 Harv. L. 

Rev. 511 (1911); Kales, Future Interests (2d ed. 1920) § 611; Simes, Future Interests (1936) § 277 et seq.; Restatement of Property (1940) § 334 et seq.; Nossaman, "Release of Powers", 56 Harv. L. Rev. 757 (1943); Note, 76

A. L. R. 1430 (1931). For a discussion of the taxation phase of powers, see Eisenstein, "Powers of Appointment and Estate Taxes", 52 Yale L. J. 296, 494 (1943).

Since case authorities were comparatively few, there was wide scope for disagreement among the theorists as to when powers could be released. Gray took a very strict view against the release of anything except general powers presently exercisable. At the other extreme, Simes thinks that all powers are releasable at common law except im- ✓ perative powers. The Restatement of Property adopts an intermediate view that although all general powers are releasable (regardless of whether they are presently exercisable) a special power can be released only when it is presently exercisable and the takers in default are all among the possible appointees, or when it is expressly made releasable by the donor. 

Pennsylvania appellate court authority on the subject apparently consists exclusively of Lyon v. Alexander, 304 

Pa. 288 (1931), Mogridge's Estate, 342 Pa. 308, 312 (1941), and Jackson's Trust, 351 Pa. 89 (1945). In all those cases the court held that a general power to appoint by will could 7. For lower court citations, see Hunter, O. C. Book (1939) "Powers of 

Appointment by Will" § 11. 5207

cas 3 

ESTATES ACT 

¶ 2b be released by the donee during his life. This is consistent with the Restatement of Property and with the weight of authority, Gray's view to the contrary notwithstanding.

As to special powers, there is language in Lyon v. Alexander, 304 Pa. at 292, indicating that special powers were not releasable, but it is uncertain whether the court was referring to all special powers or only to special powers in trust-see discussion below under ¶ 4d. 

b. Partial Release 

Another question which the case authorities left open, both in Pennsylvania and elsewhere, is whether a releasable power could be partially released in the sense of releasing the power to appoint to anyone except a designated class. 

Partial release in the sense of releasing the power over part of the property is approved in Atkinson v. Dowling, 33 S. C. 414, 12 S. E. 93 (1890),8 which was cited with ap proval in Lyon v. Alexander, 304 Pa. at 293. The Restate ment of Property also approves partial releases in § 336 but from the illustration it appears that the authors had in mind a release with respect to one of several takers in default. For the most part the authorities do not cover the question of whether a general power can, in the absence of statute, be turned into a special power by a partial release, and this was what most persons wished to do in order to save the Federal tax and still keep as much control over the property as possible. See Eisenstein, 52 Yale L. J. at 550. c. Mechanics 

The authorities were also far from definite on the subject of how a release of a power was accomplished at common law. The earlier cases on releases dealt with release by estoppel. A owns a fee simple with power to appoint it by will. During his lifetime he conveys to X. The conveyance operates as an extinguishment of the power because A is thereafter estopped from defeating X's title by appointing by will to another. It is unusual today for the

83 Ma same person to own both a power of appointment and the interest in default of appointment, but curiously enough both Mogridge's Estate, 342 Pa. 308 (1941), and Jackson's

Usually the taker in default is a person other than the owner of the power-as where a life estate and a general power to appoint by will is given to A with a gift in default of appointment to B. In such a case A acting alone cannot convey title to the remainder during his lifetime since his power is limited to exercise by will.10 However, extinguishment by deed is still possible if both A and B join in the inter vivos transfer to X. This was what was done in Lyon v. Alexander, 304 Pa. 288 (1931). Release by transfer of the property to a third person, joined in by both the owner of the power and the taker in default, is therefore clearly recognized in Pennsylvania as a proper form of release at common law. 

But this leaves open the question of how the release should be effected if no transfer to a third party is contemplated. It is stated in Lyon v. Alexander, 304 Pa. at 

293, that "the release or extinguishment of a power may take any form," so that any of the methods recognized generally would probably have been approved in Pennsyl vania. Section 336 of the Restatement of Property men tions three such methods by which the owner of a power may release it: (1) by an instrument of release for consideration or under seal to one of the takers in default, (2) by inter vivos transfer to a third party joined in by the taker in default as described above, or (3) by contract with a taker in default not to exercise this power. Similar methods are approved in Simes, Future Interests (1936) $285.

All the above methods, however, assume that the taker in default is ascertained and sui juris. Hence the principal uncertainty as to the mechanics of release prior to the statute was in the common case where the gift in default of appointment is to A's issue living at his death, or to some other unascertained class. Presumably a release in this

13. Release of Powers Under the Statute a. Validity

The act of 1943 was an attempt to clarify the uncertainties in the case law and to broaden the law of release of powers as far as good policy permitted. The provisions of that act, insofar as they defined what sort of powers can be released, remained unaffected by the 1945 amendment or the present act. The broad rule favored by Simes is adopted, and any power other than an imperative power can be released. More will be said below under 14 concerning imperative powers. Suffice it to note here that there is no other qualification to the type of power that can be released. Hence, unless the very fact that the class of appointees is restricted makes the power imperative (a conclusion which seems scarcely tenable as explained under ¶4), it now seems clear that a special power can be released contra to the Restatement and contra to the dictum in Lyon v. Alexander, 304 Pa. at 292. Also, the fact that a power is collateral (i. e. that the owner of the power has no interest in the property) does not of itself make a power unreleasable, although many collateral powers are imperative and unreleasable for that reason. 

b. Partial Release 

The power to release a power partially in all senses of the phrase is also clarified by the statute. As subsection (b) spells out, a power may not only be released as to part of the property, but also the release may restrict the class to which an appointment can be made. As explained above (¶ 2b), the authorities were not clear as to whether the latter could be done at common law. 5210

¶ 3c 

ESTATES ACT 

§3 

Gölet vill, Blond Al 10 A

In cases where the class as restricted by the release does not include the takers in default, it is probable that the statute authorizes something which the courts would not have approved in the absence of statute. Assume, for example, that A has a general testamentary power and the gift in default is to B. A cannot appoint by deed, but under the statute he could release his power to appoint to anyone except X. This is the sort of thing that will make 

Gray turn in his grave, but it seems clearly authorized by the statute. Note, however, that A still cannot appoint to 

X inter vivos without B's joinder, or commit himself to do so by contract. All he can do is release his power to appoint to anyone else, but he may still thereafter permit the property to pass in default to B. c. Mechanics 

One of the principal values of the statute is that it sets forth exactly how the release should be effected. As noted above, the case law left this matter unsettled, particularly in cases where the takers in default were unascertained or not sui juris. Subsections (a) and (c) now supply this deficiency-the former by providing for a writing signed by the owner of the power, and the latter by prescribing four optional modes of "delivery".

As to the requirement of a signed writing, it will be noted that the Restatement requirements of a seal or consideration have been eliminated. As to the delivery, four methods are presented which are sufficient to objectify the intent to release and insure its irrevocability. Any one of them can be used regardless of whether the taker in default is alive, ascertained, or sui juris. In cases of trusts, all the methods are available. In cases of legal estates in land either (1) or (4) can be used.

Certain changes have been made in subsection (c) from the earlier act. As explained below (¶9) in the discussion of the special effective date provision in subsection (e), these changes will not invalidate old releases, but they might validate prior ineffective releases and will govern 11

Secondly, the provision for filing with the recorder of deeds in clause (4) has been modified by eliminating the reference to recording in the county where the owner of the power "has a place of business".

The only other change is the elimination of delivery to a person "who could be adversely affected by an exercise of the power"-i. e. a taker in default or a presumptive taker in default. Why this was eliminated is not clear to the present writer. As explained above (¶ 2c), the methods approved by the common law were (1) a transfer of the property to a third party by the owner of the power and the taker in default, or (2) a deed of release to or a contract with the taker in default. These methods were admittedly inadequate, but it seems strange that the statute, instead of merely adding other methods, omits reference to the only methods previously known. It is believed that if a case ever arose where the parties had used a method of release recognized at common law but not mentioned in the statute the court should hold that the methods for release enumerated in the present legislation were not intended to be exclusive. Suppose, for example, the method approved in Lyon v. Alexander, 304 Pa. 288 (1931), and recognized since earliest days, was employed after January 

1, 1947—a transfer to a third party joined in by the owner of the power and the owner of a vested interest in default of appointment. Suppose further that the subject matter was personalty and no deed was recorded. The court could scarcely ignore hundreds of years of law and permit the transferors or their successors to deny the title of the transferee, merely because the statute makes no mention of this method. Furthermore, there is nothing in this section indicating that it was intended to be exclusive. Subsection (c) merely states that the release "may" be delivered in one of the prescribed methods. Of course, the careful practitioner will make certain that the statutory procedure is followed, but if the question were ever raised in litigation, it is believed that the common law methods of release should also be recognized. 5212

¶ 4. Imperative Powers a. General "Imperative" powers are mentioned twice in this section. Under subsection (a) "a power in trust which is imperative" cannot be released, and under subsection (b) a partial release of a non-imperative power will not in itself make the power imperative. The latter provision merely restates a result which the courts would undoubtedly have reached anyway and is not likely to cause any trouble. 

Questions might well arise under subsection (a), however, with regard to whether a power is imperative so that it cannot be released.

An imperative power, or "power in trust" as it is more frequently termed,12 is a power which the donee is said to have a "duty" to exercise. The concept is an elusive one and the Pennsylvania authorities on the subject are few. Much has been written by the property theorists on the question of when a power is imperative and the effects of finding that it is so. See generally, Simes, Future Interests (1936) §§ 247, 280 et seq., 287;

Tiffany, Real Property (3rd ed. 1939) § 683; Restatement of Trusts (1935) § 27, comment b; Restatement of Prop erty (1940) $367, comment c; Gray, "Powers in 

Trust... "' 25 Harv. L. Rev. 1 (1911); Note, 80 A. L. R. 

503 (1932). Unfortunately, however, the authorities do not even agree as to how the problem should be approached. 

The principal difficulty in defining the term is due to the fact that all the cases at common law where the imperative or non-imperative nature of a power is discussed can be explained away on other grounds. b. Cases on Disposition in Default of Appointment 

By far the most numerous class of cases dealing with imperative powers, or so-called powers in trust, are those where the question is what to do with the property when a power is not validly exercised. A (whose only heir is X) 

12. Note that the phrase "power in trust" does not mean that the power is contained in a trust as opposed to a legal estate but rather, as explained in the text, that the owner of the power is a sort of fiduciary with regard to it and has a duty to exercise it. The synonym, "imperative power," seems more descriptive. 5213

§cos 

ESTATES ACT 

¶ 4b gives B a power to appoint among C, D and E. B fails to appoint. According to some authorities the disposition of the property depends on whether the power is imperative. 

If the power is merely discretionary, the property reverts to A's estate and passes to his heir X. If the power is imperative, the property is awarded to C, D, and E in equal shares.

Necessarily, such a question arises only when (a) the power is a special one to appoint to a restricted class of possible appointees, and (b) there is no express gift in default of appointment. Perhaps because of this it is often said that a power is not imperative if it is general,13 or (even if it is special) if the instrument creating the power contains an express gift over in default of appointment, other than a general residuary clause.14 

Where the power is special and there is no gift in default of appointment, the tendency (exhibited in the cases from England and elsewhere discussed in the texts cited above) is to hold that in default of appointment the property is awarded to the class of possible appointees rather than back to the estate of the donor. For the most part, the few Pennsylvania cases on the point seem in harmony with this view. 

In McKonkey's Appeal, 13 Pa. 253 (1850), the widow was given real and personal property for life "having full confidence that she will leave the surplus to be divided at her decease justly amongst my children." There was no gift over in default of appointment. It was said that the widow had "a power in the nature of a trust" (at p. 258) and upon her failure to exercise it validly, 15 it passed equally to the children.

In Russell v. Kennedy, 66 Pa. 248 (1870), the widow was given an estate in certain property "during her natural life, then to be divided amongst the children as she direct." 

The widow having failed to appoint validly, it was held that the property passed to the children. There was no discussion of the nature of the power. 

In Hays's Estate, 286 Pa. 520 (1926), a daughter of testator was given a life estate "with the power to appoint among her children or their issue."

There was a gift over in default of issue, but no gift over in case there were issue but no appointment. The nature of the daughter's estate was litigated during her life, she then having issue. By way of dictum the court said (at p. 527) that in default of appointment the issue would take. 

Jones v. Mackie, 49 D. & C. 459 (C. P. Susq. 1943), is the only Pennsylvania case found giving much attention to the theory of imperative powers. There the will gave a life estate to the testator's son and provided that the son should have "the power of disposition of said real estate, the use of which is so devised to him by Will limiting such power of disposition however to the wife and children of [the son] or to his brothers and sisters among any or all of the same in such proportions as he may see fit. . 

There was a gift over in default of living relatives of the class described, but no gift over in default of appointment. 

The son did not exercise the power properly and was survived by a brother and a sister. It was held that the property passed to the brother and sister rather than back to the son's estate. The court discussed the theory of imperative powers (at 486) but did not expressly base the decision on this ground.

On the other side of the balance sheet, however, there is at least one case indicating that a special power with no gift over in default of appointment is not necessarily imperative. In Keene's Estate, 221 Pa. 201 (1908), testator's niece was given a life estate with remainder to her issue. 

If she died unmarried, she was given the "power to devise [the estate] to whichever of her brothers she will consider most worthy to inherit her bequest and mine, the interest only to them, to their children, lawful issue, absolutely." 5215

§cos 

ESTATES ACT 

¶ 4c The niece died a widow without issue. Issue of one of her brothers survived. In the course of its opinion (at 210) the court rejected the argument that the power "amounted to a trust in favor of the possible appointees." The court said that "certainly this cannot be the law, for the power was only to be exercised in the event of [her] dying unmarried and was not an absolute imperative power to make an appointment, and even if she remained unmarried, under the power she could designate 'whichever of her brothers she will consider most worthy to inherit her bequest and mine.' It would seem necessarily to follow that possible beneficiaries in the event of a discretionary power being exercised in their favor can claim no rights as cestui qui trustent before the exercise of the power. In the present case the power was never exercised and no right vested in possible contingent beneficiaries under an unexercised discretionary power of appointment." What the conditional nature of the power had to do with the question of whether it was imperative when the condition was fulfilled is difficult to understand, and with that eliminated this case seems inconsistent with the other cases discussed. 

c. Questionable Significance of These Cases 

Up to now it has been assumed that a power is imperative if the award by the court in default of appointment is to the class of possible appointees. Another cloud is thrown over the entire subject, however, by the fact that this is not necessarily so. This is where the theorists disagree. 

The subject is extensively discussed in Simes at §§ 287 and 288, where the relevant authorities are cited. Simes himself agrees with Kales that the cases where the class of possible appointees take the property are to be explained on the theory that the power was imperative. Gray on the other hand explains the same cases on the ground that the court merely found an implied gift in default of appointment to the favored class.18 The Restatement of Trusts in the comments to $27 suggests that both theories are proper depending on the facts of the case-i. e., the class. of possible appointees will take either if the donor of the 

25 Harv. L. Rev. 1, 3 (1911). 

16. Gray, "Powers in Trust 5216

¶ 4d 

ESTATES ACT 

8 3 power intended to impose a duty on the donee to exercise it, or if the donor implied a gift to the class in default of appointment. The comments to § 367 of the Restatement of 

Property also mention both theories and point out that in the usual case of this sort it makes no difference which one is adopted.

Hence, it can be argued that none of the cases on the disposition of unappointed property controls whether a power is imperative within the meaning of the statute, because they all can be explained away on the implied gift theory. Such explaining away would not be difficult in 

Pennsylvania because as shown above there is little discussion of either theory in our cases of this sort. In Mc- 

Konkey's Appeal, 13 Pa. at 258 the power was said to be "in the nature of a trust" but in that case there was unusual language in the will of the donor of the power expressing "confidence" that his widow would appoint. In

Jones v. Mackie (the only case where the question is really discussed) the Orphans' Court mentioned both theories and the decision seems based more on the ground of implied gift than on the imperative nature of the power. (See 49 D. & C. at 490.) 

d. Cases on Release of Imperative Powers at Common Law 

If Gray's theory is followed and the cases dealing with disposition in default of appointment considered of no significance in determining whether a power is imperative, there is little authority remaining to determine whether a power is imperative within the meaning of this section of the Estates Act. The only other cases relevant to the question are those involving release of powers at common law. 

Here again, however, many such cases can be explained on other grounds, because according to some authorities the imperative or non-imperative nature of a power was not the test in determining whether it was releasable at common law. Gray, for example, thought that truly imperative powers were rare, but this did not affect his view that most powers were not releasable. Hence, the earlier cases on release are significant only when a power is held to be unreleasable because it is imperative. 5217

¶ 4d 

ESTATES ACT 

The only relevant Pennsylvania authority of this sort that has been found is the following statement from Lyon v. Alexander, 304 Pa. at 291-2: 

"For all practical purposes there may be said to be two marked differences in powers of appointment; they can be summarized as general and special powers. The general are those in which the donee of the power may appoint to anyone, and the special, in which the donee of the power is restricted to passing on the property to certain specified individuals or to a specific class of individuals. In the latter case, there is a sound reason why the repository of the power should not be permitted to extinguish it, because the testator has indicated the persons to whom the property shall go and there is reposed in the appointee of the power a confidence, something partaking of the nature of a trust; but where the power is a general one under which the donee may appoint to anyone, the testator has completely relinquished all dead hand dominion over the property and has placed it for all practical purposes as completely within the control of the donee of the power as though a fee had been created in him. 

There is neither a trust nor an obligation in the nature of a trust because the power is not coupled with a duty." This seems clear authority to the effect that general powers are necessarily non-imperative.17 The rather careless dictum concerning special powers, on the other hand, cannot be taken too literally. The court seems to say that all special powers are powers in trust, but this is contrary to the generally accepted view that an express gift over in default of appointment makes even a special power non-imperative.18 The latter view was the basis for the decision in Atkinson v. Dowling, 33 S. C. 414, 424, 12 S. E. 

93, 95 (1890), (which was cited with approval in Lyon v. 17. In most cases this cannot be doubted. Query, however, whether a general imperative power cannot be imagined. Consider, for example, the collateral power given to the executors in Dormer's Est., 348 Pa. 356 (1944), to dispose of testator's estate as they saw fit. Perhaps, however, such a power would be considered special since the executors could not have appointed to themselves. 

18. See authorities supra note 14. 5218

¶ 4d §

ESTATES ACT 

Alexander) where a special power was held non-imperative and therefore releasable because of the express gift over in default of appointment. If the dictum in Lyon v. Alexander is so qualified, the rule would seem to be that all special powers unaccompanied by a gift over in default of appointment are imperative for purposes of release as well as for purposes of disposing of unappointed property. 

On the other hand, the way seems open for Pennsylvania to adopt a still more limited view as to what powers are truly imperative. The cases at common law actually holding that a power cannot be released because it is imperative are not numerous and for the most part concern powers lodged in a trustee or other person having no beneficial interest in the property.19 In such cases the terms "imperative powers" and "powers in trust" seem appropriate to describe the actual situation. In the absence of controlling authority, therefore, our court might adopt the more realistic view that a power is imperative (in the sense that it is unreleasable under the statute) only in cases where it is evident that the power was given for the benefit of the class of possible appointees rather than for the accommodation of the donee of the power. For example, if a trustee is directed to distribute income to such of testator's children as the trustee considers most in need from time to time, it seems plain that the testator was thinking primarily of caring for his children and it is not unreasonable to say that he imposed a duty on the trustee in this respect. 

On the other hand, if the testator leaves part of his estate to his sister for life with a power to appoint the principal among her issue at her death, the primary purpose of the trust is to benefit the sister by giving her various incidents of ownership in the property. To say that the testator intended to impose a "duty" on the sister to exercise the power merely because the draftsman forgot to insert a gift in default of appointment sounds like lawyer talk of the worst sort. True, the property should probably be awarded to the sister's issue if she fails to appoint, but this result can be reached by the implied gift theory without labelling the power imperative for purposes of release. 

19. See Simes, Future Interests (1936) § 281, cf. § 284. 5219

§4e 

ESTATES ACT e. Summary 

From the above discussion, it is evident that the Pennsylvania courts will have a wide latitude in determining what powers are imperative within the meaning of the present section. The following conclusions can be ventured: 

1. A general power is never imperative. 

2. It is reasonably certain that a special power with an express gift over in default of appointment is not imperative, in spite of the dictum in Lyon v. Alexander, 304 Pa. at 292. 

3. It might well be held that all special powers where there is no express gift over in default of appointment are imperative. 

4. On the other hand, the way is open for the court to adopt the more realistic view that only those special powers are imperative where it is evident that the donor of the power was thinking primarily of the welfare of the class of appointees rather than the accommodation of the donee of the power. Under this view cases of imperative powers will for the most part be confined to powers vested in a trustee or other disinterested party, or where the donor's instrument contains unusual language. 

5. Release and Disclaimer of Interests at Common Law a. General 

Terms such as release, renunciation, disclaimer, etc., are often loosely used, but it is plain that there are at least two distinct concepts to which such terms are usually applied. (1) The first is when the beneficiary of an inter vivos or testamentary gift refuses to accept it so that title never passes to him. This is usually called renunciation or disclaimer. (2) The second is where a person who already owns an interest in property divests himself of that interest in favor of one having another interest in the same property. This is usually called release, or, when a tenant for life or years gives up his estate in favor of a remainderman, a surrender. 5220

¶ 5a 

ESTATES ACT 

cos With the possible exception of cases involving spendthrift trusts, it was well settled at common law that "no person can be compelled to accept a gift against his will" and that a timely renunciation or disclaimer "will relate back to the moment when the gift was made and prevent it from ever taking effect." Bute's Estate, 355 Pa. 170, 173-4 (1946). Consequently, there are no limitations on the kind of estate that can be renounced. The beneficiary simply refuses to accept the attempted gift and the ownership remains in the donor or (in the case of a testamentary gift) in his estate to pass under section 14 (9) or (10) of the Wills Act or by intestacy. Once a gift has been accepted, however, it is too late to renounce it, and acceptance can be express, implied, or presumed from silence.2 20 Release, on the other hand, is a type of conveyance. At early law, conveyance by release or surrender obviated the necessity of livery of seisin and (in certain cases) words of inheritance. Hence it was often important in the early cases to determine whether release was possible, and there were various more or less arbitrary rules governing the question. 

The owner of an executory interest could release to the owner of the fee; a remainderman could release to a life tenant; one joint tenant could release to the other. But a release could not be made to one having neither a vested estate nor actual possession; and for obscure reasons one tenant in common could not release to the other. See, gen erally, Tiffany, Real Property (3d ed. 1939) §§ 954 (release) 

and 960 et seq. (surrender);

Simes, Future Interests (1936) 

§ 710; Restatement of Property (1936) § 29. Today, livery of seisin has passed away, the necessity for words of inheritance has been abolished by statute,21 and for the most part all forms of interests and expectancies are freely alienable either at law or in equity.22 Hence, the distinction between release and other modes of conveyance is of little or no significance in modern law. It is only necessary to note the general nature of the concept in view of the fact

¶ 6. Release and Disclaimer of Interests Under the Statute a. General

As previously explained (1), the act of 1943 was amended in 1945 to permit the release or disclaimer of interests as well as powers and this is continued by the present act although an exception as to spendthrift income is inserted. Aside from the provisions relating to spendthrift trusts and the mechanics of accomplishing a release or disclaimer, the statute will have little effect on prior case law.

The word "release" with reference to an interest in property presumably is used in accordance with its common meaning as explained above-a form of transfer where the prior ownership in the releasor is conceded. The obsolete common law restrictions on what kinds of interests can be released to whom are no doubt removed by the statute which permits the release of "any" interest, but as already pointed out the common law restrictions were of no practical consequence in modern law anyway. The fundamental idea of a release as a transfer to someone else having an interest in the same property, however, will probably continue. It would not be plausible to construe the statute to authorize a "release" in thin air so that the property would revert to the donor. It would seem that this can be done by way of renunciation or not at all. 

The word "disclaimer" is a frequently used synonym for renunciation,28 and is undoubtedly so used in the statute. 

27. See Griswold §§ 522 and 523. 

28. So used by Scott, the Restatement, Griswold, etc.

, supra in the text, ¶ 5a & b. 5223

§ESTATES ACT 

¶ 6b Hence an interest can be disclaimed under the statute only if it has not been previously accepted-expressly or by implication. 

b. Mechanics 

The mechanics for releasing or disclaiming an interest set forth in subsection (c) are quite different from what would be required at common law. Prior to the statute, a release with respect to real property was accomplished by a sealed writing delivered to the releasee.29 Disclaimer or renunciation, on the other hand, involved no transfer of title and could be accomplished "by any unequivocal act which shows such 'intention." 30

As in the case of powers, discussed above (¶ 3c), the statute requires a signed writing for either release or disclaimer (but no seal) in subsection (b) and in subsection (c) lists permissible modes of delivery. Delivery to the persons who would benefit by the release or disclaimer is excluded by the new act. Hence the orthodox mode of effecting a release at common law is not provided for, and the mechanics for effecting a disclaimer are to this extent narrower than under the 'case law. As pointed out under ¶ 3c, however, the statute should probably be construed as enabling rather than restrictive. Hence any form of release or disclaimer which would comply either with the statute or the common law should be recognized, although the contrary can be argued. 

c. Spendthrift Trusts 

The act of 1945 had attempted to make all interests releasable and disclaimable regardless of spendthrift restrictions. Presumably under the act of 1945 a spendthrift income beneficiary could release his estate to the remainderman, terminate the trust, and obtain an agreed share of the principal. This was rather shocking to bench and bar and in one case the act was held unconstitutional in this respect as applied to a trust created prior to 1945.31

Trusts which provide for some flexibility by way of making principal available to income beneficiaries when needed are becoming increasingly common. Taxwise, it is sometimes advisable for the beneficiary of such a trust to relinquish such interests in the principal and limit himself to income.

Where the life tenant is given the power to consume, this would seem to be in the nature of a power to appoint to one's self presently exercisable. As such it is clearly non-imperative and releasable under this section. 

When the trustee is given discretionary power to use principal for the support of an income beneficiary if needed, the power as such would seem to be imperative and unreleasable by the trustee. However, it can be reasoned in such case that there is a corresponding contingent interest in an indeterminate amount of principal owned by the life tenant, and that this interest in the principal can be released or disclaimed by the beneficiary regardless of spendthrift provisions. ¶ 8. A distinction between grantees and devisees in this respect would be arbitrary, however, and it seems plain that the Legislature intended to protect those claiming through the appointee rather than the appointee himself.

COMMISSIONERS' COMMENT- 

This subsection is intended to disturb the common law rule as little as possible, but to make actualities at the end of the period, rather than possibilities as of the creation of the interest, govern, and to provide a more equitable disposition of void gifts. *The provisions outlined within the brackets are discussed separately infra. 5251

ESTATES ACT 

By regarding actualities at the end of the period, the unrealistic results based on purely theoretical possibilities are avoided. The possibility test seems peculiarly inappropriate in most Pennsylvania cases because by the time the courts do decide upon the validity of the remainders, possibilities have become actualities. This results because (1) the modern tendency is to uphold valid life estates even though the ultimate remainder seems obviously void, and (2) the court refuses to decide on the validity of future estates until the termination of the valid life estates. See Quigley's Est., 329 Pa. 281, on both points.

Gifts to a class, the membership of which is still subject to increase at the expiration of the period, are treated in the same manner as contingent interests although there may have been a technical vesting in some of the members. This is in accord with the common law which invalidates the entire class gift if the class will not be closed within the period. See Simes, Future Interests, Sections 498 and 499. It also seems the most sensible solution in such cases. It will be noted that most class gifts do not vest at all until the class is determined so that this provision is necessary only for those cases where a technical vesting occurs as each member of the class is born. 

Old Law

There was no prior statute on perpetuities in Pennsylvania except that relating to cemetery trusts (see § 4 (b) (2) infra). In all other respects the common law rule was followed. 

Contrary to the common law, the permissible period for vesting will be measured by actual rather than possible events in cases subject to the present act. The interests which actually vest in time will be valid, so that no conveyance after January 1, 1948, will be stricken down in its entirety. ¶ 1. General Summary of Sections 4 and 5 

Sections 4 and 5 of the Estates Act represent a novel attempt to change the common law rule against perpetuities in a way which has not hitherto been attempted either in Pennsylvania or elsewhere. The two sections should of course be read in their entirety prior to a study of the particular provisions. The key provisions are the opening sentence of section 4 (b), providing for the measuring of the permissible period by actualities rather than possibilities, and section 5 (c) vesting all interests which have not theretofore vested in the person receiving the income at the end of the period. The new statute has already caused some comment in the law reviews and student note material on the subject will be found in 60 Harv. L. Rev. 1174 (1947), 23 N. Y. U. L. Q. 511 (1948), and 97 U. of Pa. L. Rev. 263 (1948). 

The general effect of the new statutory provisions can be best understood by comparing the common law rule with 5253

ESTATES ACT 

¶1 that of the statute as it would operate on a common type of case: Testator leaves the residue of his estate in trust to pay the income to A for life (A being childless at testator's death), then to pay the income to A's first-born child for life, and to pay the principal to the issue of A's child living at such child's death, or in the absence of issue to X. 

A is survived by his child B who dies survived by his only child C. At common law the remainder would clearly have been invalid because at testator's death it was impossible to predict with certainty that the remainder would vest within twenty-one years of A's death. It is conceivable that the entire trust would have been stricken down, life estates and all, but it is far more likely that the court would have upheld the life estates of A and B (since these estates would necessarily vest at or before A's death) and postponed passing on the remainder until B died. At that time the remainder would have been declared invalid because it might not have vested in time-viewing possibilities as of the time of testator's death. This void interest would then be awarded back to testator's heirs as of the time of his death or rather to the estates of such heirs, as by this time they would undoubtedly all be dead. 

If the same testator died after January 1, 1948, the result under the statute would be quite different. By the terms of subsection (b) the court could in no event declare an interest invalid until twenty-one years after the death of A (the life in being), because any interest which actually vested within that period would be valid, regardless of what the possibilities were at testator's death. Hence A's and 

B's life estates would necessarily be good. C's interest would also be valid if it in fact vested in time. If, for example, B survived A by only fifteen years, C's remainder would take effect and no interest would be invalid. If, on the other hand, B survived A by thirty years, C's remainder would be void. In the latter case, however, the void interest would by the terms of section 5 (c) vest in B (who was receiving the income when the period expired) rather than in testator's heirs. Thus, the statute makes two, and only two, important changes in the common law rule against perpetuities: (1) an interest is invalid only if it actually fails to vest within a 5254

ESTATES ACT 

life in being and twenty-one years, and (2) the void interest in most cases is awarded to the income beneficiary at the end of the period instead of reverting to the estate of the donor. The other provisions of section 4 and 5 are relatively unimportant because for the most part they merely restate what was probably the law prior to the statute. In effect, all the statute does is to insert the following saving clause in every will and deed after January 1, 1948: "Notwithstanding any provisions of this trust, any interest which has not vested within the period allowed by the rule against perpetuities as measured by actualities shall at the expiration of such period vest absolutely in the person or persons then receiving the income." Such clauses were not uncommon in well drafted instruments in the past (cf. 

Friday's Estate, 313 Pa. 328 (1933)), so that the statute does not represent such a radical departure from prior practice as might be supposed. From the above example it will be seen that these sections of the Estates Act, which will apply only to wills and deeds taking effect after January 1, 1948, are not likely to play an important part in our cases for some years to come. 

The only immediate effect will be that no trust subject to this act will be stricken down in its entirety on the ground that it is impossible to separate the good estates from the bad-as in Johnston's Estate, 185 Pa. 179 (1898). As pointed out below, however, such cases were becoming rare even under the old law. The tendency has long been to uphold the valid life estates and postpone decision on remote remainders until the valid estates are terminated. 

The present act merely makes this practice mandatory in all cases governed by the act. Aside from this, the practicing attorney is not likely to meet these sections in litigation for some time.

From the standpoint of the draftsman preparing wills and deeds of trust now with a view to avoiding trouble in the future, these sections are likewise of no great importance. Sections 4 (b) (3) dealing with pension trusts and 

4 (c) governing revocable trusts will allay certain fears that have existed in the past, but, as will be pointed out in the separate discussion of these clauses, they probably clarify rather than change the prior law. As to the sub- 5255

ESTATES ACT 

¶ 2a stantive change from prior law in the opening sentence of section 4 (b), it will be noted that the permissible period for vesting remains the same as it was at common law. 

Hence, at the time the instrument is prepared the same caution will be exercised to avoid the possibility of a violation under the new law as under the old. Certainly no careful draftsman will take the chance of all interests actually vesting in time if there is a possibility that they will not. 

As in the past, saving clauses should be inserted to provide an alternative disposition in accordance with the client's wishes in all cases where the primary plan might result in a too long postponement of vesting. These sections of the act were designed rather to give relief to the client of the unwary draftsman. As pointed out above, the statute merely inserts a saving clause in instruments where the attorney has forgotten to do so. 2. Background a. History of Common Law Rule 

The common law rule against perpetuities, upon which the present statute is based, was designed for a specific social purpose, although in the course of years it came to be applied as a lifeless formula. With the present statutory modification of the rule, novel questions are likely to arise requiring the reexamination of premises in order to determine the legislative intent. Fortunately, more is known of the origin and purpose of the rule against perpetuities than many rules of law. 

The standard works such as Simes,¹ Tiffany,2 Kale and, of course, Gray all have good passages on the history of the rule and there is a particularly good analysis in the "In troductory Note" to Division IV, Part I, of the Restate ment of Property." As there explained in detail, the modern common law rule against perpetuities represents the last phase of a legal war which raged for centuries over attempts to create the equivalent of an indestructible estate tail.

Originally, an estate given to A and the heirs of his body passed from generation to generation and the tenant at any particular time had no power to cut off subsequent estates, but by the middle of the thirteenth century it was settled that the tenant, if he had issue, could destroy the estate by conveying a fee to a third party. Then in 1285 the sanctity of this type of limitation was restored by the statute De Donis Conditionalis" and what then became known as an estate tail again became indestructible. 

The reaction to this form of "perpetuity" came a couple of centuries later. Late in the fifteenth century judicial blessing was given to the device of "barring the entail" by suffering common recovery-a trick by which title to the fee was indirectly transferred to a third person by allowing him to take judgment by default in a collusive suit. Since then, a tenant of entailed property has had the power to convey a fee." 

The left wing having succeeded in finding a device to circumvent the statute De Donis, the forces of the right now began to circumvent the circumvention. New attempts were made to create an indestructible estate which would necessarily pass down a family from generation to generation-notably by attempts to create indestructible executory interests to arise in the future. But, as Gray puts it, the courts "having been warned by the history of estates tail, timely took the matter in hand . . Forfeiture provisions were held invalid and unvested future estates were held destructible by the first taker. Thus, during the sixteenth and early seventeenth centuries unascertained future interests were not permitted to interfere with the alienability of property. The now-familiar contingent remainder and executory interest did not exist as indestructible estates so that living persons could at any time convey a fee. 

It was against this background that the common law rule against perpetuities was developed. It would be less

misleading if the rule were described in the affirmative-a rule permitting the creation of unvested future estates which the first taker could not destroy, provided that the estate did not remain unvested for too long a time. This is what was finally settled in 1685 by the famous Duke of Norfolk's Case. Stripped of its technicalities, the conveyance in that case purported to give a fee to Henry subject to divestment if the earldom descended upon Henry during his life in which case there was a gift over to Charles. Henry tried to destroy the executory interest in 

Charles by conveying a fee to a third person. The court held that this attempt to cut off Charles was ineffective. 

The gift over to Charles was bound to vest, if at all, prior to Henry's death, and it was decided that vesting could remain suspended at least this long. Later the period was extended to twenty-one years after the death of a life in being, and this became the common law rule against perpetuities. In the words of Gray, "the ingenuity of conveyancers, aided by the inadvertence of the judges, created a class of future estates which the courts held to be indestructible; thereupon it became necessary to make a new rule for the restraint of indestructible future interthis rule is the Rule against Perpetuests; and ities."⁹ 

b. Purpose of Common Law Rule 

It is clear from the cases in which the rule against perpetuities was thus developed that the concern of the courts was to prevent indirect restraints on alienation by the creation of estates which could not be "docked". In fact, long before the Duke of Norfolk's Case the word "perpetuity" was used to describe an inalienable estate.¹º The attitude of the courts was summed up in Scatterwood v. 

Edge, 1 Salk 229, 91 Eng. Reprints 203 (1699) where a perpetuity was said to be "an estate unalienable, though all mankind join in the conveyance.' "? This mode of describing a perpetuity has remained popular to the present day. Thus as late as 1922 in Lilley's Estate, 272 Pa. 143, 8. 3 Ch. Cas. 1 (1682, 1685).

The definition of a perpetuity as an estate which remains inalienable has been criticized severely by Gray,¹¹ and it is true that it is inexact for more than one reason. 

In the first place the definition is far too broad, for it would include estates subject to direct restraints. As Gray has pointed out, the law of perpetuities and the law of restraints. "having originally a common purpose, have had a separate development. The attempts to combine them have led to much confusion." 12 On the other hand, the definition is too narrow in certain respects because the test of inalienability will not always give the correct answer under the common law rule against perpetuities as finally developed. 

A contingent remainder in an ascertained person, for example, is freely alienable in modern law,13 but if it remains unvested beyond the period it is nevertheless objectionable as a perpetuity.14

The definition of a perpetuity as an inalienable estate, therefore, is not precise. However, as even Gray admits, the concern of the courts for the alienability of property was what produced the rule. "As has been said, the tying up of property was attempted in two ways, first by making vested estates inalienable, and when the judges stopped this, then by the creation of indestructible future contingent estates; and to restrain these last the rule against perpetuities was devised. The tying up of property is therefore restrained, as to present estates, by making them alienable, and, as to future estates, by subjecting them to the Rule against Perpetuities." 15 Or, as the court said in

One question which has been given inadequate attention by those who have analyzed the purpose of the rule against perpetuities is why the rule should apply to interests in trust where the trustee is given the power of sale.16 

Most discussions of the social policy behind the law of perpetuities deal only with the alienability of a particular piece of real estate. In modern times, however, the rule is most frequently applied to trusts where the trustee is empowered to convey the fee of any part of the corpus at any time. Whether the courts were conscious of this distinction when the rule was developed is doubtful, but the policy of applying the rule even though title to specific property is freely alienable by the trustee is probably sound. Perpetual trusts are socially and economically undesirable not only because specific items of property might be taken out of commerce, but also because such trusts tend to hinder redistribution of wealth, to eliminate a portion of a nation's capital from speculative enterprises, and to increase the number of persons who have no control over the management of their property. Regardless of whether the title to 

Blackacre is frozen, therefore, it can be argued that the power of the dead hand should be restrained in the interests of a fluid economy and a free society. 02 In any event, it is settled that the rule applies regardless of the powers of the trustee, and this should be kept in mind when it is said that the rule is designed to encourage the free flow of property. The policy of the law is to promote alienability not only of specific items of property but also of property rights in the abstract. The rule against perpetuities strikes a balance between this interest of society in the free flow of property and the normal desire of the individual to provide for his family after his death. c. True, certain changes have been made in the mechanics of the rule as a vehicle for expressing this policy, but even these changes are of a relatively minor nature and for the most part the common law rule remains intact. In fact, many arbitrary and illogical features of the common law rule were incorporated into the statute because of a desire to disturb the old law as little as possible. Aside from the provisions for disposing of void interests in section 5, the only change intended from the old law was the use of actualities rather than possibilities in measuring the period. 

In all other respects, an attempt was made to restate the prior law, or at most (as in clauses (3) and (4) of subsection (b) and in subsection (c)) to provide the answers to certain undecided questions consistently with what the courts would probably have held. Thus, as more fully explained below, the permissible period remains the same, the rule still relates to vesting and not to enjoyment, and all interests which were exempt from the common law rule are still exempt under section 4 (b) (1) infra. It is possible, of course, that the courts will decide that other changes were unwittingly made, but if this turns out to be the case, it can be safely said that any such change was not contemplated by the drafters. 

For these reasons, the case law prior to statute will continue to be important in construing the present statute. 

The answer to most questions will still be found in the standard works on perpetuities, and the Pennsylvania material collected in Foulke 18 and elsewhere will continue to be useful.
