derstand. The policy of the law is to prevent the fettering of property for more than a certain period. Yet, as the case law developed, this period was measured not by what actually occurred, but by what might have happened in the light of theoretical possibilities at the time the conveyance was made. This would have made some sense if in all cases the attempted conveyance were declared either valid or invalid in toto and if the courts would necessarily pass on the question at the beginning. In the great majority of cases, however, the court would do no such thing. It would ✓ uphold the life estates and refuse to pass on the validity of the ultimate interest until it had ripened, but then, instead of looking to see if there had actually been a postponement of vesting for too long a time, the court would shut its eyes to what did happen and strike down the remainder if at the time of the conveyance there had been even a possibility of the remainder's not vesting in time. This Alice-in- 

Wonderland logic of saying that something is bad because it might have been bad even though it turned out to be good was primarily responsible for the common law rule's becoming a mental exercise for lawyers rather than an effective instrumentality for carrying out an important social policy. The possibility test was carried to an extreme in cases where the theoretical possibilities which resulted in the invalidity of the ultimate interest were so improbable that they were fantastic to any but the legal mind. In Leach's "Perpetuities in a Nutshell", 51 Harv. L. Rev. 638 (1938), three "frequently recurring types" of such cases are noted. 

The first was the "fertile octogenarian" type: Testator leaves his estate to his eighty year old sister for life, then to her children until the death of the survivor, with remainder to her grandchildren then living. The remainder was bad, because the common law, refusing to recognize any age limit to fertility, supposes that the sister might have other children. See Coggins Appeal, 124 Pa. 10 (1889).19 19. The ages of the life tenants who were supposed to have other children in that case were not given, but the unlikelihood was mentioned by the 

Orphans' Court, 124 Pa. at 17. Cf. List v. Rodney, 83 Pa. 483 (1877), recognizing unlimited fertility in connection with another problem, and Wright's 5262

ESTATES ACT 

 The second type is well illustrated by Disston's Estate, 46 D. & C. 496 (O. C. Phila. 1942), aff'd., 346 Pa. 129 (1944).

Testatrix had five sons when she died, all of whom were married except the youngest who was then forty years old. 

She left life estates for her sons followed by life estates for their widows with remainders over to a class of descendants living at the deaths of the survivors of her sons "and their wives." It was held that the remainders were void because the youngest son might have married (or the older sons might have remarried) a woman born after testatrix's death and this woman might have survived all the sons and other wives by more than twenty-one years. Of course, her son did no such thing, but the possibility of this happening made the remainders bad. Leach calls this sort of case the "unborn widow" type.

The third of Leach's types he calls the "administrative contingency type" which the layman should enjoy because it represents an unconscious satire on the dilatory lawyer. 

Testator leaves his estate to such of his issue as are living when his estate is settled. The common law took note of the possibility of its own sluggishness and the gift was bad because the estate might not be settled for more than twenty-one years. No very good example of this sort of decision has been found in Pennsylvania, but the cases from other jurisdictions are collected in 13 A. L. R. 1033 (1921). (Note that the courts were inclined to avoid this result by construing the instrument as creating vested estates whereever possible.) To be distinguished from the true "administrative contingency" type of case are such cases as 

Wraught's Estate, 347 Pa. 165 (1943), and others in 142

A. L. R. 136 (1943), where no perpetuity objection arises because the gift over is tied to the death of a living person (e. g. a gift to issue living at the widow's death if she dies before the estate is settled).

13 remoteness. The violation of the rule was the result of bad draftsmanship on the part of the scrivener rather than an attempt on the part of the testator to tie up property for too long a time. Under the statute, the remainders would be good in all the above examples, and these cases probably account for a large percentage of perpetuity litigation. 

There are, of course, other cases where the possibility of interests remaining unvested for too long a time is more than purely theoretical. If, for example, remaindermen are to be determined on the death of the survivor of the conveyor's grandchildren and his children are not advanced in years at his death, there might well be a postponement of vesting beyond a life in being and twenty-one years. In such cases, the common law possibility test was plausible if the court could be persuaded to determine in advance whether the interests were good or bad. 

Johnston's Estate, 185 Pa. 179 (1898), is an example of where the common law rule worked well because the court struck down the entire limitation at the very beginning. 

Testator had attempted to create a trust to pay the income to his issue for seventy-five years and at the end of that period to pay the principal to his issue then living. The court held that the whole trust was void because it would have served no purpose to attempt to separate the good estates from the bad.20 If all cases had been as simple as that one, there would have been no need to change the common law rule.

Decisions such as Johnston's Estate, however, were rare and becoming rarer in Pennsylvania. More often the court would uphold such of the life estates as would necessarily vest in time and would not even pass on the validity of the remote estates until the valid life interests had terminated. The rule was that the life estates would be allowed to stand unless it was plain that testator, had he known of the remainder's invalidity, would have preferred the whole scheme to fall. Since in most cases it was easy to find that testator was primarily interested in the life beneficiaries rather than in the remote remaindermen, it

 became the practice to uphold the life interests in all except the most unusual cases. 

The cases of both sorts are extensively reviewed in 

Quigley's Estate, 329 Pa. 281 (1938), and Laucks Estate, 358 Pa. 369 (1948),21 which are good examples of where the common law rule worked badly. In Quigley's Estate testator provided for a trust to pay the income to his son for life. The provisions for the disposition of income and principal following the death of the son became so involved that no one was quite sure what they meant. Under one possible construction there would be a suspension of vesting for too long a time, but the trustees argued for a construction under which all gifts would necessarily vest in time. The court held (1) that the life estate to the son was necessarily good, regardless of what was supposed to happen to the estate thereafter, (2) that even if some of the later income gifts and the ultimate gift of principal were bad under the rule against perpetuities, testator would not have wanted his whole trust to fail, (3) that therefore the estate must be awarded to the trustees for the benefit of the son in any event, and (4) all other questions were moot for the time being so that the disputed provisions in the will would not be construed until the son's death, even under the Declaratory Judgment Act. 

This upholding of the life estates and the postponement of decision on the validity of the remainders represented a conscientious attempt to soften the effect of the rule, but the practice destroyed the last vestige of logic in the common law possibility test. In Quigley's Estate, for example, the life estate of the son was upheld and the construction of the will in other respects was postponed. On his death, it is probable that the court will also uphold the next estate since it must necessarily vest in time. During all this time the remainder (or reversion, as the case may be) remains inalienable because nobody knows what the will means. At some time in the future, however, the terrible day will arrive when the court must meet the question of whether the later gifts of income and principal are valid. 

Suppose (as often is the case) things work out in such a

¶ 3 way that the principal in fact becomes distributable within twenty-one years after the son's death. Nevertheless, the ultimate gifts will be invalid under the common law rule if the will is construed in such a way that all interests might not have vested in time. The court in 1980 will decide the case as if it were being decided in 1934. 

The present statutory correction of this practice was not the only conceivable one. The possibility test might have been preserved and it might have been provided that in all cases the entire limitation, life estates and all, must either stand or fall together. There is something to be said for this solution from a practical standpoint, but it would have had some harsh results, particularly if an entire trust were stricken because of a merely theoretical possibility of remotedness. Another possible solution would have been to continue the common law practice in all respects but require the court to pass on the validity of the remainders at the beginning, so that the ultimate interests could be fixed and alienable during the period of the valid life estates. This would have been of some help so far as it went, but there were doubts as to both the propriety and constitutionality of such a statutory provision. 

There is wisdom in the rule that questions of future property rights should not be decided at a time when the parties who will be most interested are not yet born so that their case must be argued by a trustee ad litem. Furthermore, the courts might have regarded such a statute as an attempt to impose upon them the non-judicial duty of deciding moot questions. In view of these considerations, it seemed that the best solution was to preserve the practice of upholding the life interests together with the practice of postponing decision on the validity of the ultimate interests, but to abolish the possibility test altogether and permit the court to decide the case on the basis of what actually happened as of the time the permissible period expired.22 22. Another possible solution would have been to permit the court to strike down the entire trust in those rare cases where the good and the bad interests were inseparable and to provide for the measuring of the period by actual events only in those cases where the valid estates were upheld and the decision postponed. It was thought, however, that this would only cause additional questions and litigation and would complicate the provisions of §5 5266

¶ 4. Separation of Good from Bad Gifts Mandatory under

In cases such as Quigley's Estate, 329 Pa. 281 (1938), considered above, the operation of the statute will be fairly simple. Decision on the validity of the ultimate interests will be postponed as in the past, but when the permissible period has actually run its course the court will look at what actually occurred to determine whether all interests have vested in time-instead of pretending that the case were being decided at testator's death.

In cases such as Johnston's Estate, 185 Pa. 179 (1898), where the entire trust would have failed at common law, the effect of the statute will be somewhat more drastic.23 

If section 4 and section 5 are read together it is impossible to avoid the conclusion that all conveyances must be allowed to run until twenty-one years after the death of the last life in being regardless of how inseparable the good estates seem from the estates which might turn out to be bad. If section 4 (a) does not make this clear in itself,24 section 5 (c) certainly does, because the latter section assumes that there will be a person "entitled to the income at the end of the period 99 This might be unfortunate in certain rare cases. It might be better to throw out entirely a testamentary trust to pay income forever to such of testator's issue as are living when the income accrues. Nevertheless it would seem mandatory under the statute to allow such a trust to continue until twenty-one years after the death of the last survivor of testator's descendants who were living when he died. This is a necessary evil which the drafters of the statute were well aware of, but, as explained, it seemed impossible to eliminate cases of this sort from the operation of the statute without making the whole scheme hopelessly complex. Measuring the Period a. Lives in Being 

Actual rather than possible events will be used in measuring the period, but the period itself remains that "allowed by the common law rule against perpetuities"i. e. a life in being at the time of the conveyance plus twenty-one years. The older cases will continue to govern the question of what is the permissible period. 

25. See ¶ 5a infra for further discussion of Johnston's Estate. See also discussion of Lilley's Estate under §5 (¶5a) for an even more difficult type of case. 5268

¶ 5a 

ESTATES ACT 

 There is considerable case law on who can be considered a "life in being." The best treatment of this question is under section 374, comments j to 1 of the Restatement of Property (1944).26 The life in being is the survivor of persons named or described by the conveyor in connection with the gift in question. Thus, the conveyor may expressly designate a class of persons whose lives are to be the measure of the trust-and these persons do not necessarily have to be beneficiaries of or have any relation to the gift. He can apparently name as many living persons as he wishes in this connection subject to the qualification that they must not be so numerous as to preclude the possibility of proof. If no persons are expressly designated as the measuring lives, the period will be measured by the survivor of persons living at the time of the conveyance and having a reasonable relation to the gift. These authorities will continue to be as important as heretofore-the only difference being that the court will look to see how long the life in being actually lives, rather than assuming that he might have died the day after the conveyance. 

In the ordinary case, the settlor or testator does not expressly designate the lives in being but little difficulty is encountered in determining which lives have a reasonable relation to the gift within the meaning of the above rule. 

Thus, if there is a devise to A for life, then to A's children for their lives, with remainders over," the lives in being are plainly A and such of his children as are living at testator's death.

A somewhat more difficult case would be the following: Testator gives his estate to trustees to pay the income to his children and grandchildren with remainder to such of his grandchildren as reach the age of twenty-five. A similar gift was held bad at common law in Coggin's Appeal, 124 Pa. 10 (1889), because a grandchild might have been born after testator's death and he might have been under the age of twenty-five, twenty-one years after the

Under the statute, the choice of the life in being will be the same-i. e. the survivor of testator's children and grandchildren living at his death. These are all the persons having a reasonable relation to the gift and testator has mentioned no others.28 The trustees will carry out the trust according to its terms until twenty-one years after the death of the last survivor of such children and grandchildren. It may be that no other grandchildren will be born after testator's death, in which event the remainders will clearly vest in time. But even if a grandchild is born after testator's death, the gift to him will not necessarily be bad. Such grandchild might (and probably will) reach twenty-five prior to twenty-one years after the death of the other grandchildren. In the unlikely event that a grandchild is still under twenty-five twenty-one years after the death of the survivor of the lives in being, then the gift of the principal will be void and will pass according to section 5 of the act. 

In another type of case the lives in being were irrelevant at common law because the time for ultimate vesting was the end of a stated number of years with no reference to births or deaths of designated persons-as in Johnston's Estate, 185 Pa. 179 (1898), where the remainder was to go to testator's issue living 75 years after his death. At common law it was unnecessary to consider lives in being in such a case because all living persons might have died the day after testator anyway. Hence, the simple term of twenty-one years was used as the permissible period. See also Barton v. Thaw, 246 Pa. 348, 355 (1914). Under the statute, it is submitted that lives in being reasonably related to the gift should be used in measuring the period for actual vesting. With the possibility test discarded, it is no longer necessary to assume that everyone will die the day after testator's death, so that the reason for not con- 28. The children are measuring lives, not merely because they are income beneficiaries, but because they, as parents of the grandchildren, are related to the gift. As pointed out above, this is permissible as there is nothing in the rule against perpetuities which requires that the measuring lives be connected with the gift. Thus, a gift to testator's oldest male descendant living twenty-one years after the death of the survivor of such of testator's descendants as are living at testator's death was good at common law and will necessarily be good under the statute. Friday's Estate, 313 Pa. 328 (1933), is a Pennsylvania case of this sort.29

Courts and textwriters never tire of reiterating that the rule against perpetuities prohibits the postponement of vesting for too long a time but does not concern itself with postponed enjoyment.86 The statute in no way affects this aspect of the rule and the test remains whether an interest vests in time regardless of when it is to come into enjoyment. For example, a life estate to A followed by a life estate to A's unborn child with remainder on the child's death to the X corporation was good at common law and will necessarily be good under the statute, because the life estate in the unborn child must vest at or before the death of A and the remainder in X is vested from the beginning.37

In fact the bulk of perpetuity cases seem to involve disputes concerning the interpretation of instruments to determine when the various interests vest rather than disputes concerning the operation of the rule itself. Many such cases turn on whether an interest is contingent or is vested subject to divestment. 

The former is objectionable under the rule while the latter is not. An estate remains contingent so long as it is subject to a condition precedent-as a remainder "to A if living." But an interest can still be vested although it is subject to divestment on breach of condition subsequent -as a gift "to A in fee but if A dies survived by issue then to his issue." 39. The decision is sound and follows the Restatement view, but there is an age-old split on this precise question.40 

The old cases will continue to be as important under the present statute to determine whether an interest has actually vested in time as they were formerly to determine whether an interest would necessarily vest in time.

17. Reversions

The common law dogma is that any reversion is vested.42 Hence, no such interest would be void under section 4 (b). If there were any doubt on the subject it would be removed by section 4 (b) (1), exempting all interests exempt at common law, because reversions have never been subject to the rule.43 

The simplest type of case, where there is a complete failure to dispose of the remainder in fee after life estates, should give no trouble-a devise to A for life, then to A's unborn child for life with no provision in the will for the disposition of the estate on A's child's death. There is a simple reversion of the fee remaining in testator's heirs subject to the life estates. This reversion is vested from the moment of testator's death and is clearly a valid interest. There would be no void gift under section 4 (b) and nothing to dispose of under section 5.44 

Another case which should give no trouble is the ordinary case where there are cross remainders and hence no reversion at all-a devise to A for life then to A's unborn child for life with remainder in fee to the child's issue living at his death, or in the absence of issue to X. Under 

McCreary's Estate, 354 Pa. 347 (1946), discussed above (16), the remainders to the issue and to X are both contingent and together they exhaust the entire fee. Hence if A's child is still living twenty-one years after A's death the remainder is void under section 4 (b) and the entire

¶ 8. Class Gifts 

The reference in section 4 (b) to interests in members of a class the membership of which is subject to increase at the expiration of the period was inserted to preserve the common law rule applicable to certain types of class gifts where the members have technically vested interests but the class is subject to open. a. Entire Gift Contingent 

In the type of class gift most frequently found in well drafted instruments, there is no vesting at all until the class is finally determined-as a remainder on the death of A to his children "then living". No special provision is necessary for class gifts of this sort since they will stand or fall in their entirety under the general requirement that all interests must vest within the period. 

b. Class Subject to Increase 

It is necessary to consider the special provision for class gifts only in a case where the words "then living" are omitted. Suppose, for example, a will provides for a testamentary trust to pay the income to A for life, then to A's children for their lives (A being childless on testator's death) and on the death of the survivor of A's children to pay the principal per capita to A's grandchildren. 5277

ESTATES ACT 

¶ 8b After testator's death A has a child B who has children of his own. Twenty-one years after A's death, B is still living and has had two children, X and Y, both of whom are also living. Under general principles of property law, X and Y have vested interests although the class of remaindermen remains open to let in possible other children of B. X, for example, has an interest in the remainder which vested at the moment of his birth and cannot be wholly divested even if he dies before his father B, because there was no condition in the will that he must be living at B's death. However, the size of the interest X will ultimately enjoy cannot be determined because his presumptive share is decreased each time B has another child. If B has no other children beside X and Y, X's interest will be one-half, but if B has five more children, X's share will be reduced to oneseventh.

In view of this uncertainty as to the size of X's share, the common law treated it in the same manner as a contingent interest so far as the rule against perpetuities was concerned. The common law rule was that the class must necessarily close within the period." Under the statute, the class must actually close within the period even though it might not have. On the facts suggested the entire remainder would be void, but if B had died within twenty-one years after A's death the class would actually have closed in time and all gifts would be good under the statute. The practice of treating class gifts in the same manner as contingent gifts for perpetuity purposes until the class is closed has been criticized.48 Why cut off X and 

Y merely because another child of B might be born who would necessarily have to be excluded? On the whole, however, the rule seems sensible. If the entire gift is stricken down there is more likelihood in most cases of a fair division ultimately being accomplished through the

No special provision was necessary for gifts to a class subject to decrease in number, as such gifts can be handled under the general requirement of vesting. It would seem that on proper analysis there is only one type of case where there is a vesting in members of a class which is subject to decrease but not to increase; in all such cases the interest of each member is vested subject to divestment and should be treated accordingly. An instance of such a case is the following: A bequest of $10,000 to A for life (A being childless on testator's death) with remainder in fee to A's children living at his death payable to each such child when he reaches the age of thirty, but if any child dies before reaching thirty leaving issue surviving him, his share to pass to his issue. On the death of A each child has a vested interest subject to divestment if he dies leaving issue. As explained above under ¶ 6 and below under section 5 (¶ 4a), both at common law and under the statute the gifts to the children are valid and the law strikes down the divesting contingencies which last too long rather than striking down the gifts themselves. At common law all the children of 

A living at A's death took indefeasible interests.40 Under the statute, the interests would remain defeasible until twenty-one years after A's death and only then would the defeasance clause and gifts over be stricken down giving all children who had not previously died leaving issue an indefeasible interest regardless of whether they had reached thirty.

The scheme of the statute bears a deceiving resemblance to the common law rule as to testamentary powers of appointment. Actually the statute goes much further. 

The common law rules applicable to powers of appointment (other than general powers to appoint by deed-see infra section 4 (c)) are reviewed in Warren's Estate, 320 Pa. 112 (1936), and reaffirmed in Lewis's Estate, 349 Pa. 571 (1944). 

In Warren's Estate, testator had given his daughter a life estate with a general power to appoint by will. She appointed in trust for her children with contingent remainders over at the death of the survivor of them. The Orphans' 

Court, which was affirmed per curiam, upheld the appointment, recognizing the following principles: (1) The rule against perpetuities runs from the creation of the power and not the death of the donee. (2) If the power must necessarily be exercised within the permissible period, the fact that the donee might appoint in trust and postpone vesting for too long a time is of no consequence unless she in fact does so. (3) If the donee postpones vesting until the death of persons described as a class but who were in fact all alive at the death of the donor, the appointment is valid. 

It was found in Warren's Estate that the daughter's only children were in fact both born before their grandfather's death so that the appointment was valid. Actualities as of the date of the appointment were regarded in determining whether a designated life was "in being"" when the donor died. To this extent, the rule that the will of the donee is read into the will of the donor was qualified. 

But the possibility test was applied in all other respects. 5281

ESTATES ACT 

¶ 9b Plainly the statute goes further than this in that it provides that actualities both before and after the appointment will be regarded in determining whether the remainder vests in time. Following are examples of cases where the remainder would necessarily have been bad at a common law but might turn out to be good under the statute: 

1. Testator gives the income to his descendants and principal as the survivor of his grandchildren appoints by will. In this type of case Warren's Estate would have been of no help at common law because the power might have been exercised after the permissible period. Thus the power itself would have been invalid regardless of how it was exercised. Under the statute, however, the court will wait to see if the surviving grandchild dies within twenty-one years after the death of the survivor of such of testator's descendants as were living at the testator's death. If the surviving grandchild does in fact die within this period and appoints outright, the appointment is good. 

2. Testator gives a life estate to his daughter with a general power to appoint principal. She appoints income to her "children" with contingent remainders over at the death of the survivor. So far the case is like Warren's Estate. Let us suppose, however, that the daughter had three children, one of whom was born after testator's death. At common law this would take the case out of the rule of Warren's Estate and the remainder would be void. See McCreary's Trust, 354

Pa. 347 (1946). Under the statute, however, the appointed remainder will be valid if it in fact vests within twenty-one years after the death of the survivor of the two children who were alive when testator died. b. Appointment Invalid for Another Reason 

Lewis's Estate, 349 Pa. 571 (1944), reversing 49 D. &

C. 173 (O. C. Phila. 1943), aside from its importance as a re-affirmation of the rules of Warren's Estate, suggests an additional prceaution to be taken in applying the present sections to cases involving powers. In Lewis's Estate testator's daughter was given a special power to appoint 5282

9c 

ESTATES ACT 

 among her descendants. Instead, she attempted to include her husband and charities in the appointment as well as her children. The Supreme Court held that since she attempted to appoint beyond the restricted class, the entire appointment failed, including the attempted gifts to her children. Hence, since this part of the decision was based on the law relating to powers, rather than the law of perpetuities, it will not be affected by the present sections. 

If the donee's appointment is objectionable because it attempts to postpone vesting for too long a time, then under the present section, the valid income estates would necessarily be good and the court could not strike down the entire appointment. But if, as in Lewis's Estate, the appointment is objectionable for a reason other than a postponement of vesting, then the court will still be at liberty to decide that the various appointed estates are inseparable and that the appointment must fail in its entirety. Also the disposition of the void gift will be different. As explained under section 5 (5c), an appointed interest which is void only because it remains unvested beyond the period should pass under the statute. If the appointment is bad for another reason, however, the gift will pass under the provision for default of appointment in the will of the donor of the power.

¶ 1. General 

As explained in the general discussion of section 4 (a) & (b) the rule against perpetuities was invented as a curb on the use of contingent and executory interests to create what would amount to indestructible estates tail. Yet, if applied too literally, the rule would strike down other types 5301

ESTATES ACT 

¶ 1 of projects having a social value outweighing the disadvantage involved in the fettering of property. The common law courts realized this and made appropriate exceptions to the rule.

It was essential, therefore, to provide in the statute for exceptions to the general requirement of vesting within the period. This is done by clauses (1) to (4) of section 

4 (b). Certain types of conveyances, which either were or might have been subject to the common law rule, are excepted specifically-cemetery trusts by clause (2), pension. trusts by clause (3) and trustees' powers by clause (4). 

Clause (1), considered here, is a more general provision excepting all interests which were not subject to the common law rule. This will make the statute inapplicable not only to interests which the common law courts recognized as legitimate perpetuities for reasons of policy (such as charitable trusts) but also to interests which were illogically exempt for historical reasons (such as possibilities of reverter).

By referring generally to interests exempt at common law rather than attempting to enumerate all of them, this clause should preserve the fluidity of the case law on this aspect of the rule. Certain interests were clearly exempt at common law, but there are many situations where the case law on perpetuities has not yet frozen into rigid rules. 

With the common law" a part of the statute, the way should be clear for the courts to make new exceptions or overrule old ones without being hamstrung by the statute. 

It is to be hoped that the courts will recognize the freedom the statute gives them in this regard as new and unthoughtof problems arise in the future.¹

Often it is difficult to determine whether a certain type of case represents a real exception to the rule or whether it satisfies the rule according to its terms in that the interests are vested. In each type of case there are two questions to be answered: (1) Is a suspension of vesting for 1. The change in the wording of the act from that in the earlier draft originally published is significant. In the earlier draft the clause read: "Interests which have not heretofore been subject to the common law rule against perpetuities." The language was amended before submission to the Legislature for the purpose of avoiding any implication that the case law or the subject was to be frozen as of 1948. 5302

ESTATES ACT 

 too long a time really involved? (2) If so, does the social policy which underlies the rule against perpetuities require that such a suspension be declared unlawful?

Thus, reversions were said to be vested interests at common law so that it is not necessary to consider them as exceptions to the rule. The subject is treated at ¶7 under section 4 (a) & (b), supra. 

3. Reverters and Rights of Re-entry 

Certain types of interests remaining in the conveyor do not attain to the dignity of true reversions and are not regarded as vested estates at common law. These are possibilities of reverter and rights of re-entry for breach of condition.² An example of a possibility of reverter is the interest remaining in the conveyor after a grant to A and his heirs so long as the old oak tree stands. A right of re-entry remains in the conveyor in the case of a grant to A and his heirs with a provision for forfeiture if the premises are ever used for the sale of liquor. The distinction between the two is often narrow, but for present purposes the distinction is unimportant because neither reverters nor rights of re-entry were subject to the common law rule against perpetuities. See Pennsylvania Horticultural Society v. Craig, 240 Pa. 137 (1913); Erie v. Pennsylvania R. R., 246 Pa. 238, 241 (1914); Simes, Future In terests (1936) §§ 506 and 507; Restatement, Property (1944) § 372. 

It has frequently been pointed out that the exemption of these interests from the rule is supported by neither logic nor policy. Perhaps the door is not yet shut to rectifying the doctrine by court decision. Under the cases now on the books, however, these interests must be regarded as outside the common law rule and hence exempt by this clause of the statute. 

2. Described more broadly as "powers of termination" in Restatement, Property (1943) § 155. 

3. See Gray, Perpetuities (4th ed. 1942) § 304; Simes, Future Interests 

(1936) § 506.

14 Note that we are concerned here only with the case where there is no attempted gift over to another on the termination of the special limitation or breach of the condition. If after providing for the gift to A the instrument purports to make a gift to B when the oak tree falls or when the premises are used for the sale of liquor in the examples given, B's interest is plainly void under the rule and will vest in A under section 5 (b). The identical interest remaining in the conveyor, on the other hand, is considered valid. See further discussion of this distinction under section 5 (4c). ¶ 4. Charities

It is sometimes said that gifts to charities are exempt from the rule against perpetuities. This is not strictly true. A gift to charity which remains subject to a condition precedent at the expiration of the period is just as objectionable as any other remote gift. It is more helpful to say that for purposes of applying the rule, charity in the abstract is regarded as a beneficiary in which an interest can vest. 

Suppose, for example, a trust to pay the income to X hospital perpetually. It might be suggested that there is never any vesting in such a trust and that in any event a suspension of alienability results which is directly contrary to the policy of the rule. Or, if the patients who actually benefit from the gift are regarded as the beneficiaries, there would plainly be a postponement of vesting beyond the period. In effect, however, the law regards the charitable purpose itself as a sort of beneficiary. So regarded, the gift vests immediately and is valid.* 

Suppose, on the other hand, a testator creates a trust to pay the income to his issue perpetually with a gift to the X hospital if his issue should ever fail. Here, even

Hence, the gift to X hospital was necessarily bad at common law and would be bad under the statute if any of testator's issue were still living at the end of the period. To this extent the rule against perpetuities definitely does apply to charitable gifts.5

Note that charity in the abstract is the beneficiarynot the X hospital. This distinction is important in the following type of case: a trust to pay the income to X hospital perpetually, but if the X hospital ever closes, then to pay the income perpetually to the Y home for orphans. 

Let us suppose that after the expiration of the period (probably a simple 21 years, since no lives in being are involved) the X hospital closes. Is the gift to the Y home for orphans valid? The answer is yes. It is not necessary that the interest be vested in any particular institution. 

All that is required is that before the end of the period the property be unconditionally destined to charity generally.® 

Many cases concerning the application of the rule against perpetuities to charities involve the broader question of whether a particular gift is in fact charitable, as in Tollinger's Estate, 349 Pa. 393 (1944). The concept of a charitable purpose with respect to perpetuities is as broad as with respect to other legal problems, such as cy pres and accumulations. There is a definition of charitable purpose in section 1 (1) of this act. Strictly that definition does not apply here because there is no direct reference to charities in section 4 (b) (1). However, section 1 (1) merely restates the common law definition, so that the cases and principles there discussed will be equally applicable here. ¶ 5. Options

The rule condemning options which might be exercised at a remote time is generally recognized and probably represents sound policy." The fettering of property caused by such agreements is particularly evident if the option. price is greater than the market value of the property. 

The owner of the option will of course not exercise it nor will its value be readily ascertainable for purposes of release to the owner of the fee. On the other hand, the owner of the fee will naturally be unwilling to develop the property.

It would seem, however, that even regarded as a personal right the unlimited option contract with regard to a particular item of property is void under the better view. According to the Restatement, the doctrine applies with respect to both real and personal property, and if the agreement is breached an action will not lie for damages. See general discussion of contract rights, ¶ 8 infra.

Where the holder of the option is the tenant under a long term lease such an agreement tends to sponsor rather than hinder the development of the property. A similar exception is made by the Restatement where the option relates to unissued shares of a corporation.¹2 

These exceptions indicate that the doctrine of Barton v. Thaw cannot be regarded as a blanket condemnation of all remote options. Properly stated the rule should be that an option which remains outstanding after the permissible period is void as a perpetuity unless there is no potential fettering of property or unless such fettering is outweighed by other considerations of policy. 

16. Easements and Profits

The subject of easements and profits under the rule against perpetuities is carefully analyzed in the comments to section 399 of the Restatement of Property (1944). 

Ordinarily an easement creates a present, vested interest and the fact that such interest may extend for a remote period is irrelevant so far as the law of perpetuities is concerned. This is so even if the right is to cut timber or remove coal with a provision for payment at the time the right is exercised.

If land is granted to A and his heir with the provision that upon the failure of A's issue at any time in the future, B shall have the right to remove coal from the premises, there is no reason why the interest of B should not be subject to the rule. Nor is there any reason why an option to mine coal in the future, conditional upon the payment of a fixed sum, should not be subject to the rule of Barton v. 17. Mortgages and Security Transactions 

Gray has pointed out that long term mortgages might violate the letter of the rule against perpetuities in that the interest of the mortgagor remains conditional until maturity. He suggested, however, that they should be allowed as exceptions to the Rule. In Knightsbridge Estates Trust v. Byrne, (1938) Ch. 741, (1939) Ch. 441, the Chancellor and Court of Appeals considered the problem and decided that the rule was never designed to strike down interests of this sort, and that the rights of the mortgagor were unobjectionable in a mortgage for a term of more than twentyone years. The House of Lords affirmed with only a passing reference to the problem.15 

Whatever the rationale, it seems clear that mortgages are not subject to the common law rule and hence will be excepted from the statute by section 4 (b) (1). The 

Knightsbridge case is valuable not only as a clear holding to the effect, but also as an example of the refusal of the courts to strike down remote interests which do not constitute the sort of thing the rule was designed to prevent. 

As such, the case should have a broader significance. 

Other types of security transactions where a technical violation of the rule is more apparent should also be exempt for the same general reason, wherever it appears that no fettering of property or a justifiable one is involved. Again it becomes evident that the rule against perpetuities does not necessarily strike down interests which remain contingent beyond the permissible period. If the transaction involves values other than the desire to perpetuate the prestige of a family name, premises must be re-examined to determine whether the game is worth the candle.

8. Contractual Rights-Insurance 

The dogma is that "a transaction which is exclusively contractual is not subject to the rule against perpetuities." 

Restatement of Property (1944) § 401.16 The word "exclu sively" is important because, as pointed out above (under ¶ 5-"Options"), a contract giving potential rights in particular property might create an interest in such property and make the transaction subject to the rule. But an ordinary contract unrelated to any specific property, even when the promisee remains unidentified until a remote time, is said to involve "no fettering of any property and hence there is no occasion for applying the rule against perpetuities.'' 17

The conclusion is probably correct for historical reasons, but the justification for the exemption seems fallacious. Under the same reasoning, trusts where the trustee has the power of sale, or where the corpus consists of debts of a third person would not be subject to the rule regardless of when the beneficial interests vested. Plainly, however, the rule applies whether or not title to a particlar piece of land or a particular tangible chattel is fettered, and as pointed out at ¶ 2b under section 4 (a) & (b) the policy of the law in this respect seems sound. 

A simple contract by A to pay B $1000 a hundred years hence is unobjectionable under any theory, because even if the rule against perpetuities applied to contracts, B would have what amounts to a vested remainder subject to a term of years. Suppose, however, A promises to pay $1000 to such of B's issue as are living a hundred years hence. According to the Restatement and such cases as there are on the subject, this contract is unobjectionable under the rule. 

Yet, in the first case (where B was the sole obligee) if B had assigned A's note to X in trust to pay the principal to such of B's issue as might be living a hundred years hence, the trust would violate the rule.

Honorary Trusts-Validity Apart from Rule Against Perpetuities 

So-called "honorary trusts", where no particular beneficiary is named but the trustee is directed to use property for a specific non-charitable purpose, raise problems which continue to baffle the theorists. Such trusts are objectionable for a number of reasons apart from the rule against perpetuities: the absence of a beneficiary is aesthetically offensive, and the existence of a duty with no person capable of enforcing it is said to be illusory. The subject is extensively treated in Scott on Trusts (1939) 

§ 124 et seq. According to Scott and the Restatement of 

Trusts § 124, an honorary trust (which does not violate the rule against perpetuities and is not contrary to public policy) creates a power in the trustee to apply property for the designated purpose; there is no enforceable duty to do so, but if the trustee fails to use the property as directed, he holds it on resulting trust for the next of kin or residuary beneficiaries. 

In Devereux's Estate, 48 D. & C. 491, 499 (O. C. Phila. 

1943), the court expressed the opinion that Pennsylvania goes further than the Restatement and recognizes directions of this sort as true trusts, imposing a duty on the 1. Designated as such because, there being no beneficiaries to call the trustee to account, the trustee is on his honor. The term might not be entirely appropriate in Pennsylvania in view of what the court said in Devereux's Estate, infra in the text. 5352

ESTATES ACT 

§ 4 (b) (2) trustee which the court itself will enforce if necessary.✓ 

After considering such cases as Stoffel's Estate, 295 Pa. 

248 (1929), and others, the court in Devereux's Estate concluded (at p. 500) "that in Pennsylvania this type of bequest is regarded as a trust, possessing all the essential incidents thereof; that the trustee becomes vested with a legal estate-not merely a power-with the duty of applying it to the purpose of the trust; that the lack of a cestui que trust, which normally results in there being no one having standing to compel the trustee to perform, is here supplied by the power and implementation of orphans' courts to supervise and control the activities of the trustee, suo moto, or upon the application of or on the failure of the testator's next of kin."2

As already indicated, honorary trusts are sometimes completely void because they are capricious and against public policy. Thus, in Palethorp's Estate, 249 Pa. 389, 410 (1915), testator had directed that $150,000 be set aside for the care of the family burial lot, providing among other things that a person be employed perpetually to "show people where it is". The latter provision was invalidated and the amount of the trust reduced to $10,000. It is plain that the court considered the provision for a guide objectionable quite apart from the rule against perpetuities. The case is similar in a great measure to Detwiller v. Hartman, 37 N. J. Eq. 347, where a testator directed the maintenance of a military band to march to his grave on the anniversary of his death and other holidays and play funeral marches and other appropriate music, and it was held that the object of the testator was to perpetuate the memory of his family name in a manner which could confer no public benefit or use. So certainly would be this testator's direction for a perpetual barker." Note that Palethorp's Estate is also authority for the reduction of honorary trusts of excessive amounts, even in the absence of a specific capricious direction.

3. Honorary Trusts-Perpetuity Objection 

The various explanations as to why an honorary trust of unlimited duration is objectionable as a perpetuity are reviewed in Scott on Trusts (1939) § 124.1.4 While the authorities disagree as to the theory of the objection, they all seem to agree that if a trust for a non-charitable purpose might last more than a life in being and twenty-one years it violates the rule against perpetuities, or (according to Gray) an analogous rule of law. See, for example, Stephan's Estate, 129 Pa. Super. 396 (1937).

Under the general provisions of 4 (a) and (b) of the present statute, it would seem that honorary trusts of any sort (assuming the requirements discussed under the preceding heading are satisfied) should be allowed to run the permissible period before being stricken, although this might raise some insoluble problems under section 5. Suppose a testator provides for a trust of a reasonable sum to use the income for the care of his parrot and on the death of the bird to distribute the principal to testator's descendants then living. At common law the trust would have been bad from the beginning because the care of the parrot might last more than the permissible period and the re-

4. Cemetery Trusts

The usual trust for the upkeep of graves and burial places could scarcely be called capricious—if they were, an ordinary direction for the erection of a tombstone would be invalid. Of course, if the amount directed to be retained is excessive the court will cut it down, and if there are collateral provisions for brass bands and guides, the court will have no trouble eliminating these from the legitimate provisions as in Palethorp's Estate, 249 Pa. 389 (1915), discussed above. Subject to those qualifications, however, it seems clear that cemetery trusts were generally valid at common law but that if the duration of such a trust was not properly limited, it was objectionable as a perpetuity. 

If the grave was situated in a churchyard, the court might have strained a point to regard it as charitable, but unless some connection with a charity could be shown, the trust was bad, in the absence of statute, if it was to last for more than a life in being and twenty-one years. See generally Scott on Trusts (1939) § 124.2; Deaner's Estate, 98 

Pa. Super. 360, 364 (1929).

Apparently the question was seldom raised in Pennsylvania but in Trustees of M. E. Church of Wells v.

Gifford, 5 County 92 (O. C. Bradford 1888), a perpetual trust for the upkeep of a grave was declared void. The rule against perpetuities was not mentioned, but the court was plainly more shocked by the unlimited duration of the trust than by its purpose. "... Under this will

Since that time, trusts for the upkeep of graves have been exempt from the rule against perpetuities. The present statute merely continues the act of 1891.

As pointed out in the Commissioners' comments, the phrase to the effect that such trusts should be considered "charitable" has been omitted in order to avoid the implication that such trusts are to be considered as charities for other purposes such as cy pres, accumulations, mortmain restrictions and the like-but in this the new act merely confirms the results already reached by the cases." 

In other respects also the new provision conforms to what would undoubtedly have been construed as the law under the act of 1891. 12. Background 

The genesis of this flurry of statutory provisions is well known. Due to their tax advantages pension trusts for employees have in recent years become tremendously popular. It was often impossible, however, to draw up a workable trust of this sort without providing for a suspension of vesting which might last for more than a life in being and twenty-one years. The benefit to the deceased or retired employee would generally be contingent upon a number of factors and the trust could not feasibly be limited to those who were employed or in being at the time of its creation. True, new contributions were usually made for new employees, but quite apart from the necessary mingling of the funds, no contribution could be definitely earmarked for any particular employee even as to amount because other factors beside length of service usually entered into the calculations of the benefit. Saving clauses, such as one would put in a will when a technical violation of the rule is feared, could not be inserted without giving the employees at the end of the period a windfall or providing for a reversion to the corporation which might have been regarded as objectionable taxwise under the requirements of the Revenue Code. 

The potential invalidity of such trusts was not too serious as a practical matter. The corporation itself would be the only party in a position to complain, and this was scarcely likely. Nor was it likely that a Washington theorist would upset the Government's policy with regard to such trusts by questioning their effectiveness. Furthermore, an attack on a bona fide pension trust as a violation of the rule against perpetuities, even if attempted, would probably have been unsuccessful. Admittedly many such plans involve a long suspension of vesting and a fettering of property. So do long term mortgages (according to 

Gray) and charitable trusts, although such transactions were exempt from the rule at common law. As pointed out in the discussion of clause (1) of this subsection, the rule against perpetuities was not designed and has not been applied as a blanket condemnation of all suspension of vesting beyond the period. A pension trust is certainly 5403

§(b) (3) 

ESTATES ACT 

[3 outside the purpose of the rule and it is difficult to imagine an enlightened court's not recognizing such a trust as an exception. 

The general question of the validity of pension trusts under the common law of perpetuities is discussed in detail by Lauritzen in 24 Taxes 519 (1946). See also Simes, "Trends in the Law" 44 Mich. L. Rev. 833, 837 (1946).

With the passage of the present acts, Pennsylvania has joined several other states in specifically exempting trusts of this sort from the rule against perpetuities in order to eliminate any possible doubt. 

¶ 3. General 

The wording of clause (3) was carefully drafted in an attempt to make it broad enough to validate a variety of transactions without opening the door to real evasions of the rule against perpetuities. The exemption applies not only to pension trusts and profit sharing plans but to any other "employee benefit plan" whatever it might be called. 

Note also that the benefits under the plan need not be limited to employees but may include "their families or appointees." Thus, provisions for widows' and children's benefits or benefits to pass under the employee's will or under a beneficiary designation will not be fatal. Nor will provisions for benefits to those outside the class (such as a provision for a reversion to the corporation in case of liquidation) be objectionable so long as the trust is "primarily" for the employees, their families or appointees. 

On the other hand, there are various limitations to the exemption which can be enumerated as follows: (1) The trust must be "bona fide". The courts will be able to read as much or as little into this requirement as they wish. Admittedly a vague term, it was inserted to discourage evasions without hamstringing the court by a rigid limitation. A typical case where this requirement of good faith might be useful would be where a settlor attempts to use a pension trust as a form for creating a perpetuity for his issue-as by organizing a family corporation with his descendants as the only employees. It should be per- 5404

ESTATES ACT 

missible to inquire into a settlor's motives in such a case in view of the requirement that the trust be created in good faith. (2) The trust must be created "inter vivos". 

Gifts by will in favor of employees where vesting is postponed too long will not be exempt, at least by this particular clause of the statute. See Lauritzen's article and discussion supra (12) for possible defenses of such trusts at common law. Note also that a testamentary trust for employees will be permitted to run the actual period of the rule in any event under the general provisions of section 4 (a) and (b). (3) The employees must be "business employees". The intent here was to exclude trusts for domestic servants and the like. 

4. Validation of Old Trusts 

As already noted, this clause will apply only to trusts created on or after January 1, 1948, although the similar provision in the act of 1947, P. L. 477, 20 P. S. § 3261, will except from the common law rule those trusts created between June 5, 1947 and January 1, 1948, and will make attack on trusts created prior to June 5, 1947, impossible after two years from that date. Thus, the only remaining risk of invalidity is with respect to trusts created before June 5, 1947, and even this will disappear after June 5, 1949. If, in spite of this and in spite of the improbability of anyone's ever attacking a pension trust, it is thought advisable to eliminate any doubt as to old pension trusts, this can easily be done. Assume for the sake of argument that the trust is wholly or partially invalid. At common law this would result in a reversion by operation of law in the corporation itself. If, therefore, the corporation were to make a transfer of this reversion to the trustee under the same deed of trust to be held and applied as therein directed, this transfer, having been made after January 1, 1948, would be subject to the Estates Act. Hence the new trust created by the transfer of the supposed reversion. from the old trust would be exempt from the rule against perpetuities. 5405 [The next page is 5451]

COMMISSIONERS' COMMENT-This clause is included to clarify and change the common law rule as to such interests which either might be or definitely are subject to the present rule against perpetuities.

Old Law 

There was no earlier statute on the subject. At common law remote powers to sell and the like were probably valid, but powers to determine what is principal and what is income would probably have been treated as powers of appointment and hence void if exercisable after the permissible period. Discussion 

1. Power to Sell, Lease, Mortgage, Etc. 

¶2. Powers over Principal and Income.

This clause removes certain theoretical doubts concerning powers of sale and the like, and changes the law with respect to powers over principal and income. 

1. Power to Sell, Lease, Mortgage, Etc.

This clause was inserted in order to put an end to fears concerning the validity of trustees' powers in trusts which endure beyond the period allowed by the rule although all the beneficial interests vest in time. The problem does not arise in the usual case where no vesting occurs until the time for distribution. Suppose, however, a devise of Blackacre in trust to pay income to A for life, then to A's unborn 5451

§ (b) (4) 

ESTATES ACT 

1 child for life, with remainder in fee to the X corporation. 

All the estates necessarily vest at or before A's death so that there is no violation of the rule against perpetuities even at common law. Suppose, now, that the trustee in this case were given the power to sell Blackacre at any time and reinvest the proceeds. The theorists generally agreed that there was nothing objectionable about such a power, but for some reason the bench and bar continued to be haunted by the superstition that powers of this sort were void as perpetuities.¹ The fallacy probably arose from the deceptive resemblance of the above case to other types of cases where there was a real objection. 

In the first place, the trustee's power of sale in the above case has been confused with powers to appoint beneficial interests. As was pointed out in the discussion of section 4 (a) & (b), ¶ 9, a testamentary power of appointment which might be exercised more than twentyone years after the death of the lives in being was void as a perpetuity at common law. Plainly there is no similarity between such a power of appointment and a trustee's power to sell, except that they are both called powers. 

Some early English decisions confused the two types of powers, however, and the law has been clouded ever since. 

The second type of case which might give the erroneous impression that a trustee's power of sale must not endure beyond the permissible period is where a vesting of the beneficial interests is tied to the exercise of the power. Suppose, for example, Blackacre is devised to trustees to sell and distribute the proceeds to such of testator's issue as are living when the property is sold. This was plainly objectionable as a perpetuity at common law, not because the power might be exercised beyond the period, but because the beneficial interests might not vest in time. The case is quite different from the ordinary trust for the sale of a property where all interests are vested from the beginning and the sale is the occasion for distribution rather than ascertainment of the beneficiaries. 

1. See generally Gray, Rule Against Perpetuities (4th ed. 1939) §§ 481, 487 

et seq.; Simes, Future Interests (1936) $539; Restatement, Property (1944) § 382; Leach "Powers of Sale in Trustees and the Rule Against Perpetuities," 47 

Harv. L. Rev. 948 (1934). 5452

ESTATES ACT 

§ 4 (b) (4) In the latter case the owners of this beneficial interest can terminate the trust by agreement at any time so that there is never any fettering of property. 

Trusts to facilitate sales suggest a third type of case involving powers of sale where the trust is objectionable for another reason. Suppose in the example originally given (a trust for A for life, then for A's unborn child. for life with remainder to the X corporation) there is a spendthrift provision applicable by its terms to any income beneficiary. There is still no violation of the rule against perpetuities, but there might be a violation of an analogous rule of law prohibiting trusts which remain indestructible beyond a life in being and twenty-one years.2 

The policy of both rules is the same but they are historically separate and distinct. The law frowns on the fettering of property beyond a certain period. The rule against perpetuities prevents indirect fettering which might be caused by the creation of contingent future estates. The law of restraints prevents direct fettering, for the most part by prohibiting them absolutely, although certain types of direct restraints on equitable interests have been upheld for reasons of public policy—such as spendthrift and separate use provisions in trusts. There is a sound doctrine, however, that even these legitimate direct restraints should not be permitted to last beyond a life in being and twenty-one years. Otherwise the conveyor will be able to do directly what the rule against perpetuities prohibits him from doing indirectly. Thus, in the example given, A's child and X could not join in terminating the trust if the spendthrift provision were considered valid, and the property would be fettered beyond the period allowed by the rule against perpetuities. For this reason the spendthrift provision is probably invalid as to A's child's interest at least after twenty-one years have elapsed from 

A's death.

It will be seen immediately that the objection to the spendthrift clause in the case suggested has nothing to do with the trustee's power of sale. Indeed the restraint would be even more objectionable if the trustee had no 2. Nevertheless, it was thought advisable to eliminate any doubt on the subject by the insertion of the present clause. Like the corresponding provision in the Restatement of Property (1944) § 382, the clause covers not only powers of sale but also powers to mortgage, to lease, to name successor trustees, and any other power which contributes "to the effective management of trust estates. Also like the Restatement, the statute does not require that such powers be given to the trustee. The beneficiaries might be given the power to name successor trustées, for example, or in an unusual case a person other than the trustee might be given the power of sale. 

On the other hand, the exception only relates to administrative powers themselves. A postponement of vesting until property is sold will still be objectionable if the property actually remains unsold at the expiration of the period. And there is nothing in this clause affecting the law relating to indestructible trusts, whatever the Pennsylvania law on that subject might be. 

2. Powers over Principal and Income

In one respect this clause goes further than merely restating the enlightened view at common law. Under the statute a power "to determine what is principal and what is income" is excepted from the rule so that such a power can continue beyond the period. A power of this sort is a little different from purely administrative powers in that it affects the beneficial interests. Hence, it would probably have been invalid at common law in a trust which was to last beyond a life in being and twenty-one years, although no case dealing with the question has been found. With the increasing complexity of principal and income problems, however, it is certainly reasonable to permit such powers to extend for the full duration of the trust. 

Note that the apparent broadness of the exception of "powers to determine what is principal and what is in- 5455

12 come" is limited by the phrase at the beginning of the clause to the effect that the power must "contribute to the effective management of trust assets." The intent was merely to allow the trustee leeway with respect to receipts and expenses in the twilight zone between items which are clearly principal and those which are clearly income. In this regard, the clause is comparable to section 6 (8) of this act making a similar exception to the law of accumulations. 5456 [The next page is 5501]

ESTATES ACT §4. RULE AGAINST PERPETUITIES (Continued) 

(c) Time for Beginning Period

The period allowed by the common law rule against perpetuities under subsection (b) of this section shall be measured from the expiration of any time during which one person while living has the unrestricted power to transfer to himself the entire legal and beneficial interest in the property.

COMMISSIONERS' COMMENT-The period would begin as of the death of a donee of a power who could appoint by deed or by will (Mifflin's Ap., 121 Pa. 205), but not where the power is to appoint by will alone: Lawrence's Est., 136 Pa. 354. For revocable trusts the period would begin as of the settlor's death. 

For an unfunded life insurance trust the period would be measured from the insured's death unless the trust was irrevocable and the policies were also irrevocably assigned to the trustee See Leach, 51 Harv. L. R. 638, 662. 

Old Law

There was no earlier statute on the subject. The Supreme Court had held that the common law period did not run while one person had a general power to appoint by deed, and there were other indications that the rule did not run while the remote interests were destructible. 

This section restates the common law rule.

Discussion 

1. Unrestricted Power in One Person. 

12. Restricted Powers. 

1. Unrestricted Power in One Person

This section is in accord with the common law which has always recognized that destructible estates are not forbidden by the rule against perpetuities regardless of their remoteness. As emphasized in the short history of the common law rule under section 4 (a) & (b) (12), from the earliest time it was only the indestructible future estate which was called a "perpetuity." The estate tail was a "perpetuity" under the Statute De Donis, but only until 5501

§ (c) ESTATES ACT 

¶ 1 the common recovery was invented as a device to bar the entail. The contingent remainder, on the other hand, became a potential "perpetuity" only after it was recognized as indestructible by the first taker. 

The modern authorities have also recognized that the period of the rule against perpetuities does not begin to run until the future estate becomes indestructible. There is some disagreement concerning cases of qualified destructibility (see below) but the authorities generally agree that if one person has a power to transfer the fee to himself, there is no fettering of property until that power expires. See Restatement, Property (1944) § 373; Leach, "Perpetuities in a Nutshell," 51 Harv. L. Rev. 638, 662 (1938); Simes, Future Interests (1936) § 515 et seq. 

In Pennsylvania it was long ago recognized that destructible estates were not within the purview of the rule. 

In Mifflin's Appeal, 121 Pa. 205 (1888), a life tenant with a general power to appoint the fee by deed or will appointed by will in trust to her children for their lives with remainder to their issue. It was held that the period of the rule was to be measured from the exercise of the power and not the date of the original deed, because the power could have been exercised by deed so that the fee was "neither inalienable nor indestructible" until the testatrix died. In Phillips's 

Estate, Phila. Legal Int. Nov. 17, 1947, p. 1 (O. C. Phila. adjudication Oct. 15, 1947) the same principle was applied to a revocable insurance trust. Since the settlor could have destroyed all future estates at any time during his lifetime, the period of the common law rule against perpetuities did not begin to run until settlor's death. And in McCreary's 

Trust, 354 Pa. 347, 349 (1946), section 373 of the Restatement of Property is quoted with approval. 

The principle that destructible estates are not subject to the rule is so clear from both history and authority that the only wonder is that it was ever questioned. The doubts on the subject probably arose from the frequent definition of a perpetuity as an estate which might remain unvested for a remote time. Under that definition, the contingent remainders in Mifflin's Appeal would have been perpetuities, because the case was not decided on the ground that 5502

¶

ESTATES ACT 

the donee of the power had a fee. The explanation of 

Mifflin's Appeal is rather that the common law rule against perpetuities did not strike down all remote unvested interests but only interests which remained both unvested and indestructible for too long a time.¹ 

Whether the power is exercised was of no moment so long as it existed. Thus, there was no real cause for concern when a court in another connection would say that a power to revoke which remains unexercised at the death of the owner is "a dead thing”—as in Murphey v. C. I. T., 347 Pa. 591 (1943), dealing with the immunity of the principal of a revocable trust from attack by the settlor's creditors. It is perfectly true that under property concepts even an unrestricted power over the fee is not the fee. Nevertheless, the existence of the power prevented the fettering of property which the common law rule against perpetuities was designed to prohibit. 

The present provision of the Estates Act merely continues this ancient principle of the common law. It should apply in the following common types of cases: 

1. A life estate coupled with a general power to appoint the remainder by deed. The period of the rule will begin to run only from the exercise of the poweror from the death of the donee, if the power remains unexercised.2 

2. A trust with a general power to revoke in the settlor. The period of the rule will begin to run at the settlor's death." 3. An unfunded insurance trust where settlor retains control of the policies. The period will run from settlor's death. (There is really no problem here, because if settlor remains the owner of the policies, there is no corpus and hence no trust at all until settlor dies.) 

4. A testamentary trust to pay income to testator's son for life, then to the son's children for their lives 1. And even this was subject to the exceptions discussed under sections

2. Restricted Powers 

By the wording of this subsection, the power must be (1) in one person, (2) unrestricted, (3) sufficiently general to enable the owner to transfer the fee to himself, and (4) exercisable during the owner's life. These limitations are also in harmony with the better view at common law. The subject is discussed in detail in Simes, Future Interests (1936) $$ 514 et seq. and 538. There has been some dissent 5504

ESTATES ACT § 4 (c) 

from this view on the ground that if the fee is legally alienable within the period-even though the concurrence of two or more persons is necessary, or even though the power can be exercised by will only-the purpose of the rule is not violated in spite of the remoteness of vesting. If a conveyance is made to A in fee but if A's issue should ever die out at any time then to B in fee, A and B together have the power to convey the fee at modern law. As Simes points out, however, there is a practical fettering if human nature is taken into account. B is not likely to release his interest for nothing and there is no way of valuing this interest if A wants to buy him off. Thus, the practical fettering is greater than if both interests were vested-as where A has a life estate and B a vested remainder. Similarly, if there is a devise to A for life with general power to appoint the remainder by will followed by remote gifts over (other than to A's heirs) in default of appointment, it can plausibly be argued that A's power being absolute at the moment of his death the period of the rule should be tolled at that time. Realistically, however, A, if he is human, will not have the same motive to cut off the remote interests as he would if he had the power to appoint to himself by deed. 

The giants of property law have wrangled over this question, but Pennsylvania and most American jurisdictions have taken the view that a power to appoint by will only is not enough to toll the running of the period. See discussion of "Powers of Appointment” (¶ 9a) under section 4 (a) & (b) supra. The present provision of the statute adopts this strict view in all cases. Following are examples of where this subsection would not apply to toll the running of the period: 

1. The life beneficiary of a trust is given the power to terminate the trust if he pays $10,000 to his child. 

The power is restricted and hence is insufficient to toll 5. Historically, the unbending insistence on vesting was probably due to the fact that unvested interests were inalienable at early common law. See dis cussion of "Future Interests . under §1 (a) (14) of the Wills Act for the Pennsylvania cases on the alienability of such interests under modern law. 

6. See summary of the conflicting views in Simes, Future Interests (1936) 

§ 538.

2. An inter vivos trust revocable by settlor with the consent of his wife. The power is restricted so that the period of the rule is measured from the date of the deed. 

3. General power to revoke subject to a life estate in settlor's wife. The power is not over the entire interest and hence is insufficient-unless the wife predeceases the settlor, whereupon (under the actuality test in § 4 (b)) the future estates would become destructible and the running of the period would be tolled under this subsection (c). 

4. Estates to A for life, then to A's unborn child for life, then in fee to B if living otherwise to C. After

5. A trust giving a life estate to A (who is childless at the time of the conveyance), followed by life estates to A's children for their lives with power in the survivor of A's children to appoint the remainder in fee by deed. This in effect was In re Hargreaves, L. R. 5 Eq. 383 (1868), where the remainder was held bad at common law. It would also be bad under the statute, unless the last survivor of A's children were ascertained within twenty-one years of A's death. The fact that all of A's children could join in conveying the fee after A's death is insufficient because the power is not in one person. 

6. Life estate to A and a general power in A to appoint the remainder in fee by will, with a gift in default of appointment to A's children. The power is broad enough to permit A to appoint to his own estate. 

Nevertheless the power, which cannot be exercised by A "while living," is insufficient to toll the running of the period. See McCreary's Trust, 354 Pa. 347, 350 (1946). Note that the gift in default of appointment to designated persons (rather than to the donee's 5506
