85. RULE AGAINST PERPETUITIES DISPOSITION WHEN INVALIDITY OCCURS. 

(a) Valid Interests Following Void Interests. 

A valid interest following a void interest in income shall be accelerated to the termination date of the last preceding valid interest. 

(b) Void Interests on Condition Subsequent or Special Limitation. 

A void interest following a valid interest on condition subsequent or special limitation shall vest in the owner of such valid interest. 

COMMISSIONERS' COMMENT- (c) Other Void Interests. 

Any other void interest shall vest in the person or persons entitled to the income at the expiration of the period described in Section 4 (b). 

Another significant change in present law does not involve the rule against perpetuities itself, but rather the question of what should be done with interests which are held to be void under the rule. Under the law in effect until the effective date of this act such void gifts (a) fall into the residue, or (b) pass to other residuary beneficiaries under section 15 (c) of the Wills Act of 1917, or (c) pass to the settlor's heirs or next of kin as of the date of his death. While these results seem appropriate in cases of lapsed gifts, they are not appropriate when applied to gifts void as perpetuities.

One objection to the law as it has been heretofore is a purely practical one. In most cases where prior gifts were upheld and only the remote remainders were invalidated, those who took the void gifts were deceased when the remainders came into enjoyment and the perpetuity questions were decided. 

It therefore became necessary to trace each reversion through one or more estates with consequent administration and tax difficulties.

A more serious objection to the former law arose in all cases where the invalid limitation was in favor of the settlor's descendants or of other primary objects of his bounty and the gift was either not in the residuary clause of the will or comprised only part of the residuary gift. In such a case the void remainder might be wholly or partially diverted from the family, or to another branch of the family which had already received its full share of the estate, without leaving any share to the issue of the income beneficiary. Perfect justice cannot be done 5551

§ 

ESTATES ACT 

in all cases, but an award of the void interests to the income beneficiaries at the expiration of the period will bring about equitable distribution in accordance with the settlor's most probable intent in all except the most unusual cases. Void remainders are usually to the issue of a life tenant, so that the void gift will usually go to the parent of the disappointed remainderman. In the rare cases where this will not be the result, the award to the last valid life tenant may be arbitrary, but no more so than dispositions which have taken place under the former law. [Subsection (a)] This is in accord with general principles of law which favor acceleration in the absence of some definite reason to the contrary. [Subsection (b)] Special provision for estates on condition subsequent or special limitation is necessary in order not to change the very sensible results reached by the common law in cases of remote conditions subsequent followed by void gifts over. In such cases the first taker is awarded the estate freed of the condition: Cf. 

Bilyeu's Est., 346 Pa. 134. It will be seldom indeed that the owner of the estate on a remote condition subsequent or on a special limitation is not also the income beneficiary at the expiration of the period so that he will be covered in any event by the general provisions of subsection (c) infra. However, the unusual situation where this might not be the case is provided for. 5?]. [Subsection (c)] See comment to section 4 (a) [general comment to section 

Old Law 

Under prior case law valid remainders following void income estates were accelerated and estates subject to a remote condition subsequent took free of the condition. In other cases the void interest reverted to the estate of the conveyor and passed as undisposed of property except in those cases covered by section 15 (c) of the Wills Act of 1917, P. L. 403 (lapsed and void devises and legacies falling into residue or passing to other residuary legatees) which is now replaced by section 14 (9) & (10) of the present Wills Act. 

Subsection (a) restates the common law. Subsection (b) restates the common law as to interests on conditions subsequent but changes it as to gifts on special limitation. Subsection (c) changes the common law by awarding the void interest to the person entitled to the income at the end of the period rather than allowing it to pass by intestacy or under section 14 (9) and (10) of the Wills Act. 5552

Cases of Reverters and Rights of Re-entry Distinguished. ¶ 1. General

This section has already been discussed in a general way under section 4 (a) & (b) (1). As there explained, section 5 represents the second of the two important changes from prior law accomplished by the statute. Subsections (a) and (b) of section 5 will apply to unusual cases and for the most part restate the common law applicable to these situations. Subsection (c), however, will radically change prior law with respect to the disposition of void perpetuities in the great majority of cases. 

The reasons for changing the prior law in this respect are adequately explained in the Commissioners' comments. 

An example of the unsatisfactory results required by the old law would be the following: Testator leaves the residue of his estate one-half outright to his son A and the other half in trust to pay the income to his daughter B (who is childless at testator's death), then to B's children for their lives with remainder to such children's issue living at their respective deaths. At common law the remainders would be clearly void although the life estates in B and B's children would probably have been upheld. When these life estates terminated the void remainders would presumably have passed under section 15 (c) of the Wills Act of 1917 (section 14 (10) of the present act) to A, as the other 5553

§ ESTATES ACT 

¶ 2 residuary legatee. By that time A would no doubt be dead and it would be necessary to trace the interest through his estate and perhaps through the estates of those entitled to A's estate, presumably paying taxes and possibly opening administrations all the way down the line. The result of all this would be that A's branch of the family would end up with the whole residuary estate of the original testator and B's grandchildren would be cut off entirely. Possibly the court would find a "contrary intention" and refuse to apply 15 (c) in this situation,2 but even if a partial intestacy were declared A's branch would eventually receive threequarters of the estate and B's branch only one-quarter. 

Under the Estates Act, the results in the above case should be somewhat fairer. In the first place, all the remainders might actually vest in time under section 4 (b) so that there would be no invalidity. But even if some or all of B's children were still living twenty-one years after the death of all lives in being, the void remainders would vest pursuant to section 5 (c) in the children of B who were receiving the income. Thus, the policy of the law will be upheld with a minimum of administrative complication and disruption of the testator's plan.

Of course, the old law would not be so harsh nor the new act so fair in all types of cases. It is believed, however, that the statute will at least avoid the inconvenience of awarding void interests to the estates of persons long since deceased and will accomplish substantial justice in most cases.

4. Subsection (b) a. Estates on Condition Subsequent 

Subsection (b) preserves the common law rule as to estates which by the terms of the instrument have vested in time but are subject to divestment with a gift over on breach of a remote condition subsequent. The owner of the vested estate at common law simply took free of the condition." 

Betts v. Snyder, 341 Pa. 465 (1941), is a good example. Testator gave a remainder, which would necessarily vest in time, in fee to A and B. Following these gifts there were elaborate directions for the care of his farm, prohibitions against the use of liquor on the premises, etc. with a gift over to the S. P. C. A. if any of these conditions were violated. The gift over to the S. P. C. A. was clearly void as a perpetuity and the court held that A and B took a fee simple absolute. Bilyeu's Estate, 346 Pa. 134 (1943), and 

Brady's Estate, 47 D. & C. 458 (O. C. Phila. 1943), are other examples of cases applying this principal. In each of the latter cases there were gifts on the death of a child to grandchildren then living with gifts over to another if a grandchild died before reaching the age of 25. The gifts to grand-" children were construed as vested from the time of the life tenant's death subject to divestment in case of death before reaching 25. Hence the gifts over were void and the grandchildren took free of the divesting condition. 

The only real question in any of these cases was one of construction. The estate given to the first taker must first be construed as vested subject to divestment by the event which gives life to the gift over, rather than subject to a condition precedent. Once that was determined, however, there was no real question as to the operation of the rule against perpetuities.

b. Estates on Special Limitation 

Subsection (b) restates the common law as to estates vested subject to divestment, but changes it with respect to the closely analogous case of an estate on "special limitation." The most common form of such an estate is the base or determinable fee-to A and his heirs so long as the old oak tree stands. The broader term was used in the statute because estates other than fees are sometimes (if rarely) subject to special limitations." The Restatement of 

Property (1936) § 23 defines a special limitation as "that part of the language of a conveyance which causes the created interest automatically to expire upon the occurrence

The common form of such estates, the determinable fee, is defined in § 44 of the Restatement as the estate created by a conveyance which "(a) creates an estate in fee simple. and (b) provides that the estate shall automatically expire upon the occurrence of a stated event." This definition is quoted in Betts v. Snyder, 341 Pa. 465, 469 (1941).10

At common law a remote gift over on the termination of a determinable fee was of course void as a perpetuity but the result of this invalidity was quite different from the result described above where the void interest followed an estate subject to divestment. In the case of the determinable fee the invalidity of the gift over did not enlarge the estate of the first taker. His estate still remained determinable and a possibility of reverter arose in the grantor in place of the void gift over. 

The distinction between the two types of cases under the common law rule against perpetuities is discussed in 

Betts v. Snyder, 341 Pa. 465 (1941). In that case the will was construed as creating a fee subject to divestment, so that the remaindermen were held to take the fee freed of the remote condition. §

Lilley's Estate, 272 Pa. 143 (1922), testator directed that income be accumulated for 99 years whereupon the principal and accumulations were to be distributed to the then living heirs of A and B.12 The whole trust was stricken down in that case, but under section 4 (b) of the present statute it would seem that such a solution is no longer possible. There is no perpetuity if all interests in fact vest in time, so that the trust must be allowed to run until the expiration of the permissible period.18 Suppose this period expired 50 years after the testator's death, and it thus became necessary to determine who was entitled to the void remainder. By the terms of the will no one would be entitled to the income. However, the direction to accumulate income is as unlawful under section 6 of the Estates Act as the postponement of the vesting of the remainder is unlawful under section 4 (b). In order to dispose of the void remainder under 5 (c), therefore, it would first be necessary to determine who was entitled to the income under section 8 of the act dealing with the disposition of released income subject to a void direction to accumulate. Clause (b) (2) of section 8 would probably apply so that the persons who were presently the heirs of A and B would be entitled to the income. After this was determined, section 5 (c) would be applied and the void remainder would be awarded to the same persons. 

Cases are conceivable where the solution is not so easy. Suppose at the end of the period the income is subject to a direction to accumulate which is lawful under section 6-as a will providing for income to be paid sucsessively to the first-born child of each generation, with a provision for accumulation and capitalization of income during any minority. cos b. Alternative Disposition by Testator 

If the settlor or testator makes an alternative lawful disposition which is to take effect if his primary plan results in an unlawful suspension of vesting, such alternative provision should clearly take precedence over the present section of the statute. There would simply be no void interest to dispose of under section 5, because by the terms of the instrument the primary plan was to continue only if it were lawful. Thus, if a testator provides for remote interests in the issue of A but then directs distribution to B in case the interests in A's issue do not vest before the expiration of the period allowed by law, the alternative provision would clearly take effect if the gift to A's issue turned out to be too remote and there would be no occasion for applying section 5 of the statute. 

If, however, the choice between two alternative provisions is made to depend on some circumstance other than vesting in time, there would be no justification for giving the secondary disposition effect unless the named contingency occurred. Suppose, for example, the estate is left to A for life and then to his unborn children for their lives with remainder on the death of the survivor to grandchildren then living but if A dies without issue, then to B. At the end of the period, children of A are still living and the remainder has not vested. The void remainder should be awarded to A's children under section 5 (c). There would be no justification for awarding it to B who was to take only if A died without issue.

86. INCOME ACCUMULATIONS WHEN VALID (a) General. 

No direction or authorization to accumulate income shall be void, except as herein provided. 

(b) Void Accumulations; Exceptions. 

Upon the expiration of the period allowed by the common law rule against perpetuities as measured by actual rather than possible events, any direction or authorization to accumulate income shall be void. 

This subsection shall not apply to: (1) Directions or authorizations to accumulate income in a trust for any charitable purpose or purposes; (2) Directions or authorizations to accumulate income in a bona fide trust inter vivos primarily for the benefit of business employes, their families or appointees, under a stock bonus pension, disability or death benefit, profitsharing or other employe benefit plan. 

(c) Time for Beginning Period. 

The period allowed by the common law rule against perpetuities under subsection (b) of this section shall be measured from the expiration of any time during which one person while living has the unrestricted power to transfer to himself the entire legal and beneficial interest in the property. -Substituted for repealed §6 by 

Amendment of 1955-6, P.L. 1073, applicable to conveyances on or after April 1, 1956. 

COMMISSIONERS' COMMENT-Sections 6 and 7 replace Sections 6, 7, and 8 of the 1947 act. The 1947 act continued in modified form the complicated rules in operation since the original Act of 1853, April 18, P.L. 503. The new provisions are intended to return to the Common Law Rule against Accumulations (cf. Restatement, Property, § 441), except that the period is to be measured by actual, rather than possible, events, consistent with Sections 4 and 5 of the present act. It is hoped that the new rule will reduce litigation and enable Pennsylvania to compete on a more favorable basis with states which have no statute against accumu- 5601

cos [

ESTATES ACT 

lations. The decision to relax the statutory rule against accumulations in Pennsylvania was reached only after a thorough study, including consideration of the views of leading authorities (who were unanimous in their approval of the suggested change) and of reports indicating that states having no statutes against accumulations have experienced little or no difficulty with unreasonable accumulations.

Old Law 

See under tab entitled "Repealed Sections".

The statutory prohibition against accumulation of income has now been abolished for all practical purposes as to conveyances effective on or after April 1, 1956. The present section which is substituted for old § 6 merely restates the common law rule against accumulations (no accumulation permissible after period of rule against perpetuities has expired) and makes it plain that such rule is measured by actualities rather than possibilities. Discussion 

11. Background-Reason for the Change 2. Analysis of Present Statute Examples 

3. Exceptions 

14. Time for Beginning Period 

1. Background-Reason for the Change 

The amending Act expressly repeals old §§ 6, 7 and 8 of the Act and substitutes this new $6 and $7 (discussed infra). Thus ends over one hundred years of restrictive legislation in Pennsylvania with respect to accumulations of income. The new provision is liberalizing rather than restrictive. It merely restates the common law rule against accumulations (no accumulation valid after the expiration of the period of the rule against perpetuities) and modifies that rule to provide that the permissible period is measured by actual rather than possible events. This modification of the common law rule was necessary in the interest of consistency in order to conform to the statutory modification of the rule against perpetuities contained in § 4 of the 5602

¶ 

ESTATES ACT 

$6 Act.

Otherwise, a simple repeal of § 6 would have been just as effective. 

As indicated by the Commisioners' Comment this change was recommended after careful consideration of the opinions of the property experts and the experience of lawyers in other states having no statutory restriction on income accumulations. It was discovered that only fourteen states in this country had such statutes and that these were by no means the most populated and industrialized states (New York and Pennsylvania being the only two such states on the eastern seaboard). See Restatement, Property (1944 and Supp. 1948), Introductory Note to Chap. 36 preceding § 445. The reports from attorneys in states having no such statute indicated that wills providing for unreasonable noncharitable accumulations were apparently rare or nonexistent. This is understandable. There are no doubt many testators even today who would like to create the equivalent of an indestructible estate tail by providing that their descendants should be entitled to only the income in perpetuity. Hence the rule against perpetuities still performs an important function. However, there is not the same natural desire to provide unreasonable accumulations. If a person wants to benefit individuals (as opposed to charities which have always been exempt from the rule against accumulations anyway) he usually wants to benefit those of his own or succeeding generation in preference to more remote descendants. A man might wish to endow his family perpetually, but it is unlikely that he would wish to deprive his children of income in order to favor remote descendants who may not even be born. So far as could be ascertained, Mr. Thellusson was unusual, if not unique, in this respect.

The property experts consulted included Professors 

W. Barton Leach of Harvard, Richard R. Powell of Columbia, and Lewis M. Simes of Michigan. They all agreed that the common law rule against accumulations was sufficient to prevent abuse and that the statutory regulations of accumulations were unnecessarily restrictive and caused much litigation. Of particular aid to the Advisory Committee was Prof. Simes' lecture on "The Policy Against 5603

$ESTATES ACT 

cos ¶ 2 Accumulations" (now in Public Policy and the Dead Hand, Thos. H. Cooley Lectures, 6th Series, published by the 

University of Michigan School of Law in 1955), the manuscript of which was submitted to the Committee. 

Aside from being a breeder of litigation, the old statute deprived Pennsylvanians of the benefit of many useful devices in estate planning. See the article in the May 1956 issue of Fiduciary Review. As there pointed out, it will now be possible for the first time in Pennsylvania to provide for discretionary accumulation trusts so as to reduce the impact of income taxes on beneficiaries who might be receiving more income than they need, to authorize the executor of a non-liquid estate to borrow money for the payment of death taxes and amortize the loan out of income, to provide for the amortization of mortgages out of income which the testator so amortized during his lifetime, and to provide for the payment of insurance premiums out of income. All these provisions would have been invalid prior to the present amendment. Hence those interested in estate planning were particularly in favor of abolishing the statutory rule against accumulations. 

2. Analysis of Present Statute-Examples 

Present § 6 is more significant in what it does not say than in what it says. Accumulations are now valid without qualification within the period of a life or lives in being and twenty-one years as measured by actual rather than possible events. Thus, trusts to which the new provision has no application will constitute all but a very small portion of trusts that a settlor or testator is likely to create. 

In the first place the rule will have no application to any trust which terminates within the period allotted by the rule against perpetuities. This will include the vast majority of carefully drafted instruments. 

Example: The common case of a trust to last during the lives of testator's children with distribution of principal completed at the death of the survivor of the children. Such a trust can include any provision for accumulation which the testator wishes. 5604

ESTATES ACT 

CO cos In the second place, the new statute will have no application to many trusts which violate the rule against perpetuities, for the simple reason that the rule against perpetuities itself will result in the termination of the trust at the end of the permissible period. 

Example: A will provides for distribution of income to testator's issue living from time to time in perpetuity, with a provision to accumulate and add to principal 10% of the income each year. Twenty-one years after the death of the last survivor of the issue living at testator's death, the interests of the subsequent beneficiaries will be invalid under § 4(b) and will be awarded to the issue then living under § 5(c) of the Act. Hence the trust will terminate by operation of law at the same time that any provision for accumulation would have been invalid under § 6. 

The only case where the present section will have any significant application is the relatively rare case of a trust existing validly (with all future interests vested) after the period of the rule against perpetuities has expired. 

Example: Income to A for life, then to A's unborn son for his life, vested remainder in X, with provision for accumulating and adding to principal 10% of the income each year. There is no violation of the rule against perpetuities because all interests are vested upon the death of A. However if the trust is still in existence twenty-one years after A's death, the provision for accumulating 10% of the income will become invalid under § 6. (Note that this 10% of income will then be paid to X-not A's son-see § 7 infra.) 

The present $ 6 will also be applicable to the even rarer case where the rule against perpetuities is violated but the trust can validly continue during the balance of a life estate which vested in time. 

Example: To A for life, then to A's unborn son for life, then to A's unborn grandson for life, vested remainder in X with provision for accumulating 10% of 5605

сбо CO 

ESTATES ACT 

the income as above. Twenty-one years after A's death, the life estate in the grandson (if it is not already vested) will be declared void and pursuant to § 5(a) the remainder in X will be accelerated to the death of 

A's son.

However the life estate in A's son is still valid so that for the balance of his life the provision for accumulation of income is invalid. 

As stated in the Commissioner's Comment, the new section is intended to restate what is supposed to be the common law rule against accumulations, modified only so as to measure the period by actual events. Hence, authorities dealing with the common law rule should be helpful in construing this section. Actually, however, very little common law authority exists in this brand of the law. It has been reasonably well established since Thelluson v. Woodford, 11 

Vesey Jr. 112 (1805) that in the absence of statute there is no objection to accumulations within the period of the rule against perpetuities. On the other hand, the converse-that accumulations after the perpetuity period has expired are bad-finds little support in the cases, because there is little authority one way or the other on the subject. Sufficient authority was found, however, to form a basis for §§ 441444 of the Restatement of Property which will be found more helpful as an authority than the cases which inspired it. For a documented discussion of the common law on the subject, see Simes, Future Interests (1936) § 586 et seq. 

13. Exceptions

After the period of the rule against perpetuities has expired all provisions for accumulation of income are invalid with the two exceptions noted-accumulations for a charity and accumulations in a pension or profit sharing plan. Both of these exceptions were in old § 6 and discussion of them will be found in [ 8 and 9 under old § 6-see "Repealed Sections".

Note that the other exceptions in old $6 are not continued. Hence, except for charitable trusts and pension trusts, all directions or authorizations to accumulate income after the perpetuity period are invalid, including those 5606

¶ 

limited to minority or incompetency, those inserted in the interest of judicious management, and so-called "principal and income" clauses where the trustee is given discretion ✔ to allocate receipts and expenses between principal and income. In this last respect there is a serious conflict between present § 6 and § 4(b)(4) covering perpetuities. 

That clause exempts from the statutory rule against perpetuities inter alia, powers to determine what is principal and what is income (see ¶ 2 under that section). Hence, a principal and income clause is saved from invalidity under § 4(b) (4) but insofar as such a clause authorizes the trustee to give the income beneficiary less than the income as defined by law, it would no doubt be an invalid accumulation under § 6-see Maris's Estate, 301 Pa. 20 (1930) and discussion of old § 6 at ¶ 11 under "Repealed Sections". 

Another respect in which the present section does not conform with the perpetuity provisions in § 4(b) is that there is no exception for cemetery trusts after the period has expired. There is no real inconsistency here, however. 

Since 1891 cemetery trusts have been exempt from the rule against perpetuities, but they have never been exempt from the rule against accumulations. See § 4(b)(2), Commissioner's Comment and ¶ 4.

Whether the exceptions to present § 6 should have been expanded, particularly with respect to administrative powers over principal and income, is certainly open to question. However, the lack of more liberal provisions in this respect are of little consequence, because as above noted, the cases where the present statute will have any application at all will be few and far between. 

4. Time for Beginning Period

The definition in subsection (c) of § 6 is taken verbatim from subsection (c) of § 4 dealing with perpetuities, so that the measure of the permissible period will be the same in both cases.

What is said under the discussion of § 4(c) is therefore applicable to § 6(c) also. Thus, for example, the perpetuity period in a revocable inter vivos trust will begin only at the death of the settlor. 5607 [The next page is 5651]

Discussion Section 8 of the act (now repealed) contained elaborate provisions for the disposition of income subject to an invalid direction or authorization to accumulate. The problem was complex under the old law, because accumulations could be invalid during a period when future interests remained unvested. With the repeal of old § 6 and the adoption of present § 6 providing that accumulations are invalid only after the expiration of the perpetuity period, the problem is considerably simplified because at the time when invalidity commences, all possible interests in the trust will necessarily be vested, either by the terms of the instrument or by operation of law under §§ 4 and 5 of the act. Hence, it was thought to be unnecessary to continue the complicated alternative provisions of § 8. 

5651

$

ESTATES ACT 

In many cases there will be no question as to who is entitled to the released income. 

Example: Life estate to A, followed by a direction to pay one-half of the income to A's unborn son during his life and to accumulate and add to principal the other half of the income during the same period, with vested remainder in X. As noted under § 6, 12 there is no violation of the statutory rule against perpetuities in such case because all interests necessarily vested in time. However, twenty-one years after A's death, the direction to accumulate one-half the income would be invalid and would be paid to the estate of X who has a vested interest in this half of the income. 

In other words, when the accumulations become invalid under the new provision of § 6, there will always necessarily be a vested remainder or reversion, so that the problem of accelerating contingent interests does not exist. Hence, any income not actually given to the income beneficiary will go to the vested remainderman. On the other hand, it is not impossible to imagine cases where some question will arise under the present provision. 

Example: To A for life then to A's unborn child for life, vested remainder in X, with a provision authorizing the trustee to allocate receipts and expenses between income and principal as he thinks proper. 

Twenty-one years after A's death the direction to allocate receipts and expenses becomes invalid insofar as it authorizes the trustee to allocate to principal what the law regards as income (see § 6, ¶ 3). In such a case A's child could well argue that the income had "vested" in him so that he should get all the legal income. On the other hand X would argue that A's child was given only what the trustee considered to be income so that all other legal income should be paid currently to X. DESIGNATION OF INSURANCE BENEFICIARIES NOT TESTAMENTARY 

The designation of beneficiaries of life insurance shall not be considered testamentary, regardless of whether the insurance contract designates the ultimate beneficiaries or makes the proceeds payable, directly or indirectly, to a trustee of a trust under a will or under a separate trust instrument which designates the ultimate beneficiaries, and regardless of whether any such trust is amendable or revocable, or both, or is funded or unfunded, and notwithstanding a reservation to the settlor of all rights of ownership in the insurance contracts. Unless otherwise expressly provided in the conveyance, funds or other property so passing to a trust under a will shall become and be a part of the testamentary trust to be administered and disposed of in accordance with the provisions thereof, without forming any part of the testator's estate for administration by his personal representative. 

-Added by Amending Act No. 377 of 

1957, effective July 11, 1957.

COMMISSIONERS' COMMENT This section would replace Section 8 

of the Estates Act which was omitted when the rule against accumulations was changed. It has two purposes. The most important is to make it clear that unfunded insurance trusts are not testamentary and to that extent the law as stated in Brown 

Est., 384 Pa. 99, is changed. Its second purpose is to make provision for the pouring-over of the assets of an inter vivos trust to a testamentary trust. In this latter respect it is intended to be a counterpart of the proposed new Section 14.1 of the Wills Act. 

Old Law 

There was no prior statute on the subject. The case law had become confused.

For the most part the new section merely restates settled principles of law, but it should eliminate the confusion caused by Brown Est., 384 Pa. 99 (1956). 5701

Discussion Theoretically, it could be argued that the designation of life insurance beneficiaries is a testamentary act because the usual reservation of the right to change the beneficiary prevents the transaction from being a completed inter vivos gift. However, surprisingly enough, the question has seldom been raised. Insurance proceeds are universally held to be payable to the named beneficiary regardless of whether the beneficiary designation conforms to the Statute of Wills. The best rationale is that insurance in this respect is a time-honored exception to the ordinary rules governing wills and testamentary rights. See generally discussion in Couch, Insurance (1929 and Supp. 1950) § 306 at n. 13 et seq. Cf. Discussion under Wills Act § 1, ¶ 8c and the discussion of the analogous problem of "p.o.d." U.S. 

Saving Bond under Intestate Act § 1, ¶ 4f and Wills Act 

§ 1, ¶ 8e. 

If the designation of an individual beneficiary of an insurance policy is not testamentary, it is difficult to see how making insurance payable to the trustee of a revocable trust which in turn names the ultimate beneficiary makes the transaction more (rather than less) testamentary. Nevertheless, just such a suggestion was made by the Orphans' 

Court in Brown Est., 4 D. & C. 2d 722 (1956) and the Supreme Court adopted this opinion in affirming per curiam, 384 Pa. 99 (1956). The case involved the rights of an electing spouse under § 11 of the Estates Act. It is difficult to extract the holding from the dicta in the opinion, but a reasonable interpretation of the holding is that insurance payable to a revocable unfunded insurance trust is subject to the claims of the electing spouse both (1) because the transaction was testamentary at common law and (2) because the transaction was subject to the spouse's election under § 11 of the Estates Act. The latter part of the holding was corrected by the amendment to § 11 of the Estates Act in the Act of 1955-6 P. L. 1073. The first part of the holding, that insurance trusts are testamentary, is corrected by the addition of this new § 8 of the Estates Act by the amendment of 1957. It should now be clear that the designation of beneficiaries of insurance-whether in trust or otherwise- 5702

ESTATES ACT 

8 cas is not a testamentary act, regardless of the usual powers to revoke or change beneficiaries. Hence, the designation need not conform to the execution requirements of the Wills Act and (unless the insured's estate is beneficiary) the proceeds will not be subject to the claims of the decedent's creditors. 

The amendment should also eliminate a possible argument that (independent of § 11 which now expressly excludes insurance from its scope) revocable insurance trusts can be reached by the electing spouse under § 8 of the Wills Act. 

Whether contrary results would have flowed from the opinion in Brown Est. is questionable in any event, but the present section will lay to rest any doubt on this subject. 

As indicated in the Commissioner's Comment, the second purpose of this amendment is to provide a counterpart to § 14.1 of the Wills Act as amended by Act No. 378 of 

1957. That amendment to the Wills Act codified and liberalized to a considerable extent the law with respect to wills adding to inter vivos trusts. The present section of the 

Estates Act, inter alia, deals with the converse of this situation—insurance payable to trustees under a will. It is doubtful whether this aspect of the new provision will have any effect one way or another on prior law. Its value in this respect is largely aesthetic-something to balance the new § 14.1 of the Wills Act. So far as is known, insurance payable to a trustee under a will (as opposed to the executor) would form no part of the testator's estate in any event, so that the last sentence merely restates the common law. On the other hand, the last sentence may have some procedural value in that it will now be clear that the trustee who receives the insurance proceeds in such a case will be accountable for them in the court having jurisdiction of the trust under the will and under that trust's term and number. 

It may be suggested that the second sentence of this section was intended to change the rule of Myers's Estate, 309 Pa. 581 (1933), holding that insurance payable to trustees subject to trusts set forth in the will are subject to Pennsylvania inheritance tax. The present author sees no basis for such a construction and feels sure that no such change in the inheritance tax law was intended. The reason- 5703

ing of the Court in Myers's Estate was not that the proceeds were taxable because they became part of the estate, but simply that they were taxable because the ultimate beneficiaries were named in the will rather than in the insurance policy. § 9. COMBINATION OF CHARITABLE TRUSTS 

Whenever two or more trusts heretofore have been or hereafter shall be created for substantially the same charitable purposes, and the court having jurisdiction over any such trust, upon the application of any party in interest, shall find that they can be more effectively administered if they are combined, the court in its discretion, after such notice as the court shall direct, may combine them in the manner and to the extent that the court shall approve, but not so as to violate any express provision to the contrary in any conveyance creating any of the trusts so combined. 

COMMISSIONERS' COMMENT-This section is based on the Act of 

1933, P. L. 271, 10 PS 16. In most circumstances where a trust fails it can be awarded cy pres under section 10. However, there are numerous instances where charitable trusts of small amounts should not be applied cy pres but where they can be more effectively administered if combined-particularly for purposes of investment. It was thought preferable to make this section apply to all cases where a combination of charitable trusts would provide for more effective administration than to confine its application, as in the 1933 act, to cases where "the income from the trust estates set apart for the purposes of the trusts is insufficient or inadequate.' 

Old Law 

Section 1. Whenever two or more trusts for charitable or benevolent purposes have been established, or shall hereafter be established, by the same donor or testator, or by separate donors or testators, and for any cause or reason the income from the trust estates set apart for the purposes of the trusts is insufficient or inadequate to carry out effectively and efficiently the purposes expressed by the donors of the trusts through separate administration of the trusts, and the charitable or benevolent purposes of the trusts are of the nature that they may be more effectively and efficiently carried out if the same are combined, the trustees of the trusts may, in their discretion, join in a petition to the orphans' court having jurisdiction over the accounts of any one of the trustees setting forth such facts, and the court being satisfied with the truth thereof, may order and empower said trustees to carry out the purposes of the trusts by combining the trusts in the manner and to the extent that such court shall approve, provided that such combination shall not be authorized where it would violate any specific provision to the contrary in the will or other instrument creating the trust. 

Act of 1933, P. L. 271.

The only significant change is the elimination of the requirement that the income from the trusts be insufficient for their purposes. 5751

1. General

The effect of this revision of the act of 1933 can be best understood by considering it in connection with Williams's Estate, 52 D. & C. 107 (O. C. Tioga 1944), the only reported case mentioned in Purdon under the old act. The testatrix left a fund to be used to run a home for aged women in the house where she had resided. The fund was insufficient and the surviving executrix (who was also named trustee) joined with the trustees of "The Green Home" (a home for aged men and women established some years earlier under another will) in presenting a petition to combine the trusts under the act of 1933. The petition was dismissed for the following reasons: (1) There having been no decree of distribution entered in the Williams estate and no steps having been taken to establish the Williams home, that trust had not been "established" within the meaning of the act of 1933. (2) There was no allegation that the income from the Green trust was insufficient for its purpose, and the act of 1933 required that the income from the "trust estates" (i. e. both of them) be insufficient. (3) The petition indicated that it was "absorption [of the Williams trust by the Green trust] that is contemplated, not combination." (4) The granting of the petition would have violated specific provisions in the Williams will (that the home should bear the Williams name, should be exclusively for women, etc.) contrary to the proviso of the act of 1933. 

Turning to the present act, several changes from the act of 1933 of varying degrees of importance will be noted. 

First, the word "created" has been substituted for "established," but it is doubtful that any great significance can be attached to this stylistic change. In any event the first ground mentioned above for the decision in Williams's 5752

-- 
ESTATES ACT § 9 MANDALA 

Estate is questionable even under the old wording. That a decree directing distribution by the executrix to herself as trustee is necessary for either the establishment or the creation of a trust seems contrary to general principles.¹ 

Second, the requirement that the trusts to be combined be "for substantially the same charitable purpose" has been added in the new act. This was probably implicit in the act of 1933, however, as it would be difficult to imagine how a combination of two entirely different charitable trusts would enable them to be carried out more "effectively and efficiently." Third, the application may now be made by "any party in interest,” although in the usual case the trustees will undoubtedly join in the petition as required by the old act. Fourth, and most important, the necessity for showing that "the income from the trust estates . . is insufficient " has been eliminated in the new act. 

This will change the second ground for the decision in Williams's Estate and will remove the principal barrier to combining trusts under the old act. Aside from purely stylistic changes, the other requirements of the act of 1933 remain unchanged. The jurisdiction is concurrent among all the courts having jurisdiction over the various trusts. It must be shown that the combination will contribute to more effective administration, and no "express provision" in any of the trusts may be violated. Note also that whether combination is granted remains discretionary with the court and the court has wide latitude in determining the nature of the relief. Combination for investment purposes without destroying the identities of the participating trusts, for example, might be appropriate in certain cases, while other schemes of partial combinations might be suitable in others. 

12. Cy Pres Distinguished 

The main value of Williams's Estate, 52 D. & C. 107, is that it illustrates how this section of the Estates Act

ESTATES ACT 

should not be used as a substitute for cy pres. The reference to insufficiency of income in the old act caused confusion in this regard which should not exist to the same extent under the present act. Cy pres under section 10 involves a modification or at the least an implementation of the charitable purpose set forth in the instrument which otherwise could not be carried out. The present section is far narrower in its scope in that it contemplates no change in the charitable purpose other than in the mechanics of administration. On the other hand, there is no condition. precedent of failure or impossibility under the present section. It is true that the two sections are analogous and have a common tradition, but the distinction between the two is not illusory.

The court pointed out in Williams's Estate, 52 D. & C. at 115, that the petition there was "not a petition to combine the charities, but for a decree directing the distribution of the Williams property to the Green fund. Such was certainly not the intent of the statute, and our exercise of jurisdiction thereunder and under the circumstances here presented would merely amount to applying the power we always had under the cy pres doctrine, with the added condition that no other charity shall be allowed to compete with The Green Home for the gift." The significance of 

Williams's Estate in this respect is emphasized by the fact that in subsequent cy pres proceedings the Green Home lost and a different charity was awarded the fund: Wil liams's Estate, 353 Pa. 638 (1946).

In certain cases the proper section to proceed under will be clear. A case where the present section would be the only one available would be where there are two funds destined for the same charitable use and each trust is capable of operating alone although investment problems could be simplified and duplication of clerical work eliminated by combining them. On the other hand, there will no doubt be border-line cases where either combination or cy pres could be plausibly sought-as where one of the trusts is not self-sustaining. The tactical advantage in the stronger charity's eliminating competition by proceeding under the present section is plain, but as Williams's 5754

¶ 

ESTATES ACT 

89 Estate, 52 D. & C. 107, illustrates, the court in such cases will probably interpret strictly the requirement that the two purposes be "substantially the same" and that no violation of any "express provision" of either trust be caused. 

¶3. Non-Profit Corporation Law Distinguished 

A charitable corporation is in a sense a charitable trust for the purposes set forth in its charter. See Craig's 

Estate, 356 Pa. 564, 569 (1947). It seems clear, however, that the present section was not intended to apply to cases already covered by the non-profit corporation law. "Combinations" of charitable corporations will still be governed primarily by the merger provisions in section 801 et seq. of of the act of 1933, P. L. 289, as amended, 15 P. S. § 2851801 et seq. 

However, as Craig's Estate shows, the orphans court sometimes retains jurisdiction over particular funds given to a charitable corporation by a testator who directs the segregation and preservation of the principal. Conceivably one such trust could be combined with another under this section of the Estates Act. Also, a non-corporate charitable trust could conceivably be combined with one administered by a charitable corporation (subject to the qualifications discussed above that this section should not be used as a substitute for cy pres), although such combination might be disallowed on the ground that it will merely be a clever dodge to terminate the individual trust contrary to Yeager's Estate, 354 Pa. 463, 467 (1946).

Where both segregated funds are held by the same charitable corporation, combination will usually be unnecessary, since the corporation can solve its investment problems by creating a common trust fund under section 318 of the act of 1933, P. L. 289, as amended by the act of 1947, P. L. 196, 15 P. S. § 2851-318.

§ 10. ADMINISTRATION OF CHARITABLE ESTATES 

Except as otherwise provided by the conveyor, if the charitable purpose for which an interest shall be conveyed shall be or become indefinite or impossible or impractical of fulfilment, or if it shall not have been carried out for want of a trustee or because of the failure of a trustee to designate such purpose, the court may, on application of the trustee or of any interested person or of the Attorney General of the Commonwealth, after proof of notice to the Attorney General of the Commonwealth when he is not the petitioner, order an administration or distribution of the estate for a charitable purpose in a manner as nearly as possible to fulfil the intention of the conveyor, whether his charitable intent be general or specific.

COMMISSIONERS' COMMENT This section is intended to supplant the five conflicting and inconsistent statutes on the cy pres principle, namely: (1) Act of 1855, P. L. 328, 10 PS 13; (2) 

Act of 1876, P. L. 211, 10 PS 15; (3) Act of 1885, P. L. 259, 20 PS 196; (4) Act of 1889, P. L. 173, 10 PS 14, and (5) 

Act of 1895, P. L. 114, 10 PS 13.

Section 10 is in accordance with the strong tendency of the courts to apply cy pres whenever possible and to limit very narrowly the right of next of kin to get the property back. To reach this result the section goes the whole way and lip service to a "general charitable intention" will no longer be required.

Except where the conveyor makes an alternative gift, the only question which will be before the court will be whether the original gift has failed and if so to what other charity the fund shall be awarded. The conveyor's heirs, next of kin and residuary beneficiaries will no longer be in a position to bargain with expectant charities.

3. Application to Charitable Corporations. 

14. Effective Date. ¶ 1. History 

This is an attempt to clarify our cy pres law which has been in a state of confusion since 1885. All the earlier statutes are repealed (section 20) and replaced by the present section which is designed to simplify the law and to eliminate so far as possible the claims of next of kin in all cases where a charitable gift fails for any of the reasons stated.

The doctrine of cy pres arose in the chancery courts in England. The chancellor, in his dual capacity of both an executive and a judicial officer, applied two kinds of cy pres. Prerogative cy pres consisted of appropriating on behalf of the crown an illegal charitable gift and awarding it to another charity. The donor's intent was a matter of 5803

§ 

ESTATES ACT 

11 no consequence in prerogative cy pres; an Irishman's gift to the Pope might be awarded to the Church of England. 

Judicial cy pres, on the other hand, was performed by the chancellor in his capacity of a judge. The purpose here was to carry out the donor's general intention as closely as possible, either by way of supplementing his directions. or by way of modifying the terms of the gift when exact conformity was impossible. It was this latter type of cy pres which most American courts inherited.¹ 

In Pennsylvania, it was said that the doctrine did not exist prior to statute. Failing to distinguish between the two types of cy pres, Chief Justice Gibson in Methodist 

Church v. Remington, 1 Watts 219, 227 (1832), said that "no court here possesses the specific powers necessary to give effect to the principle of cy pres, even were the principle itself not too grossly revolting to the public sense of justice to be tolerated in a country where there is no ecclesiastical establishment"? Later, however, in Philadel phia v. Girard Heirs, 45 Pa. 9, 28 (1863), judicial, as opposed to prerogative, cy pres was expressly recognized as part of our non-statutory law. 

In the June, 1946, issue of the Fiduciary Review, there is an excellent analysis of the various statutes intended to cover the subject of cy pres in Pennsylvania. Toner's 

Estate, 260 Pa. 49 (1918), also contains a review of our cy pres legislation prior to the present act. Briefly, the act of 1855, P. L. 328, provided a system consistent with the 

English doctrine: where possible the court was directed to approximate the donor's intent-otherwise there was an escheat. The act of 1876, P. L. 211, was a peculiar statute purporting to give the court power to award class gifts of 

1. See Scott's Estate, 28 Dist. 292, 294 (C. P. Phila. 1919); Scott, Trusts (1939) $399.1. 

2. Cf. Witman v. Lex, 17 S. & R. 88, 92 (1827), where Gibson qualified his theory, to the extent of holding that a gift to an unincorporated charity was not void for uncertainty "provided there be a discretionary power vested anywhere over the application of the testator's bounty to those objects." It was also held, prior to statute, that a charitable trust would not fail for want of a trustee McGirr v. Aaron, 1 P. & W. 49 (1829). At what point the doctrine of cy pres is reached along this line of decisions might be the subject of theoretical argument. It is fair to say, however, that these holdings are not in conflict with Gibson's doctrine that prior to the statute our courts did not have the power to exercise the cy pres power in the sense of modifying and thus saving a gift which had failed according to its terms.

1885, P. L. 259, was the one which caused the real trouble. 

It provided that when the object of a charitable gift in a will failed for uncertainty, object ceasing, etc., the property should be awarded to the next of kin. This was in direct conflict with the act of 1855 in the cases it covered. The cy pres power was reaffirmed, four years later, however, by the act of 1889, P. L. 173, which, like the other acts, quietly ignored its predecessors and simply restated the cy pres doctrine in much the same language as the act of 1855except that there was no provision for escheat in cases where approximation of the donor's intent was impossible. 

Finally, to top off the confusion the act of 1855 was amended in minor respects by the act of 1895, P. L. 114,* thus negativing any suggestion that it had been impliedly repealed by the intervening statutes. 

So the law stood prior to the present act. As can be seen, the central problem facing the courts in attempts to harmonize these statutes was what to do with the act of 1885 which seemed to abolish (as to the cases it covered) the doctrine which all the other acts affirmed. It was generally agreed that cy pres, if it had been temporarily abolished in such cases, was reinstated by the act of 1889. 

As of that date, the conflicting statutes could be reconciled by saying that in all cases the donor's general charitable intent would be approximated as closely as possible, but that where the intent. was so specific that it could not be approximated the property would escheat under the act of 1855 in the case of a deed or would go to the next of kin under the act of 1885 in the case of a will.5 

Strictly, the reenactment of the act of 1855 by the amendment of 1895 would not change this result because 3. By its terms it applied to any class gift of income, whether charitable or not. But the "cy pres” power it purported to give was conditioned upon there being no heirs of the testator-a situation which is theoretically impossble-unless "no known heirs" was intended in which event it would conflict with the escheat statute in non-charitable uses.

On the other hand, the easiest and most sensible solution was to ignore the troublesome act of 1885 altogether so that there would be either cy pres or escheat in all cases and next of kin would have no interest in the proceeding. There was a marked tendency to this latter view in some of the more recent cases. In 

Wilkey's Estate, 337 Pa. 129, 135 (1940), for example, the court said that if the act of 1885 "was not technically repealed, it was at least so devitalized as to make its subsequent operative force practically negligible."" 

Unfortunately, however, no case seems to have been taken to the appellate courts where it was necessary actually to decide what should become of the property if approximation of a testator's intent was impossible. As a result, the door was left open for a decision such as 

Hildebrand's Estate, 47 D. & C. 537 (O. C. Northamp.

Estate would probably have been reversed if it had been appealed, but it illustrates how prior to the present act the next of kin always had a possible argument in cy pres cases, slim though their chance of success might be.

The present act wipes the slate clean by repealing all the prior acts as to future conveyances in section 20 and setting forth in the present section a single rule to govern all cases. a. Alternative Gift in Instrument

Randall's Estate, 341 Pa. 501 (1941), the court at one point said it was refusing cy pres for this reason, but that was a case where the testator made an express provision for a reversion if the charity should fail. (See 12a above.)

Hence, the talk about whether the charitable intent was general or specific was quite irrelevant. The estate given to the charity simply expired by its terms and there was nothing left for the court to award cy pres. 

The present act expressly eliminates the requirement of a "general" charitable intent and directs that the donor's gift must be approximated regardless of "whether his charitable intent be general or specific". In view of what has been said, this new language will probably have little effect on the actual results of our cases. It should serve a practical purpose, however, in eliminating one of the possible arguments of next of kin when a case for cy pres arises.

The act of 1855 provided that if approximation of the testator's intention could not be done "consistently with law and equity" the fund should be awarded to the Commonwealth. As noted above (T1), the law in this respect $399.

The present act is based on the more realistic assumption that the donor's intent can always be approximated to a greater or lesser degree. The absolutely unique is a philosophical impossibility, much as this might be doubted by the student of wills. Naturally a closer approximation of the donor's original plan will be more feasible in some cases than others, but this is a relative matter. Some sort of approximation is now mandatory in all cases.19 Both next of kin and the Commonwealth are now eliminated as alternative distributees, although a case is conceivable where the Commonwealth might claim as the charity which will fulfil the original intent more nearly than any other-claiming under the cy pres doctrine rather than against it.

§ 11 

§ 11. POWERS OF APPOINTMENT-RIGHTS OF SURVIVING 

SPOUSE A conveyance of assets by a person who retains a power of appointment by will, or a power of revocation or consumption over the principal thereof, shall, at the election of his surviving spouse, be treated as a testamentary disposition so far as the surviving spouse is concerned to the extent to which the power has been reserved, but the right of the surviving spouse shall be subject to the rights of any income beneficiary whose interest in income becomes vested in enjoyment prior to the death of the conveyor. 

COMMISSIONERS' COMMENT This section preserves for the surviving spouse the right to share in the decedent's assets where the decedent has retained important rights of ownership at death. 

Rights of the surviving spouse in such circumstances have been recognized in other states: cf. Newman v. Dore, 275 N. Y. 371, annot. 12 Temple L. Q. 129, 36 Mich. L. R. 496. However,

Pennsylvania has given little opportunity to the surviving spouse to share when legal title has passed from the decedent prior to death: cf. Beirne v. Continental-Equitable T. & T. Co., 307 Pa. 570; Windolph v. Girard Trust Co., 245 Pa. 349; 

Rynier Est., 347 Pa. 471; contra Diedel's Est., 32 D. & C. 

685. Indeed, the situation in Pennsylvania has been such that it was stated correctly that "It is only the stupid husband, who, against his wishes, would be forced to allow his wife to share in his personalty.": Comment (1939) 5 Univ. of Pitts. L. Rev., 78, p. 87.

Section 11, in respect to powers of appointment completes the plan suggested by section 8 (c) of the Wills Act of 1947. 

The surviving spouse will have the right to reach assets of a trust created by the decedent where power of appointment is retained by the decedent, but not where the trust was created by another. "power of appointment" and not "general power of appointment" is employed so that this section can not be avoided by creating special powers giving the right to appoint to a class including every one but the spouse or some other designated individuals. "but the right of the surviving spouse shall be subject to the rights of any income beneficiary whose interest in income becomes vested in enjoyment prior to the death of the conveyor" is included for two reasons: (1) It might prove harsh to withdraw income from persons who have been receiving it. (2) It seemed proper to permit the surviving spouse to share in property of which the decedent had the beneficial enjoyment at his death, but not to permit a sharing in property over which the decedent retained control but which he did not enjoy beneficially. 5851

§ 

ESTATES ACT 

Old Law

There was no earlier legislation on inter vivos transfers of personalty in fraud of marital rights. Under our cases, such transfers could not be attacked by the spouse even when a life interest and a power of revocation were reserved, and when the transfer was made for the purpose of barring the spouse from a share in the estate. Where a general power of appointment was reserved the property could probably have been reached by the spouse, but the case law was uncertain. 

The new provision changes the prior case law by permitting the spouse to take against inter vivos transfers where one of the enumerated powers has been reserved, regardless of the good faith of the donor. Its principal application will be in cases involving transfers of personalty, since conveyances of real estate during coverture are restricted by section 5 of the Intestate Act and the 

Married Women's Property Act.

¶ 7. Effect of Election on Spouse's Share in Other Prop erty. 

1. Personalty-Common Law a. Background

At early common law, a man could do whatever he pleased with his personal property, and it was impossible for him to transfer it in fraud of his wife's rights because his wife had no interest which could be affected by any transfer he might make. This absolute dominion was infringed when the wife was given the power to share in a deceased husband's personalty against his will. His power to transfer personalty inter vivos remained unfettered, but it became possible for his wife to argue that he could not use this power as a device to deprive her of enforceable rights against his estate after he died.¹ In the meantime, married women were given free dominion over their personal property subject to a corresponding power of the husband to take against the will, so that a similar problem existed as to a woman's inter vivos transfers in fraud of marital rights.2 This was the background for the confusing line of cases that followed.³

ESTATES ACT b. General Rules-Motive of Donor Irrelevant 

It will first be noted that the inter vivos transaction must be effective generally to pass title to the property. If delivery or some other element of gift is lacking (as in 

Tunnell's Estate, 325 Pa. 554 (1937)) no title will have passed from the decedent so that the property can be claimed as part of his estate for the benefit of any party in interest. Nor will title pass if the gift was made under undue influence (as in Miskey's Appeal, 107 Pa. 611 (1883)). Such matters are discussed under section 1 (4) of the Intestate Act. Here we are concerned rather with the question of whether a transfer of ownership, good as to the decedent's relatives and beneficiaries, can be attacked by the spouse on the ground that it was in fraud of marital rights.

In determining whether an otherwise valid gift of personalty is fraudulent as to the spouse, it can be said with a fair degree of certainty that under the case law prior to this act the motive of the donor to exclude the spouse was insufficient to render the transaction vulnerable. This was established by a line of cases culminating with Beirne v. 

Continental-Equitable Title & Trust Company, 307 Pa. 570 

(1932), where Justice Kephart dissented on this very point. 

It had been found as a fact in that case that the husband created the trust for the purpose of preventing his spouse from sharing in the property after his death, but the majority reversed the court below which had based its finding of fraud on this fact alone. Such a purpose was said to be insufficient to establish the necessary "fraudulent intent" and this ruling has been followed in subsequent cases. It is theoretically possible that some other intent on the part of the donor would have tainted the transaction. with fraud. However, the nature of this hypothetical "fraudulent intent" has never been judicially defined, and it is difficult to imagine what sort of motive would constitute stronger grounds for a finding of fraud than an (1937); Fiduciary Review, October, 1943, and April, 1944. For cases in other jurisdictions, see Notes, 157 A. L. R. 1184 (1945); 36 Mich. L. Rev. 496 (1938); 

44 Mich. L. Rev. 151 (1945); Cahn, "Restraints on Disinheritance," 85 U. of 

Pa. L. Rev. 139, 149 (1936). 

4. E. g. Orth v. Doench, 309 Pa. 240, 242 (1932); DeNoble v. DeNoble, 331 

Pa. 273, 277 (1938); Fritz' Est., 135 Pa. Super. 463, 468 (1939). 5854

¶ 1c 

intent to bar the spouse from a share in the property.5 

Hence, a practical working rule under the case law as it stood prior to this act was that the motive of the donor was irrelevant in determining whether an inter vivos gift of personalty was in fraud of marital rights. This principle will not be affected by the present statutory provision. 

If the intent of the donor is irrelevant, it would seem that the only possible ground upon which one spouse might attack the inter vivos transfer of personalty by the other would be that the donor retained so many incidents of ownership that the property was still subject to the interest of the surviving spouse at the donor's death. As already noted, the retention of too many incidents of ownership might negative the whole idea of a present gift so that no title at all will have passed to the donee. There is reason to believe, however, that there was a small class of transactions in the twilight zone, where the title passed under general principles of property law but the donor could still be considered as the owner by the surviving spouse. There is an exact analogy in this respect in cases concerning the rights of creditors who are sometimes permitted to attack a transfer which is valid as to the donor and his heirs." 

It is this theory which forms the basis for the present section of the Estates Act, which provides that certain transfers, while not testamentary generally, may be treated as testamentary by the surviving spouse. Before discussing the effect of the new statutory provision, however, the cases before the act will be examined to determine to what extent this principle was recognized at common law.

e. Notes Payable at Death 

Another device to make a gift while still retaining enjoyment and dominion over the property is to execute sealed notes in favor of the beneficiary payable at the donor's death. If such notes are properly delivered, a valid gift of a future interest is accomplished. While the gift of the notes is theoretically irrevocable, the donor parts with neither dominion over nor enjoyment of his property during his lifetime; he can even render himself insolvent so that the notes become worthless if he so desires. 

In spite of the fact that such a transaction represents a rather shameless substitute for a testamentary gift, it has generally been assumed, and probably correctly, that a transfer of this sort could not have been attacked by the surviving spouse under our case law. This seems to be the holding in Rynier's Estate, 347 Pa. 471 (1943). However, the matter is not entirely open and shut. In the first place, if such notes are executed against real estate, the case might be governed by a different line of decisions.

However, a careful reading of Rynier's Estate and Hummel's Estate will indicate that the holdings of those cases are not actually inconsistent. In both cases the notes were paid to the obligee. 

In Hummel's Estate, however, the question was what share of the remaining assets the spouse was entitled to, and it was held that the spouse's share of one half must be measured before the notes were paid. It so happened that the estate was large enough for both the holders of the notes and the spouse to be paid in full, so that it was not decided whether the rights of the spouse or of the donees were superior. The point is, however, that the notes were paid at the expense of the beneficiaries under the will, but not at the expense of the electing spouse. In Rynier's 

Estate, the Supreme Court merely held that the notes must be paid. There was no decision on how the remaining assets should be divided as between the spouse and the other next of kin and this was scarcely odd, because the payment of the notes consumed "practically the whole of decedent's estate". It might be profitable to bear in mind the limited nature of the holding in Rynier's Estate in future litigation, however, where there might be a sizable estate remaining after the notes are paid. Hummel's 

Estate might still be law in measuring the spouse's share in what remains. 2. Personalty-Transactions Covered by This Section a. General Motive of Donor Irrelevant 

As indicated in the discussion above (¶ 1b), the problem of inter vivos transfers in fraud of marital rights can be approached from the standpoint of the donor's intent or from the standpoint of whether the donor has retained too many incidents of ownership for the gift to be effective as against the spouse. In section 33 of the Model Probate 

Code, the former approach is adopted and any type of transfer where fraud can be proved is made ineffective so far as the spouse is concerned. Pennsylvania, however, has rejected any solution of this type and thus has avoided the difficulties of prying into the donor's motive. Instead, it is provided in the present section that when certain powers over the property are retained by the donor, the surviving spouse may treat the transfer as testamentary, regardless of its purpose. 

Like the common law, the present provision operates only where the decedent has reserved powers in his own transfer. The spouse still has no enforceable interest in property subject to the decedent's power of appointment given by the will or deed of another. Indeed, section 8 of the Wills Act expressly excludes an electing spouse from such property. In making this distinction the present provision seems to be based on the philosophy that the spouse shares only because of some sort of a constructive fraud, which is, however, conclusively presumed where a person gives away property retaining incidents of ownership. b. Consideration Irrelevant

At common law the indications were clear that the receipt of value by the transferor would negative the possibility of fraud.18 This will no longer be so in cases covered by the present section, which is not limited to voluntary transfers. This omission will cause hardship only 

18. Cf. Overbeck v. McHale, 354 Pa. 177, 179 (1946). 5861

in the most unusual case, however, because ordinarily no one would give value for property which remains subject to the transferor's power of appointment, consumption, or revocation.19 

c. Reservation of Life Interest Irrelevant 

One of the more startling aspects of the present provision is that the reservation of income by the donor has no effect on the vulnerability of the gift. The theory probably is that since the spouse's rights arise only on the donor's death, the disposition of income before that time is a matter of no concern. This concept was favored over the philosophy that the spouse is entitled to a share of the property actually being enjoyed by the decedent during his life. Thus, under this section, a wealthy man can easily pauperize his wife after his death by transfering all his property in trust reserving the income to himself but reserving no power over the principal. On the other hand, the widow might inherit from her deceased husband more property than he enjoyed during his life, if he has made a substantial gift of both income and principal reserving a power to appoint the remainder by will. d. Powers of Appointment 

It has been suggested above (11d) that even prior to the present act a surviving spouse would probably have been permitted to reach the principal of a trust where the settlor had retained the life income and a general testamentary power of appointment over the principal. The present section goes much further. Not only will it be irrelevant whether or not a life estate has been reserved, but the section is not even limited to cases where the reserved power is general. If the provision is literally construed, the spouse will now be able to reach the principal even though a testamentary power is to appoint among a very limited number of persons, and even though it is a so-called "imperative" power where the beneficiaries within the class have a vested interest which takes effect even 19. But see discussion of Rynier's Estate, ¶ 2f infra in the text.

5862

¶ 2d

when the power is not exercised.20 Thus, where there is a life estate to settlor and remainder to issue, the spouse will be barred. But if the remainder is to issue "in such proportion as settlor may by will appoint" it would seem that the spouse may treat the transfer as ineffective to bar her rights. It is conceivable that the court will balk at the application of this section in extreme cases where no real enjoyment or dominion has been reserved, but it will be difficult to limit its operation by judicial construction to the cases which the drafters probably had in mind. 

It will be noted that there is no mention in the section of the reservation of a power to appoint by deed. It might be held that such a power is tantamount to a power to revoke or consume. However, there would seem to be a theoretical and even a practical difference in most cases. 

It will first be noted that if any power to appoint by deed is exercised by the donor before his death, the effect is the same as if he created an irrevocable trust with remainders over at the time the power was exercised. At the time of death no power remains, so that there would be no possible argument for applying this section. A trust where an inter vivos power is reversed takes on testamentary aspects only where the power remains unexercised at death, but even here it is similar to a power of revocation only if the power is broad enough to enable the settlor to appoint to himself. If the power to appoint by deed is special, there is no resemblance to a power of revocation or consumption. Hence, the only case where the reservation of a power to appoint by deed could possibly be attacked by the surviving spouse is where such a power is unlimited and remains unexercised at the settlor's death. In such a case, the court might hold that a power to revoke or consume had been in effect reserved, or it might hold that the transfer could be attacked by the spouse even in the absence of statute.21 

No additional problem is raised by a case where there is a power to appoint either by deed or will. If the power to appoint by deed is exercised, no power over the prin- 20. Imperative powers are discussed under section 3 (4) of the present act. 

21. Cf. Diedel's Trust, 32 D. & C. 685 (O. C. Phila. 1938). 5863

e. Power of Revocation or Consumption-Trusts 

The provision that the reservation of a power of revocation or consumption will enable the spouse to treat the transfer as testamentary was clearly intended to overrule the Beirne and Windolph cases considered above.22 Trusts where such a power extends to only part of the trust assets are considered below (¶ 3c). f. Transfers Not in Trust-in General 

The references to "principal" and "income" in the present section indicate that the drafters were thinking primarily of trusts where one of the enumerated powers was reserved. Those words, however, will not necessarily limit the operation of the provision to such transactions. 

It is difficult to imagine a reservation of a power to appoint personal property except in connection with a trust, but there are several ways in which powers of consumption or revocation can be in effect reserved when a gift of a future interest in personalty is made. So-called "tentative trusts", for example, are revocable by the donor, and although they bear little resemblance to a true trust such gifts should be within both the policy and the literal terms of the present provision. As noted under ¶ 1f, tentative trusts can probably be reached by an electing spouse even in the absence of statute. 

A less clear case is where the donor makes a gift of his own obligations payable at death-as in Rynier's Estate.23 If such notes are properly delivered, the notes themselves cannot be recovered back from the donee or escrow, but the donor will retain the full power to consume the property from which the notes will be paid. It is uncertain how broadly the statutory provision will be 22. Supra. lc at footnote 9.
