§ cas construed in a case of this type where there is a creation of a contract right rather than a "conveyance" of specific property but where it can be argued that practically speaking a power to consume is retained. The definition of "conveyance" in section 1 (2) and the discussion under that section should be consulted in this regard. The problem must be approached with caution in view of the absence of any saving clause in the present section relating to transfers made for value received (see ¶ 2b, supra). A transferee will not ordinarily give value for property which remains subject to a power. In the case of notes payable at death, however, the transferee might do just that and assume the risk of the maker's being solvent at death. In order to avoid embarrassment in a case where consideration is given, therefore, the courts would probably be inclined to hold that this sort of transfer, even when voluntary, is outside the scope of the present section on the ground that the notes themselves cannot be revoked or consumed. This does not necessarily mean that the spouse would be without a remedy, because, as pointed out under 1e, there is a chance that the court might distinguish Rynier's Estate and grant relief to the spouse under our case law. 

Other cases where a person retains power to consume property which will pass to a named beneficiary at death can be imagined. Could it be argued that the creator of a joint bank account, for example, has made a transfer reserving a power of consumption so that this section would overrule Orth v. Doench, 309 Pa. 240 (1932)?

Probably not, because such transfers are theoretically irrevocable; see discussion under section 1 (¶4f) of the Intestate Act. g. Insurance and Insurance Trusts

In the usual life insurance policy the insured reserves the power to change the beneficiary or to surrender the policy for cash. When a premium is paid on such a policy, does the insured make a "conveyance of assets" reserving "a power of revocation or consumption"? Senate Bill

No. 753 of the 1949 Session would have made this section 5865

§ 

ESTATES ACT 

¶ 2g inapplicable to insurance but that bill died in committee so that the question remains open. 

Again, reference should be made to the definition of conveyance" in section 1 (2) of the act and the discussion there of whether insurance falls within that definition. Even assuming that a "conveyance" of some sort has been made when insurance is purchased there is the additional problem under the present section of whether the reserved powers relate to the assets conveyed. The authorities on insurance in community property states referred to under section 1 (2) will be of some assistance in this regard. By analogy to those authorities there are at least three possible views that can be advanced as to the application of section 11 of the Estates Act to insurance. (1) It can be said that the proceeds represent the premiums so that the electing spouse can share in the entire fund. (2) It can be argued that the premiums are distinct from the proceeds so that the reserved powers do not relate to the assets conveyed. (3) Finally, there is the intermediate view that only the cash surrender value at the date of death represents assets conveyed subject to a power so that a share of only a portion of the proceeds can be claimed by the spouse. If either theory (1) or (3) is adopted, an additional problem of proration will arise in cases where some premiums were paid before and some after the effective date of the act. Somewhat analogous cases also arise in connection with the rule against perpetuities: see discussion of "Contractual Rights" 

under section 4 (b) (1) (8).

It is difficult to predict how the courts will treat insurance transactions under this section. A lot of trouble will be avoided if it is held that the section has no application. 

In the usual case the social purpose of the present section will not be served by allowing the spouse to share in insurance, and a convincing logical argument can be made for exempting insurance altogether. In addition to the argument that no "conveyance" has been made as the term is defined in section 1 (2), it can be argued that the power to change beneficiaries in an insurance policy certainly cannot be called a "power of appointment by will" and that 

5866

¶ 2h 

the power to surrender the policy for cash cannot be termed a "power of revocation or consumption" because it extends only to the cash surrender value which disappears at death and cannot be traced to the proceeds. 

On the other hand, a case can well be imagined where the purpose of the statute would seem to favor the spouseas where a large single premium policy is purchased with the aim of excluding the spouse. In such a case the court would be more sympathetic to the spouse's case, and the above logical arguments are by no means unanswerable. 

Whatever rule is applied to insurance owned outright should also apply to unfunded insurance trusts. Such trusts are often dressed up to look like present transfers but unless the policies are assigned to the trustee there is really no trust until the insured's death because there is no corpus. A funded insurance trust with the policies assigned to the trustee, on the other hand, is a true trust and if such a trust were revocable the present section would certainly apply to the securities transferred to the trustee. If the section does not apply to insurance owned outright, however, it might be questioned whether it should apply to that part of the corpus represented by the insurance proceeds, even in the case of a revocable funded trust, because the insured has reserved no more power over the policies after the transfer than before.

The whole subject of the applicability of this section to insurance will necessarily remain in doubt until the Supreme Court passes on the question. The course of the law in this respect might well depend a great deal on the equities of the first case to arise. h. Antenuptial Transfers

Nothing in the present section will restrict its operation to transfers during coverture. This seems consistent with the theory that the intent of the donor is irrelevantthe only question being whether sufficient attributes of ownership have been reserved. It would seem clear, therefore, that an antenuptial transfer could be attacked under the present provision, and it probably would make no difference how long before the marriage the transfer was made. 5867

§ ¶ 21 

ESTATES ACT i. Effective Date 

Attention is called to section 21 of the present act which provides that the act shall affect, only "conveyances" on or after January 1, 1948. Problems are likely to arise in this connection where a revocable trust is created before that date and the settlor dies thereafter. Ordinarily the new act will not apply, but in certain cases the decision might be a close one-as where the settlor has radically amended the trust after the effective date of the act. Such cases will raise a question as to the meaning of the word "conveyance" as defined by section 1 (2) of this act, where the subject is discussed generally. 

13. Personalty-Share Taken by Electing Spouse a. General 

The size of the electing spouse's share under the present section is limited (1) by the provision that the spouse may treat the transfer as "testamentary," (2) by the provision that the spouse shares "to the extent to which the power is reversed," and (3) by the provision that the spouse's interest is subordinate to estates vested in enjoyment prior to the donor's death. 

b. Transfer Treated as Testamentary 

The spouse is permitted to treat the transfer as "testamentary." In other words, as to the spouse, the transfer is treated as a gift in the will. Hence, if the spouse elects to claim under this section, he takes only the share set forth in section 8 of the Wills Act, which, unlike the Intestate Act, provides for no allowance and limits the share to onehalf even in the most favorable situation. 

c. Extent to Which Power is Reserved 

The provision that the spouse may treat the transfer as testamentary only "to the extent to which the power has been reserved" will be helpful in determining what, if any, 5868

13c 

share the spouse is entitled to in many cases, although the language is not as precise as it might be. 

The easiest case will be where the decedent has set up an inter vivos trust reserving a power over only a fractional part of the principal. Clearly the surviving spouse will have no interest in the part of the principal not subject to the power. The ambiguity in the provision lies in its failure to specify when the extent of the power is to be determined. A consideration of the various cases that might arise, however, will make it clear that the date of death should be controlling in this respect and that the section should be interpreted as if it read "to the extent to which the power has been reserved at the decedent's death." 

Such a construction is primarily necessary in order to avoid results which the Legislature could not possibly have contemplated in cases where a power originally reserved has been released, has been exercised irrevocably, or has expired prior to the death of the transferor. Suppose, for example, a testamentary power of appointment has been reserved in an inter vivos trust but the settlor releases the power (pursuant to section 3 of this act) some years prior to his death. Or, suppose a power to appoint by deed or will has been reserved and is irrevocably exercised by deed prior to the settlor's death. In all such cases, the effect is exactly the same as if an irrevocable trust reserving no power over the principal were created at the time the power was released or exercised. It would be strange indeed if the spouse could attack the transfer on the ground that the decedent once had a power over the principal at some time in the past. Or, suppose a contingent power to appoint is reserved in favor of the survivor of joint settlors and the decedent dies first so that his power never materializes. It is difficult to imagine how the present section could be construed in such a case unless the power owned at the date of death is viewed as controlling. 

A third type of case is where the settlor reserves a power to consume principal in an amount not exceeding, say, $5000 in any one year. Assuming that the solution to the other cases suggested is correct, it would seem inevitable that the surviving spouse should be limited to a share 5869

§ 

ESTATES ACT 

¶ 3d in $5000. That is the extent of the settlor's power over the principal at his death, and any other interpretation of the statute leads to the absurdities already noted. 

d. Estates of Enjoyment Saved 

The last phrase of the section, subordinating the spouse's interest to income estates which have vested in enjoyment, was necessary to prevent inequities which might otherwise arise in cases where the transferor did not reserve a life interest in himself. A typical case where this clause would operate would be the following: Settlor creates a revocable inter vivos trust, income to be paid to his sister for life with remainders over, and dies before his sister. Settlor's widow can treat the transfer as testamentary because the trust was revocable, but she may not interfere with the life estate of the sister. However, the income estate must have vested in enjoyment prior to the settlor's death. The spouse's rights in the above case would not be affected by any income estates (even though given to named persons so that they were vested in interest) following the estate of the sister. Neither would the spouse be affected by income estates arising on the death of the settlor as where a life interest has been reserved in a revocable trust followed by life estates to children. The estate must vest in enjoyment "prior to" (not "at") the settlor's death. It will be noted that no saving clause was necessary in favor of interests in principal coming into enjoyment prior to the settlor's death, for in such a case the trust would be terminated as to that principal and any reserved power over it would have expired. 

14. Personalty-Effect of Election on Interests of Other Parties (Abatement) 

The statute gives no hint as to what effect an election. by the spouse under this section will have on the interests of donees under the deed and beneficiaries under the will. 

And because of the scarcity of cases where the spouse was permitted to attack a generally valid transfer at common law, little help is given by decisions prior to the present act. 5870

§ 11 

ESTATES ACT 

In the analogous case where a widow pursues real estate conveyed by her husband inter vivos without her joinder under section 5 of the Intestate Act, the problem is relatively simple because she asserts her dower interest in the particular piece of land conveyed. Similarly, when a widow takes real estate against the will under section 8 of the Wills Act she becomes tenant in common to the extent of her share in each parcel of land the decedent owned. 

In the case of personalty, however, the problem is more complex. The most helpful analogy in applying the present section will be in cases dealing with abatement of legacies where the spouse takes personalty against the will under section 8 of the Wills Act. As stated in the discussion of that section (at ¶6), the primary rule is that the testator's plan should be disturbed as little as possible, although various rules of abatement are applied in the absence of a contrary intent appearing in the will. These cases will be of some help, but the real difficulty under the present section will lie in determining what status the inter vivos gift should have when general principles of abatement are applied.

Suppose the decedent created a revocable inter vivos trust of securities in favor of himself for life with remainder over to his sister. By will he bequeaths his personal effects to his niece, a pecuniary legacy to his nephew, and the residue to his brother. The widow elects to take against the trust under this section and against the will under section 8 of the Wills Act. Assuming there are no children, she will be entitled to a sum equal to one-half the combined value of the testamentary estate and the trust estate. But it is uncertain how the burden of this election will be distributed among the other parties in interest. 

Perhaps the simplest solution would be to follow the analogy of dower in aliened real estate and hold that the trust estate and the testamentary estate abate pro rata. In the example, this would mean that the sister as remainderman of the trust would have her gift reduced by one-half, and the testamentary gifts would abate as in any other case of election. 

Another solution would be to give the inter vivos donee a preference over the beneficiaries under the will, so that 5871

§ 

ESTATES ACT 

14 the entire burden would if possible be borne by the testamentary estate-even to the extent of wiping it out entirely-and the inter vivos gift reduced only to the extent that the widow's share exceeded the testamentary estate. 

This was substantially what was done in Hummel's Estate, 161 Pa. 215 (1894), discussed above (1e) in connection with the common law on notes payable at death. In that case the court (which seemed rather overimpressed by the seal on the notes) apparently regarded the donees as creditors, so that the decision might be confined to cases where the subject matter of the gift was the decedent's own obligation. But this method of handling the problem might be adopted generally on the ground that the inter vivos donee is more likely to be the primary object of decedent's bounty. 

A third possible solution would be to regard the inter vivos gift as testamentary for the purpose of applying rules of abatement discussed under section 8 of the Wills Act. 

It will be noted that this method is not required by the present section which merely provides that the transfer is to be regarded as testamentary so far as the spouse's rights are concerned. Nevertheless, the analogy might be appealing as an intermediate position giving the inter vivos donee an advantage over some of the testamentary beneficiaries but not all of them. The difficulty would be in deciding whether the inter vivos gift should be regarded as a pecuniary or a specific legacy under the rules of abatement. 

An inter vivos trust of securities, for example, would be in the form of a specific gift, but in substance it would bear a closer resemblance to a pecuniary legacy. 

Other possible solutions can probably be thought of, but how the courts will handle the problem cannot be predicted. It might make a difference how the question arises. 

In most situations the first solution suggested (treating the inter vivos gift and the testamentary estate separately, so that each abates proportionately) would probably constitute the best working rule in that it would prevent too heavy a burden falling on the residuary legatees. However, if the donor dies intestate, his plan would be least disturbed by adopting the second or third alternative and favoring the donee over the heirs at law. The second solu- 5872

ESTATES ACT 

§ 11 tion would also give the spouse more adequate protection when an inter vivos trust is set up in another jurisdictiona situation discussed below under the next heading. 

Other problems might arise concerning abatement within the inter vivos trust (assuming it bears at least some of the burden of the election). And a pretty problem of sequestration might be presented by a case where the spouse is given a life estate in a revocable inter vivos trust but elects to claim rights under this section instead.24 

5. Personalty-Conflict of Laws 

A novel question of conflicts will be presented where an inter vivos trust reserving one of the enumerated powers is set up in another state and the decedent dies domiciled in Pennsylvania, or vice versa. The general rule is that the rights of a surviving spouse in a decedent's personality are determined by the law of the decedent's domicil at his death.25 However, that rule assumes that the decedent died owning the property. Here the question is whether the settlor during his lifetime succeeded in giving the property away in such a manner as would put it beyond the reach of the spouse. Hence the law governing the validity and effect of the inter vivos transfer would seem to be controlling. 

Unfortunately the authorities are far from uniform on the rules of conflicts applicable to trusts inter vivos of personal property.26 Not only are the basic rules uncertain, but it makes a difference what kind of personalty is transferred.

Preliminarily it will be noted that the "seat" of the trust will be the place where the trust is to be administered (the office of the corporate trustee-unless the settlor designate another place in the instrument), so that the trustee will be accountable there. Hence, if the trustee is in another state, the courts of that state will ordinarily have 24. Cf. cases discussed under section 8 (¶ 6c) of the Wills Act.

It is important to distinguish between these rules of jurisdiction (which are relatively clear) and the question of what law will be applied by the proper court. It is also important to distinguish between questions involving the effectiveness or validity of a transfer in trust and questions regarding its administration. The law of a trust's situs usually governs questions of administration, but here we are concerned with whether the original transfer was effective to bar the spouse. With this in mind, let us suppose a Pennsylvania domiciliary takes stocks and bonds to New York and there transfers them to a New York trust company under a deed of trust expressly declaring an intention that the law of New York should govern. Let us assume further that the trust is of such a nature that the spouse could reach the assets on the death of the settlor under this section of the Pennsylvania act, but that it would be invulnerable to attack by the spouse in New York. On the facts given, it would seem that the effect of the transfer would be governed by New York law and that the spouse would be barred. This result would follow in part from section 12 (a) of the New 

York Personal Property Law (Consol. Laws C. 41) which permits foreign settlors to adopt the law of New York in this situation.

Even apart from that section of the New York statute, however, the same result would seem to follow. In Hutchinson v. Ross, 262 N. Y. 381, 187 N. E. 65 (1933), a husband created a trust with a New York trust company of securities located in New York. The settlor was domiciled in 

Quebec and under the law of that province the transfer was ineffective because it was contrary to the terms of an antenuptial agreement with his spouse. In New York, the trust was valid and irrevocable. There was no express declara-

In so deciding the New York court followed section 294 (1) of the Restatement of Conflicts which provides that the validity of an inter vivos trust of chattels is governed by the law of the state where the chattels are situated at the time the trust was created. An equally important point of the decision was that stocks and bonds are to be considered tangible property having a situs where the certificates and bonds are situateď rather than as intangible choses in action. The court said: "Intangible property, like shares of corporate stock or deeds, may for practical purposes be merged and embodied in documents like stock certificates or bonds, which like bills and notes are 'instrumentalities of trade and commerce.' 'They pass from hand to hand and properly are governed by the rule relating to the transfer of tangibles'

Such documents and the personal property merged or embodied in them have, like tangible chattels, a situs apart from the domicle of the owners." 

So much for the law of New York with respect to trusts of stocks and bonds. If the same settlor had created his trust in some other jurisdiction, however, other rules of conflicts might be applied.28 The decision in Hutchinson v. 

Ross is a clear-cut and satisfactory authority on the question, supported by the Restatement, so that it might well be followed in other jurisdictions. On the other hand, other courts (and even New York itself) might balk at making the location of the securities at the time of the transfer controlling in all cases.

Many courts, rather than regarding any one factor as conclusive, follow the cruder practice of "balancing the contacts"; the residences of the various parties, the place where the deed was executed, the location of the property, -even the state of incorporation of the companies issuing 28. Other courts might follow the cases dealing with testamentary trusts and make the domicile of the settlor controlling. As to a provision in the instrument designating the law of settlor's choice, a court might view this as significant even in the absence of a statute such as the New York act, but on the other hand, it might be held that such provisions are irrelevant on the ground that it is impossible for the intention of the parties to a transaction to affect its validity. 

Suppose now that the situation is reversed and a New York domiciliary sets up a trust of stocks and bonds with a Pennsylvania trust company. Here the Pennsylvania court would have jurisdiction and out rules of conflicts would be applied in the first instance. Such Pennsylvania cases as there are on the subject leave the question in doubt. 

A dictum in Lines v. Lines, 142 Pa. 149, 165 (1891), is in harmony with Hutchinson v. Ross. There a Pennsylvania domiciliary, while in New York, transferred stocks and bonds to a New York trust company in trust. There were various grounds for the decision that the spouse could not attack this transfer (among them, the fact that Pennsylvania had no jurisdiction over the trust anyway), but the court indicated that in its opinion the effect of such transfer on the rights of the spouse was governed by New York law. It would seem to follow that our law would govern if a resident of New York created a trust of securities in Pennsylvania, naming a Pennsylvania trust company. A seemingly contrary decision, however, is Fowler's Appeal, 125 Pa. 388 (1889). That case concerned the applicability of our statute against accumulations and the court said (at 

393): "The Settlor was a citizen of Illinois and died there; the deed of trust was made there; the securities are those of foreign corporations and Mrs. Fowler (the life beneficiary) is a citizen of Colorado. I do not understand it to be denied that the trust is valid by the law of the state where it was made and of the state where it is enjoyed; and the mere fact that the trustee happens to be a Pennsylvania corporation cannot invalidate the trust. The act of 1853 [prohibiting accumulations] was only intended to 5876

¶ 

ESTATES ACT 

11 § cos apply to our citizens. "The emphasis on the act of 

1853 will be noted. It may be that the decision is confined to cases of that limited nature, but the court might say the same thing with respect to section 11 of the Estates Act. In other words, it might be admitted that the rule of the Restatement and Lines v. Lines is sound as a matter of general conflicts law, but that our statute concerning a spouse's right to take against an inter vivos trust was "only intended to apply to our citizens." Such a conclusion would be strengthened by a consideration of the results which a contrary holding would lead to. Suppose the court in the case suggested held that the 

Pennsylvania act applied to the trust created here by the foreign domiciliary. This would mean that the trust could be considered "testamentary" by the surviving spouse. But the law of decedent's domicile would plainly govern the question of what rights the spouse has in the decedent's testamentary estate. Hence whether our act would have any effect ultimately would depend on what rights the spouse had to take against the will in the foreign jurisdiction. That the Legislature contemplated such an unusual instance of renvoi is doubtful, and our courts would do well to limit this section to Pennsylvania domiciliaries, regardless of what the ordinary rules of conflicts might be. 

The above discussion has been limited to trusts of stocks and bonds. Where other types of personal property are involved, different rules apply. The principle of 

Hutchinson v. Ross, for example, can be applied only to tangible property or to an intangible represented by an essential or semi-essential document. In the case of a trust created with intangible personalty not represented by such a document, the prevailing view seems to be that the law of the settlor's domicile controls in all cases. Jackman v.

Equitable Life Assurance Society, 145 F. 2d 945 (C. C. A. 

3d, 1944), is a good case on this question where Pennsylvania rules of conflicts were applied. See also Matter of 

Weinstein, 176 Misc. 592, 28 N. Y. S. 2d 137 (1941), distinguishing Hutchinson v. Ross in this type of case. This view is also favored by Beale (Conflict of Laws § 294.4). 

Note, however, that the Restatement of Conflicts in § 294 5877

§ 

ESTATES ACT 

¶ 6 (2) takes a contrary view and declares that the validity of an inter vivos trust of choses in action is governed by the law of the place "where the transaction takes place." 

How cash is to be considered under the above rules is uncertain. Actual bills, no doubt, would be considered tangibles or at least intangibles represented by an essential document. A deposit in a bank, on the other hand, looks more like a wholly intangible obligation, although there appears to be some authority for holding that it has a situs where the bank is located rather than at the domicile of the depositor (see Morris v. Sheehan, 112 Misc. 222, 184 

N. Y. S. 121 (1920)).

As to mortgages still other rules apply. Section 226 of the Restatement of Conflicts states that the validity and effect of an assignment of a mortgage on land is determined by the law of the state where the land is. In the comment, it is indicated that the validity of the assignment of the bond supporting the mortgage might be governed. by a different set of rules. It would seem, however, that that way lies madness, and a court would more likely consider the bond and mortgage as one in applying the rules of conflicts.

By way of conclusion (or lack of one), it may be said that the rules of conflicts governing inter vivos trusts are so uncertain that there is no definite answer to any of the innumerable types of questions that might arise. In view of this uncertainty in the law, extra-legal considerations might become important. For example, if the case arises in another state, the foreign court will not be anxious to impose a restraint on alienation arising from Pennsylvania law. On the other hand, if the case arises in Pennsylvania, our courts will not be anxious to give to the spouse of the foreign domiciliary a protection which he did not enjoy at home. Hence, logically or illogically, the tendency will probably be to decide cases in such a way that the restrictions of this section do not apply in either type of case. ¶ 6. Real Estate

At common law, each spouse was protected from inter vivos conveyances of real estate by the other. The law giv- 5878

Thus dower in statutory form has been retained for the benefit of the non-joining wife and the husband is protected by his wife's inability to convey her real estate without his joinder under the Married Women's Property Act. These matters are discussed under sections 5 (a) and 5 (b) of the Intestate Act. 

In view of the protection afforded by these other statutory provisions, there was no real need for additional legislation with regard to conveyances of real estate, and the notes of the commissioners indicate that the drafters of the present section were concerned primarily with transfers of personalty. However, the section applies to conveyances of "assets" and there is nothing in that word to indicate that only personal property was intended. 

As to conveyances of real estate by either spouse during coverture, where powers of appointment, revocation or consumption are reserved, the possibility of this section's conflicting with the law of dower and such legislation as the femme sole trader acts is discussed under section 5 (a) (3g) and section 5 (b) (¶ 3g) of the Intestate Act. In a general way, it can be said that it will be a rare case where this section will have any application to a conveyance of real estate during coverture. Where the conveyance is without joinder the case will ordinarily be governed by the broader provisions of section 5 (a) of the Intestate 

Act and the Married Women's Property Act. On the other hand, if the spouse joins in a deed in which the grantor reserves powers, the conveyance is of course effective generally, and the joinder will probably also bar the spouse from claiming under this section of the Estates Act-but see discussion below under section ¶ 9. 

Antenuptial conveyances of land in fraud of marital rights are also discussed under sections 5 (a) (¶ 3k) and 5 (b) (¶ 3h) of the Intestate Act, where it is pointed out that our cases require proof of actual fraud before such a conveyance can be attacked. It seems clear that the present section will alter the case law relating to antenuptial conveyances wherever a power of appointment, revocation, or consumption is reserved by the grantor. If 5879

¶ 7. Effect of Election on Spouse's Share in Other Property 

It has been noted that when a widow claims dower in aliened lands under section 5 (a) of the Intestate Act, she is not making an election and probably may accept gifts under the will as well (see ¶ 3d and ¶ 3g under that section). Where a spouse elects to take against the will under section 8 of the Wills Act, on the other hand, he must renounce his rights under the will. As the present section is worded, it is clear that by regarding the inter vivos transfer as "testamentary" the spouse can take against it only under section 8 of the Wills Act and hence must renounce whatever is given by the will. Must he also renounce his share in other inter vivos trusts? Probably not. Suppose, for example, the decedent by deed sets up revocable trust A in which his wife is the primary beneficiary, and revocable trust B in which his sister is the primary beneficiary, and then dies leaving the rest of his property by will to his brother. Can the widow elect to take against the will and against trust B but accept her gift under trust 4? It would seem that she could, because the present section gives the spouse the option of determining whether an inter vivos transaction is testatmentary as to her.31

[9. How Effect of Section can be Avoided 

In framing the present section the drafters no doubt were thinking primarily of the case where a man, unreasonably hostile to his dutiful wife, attempts to pauperize her after his death by making an inter vivos transfer while retaining substantial dominion over the property during his lifetime. It is plain, however, that the act will have a far broader application. Like section 8 of the Wills 

Act, the provision will apply to transfers of either spouse regardless of the decedent's good faith or the fairness of other provisions made for the surviving spouse. A typical case where our statutory provisions for the surviving spouse (both here and in the Wills Act) do far more harm than good is where a wealthy man adequately provides for the support of his widow by giving her a life interest in the bulk of his estate and in the proceeds of his life insurance. Such a provision is generally part of a carefully prepared plan to minimize the tax burden and benefit the children after the widow's death. Upon the husband's death, however, our law permits the widow, who is perhaps acting on the advice of designing persons, to raise havoc with the estate plan by taking against the will, even though the testamentary provision made for her is to her best interest.38 The alert estate planner has long

The obvious way to bar the spouse is to relinquish all control over the principal. And even principal can be kept available by giving a disinterested trustee power to use it for the settlor's benefit. It is only when such a power is reserved in the settlor that the trust can be attacked by the spouse. 

There will no doubt be attempts to avoid the effect of the present provision by setting up inter vivos trusts in other jurisdictions. Quite apart from the inconvenience this entails, however, there is no guarantee that the desired result will be attained. And even if the foreign law applies, there is always the possibility that the transfer will be regarded as testamentary under the case law of the other jurisdiction; in very few cases can the decision of any court be predicted with certainty in this field of the law.34

The most satisfactory way of insuring a carefully planned estate against attack by an ill-advised spouse is to secure a release from the spouse at the time the trust is created. Assuming, as we are, that the settlor is acting in good faith and an adequate provision is made for the spouse by way of an income estate or otherwise, this solution should not be impractical in most cases. Care should be taken, however, to reduce the risk of such a release being attacked as invalid because of lack of consideration, presumed coercion, or overreaching. It is uncertain, for example, whether a naked joinder by the spouse in the trust deed would be sufficient. Such a joinder is sufficient to bar dower in aliened land under section 5 (a) of the Intestate Act, but there the statute specifically so provides. 

An enlightened court would probably hold that any clear statement of intent to waive the statutory right was sufficient to bar an election under this section on general principles of modern marital law in the absence of affirmative proof of fraud or coercion. If psychologically feasible, however, the risk of a contrary holding can be reduced if not eliminated by obtaining the spouse's signature to a written release under seal (or containing the words "intending to be legally bound") reciting her understanding of the law and the consideration she is receiving (e. g. the income estate or whatever other provision is made for her) for executing the release. Such a release should bring the transaction within the cases dealing with inter vivos agreements in bar of marital rights.35

§ 12. SPENDTHRIFT TRUSTS 

Income of a trust subject to spendthrift or similar provisions shall nevertheless be liable for the support of anyone whom the income beneficiary shall be under a legal duty to support. 

COMMISSIONERS' COMMENT-This section is based on section 19 of the Wills Act of 1917. Other acts applicable to spendthrift trusts are the Act of 1921, P. L. 434, 48 PS 136, and section 

733 of the Penal Code, 18 PS 4733. 

The Pennsylvania Bar Association Committee on the Law of Decedents' Estates and Trusts in its report made in June 1942, made the following comments on spendthrift trusts: "It is not proposed at this point to treat the general subject of spendthrift trusts even though they are often created by wills. Here will merely be discussed the inadequacy of the existing provision in Section 19 which subjects such trusts created by will to liability for the support and maintenance of the 'wife and minor children' (cf. 48 PS 136, which confers rights to proceed with levy or attachment on any estates up to 50 percent of the amount thereof for support of 'the wife or children'. In 

Stewart's Est., 334 Pa. 356 (1939) it is said that the two acts provide concurrent remedies). Why should not the provision protect any member of the family whom the beneficiary of the trust is under a legal duty to support? 

Should there be any difference whether the support is necessary for a minor child as contrasted to a disabled child who is of age or a parent who is an invalid? The 

Supreme Court in Moorehead's Est., (289 Pa. 542, 552 (1927)) has said: ""In every civilized country is recognized the obligation, sacred as well as lawful, of a husband to protect and provide for his family. * * * This case goes beyond the concern of the immediate parties to it. It affects the status of the family as being the foundation of society and civilization, and hence in a very certain sense is of wide public concern'. "In that case, however, the issue was only as to the right of the wife against the spendthrift trust in favor of her husband. "Recommendation No. 6. Spendthrift trusts hereafter becoming effective should be subjected to liability for the support of all persons whom the beneficiary is under a legal duty to support."

The recommendation of the Bar Association Committee was followed. 5901

§ 

ESTATES ACT 

Old Law

Section 19. All income whatsoever, devised or bequeathed by any will so as to be free from liability for the debts, contracts, or engagements of the beneficiary, or so as not to be subject to execution, attachment sur judgment, sequestration, or other process, shall, notwithstanding such testamentary provision, be subject to and liable for the support and maintenance of the wife and minor children of the beneficiary, and for the value of necessaries furnished to them, or any of them, where said beneficiary has refused or neglected to provide suitably for them; and all of the income of said beneficiary shall be subject to all legal process issued by any court of this Commonwealth having jurisdiction in the premises, in order to enforce such liability of said beneficiary. 

Wills Act of 1917, P. L. 403. 

Other statutes governing both inter vivos and testamentary trusts are still in effect and are referred to below in the discussion. 

The right to execute against spendthrift income is extended from cases of wives and minor children claiming against a spendthrift interest in a testamentary trust to cases of claims by anyone whom the beneficiary has a duty to support against an income interest in any trusttestamentary or inter vivos. The significance of the change, however, is somewhat lessened by the fact that the general subject is also covered by prior decisions and other statutes.

¶ 1. Ineffective Spendthrift Provisions Etc. Distinguished 

Before a problem under this section is reached, it must first be determined that the interest of the defendant is subject to a spendthrift restriction which is effective to protect his interest from ordinary creditors. Spendthrift clauses are favorites of the Pennsylvania courts which were leaders in recognizing their validity. Nevertheless, even in Pennsylvania, such clauses are not recognized as effective in all cases. 

For example, if a man creates a trust reserving to himself the income for life, any spendthrift restriction which he attempts to impose on his own right to income is invalid as to any credit. See Bowers' Trust Estate, 346 Pa. 85, 89 n. 6 (1943). Certainly, the wife or other relative could reach the reserved income just as readily as any other claimant. Also, even when the trust is created by another, it is possible for some deeds and wills to be so construed that the spendthrift clause does not protect the interest from the wife or close relative. Such was one of the alternative grounds for the decision in Moorehead's Estate, 289 Pa. 542 (1927). It must be borne in mind, therefore, that in the subsequent discussion it is assumed there is a spendthrift provision which is valid generally and which as a matter of construction purports to protect the interest from all types of claims. 

It must also be assumed that the property is still in the hands of the fiduciary and that the beneficiary is resisting the execution. For example, a husband may make a voluntary "assignment" of his spendthrift income to his estranged wife. Such "assignment" necessarily remains revocable but will be recognized as valid if the money is paid before the beneficiary changes his mind. 

See Keeler's Estate, 334 Pa. 225 (1939). In the cases to be discussed, it is assumed that no such "assignment" has 5903

§ 

ESTATES ACT 

12 been made, or that, if made, it has been revoked prior to actual payment by the fiduciary. 

12. History-Other Statutes and Cases 

The first statute of this sort was the act of 1913, P. L. 

72 (amending the act of 1867, P. L. 78). This provision, as amended in 1917, P. L. 614, and incorporated into the 

Criminal Code of 1939, P. L. 872, as section 733, 18 P. S. § 4733, gave a wife or child the right to enforce a support order obtained under that act against one-half of the husband's or father's spendthrift interest. It further provided that the writ of attachment should remain "a continuing levy" on such income "until the order has been paid in full." This was supplemented by the act of 1921, P. L. 434, 48 P. S. § 136, giving the wife or child the same right against one-half of the husband's spendthrift interest in enforcing a support order of "any court of competent jurisdiction." Independent of these acts, section 19 of the Wills Act of 1917, made the entire spendthrift income of a testamentary trust liable for the support of the beneficiary's wife and minor children but contained no language concerning the "continuing levy." In the meantime, the Supreme Court reversed its earlier decisions and held, as a matter of case law independent of statute, that a spendthrift clause in any trust was ineffective against support claims of a wife or child.¹ In Stewart's Estate, 334 Pa. 356 (1939), the court attempted to bring some semblance of order out of this curious tangle of statutes and cases.2 From that case it

In Stewart's Est., 334 Pa. 356 (1939), however, the court made it clear that "spendthrift trusts are invalid," as to claims of wives as a matter of public policy derived solely from case law. cos appears that the claimant has a choice of remedies in reaching the spendthrift interest of the defendant-at least where the claim is against the husband or father of the claimant. Where a wife had obtained a support order upon which her husband was in arrears, it was said that she could do one or both of two things: (a) She could reduce the arrearages to judgment and execute against the entire interest of the husband in the trust regardless of the spendthrift clause. This could be done either under section 19 of the Wills Act of 1917 (as to spendthrift income of a testamentary trust), or under the case law doctrine (as to any spendthrift interest, principal or income, which the husband owned in any inter vivos or testamentary trust ³). Such execution, however, would be limited to the arrearages reduced to judgment and could not be extended to future defaults. (b) In the alternative or in addition to the above remedy, the wife could proceed to enforce her claim under the act of 1921, P. L. 434, 48 P. S. § 136 (or under section 733 of the Criminal Code, 18 P. S. § 4733, if that procedure was used in establishing the right to support) against one-half of spendthrift interest (principal or income), and the writ so obtained could presumably be used for enforcing amounts which accrued after the writ was obtained. This is a purely statutory remedy so that the limits of the statute cannot be exceeded. 

3. Present Law in General 

The present section of the Estates Act takes the place of section 19 of the Wills Act of 1917 and eliminates two arbitrary restrictions in the old provision. Both testamentary and inter vivos trusts are now covered, and the section is available to anyone whom the beneficiary has a 3. Of course, if the husband only has an income estate, the wife cannot attack the principal (Buchner v. Buchner, 34 D. & C. 597 (M. C. Phila. 1939)), but it seems clear that the case law doctrine would make a gift of principal to the husband liable to attachment even though it was subject to a spendthrift restriction and was still in the hands of the fiduciary. 5905

$

ESTATES ACT 

14 legal duty to support, rather than only wives and minor children.

The significance of these changes is less than might at first appear. As pointed out under the preceding heading, the case law doctrine had already gone further than the old Wills Act and had been extended to inter vivos as well as testamentary trusts. In one respect the case law remains broader than the present section in that the statute is still limited to income. Whether the section extends or merely reaffirms the case law in making spendthrift income liable for the support of anyone whom the beneficiary has a duty to support is problematical. So far as is known, the question has arisen only in cases where a wife or a child was claiming against the husband.* 

See further discussion of this point under ¶ 7f, g and i, below.

Note also that the present act does not repeal or in any way affect the provisions in the Criminal Code of 1939 and in the act of 1921 for securing a continuing levy against one-half of the defendant's spendthrift interest. 

Those statutes remain on the books and provide alternative or additional remedies for the wife or child. 

Thus, in all cases the following sources should be examined to determine what remedy or remedies are available: (1) the present section of the Estates Act, (2) the case law as exemplified by Stewart's Estate, 334 Pa. 356 (1939), (3) the act of 1921, P. L. 434, 48 P. S. § 136, and (4) section 733 of the Criminal Code of 1939, P. L. 872, 18 P. S. § 4733. The availability of these various remedies in various types of cases is discussed below in ¶ 7.

It is clear that before a spendthrift trust is attacked under this section, under other statutes, or under the case law, the right to support must first be judically determined. by the proper tribunal. ¶ 7. Remedies Available in Particular Cases a. General

As already noted above under ¶ 2, case law and other statutes also deal with the liability of spendthrift trusts to attachment for support, and according to Stewart's Estate, 334 Pa. 356 (1939), two general types of remedies are provided: (1) attachment under the case law 12 or under this section of the Estates Act of the entire interest of the beneficiary to satisfy a fixed amount of arrearages reduced to judgment, and (2) attachment under the act of 1921, P. L. 434, 18 P. S. § 136, or under the Criminal 

Code of 1939, P. L. 872, 18 P. S. § 4733, of one-half of the beneficiary's interest to satisfy both past and future payments. Because the various statutes are worded differently, the availability of either or both of these remedies will vary according to the relationship of the parties and the nature of the claim. 

b. Wife v. Husband on Domestic Support Order 

Greatest scope is given to the wife in obtaining and enforcing a support order. In obtaining the order she may proceed under the Criminal Code of 1939, P. L. 872, 18 

P. S. § 4733, under the act of 1907, P. L. 227, as amended, 48 P. S. § 131, or under the Support Law of 1937, P. L. 

2045, as amended, 62 P. S. § 1973. In enforcing the order against the husband's spendthrift trust both remedies are available. She may attach the entire interest for arrearages under this section of the Estates Act or under the case law, or she may attach one-half of the interest to satisfy arrearages or to secure future payments under the act of 1921 or under the Criminal Code. 

c. Wife v. Husband on Foreign Support Order 

It was at one time in doubt whether a support order properly issued by the court of another state was enforceable against spendthrift trusts in Pennsylvania. Stewart's 

Estate, 334 Pa. 356 (1939), however, removed all doubt

Although there is no permanent alimony in cases of divorce a v. m. in Pennsylvania, such a decree might have been validly obtained in another state and be entitled to full faith and credit here.

The word alimony comes from the Latin "alimonia," meaning sustenance. Both literally and as the term is generally understood, therefore, a decree for alimony is a decree for support. A decree for alimony pendente lite or permanent alimony in divorce a m. et t. runs in favor of the wife while she is still married to the respondent.

On the first point, Commonwealth ex rel. Esenwein v. 

Esenwein, 348 Pa. 455 (1944), aff'd. 325 U. S. 279 (1945), and Sherrer v. Sherrer, 334 U. S. 343 (1948) must be examined. In the usual case of the Reno divorce there is no real domicile established in Nevada and the Nevada court's finding of this jurisdictional fact would not be followed if the question could be relitigated in a state where divorce has not yet been put on a commercial basis. The question, therefore, is whether the Nevada court's finding of the jurisdictional fact is subject to collateral attack here, or must be accepted as final under the full faith and credit clause of the Federal Constitution. At the time of writing the Supreme Court of the United States is having some difficulty making up its mind about such cases. For the moment the rules seem to be: (1) If the foreign proceedings were wholly ex parte (service on the defendant having been only by publication or mail) the question of domicile can be relitigated here (Esenwein case). (2) If the defendant appears in the foreign divorce proceeding, then the foreign court's finding on the jurisdictional question cannot be attacked collaterally and the divorce is good here regardless of what the actual facts might be. (Sherrer case.) 21

If the foreign decree is subject to collateral attack under the above rules and found by the Pennsylvania court to be invalid for want of jurisdiction, then it can be ignored and execution against the spendthrift trust can proceed in the usual manner. The Esenwein case, although it did not involve a spendthrift trust, is clear authority for this. 

On the other hand, if the foreign decree is not subject to collateral attack or if the divorced plaintiff's domicile 21. Exactly how much participation by the defendant in the divorce proceeding is necessary to enable the foreign court to lift itself into jurisdiction by its own bootstraps under the Sherrer doctrine is not entirely clear. Probably any appearance-even by counsel only-would suffice. At least this would seem to be the rule until the Sherrer case is overruled, qualified or explained away. 5914

¶ 12 

ESTATES ACT 

§ cos in Nevada is actually bona fide (a possible if improbable contingency), the divorce must be recognized as valid here. 

It would seem to follow in such a case that the divorce defendant's support order would necessarily become unenforceable against a spendthrift trust or otherwise-not merely because the Pennsylvania claimant has ceased to be a "wife" within the meaning of the Act of 1921, etc. (Lippincott v. Lippincott, 349 Pa. 501 (1944)) but because the support order itself would lose its foundation. This would seem to be implicit in the Esenwein decision. 

However, the same day that the United States Supreme Court laid down a reasonably definite (if somewhat illogical) rule in the Sherrer case, it proceeded to throw another cloud over the whole subject by suggesting that a person might be married for some purposes and unmarried for others in Estin v. Estin, 334 U. S. 541 (1948). In that case a wife obtained a support order in New York. 

The husband thereupon secured a Nevada divorce but, surprisingly enough, the New York Court admitted that this was one of those rare cases where the divorce plaintiff actually was "a bona fide resident of the State of Nevada.” 

Nevertheless, the New York Court held that its support order was still effective and the United States Supreme Court affirmed. The dissenting Justices, Frankfurter and 

Jackson, would have had no argument with the decision if it had been based solely and squarely on the ground that in New York a support order survives divorce. This seemed clearly contrary to fact, however, and the majority opinion hedged on this point. This led the dissenters to conclude with some justification that the majority had "reached the Solomon-like conclusion that the Nevada decree was half good and half bad," (92 L. Ed. 1085) and entitled to only one-half faith and credit.

It is therefore constitutionally possible for the Pennsylvania court to recognize the foreign divorce decree and at the same time continue its own support order. As a necessary corollary, it would also seem constitutionally possible for the Pennsylvania court to decide that its support order was still enforceable against the interest of the half-husband in a spendthrift trust. The likelihood of our 5915

§ 

ESTATES ACT 

¶9 court's taking advantage of this loop-hole in the "full" faith and credit clause, however, is remote. In all probability the logic of the Esenwein case will be followed and the foreign divorce found either wholly good or wholly bad.

In this connection it is important to bear in mind that under equitable principles a spouse who obtains or connives in obtaining an otherwise invalid foreign divorce might be estopped to question its validity. Many cases of socially accepted divorces where both parties cooperate in obtaining a Reno decree will be covered by this doctrine of estoppel if one of the conspirators has the bad grace to question in a support proceeding the validity of the divorce so obtained. The present section applies to trusts subject to spendthrift "or similar provisions." Where a trust for a minor or incompetent is subject to a valid direction to accumulate the income, the case will be governed by section 7 (subsections b and c) of this act. 5916 [The next page is 5951]

§ 13. LIMITED ESTATES IN PERSONALTY AND IN THE PROCEEDS OF THE CONVERSION OF REAL ESTATE 

A person having a present interest in personal property, or in the proceeds of the conversion of real estate, which is not in trust, and which is subject to a future interest, shall be deemed to be a trustee of such property, and not a debtor to the remainderman, with the ordinary powers and duties of a trustee, except that he shall not be required to change the form of the investment to an investment authorized for Pennsylvania fiduciaries, nor shall he be entitled to compensation as trustee. Such person, unless given a power of consumption or excused from entering security by the terms of the conveyance, shall be required to enter such security for the protection of persons entitled to the future interests as the court in its discretion shall direct. If a person having a present interest shall not enter security as directed, the court shall appoint a trustee who shall enter such security as the court shall direct, and who shall exercise all the ordinary powers and duties of a trustee, except that he shall not be required to change the form of the investment to an investment authorized for Pennsylvania fiduciaries.

COMMISSIONERS' COMMENT-This section replaces section 23 of the 

Fiduciaries Act of 1917. "Proceeds of the conversion of real estate", instead of proceeds of the "sale" of real estate, was employed so that it includes the proceeds of real estate no matter how acquired, whether from the proceeds of insur ance (cf. Uniform Principal and Income Act Section 3 (2), 

20 PS 3473), from natural resources allocated to principal (Uniform Principal and Income Act, Section 9, 20 PS 3479), from forfeited down money (Knapp's Est., 24 C. C. 119) or from the proceeds of property taken on eminent domain: Conner's 

Est., 239 Pa. 449.

Section 13 will continue to apply when the proceeds of the conversion are reinvested in real estate. 

The words "a person having a present interest * * * which is not in trust, and which is subject to a future interest" are considered an all-inclusive definition of the relationship and as making it clear that it does not include trust relationships as such. "and not a debtor to the remainderman" was added to emphasize the fact that the rule of law heretofore found in Fiduciaries Act, section 23, will no longer apply. “except that he shall not be required to change the form of the 5951

§ ESTATES ACT 

cos 13 investment to an investment authorized for Pennsylvania fiduciaries" was included to make it clear that the life beneficiary may retain the original property so long as he considers it advisable. New investments will be required to be in legal investments, as the life beneficiary is subject to "the ordinary powers and duties of a trustee". 

Consistent with Powell's Est., 340 Pa. 404, 411, and

Zehender's Est., 8 Dist. 439, there is no provision for requiring security where the life tenant is given a power of consumption or is excused therefrom. Where these features are lacking the court in its discretion can require security.

Section 23. Whenever any person is or shall be entitled to the income from the proceeds of the sale of a decedent's real estate; and whenever any personal property, or the increase, profits or dividends thereof, has been or shall hereafter be bequeathed to any person for life or for a terms of years, or for any other limited period, or upon a condition or contingency; the executor or executors, administrator with the will annexed, trustee or trustees under such will, or trustee appointed by the orphans' court to make such sale of real estate, as the case may be, shall deliver the property so bequeathed to the person entitled thereto, upon such person giving security in the orphans' court having jurisdiction, in such form and amount as in the judgment of the court will sufficiently secure the interests of the person or persons entitled in remainder, whenever the same shall accrue or vest in possession. Should such person or legatee refuse or neglect, or be unable, to enter such security, the court may, upon petition of any person interested, including the owner of any subsequent interest, vested or contingent, in such proceeds of real estate, personal property, or the increase, profits, or dividends thereof, and upon due notice to all persons interested, so far as such notice can reasonably be given, appoint a suitable person or corporation as trustee to receive and hold such proceeds of sale or personal property, invest the same in securities authorized by law, pay the income thereof, after deducting all legal charges, to the person entitled thereto; and, upon the termination of the trust, account for and pay to the persons entitled thereto the corpus of the trust fund, or transfer and deliver to them the securities in which it is invested, as the court may direct, after deducting all legal charges thereon. Such trustee shall enter such security as the court may direct. He shall not be an insurer of the trust fund, and shall be liable to the persons interested in the income or corpus of the trust fund only for such care, prudence, and diligence in the execution of the trust as other trustees are liable for.

The law is basically changed so that instruments which would have created a legal future interest in personalty now create trusts with the first taker as trustee for himself and the remainderman.

¶ 1. Legal Life Estates in Personalty at Common Law 

Comparatively little trouble is caused by wills and deeds which transfer personalty to T in trust to pay the net income to A for life and on A's death to pay the principal to B. Similar legal estates in land without the use of the trust device are also governed by reasonably coherent rules of law which are widely understood. When the same thing is attempted with personalty, however, by an instrument which without creating a trust simply provides for a gift of personalty "to A for life, remainder to B," it is fair to say that the common law was incapable of dealing logically and consistently with the problem. 

There are good discussions of the case law on future interests in personalty in Gray, Rule Against Perpetuities (4th ed. 1942) § 789 et seq.; Simes, Future Interests (1936) 

§§ 196 et seq. and 202 et seq.; and the Introductory Note preceding § 200 of the Restatement of Property (1936). It is evident from these discussions that the cases in this field of the law defy logical analysis. The original dogma was that a "gift or devise of a chattel for an hour is forever.”¹

For centuries, however, something which is at least akin 

1. Gray at § 822; Simes at § 203-quoting Brooke's Abridgement (1576), 

Devise, pl. 13. 5953

§ 

ESTATES ACT 

¶ 2a to a future interest in personal property has been recognized at law. The disagreement relates to the nature of such interest with regard both to abstract theory and concrete results.

Several reasons for the confusion are apparent. In the first place, different results are reached depending on whether concepts are borrowed from the law of bailments or the law applicable to chattels real. A piece of jewelry is given to A for life, remainder to B. If A is regarded as a sort of bailee, he has only the use of the article (as opposed to a property interest in it) and B has the ownership. But if the concepts applied to chattels real are followed, A is the owner and B has an executory interest." 

Another disturbing factor is the modern tendency to treat personalty and realty in the same manner. This wholesome development in the law usually results in simplification, but there are limits to the use of concepts derived from the medieval system of tenures in dealing with personal property. Also, the public policy with regard to bona fide purchasers and practical problems of tracing ownership are different in the case of movables than in the case of land.

Special difficulties have been encountered with regard to consumable personalty. The remainderman of real property subject to depletion-such as a coal mine-is at least certain to receive a hole in the ground, but the remainderman of a case of claret might not even get the empty bottles. For this reason, future interests in consumable personalty were not usually recognized, although the logic of saying the remainderman gets nothing because he might get nothing seems questionable.

à. Early Cases 

Pennsylvania has its own peculiar history of the law relating to legal estates in personalty. Interests in personalty analogous to vested remainders, contingent re- 2. In order to give effect to B's interest, therefore, it was necessary to regard it as an executory limitation. 5954

¶ 2a. 

Den mainders, and executory interests in land were early recognized by our courts, but the exact nature of such interests was not clearly defined, and because of the absence of separate equity courts there was originally some question as to what protection could be given to the remainderman." 

In Kinnard v. Kinnard, 5 Watts 108 (1836), and Holman's 

Appeal 24 Pa. 174 (1854), however, more or less definite rules are set forth as representing our case law in the absence of statutes.

In Holman's Appeal, it was said (p. 178): "He who has the universal usufruct of a totality of goods has also the right to enjoy and use all the movable effects according to their nature; to consume what is liable to be consumed in its ordinary use; to gather from the living creatures the profits which they yield; to receive the interest of debts which bear interest; and to make use of everything according to its natural use." Several tyes of cases are considered. The court mentions the dogma that a gift of consumables for life passes the absolute interest, although later in the opinion there is language indicating that if any of the property is found unconsumed at the life tenant's death it belongs to the remainderman. What the court says about gifts of money is particularly interesting in the light of subsequent developments. "Money in possession, or in action, is not necessarily impaired by the use, because the use of money is nothing more than the interest or dividends which may be enjoyed by the usufruct without diminishing the principal."

The Kinnard case reviews the early rule as to security. 

Where specific tangible personalty was the subject matter of the gift, no security by the life tenant was required prior to statute unless "such circumstances be shown as would render it unsafe to trust the goods . in the hands of the first legatee. 

But so far as the legacy consists of money, or is to be converted into money, before paid over, it has been the invariable practice to require security of the first legatee, notwithstanding he may be perfectly responsible "5 Watts at 109-110. 3. b. Prior Statutes and the Debtor-Creditor Theory 

The first statute on the subject was the act of 1834, P. L. 73, which in sections 46 and 49 provided that when personal property or the proceeds of real estate were held by one for life or on condition, security could be required in all cases. The same provisions were re-enacted with unimportant changes by the acts of 1869, P. L. 70, and 

1871, P. L. 269. These statutes, which merely modified the prior law relating to the entering of security, did not purport to affect the substantive law of legal life estates in personalty. They were followed, however, by a far more important change which seems to have developed purely as a matter of case law. 

In Reiff's Appeal, 124 Pa. 145 (1889), testator had directed the sale of his estate and gave a share of the proceeds to a daughter for life with remainder over. In a prior proceeding it had been held that the daughter was a legal life tenant, and she had entered security pursuant to the act of 1834. At her death, it was claimed that the fund was subject to costs of administration and principal commissions as if it had been a trust. This claim was dissallowed by the orphans' court which rather unnecessarily went on to say that the effect of the earlier decree awarding the sum to the daughter upon her entering security was "to make the sum thus received . . . a part of her individual estate. It could be invested by her in the purchase of real estate, embarked in mercantile adventures or stock speculations, or expended in her living and family expenses as she deemed advisable. The money became essentially her own; and she was simply a debtor to the parties ultimately entitled at her death, whose claim is now payable out of her estate, and, in the event of its insolvency, by her sureties upon the bond given by her as legatee for life. The remaindermen are now creditors . . ." 124 Pa. at 149. The Supreme Court affirmed per curiam on the opinion of the orphans' court. The quoted remarks cannot be explained as a construction of the act of 1834. The theory that the life tenant is a debtor in the amount originally received seems rather to be an attempt to describe without the use of trust concepts a 5956

2b 

ESTATES ACT 

§ 13 life interest in money. The court had said in Holman's 

Appeal, 124 Pa. at 178, quoted above, that money is not "impaired by use". Yet the life tenant could scarcely be expected to retain it in kind. The debtor-creditor theory was a solution born of desperation.

For better or for worse the theory of Reiff's Appeal was consistently followed (prior to the present act) in all Pennsylvania cases where money or its equivalent was given for a limited period without the creation of a trust. 

The first taker was regarded as a debtor and the remainderman as a creditor-the debt being the value of the gift when originally received. Thus, in Letterle's Estate, 248 

Pa. 95 (1915), the court definitely adopted the debtor-creditor theory as a necessary part of its decision, holding that the individual estate of the legal life tenant, rather than the remainderman, was entitled to a capital gain on securities received in kind. In Kirkpatrick's Estate, 284 Pa. 

583 (1925), it was made clear that the entering of security had nothing to do with the debtor-creditor relationship which was held to exist even though the will excused the life tenant from putting up bond. See also Gillett's Estate, 130 Pa. Super. 309, 319 et seq. (1938), reaching the same result where the life tenant had simply neglected to put up bond. 

In Weir's Estate 251 Pa. 499 (1916), the widow-life tenant had refused to enter security, and the court had appointed a "trustee" to hold the estate for her. On the widow's death, the court held that the "trustee" had merely been substituted for the widow as a debtor to the remaindermen so that he was not allowed to take credit for a capital loss. This was corrected by section 23 of the 

Fiduciaries Act of 1917 which expressly provided that a trustee appointed by the court when the income beneficiary refused to enter security should "not be an insurer of the trust fund" but should be held only to the same duty of prudence as other trustees. In other respects, however, the act of 1917 merely re-enacted with slight changes the 5. Note, however, that Weir's Est. has been explained and limited even in cases not governed by the 1917 act. Our courts ran into real difficulty in applying the debtor-creditor relationship to cases where the legal life tenant was expressly or impliedly given power to consume the corpus of the gift. As already noted, the rule of the early cases dealing with specific bequests was that an attempted gift of consumable property to A for life with remainder to B passed the whole interest to A, although Holman's Appeal, 24 Pa. 174, 178 (1854), indicates that the remainderman might be entitled to any of the property which is affirmatively shown to be unconsumed. 

A somewhat different problem was presented by a general bequest of personalty for life (or a devise of real estate for life with power of sale) where the life tenant is given the express power to use principal for his support. In Tyson's Estate, 191 Pa. 218 (1899), the court considered the dogma that an absolute interest passes to the life tenant in such a case but rejected it as anything more than a rule of construction. Hence, it was decided that the remainderman had an interest in the unconsumed portion of the property and that this was not subject to disposition by the life tenant's will. This is undoubtedly the modern view. In all cases it is necessary to construe the will to determine the extent of the life tenant's power. 

Sometimes the life tenant is given such a complete dominion that in effect an absolute interest is taken. However, the power might be so broad as to permit a gift inter vivos by the life tenant but still not permit a bequest of it by will, as in Russ's Estate, 18 D. & C. 412 (O. C. Elk 1932), and 

Welsh's Estate, 239 Pa. 616, 618 (1913). More commonly, the life tenant is limited to consumption for purposes of his own support or "comfort"-a power which would ex-

In Welsh's Estate, 239 Pa. 616, 619 (1913), it was said that the remainderman had the burden of proving that no consumption occurred and that even when sufficient funds remained in the life tenant's possession there was a presumption that the fund bequeathed was consumed before the life tenant's individual property. See also Richey's Estate, 251 Pa. 324 (1916).

The incongruity of applying the debtor-creditor theory to cases where the first taker has a power of consumption is evident. Under the debtor-creditor theory there is no tracing of particular assets to determine the value of the remainderman's interest. Prior to the present act, therefore, any actual segregation by the life tenant was of no significance because he owned the amount of the bequest outright. But if there could be no tracing of the property received, how could it be determined whether and to what extent the power of consumption had been exercised? And how were the presumptions and rules relating to burden of proof set forth in Welsh's Estate, 239 Pa. 616, 619 (1913), and Richey's Estate, 251 Pa. 324 (1916), to be applied? In short, a power of consumption implies there is something to be consumed, while the debtor-creditor theory was based on the proposition that a bequest of money or its equivalent necessarily lost its identity upon distribution to the life tenant, even though the latter accepts distribution in kind. 

No solution has yet been suggested. 

13. Problems of Interpretation-Absolute Interests and 

Trusts Distinguished

The problems so far discussed arose only if the instrument was construed to create future interests in personalty without the intervention of a trust. Frequently the intent of the donor was not entirely clear in this respect and there are many cases distinguishing legal life estates from absolute gifts on the one hand and from gifts in trust on the other.

In certain cases the instrument can be construed to vest the entire interest in the income beneficiary free of even a debtor's obligation to the remainderman. As already noted, it was at one time thought that a specific bequest of consumable property for life or of a general legacy for life with express power to consume vested the entire interest in the first taker as a matter of law. It was long ago recognized, however, that this was at most a rule of 5961

§ 13 

ESTATES ACT 

construction.10 Where there is no express gift of the remainder following a gift of income, the instrument might be construed as making an absolute gift to the life tenant regardless of whether there is a power of consumption. 

This also was stated as a rule of law in the early cases," but it is now reasonably clear that here again it is merely a matter of discovering the testator's intention.12 A third supposed rule of law was that a gift of a fee cannot be cut down by subsequent language, but this also has been explained away.13 About the only rule of this sort which can be taken very seriously today is the rule that a gift of income unlimited as to duration is a gift of the absolute interest. This is still good law,14 although a lesser estate will be construed if there is other language in the will indicating that this was intended.15 

Another line of cases deal with the question of whether poorly drawn wills (which clearly limit the first taker to a life interest) show an intent to create a legal life estate or a trust with the life tenant himself as trustee. It is understandable that recent cases (not governed by the present act) show a tendency to adopt the latter construction wherever possible. In this way the gift is made subject to familiar trust principles and the confusion of the debtor-creditor relationship is avoided. Erdman's Estate, 352 Pa. 158, 161 (1945), is an example.16
