5962

¶ 4a § 

ESTATES ACT 4. Present Statute a. General

This section of the Estates Act is an attempt to avoid the confusion in the law of legal life estates in personalty by the simple expedient of eliminating them. The feeling was that legal estates of this sort served no useful purpose that could not be better served by the use of a trust. As 

Simes aptly remarks,¹7 "it may almost be said to be a slip in draughtsmanship to create future interests in chattels personal without the intervention of a trust." It might be added that a trust is far nearer to the layman's conception of what happens when he leaves his personal estate to one for life with remainder over than the strange results dictated by our case law and earlier statutes. 

It was therefore provided that all provisions of this sort in conveyances taking effect after January 1, 1948, shall be treated as creating trusts with the first taker as trustee for himself and the remainderman. If the first taker refuses to put up the required bond, a trustee is appointed by the court under a provision similar to that in the act of 1917. Note that the new act goes far beyond providing a rule of construction. The law creates the trust regardless of the conveyor's intent and future interests in personalty without a trust in instruments governed by the present act are legal impossibilities. 

b. Types of Property Covered 

The statute covers all estates "in personal property or in the proceeds of the conversion of real estate." The same rule will now govern a gift of a specific piece of jewelry, a pecuniary legacy, or a gift of the whole or part of residuary personalty. In addition, the statute covers the proceeds of the conversion of real estate. The usual case of the latter sort is where Blackacre is left to A for life with remainder to B and the executor sells Blackacre for the payment of the decedent's debts. Theoretically, the balance of cash passes to the distributees as real estate, but for purposes of this section it is treated in the same 

17. Future interests (1936) § 209. 

5963

§ ESTATES ACT 

4b manner as a pecuniary legacy-just as under the earlier acts.18 

Other situations where real estate not in trust is subject to future interests and is converted into money can easily be imagined-as a sale of real estate under the Price Act (in which event this section should be read as supplementing sections 10 and 13 of that act, 20 P. S. §§ 1644 and 

1624) or a taking by eminent domain. As explained in the 

Commissioners' comments the word "conversion" was used rather than the old reference to "sales" of real estate, so as to include all transactions of this sort. The term is thus used in the sense of actual conversion-not conversion in the theoretical, legal sense. Many sales do not result in a theoretical conversion because the proceeds remain real estate for certain purposes, but the act obviously applies nevertheless. Indeed, if the act only applied to theoretically converted land (as where the testator directs a sale in the will) the reference to proceeds of real estate would have been unnecessary since such a gift would be of "personal property."

The section makes no attempt to abolish legal life estates and the like in real estate which remains unconverted. In the comments to the draft of the Estates Act circulated among members of the Bar prior to enactment, there was a rather extensive discussion of the advisability of extending this section to include all forms of property. 

Several advantages of a trust over legal estates, even when the subject matter is land, were pointed out. These are also set forth in detail in the September, 1946, issue of the Fiduciary Review, and should be considered by attorneys drafting wills which devise life interests in real estate. 

Where a trustee is appointed, problems of jurisdiction and procedure in preventing waste, paying taxes and the like are avoided, and all parties benefit by the trustee's broader powers to lease, improve and insure the property. 

However, legal life estates and future interests in real estate have given comparatively little trouble to the courts and are governed by more or less settled principles which antedate the law of trusts. It was decided, therefore, that 

18. See Duval's Appeal, 38 Pa. 112, 120 (1861), and supra ¶ 2c. 5964

¶ 4c 

there was no compelling reason for a change with regard to land, and the present section was drafted accordingly. 

Nevertheless, as the Commissioners' comments point out, the present section will apply to real estate in certain rare cases-as where the life tenant as trustee of personalty invests in a mortgage which is subsequently foreclosed. 

c. Types of Estates Covered 

The statute applies only when there is a present interest which is (1) subject to a future interest and (2) not in trust that is, not subject to a trust other than the trust which the statute itself imposes. 

As to the first requirement, the earlier cases discussed above under ¶ 3 will still be authority to determine whether the first taker has in effect been given an absolute interest, in which event there will be no outstanding future interest. 

But if the first taker is limited to a life interest, a term of years, or if his otherwise absolute interest is subject to a lawful condition, the statute will apply. The nature of the future interest is irrelevant. It might be analogous to what in the case of land would be called a vested remainder, a contingent remainder, or an executory interest. Or, the future interest might not be expressly given but simply remain in the donor or his estate-like a reversion, right of re-entry, or possibility of reverter. As noted under ¶ 3, the absence of a gift over might be some indication that the first taker is entitled to an absolute estate, but not necessarily.

In certain cases it might require construction to determine whether the will has created a future interest in the property or has merely imposed an obligation in the nature of a charge on the beneficiary of the absolute interest-as a bequest of the residue to A provided he pay B $1000 when 

B becomes of age. See Ivison's Estate, 257 Pa. 297 (1917), for a will which would have raised a nice question of construction in this respect had the present act been in effect. 

The section is not limited to wills, although an inter vivos instrument purporting to create a future interest in personalty without an express trust would be something of a novelty. All the cases of this sort that have been exam- 5965

§ 

ESTATES ACT 

¶ 4d ined involved testamentary gifts. However, the creation of legal future interests in personalty seems clearly possible by inter vivos gift,19 and this section, like all the other sections of the Estates Act, was clearly intended to cover inter vivos as well as testamentary transactions. It might even be suggested that the statute would apply to an ordinary bailment. A bailment at will probably creates merely a license and no "present interest" in the bailee. 

The bailee of hired goods for a term, however, might be said to have an "interest" in the bailed property at least as real as that of a legal life tenant in view of the close historical connection between the two fields of the law noted above under ¶ 1. On the other hand, to apply the statute to such transactions would probably extend it beyond its purpose.

As to the requirement that the property is not already subject to a trust, the cases discussed above under 13 (last paragraph) will continue to be controlling. Since the principal results will now be the same whichever way the decision goes, the point will probably seldom be litigated, except perhaps with regard to commissions or the necessity of giving bond. d. Powers of the Trustee in General Power of Sale 

The first taker, who becomes a trustee for himself under the statute, or the trustee appointed by the court in cases where the first taker refuses to enter security, has the "ordinary powers and duties of a trustee," with certain exceptions discussed separately below. A purist might find this language objectionable on the ground that there are no "ordinary" powers and duties of a trustee because such powers and duties vary so much with the circumstances and the type of trust involved. If a common sense approach is adopted, however, there should be no difficulty in interpreting this part of the statute. The problem is no different than that presented when the first taker refused to enter security and a trustee was appointed by the court under section 23 of the act of 1917. The present law merely 

19. Cf. Knoll v. Hart, 308 Pa. 223 (1932), finding that the intent was testamentary in that case but recognizing the possibility of such estates. 5966

¶ 4d 

carries this idea a step further by providing that the first taker also acts as trustee if he is willing to accept the responsibility. Reported cases of trusts created by statute under the 1917 act are rare,20 but the scarcity of authority is some indication that the old act worked well where trustees were appointed. 

True, the powers and duties of the statutory trustee will not be the same in all cases. The instrument creating the interest should simply be read as if the words "in trust" had been employed-naming the first taker as trustee.21 Thus, the answer to the all-important question of whether a power of sale is an "ordinary" power of a trustee will depend primarily on the terms of the Fiduciaries Act which is being revised at the time of writing. Whatever that act provides, however, will no doubt be subject to a contrary intent appearing either expressly in the instrument or impliedly from the nature of the gift. Thus even under the 1917 act a power of sale would plainly be present where the subject matter of the gift was money or its equivalent. A pecuniary legacy to A for life must be made productive, and A as trustee would plainly have the power to sell whatever he invested in or elected to receive in kind. The same would be true of a gift of the residue of the personal estate or a share thereof, which, as already explained, is the equivalent of a money gift because of the theoretical duty on the part of the executor to liquidate. 

Where the gift is of specific property, the probable intention of the donor must be examined. If a rare painting or heirloom is given to A for life, a power of sale could scarcely be considered as one of A's "ordinary" powers as trustee. On the other hand, where there is a specific gift of securities for life, a power of sale might well be implied even under the act of 1917.22

e. Investment Powers-Retention of Property Received 

The investment powers of the statutory trustee will be governed by the legal investment provision for fiduciaries generally in the Fiduciaries Act or other statute 23-unless, of course, the instrument gives broader investment powers, but this would be unusual where no trust is expressly created. As to the power to retain property received, the present section provides that the trustee "shall not be required to change the form of the investment to an investment authorized for Pennsylvania fiduciaries." In the case of a specific bequest of unique property, such as a valuable painting, to A for life, the trustee, as explained under the preceding subheading, would probably have no power to sell the property, much less a duty to do so, even if the statute had been silent on the subject. As also explained above, a power to sell might be given by the Fiduciaries Act or implied by the instrument where the subject matter of a specific gift is not unique-as a specific bequest of securities-but this provision in the statute will make it clear that the trustee has no duty to sell.

Discussion 

11. Cross-Reference. 

12. Conveyance to Grantor's Own Heirs. 

11. Cross Reference 

This clause is identical with section 14 (4) of the Wills Act where the various problems which arise in cases of this sort are discussed. In nearly all cases the question will be identical whether the gift is by will or inter vivos. 

2. Conveyance to Grantor's Own Heirs

One problem which does not arise in modern law with respect to wills is presented where there is an inter vivos transfer (usually of a future interest) to the grantor's own heirs. At common law the heir and the ancestor were one, so that an attempted transfer of a present or future interest by will or deed to one's own heirs was considered a transfer to one's self and therefore a legal nullity. This was in harmony with medieval concepts and served to prevent evasion of feudal burdens by the device of making title pass to the heir by purchase rather than by descent.2 The rule was grounded in the same concepts and sometimes overlapped both the Rule in Shelley's case and the rule that a living person can have no heirs. It was independent of both rules, however, as illustrated by the fact that it applied to many cases where the other two rules would not apply. For example, the gift to heirs was a nullity at common law in the case of a direct devise in fee to testator's own heirs, or the case of an inter vivos transfer by A to B and his heirs during the life of A with remainder in fee to A's heirs. Similar to the Rule in Shelley's case, however, it was a rule of law and not of construction.3 

With the disappearance of feudal tenures, the rule lost its significance in cases of wills because the same person takes anyway and it is now immaterial whether he takes by descent or by purchase. In cases of inter vivos transfers, however, the rule if applied would mean that the grantor would still own the future interest which he at- 

1. See, generally, Simes, Future Interests (1936) § 144 et seq. 

2. Simes § 145. Cf. discussion under Wills Act § 16 ( 1b) of the medieval philosophy and economic considerations which gave rise to rules of this sort. 

3. See Simes § 147 and discussion of Brolasky's Estate infra in the text. 6002

ESTATES ACT 

§ 14 (1) 29 tempted to grant to his heirs. Hence, the reversion would pass by a subsequent deed of the property or under the grantor's will. Of course this rule has absolutely no justification in modern times and should have been discarded when the reason for it vanished.

Nevertheless, in Brolasky's Estate, 302 Pa. 439 (1931), our Court dusted off this moldy rule of the common law and applied it to a declaration of trust executed in 1863. Taking a rather narrow view of stare decisis, the Court felt compelled to follow the English common law and cases in other jurisdictions, although no controlling Pennsylvania authority was cited. The grantor's intent was considered important but only to the extent that it is important in applying the Rule in Shelley's case-i. e. the rule applies unless there is something showing that the word "heirs" is used as a word of purchase, such as "children." Hence, the word "heirs" having been construed literally, the remainder was held to be a nullity as a matter of law.

In the same case, however, it was said (302 Pa. at 444) that the rule had been changed by the act of 1923, P. L. 914 as to deeds executed after that date. This conclusion might be questioned as a matter of pure logic, but it is almost inconceivable that the court would have such enthusiasm for the ancient doctrine that it would fail to follow the Brolasky dictum in a case involving a post-1923 deed. 

And if the act of 1923 was sufficient to abolish the old rule, certainly the broader provision in the present section of the Estates Act has the same effect. 

For all practical purposes, therefore, it may be assumed that the recently resurrected rule invalidating transfers to one's own heirs has once more been laid to rest and will have no effect on deeds subsequent to 1923. 

4. Cf. discussion of the Rule in Shelley's Case under Wills Act § 16 (¶ 1c). 

5. In many cases the act of 1923 and the present section of the Estates Act create a class of artificial heirs other than those who would take by actual intestacy. In such cases it is fair to say that the act of 1923 abolished the common law rule nullifying transfers to one's own heirs, because that rule was based or the fact that the transfer was made to the same persons who would take by descent. In the cases where the coming into enjoyment coincides with the death of the ancestor (a deed by A to B and his heirs for the life of A, remainder in fee on A's death to A's heirs) it is difficult to see how the act of 1923 or the present Act which merely provides a rule of construction would have any effect one way or the other. 6003 [The next page is 6051]

§ 15 

ESTATES ACT § 15. ESTATES PUR AUTER VIE 

An interest conveyed to a person for the life of another, whether or not such conveyance is to him and his heirs, shall, on his death before expiration of the interest, be considered as personal property forming a part of his estate and shall be subject to distribution in like manner as a lease for a term of years.

COMMISSIONERS' COMMENT-Section 1 of the Wills Act of 1917, un like the Wills Act of 1947, includes specific reference to estates pur auter vie. There is no secial mention of estates pur auter vie in the Intestate Act of 1917, or in the Intestate Act of 1947. 

Section 11 (g) of the Fiduciaries Act of 1917 provides that estates pur auter vie, unless such estates have been limited to the decedent and his heirs, shall be included in the inventory. 

At common law, the estate pur auter vie was not an estate of inheritance; the interest of the tenant terminated upon his death, even though he died before the cestui que vie. Section 

15 changes the property interest of a tenant pur auter vie by enlarging it to an estate of inheritance. This provision is more logically in this act than in the Wills Act or the Intestate Act. 

The phrase "shall be subject to distribution in like manner as a lease for a term of years" is taken from the Fiduciaries Act. 

Its inclusion is desirable to avoid various questions that might arise in regard to procedure. 

Old Law

Section 1. Every person may dispose by will of his or her real estate, whether such estate is held in fee simple or for the life or lives of any other person or persons.

Wills Act of 1917, P. L. 403. 

Section 11 (g). All estates in lands or tenements of which the decedent was seised, at the time of his decease, for the life or lives of another person or persons, shall, unless such estate have been limited to the decedent and his heirs, go to the executors or administrators of such decedent, and be included in the inventory, and be subject to distribution in like manner as leases for terms of years. 

Fiduciaries Act of 1917, P. L. 447.

1. Common Law Rule At common law the estate pur auter vie was not an estate of inheritance. If property were limited to A for the

12 life of B, and A predeceased B, the interest of A ceased and the ownership of the property for the rest of B's life passed to the first person to take possession of it. If the estate were limited to A "and his heirs" for the life of B, and A predeceased B, the interest in the property for the rest of B's life passed to A's heirs who took as purchasers from the original conveyor. In neither case did any interest pass through the estate of A or under his will.2 ¶ 2. Statutes The common law rule was early changed in England by the Statute of Frauds. In Pennsylvania, section 1 of the Wills Act of 1833, P. L. 249, and section 9 of the act relating to executors and administrators of 1834, P. L. 73, contained provisions identical with the corresponding sections of the Wills Act and Fiduciaries Act of 1917 quoted above. It will be noted that the Fiduciaries Act did not apply to estates limited to the tenant and his heirs, and that the provision in the Wills Act was probably too general to have any effect at all on the common law rule. 

No case has been found referring to these provisions of the acts of 1833, 1834, and 1917. In fact there is no evidence that the courts have been aware of the problem. Perhaps this is a situation where the common law has been reformed through ignorance. Nevertheless, legislation is technically necessary and it seems logical that the provision should be in the Estates Act, because it involves both wills and intestacies and concerns a substantive rule of property. 

The present section makes estates pur auter vie property of the estate of the tenant who dies before the cestui que vie for all purposes regardless of whether it was limited to the tenant alone or the tenant "and his heirs."

INTESTATE ACT 

1. General

Cross References 

At common law, a man had an estate jure uxoris in real property of his wife. This estate arose immediately upon marriage and lasted during coverture-that is, until either he or his wife died. On the birth of issue, this estate was enlarged to the estate of curtesy which lasted during the lifetime of the husband even though the wife predeceased him.¹ By section 1 of the intestate act of 

1833, P. L. 315, the husband was given an estate of curtesy in his wife's realty regardless of whether there was issue born of the marriage. Thus, the estates of jure uxoris and curtesy were merged and the husband upon marriage became entitled to a life estate in all real estate of which the wife was seised during coverture. Unlike dower, curtesy was a present estate even while the wife lived, but like dower, it could be asserted against (1) land which the wife devised to another, (2) land as to which the wife died intestate, and (3) land which she attempted to convey without his joinder.

These three incidents of curtesy were modified and eventually superseded by three distinct types of statutory provisions, so that at the present time common law curtesy has completely disappeared and in its place are three statutory substitutes: (1) the widower's right to take against his wife's will (discussed under section 8 of the Wills Act), (2) the widower's statutory share, set forth in section 2 of the present act, in property as to which the wife died intestate, and (3) the husband's power to veto his wife's inter vivos conveyances arising from the necessity for his joinder in her deeds under the married women's property act, discussed below.

General

It will be noted that there is in this subsection abolishing curtesy no saving clause relating to inter vivos conveyances, as there was in the preceding subsection relating a.

¶ 3a to dower. This omission in the act of 1917, as re-enacted here, was not accidental. It was unnecessary to preserve the interest of the husband in real estate conveyed inter vivos by the wife because of the more complete protection afforded by statutes prohibiting absolutely a conveyance by the wife without her husband's joinder. 

At common law the wife might or might not have had a theoretical power to convey her land subject to the husband's curtesy, but she clearly does not have even this limited power under the married women's property acts. 

The inability of a married woman to make any deed at all without her husband's joinder, even subject to his interest, has apparently been in our statutory law since 1770.5 Assuming that this rule was not changed by the act of 1945 (see 3b below), it follows that a wife's deed without her husband's joinder has no effect, and apparently even she is not estopped to deny its validity." In this respect the law relating to a wife's conveyances differs from the corresponding law relating to conveyances by a husband. In the latter case, the grantee of the husband gets a fee subject to the wife's possibility of dower if she survives. The grantee of the wife, however, gets nothing except a cause of action for damages, so that all the complications of the corresponding law of dower are avoided. On the other hand, the limitation on a married woman's power to convey her real estate is the only protection a husband now has against his wife's voluntary alienation of her land. He no longer has an estate in her property, so that he is protected by her incapacity or not at all. This is demonstrated by Scaife v. McKee, 298 Pa. 33 (1929).

 tained a divorce a mensa et thoro on the grounds of adultery in 1926. In 1929, a dispute arose over whether the wife could at that time pass clear title to her real estate without her husband's joinder. It will be remembered that a divorce a mensa et thoro does not sever the marriage ties. By the act of 1927, P. L. 181, 48 P. S. § 117a, however, it is provided that a woman who has been granted such a divorce may convey her property without her husband's joinder." It was argued that the effect of the act of 1927 was simply to enable the wife to convey subject to the interest of the husband and that otherwise construed it would unconstitutionally deprive the husband of his estate of curtesy. 

The court rejected this argument, however, on the ground that the "husband never had any curtesy in the property" in view of section 4 of the act of 1917 which destroyed the husband's curtesy even as to lands purchased before the effective date of the act. Thus, while section 5 (a) of the present act continues dower in a modified form as to property aliened during coverture, curtesy is abolished absolutely. The only thing standing in the way of a wife's free power of alienation over her real estate is her incapacity under the married women's property act; when this incapacity is removed, her title is unfettered. 

b. Effect of Act of 1945 on Conveyances by Wife 

The act of 1893, P. L. 344, like its predecessors, provided expressly in section 1 that a married woman may "sell or otherwise dispose of" her real or personal property to the same extent as if unmarried "but she may not mortgage or convey her real property, unless her husband joins in such mortgage or conveyances." Section 2 of the same act relates primarily to contracts, but the prohibition against conveyances and mortgages without joinder is reinforced by an added provision that the wife "may not execute or acknowledge" a deed or mortgage.

By the act of 1945, P. L. 625, 48 P. S. §§ 31 and 32, the 

Legislature attempted to amend the act of 1893. The amendment must be read in the original to be appreciated, 8. See discussion of divorce (¶ 3b) under § 2 of this act. 

9. See discussion of this and similar acts below (¶3e). 655

INTESTATE ACT 

¶ 3b but it at least seems clear that the intent was to change the prior law relating to mortgages and surety contracts. 

It likewise seems clear to the present writer that it was not intended to disturb the prior law relating to conveyances, although this is a matter of opinion. The primary prohibition against conveyance without joinder in section 1 of the act of 1893 was stricken out entirely, so that section 1 now provides simply that a married woman may "sell or otherwise dispose of any property of any kind, real, personal or mixed . . . in the same manner and to the same extent as a married man" (the italicized words being substituted for "as an unmarried person" in the prior act). 

In section 2 of the act of 1893, however, the prohibition against executing or acknowledging a deed was retained by the amendment of 1945. It would seem, therefore, that the elimination of the primary prohibition against conveyances in section 1 was unintentional, since it is doubtful that the Legislature intended to start theoretical arguments concerning the possibility of a modern conveyance of real property without executing a deed. This conclusion is reinforced by the substitution of the words "as a married man" for "as an unmarried person" in section 1, as noted above. A married man can convey without his wife's joinder, but he cannot pass a marketable title without his wife's joinder because of her dower interest. Plainly there was some confusion in the minds of the drafters, but it seems unlikely that the Legislature intended to give a wife any new power to convey by the 1945 amendment. (Note that the act was again amended by the acts of 1947, P. L. 

60 and P. L. 352. These amendments contribute to the general confusion by adding different provisions to section 2-the second amendment ignoring the first. Neither of the 1947 amendments, however, remedies the ambiguity in sections 1 and 2 discussed above.) On the whole, therefore, the only sensible construction of the amendment of 1945 is that it gives to the wife the power to mortgage her real estate without her husband's joinder, but that there is no change in the law of a wife's conveyances where joinder by the husband is still necessary. 

This construction might make the title to the act defective 656

¶ 3c 

(it is certainly misleading) so that the whole amendment is held invalid (but see Banos v. Banos, 63 Montg. 272 (C. P. 

1947)). In either event, however, the law relating to conveyances will remain unaffected. 

c. Effect of Act of 1945 on Mortgages by Wife 

An examination of the amendment of 1945 will show that the Legislature at least intended to eliminate the requirement under the act of 1893 that the husband must join in a married woman's mortgages.10 This change is logical enough, because as noted under the preceding subsection, a husband has the corresponding power in this state to give a mortgage which will be superior to his wife's dower. If the amendment is effective at all, therefore, a married woman's mortgage without her husband's joinder executed after May 17, 1945, will create a valid encumbrance on the whole title, in the absence of fraud. 

d. Adverse Proceedings Against Wife 

The elimination of curtesy initiate should remove any doubt that might have existed concerning the effect of adverse proceedings against the wife's title. As a matter of fact, even before 1917, the husband's interest in his wife's real estate was probably not protected in such cases. 

In any event, it now seems clear that the husband has no power to prevent the loss of the wife's title to her real estate through execution on a bona fide judgment against her," a sale by her receiver in bankruptcy,12 condemnation,13 or partition proceedings.14

A fourth type of emancipation is where a husband releases his wife from her incapacity in a separation agreement under the act of 1897, P. L. 212, 21 P. S. § 52. It is open to question whether an agreement by the husband purporting to release his wife from the incapacity of coverture but not conforming with this act (as, for example, a release in an agreement other than a separation agreement) would be effective. Clearly an agreement by the husband can be effective to release any interest he might have in property which the wife still owns at her death,¹º but where the wife conveys to another the question is a little different: the husband would not be releasing a property interest in her land but would be attempting to remove a disability which the law imposesalthough it imposes this disability primarily for his benefit.

f. Forfeiture Distinguished 

The law relating to when a married woman's incapacity is removed is analogous in its practical results to the law of forfeiture of marital rights discussed under section 6 of this act. There is a distinction, however, which requires that these two aspects of the law be treated separately. 

Strictly speaking, there can be no question of forfeiture by a husband of interests in his wife's property during her lifetime, because as already explained (3a) he no longer has any present interest which he can forfeit. At her death, he will have an interest in any property she dies owning, and the question of forfeiture might arise; but while she lives he is protected only indirectly by her incapacity to deed her real estate.

This theoretical difference between the inter vivos protection provided the husband and that provided the wife might have practical consequences. It was noted under section 5 (a) (3j) that under our statutes a wife's dower is not forfeited immediately upon her misconduct. If she deserts her husband in 1925, returns to him in 1935 and he dies in 1936, it would seem that she could claim her dower in land conveyed by him without her joinder in 1930, because grounds for forfeiture are examined as of the time of death under section 6. On the other hand, if the husband deserts in 1925 and returns in 1935, the wife's deed in 1930 would be good because her capacity is judged as of the date of the deed; this was the decision in Thornton v. Pierce, 328 Pa. 11 (1937), discussed above (3e). Plainly the latter result is more desirable, in that it leaves the wife's real estate alienable during the period of marital strife, but unfortunately there is no statute permitting a husband to be declared an "homme sole trader" and to convey his real estate clear of a possible later claim by his wayward wife; his only remedy is to get a divorce a v. m.--which he may not desire. 

g. Conflict With Section 11 of Estates Act 

Section 11 of the Estates Act provides that a surviving spouse may treat "as testamentary" a conveyance of real or personal property by the deceased spouse in which a 660

Ek 1 power of appointment was reserved. A possible conflict with section 5 (a) of the present act has already been mentioned ( ¶ 3g). There is also a potential conflict of a somewhat different nature between section 11 of the Estates Act and the law relating to a married woman's conveyances. In the ordinary case where a married woman attempts to convey real estate without her husband's joinder, it has been seen that her deed is of no effect, and it is reasonably clear that nothing in section 11 of the Estates Act would give it partial effect merely because she reserved a power of appointment. If she conveys with her husband's joinder reserving a power of appointment, it would likewise seem reasonably clear that the husband could claim no rights under section 11 of the Estates Act (see discussion under ¶ 9 of that section), so that no problem would be raised. Suppose, however, the wife in Thornton v. Pierce (supra 3e and f) who conveyed without joinder during the period of the husband's desertion, had reserved a power of appointment in her deed. Under that decision there is no question that the deed is good. But could the widower on her death after reconciliation claim a share of the appointed property under the Estates Act? 

Or would her deed be effective to bar him under the act of 1855 which gave her the power of "free and absolute disposal" It is uncertain which act would prevail. b. Transfers in Fraud of Husband's Marital Rights (Antenuptial and Postnuptial)

ESTATES ACT § 15. ESTATES PUR AUTER VIE 

An interest conveyed to a person for the life of another, whether or not such conveyance is to him and his heirs, shall, on his death before expiration of the interest, be considered as personal property forming a part of his estate and shall be subject to distribution in like manner as a lease for a term of years. 

COMMISSIONERS' COMMENT-Section 1 of the Wills Act of 1917, un like the Wills Act of 1947, includes specific reference to estates pur auter vie. There is no secial mention of estates pur auter vie in the Intestate Act of 1917, or in the Intestate Act of 1947. 

Section 11 (g) of the Fiduciaries Act of 1917 provides that estates pur auter vie, unless such estates have been limited to the decedent and his heirs, shall be included in the inventory. 

At common law, the estate pur auter vie was not an estate of inheritance; the interest of the tenant terminated upon his death, even though he died before the cestui que vie. Section 

15 changes the property interest of a tenant pur auter vie by enlarging it to an estate of inheritance. This provision is more logically in this act than in the Wills Act or the Intestate Act. 

The phrase "shall be subject to distribution in like manner as a lease for a term of years" is taken from the Fiduciaries Act. 

Its inclusion is desirable to avoid various questions that might arise in regard to procedure. 

Old Law

Section 1. Every person may dispose by will of his or her real estate, whether such estate is held in fee simple or for the life or lives of any other person or persons.

Fiduciaries Act of 1917, P. L. 447.

At common law the estate pur auter vie¹ was not an estate of inheritance. If property were limited to A for the

The common law rule was early changed in England by the Statute of Frauds.3 In Pennsylvania, section 1 of the Wills Act of 1833, P. INTESTATE ACT. 

1. General

Cross References 

At common law, a man had an estate jure uxoris in real property of his wife. This estate arose immediately upon marriage and lasted during coverture-that is, until either he or his wife died. On the birth of issue, this estate was enlarged to the estate of curtesy which lasted during the lifetime of the husband even though the wife predeceased him. By section 1 of the intestate act of 

1833, P. L. 315, the husband was given an estate of curtesy in his wife's realty regardless of whether there was issue born of the marriage. Thus, the estates of jure uxoris and curtesy were merged and the husband upon marriage became entitled to a life estate in all real estate of which the wife was seised during coverture. Unlike dower, curtesy was a present estate even while the wife lived, but like dower, it could be asserted against (1) land which the wife devised to another, (2) land as to which the wife died. intestate, and (3) land which she attempted to convey without his joinder.

These three incidents of curtesy were modified and eventually superseded by three distinct types of statutory provisions, so that at the present time common law curtesy has completely disappeared and in its place are three statutory substitutes: (1) the widower's right to take against his wife's will (discussed under section 8 of the Wills Act), (2) the widower's statutory share, set forth in section 2 of the present act, in property as to which the wife died intestate, and (3) the husband's power to veto his wife's inter vivos conveyances arising from the necessity for his joinder in her deeds under the married women's property act, discussed below. 

2. Land as to Which Wife Died Intestate a. General

The interest of the husband in the estate of a woman who died intestate continued to be his common law estate 1. On the marital estates of the husband generally, see Tiffany, Real Property (3d ed. 1939) §§ 484 and 552 et seq.; Stewart, Husband and Wife (1887) § 141 et seq. and other authorities cited in note 10 under $5 (a). On the nature of a husband's curtesy as modified by the act of 1833 and subsequent statutes prior to 1917, see Commissioners v. Poor District, 169 Pa. 116 (1895). 652

¶ 2b 

of curtesy (as modified by the act of 1833) until 1917. In that year, however, curtesy was abolished by section 4 of the act of 1917 (the predecessor of the present subsection), and thereafter the husband has received an intestate portion in the same manner as other persons mentioned in the act.2 Hence, as to property owned by an intestate at death, both curtesy and dower can be forgotten. Either spouse now takes as an heir of the other the share set forth in section 2 of the present act, and there can be no question that the husband, like the wife, takes "subject to debts and charges" as provided in section 1.³ 

b. Requirement of Seisin-Future Interests 

What was said under section 5 (a) (¶ 2b) in regard to the common law requirement of seisin is also applicable here. Since the husband now takes as an heir under sections 1 and 2 of this act, he takes his share in all the intestate's estates of inheritance, regardless of whether his wife was "seised" of the estate during her lifetime. 

Thus, the last sentence of this subsection, if it has any effect at all, merely reinforces this conclusion with regard to future estates. The provision was inserted by the 

1917 Commission in order to overrule Hitner v. Ege, 23 Pa. 

305 (1854), where it was held that the husband could claim no curtesy in his wife's "estate in reversion or remainder, unless the particular estate be ended during coverture.” 

However, that case probably ceased to be law in 1917 even in the absence of the special provision relating to future estates, because common law curtesy, with all its peculiar incidents, was abolished and an ordinary intestate share substituted therefor. 

13. Wife's Power of Alienation Inter Vivos a. General

It will be noted that there is in this subsection abolishing curtesy no saving clause relating to inter vivos conveyances, as there was in the preceding subsection relating 

2. See discussion under § 2 (1) of this act. 

3. See Ladner, Real Estate Conveyancing in Pennsylvania (1941) § 141 (h), and cases in note 5 under  of this act, supra. 653

INTESTATE ACT 

¶ 3a to dower. This omission in the act of 1917, as re-enacted here, was not accidental. It was unnecessary to preserve the interest of the husband in real estate conveyed inter vivos by the wife because of the more complete protection afforded by statutes prohibiting absolutely a conveyance by the wife without her husband's joinder. At common law the wife might or might not have had a theoretical power to convey her land subject to the husband's curtesy, but she clearly does not have even this limited power under the married women's property acts. 

The inability of a married woman to make any deed at all without her husband's joinder, even subject to his interest, has apparently been in our statutory law since 1770.5 Assuming that this rule was not changed by the act of 1945 (see [ 3b below), it follows that a wife's deed without her husband's joinder has no effect, and apparently even she is not estopped to deny its validity." In this respect the law relating to a wife's conveyances differs from the corresponding law relating to conveyances by a husband. In the latter case, the grantee of the husband gets a fee subject to the wife's possibility of dower if she survives. The grantee of the wife, however, gets nothing except a cause of action for damages, so that all the complications of the corresponding law of dower are avoided. On the other hand, the limitation on a married woman's power to convey her real estate is the only protection a husband now has against his wife's voluntary alienation of her land. He no longer has an estate in her property, so that he is protected by her incapacity or not at all. This is demonstrated by Scaife v. McKee, 298 Pa. 33 (1929).

INTESTATE ACT 

It tained a divorce a mensa et thoro on the grounds of adultery in 1926. In 1929, a dispute arose over whether the wife could at that time pass clear title to her real estate without her husband's joinder. It will be remembered that a divorce a mensa et thoro does not sever the marriage ties. By the act of 1927, P. L. 181, 48 P. S. § 117a, however, it is provided that a woman who has been granted such a divorce may convey her property without her husband's joinder. was argued that the effect of the act of 1927 was simply to enable the wife to convey subject to the interest of the husband and that otherwise construed it would unconstitutionally deprive the husband of his estate of curtesy. 

The court rejected this argument, however, on the ground that the "husband never had any curtesy in the property" in view of section 4 of the act of 1917 which destroyed the husband's curtesy even as to lands purchased before the effective date of the act. Thus, while section 5 (a) of the present act continues dower in a modified form as to property aliened during coverture, curtesy is abolished absolutely. The only thing standing in the way of a wife's free power of alienation over her real estate is her incapacity under the married women's property act; when this incapacity is removed, her title is unfettered. 

b. Effect of Act of 1945 on Conveyances by Wife 

The act of 1893, P. L. 344, like its predecessors, provided expressly in section 1 that a married woman may "sell or otherwise dispose of" her real or personal property to the same extent as if unmarried "but she may not mortgage or convey her real property, unless her husband joins in such mortgage or conveyances." Section 2 of the same act relates primarily to contracts, but the prohibition against conveyances and mortgages without joinder is reinforced by an added provision that the wife "may not execute or acknowledge" a deed or mortgage.

By the act of 1945, P. L. 625, 48 P. S. §§ 31 and 32, the 

Legislature attempted to amend the act of 1893. The amendment must be read in the original to be appreciated, 8. See discussion of divorce (¶ 3b) under § 2 of this act. 

9. See discussion of this and similar acts below (¶ 3e). 655

INTESTATE ACT 

¶ 3b but it at least seems clear that the intent was to change the prior law relating to mortgages and surety contracts. 

It likewise seems clear to the present writer that it was not intended to disturb the prior law relating to conveyances, although this is a matter of opinion. The primary prohibition against conveyance without joinder in section 1 of the act of 1893 was stricken out entirely, so that section 1 now provides simply that a married woman may "sell or otherwise dispose of any property of any kind, real, personal or mixed in the same manner and to the same extent as a married man" (the italicized words being substituted for "as an unmarried person" in the prior act). 

In section 2 of the act of 1893, however, the prohibition against executing or acknowledging a deed was retained by the amendment of 1945. It would seem, therefore, that the elimination of the primary prohibition against conveyances in section 1 was unintentional, since it is doubtful that the Legislature intended to start theoretical arguments concerning the possibility of a modern conveyance of real property without executing a deed. This conclusion is reinforced by the substitution of the words "as a married man" for "as an unmarried person" in section 1, as noted above. A married man can convey without his wife's joinder, but he cannot pass a marketable title without his wife's joinder because of her dower interest. Plainly there was some confusion in the minds of the drafters, but it seems unlikely that the Legislature intended to give a wife any new power to convey by the 1945 amendment. (Note that the act was again amended by the acts of 1947, P. L. 

60 and P. L. 352. These amendments contribute to the general confusion by adding different provisions to section 2-the second amendment ignoring the first. Neither of the 1947 amendments, however, remedies the ambiguity in sections 1 and 2 discussed above.) On the whole, therefore, the only sensible construction of the amendment of 1945 is that it gives to the wife the power to mortgage her real estate without her husband's joinder, but that there is no change in the law of a wife's conveyances where joinder by the husband is still necessary. 

This construction might make the title to the act defective 656

¶ 3c 

(it is certainly misleading) so that the whole amendment is held invalid (but see Banos v. Banos, 63 Montg. 272 (C. P. 

1947)). In either event, however, the law relating to conveyances will remain unaffected. 

c. Effect of Act of 1945 on Mortgages by Wife 

An examination of the amendment of 1945 will show that the Legislature at least intended to eliminate the requirement under the act of 1893 that the husband must join in a married woman's mortgages.10 This change is logical enough, because as noted under the preceding subsection, a husband has the corresponding power in this state to give a mortgage which will be superior to his wife's dower. If the amendment is effective at all, therefore, a married woman's mortgage without her husband's joinder executed after May 17, 1945, will create a valid encumbrance on the whole title, in the absence of fraud. 

d. Adverse Proceedings Against Wife 

The elimination of curtesy initiate should remove any doubt that might have existed concerning the effect of adverse proceedings against the wife's title. As a matter of fact, even before 1917, the husband's interest in his wife's real estate was probably not protected in such cases. 

In any event, it now seems clear that the husband has no power to prevent the loss of the wife's title to her real estate through execution on a bona fide judgment against her," a sale by her receiver in bankruptcy,12 condemnation,13 or partition proceedings.¹4

Where either spouse has been granted a valid divorce a v. m., there can be no question that the woman regains her full capacity, since she is no longer married; this follows regardless of whether she was the innocent or guilty party so long as the divorce was valid.15 A divorce a mensa et thoro, on the other hand, has no effect on the marriage status,16 but it is expressly provided by the act of 1927, P. A fourth type of emancipation is where a husband releases his wife from her incapacity in a separation agreement under the act of 1897, P. L. 212, 21 P. S. § 52. This act provides for the recording of such agreements and that the wife may thereafter convey or encumber her real estate without joinder. It is open to question whether an agreement by the husband purporting to release his wife from the incapacity of coverture but not conforming with this act (as, for example, a release in an agreement other than a separation agreement) would be effective. Clearly an agreement by the husband can be effective to release any interest he might have in property which the wife still owns at her death,19 but where the wife conveys to another the question is a little different: the husband would not be releasing a property interest in her land but would be attempting to remove a disability which the law imposesalthough it imposes this disability primarily for his benefit. 

His power to do so without conforming to the act of 1897 is therefore at least questionable.20

3₤ ¶ f. Forfeiture Distinguished

The law relating to when a married woman's incapacity is removed is analogous in its practical results to the law of forfeiture of marital rights discussed under section 6 of this act. There is a distinction, however, which requires that these two aspects of the law be treated separately. 

Strictly speaking, there can be no question of forfeiture by a husband of interests in his wife's property during her lifetime, because as already explained (¶ 3a) he no longer has any present interest which he can forfeit. At her death, he will have an interest in any property she dies owning, and the question of forfeiture might arise; but while she lives he is protected only indirectly by her incapacity to deed her real estate.

This theoretical difference between the inter vivos protection provided the husband and that provided the wife might have practical consequences. It was noted under section 5 (a) (3j) that under our statutes a wife's dower is not forfeited immediately upon her misconduct. If she deserts her husband in 1925, returns to him in 1935 and he dies in 1936, it would seem that she could claim her dower in land conveyed by him without her joinder in 1930, because grounds for forfeiture are examined as of the time of death under section 6. On the other hand, if the husband deserts in 1925 and returns in 1935, the wife's deed in 1930 would be good because her capacity is judged as of the date of the deed; this was the decision in Thornton v. Pierce, 328 Pa. 11 (1937), discussed above (3e). Plainly the latter result is more desirable, in that it leaves the wife's real estate alienable during the period of marital strife, but unfortunately there is no statute permitting a husband to be declared an "homme sole trader" and to convey his real estate clear of a possible later claim by his wayward wife; his only remedy is to get a divorce a v. m.-which he may not desire. 

g. Conflict With Section 11 of Estates Act 

Section 11 of the Estates Act provides that a surviving spouse may treat "as testamentary" a conveyance of real or personal property by the deceased spouse in which a 660

3h 

INTESTATE ACT 

power of appointment was reserved. A possible conflict with section 5 (a) of the present act has already been mentioned ( ¶ 3g). There is also a potential conflict of a somewhat different nature between section 11 of the Estates Act and the law relating to a married woman's conveyances. In the ordinary case where a married woman attempts to convey real estate without her husband's joinder, it has been seen that her deed is of no effect, and it is reasonably clear that nothing in section 11 of the Estates Act would give it partial effect merely because she reserved a power of appointment. If she conveys with her husband's joinder reserving a power of appointment, it would likewise seem reasonably clear that the husband could claim no rights under section 11 of the Estates Act (see discussion under ¶ 9 of that section), so that no problem would be raised. Suppose, however, the wife in Thornton v. Pierce (supra ¶3e and f) who conveyed without joinder during the period of the husband's desertion, had reserved a power of appointment in her deed. Under that decision there is no question that the deed is good. But could the widower on her death after reconciliation claim a share of the appointed property under the Estates Act? 

Or would her deed be effective to bar him under the act of 1855 which gave her the power of "free and absolute disposal"? It is uncertain which act would prevail. h. Transfers in Fraud of Husband's Marital Rights (Antenuptial and Postnuptial) 

Authorities dealing with antenuptial and postnuptial conveyances and encumbrances in fraud of marital rights are discussed under section 5 (a) (¶ 3k). There is no reason to suppose that different rules would be applied to corresponding attempts by the wife to bar her husband from a share in her estate after her death. It is true that there is a theoretical difference between a wife's inchoate dower and the protection indirectly given the husband in modern law by the wife's incapacity to convey during coverture. But it is unlikely that a court would use this distinction as a basis for different rules in the law of fraudulent transfers. The opinion in Kirk v. Kirk, 340 Pa. 661

¶1. General

When the spouse's allowance first made its appearance in the Intestate Act by the amendment of 1909, P. L. 87, it was realized that the new provision would raise procedural problems not theretofore encountered in fixing the spouse's share. A special provision was therefore inserted, indicating how the amount of the allowance should be set apart from the decedent's property. This was first done by referring to the procedure followed in setting aside the widow's exemption. When the act was revised in 1917, certain changes were made and the new procedure was set forth in the Intestate Act itself. Thus, the policy adopted in 1833 of eliminating the procedural provisions from the Intestate Act was to this extent reversed.¹ 

The procedural provisions relating to the allowance are retained as part of the present act, but the drafters have followed the logical plan of keeping procedure separate from substance, so far as possible. Thus, the primary provision for the allowance (now raised to $10,000) is in section 2, while matters pertaining to procedure in such cases are segregated in the present section. Many of the questions that have arisen concerning the spouse's allowance are discussed under section 2. As there pointed out, segre-

gation of the procedural provisions should make it even clearer that the allowance is simply a part of the spouse's intestate share where there are collateral relatives but no issue. The interest vests at the moment of decedent's death and in no sense is it a personal right which must be asserted to be enjoyed. The present section should be understood, therefore, merely as one means of securing judicial recognition of a property right which already exists. As the court said in Buckland's Estate, 239 Pa. 608, 615 (1913), "the procedure to appraise and set apart is but a means to an end. 99 

12. Personal Estate

One important difference between this section and the corresponding provisions in the 1917 act is that there is no longer any mention of a right to claim the allowance out of specific items of personal property. It was thought that the provision allowing this in the old act was of little value, and merely added to the expense of administration when it was used. The old procedure for having specific personalty appraised and set aside was held to be optional,2 and in the average case there was no disadvantage in waiting until audit and claiming the allowance in cash. Even if the privilege were exercised, the spouse apparently had no special right to premature distribution of the chosen chattel. Indeed it would seem that the only advantage to the spouse in the old provision was that a slightly larger share in income could be gained by choosing a security of high yield.¹ In the absence of any good reason for continuing the right to select specific personal property, therefore, it was eliminated. Of course, the spouse may still claim the allow-

13. Real Estate

The provisions for claiming the allowance from real estate remain substantially the same as before, although some changes in detail have been made. As heretofore, "all or part" of the allowance may be claimed in this manner, so that there is no objection to claiming part from personalty and part from real estate. Alternative procedures are provided in the subsequent subsections for enforcing the right against real estate. It is now expressly provided in subsection (g) that the allowance may at the spouse's option be collected "in the manner provided by law for the collection of legacies." The procedure under subsections (a) to (f), however, enables the spouse to choose a particular parcel of real estate and thus provides an opportunity for gaining clear title to the homestead or any other land desired. This does not mean that the spouse may select a particular portion of a larger tract where a division would adversely affect the value of the whole, but it does mean that the spouse may select any one or more of separate tracts of land owned by the decedent regardless of the preferences of the other heirs. Thus, in Troutman's Estate, 30 Dist. 708 (0. C. Perry 1920), the widow took all of one tract worth $400 and the rest of the allowance out of a property worth $9500, over the protests of the other heirs who wanted her to take the entire allowance out of the more valuable tract."

Once the tract has been chosen, the present section has the effect of a special partition act, under which the court can enter a decree fixing the spouse's interest in a particular piece of land. It is a separate action in rem, independent of the ordinary administration of the estate, requiring separate petition and notice to interested parties as provided by rules of court. Indeed, it can be instituted even when no letters of administration have been granted.8 

The interest of the spouse is fixed by the order confirming the appraisement. This is regarded as a final decree, which can be attacked by appeal but not collaterally," and which can be recorded as evidence of title under subsection (f). 

14. Decedent's Creditors 

It is expressly provided that the right to claim the allowance from real estate is "subject to the rights of creditors and existing liens." This merely confirms the fundamental theory that the allowance is simply part of the spouse's share in the net estate, as pointed out under section 2 (5c). This principle raises special problems, however, when the allowance is claimed from specific real estate.

If the debt of decedent is in the form of a mortgage on the chosen land, the spouse will of course take subject to it, but in such a case the appraisement should represent only the value of decedent's equity in the property so that the spouse will not be prejudiced.10 The situation becomes more difficult in cases where the real estate chosen is not subject to any specific lien but where the personal estate is insolvent and all of decedent's real estate is subject to the general lien of creditors. It seems plain that the setting aside of real estate to the spouse cannot affect this lien, but on the other hand, the right to the allowance is in the was intended. The Commissioners' Comments make this plain, and otherwise subsections (a) to (f) become meaningless. The allowance may be claimed "out of real estate" and this implies that particular property may be selected by the spouse.

In other words, the right to the allowance is subordinate to creditors but superior to the rights of other heirs. It might be difficult to preserve this order of preference in various situations that might arise. It should not be impossible for the court to do so, however, through its control of sales by the administrator, or by applying principles of marshalling and contribution when a judgment lien is executed against property which has been appraised at its full value and set aside for the allowance.11 

5. Status of Title When Spouse Fails to Act 

Interesting questions can arise if the spouse fails to take action to enforce the right to the allowance. As already pointed out, the right to the allowance exists from. the moment of decedent's death, but it remains an abstract interest in the "first $10,000 in value" until it is made definite by court decree or family agreement. If the allowance is paid out of personalty, the spouse's share in each parcel of real estate is indirectly fixed at one-half. But if the allowance is not paid out of personalty and no action is taken to collect the allowance from real estate, the respective interests of the spouse and other heirs in any particular piece of decedent's land remain undefined. In such a situation, the other heirs could probably force the spouse's hand by instituting partition proceedings,12 but the spouse's creditors 18 are in a more difficult position. 13

§ 10. SPOUSE'S ALLOWANCE-PROCEDURE (Continued) (b) From Real Estate. 

If the allowance is to be set apart in whole or in part out of real estate, the appraisement of the real estate shall be made by two appraisers who shall be appointed by the orphans' court. The orphans' court of the county where letters testamentary or of administration have been granted, or should no letters have been granted then of the county within which was the family or principal residence of the decedent, shall have jurisdiction concerning the allowance, whether the real estate is situate in that county or in any other county of the Commonwealth. If the decedent was a non-resident of the Commonwealth then the appraisers shall be appointed by the orphans' court of any county wherein any real estate of the decedent shall lie, and that court shall thereupon have jurisdiction concerning the allowance with respect to all of the real estate of the decedent within the Commonwealth. When real estate is located outside of the county of original jurisdiction, the orphans' court of the county of original jurisdiction may, in its discretion, direct that an application for the appointment of appraisers shall be made to the orphans' court of the county in which the real estate is located to fix the value of such real estate. The appraisers so appointed shall fix the value of the real estate as of the date the claim is presented in court and shall receive such compensation as shall be allowed by the court appointing them. Exceptions to appraisements wherever made shall be filed with the court of original jurisdiction which may in its discretion refer the exceptions to the orphans' court of the county in which the real estate is located. Upon compliance with such requirements of notice as the court shall prescribe, the court of original jurisdiction may confirm such appraisement and set apart such real estate to the surviving spouse.

The primary jurisdiction in cases of Pennsylvania decedents where real estate is situated outside the county of decedent's domicile is now in the court of domicile rather than the court where the land is situated. § 10 (b) 

Discussion 

This subsection sets forth the basic procedure for asserting the right given by subsection (a) to claim the allowance out of real estate. As heretofore, the two appraisers are appointed by the court (which also fixes the amount of their compensation) and the details of the procedure are left to rules of court. Section 12 of the Supreme Court 

Orphans' Court Rules should be consulted as well as local rules governing such matters as notice requirements. The statutory language relating to these matters has been somewhat revised, but except for the new jurisdictional requirements where real estate is situated in another county, the practice under the earlier act will remain unchanged. 

The provision that the appraisement must be confirmed by the court implies that there is the power to review the report of the appraisers, but the cases show that the court will be loath to interfere with its appraisers' judgment. 

Some opinions indicate that the value fixed by the appraisers will be set aside only where there is evidence of fraud or collusion,¹ but it would seem that the rule is not quite this strict. A valuation which shocks the conscience of the court or which is clearly based on a mistake will probably be set aside, although the procedure in such a case is to refer the matter back for a reappraisement, as the court has no power to fix a valuation itself.³ 

An important innovation in the present statute is the express provision that the value should be fixed "as of the date the claim is presented." This is probably in accord with prior practice, although the point seems to have been seldom raised.4

The principal change is in the jurisdictional provisions which alter the former practice in cases where real estate is situated in a county other than the decedent's domicile.

(c) Real Estate Valued at More Than the Amount Claimed.

Whenever the real estate of the decedent cannot be divided so as to set apart the amount claimed in value without prejudice to or spoiling the whole or any parcel of it, and the appraisers shall value such real estate or parcel thereof at any sum exceeding the amount claimed, it shall be lawful for the orphans' court of original jurisdiction to confirm the appraisement, and to set apart such real estate or parcel thereof for the use of the surviving spouse: conditioned, however, That the surviving spouse shall pay the amount of the valuation in excess of the amount claimed without interest within six months from the date of confirmation of the appraisement. The time limit for paying the excess valuation has been shortened from one year to six months, but otherwise the changes are merely stylistic in order to clarify the practice under the old act. 

Discussion 

This subsection conforms closely to section 2 (d) of the act of 1917. The time limit for paying the surplus after confirmation of the appraisement is shortened to six months and it is now expressly provided that the payment is "without interest." The provision should be read in connection with subsection (d) governing the payment of the surplus or proceeds of sale, and subsection (f) containing a special proviso prohibiting the recording of a conditional decree until the surplus is paid. See also the discussion under subsection (e) (1) of the nature of the spouse's title prior to the payment of the surplus. 

Like the old provision, the statute does not specify who should decide whether the property can be divided without spoiling the whole. The matter is discussed in 

McClain's Estate, 4 Wash. 59 (1922), where it is indicated that the appraisers should pass on this question primarily, although their findings will of course be subject to review by the court. 1102 [The next page is 1151]

The only change is that the court is now expressly given the power to order payment of surplus to the administrator if this is deemed advisable, although payment may still be ordered directly to the parties entitled. 1151

§ (d) INTESTATE ACT Discussion 

This corresponds to section 2 (e) of the old act, except that the court may order payment of the surplus money to the administrator rather than to the heirs when this is deemed advisable. 

Literally, the spouse must pay the difference between the appraisement and the amount of the allowance claimed. 

Where the estate is solvent and direct payment to heirs is permitted, one of the persons entitled to this surplus will be the spouse himself, whose share under section 2 (3) is the allowance plus one-half of the balance. Hence, if the whole allowance is claimed from a property appraised at $15,000, the spouse's interest is the $10,000 allowance plus one-half of the surplus value, or $12,500 in all, and he will have to pay the other heirs only $2500 to obtain clear title to the property. 1152 [The next page is 1201]

¶ 1. Substantive Rights. 

2. Jurisdiction. 

¶ 1. Substantive Rights 

The provision governing income in the act of 1917 was new in that year, but for the most part it restated principles which a few lower courts had already developed by 1201

§ (e) 

INTESTATE ACT 

¶ 1 judicial decision. Under the present revision of the section, the problem is again tossed back to the courts to decide on the facts of each case. The reported cases, both prior and subsequent to the act of 1917,¹ are consistent with the general principle that income should be apportioned according to the respective interests in the corpus at the time the income accrues, and this policy will probably be followed under the present act. 

In determining an equitable proration of income in any particular case, therefore, the following principles concerning the location of title at various times will be helpful: (1) The interest in the allowance arises at the moment of death and not when it is claimed (Hast's Estate, 51 D. & C. 

314 (O. C. Fulton 1944), and cases there cited). Until it is claimed, however, it remains an abstract interest in the "first $10,000 in value" in such property as is later chosen.2 (2) When all or part of the allowance is claimed from real estate appraised at less than the amount claimed, title to such real estate vests in the spouse when the appraisement is confirmed, but title so ascertained relates back to the date of decedent's death (Nichalson's Estate, 24 Dist. 138 (0. C. Phila. 1915)). (3) When the allowance is claimed from real estate worth more than the amount of the claim, then on confirmation of the appraisement, the spouse becomes the owner of a fractional interest computed by using the amount of the allowance claimed plus one-half of the surplus as the numerator, and the amount of the appraisement as the denominator (Sexton v. Magsam, 29 Dist. 

250 (C. P. Fulton 1919)). This title also relates back to the date of decedent's death, although it lasts only until the excess is paid to the other heirs (whereupon the whole title vests in the spouse) or until sale if the excess is not paid. .

And for reasons explained under subsection (a) (¶ 2), this fraction should be computed at valuations at the time of distribution. When all or part of the allowance is claimed from specific real estate, the rents should be prorated according to the respective interests of the parties in the particular property as determined by the appraisement. If, for example, the whole allowance is claimed from a parcel of real estate valued at $20,000, the spouse should be entitled to threequarters of the rents from the date of death to the time when the excess is paid or the property sold. 

Where the property is not rented to a third party but is occupied by the spouse or one of the other heirs, it would seem that the occupant should be charged with the rental value during the period. Discussion As noted under subsection (a), the confirmation of the appraisement is the final decree vesting title in the spouse 1251

§ 10. (f) 

INTESTATE ACT 

to the selected piece of real estate where the value is less than the amount of allowance claimed. Hence this provision enabling the spouse to record the decree as evidence of his title. The provision is based on section 2 (h) of the act of 1917, but the proviso prohibiting the recording of a conditional decree prior to the payment of the excess is new. 

The purpose of this proviso is to prevent the clouding of title by the recording of conditional decrees with no evidence of whether the condition was complied with. It is consistent with the provision in subsection (d) to the effect that the title to the whole property vests only when the surplus is paid. Until that time (as noted in the discussion of subsection (e)) the spouse's interest is only a fractional share measured by the amount of the allowance claimed, plus one-half of the balance; as to the rest of the title the spouse has nothing more than an option to buy plus a power to force a sale. Once a decree is recorded pursuant to this subsection, a purchaser will be safe in accepting the deed of the spouse alone for the property set aside. In the absence of a recorded decree, all the heirs will have to join in order to pass clear title to the whole property. The most difficult job of title searching will be when one of the other heirs. wishes to convey his fractional interest in the land. Suppose, for example, decedent dies owning several parcels of real estate and is survived by a widow and a brother. 

If the brother wishes to convey an undivided one-half interest in one of the tracts of land, the purchaser should make certain that the spouse's allowance has been paid either out of personalty or other real estate; otherwise the brother's interest in the offered land remains undefined. 

If it turns out that the widow has never claimed her allowance, the brother will be unable to pass clear title to his interest without instituting partition proceedings. See discussion under subsection (a) (15) of "Status of Title When 

Spouse Fails to Act." 1252 [The next page is 1301]

§ 11. PROCEDURE TO ESTABLISH TITLE TO REAL ESTATE WHEN SPOUSE CLAIMS ENTIRE ESTATE 

The surviving spouse or his successors in interest claiming the entire estate under this act may, after the expiration of one year from the death of the decedent, present a petition to establish title to real estate in the orphans' court of the county where letters testamentary or of administration have been granted, or should no letters have been granted then of the county within which was the family or principal residence of the decedent, setting forth that the decedent died leaving no known heirs, other than the surviving spouse, entitled to take under the provisions of this act and seised of real estate which by virtue of this act has vested in the surviving spouse. If the decedent was a nonresident of the Commonwealth, the petition may be presented in the orphans' court of any county wherein any real estate of the decedent shall lie and such court shall thereupon have jurisdiction of proceedings under this section with respect to all of the real estate of the decedent within the Commonwealth. The court, being satisfied concerning the facts set forth in the petition, aided if necessary by the report of a master, may enter its decree nisi adjudging that the title to such real estate is in the surviving spouse or his successor in interest. Notice of the decree nisi shall be published for such length of time and in such manner as the court shall direct. If within six months from the last publication of such notice exceptions shall be filed with the court alleging the existence of other heirs entitled to interests in the real estate, the court after hearing thereon and upon evidence satisfactory to it, aided if necessary by the report of a master, shall vacate the decree nisi, or confirm it absolutely. If no exceptions are filed, the decree shall be confirmed absolutely. A certified copy of the decree shall be recorded in the deed book in the office of the recorder of deeds of each county where real estate of the decedent shall lie, shall be indexed by the recorder in the grantor's index under the name of the decedent and in the grantee's index under the name of the surviving spouse, and shall be registered in the survey bureau or with the proper authorities empowered to keep a register of real estate in the county. 1401
