There are several changes: (1) Reference to personal property has been omitted so that it is now clear that an award of the personal estate to the spouse may be made at the audit without special proceedings. (2) It is no longer necessary to await the settlement of the administrator's account or even the grant of letters. (3) Jurisdiction is now in the court of decedent's domicile or wherever land belonging to a foreign decedent is situated. (4) The procedure is now by petition, decree nisi (which is advertised), and a six-month period for exceptions. 

Discussion 

This is the latest version of an act of obscure origin, first enacted April 6, 1833 (P. L. 207), about two days before the Intestate Act of that year (P. L. 315). According to the Commission of 1917, "the act of 1833, April 6, does not seem to have been drafted by the Commission to revise the Civil Code, and no previous act containing similar provisions has been found." The preamble of the original act declared that its purpose was to provide a method for fixing the title to real estate when the spouse became entitled to the whole estate under the act of 1819, P. L. 25, in the absence of known heirs. This was a worthy purpose, but it seems to have been forgotten in the drafting of the substantive provisions of the act which somewhat pointlessly provided only for an order distributing personal property.¹ In 1917, the Commission revised the language so as to make it clear that a decree concerning the title to 1. The act was liberally construed according to the purpose declared in the preamble, however, and orders concerning real estate were entered even before the language was revised in 1917. See, for example, Rogers' Est., 2 Chester 500 (O. C. 1885). 1403

§ 

INTESTATE ACT 

real as well as personal estate could be entered, and incorporated the provision into the Intestate Act of that year as section 17 (b).

Although the logic of including procedural provisions of this sort in an Intestate Act can be questioned,2 section 17 (b) had some value in the act of 1917, as a method of clearing record title to real estate when the spouse was entitled to the whole estate "in default of known heirs." 

Insofar as the provision applied to the personal estate, however, it merely caused confusion. There was no reason why the court could not simply award the personalty to the spouse at the audit as in any other case, but the section made it appear that the special proceeding with additional advertising was mandatory wherever the whole estate went to the spouse.³ The drafters of the present act wisely omitted any reference to personal property, so that it is now clear that no special proceeding is necessary to secure an award of the whole personal estate to the spouse in proper cases. 

Logically, the provision could have been omitted altogether in view of the new preference given the spouse by section. 

2 (4). Since the spouse now takes the whole estate in the absence of comparatively close relatives (rather than only "in default of known heirs or kindred" under the act of 1917), there is no more necessity for a special procedure to fix title to real estate where the spouse is the sole heir than where a first cousin is the sole heir. However, there was precedent for the present provision and in the limited class of cases to which it applies it will satisfy the general need for a procedure to obtain declaratory decrees concerning title to a decedent's real estate. Discussion 

¶ 1. Procedure Under Prior Law. 

12. Present Act. 

1451

§ INTESTATE ACT 

¶1 

1. Procedure Under Prior Law 

The earlier history of this provision is traced in Lutton v. Powell, 7 D. & C. 245 (C. P. Beav. 1925). The rights of the Commonwealth have been set forth in our Intestate Act since 1787, the last important change prior to the present act being in 1923 when section 24 of the act of 1917 was amended as above set forth. 

As explained under section 3 (14), before the present act the Commonwealth never had a primary right to the estate but took only when a decedent's next of kin could not be found. The old acts imposed no limitation on the remoteness of blood relatives who could inherit, so that theoretically there was always someone with a right superior to the Commonwealth's, even if the decedent's ancestry had to be traced back to Adam. Hence the Commonwealth's claim was always in the nature of a claim for unclaimed funds, by way of escheat or a proceeding analogous thereto.

The subject of escheat and quasi escheat is of course much broader than the particular phase of it governing intestacy, and there is a conglomeration of Pennsylvania statutes dealing with the subject. These general statutes dealing with the rights of the Commonwealth to escheatable funds are reviewed in Commonwealth ex rel Reno v. Pennsylvania Company, 339 Pa. 513 (1940). So far as intestate property is concerned, however, the discussion of the vari ous acts in Lutton v. Powell, 7 D. & C. 245 (C. P. Beav. 

1925) and in Rooney's Estate, 38 D. & C. 524 (0. C. Phila. 

1940) is probably more helpful. As will be seen from those authorities, there are two types of statutory provisions: (1) those providing for actual escheat which vests indefeasible title in the Commonwealth, and (2) those providing for the turning over of property to the Commonwealth as custodian without escheat. After 1923, when the word "escheat" was eliminated from section 24 of the Intestate Act of 1917, the Commonwealth's claims in cases of intestacy seem to have been for payment of the latter typethe turning over of the property without escheat-and the courts have been sympathetic to this mode of procedure.¹

2. Present Act

The present act should change the entire theory of the earlier cases in view of the fact that the Commonwealth now takes in its own right as the decedent's heir under section 3 (6) in the absence of relatives as close as first cousins. The older authorities where the Commonwealth proceeded by way of escheat or quasi escheat will still be relevant in rare cases where a close relative is known to exist but cannot be found (cf. Vogest's Estate, 31 D. & C. 

169 (O. C. Phila. 1937)), but in the ordinary case where the Commonwealth claims under section 3 (6) on the theory that relatives with a prior right do not exist, there would seem to be no resemblance to escheat proceedings. 

The one remaining reference in the present act to the general statutes concerning the Commonwealth's claim to unclaimed funds is in regard to the manner of paying the proceeds of the estate after liquidation into the state treasury. In this respect, but in this respect only, the present Intestate Act refers to the law governing "unclaimed" funds in the hands of a fiduciary. The reference is presumably to section 1314 of the Fiscal Code of 1929, P. L. 343, 72 P. S. § 1314 concerning payment of such funds without escheat and containing almost identical language. 

This reference might affect the wording of the decree making the award to the Commonwealth,2 but it would seem unnecessary to refer to the general escheat or quasi escheat statutes for any other purpose. Thus it should be clear under the present act that no informers' fees will be payable and that no appointment of an escheator is necessary. 

Note particularly that there is no longer a reference to the Fiscal Code for the procedure to be followed in selling real estate. The procedure is now that prescribed by the Price Act and it is clear that the administrator is the one who makes the sale. This requirement for the

(11) Lapsed and Void Devises and Legacies.- 

Adopted Persons and Illegitimates. For the purposes of the foregoing clauses of this section, the words "child" or "issue" shall include persons claiming by or through adoption and an illegitimate person shall be considered the child of his mother and not of his father; 

Provided, That when the parents of a person born illegitimate shall have married each other, he shall thereafter be considered legitimate. 

COMMISSIONERS' COMMENT This is intended to give adopted children the same right of substitution as natural children, thus avoiding the effect of Russell's Est., 284 Pa. 164, where an adopted child of a niece was not permitted to receive the niece's share, and Corr's Est., 34 D. & C. 255, where an adopted child given the residuary estate was not such a lineal descendant as would defeat the substitution of issue for a deceased brother and sister. So also this clause gives full rights of substitution to illegitimates and their issue in the mother's family if there is no marriage, and in both families if the parents marry: Cf. Act of 

1901, P. L. 639, 11 PS 1; Patterson's Est., 282 Pa. 396; 

Wettach v. Horn, 201 Pa. 201.

Old Law 

There was no prior statute on adoption governing lapsed legacies. Under our case law, an adopted child was not considered a child or issue within the meaning of the anti-lapse statute.

As to illegitimates the subject was probably covered by the Act of 1901, P. L. 639, 11 P. S. § 1, which reads as follows: 

Illegitimate children shall take and be known by the name of their mother, and the common law doctrine of nullius filius shall not apply as between the mother and her illegitimate child or children. But the mother and her heirs, and her illegitimate child and its heirs, shall be mutually liable one to the other, and shall enjoy all the rights and privileges one to the other, in the same manner and to the same extent, as if the said child or children had been born in lawful wedlock.

The effect of the anti-lapse statute (clause (8) supra) in cases involving adoption is changed. As to illegitimates, 3351

¶ 1. General

This clause is new and fills in a blank space that has existed in our anti-lapse statutes since 1810. As indicated by the authorities cited in the Commissioners' Comments, the prior law is changed as to the rights of those claiming by or through adoption in cases of substitution of issue to prevent lapse. As to illegitimates, the clause continues what the law probably has been since the act of 1901, P. L. 

639, 11 P. S. §1, which has been construed as making an illegitimate the child of his mother for all purposes.¹ The present clause refers primarily to clause (8) providing for the substitution of issue of certain devisees and legatees who predecease the testator. Indirectly it also refers to clauses (9) and (10) which themselves refer to clause (8).

It will be noted that clause (8) mentions children and issue in three connections: (a) The gift is saved for the "surviving issue" of the predeceased devisee or legatee. (b) The devisee or legatee must be the testator's "child or other issue," or the testator's brother or sister, or "a child of his brother or sister." (c) The issue of a brother, sister, nephew, or niece are not substituted if the spouse or "issue" of the testator would benefit by the lapse. Under

12. Intervening Adoption or Illegitimacy 

Not only may adopted persons claim, but an intervening adoption will not break the line of issue where, for example, a child of the named legatee's adopted child is claiming as the statutory substitute-or where the named legatee is the adopted child of the testator's child. The clause applies whether the substitute is claiming "by or through" adoption. Similarly an intervening illegitimacy will not break the line between the child of an illegitimate and the illegitimate's mother (or either parent of the illegitimate in cases of legitimation by subsequent marriage), because the illegitimate is considered the mother's child for all purposes under clause (8). 

3. Adopted Child as Natural Child's "Brother"

Suppose the named legatee is the adopted child of the testator's parent. Is the adoptee a "brother" of the testator within the meaning of clause (8) if he predeceases testator but has a child who survives? This is not too clear from the wording of the present clause, but it would seem that the adoptee's child would be claiming "through" adoption and therefore would qualify as a statutory substitute. Note that the same problem does not exist with regard to illegitimacy, for both under the present clause and the act of 1901, the illegitimate is the child of his mother for all purposes. ¶4. Natural Parents of Adopted Person

Unlike section 14 (6) of this act and section 8 of the Intestate Act, the present clause does not provide that the adopted person is no longer the child of his natural parents. 

Presumably, therefore, a claim could be made under this clause (8) through either the natural or the adopted family, although the contrary could be argued. For analogous 3353

§ 14 (13) A- 

(13) Lien of Pecuniary Legacies. 

Pecuniary legacies of one hundred dollars or less shall not be a charge on any of the testator's real estate. All pecuniary legacies in excess of the principal sum of one hundred dollars shall be charged upon, and payable out of, any real estate not specifically devised, where the personal estate is or becomes insufficient for their payment. 

COMMISSIONERS' COMMENT This is similar to section 17 of the 1917 

act. Prior to the 1917 act, real estate was not available for payment of pecuniary legacies unless they were expressly charged upon it. The 1917 act made all legacies a lien. Clause (13) makes a distinction between the larger and the smaller legacies. 

This seems justified as a reasonable classification. We thus avoid the necessity of recording releases of small legacies to perfect title to real estate. This has been a frequent source of annoyance, particularly in the case of very small legacies. The words "principal sum" are used to avoid any possible question when income has accumulated. It is to be noted that a legacy of $100 would not be a charge on real estate, but that a legacy of $100.01 would be. As a practical matter the smaller legacies are usually paid first.

Old Law 

Section 17. All pecuniary legacies contained in any will shall be charged upon, and payable out of, any real estate not specifically devised, where the personal estate is insufficient for their payment, or where the personal estate, though originally sufficient, has been wasted or misapplied by the executor, unless a contrary intention shall appear by the will. 

Wills Act of 1917, P. L. 403. 

The law remains the same as under the act of 1917 with respect to legacies of over $100. The provision freeing real estate from the lien of legacies of $100 or less is new. Discussion

¶ 1. General Relation to Law of Abatement 

This clause continues section 17 of the Wills Act of 1917 when this provision was first inserted into the statute, the only change being the excepting of legacies of $100 or less. The subject of charged legacies bears a close relation to the law of abatement which at the time of writing is covered by the rather inadequate provisions in section. 

20 of the Fiduciaries Act of 1917, P. L. 447, 20 P. S. § 632, and by general case law. The relation between the two branches of the law is illustrated by Forsyth's Estate, 335 

Pa. 281, 285-6 (1939), discussed below under 15-"Contrary Intent."

The law of charged legacies will be even more closely related to the law of abatement if the Fiduciaries Act is revised as presently planned so as to provide for the administration of real estate, and more specific rules for the appropriation of assets when the net estate is insufficient. to pay all devisees and legatees. Unless and until such changes are accomplished, it would be useless to speculate on the effect they would have on this section of the Wills Act. Suffice it to say that if real estate is administered there will necessarily be a change in what a charged legacy means in terms of its enforcement. Also the abatement section of any new Fiduciaries Act that is passed will have to be read in connection with this clause in the Wills Act

2. Common Law

At early law, a decedent's land descended directly to his heirs, could not be affected by a will, and was not even chargeable with his debts, other than specialties. The law of decedents' estates has rather consistently progressed away from the dualism between real and personal property, but even though real estate was long ago made devisable and available to creditors, a decedent's personal estate was still looked upon as the primary source for the payment of debts and the only source for the payment of pecuniary legacies, unless the testator had shown a different intention in his will.

Thus, if the will contained a gift of $10,000 to A and nothing more, the decedent's real estate passed by intestacy to his heirs, free of the claim of A who took nothing if there was no personalty from which he could be paid: 

Espy's Estate, 207 Pa. 459 (1904). The same was true if testator gave $10,000 to A and "all my real estate to B"; 

A was paid from the personal estate or not at all: Wallace's Estate, 234 Pa. 459 (1912).

It was, of course, possible for the testator to provide that a legacy be charged against real estate, either expressly or by implication. Even a specific devise could be charged with a legacy as where the testator made a devise of Blackacre "subject to," "upon condition of,” or “in consideration of" the payment of a legacy. The most important cases of implied charges before the act of 1917 were those holding that a pecuniary legacy was charged against residuary real estate when the legacy was followed by a general residuary clause which blended real and personal property_"$10,000 to A and the residue of my estate, real

Fiduciary Review, July 1948; Page, Wills (3d ed. 1941) § 1437 et seq. But see Cable's Appeal, 91 Pa. 327 (1879), illustrating the possibility of a devisee being personally liable for the payment of a legacy without it being charged on the land. Note that once a charge is found there is the secondary problem of whether other real estate and the personal estate is thereby exonerated. See Hun ter, O. C. There a pecuniary gift in the residuary clause was charged against what might be termed the residue of the residue. The reasoning of the court in these cases is important to note. The decisions did not rest on the general proposition that legacies must be preferred to real estate not specifically devised but upon the theory that the "rest" or "residue" of the decedent's real estate could only mean the rest after payment of the pecuniary legacy. See Reel's Estate, 266 Pa. 221 (1920), where the rule was applied even though specific parcels of land were mentioned in the residuary clause. Thus, these decisions in no way affected the rule prior to the statute that legacies were not charged against intestate real estate or real estate devised by general terms.* 

13. Effect of Statute 

Against this background section 17 of the 1917 act was passed stating that in the absence of a contrary intent pecuniary legacies should be charged against real estate not specifically devised. The present clause re-enacts this provision as to legacies over $100. a. Intestate Real Estate

One clear effect of the statute is to change the rule in Espy's Estate, 207 Pa. 459 (1904) (supra 2), and charge legacies against land passing by intestacy when the will simply provides for a pecuniary legacy and nothing else. b. Residuary Devises

As to land passing under a general residuary clause the statute merely confirms the result reached by the cases prior to 1917.

Land specifically devised is excepted from the statute so that the prior law remains unchanged in cases where there is a non-residuary gift of land specifically identified in the will. d. Non-Residuary Devises in General Terms 

The question of whether the statute changes the rule of Wallace's Estate, 234 Pa. 459 (1912) (supra ¶2), that legacies are not charged against a non-residuary gift of "all my real estate" remains unanswered. 

At early law, a will spoke as of its date with respect to real estate so that all devises (even residuary devises) were necessarily specific." This was early changed by what are now sections 14 (1) and 14 (2) of the present act under which a will speaks as of the testator's death as to both real and personal property, and after-acquired real estate passes by what the statute since 1833 has termed a "general devise." Page believes that in view of such statutes, devises of land may in modern law "be general or residuary as well as specific. 997 In view of the language both of clause (2) and of the present clause of section 14, there clearly is such a thing as a general devise in our law today. Most authorities would no doubt agree that a residuary devise is general. 

But that is unimportant in applying the present clause because even before the statute pecuniary legacies were a charge on residuary real estate. The question is whether a devise of "my real estate" or "all my real estate" is nonspecific within the meaning of this clause. 

In Wallace's Estate, decided before there was a statute governing charged legacies. but after the act of 1833 had authorized a devise of after-acquired real estate, the lower

Persuasive arguments can be made on both sides. In support of Timothy's Estate it can be said that the average testator owns only his residence or at most a few parcels of real estate and is likely to be thinking in specific terms when he refers to "my real estate." On the other hand, a gift of "all my personal estate" is clearly general and to treat the two types of property differently seems contrary to the modern trend.

For the present clause to apply, the legacy must be not only general but "pecuniary." Suppose a testator provides for a gift of "$1000 worth of government bonds." 

As pointed out in the discussion of clauses (1) and (2) of this section, such a gift has been held to be non-specific where the question was one of ademption, and it would seem to follow that it was pecuniary, since the testator was thinking primarily in terms of value rather than specific property. .: 

By the same token, a demonstrative legacy ("$1000 out of my bank account") for purposes of ademption is said to be general insofar as the fund indicated is insufficient for its payment and hence it should to that extent be considered pecuniary within the meaning of the present clause. 5. Contrary Intent 

In Cornell's Estate, 23 D. & C. 381 (O. C. Phila. 1935) legacies of $1,000 and $50,000 were payable "out of my personal estate," and the court held that they were not charged on residuary real estate beacuse the testator had shown an intention contrary to the statute. Apparently, the court construed the will as limiting the payment of the legacy to the personal estate. In effect the court refused to construe the gift as demonstrative. This, of course, is a possible construction although in ademption cases a more definite provision is usually required to find such a limitation. 

A clearer case in this respect is Forsyth's Estate, 335 Pa. 281 (1939). There the testator expressly limited the payment of his legacies to stocks and bonds directing that his real estate should not be sold for this purpose. Of course, the court held that the statute had no application, because the testator had clearly expressed a contrary intention. The only reason the case reached the Supreme 

Court was because of the appellant's ingenious theory that 3457

§(13) 

WILLS ACT 

16 although the legacies were not payable from the land, the debts of decedent were so payable-hence that the gross value of the stocks and bonds were available for the payment of the legacies. The court rejected the contention saying that this "would be tantamount to paying appellant's bequest out of the proceeds of real estate" contrary to the testator's express direction (335 Pa. at 286). 

16. Effect of Charge-Enforcement, Discharge, etc. 

Assuming the act applies in a given case, the legacy upon probate of the will becomes a lien of record against the real estate until it is paid and marked satisfied on the records of the Orphans' Court, or otherwise discharged. 

There is a good review of the authorities on such matters by James G. Schmidt in the July 1948 issue of the Fiduciary Review.

Very briefly the law on the subject under the Fiduciaries Act of 1917, as reviewed by Mr. Schmidt, may be summarized as follows: (1) The jurisdiction for enforcement of the charge is exclusively in the Orphans' Court 10-usually by petitions to sell for the payment of a legacy under section 25 of the Fiduciaries Act of 1917, P. L. 447, as amended, 20 P. S. $ 652. (2) The usual method for the discharge of the lien is by payment and the securing from the legatee of an order to mark the legacy satisfied of record which is thereupon. filed with the clerk of the Orphans' Court. The lien may also be discharged from the land (and transferred to the proceeds or to other property) by (a) a sale for the payment of debts by order of the Orphans' Court 11 or (presumably) under a power in the will 12; (b) by a sheriff's sale on a judgment against the devisee (except in certain cases of express charges set forth in Pennsylvania Trust 

10. Clark's Est., 99 Pa. Super. 490, 496 (1930). Note that express charges as in that case often involved both (1) a charge, and (2) a personal obligation on the part of the devisee. See Logan v. Glass, 136 Pa. Super. 221, 225 (1939).

A statutory charge probably does not result in any personal obligation. 

11. Lombaert's Appeal, 99 Pa. 580 (1882). 

12. Cf. cases on lien of debts, Hunter, O. C. Book (1939) "Powers of Sale of Real Estate" § 18. The revision of the Fiduciaries Act now in progress will probably cover this point specifically. 3458

S. § 671 and § 691 which can be resorted to when the legacy is payable in the future or when the legatee cannot be found. (3) Prior to discharge, the charge is a lien of record as of the date of probate. Hence, it would be senior to liens against the devisee or heir and might have collateral effects on the discharge of such subsequent liens under the act of 1929, P. L. 874, 21 P. S. § 651. 

Attention is again called to the fact that the revision of the Fiduciaries Act which is now being prepared might have far reaching effects on some or all of the above rules. 

17. Exception of Legacies of $100 or Less

Little need be said concerning the first sentence of the present clause excepting legacies of $100 or less from the general provision. The purpose was to avoid the nuisance of removing the lien where the executor fails to secure an order of satisfaction from the legatee-or where the legatee, offended by a token legacy, refuses to accept or renounce it.

As noted in the Commissioners' comments, the measure is the "principal sum"-not the legacy plus interest. Presumably, the value of an annuity legacy (e. g. $25 a month for life) would be the principal value measured by annuity tables rather than the amount of the periodic payments in this respect.

Plainly there is no constitutional objection to this distinction between large and small legacies. Not only is the classification eminently reasonable, but the statute merely provides a rule for construing a testator's probable intent and the rule of the statute can thus be changed by any testator who so wishes.

It will be noted in this connection that the rule as to $100 legacies is subject to the opening sentence of section 14 so that this part of the clause also applies only in the absence of a contrary intent. Query, if the pre-1917 cases (discussed above) will be followed so as to create a charge in a case where the testator leaves one dollar to A and the 3459

§(13) WILLS ACT 

17 "rest" of his real and personal estate to B. It is submitted that such a construction would defeat the legislative intent and that something more definite should be required to show an intent that small legacies should be charged. Certainly no normal testator would so intend in cases where the legacy is $100 or less. 3460 [The next page is 3501]

For the purpose of creating a temporary reserve of a reasonable amount for administration of the trust, or periodic distributions in specified amounts, or the needs of a beneficiary; 

(2) Lifetime of the Settlor. 

For a period expressly measured by the lifetime of the settlor; (3) Minority.

During the minority of any beneficiary who if living at the age of twenty-one will be entitled to such accumulations and earnings thereon or to the entire income from such accumulations and earnings thereon; and a direction or authorization to accumulate income until a person reaches a designated age over twenty-one and thereafter to pay to such person, if living, such accumulations and earnings thereon or the entire income from such accumulations and earnings thereon, shall be valid during minority and shall take effect as though twenty-one had been the designated age; (4) Incompetency.

For the exclusive benefit of a person who, in the opinion of the trustee, is incompetent to receive or judiciously use the income; (5) Charity.

For any charitable purpose or purposes; 

(6) Pension or Profit-Sharing Plans. 

In a bona fide trust inter vivos primarily for the benefit of business employees, their families or appointees, under a stock bonus, pension, disability or death benefit, profit-sharing, or other employee benefit plan; (7) Insurance Premiums.

In a trust consisting of, or including, a policy or policies of insurance, a direction or authorization that the 5601

ESTATES ACT 

dividends on such policies may be applied in whole or in part for the payment of premiums on such policy or policies; 

(8) Apportionment Between Principal and Income. 

The following directions or authorizations shall be valid: a. To apply to principal in whole or in part extraordinary dividends, regardless of the form in which they are paid, and rights to subscribe to stock; b. To amortize from income premiums paid for investments which are callable or have a fixed maturity; c. To amortize from income the waste represented by the return from a wasting asset or dividends from a wasting asset corporation; d. To pay carrying charges on unproductive or underproductive property from income; e. To apply to principal in whole or in part the proceeds of the conversion of unproductive or under-productive property.

Clause (3), in permitting accumulation during any minority, is more liberal than heretofore. See McBride's Est., 152

Pa. 69; In re Trustee's Account, 87 Pitts. L. J. 79.

The validation of accumulations during minority, when the accumulation is directed to be continued beyond the minority and then paid to the former minor, is consistent with former law: Stocking's Est., 304 Pa. 476; Gray, Rule Against Per petuities (4th Ed.), sections 700, 718. However, clause (3) as proposed changes the law by permitting the designated person to receive accumulated income on reaching twenty-one when the gift of income is contingent upon survival to a designated age (cf. Lowe's Est., 326 Pa. 375) and in permitting income accumulated until the age of twenty-one to be capitalized. If the minor dies before he is twenty-one, accumulations to the date of his death, being valid, will be distributed as directed by the conveyor. [clause (4)] This is new and will validate what frequently occurs in actual practice when persons interested do not wish to secure the appointment of a guardian in the common pleas court.

The significant changes are as follows: (1) The period of accumulation during the settlor's life must now be "expressly" measured by his life. (Whether this represents a clarification or a change from prior law is uncertian.) (2) (a) Minority accumulations may now be for any minor, regardless of whether he is living at the date of the conveyance. (b) The accumulated fund may be given to another in case of death during minority. (c) The accumulation is valid even though it is capitalized, so long as the former minor receives the entire income from the accumulated fund after reaching majority. (3) Instruments providing for accumulations until an age over twenty-one are reformed by substituting twentyone as the designated age, if that will make them lawful. (4) Pension and profit-sharing plans are excepted. (5) The power of the testator or settlor to dictate his own rules as to principal and income or to give his trus- 5605

There are other changes of minor significance, but for the most part the prior law in other respects is merely restated or clarified.

3. Opening Words-Section Only Applicable to Directions and Authorizations 

It is important to bear in mind the opening words of this section when considering the various exceptions to the general rule which follow. The law is concerned only with a "direction or authorization" in the trust instrument. If the trustee withholds income of his own accord without authorization in the instrument, there is a problem of whether he is committing a breach of trust, but strictly speaking there is no problem in the law of accumulations." 

Thus, the exceptions to the general prohibition subsequently enumerated in clauses (1) to (8) in no way affect the ordinary duties of a trustee in the absence of a special provision in the trust.

It will be seen that the general prohibition expressly includes "authorizations" to accumulate as well as directions. This is probably in accord with prior law, but the wording should remove the doubt on the subject created by some early Supreme Court decisions indicating that where the trustee had discretion to distribute the income, the act of 1853 did not apply. As Mr. Foulke pointed out years ago, there was no sense in these decisions. Furthermore, there were other cases where the statute was applied, despite the fact that discretion had been given to the trustee." 

There should be no question in this regard under the present act.

It likewise seems clear that the present section, like the old act, will cover cases of implied as well as express provisions for accumulation. If the construction of the trust instrument is kept separate from the problem of accumulations, this should present no difficulty. A testator, for ex-

5. Clause (2)-Lifetime of the Settlor 

Accumulation during the life of the settlor is a traditional exception to the statutory prohibition; it was in the original Thelluson Act 14 and in the Pennsylvania act of 1853. Clause (2) should settle the long unanswered question in this state of whether an unlawful accumulation directed in an inter vivos trust should be upheld at least until the settlor dies. Suppose, for example, that a deed of trust provides that income should be accumulated for 50 years, and the settlor dies 25 years after the date of the deed. 

13. Cf. Billings's Est. (No. 2) 268 Pa. 71, 75 (1920); but see Restatement, Trusts (1944) § 439, comment i. See further discussion of support trusts under §8 (¶5b). 

14. 39 & 40 Geo. III, c. 98. 5610

¶ 

1 B

Should the trustee be permitted to accumulate at least during the settlor's life? The better view was that this was permissible under the act of 1853,15 although the only real authority on the question was an oblique Supreme Court dictum to the contrary.18 No one was quite certain of the answer. The present provision seems clear to the effect that such a provision would be bad from the beginning. 

Unless the period of accumulation is "expressly measured by the lifetime of the settlor," the whole accumulation is void.

There will no doubt be those who will disagree with this solution. Why should the policy of the law vary according to what the settlor provides? There is, however, this to be said in favor of the present provision: In a great many cases of this type the settlor might well prefer having the provision stricken down in its entirety rather than chopped off in the middle. Furthermore, the invalidation of the whole accumulation avoids the dreadful problem of what to do with the fund accumulated during the settlor's life where the ultimate beneficiaries of the accumulated fund were to have been ascertained at some later date. A provision allowing accumulation at least during the permissible period is plausible in the case of a direction to accumulate until a beneficiary reaches an age over twentyone (a problem discussed below-¶ 6e), but aside from that case, it is usually anyone's guess as to whether the settlor would have wanted the accumulation during what might turn out to be a shorter period than he had contemplated and as to what the settlor would want done with the accumulations which result. In any event, for better or worse, the drafters decided to cut the Gordian knot and permit such accumulations only if the period is "expressly measured by the lifetime of the settlor." The new provision will operate harshly in certain cases, but it is admittedly an arbitrary restriction with emphasis on certainty rather than perfect justice in every imaginable case. Thus, a di-

Suppose the settlor of an inter vivos trust directs accumulation of income until his own death or until the death of A, whichever earlier occurs. It is believed that such a direction should be valid under the present statute because the maximum period of accumulation is expressly measured by the lifetime of the settlor, and the direction is thus within the literal meaning as well as the policy of the exception in clause (2).

Assuming that the period of accumulation is expressly measured in conformity with the statute, there is no requirement in clause (2) concerning what must be done with the accumulated fund. Any direction in this regard is lawful. That capitalization of the fund is permissible is clear not only from the absence of prohibition in this section but also from the rule of construction set forth in section 7 (a). 

In this respect the present statute probably restates the prior law, but it must be admitted that the act of 1853 was ungrammatical, if not ambiguous, on this point. See Commissioners' Comments to section 7 (a). 

[6. Clause (3)-Minority 

The minority clause is perhaps the most interesting of the exceptions to the general prohibition enumerated in this section. It changes prior law on several important points and constitutes an extremely liberal provision in this branch of the law of accumulations. a. Any Minority Permissible

It will first be noted that under the present wording, accumulation is permissible during the minority of "any beneficiary." Under the Act of 1853 the minor had to be in existence when the trust began,17 although the reason for this restriction was not clear. Accumulations during minor- 

17. McBride's Est., 152 Pa. 192 (1893). 5612

The same reasoning applies whether the minor was born before or after the creation of the trust. By permitting accumulations for after-born minors, the present act eliminates an illogical restriction in the old law. In taking advantage of this relaxation of the law of accumulations, however, attorneys must be on guard to avoid a violation of the rule against perpetuities (as modified by sections 4 and 5 of the present act); the provisions of this section will clearly not validate gifts and restraints which violate some other rule of law.18 b. Gift Over on Death During Minority Permissible

The second important change from prior law is that clause (3) permits a gift over in case of death before reaching twenty-one. This is implicit in the words " who if living at the age of twenty-one will be entitled to such accumulations . "If the minor dies before reaching twenty-one, there is no prohibition against a gift over of the accumulated fund. Under prior law, such a gift over would probably have been unlawful; apparently the fund had to be held exclusively for the minor or his estate.¹9 

Again, however, there would seem to be no reason for such a restriction. The minor who dies before reaching twentyone will not get the benefit of the accumulated fund anyway, so there is no objection to allowing the fund to go to some- 

18. Compare Price, “Act Relating to Real Estate" (1874) 146. Under section 4 of the present act the common-law rule against perpetuities is modified by making actualities rather than possibilities the test in determining remoteness of vesting, but the permissible period (life in being and twenty-one years) remains the same. In drafting wills and deeds the attorney will have to take the same precautions to guard against the possibility of a violation as he took prior to the present act to avoid the certainty of a violation. Where the right to the accumulations is indefeasibly vested in the minor within the permissible period, the rule against perpetuities, strictly speaking, will not be violated merely because the income continues to be accumulated after the permissible period has expired. However, such a provision in a deed or will might violate the less familiar rule against indestructible trusts lasting beyond a life and twenty-one years. See Simes, 7 U. of Chi. L. Rev. at 410. On the whole, attorneys will be wise to limit any general clause in wills and deeds directing accumulations during minorities to beneficiaries who will be born before the death of the life in being-regardless of whether the gift of the accumulated fund is contingent upon the minor's surviving the age of twenty-one. 

19. Scattergood's Est., 28 Dist. 130 (1918). The authorities are scarce and it is not clear how the courts handled provisions of this sort under prior law even assuming the gift over was bad. Here also a possible violation of the rule against perpetuities must be guarded against, but if that rule is satisfied, the present law will clearly not be violated merely because the minor's enjoyment of the accumulation is contingent upon his living to attain majority. 

c. Permissible Capitalization of Accumulations 

Perhaps the most radical change accomplished by clause (3) is that an accumulation during minority is valid even when the minor will never receive the accumulated fund, provided he will receive the entire income therefrom upon reaching majority. Suppose, for example, a will contains a direction to accumulate and capitalize income during the minority of A, and upon A's reaching twenty-one to pay the income (from the principal as enlarged by the accumulations) to A for life with remainder at his death to B. 

Plainly such a direction would have been bad under prior law because the ultimate benefit of the accumulation enures to B, while A merely gets the income from the fund during his life.21 Under the present act the provision would be valid.

The reason for this relaxation of the rule was that the sudden payment to a twenty-one-year-old of what might be a very large sum of money out of all proportion to what he will receive in subsequent years might be just as undesirable socially as tying up the accumulated fund until his death; in any event the testator should be allowed to decide. 

This is by no means a novel idea. Back in 1871, Justice 

Paxson, then a judge of Orphans' Court, had this to say of the act of 1853: "Speaking for myself, it is difficult to see the wisdom of any Act which requires in a large estate, the accumulated income of a minor to be paid to him in all cases, upon his arrival at full age. There are many instances where such a thing would be injurious to him in the highest degree. The capitalization of the income, and pay- 

20. The present provision is in accord with Restatement, Property (1944) § 445, construing statutes requiring that the accumulation must be for the minor's benefit. 

21. Washington's Est., 75 Pa. 102 (1874); Farnum's Est., 191 Pa. 75 (1899); Lowe's Est. 326 Pa. 375, 383 (1937). 5614

¶ 6d

ESTATES ACT 

& 6 2 PA 33 Cla ment to him only of the interest after majority, would often promote his best good. There would seem to be no reason of public policy demanding such a change in the right of disposing of property." 22 

Justice Paxson's suggestion is followed in clause (3) which provides that an accumulation during minority is valid if the minor will receive either the accumulations or the "entire income from such accumulations" when he becomes of age. Perhaps the words "during his life" should have been added, but this seems plainly implied. A gift of the income from the accumulated fund for only five years after attaining majority would obviously not suffice, but on the other hand it is not necessary to give the former minor the income from the fund in perpetuity, as this would be the equivalent of the fund itself. 

In drafting instruments designed to take advantage of this new liberalization of the law, attorneys should be on guard against a literal violation of its terms. The particular beneficiary must receive at least the entire income for the rest of his life from any fund accumulated during his minority. A general minority clause in a will might run afoul of this limitation. For example, a testator with five children, only one of whom is a minor at his death, cannot lawfully provide for accumulation of the minor child's onefifth share of income and the addition of the accumulated fund to the general principal from which all five children will receive the income. Unless the youngest child is given the accumulations outright upon reaching the age of twentyone, a separate trust must be created for his benefit so that he alone will receive the "entire" income from the fund accumulated during his minority. 

d. Summary 

By way of summary, if the three changes from prior law are considered together, the following provision in a will would be valid under the present section: "To A for life, then to A's first born child for life [A now having no children], remainder in fee to X [a living person]. But if 

22. Washington's Est., 8 Phila. 182, 189 (O. C. 1871), aff'd. 75 Pa. 102 (1874), quoted in Eberly's Appeal, 110 Pa. 95, 97 (1885). 5615

ESTATES ACT 

¶ 6e A's first born child shall be a minor at the time of A's death, the trustee shall accumulate the income during the child's minority and add such accumulations to principal." Under prior law the above provision would be objectionable for three reasons: (1) the minor is not in being at testator's death; (2) the minor's estate will get no benefit from the accumulations if he dies before reaching twenty-one; and (3) even if the child reaches twenty-one, he will merely get the income from the accumulations instead of the accumulated fund itself. Under the present act none of these objections could be made. This does not mean that the lid will be entirely off. An accumulation during minority will still be valid only if the minor will receive some of the benefit of the accumulated fund-even though that benefit might be contingent upon his reaching majority and might be limited to income from the fund. A direction to accumulate during the minority of A and then to pay the accumulations to B would be just as bad under the present act as it would have been in the past. 

e. Age Over Twenty-One 

The last sentence of clause (3) deals with the all too common case where an accumulation is directed until an age over twenty-one. Testators are wont to decide for themselves what is a proper age of discretion, and this has raised some troublesome problems in the law of accumulations. 

The present provision is in accord with prior law in the simple case of a direction to accumulate until age thirty followed by an unconditional gift of the accumulated fund to the beneficiary; in such a case it was easy to allow the accumulation at least during the minority and order the accumulations paid to the beneficiary when he became of age.2 

Suppose, however, the direction is to accumulate until A reaches 30, then to pay the accumulations to A if living, but if A dies before reaching 30 to pay the accumulations to B. 

Under prior law, the direction would probably have been objectionable even if it had been limited to minority because the accumulations might not go to A, but in any event the courts refused to accelerate the contingent gift to age 23 

23. Stocking's Est., 304 Pa. 476 (1931). 

5616

Co 

ESTATES ACT 

cas EI twenty-one.24 Under the present section the contingent gift of the accumulations is not objectionable in itself, the only objectionable feature being the designation of the age over twenty-one. As a result there are two questions to be answered: Can the accumulation be permitted during minority, and can the contingent gift of the accumulated fund be accelerated? Clause (3) answers both questions in the affirmative. In effect, whenever a provision for accumulation is valid in all respects except the designated age, this clause says to the erring testator: "Although you said ‘age 

30' you meant 'age 21.'" Thus, both the period of accumulation and the gift of the accumulated fund is given effect "as though twenty-one had been the designated age.” 

7. Clause (4)-Incompetency 

Clause (4), dealing with accumulation during incompetency, has no counterpart in the act of 1853 and changes the law accordingly. It should be read in connection with subsection (c) and (d) of section 7, infra, providing that income must be available for the incompetent's support and that any surplus income accumulated must be paid to the incompetent or to his estate. 

Prior to the present act, there was undoubtedly a lot of de facto accumulation being practiced in cases of incompetent beneficiaries which was never objected to, but it seems fairly clear that under prior law a beneficiary who was not legally incompetent, or the guardian of one who was, could at any time have compelled the trustee to pay over such accumulations.25 Enforced distribution of income not needed for support is obviously pointless where there is a guardian, who will proceed to continue the accumulation anyway, so that the only effect is that commissions must be paid to both trustee and guardian. Of course, an accumulation statute can do nothing where the testator has failed to provide for such contingencies, but the law

25. See Taite's Est., 46 D. & C. 456 (O. C. Montg. 1943). Cf. Sterrett's

McManus's Estate, 361 Pa. 122 (1949) and further discussion of support trusts under 88 (5b). 5617

17 should not stand in the way of a testator who has foreseen the difficulty.

The fact that double commissions will in many cases be avoided is not a complete justification of clause (4) which permits a settlor to direct the withholding of income not only in cases of legal incompetency but also in cases where the beneficiary might be competent in the eyes of the law but not in the eyes of the trustee. One reason for this extension is a purely practical one-it will avoid the necessity of litigation in the common pleas each time the provision in the act is invoked. But beyond this, there seems to be no evil in permitting accumulation whenever the trustee believes the beneficiary is incompetent. The accumulations under clause (4) will necessarily be limited to income not needed for support. Usually the trust instrument will so provide, but even if it does not, income will be available for the incompetent's support under subsection (c) of section 7. Hence, if support trusts in general are conceded to be proper, there should be no objection to permitting accumulations of surplus income in such situations. If the beneficiary were competent, he would undoubtedly save and invest income which he had no immediate use for. In a support trust, the trustee spends the beneficiary's money for him. Should not the trustee be allowed to do what the beneficiary would do and save the income not needed? 

The principal practical value of the present law specifically authorizing accumulations during incompetency is that it will make lawful directions in the instrument concerning the investment of such accumulations. In the past, it is doubtful whether a trustee could have invested de facto accumulations of this sort at all, even in legals, without assuming the liability of an insurer. With such accumulations now lawful, it would seem clear that income withheld pursuant to a disability clause in the will or deed can at least be invested in legals, and that the investment powers in the instrument can extend to such fund if the intent so to extend it is expressed or implied in the instrument. 

The important limitation on the validity of accumulations under clause (4) is in the requirement that the accumulations must be for "the exclusive benefit" of the in- 5618

¶ 

§6 ESTATES ACT 

13 competent. These words, particularly when read with subsection (d) of section 7, indicate that to be valid the accumulated fund must ultimately go either to the beneficiary or to his estate. Hence, a mere temporary withholding is the most that is permitted under this clause.26 It might be suggested that the statute should have permitted a gift over of the accumulations on the beneficiary's death for the reasons set forth above (¶ 6b) in connection with accumulations during minority. It is believed, however, that the limitation here is a wise one. Under the incompetency provision, the trustee must be the judge of how long the income should be withheld. This discretion can be more objectively exercised if the ultimate ownership of the fund is not at stake and the size of the corpus can in no event be swelled by capitalization. 

8. Clause (5)—Charity 

Clause (5) follows the blanket exception in favor of charities contained in the act of 1853. Similar exceptions are found in the laws of some other states, although the Thelluson Act contains none.27 Considering the fascinating possibilities of long-term accumulations, it is surprising that this unqualified exemption has caused as little trouble as it has. There is indeed the case of the gentleman who attempted to pay off the entire debt of the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania with accumulations from a fund of $377.35.28 The court had some difficulty in finding a reason for refusing to enforce the trust, but succeeded in invalidating it for a reason wholly unrelated to the preposterousness of the settlor's scheme. No doubt the courts will continue to strike down the brain children of eccentric testators and 26. It is sometimes said that where the ownership of the accumulated fund remains in the income beneficiary from whom it was withheld, there is properly speaking no "accumulation" at all. Cf. Mathues's Est., 322 Pa. 358, 360 (1936). It is believed that this statement is not accurate. Where the ownership of withheld income is in a living person who has the present legal right to enforce its distribution, there is no accumulaton within the purview of the statute the beneficiary is in effect merely leaving his money in bank. 

Where, however, no one has the legal authority to demand immediate distribution of the withheld income, there is an accumulation, regardless of vested ownership, and such accumulation must come within one of the exceptions in the statute to be lawful.

Other limitations to the validity of such accumulations arise from distinctions drawn in the general law of charities. It is first necessary to establish that the purpose falls within the meaning of the word "charitable." This word is defined in section 1 (1) of the present act as including "the relief of poverty, the advancement of education, the advancement of religion, the promotion of health, governmental or municipal purposes, and other purposes, the accomplishment of which is beneficial to the community." 30 

As pointed out in the discussion of that clause of section 1, questions of this sort arise not only when the social benefit of the gift is doubtful but also where a power to select beneficiaries might be so broad as to permit the selection of non-charitable objects,31 or where individuals might get incidental benefits from the charitable accumulation.32 And finally there is the requirement that the gift to charity must be unconditional, at least at the time when the accumulation is to commence.33 

9. Clause (6)-Pension or Profit-Sharing Plans 

The law of accumulations, like the law of perpetuities, was aimed at schemes of a private nature which were deemed to have no particular social value. The prohibition in the accumulation statute is framed in broad language, however, and would apply to business transactions as well, although in the latter cases there may be considerations of policy favoring the restraint and outweighing the policy against it. ¶ 11. Clause (8)-Apportionment Between Principal and In come In interpreting trusts which direct simply that the "income" shall be paid to the life tenant it is necessary for the law to determine what this word means and consequently to draw a sharp dividing line through the twilight zone between principal and income. Having done so, the Pennsylvania courts somewhat reluctantly found it impossible to avoid the logical conclusion that it constitutes an unlawful accumulation for a testator to draw a different line and treat as principal that which the law had designated income. 

Thus, in Maris's Estate, 301 Pa. 20 (1930), a direction to capitalize stock dividends was held bad under the act of 1853, because under the law at the time of the decision such dividends were income to the extent that they were earned after decedent's death. To correct this decision, the act of 

1939, P. L. 201 was passed permitting the capitalization of extraordinary dividends or profits on the sale of stock. The present section goes further and permits the creator of the trust to designate what shall be treated as income and what as principal in a variety of situations. 

Necessarily the exception is still limited to the enumerated cases. It still is not possible for a testator to accomplish a real accumulation by directing that all rents, interests, and dividends shall be treated as principal. However, the act of 1939 is considerably broadened, and in general a testator will be able to direct or authorize the capitalization of items in the twilight zone which the law says are income but which it might have said were principal. 

The specific provisions are largely self-explanatory. It will be noted in the first place that since the adoption of 5622

¶ 

the Uniform Principal and Income Act, profits from the sale of securities are principal,37 so that it was not necessary to include in the present act this exception appearing in the act of 1939. Clause (8) deals only with items which the law designates as income, because there is nothing in the law of accumulations which would prevent a testator's designating as income that which the law considers principal. The provision in clause (8) for extraordinary dividends is a paraphrase of the act of 1939, although under the Principal and Income Act it will be useful only in cases of extraordinary dividends paid in cash or in stock or rights of another corporation. The provision in sub-clause b permitting amortization of bonds purchased at a premium will enable a testator, if he so wishes, to change the rule in section 6 of the Principal and Income Act.88 Attention should be directed to the broadness of the language used in this clause; as phrased it will apply to callable preferred stock as well as bonds purchased at a premium. 

The wasting asset provision in sub-clause c will permit a testator to modify the Pennsylvania rule concerning these investments if a depletion reserve is desired.39 The language in the act is broader than that used in the Principal and Income Act and should cover all types of wasting property-book royalties and patents, as well as mines and timber. Note, however, that under the wording of this clause, capitalization of such returns should be permissible only to an extent reasonably necessary to compensate for the waste. 

The correct percentage of returns to be capitalized will be impossible to determine with accuracy in many cases, but this necessary uncertainty should cause but little trouble. 

In practice, the courts will probably interfere with the direction of the settlor or of the trustee in such matters only where the resulting capitalization is plainly beyond all reason. The greater the uncertainty of what constitutes a

§ 7. DISPOSITION OF VALID INCOME ACCUMULATIONS. 

(a) During Lifetime of Settlor. 

Except as may be otherwise directed or authorized in the conveyance, accumulations during a period measured by the lifetime of the settlor shall be added to and form a part of the principal from which they originated. (b) During Minority.

Except as may be otherwise directed or authorized in the conveyance, accumulations during the minority of a beneficiary shall be added to any principal from which the beneficiary is to receive the income. Notwithstanding any direction or authorization to accumulate income during the minority of a beneficiary, it shall be lawful for the court, where other means for his maintenance and education shall be insufficient, to make an adequate allowance from income for such purpose. (c) During Incompetency.

Notwithstanding any direction or authorization to accumulate income for the benefit of an incompetent person, it shall be lawful for the court, where other means for such incompetent's maintenance shall be insufficient, to make an adequate allowance from income for such purpose. 

(d) Upon Competency or Death. 

Accumulations during the incompetency of a person shall be distributed to him when he shall become competent, or to his personal representative at his death.

14. Use of Income for Support of Minors and Incompetents. ¶ 1. General.

This section might be more appropriately labelled "Miscellaneous" in that it contains provisions which might become relevant in a number of situations. First, there are rules of construction with regard to accumulations during settlor's life, during minority, and during incompetency under instruments which do not make it clear what is to be done with income after it is accumulated (subsections (a), (b-first sentence) and (d)). Secondly, there is a provision (subsection (d)) covering the disposition of income accumulated during incompetency which seems to go further than providing a rule of presumed intent and might supersede an invalid direction in the will. Finally, there are provisions (subsections (b-second sentence) and (c)) permitting the court to order the release of income lawfully accumulated during minority or incompetency when it is required for the minor's or incompetent's support. 

2. Rules of Construction. 

There was nothing in the act of 1853 to assist the court in construing instruments which failed to provide what was to be done with an accumulated fund. Uusually it is safe to assume that the settlor or testator contemplated that the accumulations would be capitalized, except where this would make an otherwise valid direction unlawful.¹

This is the general theory followed in subsections (a), (bfirst sentence) and (d) of the present section. 

Thus, where the accumulation is during the life of the settlor, there is no restriction in section 6 (2) concerning what may be done with the accumulated fund. The settlor may direct such disposition of it as he pleases. But if he fails to specify what should be done with it, subsection

If this principal is given outright, the beneficiary gets both the original principal and the accumulations. If the trust continues after settlor's death, the accumulations are added to the corpus.2

A similar rule of construction governing accumulation during minority is contained in the first sentence of subsection (b). In such cases the settlor or testator is given a choice under section 6 (3) not hitherto allowed. He may either give the accumulations outright to the former minor or add them to principal from which the former minor will receive the income. If the instrument merely directs the accumulation without disposing of the accumulated fund, the latter of these two valid dispositions will be adopted under subsection (b) whenever this is possible. 

Thus, it will be capitalized if the trust continues for the benefit of the former minor. If the trust terminates at the minor's coming of age with the principal distributed to the former minor, the accumulation will be added to such principal, for certainly the former minor will "receive the income" of principal which he gets outright. If the trust continues and the former minor is a beneficiary of no part of it, it will be impossible to apply subsection (b) of this section. The accumulation will therefore be unlawful under section 6 (3), and it will be disposed of as such under section 8.

¶ 3. Does Subsection (d) Override Unlawful Direction? 

Subsection (a) and the first sentence of subsection (b) are clearly rules of construction which have no application where the disposition of the accumulated fund is "otherwise directed or authorized in the conveyance". Subsection (b), for example, would be of no help if the instrument directs distribution of the accumulation to one other than the minor. Such a direction would make the accumulation unlawful and the income would necessarily pass under section 8.

Subsection (d), however, is not so qualified. It simply states that accumulations during incompetency shall be distributed to the beneficiary or to his estate. As pointed out under section 6 (¶7), such a disposition of accumulations during incompetency is the only disposition which makes the accumulation valid in the first place. What would be the result if the instrument expressly directs that income accumulated during incompetency is to be capitalized and held for another? Does this make the accumulation invalid so that the income will pass under section 8? Or does subsection (d) of section 7 override the direction in the instrument, thus making the direction lawful? In most cases, it will probably be possible to avoid this dilemma by finding that clause (1) of section 8 would apply even if the direction is void, so that the solution would be the same under both sections-see § 8 (15). 

14. Use of Income for Support of Minors and Incompetents

The second sentence of subsection (b) continues the proviso in the act of 1853 providing for a court order to use income for the support of a minor when there is no provision to this effect in an instrument directing a valid accumulation during minority. Subsection (c) is new and makes a similar provision for the support of an incompetent. Apart from stylistic improvements, the new provisions depart from the old provision for minors by omitting the words "on the application of the guardian". 5655

ESTATES ACT 

¶ 4 This should eliminate the necessity of having a guardian appointed in all cases and enable the court, if it sees fit, to order the trustee to apply the allowance directly. 

The effect of ordering use of income for the support of a minor will be somewhat more startling in certain cases than it was under the old act, because section 6 (3) now permits capitalization of such accumulations. The instrument might provide that income should be accumulated during A's minority and added to principal, that after A comes of age income should be paid to A, and that after A's death the principal (including the accumulations) should be paid to B. If the court orders the use of income for the support of A during his minority, it will thereby be depleting B's remainder. There can be no question, however, that subsection (b) provides for just that result. 5656 [The next page is 5701]

§ 8. DISPOSITION OF INVALID INCOME ACCUMULATIONS (a) Unlawful Authorization. 

Any income authorized but not directed to be accumulated unlawfully shall be distributed as if no such accumulation had been authorized. (b) Unlawful Direction.

Any income directed to be accumulated unlawfully shall be distributed in the absence of a valid alternative direction in the following order of preference: (1) To the person or persons, if any, who are entitled to the immediate enjoyment of the income from which such accumulations were directed; (2) To the person or persons, if any, who would be entitled to the accumulations if the time fixed by the conveyance for the payment of the accumulations were accelerated to the time of the accrual of the income; (3) To the person, or proportionately to the persons, if any, who, when the income accrues, are entitled to other income from the same trust; (4) To the person or persons, if any, entitled under the residuary clause of the conveyance; (5) To the person or persons entitled to property undisposed of by the conveyance. 

COMMISSIONERS' COMMENT- 

[Subsection (a)] When there is merely an authorization to accumulate unlawfully, it is clear that the authorization can be disregarded without disrupting the conveyor's plans. [Subsection (b) (1)] Since 1853, Pennsylvania has provided that void accumulations of income "shall go to and be received by such person or persons as would have been entitled thereto if such accumulation had not been directed." 

The present rule in Pennsylvania was announced in White's Est., 8 Dist. 33, 35, by Judge Penrose, and adopted by the 

Supreme Court in Maris's Est., 301 Pa. 20, as follows: "*** the striking down of the illegal accumulation leaves the will as if it had been silent on the subject, and future gifts are not accelerated; if the accumulation relates to a vested interest taking effect in possession, the released 5701

$cos 

ESTATES ACT 

income goes at once to the beneficiary-if to an interest not vested in possession, the income goes to the residuary legatee or devisee, unless the residuary estate itself be the subject of the provision, in which case the income goes under the intestate laws to the next of kin or heirs." 

Subsection (b) (1) retains as a first preference the part of the rule in White's Estate which gives void accumulations to the person or persons who have a vested estate in immediate possession. The best illustration of such an estate is that in Maris's Estate, supra, where a primary gift of all the income to B was subsequently modified by a void direction that stock dividends be considered as principal. striking down the void accumulation the primary gift of all the income was construed as a vested estate in immediate possession and became absolute in B, as if the accumulation had never been directed. In 

The part of the rule in White's Est., 8 Dist. 33, denying the acceleration of future gifts is modified because where the conveyor has indicated who in the future should take the accumulation, his presumed intent is to give to the same person a present gift of the released income. Subsection (b) (2) as a second preference accelerates future gifts whether vested or con tingent. Illustrations of acceleration are as follows: 

1. A vested gift of the accumulations to B. payable to him after a term of years, or after a prior life estate-accelerated by immediate payment to B. 

2. A contingent gift of the accumulations to B payable to him if living after a term of years or after a prior life estate, and if not then living, payable to C. This is accelerated by immediate payment to B if living when the income accrues. 

C is eliminated because the conveyor's presumed intent was primarily to benefit B, and only secondarily to benefit C. 

3. Gifts of the accumulations to a class, whether vested or contingent, are similarly accelerated, and the members are determined at the time of the accrual of the income.

Heirs. ¶ 1. General

Provisions in the various accumulations statutes relating to the disposition of released income have in general. given more trouble than those relating to what accumulations are lawful. In the act of 1853, Pennsylvania followed the English Thellusson Act in providing that released income shall go to "such person or persons as would have been entitled thereto if such accumulations had not been 5703

§12 cos 

ESTATES ACT 

XX directed." Other states have followed the New York statute in awarding such income to the "persons presumptively entitled to the next eventual estate." Pennsyl vanians can gain some comfort from the fact that New York has had even more trouble with its provision than we have had with ours.2 In view of the marked lack of success of both provisions, it is strange that the legislatures of the various states have continued to use the same ambiguous language even in the more recent statutes. The provision in the present section is at least a worthy attempt to meet the problem instead of blindly following a rule which has been tried and found wanting.

A curious thing about this branch of the law of accumulation is that it presents an almost pure problem of draftsmanship. People can usually agree on what the most sensible disposition of released income should be in a particular case in order to carry out what would have been the testator's most probable intent if he had known of the invalidity. The problem is how to frame general rules which will bring about the proper result in the various unpredictable situations that arise. The main difficulty springs from the fact that any given provision seems to work well in some cases but not in others. The present section adopts the scheme of stating not one but several methods of handling void accumulations, and these methods are listed in order of preference.

[[3. Subsection (a)-Unlawful Authorizations 

Subsection (a) provides that all unlawful authorizations to accumulate shall be ignored. This easy solution to a class of cases is so obvious that it might easily have been overlooked. A typical case would be an instrument which gives the income to A and then authorizes the trustee to accumulate and capitalize part of it if the trustee thinks it is advisable to create a reserve against investment losses. 

The unlawful authorization will simply be ignored and the whole income paid to A. 

Often the line between an authorization and a direction to accumulate is a fine one. If a will gives the income to A and then provides that the trustee may in his discretion withhold and accumulate income not needed for A's support, it would seem clear that a case of authorization to accumulate would be presented, and if it were unlawful subsection (a) of this section would govern the disposition of surplus income. On the other hand, the will might direct the trustee to pay so much of the income as the trustee thinks proper for the support of A and to accumulate any income not needed for such purpose. This would seem to be a direction to accumulate because, while the trustee is arbiter of how much A needs for support, the trustee has no discretion with respect to the disposition of income which he considers unnecessary for this purpose. See further discussion of support trusts under ¶ 5 below. 

¶ 4. Subsection (b)-Unlawful Direction-Alternative Pro vision in Instrument

Subsection (b) controls the disposition of income unlawfully directed to be accumulated only "in the absence of a valid alternative direction" in the instrument. seems plain that such an "alternative direction" would be presented only in the relatively rare case where a cautious It 5705

cop ¶ 5a 

ESTATES ACT 

draftsman has foreseen the possibility that the primary provision for accumulation might be found to be unlawful and has expressly provided for such a contingency-as a direction to pay half the income to A and accumulate the other half, followed by a provision that if such accumulation is unlawful the income not paid to A should be paid to X. This parenthetical phrase in subsection (b), on the other hand, was certainly not designed to cover alternative provisions geared to other contingencies. An alternative direction which by the terms of the instrument is to take effect only if A predeceases the testator, for example, would not be given artificial life by this statutory provision if A in fact survives. 

5. Clause (1)-Persons Who Would Take in Absence of 

Direction a. General

In the usual case there will be no "valid alternative direction" and the disposition of income subject to an invalid direction to accumulate will be governed by clauses. (1) to (5) in order of preference. The first class of cases dealt with comprises those where the unlawful direction can be ignored without upsetting other aspects of testator's plan and without leaving income undisposed of. This sort of case is recognized with ease but defined with difficulty. 

The typical example is Maris's Estate, 301 Pa. 20 (1930).

There, testator gave the entire income to his widow with remainders over. In a separate clause, it was provided that all stock dividends should be "considered as principal." This resulted in an unlawful accumulation because such dividends were partly income under the law then in force (see § 6 (8)-11). The question therefore arose as to how the income portion of the dividends should be distributed, and it was held that it should be paid to the widow as the person under the act of 1853 who "would have been entitled thereto if the accumulation had not been directed." 

The conclusion seems clearly correct, but it is difficult to explain why. The old Pennsylvania and English provisions worked well in this particular situation. Indeed, the desirability of this result is often so compelling that the New 5706

¶ 5b 

ESTATES ACT 

§8 5. 5 FOS York courts have sometimes been forced to accept it in spite of the absence of a comparable statutory provision in that state. It is this type of case which will be covered by clause (1) of the present section, which is first in order of preference and provides that released income shall go to the "person or persons, if any, who are entitled to the immediate enjoyment of income from which such accumulations were directed." 

The idea is a difficult one to express, for this solution is appropriate only in cases closely analogous to Maris's Estate. The limitations are elusive. It is not simply a matter of having a trust instrument which makes sense if the unlawful provision is obliterated. A testator might give income to his children and then provide that the share of a wayward son shall be accumulated for his issue; in such a case the accumulation statute should not have the effect of giving a portion to the disinherited child merely because of the testator's choice of words. The distinguishing features of cases suited to this method of distributing released income seem rather to be a primary intention that the beneficiary should enjoy the whole income followed by a direction in the nature of an afterthought to accumulate a part of it unlawfully. Whether clause (1) is adequate to convey this thought remains to be seen. The similarity to the language of the old act will be noted. It is close to impossible, however, to phrase a wholly satisfactory provision of this sort, and in the last analysis the success of the provision will depend on sympathetic and intelligent construction by the courts. b. Trusts for Support

A special type of case which might be governed by clause (1) is where income is directed to be used for the support of a beneficiary. Such trusts might be treated in a number of ways depending on how they are phrased. 

In some cases, as pointed out above under ¶3, the provision for withholding income not needed for support

In other cases where the gift of income is definitely limited to what is needed. for support, there might be no express or implied direction. to accumulate the surplus income, in which event the surplus would simply pass as undisposed-of property by intestacy or otherwise, and no problem of accumulations would be raised-see discussion under section 6 (¶3 at fn.
