In cases where there is an express or implied direction to accumulate income not needed for support, the accumulation might be valid under clause (1) of section 6 (14) (temporary reserves), under clause (3) of section 6 (16) (minority), or clause (4) of section 6 (17) (incompetents). Before considering the effect of section 8 (b) on support trusts, therefore, care must be taken to ascertain if there is in fact an invalid direction to accumulate. 

If such is found to be the case, an award to the life beneficiary or his estate might well be appropriate under clause (1). 

In McManus's Estate, 361 Pa. 122 (1949), decided under the old act, the will directed that income from a trust should be used for the support of A (with no mention of accumulations at this point) and that on A's death the principal "and any accumulation of income therefrom" should be paid to B. When A died there was a dispute concerning the disposition of a fund which the trustee had accumulated from income not needed for A's support. The court decided that if there was an implied direction to accumulate surplus income it was void, and, without discussion of the problem, the accumulated fund was awarded to A's estate. The decision can be rationalized as an application of the rule of Maris's Estate. Testator first provided for use of all the income for the support of A and then as an afterthought made an incidental disposition of any accumulations held at A's death. In such a case, clause (1) of the present section should bring about a similar result. It is apparent, however, that not all support trusts containing unlawful accumulation provisions will be subject to this treatment. 5708

6. Clause (2)-Acceleration of Gift 

Unfortunately the cases are few where the unlawful direction to accumulate can simply be ignored under clause (1). More often than not, there is no one "entitled to the immediate enjoyment of income from which such accumulations were directed." The accumulation is directed for the primary purpose of making a postponed gift and the obliteration of the unlawful direction will either leave the income undisposed of or its disposition suspended. Clause (1) cannot apply, therefore, and such cases will if possible be governed by clause (2) providing for distribution to the ultimate beneficiary of the accumulated fund. The simplest case where the method described in clause (2) can be used is where the ultimate right to the accumulations is finally vested in an ascertained person—a direction to accumulate during the life of X and on X's death to distribute the accumulated fund to Y, a living person. Plainly in such a case nothing should be given to X, whose life was merely the measure of the accumulation period and who is not even a beneficiary by the terms of the trust. Since clause (1) cannot be applied, the situation is governed by clause (2) and the gift to Y is simply accelerated so that the income is paid to him as it accrues. The result in such a case is probably in accord with prior law.* 

Suppose now that the remainder is contingent-as a direction to accumulate during the life of X, and on the death of X to distribute principal and accumulations to Y, if then living, but if Y is then dead, to Z. In such a case, clause (2) would be equally applicable, although its operation becomes more complex. The gift of each item of income is accelerated to the date such item accrues, and the person entitled thereto is ascertained as of that date. One quarterly dividend, payable to stockholders of record on a date when Y is alive, will be paid to Y; the next quarterly dividend might go to Z if Y dies in the meantime. Clause (2) will also apply where the postponed gift of the accumulations is to an unascertained class-a direction to accumulate during the life of X and then distribute the accumulated fund to such of X's children as are living at 

4. See infra note 5 and § 6, ¶ 6e at footnote 23. 5709

ESTATES ACT 

[7 his death. While X is living the income will be paid to whatever children X happens to have on the date each item of income accrues. This acceleration of contingent gifts of the accumulated fund is new to the law of Pennsylvania. 

It would seem, however, to be the most sensible way of handling an awkward situation. 

Clause (2) should not be construed so literally that it would include persons entitled by way of reversion. If, in the last mentioned example, X has no children at the time the income accrues, and there is no alternative gift of the accumulations in the instrument, persons presently entitled to undisposed-of property (residuary legatees under § 14 (9) & (10) of the Wills Act, heirs at law, etc., as the case may be) should not be considered within the scope of clause (2). If such a literal construction were adopted, clauses (1) and (2) would cover all possible cases, and clauses (3) and (4) would be useless. Plainly this could not have been the Legislative intent. 

17. Clause (3)-Other Income Beneficiaries 

Assuming, therefore, that reversionary interests are not to be considered under clause (2), there will be cases where neither clause (2) nor clause (3) will apply. Where this is so, clause (3) will take effect if possible. 

The following would be an example of such a case:

Testator directs that half the income from his estate should be paid to X and the other half of the income accumulated during the life of Y, with remainders of half the principal on X's death to X's issue and the other half of the principal plus accumulations on Y's death to Y's issue then living. When the will takes effect, Y is living and has no issue. What should be done with the half of the income subject to the unlawful direction to accumulate? Clause (1) would not apply because there is no present gift of this portion of the income. Neither could clause (2) apply because, with reversions eliminated, there would be no one in existence to take. Clause (3) will therefore become operative and the released income will go to X as the person entitled to other income from the same trust. 

5. See Thistle's Est., 263 Pa. 60, 65 et seq. (1919) and § 6, 6e, at footnote 24. 5710

cos 10 11 PA Problems will no doubt arise, in determining what is "the same trust" in some cases, but the run-of-the-mill case should give no difficulty in this regard. 

¶8. Clauses (4) and (5)—Residuary Beneficiaries and Heirs 

Finally, there are clauses (4) and (5) which will apply to all cases not covered by the previous clauses-as, for example, a direction to accumulate all the income of a trust during the life of X and then distribute the accumulations to X's issue, where X has no issue at the time the income begins to accrue and there is no other income beneficiary. 

If the trust is not created by the residuary clause of the instrument, the released income will fall into the residue under clause (4). If there is no residuary clause, or if the void direction to accumulate is in the residuary clause, it would seem that clause (5) would apply and the released income would go back to the settlor if living, or under his will, or to his heirs at law, as the case may be. 

The analogy to the disposition of lapsed and void legacies under sections 14 (9) and 14 (10) of the Wills Act will be noted, except that there is no express provision in the present section in favor of other residuary legatees where the void accumulation is directed in a separate trust consisting of part of the residuary estate. It could conceivably be argued, however, that clause (4) covers such cases, or that (in cases of wills) the two acts can be read together so that the other residuary beneficiaries would take. 5711 [The next page is 5751]

London v. Kingsley, 368 Pa. 109, 116-120 (1951)—possibilities of reverter may be, "inter alia, inherited, sold and conveyed." ¶ 2e 

See First Federal v. Porter, 408 Pa. 236 (1962), Teacher v.

Super. 78 (1949), for the effect of the Act of 1812 on the construction of deeds to A and B as husband and wife when they are not in fact married: "To A and B by entireties" creates a joint tenancy, but "to A and B, his wife" creates a tenancy in common. Cf. Nolan Estate, 82 D. & C. 195, 2 Fid. Rep. 665 (O. C. Del. 1952): conveyance to two sisters "by entireties" creates joint tenancy. For the effect of deeds to three or more persons, two of whom are married, see discussion under Intestate Act, § 4 (6), ¶ 1, footnote 4. For the effect of divorce on tenancies by entireties under various statutes, see Lazare v. Lazare, 365 

Pa. 591 (1950); Christner v. Christner, 366 Pa. 41 (1950); Collins v. Wilkinson, 366 Pa. 108, 110 (1950).

INTESTATE ACT 

¶ 3a 

Note that the right to the allowance in cases of partial intestacy is now qualified by the 1956 amendment discussed under § 2 of this supplement. See Deist Estate, 75 D. & C. 145 (0. C.

Som. 1950) holding before the amendment that wife gets full share of intestate property, including the $10,000, even though she is also beneficiary under a will disposing of only part of the estate.

An important qualification to the general rule in cases like these before the 1956 amendment arises from Martin Estate, 365 Pa. 280 (1950), holding that in such cases, if the spouse takes against the will, he takes only the smaller share of the total estate set forth in section 8 of the Wills Act, and hence cannot take the $10,000 allowance even from the intestate property. § 2. SHARE OF SURVIVING SPOUSE. 

Sub-section (3) was amended as to decedents dying on or after April 1, 1956, by the Act of 1955-6, P. L. 1037, as follows: 

(3) No Issue. 

The first ten thousand dollars in value and one-half of the balance of the estate, if the decedent is survived by no issue. In case of partial intestacy, any amount received by the surviving spouse under the will shall satisfy pro tanto the ten thousand dollar allowance; or . . .

COMMISSIONERS' COMMENT ΤΟ 1956 AMENDMENT This amendment prevents the surviving spouse, provided for in part by the will, from receiving an excessive share in what does not pass by will.

The amendment will change the prior law with respect to partial intestacy. See discussion in original text under § 2, [ 5e and § 1, s 3a and 6b. The new limitation applies only to the spouse's allowance. Except for the allowance, the spouse and other heirs will continue to take their entire shares of undisposed of property in cases of partial intestacy, regardless of what they receive under the will. ¶ 3a

It was held, however, that he was nevertheless estopped from denying the validity of the decree he obtained.

INTESTATE ACT § 3. SHARES OF OTHERS THAN SURVIVING SPOUSE. 

By the Act of 1959, P. L. 1747, effective December 10, 1959 

(underlined) and by Act No. 474 of 1965, effective December 

22, 1965 (double underlined), § 3(5) was amended to read as follows: 

(5) Uncles, Aunts and Their Children and Grandchildren. 

If no grandparent survives the decedent, then to the uncles and aunts and the children and grandchildren of deceased uncles and aunts of the decedent as provided in clause (1) of section 4. 

The amendment of 1959 was not initiated by the Joint State Government Commission nor its Advisory Committee on decedents' estates. The effect of course was to include children of first cousins as possible heirs in preference to the Commonwealth for all purposes. See Verrall Estate, 25 D. & C. 2d 692, 12 Fid.

Rep. 129 (O. C. Phila. adj. 1961) where the amendment was criticized but applied. 

The Advisory Committee was unhappy about this change and made several attempts to have the 1959 amendment repealed -most recently in the 1965 Session. As a result of disagreement within the Senate, the present compromise was worked out in committee whereby children of first cousins are recognized as heirs only if no first cousins survive. This apparently created drafting problems which were solved (a little awkwardly) by a combination of changes to this section and to section 4(1) below.

It is interesting to observe that the 1965 amendment once more brings into our law a limit on representation. First cousins once removed will take the estate only if they are the closest relatives surviving. They will not "represent" their parents if a first cousin survives. See the discussion of the checkered career of the doctrine of representation in Pennsylvania under 

Intestate Act § 3 ¶ 5b.

INTESTATE ACT  

An interesting case on constructive desertion with a new twist is Archer Estate, 363 Pa. 534 (1949). There was evidence that (1) the couple separated by mutual consent, (2) the husband-decedent committed adultery, and (3) the wife-claimant committed adultery-in that order. The wife argued that she had not forfeited her intestate share because the decedent's adultery turned the separation into a desertion by the decedent (Lodge's Estate) so that her subsequent misconduct did not constitute a desertion by her (Jac's Estate). The argument was rejected, however, on the ground that the doctrine excusing a deserted wife's adultery applies only when the desertion took place at the time of the separation and not when the separation was by consent, particularly if, as in this case, the surviving spouse had no knowledge of the decedent's prior misconduct at the time she committed adultery. Following Lodge's Estate, therefore, the court held that the widow's adultery turned the separation into a desertion by her so that she was barred from sharing in the estate. See also Crater Estate, 372 Pa. 458 (1953). ¶ 4a

§7. ILLEGITIMATES. 

¶ 1 

The substantive law of illegitimates may be substantially affected by the Act of 1959 P. L. 1916, 48 P. S. § 169.1, effective 

December 17, 1959, which reads as follows: "Section 1. In all cases where a supposed or alleged marriage is contracted, which is absolutely void by reason of one of the parties thereto having a spouse living at the time of the supposed or alleged marriage, or if for any other lawful reason, the said marriage was void or voidable when contracted, all children born to such parties shall be deemed the legitimate children of both parties for all purposes. "Section 2. The provisions of this act shall not affect any property rights that have vested prior to the effective date of this act.”

In the absence of cases construing this language, no one is quite sure how the act will be interpreted. See Estate of A.B., (Reed Estate) 27 D. & C. 2d 527, 12 Fid. Rep. 471, 474 et seq. (O. C. Phila. 1962), and the article in Fiduciary Review, March 8015

INTESTATE ACT 

1960. Apart from the question of what is a "supposed or alleged marriage" and other questions discussed in those authorities, interesting conflicts with the presumption of legitimacy may arise in a case where the wrongdoer is the mother rather than the father-e.g., a woman who is already married to H1 enters into a bigamous marriage with H2. Her children by H2 would, under the common law rule, be presumed to be legitimate children of H1 in the absence of proof of non-access, but the statute would make them children of H2. 

While on the subject of the common law presumption of legitimacy, note that this presumption apparently will not help those claiming under the new act which purports only to make the children legitimate but not to make the "supposed" marriage valid. Thus if H, while married to W1, enters into a bigamous marriage with W2, the subsequent children of W2 will have to prove that they are actually children of H to get the benefit of the statute, without the aid of the common law presumption. 

In addition to the above difficulties, there is the question of the statute's conflict with section 7 of the Intestate Act in so far as illegitimate children's rights with respect to their father are concerned. The absence of any express repealer of section 7 in the 1959 act, or any reference in its title to property rights, led the auditing judge in Estate of A. B., supra, 12 Fid. Rep. at 478, to conclude that it may be unconstitutional.

Montg. 1950).

§ 17. EFFECTIVE DATE. 

The effective date provision of the Amending Act of 1955-6, P. L. 1037, reads as follows: 

Section 4. This amending act shall take effect April one, one thousand nine hundred fifty-six, and shall apply to the real and personal estates of all persons dying on or after that day. The provisions of sections ten, eleven and twelve of the "Intestate Act of 1947" repealed hereby shall remain in effect as to the estates of persons dying on or after January one, one thousand nine hundred forty-eight, and prior to April one, one thousand nine hundred fifty-six.

For the effective date provisions of the various amendments, see the full text of the amendments, pp. 13 et seq. 

There is no effective date provision for the Amending Act of 1959, P. L. 1747 so that under section 4 of the Statutory Construction Act of 1937, P. L. 1019, as amended, 46 P. S. § 504, it takes effect on the date of its enactment-December 10, 1959. 

Where (as in the 1957 amendment) the effective date provision merely states that the act takes effect "immediately", with no reference to the date of the decedent's death (as there is in the effective date provision of the original act and the 1956 and 1963 amendments), or where (as in the 1959 amendment) there is no effective date provision, presumably the date of death will control anyway. (Cf. discussion in the text of new § 14 (16) of the Wills Act.) For special problems relating to the effective date of the 1963 amendment to the Intestate Act see discussion of new  in the text. Through the doctrine of equitable election, a testator may in a sense succeed in giving away property which he neither owns nor has power to appoint. The doctrine is defined by Gibson, C. J. in Stump v. Findlay, 2 Rawle 168, 174 (1828) as follows: "If the testator devise the estate of Titius to another, and give Titius a legacy, Titius shall not hold the estate, 8023

§(a) 

WILLS ACT 

and claim the legacy; he shall not take a benefit under the instrument, without suffering the whole of it to take effect. 

And it is immaterial whether the testator believed he had a right to dispose of the estate of Titius, or intended to assume an arbitrary power. If Titius will avail himself of his bounty, he shall not disappoint his will."

The doctrine is further explained and qualified in Shelley's 

Estate, 287 Pa. 105 (1926); Witmer v. Witmer, 362 Pa. 119 (1949); Vassilakis v. Vassilakis, 371 Pa. 268, 273 (1952); Patterson Estate, 65 D. & C. 201 (O. C. Phila. 1948); Laughlin Estate, 78 D. & C. 361 (O. C. Allegh. 1951); Foust Estate, 2 Fid. Rep. 

528 (O. C. Montg. 1952); Harris Trust, 83 D. & C. 417, 3 Fid. 

Rep. 195 (O. C. Phila. 1953); Andreas Estate, 5 D. & C. 2d 777, 6 Fid. Rep. 272 (O. C. Lehigh 1956); Wisser Estate, 5 Fid. Rep. 

653 (O. C. Allegh. 1955). See other cases collected in Hunter,

Orphans' Court Commonplace Book (1939) "Election in 

Equity.'

These principles, however, have been thrown into some doubt by certain statements by the court in Peden Estate, 409 Pa. 194, 202-3 (1962). There the testator gave his wife a life interest in the residue expressly conditional upon her allowing two pieces of entireties real estate to pass to the same trust. 

The wife was declared incompetent shortly after the decedent's death and died a few months thereafter. While the widow was still living her guardian attempted to elect against the will under Section 8 of the Wills Act but failed to get court authority for such election. The lower court decided (1) that the election. against the will under the Wills Act was ineffective because of the absence of the necessary court authority during the widow's life and because no election is possible after the widow's death, but (2) that the action of the guardian was nevertheless effective as an equitable election to renounce the gift in the will and to keep the entireties property (12 Fid. Rep. 71, 76). The 

Supreme Court affirmed but unfortunately did not follow the careful reasoning of the Orphans' Court. It agreed that the election under the Wills Act was invalid and agreed that the widow's estate could keep the entireties property. However, in the last four paragraphs of its opinion the Supreme Court said that the condition in the will is invalid (for reasons which were 8024

WILLS ACT 

§1 (b) 13 not explained), so that the doctrine of equitable election had no application and the widow's estate could both keep the entireties property and accept the benefits given her under the will (presumably support for the few months she survived, although no one was claiming this). This dictum seems inconsistent with the orphans' court decision which was affirmed. ¶8g (New) Disposition of Decedent's Remains. 

See Act of 1959 P. L. 1617, effective November 30, 1959, relating to the validity of directions in wills with respect to the delivery of the decedent's remains to an Eye Bank or Body Part Bank. For the common law rule concerning the effect of testamentary directions as to burial, etc., see Hunter, Orphans' Court (2d ed. 1959), vol. 3, p. 89 (under "Funeral" § 3). 

§1 (b). WHO MAY MAKE A WILL-PERSONS IN MILITARY SERVICE AND MARINERS. 

Effective May 22, 1953 § 1 (b) was amended by the Act of 1953 P. L. 216 (supplemented to correct stylistic errors by Act of 1961, P. L. 357) as follows: 

(b) Persons in Military Service and Mariners. [Dur ing any war in which the United States is engaged, a] Any person of sound mind eighteen years of age or older and being in the Armed Forces of the United States in active service at home or abroad, or being a mariner on land or at sea, may by will dispose of all his real and personal estate subject to payment of debts and charges. [and] He may thereafter revoke such will [whether or not the United States is engaged in war and] whether or not he is still in such service or is a mariner. 

Prior to the amendment it was uncertain whether the requirement that the will be made during a "war" was satisfied if the will was made during a "police action" such as Korea or, on the other hand, if it were made after cessation of actual hostilities of a declared war but before the war was formally ended. In Harding v. Pennsylvania Mutual Life Insurance Company, 373 Pa. 270 (1953) and Beley v. Pennsylvania Mutual Life 8025

cos 

WILLS ACT 

::. 

Insurance Company, 373 Pa. 231 (1953), the word "war" in an insurance policy was interpreted (two justices dissenting) as "declared war" so as to exclude the action in Korea, but this result was reached with some reliance on the rule requiring a construction of insurance policies favorable to the insured. 

World War II was also decided to be officially ended in those cases. On the other hand "war" was interpreted in the realistic sense of actual hostilities in Thomas v. Metropolitan Life Ins. 

Co., 388 Pa. 499 (1957) (one dissent) construing "act of war" in an insurance policy; in Atlantic Refining Company v. Graham, 74 D. & C. 433, 436 (C. P. Erie 1949), dealing with the interpretation of a lease; and in Reemployment Rights of Korean 

Veterans, 5 D. & C. 2d 661 (Att'y Gen. Opinion 1954), dealing with the construction of a civil service statute. The only case found dealing with the construction of § 1 (b) of the Wills Act before the present amendment is Morgan Estate, 2 D. & C. 2d 

480, 4 Fid. Rep. 561 (O. C. Luz. 1954) where it was held that a soldier 19 years old made a valid will under this section during the action in Korea in 1950 in spite of the absence of any declared war at that time-the term "war" in the statute being construed as "war in the popular sense . . ." The court discussed but refused to follow the Harding and Beley cases.

With the words "during any war in which the United States is engaged" now deleted from the statute, this question will no longer arise in cases of decedents dying on or after May 22, 1953.

The words "whether or not the United States is engaged in war" were inadvertently retained by the 1953 amendment in the reference to revocation in the last few lines of this section, but were eliminated by the amendment of 1961. This change, of course, is stylistic only and should have no effect on the meaning of the statute.

In Churchill's Estate, 260 Pa. 94 (1918) (discussed in the original text under § 2 (1)) testator had written his name both in the testimonium clause and in the attestation clause (which referred to him in the third person) and the court held that the will was not signed at the end-the most plausible explanation for the decision being that the will was not signed at all, since the two insertions in the printed form were not intended as signatures. Along the same line it was held in Kretz Estate, 410 Pa. 

590, 597 (1963) that testator's name on an envelope containing a testamentary writing was not intended as a signature to the writing. Consistent with Churchill's Estate, the court held in 

Glace Will, 413 Pa. 91 (1964) that where a testator wrote his name in the testimonium clause and the scrivner wrote the testator's name on the signature line, the will was not signed. In 

Miller Will, 414 Pa. 385 (1964), however, the court upheld a will where the signature line of a printed form was blank but where the testator had written his name in the attestation clause and inserted the word "my" before the words "last will" in the same clause. Churchill Estate and Glace Estate were distinguished on tenuous grounds rather than overruled, so that the law in this area is in a delicate state of balance if not confusion.

§ 4. WITNESSES. 

This 4 was amended as to decedents dying on or after 

April 1, 1956 by the Act of 1955-6, P. L. 1070 as follows: 

(a) General Rule.

Except as provided in subsection (b) hereof, no will shall be valid unless proved by the oaths or affirmations of two competent witnesses. 

(b) Foreign Execution. 

A written will of a testator domiciled outside of Pennsylvania but within the United States, executed and proved in accordance with the law of his domicile, shall be effective as to property within Pennsylvania. 8033

WILLS ACT COMMISSIONERS' COMMENT TO 1956 AMENDMENT-This sub section covers the case of a will probated in another state and in accordance with the law of that state, even though the method of proof as set forth in the probate record is not in compliance with the method of proof required for the wills of Pennsylvania decedents. It has been difficult to prove such wills in Pennsylvania, especially after a lapse of many years after the death of the testator. Note the amendment of Section 306 of the Register of Wills Act of 1951 to conform with the addition of this subsection. 

In view of the liberal requirements for execution of wills in Pennsylvania it was originally thought that no special provision would be needed for proof of foreign wills. However, it was found that in some cases the far stricter requirement of a foreign jurisdiction was satisfied without satisfying the Pennsylvania requirements. For example, New Jersey requires two subscribing witnesses and in this sense is much stricter than Pennsylvania. On the other hand, a properly witnessed will can apparently be probated in New Jersey on the testimony of only one of the two subscribing witnesses-such witness testifying as to the proper execution and the proper attestation by the absent witness. When such a will was brought into Pennsylvania for the purpose of recording the transfer of title to Pennsylvania real estate, it was necessary to supplement the proof with the testimony of a second witness because, while Pennyslvania does not require subscribing witnesses, testimony of at least two witnesses was required in all cases. This caused delay and difficulty, particularly in wills executed in distant states which would not accommodate the Pennsylvania parties by adding testimony which was unnecessary in the other jurisdiction. This is now corrected by the addition of the new subsection (b) which, as the Commissioners' Comment points out, must be read in connection with § 306 of the Register of Wills Act as amended by the Act of 1955-6 P. L. 1021. Cf. amendment to § 1101 of the Fiduciaries Act by Act No. 96 of 1963. 

Note that the relaxation in the requirements for proof of foreign wills applies only to wills of testators domiciled in other states of the United States. The proof of wills of testators 8034

WILLS ACT 

84 domiciled in foreign countries and not satisfying our two witness requirement will still have to be supplemented by additional proof for the will to be effective as to Pennsylvania real estate. ¶ 2a

Suppose T, who has a valid will favoring A, changes his mind and wants to revoke it in favor of B, but is prevented from doing so by A's fraud or duress. The will is nevertheless valid and should be probated because it has never been revoked as provided by the statute. See McCloskey Estate, 6 

D. & C. 2d 97, 6 Fid. Rep. 197 (O. C. Allegh. 1956) and the dictum in Mangold v. Neuman, 371 Pa. 496, 502 (1952); cf. infra 3, fn. 3. Note, however, that B is not without a remedy in such a case, because, if he can prove the fraud, A may be forced to account as constructive trustee. See the follow-up of

By the terms of section 5 (2) the "other writing" submitted as a revocation must be capable of proof "in the manner required of wills." Hence any instrument signed by mark with only one subscribing witness (see $2 (2)) failed as a revoking writing as defined by the statute: Gray Will, 365 Pa. 411 (1950).

Actually the paper in that case contained an attempted disposi tion of the decedent's property inconsistent with the earlier will but contained no express revocation so that it would seem that subsection (2) of section 5, which requires a declaration of revocation, would be irrelevant and the revocation would have been pursuant to subsection (1) or not at all (see discussion supra under ¶ 4a). However, the court said that "the declaration of revocation need not be express" under subsection (2) so that the revocation by other writing failed only because of defective execution. The point was of no consequence in Gray 

Will but the court's statement that a "declaration" of revocation under subsection (2) can be "by necessary implication" might become significant in other cases: see 365 Pa. at 416. 

Bell Estate, 84 D. & C. 415, 3 Fid. Rep. 185 (O. C. Montg. 1953) lends further support to the proposition that a revocation by other writing under § 5 (2) need not be express. In that case decedent's will provided for certain specific gifts and pecuniary legacies of $10,000 each and left the residue to X. 87(2)-(4). MODIFICATION BY CIRCUMSTANCES DIVORCE MARRIAGE BIRTH OR ADOPTION. 

Subsection (2) was amended as to decedents dying on or after April 1, 1956, by the Act of 1955-6, P. L. 1070, as follows: 

(2) Divorce. 

If the testator is divorced from the bonds of matrimony after making a will, all provisions in the will in favor of or relating to his spouse so divorced shall [be thereby revoked] thereby become ineffective for all purposes.

COMMISSIONERS' COMMENT TO 1956 AMENDMENT This amendment eliminates any question concerning the rights of the divorced spouse if the will as probated includes provision for the surviving spouse, thus avoiding possible confusion as to what should be probated. 

This amendment makes two changes in the prior wording of the statute. In the first place the provision is extended to all provisions either in favor of or "relating to" the spouse. This wording is perhaps not so exact as it might be but the intention is clear enough. Provisions appointing the wife executor or trustee, for example, could have been construed as not "in favor of" the spouse although they clearly relate to the spouse and 8050

WILLS ACT 

§7 (2)-(4) 20 3 hence would become ineffective upon divorce under the revised wording. Likewise it would seem clear that a provision giving the spouse a power of appointment would be ineffective. The new wording confirms what probably would have been the construction of the original 1947 act, although prior to the amendment a serious question could have been raised with respect to these fringe benefits. See discussion in ¶ 2(d) under this section in the original text and compare similar cases under § 8, 4, of this Act dealing with an electing spouse. 

The second change may seem purely formal, but in fact it will be quite important to the practitioner. Under the prior wording (as pointed out in ¶ 2 (c) in the original text) the provision for the spouse was "revoked" by the divorce so that it seemed plain that the question would have to be raised as a matter of probate before the Register of Wills rather than as a matter of distribution at the audit of the account. The amendment changes this so that questions under this section will now be a matter of distribution to be decided at the audit. In this respect subsection (2) is made to conform with the other sub sections of § 7.

§ 8. CHANGE BY ELECTION OF SURVIVING SPOUSE. 

Subsection (a) was amended as to decedents dying on or after April 1, 1956 by the Act of 1955-6 P. L. 1070 as follows: 

(a) Right of Election. 

When a married person dies testate as to any part of his estate, the surviving spouse while living shall have a right of election under the limitations and conditions hereinafter stated: Provided, That the spouse so electing also must elect to take against all conveyances within the scope of subsection (a) of section 11 of the Estates Act of 1947, as amended, of which he is a beneficiary. 

COMMISSIONERS' COMMENT TO 1956 AMENDMENT [This amendment makes it clear that the surviving spouse who has elected against a conveyance will not be unduly favored. Except for this amendment, the surviving 8053

§

WILLS ACT 

spouse might be able to elect against the will and against an inter vivos conveyance not favorable to him and at the same time enjoy the benefits of a favorable inter vivos transfer. Bossler Est., 44 Schuyl. L. R. 188.

See also Section 11 of the Estates Act of 1947, as amended.]

Prior to this amendment and the corresponding amendment to § 11 of the Estates Act, the surviving spouse presumably had the option of treating inter vivos conveyances described in § 11 as testamentary or not. Hence, if a revocable trust were in her favor, a widow could refrain from exercising her right to treat it as testamentary and take under it, although she had elected to take against the will. This is now changed by the present amendment which requires the surviving spouse to be consistent with respect to all conveyances which are subject to an election. 

Note, however, that insurance and insurance trusts are now excluded from the operation of § 11 (a) of the Estates Act so that an electing spouse may still take the insurance and elect against the will. See further discussion under § 11 of the Estates Act. 13 

An interesting conflict between this section of the Wills Act and section 2 of the Intestate Act was brought to light in Martin 

Estate, 365 Pa. 280 (1950). The will of the testatrix in that case disposed of only part of the estate, leaving the rest to pass by intestacy. She was survived by a husband and collaterals but no issue. The husband elected against the will and, logically enough, claimed one-half the testamentary estate under § 8 of the Wills Act and $10,000 plus a half of the intestate property under $2 (3) of the Intestate Act. The Supreme 

Court held, however, that once there is an election against the will, § 8 of the Wills Act supersedes § 2 of the Intestate Act,

In McFerren Estate, after a gift was construed to be general, a further difficulty arose from the fact that two of the securities in question not only were not owned by the decedent at his death, but had matured or been redeemed so that they were no longer available on the market. Hence, the executor could not buy them, nor could current value be ascertained for an equivalent cash payment. The court solved the problem (Justice Stern dissenting) by awarding the cash value of the named securities as of the date of the will. Note that short of finding that the gift failed altogether, it was the only reasonable solution possible on the peculiar facts of this case. It would not seem logical to apply the same rule where the securities are available at decedent's death.

A slightly different problem arose with respect to another legacy of stock in the McFerren will. Here also the legacy was construed to be general, but in this instance the designated stock was available and still owned by the decedent. However, there had been a 212 for 1 stock split between the date of the will and the date of death. In spite of the 1917 equivalent to section 14 (1) of the present act, the court held that the will must be construed as of its date in this respect, so that the legatee got 22 times the number of shares designated. Note, however, that it was undoubtedly intended by the court that 8060

¶ 10 (New) Miscellaneous Problems. 

a. Division Among Heirs 

At common law, when a testator made a gift to heirs, the division among them was according to the intestate law, and even the words "in equal shares" in the will were insufficient to overcome this rule: see Hoch's Estate, 154 Pa. 417 (1893). The present statute continues this rule and the burden of showing a contrary intent should be at least equally heavy. Cf. Wanamaker 

Estate, 399 Pa. 274, 280 (1960), and Burleigh Estate, 405 Pa. 373 (1961), infra. b. Gifts to Heirs of Two Persons 

More difficult problems are raised if the will makes a gift to the heirs of two persons. In Love Estate, 362 Pa. 105 (1949), a will made a gift to the heirs of testator's brother and sister, both of whom had died survived by issue. Following cases dealing with gifts to children of two unmarried persons, (Cf. Moyer 

Estate, 389 Pa. 228 (1957); Campbell Estate, 395 Pa. 395 (1959); 

Platt Estate, 4 Fid. Rep. 634 (O. C. Phila. 1954)) the court refused to award half to one group of heirs and half to the other, but instead gave an equal share to each child of either ancestor and to the issue of each deceased child, just as if they were all descendants of the same person. Eleven years later, however, in Wanamaker Estate, 399 Pa. 274 (1960) the court reached the opposite conclusion and directed a stirpal distribution under a will making a gift of a remainder to the "heirs of my children ... in equal shares", and in Burleigh Estate, 405 Pa. 373 (1961), a gift of a remainder "equally to my said brother and sister, or their heirs" was interpreted to mean one-half to the heirs of the brother and the other half to the heirs of the sister living at the 8069

§(5) 

WILLS ACT 

termination of the trust in shares determined by the intestate law. There would appear to be little life left in Love Estate although the court in Burleigh Estate based its decision solely on the ground that no will has a brother. c. Ancestor Not Designated

Sometimes the will is ambiguous in that it makes a gift to heirs and fails to state whose heirs are intended-as a gift to children for life followed by a direction on the death of each child "to distribute his or her share of principal according to the intestate laws." In Harrah Estate, 67 D. & C. 69, 71-72, 364 Pa. 451, 454-5 (1950), the court impliedly approved a construction of such a clause in favor of the heirs of the life tenant -stressing the words "his or her share." For a case favoring testator's heirs under somewhat different language, see Couffer's Estate, 58 Dauph. 343 (O. C. 1947); cf. White Estate, 25

D. & C. 2d 606 (O. C. Phila. adj. 1961). Other cases are collected in Hunter's Orphans' Court Commonplace Book, "Legacies and 

Devises" 5 (j).

T3 

Bonham Estate, 393 Pa. 355 (1958)-Haydon's Estate followed. 

§ 14 (6). RULES OF INTERPRETATION-ADOPTED CHILDREN. 

The first few lines of this subsection were amended as to decedents dying on or after April 1, 1956 by the Act of 1955-6, P. L. 1070, as follows: (6) Adopted Children.

In construing clauses (8), (9) and (10) of this section, relating to lapsed and void devises and legacies, and in construing a will making a devise or bequest etc. 8070

WILLS ACT § 14 (6) 

。,k [A] #i 

COMMISSIONERS' COMMENT TO 1956 AMENDMENT-This amendment to clause 6 and the deletion of clause 11 from section 14 make it clear that the adopted child is made a member of his new family and does not remain a member of his natural family. In construing a will before this amendment, it has not been clear that an adopted child was not entitled as issue of his natural parent in the case of lapsed and void devises and legacies. See Ericsson Est., 5 Fid. Rep. 225 [4 D. &. C. 2d 

110 (O. C. Montg. 1955)].

The status of adopted children in construing § 14 (8) (antilapse) and §§ 14 (9) and (10) (which in turn refer back to § 14 (8)) was formerly governed by a separate clause, $14 (11), which was deleted from the statute by the same amendment. 

The construction of wills and the construction of other clauses of § 14 with respect to adoption will now both be governed by clause (6). This is a distinct improvement. The wording of old § 14 (11) was inferior to the wording of § 14 (6) in two respects: (a) it was not clear as to the status of collateral relatives of an adopted person; and (b) it failed to cover the status of the natural relatives of an adopted person. Both these defects are now corrected.

Since publication of the original text, there have been several important Supreme Court decisions dealing with the rights of adopted children under wills of pre-1948 decedents. 

In Howlett Estate, 366 Pa. 293 (1951), the will of a 1921 decedent made a gift to a son's "issue". It was held under section 16 (b) of the Wills Act of 1917 (which by its terms applied only to gifts to children) that the son's adopted child was not included, even though the adoption took place before the will was executed. Although this represents a rather strict construction of the 1917 Act, the decision is in line with prior cases (see discussion under 5c of the original text). 

In Collins Estate, 393 Pa. 195 (1958) (discussion in Fiduci ary Review, July, 1958, and followed in Thompson Trust, 30 D. & C. 2d 362, 13 Fid. Rep. 450 (O. C. Westmore. 1963)) the will of a 1921 decedent made a gift of a remainder to each child's "descendants" and it was held that a child's adopted children were included even though the adoptions took place some years after the decedent's death. The decision is difficult to reconcile with cases either before or after it. The decision was not (and 8072

WILLS ACT 

§14 (6) obviously could not have been) based on the Wills Act of 1917. 

Rather, the decision was based on the wording of the will-primarily the word "descendants" itself plus references to the Intestate Act in other (inapplicable) portions of the will-and the fact that since 1855 adopted persons have been considered heirs of the adopting parent. Unless the case is to be explained away as confined to the wording of the particular will, the best explanation of the decision is that a gift to "descendants" (unlike "issue", "children", etc.) suggests the law of descent and hence is equivalent to a gift to heirs and governed by a different line of cases-see above under ¶ 2.

The court has shown no inclination to extend Collins Estate. 

Thus, in Holton Estate, 399 Pa. 241 (1960), an after-adopted child was excluded from a gift in the will of a 1931 decedent to the life tenant's "children", even though there was an alternative gift to "descendants" of deceased children of the life tenant. 

And in Tower Estate, 410 Pa. 389 (1963) an after-adopted child was excluded from a gift in the will of an 1889 decedent to the life tenant's "children and issue of deceased children... in the same shares and proportions they would take in distribution under the intestate laws of Pennsylvania from their deceased parent." Indeed it may well be that the Supreme Court is regretting Collins; see for example, the last paragraph of the opinion in Tower Estate (410 Pa. at 393) where "children", "grandchildren", "issue", "lineal descendants" and "descent from me" are spoken of as "words of blood". Cf. Pennington Estate, 35 D. & C. 2d 363 (O. C. Phila. 1965) (adopted child excluded from gift to children under New Jersey law)-decision on appeal as this goes to print. 14

The hypothetical case discussed in the text has now become real in Jull Estate, 370 Pa. 434 (1952), and the decision is contrary to what was predicted. A gave B a general power of appointment. § 18. TESTAMENTARY GUARDIAN. 

Subsection (b) was amended as to decedents dying on or after April 1, 1956, by the Act of 1955-6, P. L. 1070 (underlined) and, effective September 24, 1963, by the Act of 1963, P. L. 327 (double underlined) as follows: (b) Guardian of the Estate.

Any person may by will appoint a [testamentary] guardian of [the] real or personal [estate which he shall devise, bequeath or appoint to a minor] property passing to a minor upon his death, when such property (1) Is devised, bequeathed or appointed to the minor in that person's will, or descends from that person to the minor by intestacy. (2) Is the proceeds of an insurance or annuity contract on the testator's life, unless the owner of the contract has made an inter vivos designation of a guardian therefor. (3) Arises from an inter vivos transfer, the major portion of which constituted a gift from the testator, unless the testator has made an inter vivos designation of a guardian therefor. (4) Is a cause of action arising by reason of the testatator's death. 8086

WILLS ACT 

18 § cos 1 Car SMI 1218 (8(5[B TEL B (5) Is a pension or death benefit from an employer of the testator or a society or organization of which the testator was a member. (6) Is a tentative trust of which the testator was the settlor.

COMMISSIONERS' COMMENT TO 1956 AMENDMENT-This amend ment is suggested to cover the situations not covered by the Act of 1945, April 18, P. L. 253 (No. 113). It is intended to make it possible for a person making a testamentary or inter vivos gift to a minor to provide for the management of such property until the minor attains the age of twenty-one. It was thought advisable to refer specifically to each type of situation to be covered, as there seems to be no general language which could accomplish this purpose. 

As noted in the original text, Pennsylvania in 1947 deprived the parents of any power to appoint a general guardian for the estate of a minor but gave to any testator the power to appoint by will a guardian for the property which he devised or bequeathed to the minor. This provision in the 1947 Act complemented the provisions of the Act of 1945, P. L. 253, 20 P. S. § 1178, which gave any person the power to name a guardian for minor beneficiaries of insurance policies and minor beneficiaries of gifts inter vivos. The present amendment greatly expands the power of a testator to name a guardian in his will. 

It is still impossible for a testator to appoint a guardian for benefits a minor receives from somebody else, but broadly speaking an appointment of a guardian by will can now be made effective as to most common types of property which pass from the testator to the minor. See discussion in the May 1956 issue of Fiduciary Review.

As there stated, this new amendment should be quite useful, particularly with respect to insurance in small estates. Take the case of a man with an estate of $10,000 and insurance of $20,000, both of which he wishes to go outright to his wife if she survives, otherwise to his children. In the past, it was possible to name a guardian for the insurance in the policy under the Act of 1945, 8087

§ 

WILLS ACT 

but such guardian would lack the power to use principal without court approval or to invest in nonlegals. Consequently it was often considered better practice to have minors' shares of insurance paid to a trustee under a short insurance trust. This involved not only the drafting of the insurance trust but also the revision of the beneficiary designation in the insurance to provide for payment of minors' shares to the trustee. Such procedure of course continues to be perfectly proper under the new amendment, but if the busy attorney wishes to save time and trouble he may now simply appoint a guardian for insurance proceeds in the will and give that guardian power to invest in nonlegals and use principal as well as income for the minor's support. That the instrument appointing a guardian may give him additional powers seems clear from § 1045 (a) of the Fiduciaries Act of 1949, P. L. 512, 20 P. S. § 320.1045. It would also be wise to take advantage of the other opportunities for appointing guardians given by the new amendment by making the appointment extend to all property with respect to which testator has the power to appoint a guardian and for which no trust or guardianship is otherwise provided. 

Note that § 1022 of the Fiduciaries Act, as amended by the Act of 1959, P. L. 1450, provides that no bond is required of a guardian appointed by a will "as to the property acquired under the authority of such appointment."

The enumeration in amended $18 of the new types of property to which the testamentary appointment of a guardian can extend is for the most part self-explanatory. It will be noted that clauses (2) and (3) overlap the provisions of the Act of 1945, P. L. 253, in that guardians for such property can be appointed either in the inter vivos instrument or in the will. However there is no conflict because if, for example, a testator named a guardian in a will for insurance proceeds and it turned out that he had designated another guardian for insurance proceeds in the policy itself, the appointment in the policy would prevail under the express provision of the present amendment. 

Section 18 as amended will also partially overlap the Pennsylvania Uniform Gifts to Minors Act of 1957, P. L. 358, which authorizes the donor of securities or cash to appoint a "custodian" for minor beneficiaries. Here there will be a real con- 8088

ESTATES ACT §1 (2). DEFINITIONS "CONVEYANCE". 

Effective July 25, 1961.

This section was amended by the 

Act of 1961, P. L. 844, as follows: 

(2) "Conveyance" means an act by which it is intended to create an interest in real or personal property whether the act is intended to have inter vivos or testamentary operation. Except as used in section 11, it shall include an act by which a power of appointment whenever given is exercised. 

COMMISSIONERS' COMMENT TO 1961 AMENDMENT-The pur pose of this additional phrase is an effort to make the benefits of the act available to a testator or settlor who is also the donee of a power of appointment given under an instrument antedating the effective date of the act. 

Since Pennsylvania apparently still follows the "relation back" theory as to powers of appointment, the "act (creating) an interest in real or personal property" would probably be construed to be the act of the donor in giving the power, and not the act of the donee in exercising it. Hence, under the present definition of "conveyance", an act exercising a power is excluded.

The result is that a testator or settlor who has a power of appointment over property and also property of his own, all of which he desires to convey inter vivos or by will in trust upon the same terms, cannot do so in important respects. One of the most valuable contributions of the act to progress is the abolition of the former restrictions on accumulations. But that is available to the settlor only with respect to his own property, and not with respect to property he has power to appoint under an instrument effective prior to April 1, 1956. He must either set up separate trusts for his own and the appointed estate, with different provisions, or else forego the advantages of the act.* 

As pointed out in the original text, prior to the present amendment it was doubtful how the definition of "conveyance" *[It seems plain that the comment was written when the amendment was still in the form of a suggestion, so that the results described are those under the prior law without the present amendment.] 8094

ESTATES ACT 

§1 (2) E1 PA would have been construed by the courts in cases involving the exercise of powers of appointments. Under the strict property view, the donee of a power merely fills in blanks in the instruments giving the power so that the appointment would relate back and be considered part of the conveyance by the donor. 

On the other hand, this analysis often seems artificial and courts have sometimes departed from strict property theory in these cases, as in Sinkler Trust, 3 D. & C. 2d 241 (O. C. Phila. 1955), discussed below under ¶ 2c. The present amendment adopts the more practical view and treats the exercise of the power as the conveyance in construing the Estates Act. 

To take a simple example, A dies in 1940 and by his will gives B a life estate and a power to appoint the remainder by will. B dies in 1962 exercising the power. The Estates Act applies to B's 1962 appointment, even though the act was not in effect in 1940 when A died. 

There is a good article in the January, 1962, edition of Fiduciary Review pointing out certain features of the amendment which might otherwise be overlooked and some questions that may arise under it. 

In the first place, it should be noted that only a few sections of the Estates Act use the word "conveyance". Nevertheless, the amended definition has a wider application because of the effective date provision in section 21 of the Estates Act which provides that the act shall apply to "conveyance" effective on or after January 2, 1948. Thus, by way of the back door, so to speak, all sections of the act are covered. (It is true that sections 2, 3 and 9 are excepted from section 21, but this is of no significance because those sections purport to apply to all trusts and estates regardless of when created, so that as to those sections it makes no difference whether the conveyance is regarded as the giving of the power or its exercise.) 

On the subject of effective dates, section 2 of the amendment of 1961 raises questions of its own. It provides that the amendment "shall take effect immediately" but (unlike the original act and various other amendments) does not expressly limit its own application to appointments made after its enactment. Thus, it could be argued that literally the amendment applies to all appointments after January 1, 1948 (the effec- 8095

§(2) 

ESTATES ACT 

tive date of the original act) so long as the litigation takes place after July 25, 1961 (the date of the amendment). As the Fiduciary Review points out, however, this would lead to confusion which would be compounded in the case of sections (e.g., section 

6-accumulations) where the substantive law was changed by amendments between 1948 and 1961. Furthermore, so construed, the amendment would probably be unconstitutional. Of course, if the amendment is construed merely as restating what the law was under the definition before the amendment, the question of its effective date becomes unimportant. But assuming arguendo the amendment changes prior law, it seems essential to its coherence and constitutionality to construe it to apply only to appointments becoming effective on or after July 25, 1961. Certainly the general language of the effective date section of the amendment is susceptible to such an interpretation and under familiar principles of statutory construction the sensible, prospective and constitutional construction should be adopted. See sections 52 and 56 of the Statutory Construction 

Act of 1937, P. L. 1019, 46 P. S. §§ 552 and 556. 

In applying the act in the light of the amended definition of "conveyance", special care should be taken with respect to the following sections: 

Section 4 (perpetuities): Although this section does not use the word "conveyance", it will nevertheless apply to appointments made after July 25, 1961, for reasons explained above. 

However, the amendment should not be given any more effect than its terms provide. Actualities will govern the validity of the appointment but there is nothing in the amendment to change the perpetuity period which will still run from the donor's death (See § 4(a) and (b), 9). Example: A dies in 1940 and by his will gives B a life estate and a general power to appoint the remainder by will. B dies in 1962 exercising the power by appointing to C for life, remainder to C's issue living at C's death. 

C was born in 1950 and, not being a life in being at A's death, cannot be used in measuring the period, although actualities rather than possibilities will govern the validity of the appointment. Hence, (1) if C actually dies more than 21 years after 

B's death the remainder is invalid, but (2) if C dies within 21 years of B's death the remainder is valid under the statute although it would have been bad at common law. (There is a pos- 8096

ESTATES ACT 

§1 (2) 1 A - sible constitutional objection here—Are the takers in default deprived of something by letting B do something he could not have done in 1940-but it is pretty thin; after all even at common law B could have inserted a saving provision in his appointment having the same effect as the statute.) 

Section 11 (rights of spouse in inter vivos transfers): Note that this is expressly excepted from the 1961 amendment and the implication is reasonably clear that, regardless of what prior law may have been, section 11 does not apply to appointments. 

This is consistent with section 8 (c) of the Wills Act which puts appointive property beyond the electing spouse's reach. 

Section 14 (rules of interpretation): The section now applies to appointments but in cases where the donor died before 1948, care must be taken to distinguish between questions of what the donor meant and questions of what the donee meant. 

Example: A dies in 1920 and gives B a special power to appoint by deed among A's heirs. In 1962 B appoints to C who was not an heir of A in 1920 but who would have been if A had died in 1962. To be sure, section 14 (1) of the Estates Act (meaning of gifts of heirs) governs the appointment, but it does not govern the will of A and hence will not help C in contending that he is within the class of permissible appointees. ¶ 2a

By a series of Supreme Court decisions it is now reasonably clear that (1) the Estates Act does not apply to a funded pre-1948 revocable trust, regardless of when the settlor dies, when there have been no amendments or additions since January 1, 1948 (McKean Estate, 366 Pa. 192 (1951); cf. Pennington Estate, 35 D. & C. 2d 363 (O. C. Phila. 1965)), but (2) if the dispositive provisions of a pre-1948 revocable trust are amended after January 1, 1948, so as to bring about a substantial change in the dispositive scheme, the "conveyance" takes place as of the date of the amendment so that the Estates Act applies. (Henderson Estate, 395 Pa. 215 (1959); Behan Estate, 399 Pa. 314 (1960); Huested Estate, 403 Pa. 185 (1961)). As to pourover wills adding to a revocable trust, cf. Stroud Trust, 10 

Fid. Rep. 602 (O. C. Montg. 1960) dealing with a somewhat different problem.

That the act does not apply to a pre-1948 tentative trust when the depositor died after 1948 was decided in Black Estate, 73 D. & C. 86 (0. C. Del. 1950); but see Iafolla Estate, 380 Pa. 

391 (1955) and Krasney Estate, 7 Fid. Rep. 403 (O. C. Phila. 

1957) suggesting a distinction between tentative trusts and formal revocable trusts in this respect. Note that the problem is not likely to be serious because the main effect of the Estates Act on tentative trusts is with respect to spouses' rights under section 11 and it has been held that tentative trusts are subject to election even in the absence of the Estates Act-see cases cited under that section in this supplement. ¶ 2c 

In Brown Estate, 14 D. & C. 2d 722, aff'd 384 Pa. 99 (1956) it was held that a revocable unfunded insurance trust was testamentary and hence subject to a surviving spouse's election under Section 11 of the Estates Act. This would suggest that the "conveyance" in such a case takes place when the decedent dies and the theretofore empty shell acquires a corpus. The rule of 

Brown Estate, however, was changed by two subsequent amend ments to the Estates Act: (1) The Act of April 1, 1956, P. L. 

8098

ESTATES ACT 

§1 (2) 54 1073 which took insurance and insurance trusts out of the scope of Section 11 of the Estates Act, and (2) the Act of July 11, 1957, P. L. 792 which added a new section 8 to the act declaring that insurance and unfunded insurance trusts are not testamentary. The combined effect of these two amendments created an interesting problem in cases where an insurance trust was executed before 1956 and the decedent died thereafter. The 

Supreme Court finally cut the Gordian knot in Storb Appeal, 400 Pa. 567 (1960) (discussed, sub non. Cilley Estate, in Fiduciary Review, Aug. 1960) by holding in effect that although there was a conveyance at the date of the trust, the conveyance did not "become effective" until the decedent died, so that for purposes of the Estates Act an unfunded insurance trust can be regarded as a conveyance as of the date of the decedent's death. 

See also Henderson Estate, 395 Pa. 215 (1959); Conway Trust, 9 D. & C. 2d 385, 7 Fid. Rep. 467 (O. C. Phila. adjud. 1957); Hunt 

Estate, 19 D. & C. 2d 356, 10 Fid. Rep. 33 (O. C. Del. 1959); 

Kister Trust, 16 D. & C. 2d 688, 9 Fid. Rep. 299 (O. C. Phila. adjud. 1959); Clephane Trust, 15 Fid. Rep. 188 (O. C. Montg. 

1965). This result seems sound in the case of a typical unfunded insurance trust (such as that involved in Storb Estate) where ownership of the policies (in which the trustee is named beneficiary) remains in the settlor; in such a case nothing is actually transferred to the trust until the decedent dies. However, the rule of Storb Estate would not apply as to any assets actually transferred to the trust before the settlor's death-as, for example, in the case of a funded insurance trust, or even an unfunded trust where (contrary to usual practice) the ownership of the policies is assigned to the trustee. ¶3

ESTATES ACT § 2. TERMINATION OF TRUSTS. 

Subsection (a) was amended as to conveyances effective on or after April 1, 1956, by the Act of 1955-6, P. L. 1073, by the addition of the underlined words near the beginning of the first sentence: (a) Failure of Original Purpose.

The court having jurisdiction of a trust, heretofore or hereafter created, regardless of any . . . etc. 

COMMISSIONERS' COMMENT TO 1956 AMENDMENT This amendment is included to make it possible for the court to terminate a trust under provisions of Section 2, regardless of when the trust was created. A footnote to 

Bosler Est., 378 Pa. 333, at page 339, indicates that trusts may be terminated retroactively when and if there is a failure of purpose under the circumstances specified in Section 2(a), if there is statutory authorization therefor. 

Section 2 of the original Estates Act of 1947 was effective only as to conveyances effective on or after January 1, 1948, as set forth in the effective date provision in § 21. As noted in the original text (§ 2, T 3c), however, there was a line of lower court cases where pre-1948 trusts were terminated in the absence of statutory authority on the ground of failure of purpose, in spite of a spendthrift provision or the fact that all possible parties in interest did not join in the petition to terminate. See other such cases under 3c of the present supplement. Apparently no one was indiscreet enough to appeal any of these cases to the Supreme Court until Bosler Estate, 378 Pa. 333 (1954) where the lower court had partially terminated a $20,000 spendthrift trust created by the will of a 1916 decedent in favor of testator's son, on evidence that the income would be insufficient for the son's support after his retirement in accordance with what testator expressly stated to be the purpose of the trust. 

The Supreme Court reversed saying, in part: "Certainly there is no appellate authority which holds that a partial reduction in the income of a spendthrift trust 8100

ESTATES ACT 

§2 constitutes such a failure of the purpose of the trust as to warrant its termination by judicial decree. . . . While the order made by the court below is undoubtedly well intentioned for the purpose of affording some relief to the petitioner's anxieties, it constitutes a modification of the terms of the trust that cannot, in the absence of statutory authorization, be sustained." (378 Pa. at 338-9)

At the end of the sentence last quoted the court inserted a footnote which recited the provisions of Section 2 of the Estates 

Act of 1947 and stated: "This act, not being retroactive (Section 21), is, of course, inapplicable to the present case." (378 Pa. at 339)

It was this footnote that was the inspiration of the above amendment of 1956. As stated in the Commissioners' Comment the thought was that the Supreme Court had implied that Section 2 could have applied if it had expressly been made applicable to old trusts. The big question is whether the court will give effect to the amendment or hold that the Act cannot constitutionally be applied to trusts created before its enactment. 

The constitutionality of the amendment is certainly doubtful in view of the decision in Borsch Estate, 362 Pa. 581 (1949), and

Grote Trust, 390 Pa. 261, 271 (1957), holding that spendthrift income could not be released and declaring the Act of 1943, P. L. 

797 as amended in 1945, P. L. 1337 (the predecessor of § 3 of the 

Estates Act) unconstitutional insofar as that Act purported to authorize such releases in pre-1945 trusts. See infra, this supplement, § 3, ¶ 5b. Note, however, that the constitutional problems are not the same under the two sections. Section 3 deals with voluntary releases by a beneficiary, while § 2 deals with the power of a court of equity to depart from the literal provisions of a trust in the interest of carrying out the settlor's original purpose. In Timmins Trust, 7 Fid. Rep. 453 (O. C. Montg. adjud. 1957) a 1935 spendthrift trust was terminated under the new amendment without discussion of its constitutionality. In 

Miller Estate, 27 D. & C. 2d 239, 242 (O. C. Phila. adj. 1962) and 

Irwin Estate, 28 D. & C. 2d 123, 130 (fn.) (O. C. Phila. adj. 

1962) the court expressly refrained from passing on the question. 8101

The law with respect to termination of trusts which are to last for a term of years or until the beneficiary reaches a certain age (e.g., income to A until he reaches 30, and then principal to 

A) where there is no spendthrift provision and the entire interest is vested in the income beneficiary, has become even more uncertain than heretofore. Decker's Estate, 353 Pa. 509 (1946) (cited in the text) followed a line of Pennsylvania cases holding that such trusts are not recognized as having a "special purpose," hence are "dry" (an incorrect use of the word) and may be terminated by the sole parties in interest. This was followed in Miller Trust, 2 Fid. Rep. 284 (O. C. Lehigh 1952), and Mertz

Estate, 5 Fid. Rep. 348 (O. C. Leh. 1955), where such trusts were prematurely terminated on the petition of the sole beneficiary. 

This whole line of cases has now been thrown in doubt, if not overruled, by Cannistra Estate, 384 Pa. 605 (1956). In that case income was to be paid to A and B until A reached 30, at which time A and B were to receive the principal. There were no gifts over to others and no spendthrift clause. Nevertheless, on the petition of A and B before A had reached the designated age, the court refused to terminate the trust, saying that the testator's wish to continue the trust until A reached 30 must be honored. 

On its merits, the decision is reasonable enough. However, the court's failure to expressly overrule earlier cases to the contrary leaves this branch of the law in a state of flux. (Note that

§3. RELEASE OR DISCLAIMER OF POWERS OR INTERESTS. 

Subsection (a) was amended by the Act of February 17, 1956, P. L. 1073, effective April 1, 1956 by the addition of the underlined words at the end. (a) Powers and Interests Releasable. but nothing in this section shall authorize an income beneficiary of a spendthrift trust to release or disclaim his right to such income, unless as a result of the release or disclaimer the released or disclaimed income will pass to one or more of the beneficiary's descendants. 

COMMISSIONERS' COMMENT ΤΟ 1956 AMENDMENT This amendment gives Pennsylvania residents a greater latitude in making their estate plans and avoiding unnecessary federal taxes without losing the protection the conveyor intended to provide for the beneficiaries and their families.

As pointed out in the original text (6c), the 1947 Act changed the earlier Act of 1943, P. L. 797 as amended 1945, P. L. 

1337, by adding the provision that nothing in this section should authorize the release or disclaimer of spendthrift income. The present amendment represents a partial retreat from this position. The purpose is obviously to give greater leeway for tax advantages that can sometimes be accomplished through posttestamentary estate planning. Frequently the issue of an income beneficiary are the remaindermen of a trust. In such cases the parent, who may be in a high income tax bracket and receiving more income than he needs, may prefer to disclaim or release his interest to his children. For a number of reasons, however, it is doubtful that the amendment will be as useful as the drafters apparently had hoped. 

As to disclaimers, the amendment is of little significance because disclaimers (or renunciations) of spendthrift interests are probably valid in the absence of statute regardless of who takes the disclaimed interests-see discussion under ¶ 5b in the original text and in this supplement. Acceptance is a necessary ele- 8107

§

ESTATES ACT CARE SAMSKE DEJEZETTE 

ment of a gift and it would be rather extraordinary to hold that a gift must be accepted (or that a disclaimer of it could thereafter be repudiated-which would amount to the same thing) merely because there would be a spendthrift restriction attached to it if it were accepted. In the absence of definite authority to the effect that spendthrift interests may be disclaimed at common law, however, the 1956 amendment will at least clarify the situation in cases where the disclaimed interest will pass to the disclaimer's issue. (See below under 6.1 for discussion of whether disclaimed interests pass to issue in various types of cases.)

As to releases of spendthrift interests after acceptance, the amendment will also have a limited effect for a variety of reasons.

In the first place the amendment will probably be held to be ineffective with respect to releases of spendthrift interests under most pre-1956 conveyances. In Borsch Estate, 362 Pa. 581 (1949) (cited in the original text under ¶ 6c) the court held that, although the 1945 Act purported to apply to all conveyances, past or future, it could not constitutionally be applied to enable a spendthrift beneficiary to release his interest in a trust created before the Act's enactment. This holding was confirmed by 

Grote Trust, 390 Pa. 261 (1957). By the same reasoning it would seem that the 1956 amendment cannot constitutionally be applied to allow releases of spendthrift interests in conveyances that took effect prior to the enactment of the Act of June 1, 1945, or during the period between January 1, 1948 (when releases of spendthrift income were again made unlawful) and February 17, 1956, when the present amendment was enacted. 

Indeed, it is not even clear from the rather ambiguous effective date provision of the 1956 amendment (see text at p. 4971) that it was intended to apply to old conveyances. 

The constitutional objection would not apply to releases of interests under conveyances taking effect after February 17, 1956 (or during the 1945-48 interval), but other difficulties arise from the fact that the statute permits only a disclaimer or release of a spendthrift interest and not any other form of transfer. Where there is no spendthrift provision, the statute is superfluous in authorizing releases of interests (except for pro- 8108

ESTATES ACT 

§3 57 viding the mechanics) because all sorts of present, future, vested and contingent interests are alienable in modern law without the aid of statute-see discussion under Intestate Act § 1, ¶ 2d and Wills Act § 1, ¶ 4. Hence if what purports to be a release could not take effect as such, it could take effect as another form of transfer. Where a spendthrift interest is involved, on the other hand, the only conveyance possible, after an interest has been accepted, is a "release" under the statute. 

As pointed out under ¶ 5a of the original text, a release at common law was a form of conveyance of real property available only where the transferee was already in possession so that livery of seisin was impossible-as a release by a remainderman to the life tenant-or in certain cases where the interest could not be otherwise conveyed at early common law-for example, a release of an executory interest to the owner of a defeasibly vested interest. In addition to the authorities on releases cited in the original text, see American Law of Property (1952) § 12.9; 

Powell, Real Property (1950) Vol. 2, pp. 21, 440 and 493; Simes and Smith, Future Interests (2d ed. 1956) §§ 1853 and 1855. 

Thus, if the word "release" in the statute is construed strictly according to its common law meaning the statute will be virtually useless. For example, a life tenant could not release his interest to even a vested remainderman, much less a contingent one.

A good case could be made for construing the statute more broadly. After all, it does speak in terms of a release of income, so the draftors could scarcely have had in mind the early common law usage of the term. Perhaps they intended to include what is traditionally called a "surrender." At common law, a tenant for life or for years could surrender his interest to the owner of a reversion or remainder. See American Law of Property (1952) § 12.8; Tiffany, Real Property (3d ed. 1939) § 960. 

Thus, a broadening of the definition to include surrenders would help some. However, it would seem from the nature of the transaction and from the definition which both the above authorities quote from Coke that the remainder had to be a vested one, and vested remainders in well-drawn instruments are a rarity on the modern scene. 8109

§

ESTATES ACT 

The amendment will be useful in the large majority of cases only if the common law usage of the term "release" is discarded and the amendment can somehow be construed to permit a "release" to a contingent remainderman-as where spendthrift income is left to A for life with the principal payable to A's issue living at his death and A purports to release his interest to his present issue. The difficulty is that there is no way to tell whether A's present issue will turn out to be the remaindermen and the statute could scarcely be construed to permit a "release" to a stranger to the title. But suppose the very act of release accelerated the remainder so that A's present issue thereby became vested remaindermen of the trust. If this were the result of the release, then it would be plausible enough to construe the statute to permit such releases through a bootstrap type of reasoning. However, the cases to date are against accelerating contingent remainders in cases of release (as opposed to disclaimers) of life interests. See Grote Trust, 390 Pa. 261, 270 et seq. (1957) and Matthews Trust, 28 D. & C. 2d 416, 12 Fid. Rep. 

653 (O. C. Phila. 1962). Both cases decided that attempted releases of spendthrift income interests to contingent remaindermen were invalid. True, Grote involved a 1917 trust and Matthews a 1944 decedent, so that they both could be regarded as merely extensions of Borsch Estate and not controlling in cases involving trusts created after February 17, 1956 (see discussion supra). However, the parts of those cases holding that the contingent remainders would not be accelerated in any event would seem to make releases theoretically impossible in any case where the remainders are contingent. Also, it is quite evident from the opinions in both cases that the courts had little sympathy for attempted releases of spendthrift income. 

Therefore, unless and until Grote and Matthews are modified or explained away (and anything can happen in this field of the law) it would seem that the 1956 amendment accomplished very little if anything, because (1) disclaimers of spendthrift interests are probably effective at common law anyway, regardless of who profits by them, and (2) releases of spendthrift interests will probably continue to be ineffective wherever the remainder is contingent.
