Footnote 31: 

The citation of Borsch Estate is 362 Pa. 581 (1949). See also Grote Trust, 390 Pa. 261, 271 (1957). ¶ 6.1 (New) Disposition of Disclaimed or Released Interests

When an interest is disclaimed or released, what happens to it? (a) Disclaimer.

As pointed out in the original text (¶ 5a and ¶ 6a), there is a basic difference between a release and a disclaimer. A release of an interest after it has been expressly or impliedly accepted is a transfer of an interest to a person having another interest in the same property. When an interest is disclaimed (or renounced) before it has been accepted, on the other hand, there is no transfer of anything and hence no transferee. The law must step in and award the disclaimed interest to someone. 

It will not be left hanging in the air. 

In the simplest type of case a disclaimer will result in an intestacy. A testator leaves his entire estate to A, who disclaims the gift. Obviously, the estate will pass to the heirs at law.

In somewhat more complex cases, certain provisions of the Wills Act might avoid intestacy. Suppose the testator, whose heirs at law are his children, leaves his entire estate to his nephew and the nephew disclaims. Suppose further that issue 8113

$

ESTATES ACT 

of the nephew survive the testator and are able and willing to accept the gift. Will the estate pass to the nephew's issue under the anti-lapse provisions of $14 (8) of the Wills Act on the theory that a disclaimer is the equivalent of prior death? As indicated under the Wills Act, § 14 (8), 5 of the original text, no Pennsylvania cases have been found on this question. 

Assuming § 14 (8) of the Wills Act does not apply to the disclaimed interests or that there is no occasion for applying it, an intestacy may also be avoided if there are other beneficiaries under the will who qualify under §§ 14 (9) or 14 (10) of the Wills Act. These sections provide that various types of ineffective gifts either fall into the residue or, if they are part of the residue, pass to the other residuary beneficiaries, and they expressly apply to a devise or bequest which has been "disclaimed by the beneficiary." See, generally, Seitzinger Estate, 28 D. & C. 2d 349 (O. C. Schuyl. 1961). Thus, if a testator leaves the residue of his estate to his friends A and B, and A disclaims, the entire residue would presumably pass to B under § 14 (10) of the Wills Act. Note, however, where the disclaimed interest is under a deed of trust, there is nothing in the Estates Act comparable to §§ 14 (8), (9) and (10) of the Wills Act, so there will be a reversion to the settlor or his estate-unless it passes by survivorship or to remaindermen under principles discussed below.

Cases where disclaimed interests will pass to someone other than the heirs or other beneficiaries under §§ 14 (9) and (10) of the Wills Act (or back to the settlor in the case of a deed of trust) can be imagined. Suppose the testator leaves $10,000 to his friends H and W (a married couple) and leaves the residue of his estate to X. Suppose now that H disclaims but W accepts. 

If the legacy were construed as a legacy to H and W as tenants in common, a one-half interest in the $10,000 legacy would fall into the residue and pass to X. On the other hand, a legacy to married persons is generally construed to pass to them as tenants by the entireties. Hence, it could be argued either that the entire $10,000 passes to W (on the theory that a disclaimer is the equivalent of prior death) or that the entire gift falls into the residue and passes to X on the theory that the entireties entity no longer exists. Questions of this sort were discussed 8114

ESTATES ACT 

cas §3 Th 2391 EUSA Ed in Bute Estate, 355 Pa. 170, 175 (1946), but the Court did not pass on them because on the facts of that case W (who was testator's sole heir at law) took in any event. 

Even more difficult problems arise when a life interest in a trust is disclaimed. If the remainder is not accelerated, the life estate of the disclaimer will become an estate pur auter vie in the hands of whoever is entitled to it under principles discussed above. As pointed out in ¶ 8 under §§ 14 (9) and (10) of the Wills Act, however, the remainder in such a case may be accelerated and take effect immediately, thus closing the gap left by the disclaimed life estate. Although it can fairly be said that acceleration is the rule and non-acceleration the exception, even where the remainder is contingent (if we rely on cases involving disclaimers by electing spouses discussed under Wills Act § 8, ¶ 6c), the question is said to be governed by the testator's probable intent so that the result is hard to predict in any particular case. (The subject is further confused by the disturbing tendency of our courts to discuss disclaimers and releases in the same breath-see supra under ¶ 5b, this Supplement.)

Recent cases decreeing acceleration of contingent remainders upon a disclaimer of a life interest are Chandlee Estate, 18 D. & C. 2d 783 (O. C. Phila. adj. 1959) and Kerr Estate, 36 D. & C. 2d 200, 15 Fid. Rep. 241 (O. C. Chester 1965); but see Webb Trust, 1 Fid. Rep. 347 (O. C. Montg. 1951) refusing to accelerate.

A logical approach to the problem of acceleration of remainders in cases of disclaimer is suggested in Restatement, Property (1936) § 231 et seq., and appendix to Vol. 2, p. 48 et seq.; and in Simes & Smith Future Interests (2d ed. 1956) §§ 791-804. Those authorities suggest that acceleration or nonacceleration in these cases should depend on whether it appears from the scheme of distribution that the remainder interest was postponed only for the purpose of allowing room for the life estate or for some other reason. Section 233 of the Restatement states that a remainder subject to a condition precedent is never accelerated so long as the condition precedent remains unfulfilled. In comment c, however, it is indicated that what would normally be construed as a condition precedent in such circum- 8115

§

cos 

ESTATES ACT 

stances might not be so construed for this purpose. It is said, "In resolving this preliminary problem of construction, the criterion is whether the terms and circumstances of the limitation manifest an intent to benefit persons living at the termination of the preceding interest or at the death of the person to whom such preceding interest was limited." 

For example, if a life estate is given to a testator's widow with remainder to testator's issue living at her death, it would be reasonable to assume that there was no reason to postpone the gift to the issue other than to make room for the life estate; hence, if the widow disclaims her life estate the remainder should be accelerated. As Simes and Smith put it (§ 796), all the court is doing in such a case is construing the remainder to mean issue "living at the termination of the life estate" rather than living at the widow's biological death. On the other hand, if an estate is given to testator's son for life with remainder to the son's issue living at the son's death and the life tenant disclaims, acceleration might cause an injustice by excluding children of the son born later. In the latter case there would be an obvious reason for postponing the remainder other than making room for the life estate-i.e., the inclusion of all the son's children who might be born before his death. It may be possible to reconcile at least some of the conflicting Pennsylvania authorities on this basis. 

(b) Release. 

In contrast to a disclaimer, a release of an interest which has already been accepted is simply a form of conveyance to a person having an interest in the same property. Hence the interest will pass to the party to whom it is released. If this is not clear from the instrument of release, the court may have to construe it to determine the intent of the releasor. But, unlike a disclaimer, there can be no valid release unless a releasee is designated-either expressly or by implication. (See ¶ 5a and ¶ 6a of original text and discussion supra.) 

If the release is of an interest under the will of a post-1947 decedent, some confusion in this regard might arise from the fact that §§ 14 (9) and (10) of the Wills Act purport to prescribe what happens to (inter alia) "a devise or bequest. . . which 8116

ESTATES ACT 

§3 17 23 has been released or disclaimed." As noted above, these sections logically apply to disclaimers. But could they be construed to supersede the express or implied terms of a release? 

Probably not. In the first place subsections (9) and (10) apply only "if the disposition [of the interest] . . . shall not be otherwise expressly provided for by law." In the second place § 14 is entitled "Rules of Interpretation" and subsections (9) and (10) provide rules for construing the will creating the interest -not for construing a conveyance of an interest under the will. 

It is clearly the intent of §§ 14 (9) and (10) to provide for the disposition of interests which would otherwise be left hanging in the air, and a released interest would not be left hanging if the release was effective to begin with. 

Once it is determined to whom the releasor intended to release his interest, there is the further question of what happens by way of merger of interests and acceleration of remainders as a result of the releasee's combined ownership of his own and the releasor's interest. 

Where there is no spendthrift restriction on the interest released, the answer should not be too difficult. For one thing, in the absence of a spendthrift clause, there is no need to be concerned with whether the "release" can take effect as such; if the interest in question is not releasable under a strict definition of the term, the attempted release can be given effect as an assignment. A has a life estate which is followed by a remainder to his issue living at his death. A "releases" his life estate to his present issue. There is a serious question whether such a release is possible because A's present issue may not turn out to be the actual remaindermen. However, absent a spendthrift provision, the "release" can take effect as an assignment and the only question is whether the remainder is accelerated. If it is, the present issue end up with a fee; if not, they will have an estate pur auter vie which may or may not ripen into a fee when A actually dies. The question of acceleration or non-acceleration here should be governed by the general principles of probable intent discussed above in connection with disclaimers. 

On the other hand, if A's life estate in the above case is subject to a spendthrift provision, the release is good only if it can take effect as such and only if it falls within the exception 8117

-- 
ESTATES ACT 

added by the 1956 amendment to this section of the Estates Act. 

The problems arising in such a case are treated in the discussion of the 1956 amendment, supra this supplement.

N. H. 225, 97 A. 2d 207 (1953).

Although most of the criticisms of the wait-and-see statutes seem to be motivated by nostalgia and are easily answered, the authorities cited above under 11 do raise a real question with respect to the choice of lives in being under the Pennsylvania Act and others like it. First suggested by Robert D. Risch in a student note in 60 Harv. L. Rev. 1174 (1947), the problem was later elaborated by Simes and emphasized by others who take a dim view of the wait-and-see reform. Very briefly, the problem is this: Under the common law rule the only significant measuring lives are those which the settlor or testator himself has used as a measure for the vesting of the interests, because under the possibility test it must be supposed that everyone else in the world dies the minute after the conveyance becomes effective. Under the wait-and-see doctrine, however, no such assumption can be made. Therefore, it becomes important to determine which lives in being can be considered among those that the settlor or testator might have chosen as the measure for the vesting of the interest. 

This is indeed a question that must be faced in applying the wait-and-see statutes. However, it is not as difficult or complex as the critics of the statutes seeem to think it is. Professor 

Leach, who is more relaxed about such things, puts it this way in 67 Harv. L. Rev. at 1352 (supra, ¶ 1): "If my friend Simes and I were construing that statute, we wouldn't have any trouble making it work well rather than badly; we wouldn't let it produce capricious results; 8120

ESTATES ACT 

 Ca and in the first case that came before us we would lay down our fairly comprehensive views as to application of the act as guide lines to the bar. Why should we doubt that the 

Pennsylvania court is as smart as we are? . . ."

Far from being insoluble, the question is not even as novel as might be supposed. The problem of construing the statute in this regard is similar to the problem of construing wills which provide for a trust to last "as long as the law permits" with contingent remainder at termination. At least one Pennsylvania court has shown that it is as smart as Leach and Simes in such a case. In Chambers Estate, 1 Fid. Rep. 601 (0. C. 

Phila. 1950) the court considered a will which provided for a trust to last "for as long a time as it is legal in Pennsylvania at the time of my death." Income was to be paid in the meantime to "direct heirs" living at the time of distribution and the remainder was given to "direct heirs" at termination. The decedent died in 1942 so that the case was governed by the common law. The testator was survived by two sons and some grandchildren and great-grandchildren. The court held that the trust was valid, refusing to declare it void for indefiniteness. 

After discussing the relevant authorities it was concluded that at least the two sons could be used as lives in being in measuring the period. Whether the more remote descendants who were living at the time of the decedent's death could also be used was not decided. The court relied on Fitchie v. Brown, 211 U. S. 

321 (1908) which reached a similar conclusion in construing the same type of will, and Restatement, Property (1944) § 370, comment n, which follows the Fitchie case in illustration 4. 

The question of choosing lives in being under the Pennsylvania statute is very much the same. The solution depends on which of the following classes of lives the courts will be willing to use: (1) Individuals whose lives are used by the settlor or testator for determining the time of vesting. (2) Qualified members of a class of persons whose lives are used by the settlor or testator for determining the time of vesting. (3) Remaindermen and other beneficiaries of the particular conveyance who are not measuring lives by its terms. 8121

ESTATES ACT 

(4) Other lives, in a wide spectrum ranging from those mentioned in other conveyances in the same instrument, through those having some connection with the conveyance, to complete strangers to the transaction. 

The four classes of possible measuring lives can be illustrated in terms of the following fairly simple example: Testator by his will gives $100 to a godchild and leaves the residue of his estate in trust to pay the income to his son for life, then to pay the income to the son's children (whenever born) and the survivor of them, and on the death of the survivor of the son and his children to pay the principal to the son's issue then living.

Class (1) would include only the son, a particular person named in the will whose death is a condition precedent to all succeeding interests. No one would seriously question that he is a life in being both at common law and under the statute. (Note that in the example, the son happens to be a life tenant but this is not essential. Any person whose life is a measure for vesting by the terms of the instrument, beneficiary or not, would be included in class (1).)

Class (2) would consist of those of the son's children who were born or conceived before the testator's death. This is the first point where the application of the statute will differ somewhat from the application of the common law. Assuming the son survived the testator, none of the grandchildren were significant lives in being at common law because all those who were born before the testator's death may die before the grandchildren who are, or may be, born thereafter. (Even at common law, however, the grandchildren could be used as lives in being if the son predeceased the testator, because then there could be no members of the class born after the conveyance became effec tive: see Restatement, Property (1944) § 374, comment j.) In applying the statute, it would seem reasonable to include in the class of lives in being such of the grandchildren as were in fact born or conceived before testator's death, regardless of whether the son survived. They are members of a class which the testator himself chose as measuring lives and, since we are allowed to look at what actually happened, there is no reason mentally to kill them all off the day after testator's death. 8122

ESTATES ACT 

 "Sure! 1 Class (3) would consist of any great-grandchildren or more remote descendants of the testator who happened to be living at his death. Their lives do not measure the duration of the suspension of vesting under the terms of the instrument but they are possible remaindermen of the trust. From the standpoint of policy it would seem reasonable to include as a life in being, say, a great-grandchild born before testator's death, but the advisability of proceeding cautiously in this area becomes apparent after a moment's reflection. Suppose, for example, there were an alternative gift, in default of issue at termination, to testator's then heirs under the intestate law. If all possible beneficiaries of the particular conveyance are to be included as measuring lives, it would seem necessary to include all those persons living at testator's death who might turn out to be his heirs as of the time of the death of his last grandchild. 

Class (4) would include practically anybody, depending on where one chose to draw the line, beginning with the godchild who gets the $100 legacy and ending Goodness knows wherethe testator's gardener, the judge who decides the case, or anyone in the telephone book, to mention a few of the suggestions which are made by the critics of the act and which Leach quite rightly regards as frivolous.

Almost everyone would probably agree that lives in being included in classes (1) and (2) should be used in measuring the period allowed by the statute and would probably shudder at the thought of getting into the outer fringes of class (4). 

In between, there is room for reasonable difference of opinion and it remains to be seen how the law will develop. The main area of disagreement is likely to be with respect to class (3), but even class (4) may be found tempting in certain cases. One lesson to be learned from the wealth of law review material on the question (¶1 supra) is the importance of knowing where one is going in this field. Consider for example the following cases: (a) Options. It is ironic that one of the more difficult questions with respect to measuring the period under the statute was the first to arise in litigation. In Mumma v. Hinkle, 20 

D. & C. 2d 621, 8 Fid. Rep. 290 (C. P. Dauph. 1958), 4 Villa.

L. Rev. 144, by an agreement executed in 1950, A gave B an 8123

ESTATES ACT 

option to purchase real estate for a certain price. The agreement was expressly binding on heirs, executors and assigns and there was no time limit on when the option could be exercised. 

In 1956, B attempted to exercise the option and A claimed that it violated the rule against perpetuities. It was held that the option was good under Section 4 of the Estates Act so long as it was exercised "within the lives of the contracting parties" (8 Fid. Rep. at 294). (Cf. Gilbert v. Union College, 343 S.W. 

2d, 829 (Ky. 1961) where a similar question was raised under the Kentucky wait-and-see statute, although the option in that case would have been good at common law so the decision is not so significant.) The important question with respect to options is whether the lives of the parties to the agreement may be used in measuring the statutory period or whether a simple period of twenty-one years is the limit. Since the option in the 

Mumma case was exercised within six years the exercise was valid under either theory, although the court based its decision on the fact that it was exercised during the lives of the parties. 

It will be noted that the lives of the parties to an option agreement fall within class (3)-i.e., persons who have a beneficial interest in a particular conveyance but who are not by the terms of the instrument used as a measure for the time of vesting. 

In effect, after the agreement, A has a fee simple subject to a condition and B has an executory interest which is to take effect upon the happening of the condition-i.e., his election to exercise the option. It certainly seems reasonable to include the lives of the contracting parties in measuring the period in option cases, although to do so involves using lives which are not measuring lives by the terms of the instrument. (b) Defeasible Fees Owned by Corporations, Associations,

Charitable Trusts, etc. Testator leaves his estate to a church for a particular charitable purpose and then provides that if the purpose should ever fail the estate should pass to his niece. 

This in effect is Pruner Estate, 400 Pa. 629 (1960), discussed under Estates Act § 5, 14, but that case involved a 1904 decedent and so was decided under the common law. Obviously the church cannot be used as a life in being but the niece (a class (3) life) could be. This is simply another version of the problem discussed with respect to options. 8124

ESTATES ACT 

 31 AIT (c) Period In Gross. Testator leaves his estate in trust to pay the income to his issue living from time to time with remainder to such of his issue as are living 75 years after his death. (Cf. Johnston's Estate, 185 Pa. 179 (1898).) In the original text it was suggested that the issue living at testator's death could be considered lives in being in such a case. It should be realized however that this involves getting into class (3), in that no life is specified by the testator as measuring the period of vesting. Here again, the alternative would be to hold that the trust is valid only for a period of 21 years. (d) Settlor of Irrevocable Trust. Settlor creates an irrevocable inter vivos trust to pay the income to his brother for life, then to pay the income to his brother's children and the survivor of them, and on the death of the survivor to pay the principal to his brother's issue then living with an alternative gift to charity in default of issue. The brother is childless at the time the trust is created but later has children. Twentyone years after the brother's death the children seek to terminate the trust under Sections 4 and 5 of the Estates Act but it appears that the settlor is still living. There will be a strong temptation in such a case to refuse termination on the ground that the settlor can be considered a life in being in measuring the period. Note however that this gets us into class (4) with all its resulting perils, because the settlor is neither a measuring life by the terms of the instrument nor a possible beneficiary of the trust.

It is suggested that the statute will work well if the courts stop either with class (2) or class (3) in determining what lives in being can be considered. There is much to be said for the conservative approach of considering only lives in classes (1) and (2)-i.e., lives which the testator or settlor has chosen as measuring lives for the period of vesting. This would seem to be the result called for by the Kentucky statute, supra, which contains a proviso stating that "the period shall not be measured by any lives whose continuance does not have a causal relationship to the vesting or failure of the interest." Even this narrow construction would probably save the great bulk of conveyances which were bad at common law. In only a few cases would it operate harshly-mainly in cases where no measuring lives are 8125

ESTATES ACT 

mentioned in the instrument such as those involving options, defeasible fees, and periods in gross discussed above. However, no great hardship will result in a rule limiting options to 21 years (bearing in mind that options contained in leases are exempt from the rule in any event: see § 4(b) (1) ¶5), and in other cases the harsh effects of invalidity at common law are to a large extent avoided by § 5 of the Act. 

On the other hand the statute will also be workable if lives in class (3) are included. Difficult cases can be imagined under such a construction of the statute but not insoluble ones. Furthermore, the inclusion of lives in class (3) would be supported by such authority as there is on the subject-the Mumma case on options and the persuasive authority of the Chambers and Fitchie cases and the Restatement, discussed above. 

Real difficulties will be encountered only if the lives described in class (4) (purely collateral lives who are neither measuring lives by the terms of the instrument nor beneficiaries of the conveyance) are included in measuring the period. The use of a collateral life having an intimate relationship to the conveyance (e.g., the settlor of the inter vivos trust in example (d) above) would do no harm in itself but unless the decision were limited to its facts, it would be difficult to know where to stop. ¶ 6

Also to be distinguished from cases of ordinary class gifts are separate gifts to a series of classes, where the number of 8126

§4 (b) (1) classes is finally determined within the period, but one of the classes might violate the rule. In such cases the class gifts are separable and the good ones upheld. Thus in Harrah's Estate, 364 Pa. 451 (1950), there was a gift to George for life, then to 

George's children for their lives, and on the death of each child a gift of his share of principal to his heirs. The court held that since the number of separate classes (and hence the size of each class gift) must be determined within the period, the gifts to the heirs of children of George living when the testator died are valid and separable from the invalid gifts to heirs of after-born children. See also Jones Estate, 410 Pa. 380 (1963); Smith Estate, 73 D. & C. 38 (O. C. Phila. 1950); and Restatement, Property (1944) § 389. It would seem to follow that in Harrah Estate situations arising under the statute, § 4 (b) must be applied separately to each of the various class gifts. Note the difference between this type of case and the case where there is a single gift to one class which remains open beyond the period-as a single remainder to issue living on the death of the survivor of George's children. In Caplan v. Pittsburgh, 375 Pa. 268 (1953) the city conveyed land to X and in the deed, which was duly recorded, X agreed that if the city should condemn a described portion of the land for widening a street "at any time in the future", no claim for damages would be made by X "or his successors in title".

The important distinction between a fee subject to a condition subsequent and a fee subject to a special limitation was overlooked in Pruner Estate, 400 Pa. 629 (1960) where the court (in applying the common law rule to the will of a 1904 decedent) used the two terms interchangeably but reached a conclusion which is correct only if the estate were a fee subject to a special limitation. The devise in the will was an absolute one for a particular charitable purpose, but a codicil was construed to provide that if at any time the charitable purpose could not be carried out the property should pass to the testator's niece. The trustees were in fact unable to carry out the charitable purpose according to its terms and the attempted gift over to the niece was of course too remote. If the codicil imposed a condition subsequent on the gift to the charity (a reasonable construction which the court said it adopted in several places in the opinion), then the condition would fall with the remote gift over to the neice, so that there would be nothing left but the provisions in the original will giving a fee simple absolute to the charity and the gift should have been subject to cy pres. Late in the opinion, however, the Court seemed to shift its ground and, treating the charitable gift as one on special limitation (an implausible construction in view of the fact that the provision relating to the possible failure of the charitable purpose was an afterthought added by codicil), awarded the reverter to the heirs at law. The case is discussed in Sparks, Future Interests, 36 N. Y. U. L. Rev.

§ 6. INCOME ACCUMULATIONS WHEN VALID. 

T3 

Text: 

In James Estate, 414 Pa. 80 (1964), rev'g 13 Fid. Rep. 636 (O. C. Phila. 1963), the court considered the exemption of charitable trusts from the present statutory rule against accumulations in relation to the will of a 1960 decedent who directed distribution to a charity at twenty-year intervals of 50% of the income for 220 years and 75% of the income for an additional 180 years, the balance of the income to be accumulated and all accumulated income and principal to be paid to the charity at the end of 400 years. The Supreme Court, reversing the majority of a divided Orphans' Court, held that the accumulation was void ab initio and that the income should be distributed currently to the charity. The court concluded that the accumulation provision was so unreasonable that it in effect deprived the trust of its charitable nature and therefore took it out of the statutory exemption. Assuming that the provision was that unreasonable (there was some disagreement concerning this in the lower court) the reasoning seems sound. Certainly, as the court suggested, a direction to accumulate for ten thousand years before payment to a charity would make the charitable benefit too remote to be real. However, even accepting the conclusion that the accumulation direction deprived the trust of its charitable nature, it would seem that under the terms of the statute the accumulation provision would at least be good for the period of the rule against perpetuities-probably 21 years in this case, there being no significant measuring lives. None of the judges passing on the question considered this solution, possibly because as a practical matter it would be neither here nor there. 

A similar question was raised in Morris Trust, 36 D. & C. 

2d 277, 15 Fid. Rep. 250 (O. C. Chest. 1965) where the will directed that income from a trust be paid to certain charities and added to their endowment funds, so that only income on the accumulations would be available for the charitable purposes. Distinguishing James Estate, the court held this provision was valid. 8131

§ 11. POWERS OF APPOINTMENT RIGHTS OF SURVIVING SPOUSE. 

This section was amended as to conveyances effective on or after April 1, 1956 by the Act of 1955-6 P. L. 1073, as follows: 

§ 11. Conveyances to Defeat Marital Rights. 

(a) In General. 

A conveyance of assets by a person who retains a power of appointment by will or a power of revocation or consumption over the principal thereof, shall at the election of his surviving spouse, be treated as a testamentary disposition so far as the surviving spouse is concerned to the extent to which the power has been reserved, but the right of the surviving spouse shall be subject to the rights of any income beneficiary whose interest in income becomes vested in enjoyment prior to the death of the conveyor. The provisions of this subsection shall not apply to any contract of life insurance purchased by a decedent, whether payable in trust or otherwise. 

(b) Determination of Share. 

The spouse may elect to take against any such conveyance and shall be entitled to one-third thereof if the conveyor is survived by more than one child, or by one or more children and the issue of a deceased child or children, or by the issue of more than one deceased child, and in all other circumstances one-half thereof. 8134

ESTATES ACT 

§ 11 1 

(c) Election Against Other Conveyances. 

A spouse electing under this section also must elect to take against the will, if he is a beneficiary thereunder, and against all other conveyances within the scope of subsection (a) of which he is a beneficiary. (d) Procedure.

The election to treat a conveyance as testamentary shall be made in the same manner as an election to take against the will. If there is a will, such election shall be made within the same time limitations as an election to take against the will. 

If there is no will, such election shall be made within one year of the conveyor's death, and the orphans' court, on application of the surviving spouse made within such period, may extend the time for making the election. It can be made only if there has been no forfeiture of the right to make an election. The court having jurisdiction of the deceased conveyor's estate shall determine the rights of the surviving spouse in the property included in the conveyance. 

COMMISSIONERS' COMMENT TO 1956 AMENDMENT-Subsec tion (a): The last sentence is added to eliminate uncertainties as to the application of this section to life insurance. Lower court opinions which have dealt with the subject give no clear indication of the extent to which Section 11, as drafted in 1947, would have been applied to life insurance. See Auch Est., 4 Fiduc. Rep. 

113; Brown Est., 5 Fiduc. Rep. 113.

Subsection (c): [This subsection as amended, together with Section 8 of the Wills Act of 1947 as amended, should make it clear that all of the interest passing to the surviving spouse must be taken into consideration, so that the surviving spouse cannot elect against inter vivos transfers which are unfavorable and 8135

§ESTATES ACT 

still enjoy the benefit of inter vivos transfers which are favorable.] * 66 Subsection (d): [This subsection is intended to provide the procedure needed to carry out the purpose of subsection (a). The need for such clarification was illustrated by Judge Van Roden in his article entitled 

'Rights of Surviving Spouse to Share in Assets Trans ferred by Decedent in His Lifetime", 25 Pa. Bar Assn. 

Qu. 51, 58 Dick. L. R. 70.] This amendment expands and clarifies § 11 which originally had left too much to the imagination. 

Subsection (a): The sentence added to subsection (a) provides that the purchase of insurance, even though the beneficiary can be changed by the owner of the policy at any time prior to his death, is not a revocable conveyance within the meaning of § 11-regardless of whether the insurance is payable directly to the beneficiaries or to a revocable insurance trust. This question was left open by the wording of the original Act (see discussion under 2g of the original text). In Brown Est., 384 

Pa. 99 (1956) the Supreme Court affirmed per curiam the 

Orphans' Court which had held that insurance payable to a revocable insurance trust was subject to the claim of an electing spouse both (1) because the transaction was testamentary at common law and (2) because it was subject to the spouse's election under § 11 of the Estates Act prior to the present amendment. The first part of the holding was corrected by new §8 of the Estates Act added by the 1957 amendment. The second part of the holding is corrected by the present addition to subsection (a). It now seems clear that an electing spouse may not reach insurance proceeds regardless of how they are payable. 

See Henderson Estate, 395 Pa. 215 (1959), and Hunt Estate, 19 D. & C. 2d 356, 10 Fid. Rep. 33 (O. C. Del. 1959) giving full effect to the new amendment in cases involving both insurance *The provisions of the amendment following subsection (a) were substantially revised (with the assistance and approval of a subcommittee of the Advisory Committee) after the bill had been introduced in the Legislature. Hence, the comments to subsections (c) and (d) are not strictly applicable to these provisions as finally passed. However, they are included here because they are equally appropriate to the final version of the amendment. 8136

ESTATES ACT §11 

1 payable outright to named beneficiaries and insurance payable to unfunded insurance trusts. (See discussion of these cases in connection with effective date problems under Estates Act § 1 (2) ¶ 2c.) 

Subsection (b): The share which the electing spouse takes is now spelled out in § 11 of the Estates Act instead of indicated by the implied reference to § 8 of the Wills Act. As originally written, § 11 simply stated that the spouse could consider the conveyance as "testamentary"-i.e., it was a will so far as she was concerned, so that if she elected against the will under § 8 of the Wills Act it would follow that she would be entitled to the electing spouse's share of both funds; see discussion in. original text under Estates Act § 11, 3. As pointed out in ¶ 4 of the original text, however, it was not clear under old § 11 whether the spouse took her fractional share of each fund or whether she took her fractional share of the combined funds and what was left over was allocated between the inter vivos trust and the will according to how the rules of abatement might apply to the combined fund. In addition to making clear what was implicit in the old section, therefore, subsection (b) of the amendment clarifies the law with respect to the effect of the election on the remaining assets. The spouse is entitled to "onethird [or one-half] thereof”—i.e., of the inter vivos conveyance she is electing against-and it seems clear that the determination of what the spouse gets and how the balance is distributed among the beneficiaries in a revocable trust or other conveyance is treated separately from the similar problems with respect to the election against the will. This conclusion is reenforced by the procedural provisions of subsection (d) which provides for a separate election against each fund. 

Subsection (c): This subsection effects a substantial change from the prior law in certain cases. Before the amendment the spouse had to elect against the will in order to get the benefit of § 11 with respect to the inter vivos conveyance she elected to treat "as testamentary". Conversely, however, she was not compelled to treat any particular inter vivos conveyance as testamentary. Hence if she were beneficiary of revocable Trust 

A but was excluded from revocable Trust B and under the will, she could presumably treat only Trust B as testamentary and 8137

§

ESTATES ACT 

elect against it and the will while still retaining the benefit given to her under Trust A. See discussion in original text under ¶ 7. 

This result is changed by the new subsection (c) of this section and the corresponding amendment to § 8 (a) of the Wills Act. 

The spouse can no longer pick and choose among the funds she may elect against; it is all or nothing. The one exception is that the electing spouse is not compelled to elect against a will or inter vivos conveyance of which she is not a beneficiary. See 

Hagy Estate, 15 Fid. Rep. 456 (O. C. Phila. adj. 1964) where this provision was applied literally even though the widow shared in the testamentary estate under § 7 (3) of the Wills Act as an after-married spouse. Also note that the spouse is required to elect against only those inter vivos conveyances "within the scope of subsection (a)", and that life insurance payable in trust or otherwise is now expressly excluded from subsection (a). 

Hence the spouse can elect against a will and inter vivos conveyances but still accept whatever life insurance benefits are provided for her. See Hunt Estate, 19 D. & C. 2d 356 (0. C. Del. 

1959); Clephane Trust, 36 D. & C. 2d 386, 15 Fid. Rep. 188 (0. C. 

Montg. 1965); cf. Clark Estate, 8 D. & C. 2d 665, 7 Fid. Rep. 73 (O. C. Allegh. 1956).

The way § 11 (c) of the Estates Act and amended § 8 (a) of the Wills Act will now operate in this respect can be illustrated by the following example:

The spouse is beneficiary under the will, under Trust A (a revocable trust of securities), and under Trust B (a revocable unfunded insurance trust). The spouse's child is sole beneficiary under revocable Trust C. Testator's sister is beneficiary under Trust D. If the spouse elects against Trust D, she must also elect against the will and Trust A. However she is not required to elect against 

Trust B (because insurance is not within the scope of subsection (a)) or against Trust C (because the spouse is not a beneficiary of that trust).

Note that Section 11 as revised in no way limits the rights of the spouse in intestate property. True, if there is only a partial intestacy, Section 2 (3) of the Intestate Act, as amended, now limits the spouse's right to the $10,000 allowance, and under the 8138

ESTATES ACT 

§ 11 20 17 doctrine of Martin Estate, 365 Pa. 280 (1950) (see Wills Act § 8, 13, this Supplement) a spouse who takes against a partial will cannot claim the allowance from intestate property. However, if there is a complete intestacy a spouse can take her $10,000 allowance in appropriate cases, even though she elects to take against an inter vivos conveyance, and it was so held in Hershey Estate (No. 2), 11 Fid. Rep. 122 (O. C. Fulton adj. 1960).

Subsection (d): This is a new procedural section. Prior to the amendment the mechanics for electing to treat an inter vivos conveyance as testamentary were not clear. With the addition of new subsection (d), it is now clear that the spouse files an election with respect to each conveyance and that in each case the procedures set forth in §§ 8-13 of the Wills Act must be followed. Cf. Vache Estate, 19 D. & C. 2d 392, 9 Fid. Rep. 465 (O. C. Del. 1959).

Special attention is called to the time limits in this subsection. Before the amendment, it probably would have been inferred that where the decedent died testate the election against the inter vivos conveyance would have to be made along with an election against the will within a year from probate as provided in section 11 of the Wills Act. However, prior to the amendment to section 11 of the Estates Act, there was nothing in the law which would prescribe a time limit in case the decedent died intestate. Hence, in Hershey Estate, 10 Fid. Rep. 390, 397 (0. 

C. Fulton adj. 1960) it was held that there was no time limit under the unamended statute for election against inter vivos conveyances. This is now changed by subsection (d) of the amendment which was strictly enforced in Faller Estate, 407 Pa. 73 (1962), and Vache Estate, 9 Fid. Rep. 465 (O. C. Del. 1959).

Note also that under the last sentence of this subsection, the election must be filed with the court having jurisdiction of the testamentary estate, which will determine the spouse's rights under this section, and this will not necessarily be the court which has jurisdiction over the inter vivos conveyance. In cases where the courts of more than one county are involved, this will result in something of a procedural novelty. The court having jurisdiction over the estate will be deciding the spouse's rights in an inter vivos trust which is being accounted for in another county. 

Nevertheless, that is what the amendment provides and it was 8139

In Longacre v. Hornblower & Weeks, 83 D. & C. 259, 3 Fid.

Rep. 419 (C. P. Phila. 1952), decedent in 1950 transferred securities to a broker under an agreement reciting that decedent and X were joint tenants of the property with right of survivorship, but that either of them could terminate or modify the agreement "on behalf of the joint account". After decedent's death, X claimed the securities by right of survivorship and decedent's wife W claimed a spouse's share in them under this section of the Estates Act. The court held: (1) the account was revocable by the decedent alone so far as the broker was concerned, but had the decedent done so, the withdrawn securities would have remained joint property as between decedent and X. Hence W could not take her share in the entire account. (2) However, even assuming the joint account was irrevocable so far as X's interest was concerned, nevertheless either decedent or X could have severed the tenancy and acquired a one-half interest as his own property. Hence, to the extent of the one-half interest decedent could have recaptured, the conveyance was subject to his power of revocation or consumption and W was entitled to her share as electing spouse in this one-half. See also Hagy 

Estate, 15 Fid. Rep. 456, 460 (O. C. Phila. 1965) following the same reasoning with respect to real estate held in joint tenancy.

Montg. 1965), is equally applicable to the case (inadequately discussed in the text) of a joint bank account with right of survivorship where either party can withdraw. § 21. EFFECTIVE DATE. 

For the effective date provisions of the various amendments, see the full text of the amendments, pp. 4966 et seq., and discus- 8149

§ 

ESTATES ACT 

sion of the particular sections amended where the effective date raises special problems-e.g. §§ 1 (2), 3, 8, and 14 (5).

In addition to having its own effective date provision, the Act of 1956, P. L. 1073, amended § 21 of the original act as follows: 

Section 21. Effective Date. This act shall take effect on the first day of January, one thousand nine hundred forty-eight, and, except as set forth in [section 3] sections two, three and nine hereof, shall apply only to conveyances effective on or after that day. As to conveyances effective before that day, the existing laws shall remain in full force and effect.

The thought of amending an effective date provision of a statute numbs the mind. Section 3 of the act was always specifically excepted from the effective date provision of § 21 and the omission of a similar exception as to § 9 was an inadvertence which could scarcely have caused any real ambiguity because of the fact that retroactive application of $9 was perfectly clear from its wording in the body of the act (see § 9, 14). Hence the addition of the express mention of § 9 in the exception to the effective date provision in § 21 is a mere technicality to correct something which could have been misleading in the original act. 

The addition of § 2 to the sections which are excepted from § 21, however, is illogical and confusing. Section 2 was made applicable to old trusts by the same amending Act of 1955-6 (see discussion of this amendment under § 2 in this Supplement). If § 2 had originally been applicable to old trusts, an express exception of § 2 in § 21 would have been appropriate. Originally, however, § 2 applied only to new trusts. Hence the effective date of its application to old trusts should be the effective date of the amending statute--April 1, 1956. In short it would seem logically and constitutionally impossible to amend the effective date provision of an old Act to make the old Act effective prior to the amendment-rather than effective as of the date of the amendment to all conveyances regardless of when made. 8150

Rhodes Estate, 5 Fid. Rep. 189 (O. C. Allegh. 1954). For clear holdings that, prior to the present act, a direction to accumulate, not expressly measured by the lifetime of the settlor, is valid so long as the settlor actually lives, see Sinkler Trust, 3 D. & C. 

2d 241, 5 Fid. Rep. 337 (O. C. Phila. adjud. 1954) and Parrish 

Trust, 23 D. & C. 2d 167, 11 Fid. Rep. 192 (O. C. Phila. adjud. 

1961) (cf. further discussion of this case under Estates Act $1(2), 2a). See also Leisenring's Estate, 237 Pa. 60, 66-7 (1912) where the court said in connection with another problem: "Should the construction of the will carry the accumulation beyond the statutory period within which accumulations are permissible, the law will stop the accumulations at this point, and thenceforth give the income to the next of kin. It will not declare the gift void because of such transgression, but will avoid so much of it as does transgress the restrictions of the Act of 1853. . 99 

Capitalization of income accumulated during settlor's life permissible: Wheelock Trust, 21 D. & C. 2d 753, aff'd 401 Pa. 

193 (1960); Parrish Trust, 11 Fid. Rep. 192 (O. C. Phila. adjud. 1961). 8152

Ferguson Trust, 354 Pa. 367, 372 (1946), is a definite holding that an accumulation for charity is valid even though individuals participate in the income from the accumulations until the time for distribution. 8153

Text (1st and 2nd paragraphs): 

See also Crawford Estate, 362 Pa. 458 (1949) holding that a direction to add stock dividends to principal in a pre-1939 will is void and Klauder Estate, 17 D. & C. 2d 660 (O. C. Phila. adj. 

1959)-same as to capital gains. After those cases were decided, Catherwood Trust, 405 Pa. 61 (1961), held that the Principal and Income Act applies to old trusts-in affect saying that the Legislature can do what the testator under earlier cases was not permitted to do. Still later, Pew Trust, 411 Pa. 96 (1963), to everyone's surprise, held that stock dividends of 6% or less were income at common law and always had been. The interplay of these various cases and statutes is discussed in Mc- 

Ilhenny Trust, 15 Fid. Rep. 367 (O. C. Phila. 1965) where, for reasons not clear to the present writer, a direction in a 1925 trust to allocate 1960-1963 6% stock dividends to principal was held invalid. See discussion of this case in Fiduciary Review, July, 1965, p. 2.
